The connection is thus: 'when that Sumedha, the Leader of the World, the foremost person, had attained Nibbāna through the final passing away of the aggregates.' 'With a serene and joyful mind' (pasannacitto sumano) means: 'I, with a mind made serene by faith and a heart made beautiful by gladness, performed the worship of the stūpa and the worship of the cetiya for that Blessed One, Sumedha.'

56. Ye ca khīṇāsavā tatthāti tasmiṃ samāgame ye ca khīṇāsavā pahīnakilesā chaḷabhiññā chahi abhiññāhi samannāgatā mahiddhikā mahantehi iddhīhi samannāgatā santi, te sabbe khīṇāsave ahaṃ tattha samānetvā suṭṭhu ādarena ānetvā saṅghabhattaṃ sakalasaṅghassa dātabbabhattaṃ akāsiṃ tesaṃ bhojesinti attho.

56. Regarding the phrase 'And those with taints destroyed were there': At that assembly, there were those with taints destroyed (khīṇāsavā), who had abandoned defilements, were endowed with the six supernormal knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), and possessed great psychic power (mahiddhikā), being endowed with great powers. The meaning is: 'Having gathered all those with taints destroyed there—that is, having brought them with great reverence—I gave a meal for the Sangha, a meal to be given to the entire Sangha; I fed them.'

57. Upaṭṭhāko tadā ahūti tadā mama saṅghabhattadānakāle sumedhassa bhagavato nāmena sumedho nāma upaṭṭhākasāvako ahu ahosīti attho. So sāvako mayhaṃ pūjāsakkāraṃ anumodittha anumodito ānisaṃsaṃ kathesīti attho.

57. Regarding 'An attendant was there at that time': The meaning is that at that time, during my offering of a meal to the Sangha, there was an attendant disciple of the Blessed One Sumedha, named Sumedha. The meaning is: that disciple rejoiced in my offering and honor, and having rejoiced, he spoke of its benefits.

58. Tena cittappasādenāti tena thūpapūjākaraṇavasena uppannena [P 0.0323] cittappasādena devaloke dibbavimānaṃ upapajjiṃ upagato asmīti attho, tattha nibbattomhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Chaḷāsītisahassānīti tasmiṃ vimāne cha asītisahassāni devaccharāyo me mayhaṃ cittaṃ ramiṃsu ramāpesunti sambandho.

58. Regarding 'Through that serenity of mind': The meaning is, 'Through the serenity of mind that arose on account of worshipping the stūpa, I was reborn in the world of the devas, I attained a divine mansion.' That is to say, 'I was reborn there.' Regarding 'Eighty-six thousand': The connection is, 'In that mansion, eighty-six thousand celestial nymphs delighted my mind; they caused it to be delighted.'

59. Mameva anuvattantīti tā accharāyo sabbakāmehi dibbehi rūpādivatthukāmehi upaṭṭhahantiyo mamaṃ eva anuvattanti mama vacanaṃ anukaronti sadā niccakālanti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

59. Regarding 'They attended only upon me': The meaning is that those celestial nymphs, attending with all divine sensual pleasures—sensual objects such as forms and so on—attended only upon me; they acted according to my word, always, for all time. The rest is easily understood.

Pilindavacchattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pilindavaccha is concluded.

6. Rāhulattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rāhula

Padumuttarassa [M 2.0015][V 2.0014] bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato rāhulattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi āyasmā purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ sikkhākāmānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento senāsanavisodhanavijjotanādikaṃ uḷāraṃ puññaṃ katvā paṇidhānaṃ akāsi. So tato cavitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde amhākaṃ bodhisattaṃ paṭicca yasodharāya deviyā kucchimhi nibbattitvā rāhuloti laddhanāmo mahatā khattiyaparivārena vaḍḍhi. Tassa pabbajjāvidhānaṃ khandhake (mahāva. 105) āgatameva. So pabbajitvā satthu santike anekehi suttapadehi suladdhovādo paripakkañāṇo vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahā pana hutvā attano paṭipattiṃ paccavekkhitvā aññaṃ byākaronto –

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Rāhula begins with the words 'Of the Blessed One Padumuttara.' This venerable one, having made his aspiration under former Jinas and accumulating merits that serve as a basis for liberation in various existences, was born into a good family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity and while listening to the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher establish a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those desirous of training. Aspiring to that same position himself, he performed great merit, such as cleaning and illuminating the dwelling place, and made his aspiration. Passing away from there, he wandered among devas and humans, experiencing prosperity in both realms. During this Buddha-era, dependent on our Bodhisatta, he was conceived in the womb of the princess Yasodharā and received the name Rāhula. He grew up with a great retinue of khattiyas. The account of his going forth is found in the Khandhaka. Having gone forth, he received excellent instruction from the Teacher through many discourses. His knowledge having matured, he strove diligently in insight practice and attained arahantship. Then, having become an Arahant, reflecting on his own practice and declaring his final knowledge, he said:

“Ubhayeneva sampanno, rāhulabhaddoti maṃ vidū;

Yañcamhi putto buddhassa, yañca dhammesu cakkhumā.

“Endowed with both qualities, they know me as ‘Rāhula the Good.’ For I am the son of the Buddha, and I possess the eye of wisdom in the Dhamma.

“Yañca me āsavā khīṇā, yañca natthi punabbhavo;

Arahā dakkhiṇeyyomhi, tevijjo amataddaso.

“And because my taints are destroyed, and because for me there is no future existence, I am an Arahant, worthy of offerings, endowed with the three true knowledges, and a seer of the Deathless.”

“Kāmandhā jālapacchannā, taṇhāchadanachāditā;

Pamattabandhunā bandhā, macchāva kuminā mukhe.

“Blinded by sensual passion, covered by a net, shrouded by the veil of craving, bound by the kinsman of heedlessness, beings are like fish in the mouth of a fish-trap.”

“Taṃ kāmaṃ ahamujjhitvā, chetvā mārassa bandhanaṃ;

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha, sītibhūtosmi nibbuto”ti. (theragā. 295-298);

“Having cast off that sensual passion, having cut through Māra’s bond, having uprooted craving together with its root, I have become cooled, fully extinguished.”

Catasso gāthā abhāsi. Tattha [P 0.0324] ubhayeneva sampannoti jātisampadā paṭipattisampadāti ubhayasampattiyāpi sampanno samannāgato. Rāhulabhaddoti maṃ vidūti “rāhulabhaddo”ti maṃ sabrahmacārino [V 2.0015] sañjānanti. Tassa hi jātasāsanaṃ sutvā bodhisattena, “rāhu, jāto, bandhanaṃ jāta”nti vuttavacanaṃ upādāya suddhodanamahārājā “rāhulo”ti nāmaṃ [M 2.0016] gaṇhi. Tattha ādito pitarā vuttapariyāyameva gahetvā āha – “rāhulabhaddoti maṃ vidū”ti. Bhaddoti pasaṃsāvacanameva. Aparabhāge satthā taṃ sikkhākāmabhāvena aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhākāmānaṃ yadidaṃ rāhulo”ti (a. ni. 1.209).

He spoke four verses. Therein, 'endowed with both' means he is endowed and possessed of both accomplishments: the accomplishment of birth and the accomplishment of practice. Regarding 'They know me as Rāhula the Good,' this means, 'My companions in the holy life know me as “Rāhula the Good.”' For when the Bodhisatta heard the news of his birth, he uttered the words, 'A rāhu is born, a fetter is born.' Taking this utterance as the basis, the great king Suddhodana gave him the name 'Rāhula.' Here, taking only the name derived from the expression spoken by his father at the beginning, he says, 'They know me as Rāhula the Good.' The word 'bhadda' is simply a term of praise. In the latter part of his life, on account of his desire for training, the Teacher established him in the foremost position, saying: 'Monks, foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are desirous of training is this one, that is, Rāhula.'

68. Evaṃ so pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttarassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Sattabhūmimhi pāsādeti pasādaṃ somanassaṃ janetīti pāsādo. Uparūpari ṭhitā satta bhūmiyo yasmiṃ pāsāde soyaṃ sattabhūmi, tasmiṃ sattabhūmimhi pāsāde. Ādāsaṃ santhariṃ ahanti ādāsatalaṃ nipphādetvā lokajeṭṭhassa bhagavato tādino ahaṃ santharaṃ adāsiṃ, santharitvā pūjesinti attho.

68. Thus, having attained that foremost position, he recalled his past deeds, became joyful, and revealing the account of his past conduct, spoke beginning with 'of the Blessed One Padumuttara,' and so forth. Regarding 'in the seven-storied palace': 'pāsāda' means that which generates serene confidence and gladness. The seven stories stood one above the other in that palace, hence it is a seven-storied palace; in that seven-storied palace. Regarding 'I spread a mirror': having prepared a mirror-like surface, I gave a covering to the Blessed One, the foremost in the world, the one of such a nature. The meaning is, 'having spread it, I worshipped him.'

69. Khīṇāsavasahassehīti arahantasahassehi parikiṇṇo parivuto. Dvipadindo dvipadānaṃ indo sāmi narāsabho mahāmuni gandhakuṭiṃ tehi saha upāgami pāvisīti attho.

69. Regarding 'by a thousand of those whose taints are destroyed': surrounded and encompassed by a thousand Arahants. The Lord of the Two-footed, the master of two-footed beings, the bull among men, the Great Sage, approached and entered the fragrant chamber along with them—this is the meaning.

70. Virocento gandhakuṭinti taṃ gandhakuṭiṃ sobhayamāno devānaṃ devo devadevo narānaṃ āsabho narāsabho jeṭṭho satthā bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe nisīditvā imā byākaraṇagāthāyo abhāsatha kathesīti sambandho.

70. Regarding 'illuminating the fragrant chamber': adorning that fragrant chamber, the god of gods, the bull among men, the preeminent Teacher, seated in the midst of the community of monks, spoke these verses of prophecy. This is the connection.

71. Yenāyaṃ jotitā seyyāti yena upāsakena ayaṃ pāsādasaṅkhātā seyyā jotitā pabhāsitā pajjalitā. Ādāsova kaṃsalohamayaṃ ādāsatalaṃ iva suṭṭhu samaṃ katvā santhatā. Taṃ upāsakaṃ kittayissāmi pākaṭaṃ karissāmīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

71. Regarding 'by whom this bed was illuminated': by which lay follower this bed, known as a palace, was illuminated, brightened, and made radiant. Like a mirror-surface made of bronze, it was perfectly even and spread out. The meaning is, 'I will praise that lay follower, I will make him known.' The rest is easily understood.

81. Aṭṭhānametaṃ yaṃ tādīti yaṃ yena kāraṇena tādī iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu akampiyasabhāvattā tādī agāre gharāvāse ratiṃ allīnabhāvaṃ ajjhagā pāpuṇi, etaṃ kāraṇaṃ aṭṭhānaṃ akāraṇanti attho.

81. Regarding 'This is impossible, that one of such a nature': The meaning is, 'for whatever reason one of such a nature, being of an imperturbable nature regarding desirable and undesirable things, should find delight and clinging in a household dwelling; this is impossible, it is without cause.'

82. Nikkhamitvā [M 2.0017] agārasmāti gharāvāsato nikkhamitvā taṃ tiṇadalamiva pariccajitvā subbato susikkhito pabbajissati. Rāhulo nāma [P 0.0325] nāmenāti suddhodanamahārājena pesitaṃ [V 2.0016] kumārassa jātasāsanaṃ sutvā pitarā siddhatthena, “rāhu jāto, bandhanaṃ jāta”nti vuttanāmattā rāhulo nāmāti attho. “Yathā candasūriyānaṃ vimānapabhāya kiliṭṭhakaraṇena rāhu asurindo upeti gacchati, evamevāyaṃ mama abhinikkhamanapabbajjādīnaṃ antarāyaṃ karontoriva jāto”ti adhippāyena, “rāhu jātoti āhā”ti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Arahā so bhavissatīti so tādiso upanissayasampanno vipassanāyaṃ yuttappayutto arahā khīṇāsavo bhavissatīti attho.

82. Regarding 'Having left home': having departed from household life, abandoning it like a blade of grass, he will become well-behaved and well-trained, he will go forth. Regarding 'Named Rāhula by name': The meaning is, having heard the message of the prince’s birth sent by King Suddhodana, because the father, Siddhattha, had spoken the name, saying, 'A rāhu is born, a bond is born,' he was named Rāhula. It should be understood that the intention was, 'Just as Rāhu, the lord of asuras, approaches and obscures the radiance of the moon and sun, so this one has been born as if to create an obstacle to my renunciation and going forth,' and thus he said, 'A rāhu is born.' Regarding 'He will become an Arahant': The meaning is, one so endowed with supporting conditions, engaged and striving in insight, will become an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.

83. Kikīva aṇḍaṃ rakkheyyāti aṇḍaṃ bījaṃ rakkhamānā kikī sakuṇī iva appamatto sīlaṃ rakkheyya, cāmarī viya vāladhinti vālaṃ rakkhamānā kaṇḍakesu vāle laggante bhindanabhayena anākaḍḍhitvā maramānā cāmarī viya jīvitampi pariccajitvā sīlaṃ abhinditvā rakkheyya. Nipako sīlasampannoti nepakkaṃ vuccati paññā, tena nepakkena samannāgato nipako khaṇḍachiddādibhāvaṃ apāpetvā rakkhaṇato sīlasampanno bhavissatīti evaṃ so bhagavā byākaraṇamakāsi. So evaṃ pattaarahattaphalo ekadivasaṃ vivekaṭṭhāne nisinno somanassavasena evaṃ rakkhiṃ mahāmunītiādimāha. Taṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

83. Regarding 'Like a blue jay guarding its egg': just as a blue jay, guarding its egg or seed, so should one be diligent in guarding virtue. Or regarding 'like a cāmarī guarding its tail': just as a cāmarī, guarding its tail, when its tail gets caught in thorns, would rather die than pull it free for fear of breaking it, so too should one guard virtue, even at the cost of life, without breaking it. Regarding 'Wise and endowed with virtue': 'nepakka' is called wisdom; endowed with that wisdom, one is wise. By guarding virtue so as to prevent it from becoming broken or flawed, one becomes endowed with virtue. Thus, the Blessed One made this prophecy. He, having thus attained the fruit of arahantship, one day sat in solitude and, filled with joy, spoke beginning with 'Thus I guarded, O Great Sage.' That is easily understood.

Rāhulattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rāhula is completed.

7. Upasenavaṅgantaputtattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta

Padumuttaraṃ bhagavantantiādikaṃ āyasmato upasenavaṅgantaputtattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ samantapāsādikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā satthu adhikārakammaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā [M 2.0018] devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde nālakagāme rūpasārī brāhmaṇiyā kucchimhi nibbatti, upasenotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā upasampadāya ekavassiko “ariyagabbhaṃ vaḍḍhemī”ti ekaṃ kulaputtaṃ attano santike upasampādetvā tena saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ gato. Satthārā cassa tassa avassikassa bhikkhuno saddhivihārikabhāvaṃ sutvā “atilahuṃ kho tvaṃ, moghapurisa, bāhullāya āvatto”ti (mahāva. 75) garahito “idānāhaṃ yadi parisaṃ nissāya satthārā garahito, parisaṃyeva pana nissāya [P 0.0326] satthu [V 2.0017] pasādaṃ karissāmī”ti vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahā pana hutvā sayampi sabbe dhutaṅgadhamme samādāya vattati, aññepi tadatthāya samādapesi, tena naṃ bhagavā samantapāsādikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. So aparena samayena kosambiyaṃ kalahe uppanne bhikkhusaṅghe ca dvidhābhūte ekena bhikkhunā taṃ kalahaṃ parivajjitukāmena “etarahi kho kalaho uppanno, bhikkhusaṅgho ca dvidhābhūto, kathaṃ nu kho mayā paṭipajjitabba”nti puṭṭho vivekavāsato paṭṭhāya tassa paṭipattiṃ kathesi. Evaṃ thero tassa bhikkhuno ovādadānāpadesena attano tathā paṭipannabhāvaṃ dīpento aññaṃ byākāsi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta begins with the words 'Padumuttara, the Blessed One.' This venerable one, too, having made an aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating, in various existences, merits that are a support for liberation, was born in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having come of age, he went to the Teacher, and while listening to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher establish a certain monk in the foremost position among those who are inspiring in every respect. Having made an aspiration before the Teacher and aspiring for that same position, he performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandered among gods and humans. During this Buddha's Dispensation, he took conception in the womb of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī in the village of Nālaka; his name was Upasena. Having come of age, he mastered the three Vedas. After listening to the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, he gained faith and went forth. After his higher ordination, while still a monk of less than one year's standing, thinking, 'I will expand the noble succession,' he gave the higher ordination to a clansman in his presence and went with him to the Teacher. When the Teacher heard of him, a monk of less than one year's standing, having a pupil, he rebuked him, saying: 'You are too hasty, you foolish man; you are striving for abundance' (Mahāva. 75). Being thus rebuked, he thought: 'If I have now been rebuked by the Teacher on account of the assembly, then it is on account of the assembly itself that I will inspire the Teacher's confidence.' Practicing insight meditation, he soon attained Arahantship. Having become an Arahant, he himself undertook all the ascetic practices and lived accordingly, and he encouraged others to do the same. For that reason, the Blessed One established him in the foremost position among those who are inspiring in every respect. On a later occasion, when a dispute arose in Kosambī and the Saṅgha of monks was divided in two, he was asked by a certain monk who wished to avoid that dispute: 'Now a dispute has arisen, and the Saṅgha of monks is divided in two. How should I conduct myself?' Beginning with dwelling in seclusion, the elder taught him the proper conduct. In this way, by means of giving instruction to that monk, the elder, wishing to reveal his own practice, made a further declaration.

86. So evaṃ pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaraṃ bhagavantantiādimāha. Pabbhāramhi nisīdantanti purato bhāraṃ namitaṃ onamitanti pabbhāraṃ vivekakāmaṃ vanamajjhe sayaṃjātapabbatapabbhāre nisinnaṃ naruttamaṃ bhagavantaṃ ahaṃ upagacchiṃ samīpaṃ gatoti attho.

86. He, having thus attained that foremost position, recollecting his own past deeds, and wishing to reveal the story of his past conduct out of joy, spoke the verses beginning with 'Padumuttara, the Blessed One.' Regarding the words 'seated on a slope' (pabbhāramhi nisīdantaṃ): a pabbhāra is a slope, so called because it is weighted and inclined forward. I approached the Blessed One, the supreme among men, who, desiring seclusion, was seated on a naturally formed mountain slope in the midst of the forest. 'I approached' means 'I went near'.

87. Kaṇikārapuppha disvāti tathā upagacchanto tasmiṃ padese supupphitaṃ kaṇikāraṃ disvā. Vaṇṭe chetvānahaṃ tadāti tasmiṃ tathāgatassa diṭṭhakāle taṃ pupphaṃ vaṇṭe vaṇṭasmiṃ chetvāna chinditvāna. Alaṅkaritvā chattamhīti tena pupphena chattaṃ chādetvā. Buddhassa abhiropayinti pabbhāre nisinnassa buddhassa muddhani akāsinti attho.

87. Regarding 'seeing a kaṇikāra flower' (kaṇikārapupphaṃ disvā): it means that as I was thus approaching, I saw in that place a fully blossomed kaṇikāra tree. Regarding 'having cut it at the stem then' (vaṇṭe chetvānahaṃ tadā): it means that at that time, upon seeing the Tathāgata, I cut that flower at its stem. Regarding 'having adorned it as a canopy' (alaṅkaritvā chattamhi): it means I made a canopy with that flower. Regarding 'I raised it over the Buddha' (Buddhassa abhiropayiṃ): the meaning is that I held it over the head of the Buddha who was seated on the slope.

88. Piṇḍapātañca [M 2.0019] pādāsinti tasmiṃyeva nisinnassa bhagavato piṇḍapātaṃ pakārena adāsiṃ bhojesinti attho. Paramannaṃ subhojananti sundarabhojanasaṅkhātaṃ paramannaṃ uttamāhāraṃ. Buddhena navame tatthāti tasmiṃ vivekaṭṭhāne buddhena saha navame aṭṭha samaṇe samitapāpe khīṇāsavabhikkhū bhojesinti attho.

88. Regarding 'and alms-food I gave' (piṇḍapātañca pādāsiṃ): the meaning is that I gave alms-food in a special manner to the Blessed One seated right there; that is, I fed him. Regarding 'the finest food, an excellent meal' (paramannaṃ subhojanaṃ): it means the supreme nourishment, known as excellent food. Regarding 'with the Buddha as the ninth there' (Buddhena navame tattha): the meaning is that in that secluded place, I fed eight ascetics, monks whose taints were destroyed, with the Buddha as the ninth among them.

Yaṃ vadanti sumedhoti yaṃ gotamasammāsambuddhaṃ bhūripaññaṃ pathavisamānaṃ paññaṃ sumedhaṃ sundaraṃ sabbaññutādipaññavantaṃ. Sumedho iti sundarapañño iti vadanti paṇḍitā ito kappato satasahasse kappe eso gotamo sammāsambuddho bhavissatīti sambandho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

Regarding 'whom they call Sumedha' (yaṃ vadanti sumedho): this refers to the Gotama Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is of vast wisdom (bhūripañña), whose wisdom is like the earth, the beautiful one (sumedha), endowed with omniscience and other forms of wisdom. The connection is as follows: the wise say, 'Sumedha means one of beautiful wisdom,' and 'one hundred thousand aeons from this aeon, this Gotama will become a Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha.' The rest is easily understood.

Upasenavaṅgantaputtattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta is concluded.

8. Raṭṭhapālattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla.

Padumuttarassa [P 0.0327][V 2.0018] bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato raṭṭhapālattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato uppattito puretarameva haṃsavatīnagare gahapatimahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena gharāvāse patiṭṭhito ratanakoṭṭhāgārakammikena dassitaṃ aparimāṇaṃ vaṃsānugataṃ dhanaṃ disvā “imaṃ ettakaṃ dhanarāsiṃ mayhaṃ pituayyakapayyakādayo attanā saddhiṃ gahetvā gantuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, mayā pana gahetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ mahādānaṃ adāsi. So abhiññālābhiṃ ekaṃ tāpasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tena devalokādhipacce niyojito yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā tato cuto devaloke nibbattitvā dibbasampattiṃ anubhavanto tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto manussaloke bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ samatthassa kulassa ekaputtako hutvā nibbatti. Tena samayena padumuttaro bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko veneyyasatte nibbānamahānagarasaṅkhātaṃ khemantabhūmiṃ sampāpesi. Atha so kulaputto anukkamena viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā pasannacitto parisapariyante nisīdi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Raṭṭhapāla begins with the words, 'Of the Blessed One Padumuttara,' and so forth. This venerable one, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that support liberation in various existences, was born even before the arising of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī, into a family of a great, wealthy householder. Having come of age, upon his father's passing, he became established in the household. Seeing the immeasurable, ancestral wealth shown to him by the keeper of the jewel treasury, he reflected: 'My father, grandfather, great-grandfather, and other ancestors were unable to take this much wealth with them. It is, however, fitting for me to take it with me.' Thinking thus, he gave great alms to the poor, the needy, and others. He approached a certain ascetic who possessed the higher knowledges and was directed by him toward attaining lordship in the deva world. Having performed meritorious deeds for his entire life, he passed away from there and was reborn in a deva world. Enjoying divine bliss, he remained there for the full lifespan, and passing away from there, he was reborn in the human world as the only son of a family capable of uniting a divided kingdom. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara had arisen in the world, had turned the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, and was guiding trainable beings to the secure land known as the great city of Nibbāna. Then that clansman, having gradually attained discernment, went one day with lay devotees to the monastery. Seeing the Teacher preaching the Dhamma, with a gladdened mind, he sat down at the edge of the assembly.

Tena [M 2.0020] kho pana samayena satthā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ saddhāpabbajitānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. So taṃ disvā pasannamānaso satasahassabhikkhuparivutassa bhagavato sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ patthesi. Satthā anantarāyena samijjhanabhāvaṃ disvā “ayaṃ anāgate gotamassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa sāsane saddhāpabbajitānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti byākāsi. So satthāraṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. So yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā tato cavitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito dvenavute kappe phussassa bhagavato kāle satthu vemātikesu tīsu rājaputtesu satthāraṃ upaṭṭhahantesu tesaṃ puññakiriyāsu sahāyakiccaṃ akāsi. Evaṃ tattha tattha bhave bahuṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kururaṭṭhe thullakoṭṭhikanigame raṭṭhapālaseṭṭhino gehe nibbatti, tassa bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ samatthakule nibbattattā raṭṭhapāloti vaṃsānugatameva nāmaṃ ahosi. So mahatā parivārena vaḍḍhanto anukkamena yobbanappatto mātāpitūhi patirūpena dārena saṃyojito mahante [P 0.0328] ca yase patiṭṭhāpito dibbasampattisadisasampattiṃ paccanubhoti.

At that time, the Teacher placed a certain monk in the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith. Seeing this, with a gladdened mind, he gave a great offering for seven days to the Blessed One, who was surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, and aspired to that position. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled without obstruction, prophesied: 'In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Enlightened One named Gotama, this one will be the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith.' Having paid homage to the Teacher and the community of monks, he rose from his seat and departed. He performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, and after passing away, he wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Ninety-two aeons from the present, during the time of the Blessed One Phussa, when the Teacher was being attended upon by his three step-brothers, the princes, he assisted them in their meritorious deeds. Thus, accumulating much wholesome merit in various existences and wandering only in good destinations, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in the Kuru country, in the market town of Thullakoṭṭhika, in the house of the merchant Raṭṭhapāla. Because he was born into a family capable of uniting a divided kingdom, his name was Raṭṭhapāla, a name passed down through his lineage. Growing up with a large retinue, he gradually reached youth, was joined by his parents to a suitable wife, and, established in great renown, he experienced a fortune like that of the gods.

Atha [V 2.0019] bhagavā kururaṭṭhe janapadacārikaṃ caranto thullakoṭṭhikaṃ anupāpuṇi. Taṃ sutvā raṭṭhapālo kulaputto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitukāmo sattāhaṃ bhattacchedaṃ katvā kicchena kasirena mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā satthu āṇattiyā aññatarassa santike pabbajitvā yonisomanasikārena kammaṃ karonto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthāraṃ anujānāpetvā mātāpitaro passituṃ thullakoṭṭhikaṃ gantvā tattha sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caranto pitu nivesane ābhidosikaṃ kummāsaṃ labhitvā taṃ amataṃ viya paribhuñjanto pitarā nimantito svātanāya adhivāsetvā dutiyadivase pitu nivesane piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā alaṅkatapaṭiyatte itthāgārajane upagantvā “kīdisā nāma tā, ayyaputta, accharāyo, yāsaṃ tvaṃ hetu brahmacariyaṃ carasī”tiādīni (ma. ni. 2.301) vatvā palobhanakammaṃ kātuṃ āraddhe tassādhippāyaṃ viparivattetvā aniccatādipaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammaṃ kathento –

Then the Blessed One, while wandering on tour through the countryside in the Kuru country, arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. Hearing of this, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Teacher. Having heard the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, he gained faith and desired to go forth. After abstaining from food for seven days, with difficulty and hardship he gained his parents' permission. He then approached the Teacher, requested to go forth, and by the Teacher's instruction, went forth under a certain elder. Applying himself to the practice with wise attention, he developed insight and attained arahantship. Having attained arahantship, he obtained the Teacher's permission and went to Thullakoṭṭhika to see his parents. There, while wandering for alms from house to house in sequence, he received stale barley-meal at his father's residence. Consuming it as if it were ambrosia, he was invited by his father for the next day and accepted. On the second day, after consuming the almsfood at his father's residence, he approached the women of the inner chambers, who were adorned and prepared. When they began their work of temptation, saying, 'Of what kind, noble son, are the nymphs for whose sake you lead the holy life?' and so on, he turned their intention around and, teaching the Dhamma connected with impermanence and so forth, said:

“Passa [M 2.0021] cittakataṃ bimbaṃ, arukāyaṃ samussitaṃ;

Āturaṃ bahusaṅkappaṃ, yassa natthi dhuvaṃ ṭhiti.

Behold this decorated image, a body of sores, built up, diseased, and of many thoughts, for which there is no lasting stability.

“Passa cittakataṃ rūpaṃ, maṇinā kuṇḍalena ca;

Aṭṭhiṃ tacena onaddhaṃ, saha vatthehi sobhati.

Behold this decorated form, with jewels and earrings; a frame of bones bound up with skin, it shines together with its clothes.

“Alattakakatā pādā, mukhaṃ cuṇṇakamakkhitaṃ;

Alaṃ bālassa mohāya, no ca pāragavesino.

Feet dyed with lac, a face smeared with powder; enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the farther shore.

“Aṭṭhāpadakatā kesā, nettā añjanamakkhitā;

Alaṃ bālassa mohāya, no ca pāragavesino.

Hair arranged in eight plaits, eyes smeared with collyrium; enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the farther shore.

“Añjanīva navā cittā, pūtikāyo alaṅkato;

Alaṃ bālassa mohāya, no ca pāragavesino.

Like a new, decorated collyrium pot, this foul body is adorned; enough to delude a fool, but not one who seeks the farther shore.

“Odahi [P 0.0329] migavo pāsaṃ, nāsadā vāguraṃ migo;

Bhutvā nivāpaṃ gacchāma, kandante migabandhake.

The hunter set the snare; the deer did not approach the net. Having eaten the bait, we depart, while the deer-trappers lament.

“Chinno [V 2.0020] pāso migavassa, nāsadā vāguraṃ migo;

Bhutvā nivāpaṃ gacchāma, socante migaluddake”ti. (ma. ni. 2.302; theragā. 769-775);

The hunter's snare is cut; the deer did not approach the net. Having eaten the bait, we depart, while the deer-hunters grieve.

Imā gāthāyo abhāsi. Imā gāthā vatvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rañño korabyassa migājinavanuyyāne maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nisīdi. Therassa kira pitā sattasu dvārakoṭṭhakesu aggaḷaṃ dāpetvā malle āṇāpesi “nikkhamituṃ mā detha, kāsāyāni apanetvā setakāni nivāsāpethā”ti. Tasmā thero ākāsena agamāsi. Atha rājā korabyo therassa tattha nisinnabhāvaṃ sutvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā “idha, bho raṭṭhapāla, pabbajanto byādhipārijuññaṃ vā jarābhogañātipārijuññaṃ vā patto pabbajati, tvaṃ pana kiñcipi pārijuññaṃ anupagato eva kasmā pabbajasī”ti pucchi. Athassa thero “upaniyyati loko addhuvo, atāṇo loko anabhissaro, asaraṇo loko sabbaṃ pahāya gamanīyaṃ, ūno loko atitto taṇhādāso”ti (ma. ni. 2.305) imesaṃ catunnaṃ dhammuddesānaṃ attanā viditabhāvaṃ kathetvā tassā desanāya anugītiṃ kathento –

He spoke these verses. Having spoken these verses, he rose into the air and sat down on the auspicious stone slab in King Koravya’s Migājina deer park. It is said that the elder’s father had the bolts put on the seven gateways and ordered the strongmen, “Do not let him leave; take away his saffron robes and clothe him in white garments.” Therefore, the elder went through the air. Then King Koravya, hearing that the elder was seated there, approached him and exchanged friendly and courteous greetings. He then asked, “Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, those who go forth usually do so having met with decay through sickness, or decay through old age, wealth, or relatives. But you have met with no such decay—why then have you gone forth?” Then the elder, explaining that he himself had understood these four summaries of the Dhamma: “The world is swept away, it is unstable; the world is without shelter, without a protector; the world is without refuge, one must go on, leaving everything behind; the world is deficient, insatiate, a slave to craving,” recited a verse in accordance with that teaching, saying:

“Passāmi [M 2.0022] loke sadhane manusse, laddhāna vittaṃ na dadanti mohā;

Luddhā dhanaṃ sannicayaṃ karonti, bhiyyova kāme abhipatthayanti.

“I see people in the world with possessions who, having obtained wealth, do not give because of delusion; greedy, they make a hoard of wealth, and further crave for pleasures.

“Rājā pasayhappathaviṃ vijetvā, sasāgarantaṃ mahimāvasanto;

Oraṃ samuddassa atittarūpo, pāraṃ samuddassapi patthayetha.

“The king, having conquered the earth by force and dwelling on the earth up to the ocean’s shore, not satisfied with this side of the sea, would yearn for the other side of the sea as well.

“Rājā ca aññe ca bahū manussā, avītataṇhā maraṇaṃ upenti;

Ūnāva hutvāna jahanti dehaṃ, kāmehi lokamhi na hatthi titti.

“A king and many other people, their craving unappeased, go to death; still unfulfilled they abandon the body, for in the world there is no satisfaction with sensual pleasures.

“Kandanti [P 0.0330] naṃ ñātī pakiriya kese, ‘aho vatā no amarā’ti cāhu;

Vatthena naṃ pārutaṃ nīharitvā, citaṃ samodhāya tato ḍahanti.

“His relatives wail for him, with dishevelled hair, and say, ‘Alas, that he was not immortal!’ Having wrapped him in a cloth and carried him out, they build a pyre and then burn him.

“So ḍayhati sūlehi tujjamāno, ekena vatthena pahāya bhoge;

Na mīyamānassa bhavanti tāṇā, ñātī ca mittā atha vā sahāyā.

“He is burned, prodded by stakes, with but a single cloth, having abandoned his possessions; for one who is dying, there are no protectors, neither relatives, nor friends, nor companions.

“Dāyādakā [V 2.0021] tassa dhanaṃ haranti, satto pana gacchati yena kammaṃ;

Na mīyamānaṃ dhanamanveti kiñci, puttā ca dārā ca dhanañca raṭṭhaṃ.

“His heirs take his wealth, but the being goes according to his kamma; nothing follows the dying one, neither children, nor wife, nor wealth, nor kingdom.

“Na dīghamāyuṃ labhate dhanena, na cāpi vittena jaraṃ vihanti;

Appaṃ hidaṃ jīvitamāhu dhīrā, asassataṃ vippariṇāmadhammaṃ.

“Not by wealth is long life obtained, nor by riches is aging overcome. The wise say this life is short, impermanent, and subject to change.

“Aḍḍhā [M 2.0023] daliddā ca phusanti phassaṃ, bālo ca dhīro ca tatheva phuṭṭho;

Bālo hi bālyā vadhitova seti, dhīro ca no vedhati phassaphuṭṭho.

“Both the rich and the poor experience contact; the fool and the wise are touched by it equally. The fool, because of his folly, lies as though slain; but the wise man does not tremble when touched by contact.

“Tasmā hi paññāva dhanena seyyā, yāya vosānamidhādhigacchati;

Abyositattā hi bhavābhavesu, pāpāni kammāni karoti mohā.

“Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth, by which one attains consummation here; for being unsettled in existence after existence, one does evil deeds out of delusion.

“Upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ, saṃsāramāpajjaparamparāya;

Tassappapañño abhisaddahanto, upeti gabbhañca parañca lokaṃ.

“He enters a womb and the next world, falling into saṃsāra in succession. The one of little wisdom, placing faith in that, enters a womb and the next world.

“Coro [P 0.0331] yathā sandhimukhe gahīto, sakammunā haññati pāpadhammo;

Evaṃ pajā pecca paramhi loke, sakammunā haññati pāpadhammo.

“Just as a thief of evil nature, caught at a break-in, is destroyed by his own deed; so too a person of evil nature, after death in the next world, is destroyed by their own deed.

“Kāmā hi citrā madhurā manoramā, virūparūpena mathenti cittaṃ;

Ādīnavaṃ kāmaguṇesu disvā, tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rāja.

“Sensual pleasures are indeed diverse, sweet, and delightful; they agitate the mind with their varied forms. Having seen the danger in sensual qualities, therefore I have gone forth, O king.

“Dumapphalānīva patanti māṇavā, daharā ca vuḍḍhā ca sarīrabhedā;

Etampi disvāna pabbajitomhi rāja, apaṇṇakaṃ sāmaññameva seyyo.

“Like fruits from a tree, people fall, both young and old, at the breaking up of the body. Seeing this too, I have gone forth, O king; unquestionably, the ascetic life is indeed better.

“Saddhāyāhaṃ pabbajito, upeto jinasāsane;

Avañjhā mayhaṃ pabbajjā, anaṇo bhuñjāmi bhojanaṃ.

“Through faith I went forth, entered the Victor's dispensation; my going forth is not in vain, I eat my food without debt.

“Kāme ādittato disvā, jātarūpāni satthato;

Gabbhāvokkantito dukkhaṃ, nirayesu mahabbhayaṃ.

“Seeing sensual pleasures as ablaze, gold and silver as a weapon, descent into the womb as suffering, and great terror in the hells—

“Etamādīnavaṃ [M 2.0024][V 2.0022] ñatvā, saṃvegaṃ alabhiṃ tadā;

Sohaṃ viddho tadā santo, sampatto āsavakkhayaṃ.

“—having known this danger, I then found spiritual urgency. Pierced by that, I became tranquil and have reached the destruction of the taints.

“Pariciṇṇo mayā satthā, kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ;

Ohito garuko bhāro, bhavanetti samūhatā.

“The Teacher has been attended to by me, the Buddha's Teaching has been done; the heavy burden has been laid down, the guide to existence is uprooted.

“Yassatthāya pabbajito, agārasmānagāriyaṃ;

So me attho anuppatto, sabbasaṃyojanakkhayo”ti. (theragā. 776-793) –

“For the sake of which I went forth from home to homelessness, that goal of mine has been attained: the destruction of all fetters.”

Imā gāthā avoca. Evaṃ thero rañño korabyassa dhammaṃ desetvā satthu santikameva gato. Satthā ca aparabhāge ariyagaṇamajjhe nisinno theraṃ saddhāpabbajitānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

He spoke these verses. Thus, the Elder, having taught the Dhamma to King Korabya, went to the Teacher’s presence. And the Teacher, later, seated amidst the assembly of noble ones, placed the Elder in the foremost position among those who had gone forth in faith.

97-8. Evaṃ [P 0.0332] so thero pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttarassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Varanāgo mayā dinnoti tassa bhagavato rūpakāye pasīditvā varo uttamo seṭṭho īsādanto rathīsāsadisadanto urūḷhavā bhāravaho rājāraho vā. Setacchattopasobhitoti hatthikkhandhe ussāpitasetacchattena upasevito sobhamāno. Punapi kiṃ visiṭṭho varanāgo? Sakappano hatthālaṅkārasahito. Saṅghārāmaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa vasanatthāya ārāmaṃ vihāraṃ akārayiṃ kāresiṃ.

Thus, the elder, having attained that supreme position, recollected his past deeds and, filled with joy, proclaimed his former conduct, beginning with “To the Blessed Padumuttara…” “A splendid elephant was given by me” means, delighting in the physical form of that Blessed One, it was a superior, excellent, and foremost tusker, whose tusks were like chariot-shafts, a mighty bearer of burdens, worthy of a king. “Adorned with a white parasol” means resplendent, attended by a white parasol raised upon the elephant’s back. What further distinguished that splendid elephant? It was caparisoned, complete with elephant ornaments. “For the Sangha’s dwelling” means I caused a monastery to be built, a sanctuary for the community of monks headed by the Buddha.

99. Catupaññāsasahassānīti tasmiṃ kārāpite vihārabbhantare catupaññāsasahassāni pāsādāni ca ahaṃ akārayiṃ kāresinti attho. Mahoghadānaṃ karitvānāti sabbaparikkhārasahitaṃ mahoghasadisaṃ mahādānaṃ sajjetvā mahesino munino niyyādesinti attho.

99. “Fifty-four thousand” means, within the monastery that was caused to be built, I had fifty-four thousand palaces constructed. “Having made a great offering like a flood” means, having prepared a great gift equal to a great flood, complete with all requisites, I presented it to the Great Sage, the Silent One.

100. Anumodi mahāvīroti caturāsaṅkhyeyyasatasahassesu kappesu abbocchinnaussāhasaṅkhātena vīriyena mahāvīro sayambhū sayameva bhūto jāto laddhasabbaññutaññāṇo aggo seṭṭho puggalo anumodi vihārānumodanaṃ akāsi. Sabbe jane hāsayantoti sakalānantāparimāṇe devamanusse hāsayanto santuṭṭhe [M 2.0025] kurumāno amatanibbānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ catusaccadhammadesanaṃ desesi pakāsesi vivari vibhaji uttānī akāsīti attho.

100. “The Great Hero rejoiced” means: the Great Hero—who by his effort, known as uninterrupted striving over four incalculable hundred thousand eons, became self-existent, self-arisen, having obtained omniscient knowledge, the foremost, the best person—rejoiced; he gave the dedication for the monastery. “He caused all people to rejoice” means: causing all infinite and immeasurable gods and humans to rejoice, making them content, he taught, explained, revealed, analyzed, and made plain the teaching of the four truths connected with deathless Nibbāna; this is the meaning.

101. Taṃ [V 2.0023] me viyākāsīti taṃ mayhaṃ katapuññaṃ balaṃ visesena pākaṭaṃ akāsi. Jalajuttamanāmakoti jale jātaṃ jalajaṃ padumaṃ, padumuttaranāmakoti attho. “Jalanuttamanāyako”tipi pāṭho. Tattha attano pabhāya jalantīti jalanā, candimasūriyadevabrahmāno, tesaṃ jalanānaṃ uttamoti jalanuttamo. Sabbasattānaṃ nāyako uttamoti nāyako, sambhāravante satte nibbānaṃ neti pāpetīti vā nāyako, jalanuttamo ca so nāyako cāti jalanuttamanāyako. Bhikkhusaṅghe nisīditvāti bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhe nisinno imā gāthā abhāsatha pākaṭaṃ katvā kathesīti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

101. “He prophesied that for me” means: he made that power of merit done by me especially manifest. “Named Jalajuttama” means: ‘jalaja’ is that which is born in water, a lotus; the meaning is ‘named Padumuttara’. “Jalanuttamanāyaka” is also a reading. In that case, ‘jalanā’ are those who shine by their own radiance, that is, the moon, sun, devas, and Brahmās; ‘Jalanuttama’ is the supreme among those who shine. ‘Nāyaka’ is the supreme leader of all beings; or, he is the ‘Nāyaka’ because he leads, he brings, beings who have accumulated the requisites to Nibbāna. He is both Jalanuttama and Nāyaka, thus he is Jalanuttamanāyaka. “Having sat in the Sangha of bhikkhus” means: seated in the midst of the Sangha of bhikkhus, he spoke these verses, having made them clear; this is the meaning. The rest has a plain meaning.

Raṭṭhapālattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla is concluded.

9. Sopākattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sopāka

Pabbhāraṃ sodhayantassātiādikaṃ āyasmato sopākattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato [P 0.0333] kāle aññatarassa kuṭumbikassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ disvā bījapūraphalāni satthu upanesi, paribhuñji bhagavā tassānukampaṃ upādāya. So bhikkhu satthari saṅghe ca abhippasanno salākabhattaṃ paṭṭhapetvā saṅghuddesavasena tiṇṇaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ khīrabhattaṃ adāsi. So tehi puññehi aparāparaṃ devamanussesu sampattiyo anubhavanto ekadā manussayoniyaṃ nibbatto ekassa paccekabuddhassa khīrabhattaṃ adāsi.

The Apadāna of the venerable Sopāka, beginning with “While cleaning the slope...”. He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that are a supporting condition for turning away from the round of rebirths, was reborn as the son of a certain householder in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. One day, seeing the Teacher, he offered citron fruits to the Teacher. The Blessed One partook of them out of compassion for him. He, being exceedingly pleased with the Teacher and the Sangha, established a ticket-food offering and, by way of dedicating it to the Sangha, gave milk-rice to three bhikkhus for as long as they lived. Through those merits, wandering from one existence to the next among devas and humans and experiencing prosperity, he was once reborn in the human realm and gave milk-rice to a Paccekabuddha.

Evaṃ tattha tattha puññāni katvā sugatīsuyeva paribbhamanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde purimakammanissandena sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarāya duggatitthiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Sā taṃ dasamāse kucchinā pariharitvā paripakke gabbhe vijāyanakāle vijāyituṃ asakkontī mucchaṃ āpajjitvā bahuvelaṃ matā viya nipajji. Ñātakā “matā”ti saññāya susānaṃ netvā citakaṃ āropetvā [M 2.0026] devatānubhāvena vātavuṭṭhiyā uṭṭhitāya aggiṃ adatvā pakkamiṃsu. Dārako pacchimabhavikattā devatānubhāveneva arogo hutvā mātukucchito nikkhami. Mātā pana kālamakāsi. Devatā manussarūpenupagamma taṃ gahetvā susānagopakassa gehe ṭhapetvā katipāhaṃ kālaṃ patirūpena āhārena posesi. Tato paraṃ susānagopako attano puttaṃ katvā vaḍḍhesi. So [V 2.0024] tathā vaḍḍhento tassa puttena suppiyena nāma dārakena saddhiṃ kīḷanto vicari. Tassa susāne jātasaṃvaḍḍhabhāvato sopākoti samaññā ahosi.

Thus, having performed meritorious deeds in various places and wandering only among good destinations, during the arising of this Buddha, as a result of his past kamma, he took conception in the womb of a certain poor woman in Sāvatthī. She carried him in her womb for ten months, and when her womb was mature, at the time of birth, being unable to deliver, she fainted and lay for a long time as if dead. Her relatives, perceiving that she was dead, took her to the charnel ground and placed her on a pyre. But when, through the power of the devas, wind and rain arose, they departed without setting the fire. The boy, because it was his final existence, emerged from his mother’s womb without illness, solely through the power of the devas. The mother, however, passed away. A deva, approaching in human form, took him and placed him in the house of the charnel ground keeper, nourishing him for some days with suitable food. Thereafter, the charnel ground keeper adopted him as his own son and raised him. As he was thus growing up, he would play and wander about with the keeper’s son, a boy named Suppiya. Because he was born and raised in the charnel ground, the designation ‘Sopāka’ arose for him.

Athekadivasaṃ sattavassikaṃ taṃ bhagavā paccūsavelāyaṃ ñāṇajālaṃ pattharitvā veneyyabandhave olokento ñāṇajālassa antogataṃ disvā susānaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Dārako pubbahetunā codiyamāno pasannamānaso satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Satthā tassa dhammaṃ kathesi. So dhammaṃ sutvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pitarā “anuññātosī”ti vutto pitaraṃ satthu santikaṃ ānesi. Tassa pitā satthāraṃ vanditvā “imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājetha, bhante”ti anujāni, taṃ pabbājetvā bhagavā mettābhāvanāya niyojesi. So mettākammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā susāne viharanto nacirasseva mettājhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi. Arahā hutvāpi aññesaṃ sosānikabhikkhūnaṃ mettābhāvanāvidhiṃ dassento “yathāpi ekaputtasmi”nti (theragā. 33) gāthaṃ abhāsi. Idaṃ [P 0.0334] vuttaṃ hoti – yathā ekaputtake piye manāpe mātā pitā ca kusalī ekantahitesī bhaveyya, evaṃ puratthimādibhedāsu sabbāsu disāsu kāmabhavādibhedesu vā sabbesu bhavesu daharādibhedāsu sabbāsu avatthāsupi ṭhitesu sabbesu sattesu ekantahitesitāya kusalī bhaveyya “mitto, udāsino, paccatthiko”ti sīmaṃ akatvā sīmāya sambhedavasena sabbattha ekarasaṃ mettaṃ bhāveyyāti imaṃ pana gāthaṃ vatvā “sace tumhe āyasmanto evaṃ mettaṃ bhāveyyātha, ye te bhagavatā ‘sukhaṃ supatī’tiādinā (a. ni. 11.15; pari. 331; mi. pa. 4.4.6) ekādasa mettānisaṃsā ca vuttā, ekaṃsena tesaṃ bhāgino bhavathā”ti ovādaṃ adāsi.

Then one day, at dawn, the Blessed One, spreading out the net of his knowledge and surveying the kinsmen to be tamed, saw that seven-year-old boy caught within his net of knowledge and went to the charnel ground. The boy, being urged by a past cause, approached the Teacher with a mind of faith, paid homage, and stood to one side. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he asked for the going forth. When he was asked, “Have you been permitted by your father?” he brought his father to the Teacher. His father paid homage to the Teacher and gave his consent, saying, “Venerable sir, please give the going forth to this boy.” Having given him the going forth, the Blessed One instructed him in the development of loving-kindness. He, having taken up the meditation subject of loving-kindness, while dwelling in the charnel ground, before long made the mettā-jhāna his basis, developed insight, and realized Arahantship. Even after becoming an Arahant, while showing the method for developing loving-kindness to other bhikkhus dwelling in the charnel ground, he spoke the verse beginning, “Just as for an only son…” (Theragāthā 33). This is what was said: Just as a mother and father are skilled and solely intent on the welfare of their dear and beloved only son, so too should one be skilled and solely intent on the welfare of all beings situated in all conditions—such as being young and so on—in all directions—such as the east and so on—and in all states of existence—such as the kāma-existence and so on. Without making a boundary such as ‘friend,’ ‘neutral one,’ or ‘enemy,’ one should develop loving-kindness with a single taste everywhere by breaking down the boundaries. Having spoken this verse, he then gave this exhortation: “Venerables, if you were to develop loving-kindness in this way, you would, without a doubt, become partakers of those eleven benefits of loving-kindness spoken of by the Blessed One, beginning with, ‘One sleeps in comfort…’ (Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.15; Parivāra 331; Milindapañha 4.4.6).”

112. Evaṃ [M 2.0027] so pattaphalādhigamo attano katapuññaṃ paccavekkhitvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ dassento pabbhāraṃ sodhayantassātiādimāha. Tattha pabbhāranti silāpabbatassa vivekaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ pabbajitānurūpattā iṭṭhakapākāraṃ katvā dvārakavāṭaṃ yojetvā bhikkhūnaṃ vasanatthāya adāsi, pakārena bharo patthetabboti pabbhāro, taṃ sodhayantassa mama santikaṃ siddhattho nāma bhagavā āgacchi pāpuṇi.

112. Thus he, having attained the fruit, reflecting on the merit he had performed, and with joy arisen, related the story of his past deeds, speaking the verse beginning, 'While cleaning the mountain slope…' Therein, 'mountain slope' means a secluded place on a rocky mountain. As it was suitable for those who have gone forth, having made a brick enclosure and fitted a door-leaf, he gave it to the bhikkhus for their residence. Because it is a support (bharo) to be desired (patthetabbo) in a special way (pakārena), it is called a 'pabbhāra'. While I was cleaning it, the Blessed One named Siddhattha approached and arrived in my presence.

113. Buddhaṃ upagataṃ disvāti evaṃ mama santikaṃ āgataṃ disvā tādino iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu akampiyasabhāvattā tādiguṇayuttassa lokajeṭṭhassa buddhassa santharaṃ tiṇapaṇṇādisantharaṃ kaṭṭhattharaṃ paññāpetvā niṭṭhāpetvā pupphāsanaṃ pupphamayaṃ āsanaṃ ahaṃ adāsiṃ.

113. Regarding 'Seeing the Buddha approaching': thus, seeing him coming into my presence, I prepared and finished a spread of grass, leaves, and so forth, and a wooden platform for the Buddha, the Foremost in the World, the 'Such-like One' (tādino), who, due to his unshakable nature amidst the agreeable and disagreeable, is endowed with that quality of 'suchness'. I then offered a flower-seat, that is, a seat made of flowers.

114. Pupphāsane [V 2.0025] nisīditvāti tasmiṃ paññatte pupphāsane nisīditvā lokanāyako siddhattho bhagavā. Mamañca gatimaññāyāti mayhaṃ gatiṃ āyatiṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ aññāya jānitvā aniccataṃ aniccabhāvaṃ udāhari kathesi.

114. Regarding 'Sitting on the flower seat': the Blessed One Siddhattha, the Guide of the World, sat down on that prepared flower seat. Regarding 'And knowing my destiny': having known my destiny—my future place of rebirth—he declared and spoke of impermanence, the state of being impermanent.

115. Aniccā vata saṅkhārāti vata ekantena saṅkhārā paccayehi samecca samāgantvā karīyamānā sabbe sappaccayadhammā hutvā abhāvaṭṭhena aniccā. Uppādavayadhamminoti uppajjitvā vinassanasabhāvā uppajjitvā pātubhavitvā ete saṅkhārā nirujjhanti vinassantīti attho. Tesaṃ vūpasamo sukhoti tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ visesena upasamo sukho, tesaṃ vūpasamakaraṃ nibbānameva ekantasukhanti attho.

115. Regarding 'Truly, conditioned things are impermanent': indeed, absolutely, conditioned things—being produced by the coming together and assembling of conditions, and thus being phenomena that are dependently arisen—are impermanent in the sense that they cease to be. Regarding 'They are of the nature of arising and vanishing': having arisen, they have the nature of perishing; having arisen and come into being, these conditioned things cease, they perish—this is the meaning. Regarding 'The stilling of them is bliss': the complete stilling of those conditioned things is bliss; the meaning is that Nibbāna, which brings about their stilling, is itself absolute bliss.

116. Idaṃ vatvāna sabbaññūti sabbadhammajānanako bhagavā lokānaṃ jeṭṭho vuḍḍho narānaṃ āsabho padhāno vīro idaṃ aniccapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ [P 0.0335] dhammadesanaṃ vatvāna kathetvā ambare ākāse haṃsarājā iva nabhaṃ ākāsaṃ abbhuggamīti sambandho.

116. Regarding 'Having said this, the All-Knowing One': the Blessed One, the knower of all phenomena, the eldest and most senior of the worlds, the bull among men, the foremost hero, having spoken and taught this Dhamma discourse connected with impermanence, rose up into the sky, into the firmament, like a swan-king. This is the connection.

117. Sakaṃ diṭṭhiṃ attano laddhiṃ khantiṃ ruciṃ ajjhāsayaṃ jahitvāna pahāya. Bhāvayāniccasaññahanti anicce aniccanti pavattasaññaṃ ahaṃ bhāvayiṃ vaḍḍhesiṃ manasi akāsiṃ. Tattha kālaṃ kato ahanti tattha tissaṃ jātiyaṃ tato jātito ahaṃ kālaṃ kato mato.

117. Regarding 'Having abandoned one's own view': having abandoned and given up one's own view, doctrine, preference, liking, and disposition. Regarding 'I cultivated the perception of impermanence': I developed, increased, and brought to mind the perception that occurs as 'impermanent' in regard to what is impermanent. Regarding 'There I passed away': there, in that birth, from that birth, I passed away, I died.

118. Dve [M 2.0028] sampattī anubhotvāti manussasampattidibbasampattisaṅkhātā dve sampattiyo anubhavitvā. Sukkamūlena coditoti purāṇakusalamūlena, mūlabhūtena kusalena vā codito sañcodito. Pacchime bhave sampatteti pariyosāne bhave sampatte pāpuṇite. Sapākayonupāgaminti sakaṃ pacitabhattaṃ sapākaṃ yoniṃ upāgamiṃ. Yassa kulassa attano pacitabhattaṃ aññehi abhuñjanīyaṃ, tasmiṃ caṇḍālakule nibbattosmīti attho. Atha vā sā vuccati sunakho, sunakhocchiṭṭhabhattabhuñjanakacaṇḍālakule jātoti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

118. Regarding 'Having experienced two kinds of success': having experienced the two kinds of success known as human success and divine success. Regarding 'Urged by the root of merit': urged or impelled by an ancient wholesome root, or by wholesome kamma that has become a foundation. Regarding 'When the final existence was attained': when the final existence was attained, was reached. Regarding 'I was reborn in a Sopāka womb': I approached a womb where one cooks for oneself (sakaṃ pacati). The meaning is: I was reborn in an outcaste (caṇḍāla) family, whose own cooked food is not to be eaten by others. Alternatively, 'sā' is a term for a dog (sunakha); the meaning is: born in an outcaste family that eats food left over by dogs. The rest has a clear meaning.

Sopākattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sopāka is concluded.

10. Sumaṅgalattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sumaṅgala.

Āhutiṃ [V 2.0026] yiṭṭhukāmotiādikaṃ āyasmato sumaṅgalattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto piyadassissa bhagavato kāle rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. So ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ nhatvā ekacīvaraṃ ṭhitaṃ disvā somanassappatto apphoṭesi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyā avidūre aññatarasmiṃ gāmake tādisena kammanissandena daliddakule nibbatti, tassa sumaṅgaloti nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto khujjakāsitanaṅgalakuddālaparikkhāro hutvā kasiyā jīvikaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ raññā pasenadinā kosalena bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca mahādāne pavattiyamāne dānūpakaraṇāni gahetvā āgacchantehi manussehi saddhiṃ dadhighaṭaṃ gahetvā āgato bhikkhūnaṃ sakkārasammānaṃ disvā “ime samaṇā sakyaputtiyā sukhumavatthanivatthā subhojanāni bhuñjitvā nivātesu senāsanesu viharanti, yaṃnūnāhampi pabbajeyya”nti cintetvā aññataraṃ mahātheraṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano pabbajādhippāyaṃ nivedesi. So taṃ karuṇāyanto pabbājetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ [P 0.0336] ācikkhi. So araññe [M 2.0029] viharanto ekakavihāre nibbinno ukkaṇṭhito hutvā vibbhamitukāmo ñātigāmaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge kacchaṃ bandhitvā khettaṃ kasante kiliṭṭhavatthanivatthe samantato rajokiṇṇasarīre vātātapena sussante khettaṃ kassake manusse disvā “mahantaṃ vatime sattā jīvikanimittaṃ dukkhaṃ paccanubhavantī”ti saṃvegaṃ paṭilabhi. Ñāṇassa paripākagatattā cassa yathāgahitaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So aññataraṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upagantvā vivekaṃ labhitvā yonisomanasikaronto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggapaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The verse beginning, 'Desiring to make an offering…' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Sumaṅgala. This venerable one, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and having accumulated merits that serve as a foundation for liberation in various existences, was reborn as a tree deity in the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī. One day, seeing the Teacher standing in a single robe after bathing, he was filled with joy and applauded. Through that meritorious deed, while wandering through existences among devas and humans, he was reborn in this Buddha-dispensation into a poor family in a small village not far from Sāvatthī, as a result of that kamma. He was given the name Sumaṅgala. When he came of age, equipped with a small plow and a hoe, he made his living by farming. One day, when King Pasenadi of Kosala was making a great offering to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he came along with the people who were arriving carrying the requisites for the offering, bringing a pot of curd. Seeing the honor and respect being given to the bhikkhus, he thought: 'These recluses, sons of the Sakyan, wear fine robes, eat good food, and dwell in lodgings sheltered from the wind. Why should I not also go forth?' Having thought thus, he approached a certain great elder and informed him of his intention to go forth. Out of compassion for him, the elder gave him the going forth and instructed him in a meditation subject. While dwelling in the forest, living alone, he became disenchanted and discontented. Desiring to leave the monastic life, he was going to his relatives' village when, on the way, having tucked up his robe, he saw farmers plowing a field. They wore soiled clothes, their bodies were covered all over with dust, and they were withering in the wind and sun. Seeing these farmers, he gained a sense of spiritual urgency, thinking: 'Indeed, what great suffering these beings experience for the sake of their livelihood!' And because his knowledge had reached maturity, the meditation subject he had undertaken became present to his mind. He went to the foot of a certain tree, and having found seclusion and applying wise attention, he developed insight and, by the sequence of the paths, attained Arahantship.

124. Evaṃ so pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento āhutiṃ yiṭṭhukāmohantiādimāha. Tattha āhutinti annapānādianekavidhaṃ pūjāsakkārūpakaraṇaṃ. Yiṭṭhukāmoti yajitukāmo, dānaṃ dātukāmo ahaṃ. Paṭiyādetvāna bhojananti āhāraṃ paṭiyādetvā nipphādetvā. Brāhmaṇe paṭimānentoti paṭiggāhake suddhapabbajite pariyesanto. Visāle māḷake ṭhitoti parisuddhapaṇḍarapulinatalābhirāme vipule māḷake ṭhito.

124. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship, recollecting his past deeds with joy, and revealing the Apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke beginning with, 'Desiring to offer a sacrifice.' Herein, 'sacrifice' means various kinds of requisites for offerings and honors, such as food and drink. 'Desiring to offer a sacrifice' means desiring to perform a sacrifice, desiring to give a gift. 'Having prepared food' means having prepared and produced nourishment. 'Awaiting brahmins' means searching for pure renunciants, suitable recipients. 'Standing in a spacious hall' means standing in a vast pavilion, delightful with its clean, white-sanded floor.

125-7. Athaddasāsiṃ sambuddhantiādīsu mahāyasaṃ mahāparivāraṃ sabbalokaṃ sakalasattalokaṃ vinetānaṃ visesena netāraṃ nibbānasampāpakaṃ sayambhuṃ sayameva bhūtaṃ anācariyakaṃ [V 2.0027] aggapuggalaṃ seṭṭhapuggalaṃ bhagavantaṃ bhagyavantādiguṇayuttaṃ jutimantaṃ nīlapītādipabhāsampannaṃ sāvakehi purakkhataṃ parivāritaṃ ādiccamiva sūriyamiva rocantaṃ sobhamānaṃ rathiyaṃ vīthiyaṃ paṭipannakaṃ gacchantaṃ piyadassiṃ nāma sambuddhaṃ addasinti sambandho. Añjaliṃ paggahetvānāti bandhañjalipuṭaṃ sirasi katvā sakaṃ cittaṃ attano cittaṃ pasādayiṃ itthambhūtassa bhagavato guṇe pasādesiṃ pasannamakāsinti attho. Manasāva nimantesinti cittena pavāresiṃ. Āgacchatu mahāmunīti mahito pūjāraho muni bhagavā mama nivesanaṃ āgacchatu.

Then I saw the Fully Enlightened One of great fame and with a great retinue, the trainer of the entire world, of all beings, the special leader of those to be trained, the one who brings about Nibbāna, the Self-become One who arose by himself without a teacher, the foremost individual, the supreme person, the Blessed One endowed with qualities such as fortune, the radiant one possessing rays such as blue and yellow, honored and surrounded by disciples, shining and splendid like the sun, walking along the road—I saw the Fully Enlightened One named Piyadassī. This is the connection. Having raised my hands in reverential salutation, having placed my joined palms on my head, I gladdened my own mind; that is, I made my mind serene with the virtues of such a Blessed One. With my mind alone, I invited him. 'May the Great Sage come' means: may the Blessed One, the Sage worthy of honor, come to my dwelling.

128. Mama saṅkappamaññāyāti mayhaṃ cittasaṅkappaṃ ñatvā loke sattaloke anuttaro uttaravirahito satthā khīṇāsavasahassehi arahantasahassehi [M 2.0030] parivuto mama dvāraṃ mayhaṃ gehadvāraṃ upāgami sampāpuṇi.

128. 'Knowing my intention' means: knowing my mind's intention, the Teacher, who is unsurpassed and without superior in the world of beings, surrounded by thousands of Arahants whose taints are destroyed, approached my door—my house's door—and arrived.

129. Tassa sampattassa satthuno evaṃ namakkāramakāsiṃ. Purisājañña purisānaṃ ājañña, seṭṭha, mama namakkāro te tuyhaṃ atthu bhavatu. Purisuttama purisānaṃ uttama adhikaguṇavisiṭṭha te tuyhaṃ mama namakkāro atthu. Pāsādaṃ pasādajanakaṃ mama nivesanaṃ [P 0.0337] abhiruhitvā sīhāsane uttamāsane nisīdatanti āyācinti attho.

129. To that Teacher who had arrived, I made this salutation: 'O thoroughbred among men, O best of men, may my homage be to you. O supreme among men, distinguished by superior qualities, may my homage be to you.' The meaning is: they entreated him, saying, 'Having ascended the delightful palace, my dwelling, please sit on the lion-seat, the supreme seat.'

130. Danto dantaparivāroti sayaṃ dvārattayena danto tathā dantāhi bhikkhubhikkhunīupāsakaupāsikāsaṅkhātāhi catūhi parisāhi parivārito. Tiṇṇo tārayataṃ varoti sayaṃ tiṇṇo saṃsārato uttiṇṇo nikkhanto tārayataṃ tārayantānaṃ visiṭṭhapuggalānaṃ varo uttamo bhagavā mamārādhanena pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā pavarāsane uttamāsane nisīdi nisajjaṃ kappesi.

130. 'The tamed one surrounded by the tamed' means: he himself is tamed by means of the three doors, and he is surrounded by the fourfold assembly of tamed ones, namely monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. 'The one who has crossed, the best of those who help others cross' means: he himself has crossed over from the cycle of existence, has emerged and gone beyond, and is the best, the supreme among distinguished individuals who help others cross. Having ascended the palace through my invitation, the Blessed One sat on the excellent seat, the supreme seat; he took his seat.

131. Yaṃ me atthi sake geheti attano gehe yaṃ āmisaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ sampāditaṃ rāsikataṃ atthi. Tāhaṃ buddhassa pādāsinti buddhassa buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa taṃ āmisaṃ pādāsiṃ pa-kārena ādarena vā adāsinti attho. Pasanno sehi pāṇibhīti attano dvīhi hatthehi passannacitto gahetvā pādāsinti attho.

131. 'Whatever I have in my own home' means whatever material offering is prepared, procured, and collected in my own house. 'That I gave to the Buddha' means: I gave that material offering to the Sangha headed by the Buddha; 'pādāsiṃ' means I gave (adāsiṃ) in a special manner or with respect. 'With a serene mind, with my own hands' means: with a serene mind, I took it with my own two hands and gave it.

132. Pasannacitto pasāditamanasaṅkappo sumano sundaramano. Vedajāto jātavedo uppannasomanasso katañjalī sirasi ṭhapitaañjalipuṭo buddhaseṭṭhaṃ namassāmi seṭṭhassa buddhassa paṇāmaṃ karomīti attho. Aho buddhassuḷāratāti paṭividdhacatusaccassa satthuno uḷāratā mahantabhāvo aho acchariyanti attho.

132. 'With a serene mind' means with a mind and intention made serene; 'joyful' means having a beautiful mind. 'Filled with rapture' means with joy arisen, with uplifted joy; 'with hands raised in homage' means with cupped hands placed upon the head. 'I pay homage to the supreme Buddha' means I make obeisance to the foremost Buddha. 'Oh, the eminence of the Buddha!' means the greatness, the magnificence of the Teacher who has penetrated the four noble truths—oh, how wonderful!

133. Aṭṭhannaṃ [V 2.0028] payirūpāsatanti payirupāsantānaṃ bhuñjaṃ bhuñjantānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ ariyapuggalānaṃ antare khīṇāsavā arahantova bahūti attho. Tuyheveso ānubhāvoti eso ākāsacaraṇaummujjananimujjanādiānubhāvo tuyheva tuyhaṃ eva ānubhāvo, nāññesaṃ. Saraṇaṃ taṃ upemahanti taṃ itthambhūtaṃ tuvaṃ saraṇaṃ tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ parāyananti upemi gacchāmi jānāmi vāti attho.

133. 'Attended by eight' means that among the eight noble individuals who were attending and partaking, many were Arahants whose taints were destroyed. 'This is your power' means this power of walking in the sky, emerging and submerging, and so forth, is your power alone, and not of others. 'I go to you for refuge' means I go to you, who are such, for refuge, protection, shelter, and final resort; that is, I approach, go to, or understand.

134. Lokajeṭṭho [M 2.0031] narāsabho piyadassī bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe nisīditvā imā byākaraṇagāthā abhāsatha kathesīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

134. The world's chief, the bull among men, the Blessed One Piyadassī, having sat amidst the community of monks, spoke these verses of declaration; that is, he uttered them. The rest is easily understood.

Sumaṅgalattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sumaṅgala is complete.

Dutiyassa sīhāsanavaggassa vaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the second chapter, the Sīhāsana Vagga, is complete.

3. Subhūtivaggo

3. The Chapter on Subhūti

1. Subhūtittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Subhūti

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ [V 2.0029] āyasmato subhūtittherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto ito kappasatasahassamatthake anuppanneyeva padumuttare bhagavati lokanāthe haṃsavatīnagare [P 0.0338] aññatarassa brāhmaṇamahāsālassa ekaputtako hutvā nibbatti, tassa nandamāṇavoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto attano parivārabhūtehi catucattālīsāya māṇavasahassehi saddhiṃ pabbatapāde isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañcābhiññāyo ca nibbattesi. Antevāsikānampi kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. Tepi nacirasseva jhānalābhino ahesuṃ.

3. 'Not far from the Himālaya' and so forth is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Subhūti. He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of former Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a supporting condition for turning away from the cycle of rebirths in various existences, one hundred thousand aeons ago, before the Blessed One Padumuttara, the Lord of the World, had arisen, was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī as the only son of a certain wealthy brahmin. They gave him the name Nandamāṇava. Having come of age, he learned the three Vedas, but seeing no essence in them, he went forth into the ascetic life at the foot of a mountain, together with his retinue of forty-four thousand young men, and he brought into being the eight attainments and the five supernormal knowledges. He also taught the meditation subjects to his resident pupils. They too, before long, became attainers of jhāna.

Tena ca samayena padumuttaro bhagavā loke uppajjitvā haṃsavatīnagaraṃ upanissāya viharanto ekadivasaṃ paccūsasamaye lokaṃ volokento nandatāpasassa antevāsikajaṭilānaṃ arahattūpanissayaṃ, nandatāpasassa ca dvīhaṅgehi samannāgatassa sāvakaṭṭhānantarassa patthanaṃ disvā pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā pubbaṇhasamaye pattacīvaramādāya aññaṃ kañci anāmantetvā sīho viya ekacaro nandatāpasassa antevāsikesu phalāphalatthāya gatesu “buddhabhāvaṃ me jānātū”ti passantasseva nandatāpasassa ākāsato otaritvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi. Nandatāpaso buddhānubhāvañceva lakkhaṇapāripūriñca disvā lakkhaṇamante sammasitvā “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato nāma agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto rājā hoti cakkavattī, pabbajanto loke vivaṭacchedo [M 2.0032] sabbaññū buddho hoti, ayaṃ purisājānīyo nissaṃsayaṃ buddho”ti ñatvā paccuggamanaṃ katvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā adāsi. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane. Nandatāpasopi attano anucchavikaṃ āsanaṃ gahetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tasmiṃ samaye catucattālīsasahassajaṭilā paṇītapaṇītāni ojavantāni phalāphalāni gahetvā ācariyassa santikaṃ sampattā buddhānañceva ācariyassa ca nisinnākāraṃ oloketvā āhaṃsu – “ācariya, mayaṃ ‘imasmiṃ loke tumhehi mahantataro natthī’ti vicarāma, ayaṃ pana puriso tumhehi mahantataro maññe”ti. Nandatāpaso – “tātā[V 2.0030], kiṃ vadetha, tumhe sāsapena saddhiṃ aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyojanasatasahassubbedhaṃ sineruṃ upametuṃ icchatha, sabbaññubuddhena saddhiṃ mā maṃ upamitthā”ti āha. Atha te tāpasā – “sace ayaṃ orako abhavissa, na amhākaṃ ācariyo evaṃ upamaṃ āhareyya. Yāva mahāvatāyaṃ purisājānīyo”ti pādesu nipatitvā sirasā vandiṃsu. Atha te ācariyo āha – “tātā, amhākaṃ buddhānaṃ anucchaviko deyyadhammo natthi, bhagavā ca bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ idhāgato, tasmā mayaṃ yathābalaṃ deyyadhammaṃ dassāma, tumhehi yaṃ yaṃ paṇītaṃ phalāphalaṃ ābhataṃ, taṃ taṃ āharathā”ti āharāpetvā sahattheneva dhovitvā sayaṃ [P 0.0339] tathāgatassa patte patiṭṭhāpesi. Satthārā phalāphale paṭiggahitamatte devatā dibbojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu. Tāpaso udakampi sayameva parissāvetvā adāsi. Tato bhojanakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā nisinne satthari sabbe antevāsike pakkositvā satthu santike sāraṇīyaṃ kathaṃ kathento nisīdi. Satthā “bhikkhusaṅgho āgacchatū”ti cintesi. Satthu cittaṃ ñatvā satasahassamattā khīṇāsavā āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having arisen in the world, was dwelling near the city of Haṃsavatī. One day, while surveying the world at dawn, He saw the strong supporting condition for Arahantship in the matted-hair ascetic disciples of the ascetic Nanda, and also the aspiration of Nanda the ascetic for the rank of a disciple endowed with two qualities. Early in the morning, after attending to His bodily needs, He took His bowl and robe in the forenoon and, without informing anyone, went forth alone like a lion. While the disciples of Nanda the ascetic were away gathering fruits, He thought, 'Let him know my state of Buddhahood,' and, as Nanda the ascetic was watching, He descended from the sky and stood upon the earth. Seeing the Buddha's majesty and the perfection of His marks, Nanda the ascetic reflected upon the science of the marks and knew: 'A person endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, becomes a wheel-turning monarch; if he goes forth, he becomes in the world a Buddha, an All-Knowing One who removes the veil. This thoroughbred of men is undoubtedly a Buddha.' Recognizing this, he went forth to meet Him, paid homage with the five-point prostration, prepared a seat, and offered it. The Blessed One sat upon the prepared seat. Nanda the ascetic also took a seat suitable for himself and sat to one side. At that time, forty-four thousand matted-hair ascetics, having gathered excellent and nourishing fruits, arrived in the presence of their teacher. Seeing the manner in which the Buddha and their teacher were seated, they said: 'Teacher, we have lived thinking, "In this world, there is no one greater than you." But this man, we think, is greater than you.' Nanda the ascetic said: 'Dear sons, what are you saying? You wish to compare Mount Sineru, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, with a mustard seed. Do not compare me with the All-Knowing Buddha.' Then those ascetics, thinking, 'If this man were inferior, our teacher would not have brought forth such a comparison. How great, indeed, is this thoroughbred of men!' fell at His feet and paid homage with their heads. Then their teacher said to them: 'Dear sons, we have no offering suitable for a Buddha. The Blessed One has come here at the time for the alms round. Therefore, let us give an offering according to our ability. Whatever excellent fruits you have brought, bring them forth.' Having had them brought, he washed them with his own hands and himself placed them in the Tathāgata's bowl. As soon as the Teacher had accepted the fruits, the deities infused them with divine essence. The ascetic also personally strained water and offered it. After the meal was finished and the Teacher was seated, he called all his disciples, and sat down near the Teacher, engaging in friendly conversation. The Teacher thought, 'Let the community of monks come.' Knowing the Teacher's thought, about one hundred thousand Arahants, whose corruptions were destroyed, came, paid homage to the Teacher, and stood to one side.

Atha nandatāpaso antevāsike āmantesi – “tātā, buddhānaṃ nisinnāsanampi nīcaṃ, samaṇasatasahassassapi āsanaṃ natthi. Tumhehi ajja uḷāraṃ bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca sakkāraṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, pabbatapādato vaṇṇagandhasampannāni pupphāni āharathā”ti āha. Acinteyyattā iddhivisayassa te muhutteneva vaṇṇagandharasasampannāni pupphāni āharitvā buddhānaṃ yojanappamāṇaṃ pupphāsanaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Aggasāvakānaṃ tigāvutaṃ, sesabhikkhūnaṃ [M 2.0033] aḍḍhayojanādibhedaṃ, saṅghanavakassa usabhamattaṃ paññāpesuṃ. Evaṃ paññattesu āsanesu nandatāpaso tathāgatassa purato añjaliṃ paggayha ṭhito, “bhante, amhākaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya imaṃ pupphāsanaṃ āruyha nisīdathā”ti āha. Nisīdi bhagavā pupphāsane. Evaṃ nisinne satthari satthu ākāraṃ ñatvā bhikkhū attano attano pattāsane nisīdiṃsu. Nandatāpaso mahantaṃ pupphacchattaṃ gahetvā tathāgatassa matthake dhārento aṭṭhāsi. Satthā “tāpasānaṃ ayaṃ sakkāro mahapphalo hotū”ti nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajji. Satthu samāpannabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhikkhūpi samāpattiṃ samāpajjiṃsu. Tathāgate sattāhaṃ nirodhaṃ samāpajjitvā nisinne antevāsikā bhikkhācārakāle sampatte vanamūlaphalāphalaṃ paribhuñjitvā sesakāle buddhānaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhaṃsu. Nandatāpaso pana bhikkhācārampi agantvā pupphacchattaṃ dhārentoyeva sattāhaṃ pītisukheneva vītināmesi.

Then the ascetic Nanda addressed his disciples: 'Dear sons, the seat on which the Buddha is sitting is low, and there are no seats for a hundred thousand monks. Today it is fitting that you should perform a magnificent act of reverence for the Blessed One and the community of monks. Bring flowers endowed with color and fragrance from the foot of the mountain.' Due to the inconceivable nature of the domain of psychic power, in a single moment they brought flowers endowed with color and fragrance and prepared a flower-seat for the Buddha measuring one yojana. For the chief disciples, they prepared seats measuring three gāvutas; for the remaining monks, seats of various sizes, such as half a yojana; and for the most junior monk of the community, a seat measuring one usabha. When the seats were thus prepared, the ascetic Nanda stood before the Tathāgata with his hands raised in reverence and said: 'Venerable Sir, for our welfare and happiness for a long time to come, please ascend this flower-seat and be seated.' The Blessed One sat upon the flower-seat. When the Teacher was thus seated, the monks, knowing the Teacher's intention, sat down on their own allotted seats. The ascetic Nanda, taking a large floral parasol, stood holding it over the Tathāgata's head. The Teacher, thinking, 'May this act of reverence by the ascetics be of great fruit,' entered the attainment of cessation. Knowing that the Teacher had entered this attainment, the monks also entered that same attainment. While the Tathāgata remained seated for seven days, having entered the attainment of cessation, his disciples, when the time for the alms round came, would consume forest roots and fruits, and for the remaining time, they stood with their hands raised in reverence towards the Buddha. The ascetic Nanda, however, did not go for alms but, while holding the floral parasol, passed those seven days in rapture and happiness alone.

Satthā nirodhato vuṭṭhāya araṇavihāriaṅgena dakkhiṇeyyaṅgena cāti dvīhi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ ekaṃ sāvakaṃ “isigaṇassa pupphāsanānumodanaṃ karohī”ti āṇāpesi. So cakkavattirañño santikā paṭiladdhamahālābho mahāyodho viya tuṭṭhamānaso attano visaye ṭhatvā tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ sammasitvā [V 2.0031] anumodanamakāsi. Tassa desanāvasāne satthā sayaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Satthu desanāvasāne sabbepi catucattālīsasahassatāpasā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthā – “etha bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tesaṃ tāvadeva kesamassū antaradhāyiṃsu[P 0.0340]. Aṭṭha parikkhārā sarīre paṭimukkāva ahesuṃ. Te saṭṭhivassikattherā viya satthāraṃ parivārayiṃsu. Nandatāpaso pana vikkhittacittatāya visesaṃ nādhigañchi. Tassa kira araṇavihārittherassa dhammaṃ sotuṃ āraddhakālato paṭṭhāya – “aho vatāhampi anāgate ekassa buddhassa sāsane iminā sāvakena laddhaguṇaṃ labheyya”nti cittaṃ udapādi. So tena vitakkena maggaphalapaṭivedhaṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Tathāgataṃ pana vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha sammukhe ṭhito evamāha – “bhante, yena bhikkhunā isigaṇassa pupphāsanānumodanā katā, ko nāmāyaṃ tumhākaṃ sāsane”ti? “Araṇavihāriaṅgena ca dakkhiṇeyyaṅgena ca etadaggaṭṭhānaṃ patto eso bhikkhū”ti. “Bhante, yvāyaṃ mayā sattāhaṃ pupphacchattaṃ dhārentena [M 2.0034] sakkāro kato, tena adhikārena aññaṃ sampattiṃ na patthemi, anāgate pana ekassa buddhassa sāsane ayaṃ thero viya dvīhaṅgehi samannāgato sāvako bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi.

The Teacher, having emerged from cessation, commanded a disciple endowed with two qualities—dwelling without conflict and being worthy of offerings—saying, 'Perform the rejoicing in the flower seat for the group of seers.' That disciple, like a great warrior delighted in heart upon receiving great wealth from the presence of a wheel-turning monarch, stood firm in his domain, contemplated the Three Baskets of the Buddha's word, and performed the rejoicing. At the end of his discourse, the Teacher himself taught the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the Teacher's discourse, all forty-four thousand ascetics attained arahantship.
