The Teacher extended his hand, saying, 'Come, monks.' Instantly, their hair and beards disappeared. The eight requisites were placed upon their bodies. They, like elders of sixty years, surrounded the Teacher. However, the ascetic Nanda, due to his distracted mind, did not achieve any special attainment. It is said that from the moment he began to listen to the Dhamma of the Elder who dwells without conflict, the thought arose in him: 'Oh, may I too in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, attain the qualities gained by this disciple.' Due to that thought, he was unable to realize the path and fruition. Yet, having paid homage to the Tathāgata and raised his hands in reverence, he stood before him and said: 'Venerable sir, by which monk was the rejoicing in the flower seat performed for the group of seers? What is his name in your dispensation?' 'That monk has reached the foremost position through the quality of dwelling without conflict and the quality of being worthy of offerings.' 'Venerable sir, for the honor I have done by holding the flower parasol for seven days, I do not aspire for any other attainment through that merit; but in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, may I become a disciple endowed with these two qualities like this elder.' Thus he made his aspiration.

Satthā “samijjhissati nu kho imassa tāpasassa patthanā”ti anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ pesetvā olokento kappasatasahassaṃ atikkamitvā samijjhanakabhāvaṃ disvā, “tāpasa, na te ayaṃ patthanā moghaṃ bhavissati, anāgate kappasatasahassaṃ atikkamitvā gotamo nāma buddho uppajjissati, tassa santike samijjhissatī”ti dhammakathaṃ kathetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Nandatāpaso yāva cakkhupathaṃ na samatikkamati, tāva satthu bhikkhusaṅghassa ca añjaliṃ paggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. So aparabhāge kālena kālaṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ suṇitvā aparihīnajjhānova kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbatto. Tato pana cuto aparānipi pañca jātisatāni pabbajitvā āraññakova ahosi, kassapasammāsambuddhakālepi pabbajitvā āraññako hutvā gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūresi. Etaṃ kira vattaṃ aparipūretvā mahāsāvakabhāvaṃ pāpuṇantā nāma natthi, gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pana āgamaṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. So vīsativassasahassāni gatapaccāgatavattaṃ pūretvā kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsadevaloke nibbatti.

The Teacher, wondering, “Will this ascetic’s aspiration be fulfilled?” sent forth his knowledge of the future and, looking ahead, saw its fulfillment after the lapse of a hundred thousand aeons. “Ascetic, your aspiration will not be in vain. In the future, after the lapse of a hundred thousand aeons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In his presence, your aspiration will be fulfilled,” he declared, delivering a discourse. Then, surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus, he soared into the sky. The ascetic Nanda stood with joined hands until the Teacher and the Sangha of bhikkhus had passed beyond his sight. Later, from time to time, he approached the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and without losing his meditative attainments, passed away to be reborn in the Brahma world. After passing away from there, for another five hundred lives he went forth and was a forest-dweller. Even during the time of Kassapa, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, he went forth and became a forest dweller, fulfilling the practice of going and returning. It is said that none attain the state of a great disciple without completing this practice. The practice of going and returning should be understood in the manner stated in the commentaries on the Āgamas. Having fulfilled this practice for twenty thousand years, he passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world.

Evaṃ so tāvatiṃsabhavane aparāparaṃ uppajjanavasena dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato cuto manussaloke anekasatakkhattuṃ cakkavattirājā padesarājā ca hutvā uḷāraṃ manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā amhākaṃ bhagavato uppannakāle sāvatthiyaṃ sumanaseṭṭhissa gehe anāthapiṇḍikassa [P 0.0341] kaniṭṭho hutvā nibbatti. Subhūtītissa nāmaṃ ahosi.

Thus, he experienced divine prosperity by being reborn repeatedly in the Tāvatiṃsa existence. Then, having passed away from there, he became a wheel-turning monarch and a regional king many hundreds of times in the human world, experiencing abundant human prosperity. When our Blessed One arose, he was reborn in Sāvatthī, in the household of Sumanaseṭṭhi, as the younger brother of Anāthapiṇḍika. His name was Subhūti.

Tena [V 2.0032] ca samayena amhākaṃ bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko anupubbena rājagahaṃ gantvā tattha veḷuvanapaṭiggahaṇādinā lokānuggahaṃ karonto rājagahaṃ upanissāya sītavane vihāsi. Tadā anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi sāvatthiyaṃ uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā attano sahāyassa rājagahaseṭṭhino gehaṃ gantvā buddhuppādaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ sītavane viharantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya [M 2.0035] satthāraṃ sāvatthiṃ āgamanatthāya yācitvā tato pañcacattālīsayojane magge yojane yojane satasahassapariccāgena vihāre patiṭṭhāpetvā sāvatthiyaṃ aṭṭhakarīsappamāṇaṃ jetassa kumārassa uyyānabhūmiṃ koṭisanthārena kiṇitvā tattha bhagavato vihāraṃ kāretvā adāsi. Vihāramahadivase ayaṃ subhūtikuṭumbiko anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhinā saddhiṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto saddhaṃ paṭilabhitvā pabbaji. So upasampanno dve mātikā paguṇā katvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathāpetvā araññe samaṇadhammaṃ karonto mettājhānaṃ nibbattetvā taṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

At that time, our Blessed One had arisen in the world and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma. Gradually, he went to Rājagaha and, benefiting the world by accepting the Veḷuvana and other offerings, he dwelt in Sītavana near Rājagaha. Then, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, having taken goods for trade from Sāvatthī, went to the house of his friend, the chief merchant of Rājagaha. Hearing about the appearance of the Buddha, he approached the Teacher dwelling in Sītavana. At the very first sight, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry. He then invited the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī. Along the forty-five yojana journey, he established monasteries at every yojana, spending a hundred thousand for each. In Sāvatthī, he bought Prince Jeta’s park, measuring eight karīsas, by covering it with a crore of coins. There, he built a monastery for the Blessed One and offered it to him. On the great day of the monastery’s dedication, this householder Subhūti went with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. While listening to the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth. After ordination, he mastered the two Mātikās, received instruction in a meditation subject, and practiced the ascetic life in the forest. Developing loving-kindness meditation as his basis, he cultivated insight and attained arahantship.

So dhammaṃ desento yasmā satthārā desitaniyāmena anodissakaṃ katvā deseti, tasmā araṇavihārīnaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Yasmā ca piṇḍāya caranto ghare ghare mettājhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya bhikkhaṃ paṭiggaṇhāti “evaṃ dāyakānaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatī”ti, tasmā dakkhiṇeyyānaṃ aggo nāma jāto. Tena naṃ bhagavā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ araṇavihārīnaṃ dakkhiṇeyyānañca yadidaṃ subhūtī”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 201) dvayaṅgasamannāgate aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Evamayaṃ mahāthero attanā pūritapāramīnaṃ phalassa matthakaṃ arahattaṃ patvā loke abhiññāto abhilakkhito hutvā bahujanahitāya janapadacārikaṃ caranto anupubbena rājagahaṃ agamāsi.

Because he taught the Dhamma without specifying a recipient, in the manner taught by the Master, he became known as the foremost among those who dwell without conflict. And because, while wandering for alms, he would enter the absorption of loving-kindness at each and every house, and having emerged from it, would accept the alms-food, thinking, “In this way, it will be of great fruit for the donors,” he became known as the foremost among those worthy of offerings. For this reason, the Blessed One placed him in the foremost position endowed with two factors, declaring: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who dwell without conflict and are worthy of offerings, Subhūti is the foremost.” Thus this great elder, having attained Arahantship—the pinnacle of the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled—became renowned and distinguished in the world. Wandering on tour through the country for the welfare of the multitude, he in due course arrived at Rājagaha.

Rājā bimbisāro therassa āgamanaṃ sutvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā “idheva, bhante, vasatha, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vo karissāmī”ti vatvā pakkanto vissari. Thero senāsanaṃ alabhanto abbhokāse vītināmesi. Therassānubhāvena devo na vassati. Manussā avuṭṭhitāya upaddutā rañño nivesanadvāre ukkuṭṭhiṃ akaṃsu. Rājā “kena nu kho kāraṇena devo na vassatī”ti vīmaṃsanto “therassa abbhokāsavāsena maññe na vassatī”ti cintetvā tassa paṇṇakuṭiṃ kārāpetvā “imissaṃ, bhante, paṇṇakuṭiyaṃ vasathā”ti vatvā vanditvā pakkāmi. Thero kuṭiṃ pavisitvā tiṇasanthārake pallaṅkena nisīdi. Tadā devo thokaṃ [P 0.0342] thokaṃ phusāyati, na sammādhāraṃ anupavecchati. Atha thero lokassa avuṭṭhikabhayaṃ vidhamitukāmo [M 2.0036] attano ajjhattikabāhiravatthukassa [V 2.0033] parissayassa abhāvaṃ pavedento “channā me kuṭikā”ti (theragā. 1) gāthamāha. Tassattho theragāthāyaṃ vuttoyeva.

King Bimbisāra, hearing of the elder’s arrival, approached him, paid homage, and said, “Venerable sir, please dwell right here. I will have a dwelling place made for you.” Having said this, he departed and forgot. The elder, not receiving a lodging, passed the time in the open. Through the elder’s spiritual power, it did not rain. The people, afflicted by the drought, raised a clamor at the king’s palace gate. The king, investigating, “For what reason, I wonder, does it not rain?” thought, “I suppose it does not rain because of the elder’s dwelling in the open.” He had a leaf-hut built for him, and saying, “Venerable sir, please dwell in this leaf-hut,” he paid homage and departed. The elder entered the hut and sat cross-legged on a spread of grass. Then it drizzled a little, but a steady downpour did not ensue. Then the elder, wishing to dispel the world’s fear of the drought and to make known the absence of any danger to himself based on internal or external things, uttered the verse beginning: “My little hut is roofed” (Theragā. 1). Its meaning is stated in the Theragāthā itself.

Kasmā panete mahātherā attano guṇe pakāsentīti? Iminā dīghena addhunā anadhigatapubbaṃ paramagambhīraṃ ativiya santaṃ paṇītaṃ attanā adhigatalokuttaradhammaṃ paccavekkhitvā pītivegasamussāhitaudānadīpanatthaṃ sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvavibhāvanatthañca paramappicchā ariyā attano guṇe pakāsenti. Yathā taṃ lokanātho bodhaneyyānaṃ ajjhāsayavasena “dasabalasamannāgato, bhikkhave, tathāgato catuvesārajjavisārado”tiādinā (a. ni. 10.21; ma. ni. 1. 148 atthato samānaṃ) attano guṇe pakāseti. Evamayaṃ therassa aññābyākaraṇagāthāpi ahosīti.

Why, then, do these great elders make known their own qualities? Having reviewed the supremely profound, exceedingly peaceful, and sublime supramundane Dhamma which they themselves had realized—something never before attained over this long period—the noble ones, who are of utmost fewness of wishes, make known their own qualities in order to express an inspired utterance, being impelled by a surge of joy, and to reveal the liberating nature of the Teaching. It is just as the Lord of the World, according to the dispositions of those to be trained, makes known his own qualities, saying: “Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers and is expert in the four kinds of fearlessness,” and so on. In this way, this was also the elder's verse of declaration of final knowledge.

1. Evaṃ so pattaarahattaphalo pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno ca attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Tattha himavantassāti himālayapabbatassa avidūre āsanne samīpe pabbatapāde manussānaṃ gamanāgamanasampanne sañcaraṇaṭṭhāneti attho. Nisabho nāma pabbatoti pabbatānaṃ jeṭṭhattā nāmena nisabho nāma selamayapabbato ahosīti sambandho. Assamo sukato mayhanti tattha pabbate mayhaṃ vasanatthāya assamo araññāvāso suṭṭhu kato. Kuṭirattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānavatiparikkhepādivasena sundarākārena katoti attho. Paṇṇasālā sumāpitāti paṇṇehi chāditā sālā mayhaṃ nivāsanatthāya suṭṭhu māpitā niṭṭhāpitāti attho.

1. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship and reached the foremost position, he recollected his past deeds, became filled with joy, and, in order to make known the story of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning: “Not far from the Himālaya…” Therein, not far from the Himālaya means in the vicinity, near, close to the foot of the Himālaya mountain, in a place suitable for people’s coming and going. A mountain named Nisabha: because it was the chief among mountains, there was a rocky mountain named Nisabha; this is the connection. My hermitage was well-made: on that mountain, a hermitage, a forest dwelling, was well-made for me to reside in. This means it was made in a beautiful manner, with a hut, a place for the night, a place for the day, a fence, an enclosure, and so on. A leaf-hall was well-constructed: a hall covered with leaves was well-constructed and completed for my dwelling.

2. Kosiyo nāma nāmenāti mātāpitūhi katanāmadheyyena kosiyo nāma. Uggatāpano pākaṭatapo ghoratapo. Ekākiyo aññesaṃ abhāvā ahaṃ eva eko. Adutiyo dutiyatāpasarahito jaṭilo jaṭādhārī tāpaso tadā tasmiṃ kāle nisabhe pabbate vasāmi viharāmīti sambandho.

2. Kosiya by name: my name was Kosiya, the name given by my parents. Of fierce asceticism: of manifest asceticism, of terrible asceticism. Alone: because there were no others, I was just one, alone. Without a second: devoid of a second ascetic. A matted-hair ascetic: an ascetic wearing matted hair. At that time, I lived and dwelt on Mount Nisabha; this is the connection.

3. Phalaṃ mūlañca paṇṇañca, na bhuñjāmi ahaṃ tadāti tadā tasmiṃ nisabhapabbate vasanakāle tiṇḍukādiphalaṃ muḷālādimūlaṃ, kārapaṇṇādipaṇṇañca rukkhato [M 2.0037] ocinitvā na bhuñjāmīti attho. Evaṃ sati kathaṃ jīvatīti taṃ dassento pavattaṃva supātāhanti [P 0.0343] āha. Tattha pavattaṃ sayameva jātaṃ supātaṃ attano dhammatāya patitaṃ paṇṇādikaṃ nissāya āhāraṃ katvā ahaṃ tāvade tasmiṃ kāle jīvāmi jīvikaṃ kappemīti sambandho. “Pavattapaṇḍupaṇṇānī”ti [V 2.0034] vā pāṭho, tassa sayameva patitāni paṇḍupaṇṇāni rukkhapattāni upanissāya jīvāmīti attho.

3. And I did not eat fruit, root, or leaf then: this means that at that time, while dwelling on Mount Nisabha, I did not eat fruit such as tinduka, root such as lotus-stalk, or leaf such as kārapaṇa, after picking them from a tree. This being the case, how did he stay alive? To show this, it is said: pavattaṃva supātāhaṃ. Therein, pavattaṃ means what has come about by itself; supātaṃ means what has fallen by its own nature. Relying on such leaves and so on for my food, I lived and sustained myself at that time; this is the connection. Or else the reading is pavatta-paṇḍupaṇṇāni (naturally fallen withered leaves), and the meaning is: I lived relying on withered tree leaves that had fallen by themselves.

4. Nāhaṃ kopemi ājīvanti ahaṃ jīvitaṃ cajamānopi pariccāgaṃ kurumānopi taṇhāvasena phalamūlādiāhārapariyesanāya sammā ājīvaṃ na kopemi na nāsemīti sambandho. Ārādhemi sakaṃ cittanti sakaṃ cittaṃ attano manaṃ appicchatāya santuṭṭhiyā ca ārādhemi pasādemi. Vivajjemi anesananti vejjakammadūtakammādivasena anesanaṃ ayuttapariyesanaṃ vivajjemi dūraṃ karomi.

4. I do not corrupt my livelihood: even while giving up my life, while making a sacrifice, I do not corrupt or destroy my right livelihood by searching for food such as fruits and roots out of craving; this is the connection. I satisfy my own mind: I satisfy and gladden my own mind with fewness of wishes and with contentment. I avoid improper seeking: I avoid and keep at a distance improper seeking, that is, unsuitable searching by such means as practicing medicine or acting as a messenger.

5. Rāgūpasaṃhitaṃ cittanti yadā yasmiṃ kāle mama rāgena sampayuttaṃ cittaṃ uppajjati, tadā sayameva attanāyeva paccavekkhāmi ñāṇena paṭivekkhitvā vinodemi. Ekaggo taṃ damemahanti ahaṃ ekasmiṃ kammaṭṭhānārammaṇe aggo samāhito taṃ rāgacittaṃ damemi damanaṃ karomi.

5. "A mind associated with lust" means: whenever a mind connected with lust arises in me, I myself reflect upon it; having investigated it with knowledge, I dispel it. "Being one-pointed, I tame it" means: I, being foremost and concentrated upon a single meditation object, tame that lustful mind; I bring it under control.

6. Rajjase rajjanīye cāti rajjanīye allīyitabbe rūpārammaṇādivatthusmiṃ rajjase allīno asi bhavasi. Dussanīye ca dussaseti dūsitabbe dosakaraṇavatthusmiṃ dūsako asi. Muyhase mohanīye cāti mohitabbe mohakaraṇavatthusmiṃ moyhasi mūḷho asi bhavasi. Tasmā tuvaṃ vanā vanato araññavāsato nikkhamassu apagacchāhīti evaṃ attānaṃ damemīti sambandho.

6. "You are attached to what is enticing" means: in an object that is enticing, that is to be clung to, such as a visible form, you are attached; you are one who clings. "And you are hostile towards what is provocative" means: in an object that is provocative, a cause for aversion, you are one who is hostile. "And you are deluded by what is deluding" means: in an object that is deluding, a cause for delusion, you are deluded; you are one who is bewildered. "Therefore, you should leave the forest, depart from the wilderness-dwelling." Thus, "I tame myself"—this is the connection.

24. Timbarūsakavaṇṇābhoti suvaṇṇatimbarūsakavaṇṇābho, jambonadasuvaṇṇavaṇṇoti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

24. "Having a radiance like the Timbarūsaka fruit" means having a radiance like a golden Timbarūsaka fruit, which is to say, having the color of jambonada gold. The rest is easily understood.

Subhūtittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Subhūti is concluded.

2. Upavānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upavāna

Padumuttaro [M 2.0038] nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato upavānattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle daliddakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavati parinibbute tassa dhātuṃ gahetvā manussadevanāgagaruḷakumbhaṇḍayakkhagandhabbehi sattaratanamaye sattayojanike thūpe kate tattha sudhotaṃ attano uttarasāṭakaṃ veḷagge laggetvā ābandhitvā dhajaṃ katvā pūjaṃ akāsi. Taṃ gahetvā abhisammatako [P 0.0344][V 2.0035] nāma yakkhasenāpati devehi cetiyapūjārakkhaṇatthaṃ ṭhapito adissamānakāyo taṃ ākāse dhārento cetiyaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. So taṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānaso hutvā tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā upavānoti laddhanāmo vayappatto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto arahattaṃ patvā chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Yadā bhagavato aphāsu ahosi, tadā thero uṇhodakaṃ tathārūpaṃ pānakañca bhesajjaṃ bhagavato upanāmesi. Tenassa satthuno rogo vūpasami. Tassa bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsi.

"The Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth, is the Apadāna of the venerable Upavāna. This venerable one, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences that serve as a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in a poor family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, he took a relic. When a stūpa of seven yojanas, made of the seven kinds of jewels, was built by humans, devas, nāgas, garuḍas, kumbhaṇḍas, yakkhas, and gandhabbas, he made an offering there by attaching his own well-washed upper robe to the tip of a bamboo, tying it, and making it into a banner. A yakkha general named Abhisammata, appointed by the devas to protect the offerings to the cetiya, took it and, with an invisible body, held it in the sky and circumambulated the cetiya three times. Seeing this, his mind became serene with even greater joy. Through that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī during this Buddha-dispensation and was named Upavāna. Having come of age, he saw the Buddha's power at the dedication of Jetavana and, gaining faith, went forth. Practicing insight meditation, he attained arahantship and became endowed with the six supernormal knowledges. When the Blessed One was indisposed, the elder brought warm water, a suitable beverage, and medicine to the Blessed One. Through this, the Teacher's illness subsided. The Blessed One gave his blessing in appreciation.

52. Evaṃ so pattaarahattaphalo adhigataetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Tattha sabbesaṃ lokiyalokuttaradhammānaṃ pāragū pariyosānaṃ nibbānaṃ gato patto padumuttaro nāma jino jitapañcamāro bhagavā aggikkhandho iva chabbaṇṇā buddharaṃsiyo jalitvā sabbalokaṃ dhammapajjotena obhāsetvā sambuddho suṭṭhu buddho avijjāniddūpagatāya pajāya savāsanāya kilesaniddāya paṭibuddho vikasitanettapaṅkajo parinibbuto khandhaparinibbānena nibbuto adassanaṃ gatoti sambandho.

52. Thus, he who had attained the fruit of arahantship and reached the foremost position, remembering his past deeds, out of joy proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with the words, "The Victor named Padumuttara." Therein, the Victor named Padumuttara, who had gone to the further shore of all worldly and supramundane phenomena, that is, had reached Nibbāna, the culmination; who had conquered the five Māras; the Blessed One, like a mass of fire, having blazed forth the six-colored Buddha-rays and illuminated the entire world with the lamp of the Dhamma, is the Sambuddha, the perfectly awakened one. He is awakened from the sleep of defilements with their latent tendencies for the sake of the people for whom the sleep of ignorance has been dispelled; his lotus-like eyes are fully blossomed. He is completely extinguished, extinguished by the final extinguishment of the aggregates, gone to invisibility—this is the connection.

57. Jaṅghāti cetiyakaraṇakāle upacinitabbānaṃ iṭṭhakānaṃ ṭhapanatthāya, nibandhiyamānasopānapanti.

57. "Jaṅghā" means a row of steps being constructed for the purpose of placing the bricks that are to be piled up at the time of building the cetiya.

88. Sudhotaṃ [M 2.0039] rajakenāhanti vatthadhovakena purisena suṭṭhu dhovitaṃ suvisuddhakataṃ, uttareyyapaṭaṃ mama uttarasāṭakaṃ ahaṃ veḷagge laggitvā dhajaṃ katvā ukkhipiṃ, ambare ākāse ussāpesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

88. "Well-washed by a washerman" means thoroughly washed and made perfectly pure by a man who washes clothes. "My upper garment" means: I attached my upper robe to the tip of a bamboo, made it into a banner, and raised it up. The meaning is that I hoisted it in the air, in the sky. The rest is easily understood.

Upavānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upavāna is concluded.

3. Tisaraṇagamaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tisaraṇagamaniya

Nagare bandhumatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato tisaraṇagamaniyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle bandhumatīnagare kulagehe nibbattitvā andhamātāpitaro upaṭṭhāsi. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi – “ahaṃ mātāpitaro upaṭṭhahanto pabbajituṃ na labhāmi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ tīṇi saraṇāni [P 0.0345] gaṇhissāmi[V 2.0036], evaṃ duggatito mocessāmī”ti nisabhaṃ nāma vipassissa bhagavato aggasāvakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tīṇi saraṇāni gaṇhi. So tāni vassasatasahassāni rakkhitvā teneva kammena tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatto, tato paraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthinagare mahāsālakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto sattavassikova dārakehi parivuto ekaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ agamāsi. Tattha eko khīṇāsavatthero tassa dhammaṃ desetvā saraṇāni adāsi. So tāni gahetvā pubbe attano rakkhitāni saraṇāni saritvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ arahattappattaṃ bhagavā upasampādesi.

"In the city of Bandhumatī," and so forth, is the Apadāna of the venerable Tisaraṇagamaniya. He, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated, in various existences, merits that serve as a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in a family home in the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī and attended to his blind parents. One day he thought: “While attending to my parents, I cannot go forth. Let me now take the three refuges; in this way I will be freed from a bad destination.” He approached Nisabha, the chief disciple of the Blessed One Vipassī, and took the three refuges. Having protected them for a hundred thousand years, by that same deed he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Thereafter, wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of good fortune, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn into a great Sāla family in the city of Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, at the age of seven, surrounded by boys, he went to a monastery. There, a certain elder who was a destroyer of the cankers taught him the Dhamma and administered the refuges. Having taken them, he recalled the refuges he had protected in the past, developed insight, and attained arahantship. The Blessed One gave the higher ordination to him who had thus attained arahantship.

106. So arahattappatto upasampanno hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nagare bandhumatiyātiādimāha. Tattha mātu upaṭṭhāko ahunti ahaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ upaṭṭhāko bharako bandhumatīnagare ahosinti sambandho.

106. Having attained arahantship and been given the higher ordination, recalling his past deeds and out of joy, he proclaimed the Apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with “In the city of Bandhumatī…” The connection here is: “I was a supporter of my mother” means “I was a caretaker and provider for my parents in the city of Bandhumatī.”

108. Tamandhakārapihitāti [M 2.0040] mohandhakārena pihitā chāditā. Tividhaggīhi ḍayhareti rāgaggidosaggimohaggisaṅkhātehi tīhi aggīhi ḍayhare ḍayhanti sabbe sattāti sambandho.

108. “Enveloped in darkness” means covered, obscured by the darkness of delusion. “Burning with three fires” means all beings are burned, are scorched, by the three fires, namely, the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion. This is the connection.

114. Aṭṭha hetū labhāmahanti aṭṭha kāraṇāni sukhassa paccayabhūtāni kāraṇāni labhāmi ahanti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

114. “I obtain eight causes” means “I gain eight reasons, conditions that are the basis for happiness.” The remainder is easily understood.

Tisaraṇagamaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tisaraṇagamaniya is concluded.

4. Pañcasīlasamādāniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcasīlasamādāniya

Nagare candavatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato pañcasīlasamādāniyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto anomadassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto purimabhave katākusalakammānurūpena daliddo hutvā appannapānabhojano paresaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīvanto saṃsāre ādīnavaṃ ñatvā pabbajitukāmopi pabbajjaṃ alabhamāno anomadassissa bhagavato sāvakassa nisabhattherassa santike pañca sikkhāpadāni samādiyi. Dīghāyukakāle uppannattā vassasatasahassāni sīlaṃ paripālesi. Tena kammena so devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ mahābhogakule nibbatto. Mātāpitaro sīlaṃ samādiyante disvā attano sīlaṃ saritvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patvā pabbaji.

The account beginning with “In the city of Candavatī” is the Apadāna of the Venerable Pañcasīlasamādāniya Thera. He, too, having made an aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences as a basis for liberation, was, during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, born into a certain family. Due to unwholesome kamma done in a past existence, he was poor, with little food and drink, and lived by working for others as a hired laborer. Knowing the danger in saṃsāra, though he wished to go forth, he could not obtain the going forth. Instead, he undertook the five training precepts in the presence of the Elder Nisabha, a disciple of the Blessed One Anomadassī. Because he was born in a time of long lifespans, he protected these precepts for a hundred thousand years. Through that kamma, he wandered on among devas and humans until, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn into a wealthy family in Vesālī. Seeing his parents undertaking the precepts, he recalled his own precepts, developed insight, attained arahantship, and went forth.

134. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto udānavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento [V 2.0037] nagare candavatiyātiādimāha. Bhatako [P 0.0346] āsahaṃ tadāti tadā mama puññakaraṇakāle ahaṃ bhatako bhatiyā kammakārako āsiṃ ahosiṃ. Parakammāyane yuttoti bhatiyā paresaṃ kammakaraṇe āyutto yojito okāsābhāvena saṃsārato muccanatthāya ahaṃ pabbajjaṃ na labhāmi.

134. Recalling his past deeds, with joy arisen, he proclaimed the Apadāna of his former conduct by way of an inspired utterance, speaking the verse beginning with “In the city of Candavatī…” “I was a laborer then” means “at that time, when I was making merit, I was a wage-earner, a worker for hire.” “Engaged in others' work” means being employed in doing the work of others for a wage, and due to a lack of opportunity, for the sake of release from saṃsāra, I did not obtain the going forth.

135. Mahandhakārapihitāti mahantehi kilesandhakārehi pihitā saṃvutā thakitā. Tividhaggīhi ḍayhareti narakaggipetaggisaṃsāraggisaṅkhātehi tīhi [M 2.0041] aggīhi ḍayhanti. Ahaṃ pana kena upāyena kena kāraṇena visaṃyutto bhaveyyanti attho.

135. “Enveloped in great darkness” means covered, enclosed, and blocked by the great darkness of the defilements. “Burning with three fires” means they are burned by the three fires, namely, the fire of hell, the fire of the ghost realm, and the fire of saṃsāra. “But by what means, for what reason, might I be disjoined from this?”—this is the meaning.

136. Deyyadhammo annapānādidātabbayuttakaṃ vatthu mayhaṃ natthi, tassābhāvena ahaṃ varāko dukkhito bhatako bhatiyā jīvanako yaṃnūnāhaṃ pañcasīlaṃ rakkheyyaṃ paripūrayanti pañcasīlaṃ samādiyitvā paripūrento yaṃnūna rakkheyyaṃ sādhukaṃ bhaddakaṃ sundaraṃ katvā paripāleyyanti attho.

136. “I have no gift-worthy object,” meaning, no item suitable for giving, such as food and drink. Due to this lack, I, a wretched and suffering wage-earner, live by hire. “Surely I should protect the five precepts,” meaning, having undertaken the five precepts, I should fulfill them; surely I should protect them, having made them good, auspicious, and beautiful, I should maintain them perfectly. This is the meaning.

148. Svāhaṃ yasamanubhavinti so ahaṃ devamanussesu mahantaṃ yasaṃ anubhaviṃ tesaṃ sīlānaṃ vāhasā ānubhāvenāti attho. Kappakoṭimpi tesaṃ sīlānaṃ phalaṃ kittento ekakoṭṭhāsameva kittaye pākaṭaṃ kareyyanti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

148. “Thus, I experienced fame” means “I experienced great fame among devas and humans through the strength, the power of those precepts”; this is the meaning. “Even if I were to praise the fruit of those precepts for a koṭi of aeons, I would only declare a single portion”; this is the meaning. The remainder is easily understood.

Pañcasīlasamādāniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcasīlasamādāniya is concluded.

5. Annasaṃsāvakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Annasaṃsāvaka

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhantiādikaṃ āyasmato annasaṃsāvakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto piṇḍāya carantaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇabyāmappabhāmaṇḍalopasobhitaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā gehaṃ netvā varaannapānena santappetvā sampavāretvā bhojesi. So teneva cittappasādena tato cuto devaloke nibbattitvā dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato cavitvā manussaloke nibbattitvā manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato aparāparaṃ devamanussasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto sāsane pasīditvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So pubbe katapuññanāmavasena annasaṃsāvakattheroti pākaṭanāmo ahosi.

The account of the Venerable Annasaṃsāvaka Thera begins with “The golden-colored Sambuddha,” etc. This elder, too, having made an aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a support for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born into a certain family home. He saw the Blessed One, who was wandering for alms, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and a fathom-wide halo of light. With a serene mind, he invited the Blessed One, led him to his home, satisfied him with excellent food and drink, offered it formally, and served him a meal. Through that very serenity of mind, after passing away from that life, he was reborn in the heavenly world and experienced divine fortune. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the human world and experienced human fortune. Thereafter, he repeatedly experienced the fortunes of devas and humans until, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a certain family, gained faith in the Teaching, went forth, cultivated insight, and attained arahantship.

155-6. So [M 2.0042][V 2.0038] aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto “evaṃ mayā iminā puññasambhārānubhāvena pattaṃ arahatta”nti attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ udānavasena pakāsento suvaṇṇavaṇṇantiādimāha[P 0.0347]. Tattha suvaṇṇassa vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa bhagavato soyaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, taṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ siddhatthanti attho. Gacchantaṃ antarāpaṇeti vessānaṃ āpaṇapantīnaṃ antaravīthiyaṃ gacchamānaṃ. Kañcanagghiyasaṃkāsanti suvaṇṇatoraṇasadisaṃ bāttiṃsavaralakkhaṇaṃ dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇehi sampannaṃ lokapajjotaṃ sakalalokadīpabhūtaṃ appameyyaṃ pamāṇavirahitaṃ anopamaṃ upamāvirahitaṃ jutindharaṃ pabhādhāraṃ nīlapītādichabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo dhārakaṃ siddhatthaṃ disvā paramaṃ uttamaṃ pītiṃ alatthaṃ alabhinti sambandho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

155-6. Then, at a later time, recollecting his past deeds, he became joyful and, thinking, 'Thus, through the power of this accumulation of merit, I have attained arahantship,' he revealed the account of his past conduct by way of an inspired utterance, speaking the verse beginning 'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ,' etc. Herein, 'golden-colored' means the Blessed One whose color is like the color of gold; thus, the golden-colored Sambuddha, Siddhattha, is the meaning. 'Walking among the shops' means walking in the street between the rows of merchants' shops. 'Resembling a golden archway' means like a golden archway, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks, the light of the world, being a lamp for the entire world, immeasurable, without measure, incomparable, without comparison, the bearer of splendor, the holder of the six-colored Buddha-rays such as blue and yellow. Seeing Siddhattha, 'I obtained supreme, excellent joy'—this is the connection. The rest is easily understood.

Annasaṃsāvakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Annasaṃsāvaka is concluded.

6. Dhūpadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhūpadāyaka

Siddhatthassa bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato dhūpadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto siddhatthe bhagavati cittaṃ pasādetvā tassa bhagavato gandhakuṭiyaṃ candanāgarukāḷānusāriādinā katehi anekehi dhūpehi dhūpapūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññena devesu ca manussesu ca ubhayasampattiyo anubhavanto nibbattanibbattabhave pūjanīyo hutvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto puññasambhārānubhāvena sāsane pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patvā katadhūpapūjāpuññattā nāmena dhūpadāyakattheroti sabbattha pākaṭo. So pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ dassento siddhatthassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Siddho paripuṇṇo sabbaññutaññāṇādiguṇasaṅkhāto attho payojanaṃ yassa bhagavato soyaṃ siddhattho, tassa siddhatthassa bhagavato bhagyādiguṇavantassa lokajeṭṭhassa sakalalokuttamassa tādino iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu [M 2.0043] tādisassa acalasabhāvassāti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Dhūpadāyaka, beginning with 'Siddhatthassa bhagavato,' etc. This elder, too, having made an aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a support for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born into a family household. Having gained faith in the Blessed One Siddhattha, he offered incense worship in the Blessed One's perfumed chamber with many incenses made from sandalwood, agarwood, black aloeswood, and so forth. By that merit, he experienced both divine and human prosperity among devas and humans. Having become one worthy of honor in each successive existence, he was born into a family household in this Buddha-era. By the power of his accumulated merit, he went forth in the Teaching, developed insight, attained Arahantship, and became widely known everywhere as Dhūpadāyaka Thera by name, due to the merit of his incense offering. Having attained the fruit of Arahantship, recollecting his past deeds, filled with joy, revealing the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verse beginning 'Siddhatthassa bhagavato,' etc. 'Siddhattha' means the Blessed One for whom the meaning or purpose, consisting of qualities like omniscience, is accomplished and perfected. The meaning is: of that Blessed One Siddhattha, who possesses qualities like fortune, who is the foremost in the world, the supreme of the entire world, a 'Tādī'—one who is unshakeable amidst desirable and undesirable things. The rest is clear in meaning.

Dhūpadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhūpadāyaka is concluded.

7. Pulinapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pulinapūjaka

Vipassissa [V 2.0039] bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato pulinapūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto sāsane pasannacitto cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇesu [P 0.0348] purāṇavālukaṃ apanetvā navaṃ muttādalasadisapaṇḍarapulinaṃ okiritvā māḷakaṃ alaṅkari. Tena kammena so devaloke nibbatto tattha dibbehi ratanehi vijjotamāne anekayojane kanakavimāne dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato cuto manussaloke sattaratanasampanno cakkavattī rājā hutvā manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā aparāparaṃ saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto sāsane pasanno pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So attano katapuññanāmasadisena nāmena pulinapūjakattheroti pākaṭo.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pulinapūjaka, beginning with 'Vipassissa bhagavato,' etc. This elder, too, having made an aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a support for liberation. At the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born into a certain family. With a mind serene in the Teaching, he removed the old sand from the courtyards of the shrine and the Bodhi tree, and scattered new white sand resembling strings of pearls, adorning the platform. By that deed, he was reborn in the heavenly world. There, in a golden mansion many yojanas wide, shining with divine jewels, he enjoyed divine prosperity. Passing away from there, he was born in the human world, becoming a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures and experiencing human prosperity. Wandering on again and again, in this Buddha-era, he was born into a wealthy family. With a serene mind towards the Teaching, he went forth, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. He became widely known as Pulinapūjaka Thera by a name similar to the meritorious deed he had performed.

165. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ dassento vipassissa bhagavatotiādimāha. Tattha vividhaṃ passatīti vipassī, vivicca passatīti vā vipassī, vividhe attatthaparatthādibhede atthe passatīti vā vipassī, vividhe vohāraparamatthādibhede passatīti vā vipassī, tassa vipassissa bodhiyā pādaputtame uttame bodhirukkhamaṇḍalamāḷake purāṇapulinaṃ vālukaṃ chaḍḍetvā suddhaṃ paṇḍaraṃ pulinaṃ ākiriṃ santhariṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

165. Recollecting his past deeds, with joy arisen, revealing the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verse beginning 'Vipassissa bhagavato,' etc. Herein, 'Vipassī' means one who sees in various ways; or, one who sees in seclusion; or, one who sees various meanings, such as benefit for oneself and benefit for others; or, one who sees various distinctions, such as conventional and ultimate truth. For that Vipassī, at the supreme tree, the Bodhi tree, on the excellent terrace of the Bodhi-tree precinct, having cast aside the old sand, I scattered and spread pure white sand. The rest is easily understood.

Pulinapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pulinapūjaka is concluded.

8. Uttiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uttiya

Candabhāgānadītīretiādikaṃ [M 2.0044] āyasmato uttiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle candabhāgānadiyaṃ susumāro hutvā nibbatto nadītīraṃ upagataṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto pāraṃ netukāmo tīrasamīpeyeva nipajji. Bhagavā tassa anukampāya piṭṭhiyaṃ pāde ṭhapesi. So tuṭṭho udaggo pītivegena mahussāho hutvā sotaṃ chindanto sīghena javena bhagavantaṃ paratīraṃ nesi. Bhagavā tassa cittappasādaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ ito cuto devaloke nibbattissati[V 2.0040], tato paṭṭhāya sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto ito catunnavutikappe amataṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti byākaritvā pakkāmi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Uttiya, beginning with 'Candabhāgānadītīre,' etc. He too, having made an aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences as a support for liberation, was reborn as a crocodile in the Candabhāgā River during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Seeing the Blessed One approaching the riverbank, with a serene mind and wishing to carry him across, he lay down right near the shore. Out of compassion for him, the Blessed One placed his feet on its back. Delighted and elated, filled with great enthusiasm by the force of his rapture, he cut through the current and with swift speed carried the Blessed One to the far shore. The Blessed One, knowing the serenity of his mind, declared: 'Passing away from here, this one will be reborn in the deva world. From then on, wandering only in happy destinations, he will attain the Deathless ninety-four aeons from now.' Having made this prediction, he departed.

So tathā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbatti, uttiyotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto “amataṃ pariyesissāmī”ti paribbājako hutvā ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho hutvā sāsane pabbajitvā sīladiṭṭhīnaṃ avisodhitattā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto aññaṃ bhikkhuṃ visesaṃ nibbattetvā aññaṃ byākarontaṃ disvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā saṅkhepena ovādaṃ yāci. Satthāpi tassa[P 0.0349], “tasmātiha tvaṃ, uttiya, ādimeva visodhehī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.382) saṅkhepeneva ovādaṃ adāsi. So satthu ovāde ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ ārabhi. Tassa āraddhavipassakassa ābādho uppajji. Uppanne ābādhe jātasaṃvego vīriyārambhavatthuṃ ñatvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Thus, wandering only in happy destinations, in this Buddha-era he was reborn at Sāvatthī as the son of a certain brahmin, and they gave him the name Uttiya. When he came of age, thinking, 'I will seek the Deathless,' he became a wanderer. One day, seeing the Blessed One, he approached, paid homage, and after hearing the Dhamma, gained faith and went forth in the Teaching. However, because his virtue and views were not purified, he was unable to bring about any special attainment. Seeing other monks bring about special attainments and declare final knowledge, he approached the Teacher and requested a brief exhortation. The Teacher gave him a brief exhortation beginning with the words, 'Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the very beginning,' and so on (SN 5.382). Abiding in the Teacher’s exhortation, he began insight practice. For him who had begun insight practice, an illness arose. When the illness arose, he became filled with spiritual urgency and, knowing this to be a basis for arousing effort, he developed his insight and attained Arahantship.

169. Evaṃ so katasambhārānurūpena pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento candabhāgānadītīretiādimāha. Tattha candabhāgānadītīreti parisuddhapaṇḍarapulinatalehi ca pabhāsampannapasannamadhurodakaparipuṇṇatāya ca candappabhākiraṇasassirīkābhā nadamānā saddaṃ kurumānā gacchatīti candabhāgānadī, tassā candabhāgānadiyā tīre susumāro ahosinti sambandho. Tattha [M 2.0045] susumāroti khuddakamacchagumbe khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ karonto māretīti susumāro, caṇḍamaccho kumbhīloti attho. Sabhojanapasutohanti ahaṃ sabhojane sakagocare pasuto byāvaṭo. Nadītitthaṃ agacchahanti bhagavato āgamanakāle ahaṃ nadītitthaṃ agacchiṃ pattomhi.

169. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship in accordance with his accumulated requisites, he recalled his past deeds and declared his former life story, beginning with the words, 'On the bank of the Candabhāgā River.' Therein, 'on the bank of the Candabhāgā River' means: the Candabhāgā River is so called because it flows making a roaring sound, having pure white sandy banks and being full of lustrous, clear, sweet water. 'On the bank of that Candabhāgā River, there was a crocodile'—this is the connection. Therein, 'crocodile' (susumāro) means: it kills small shoals of fish, making them into pieces; thus it is a 'susumāro,' meaning a fierce fish, a crocodile. 'I was intent on my food' means: I was intent on and occupied with my own food in my feeding ground. 'I went to the river ford' means: at the time of the Blessed One's arrival, I went to the river ford; I arrived.

170. Siddhattho tamhi samayeti tasmiṃ mama titthagamanakāle siddhattho bhagavā aggapuggalo sabbasattesu jeṭṭho seṭṭho sayambhū sayameva bhūto jāto buddhabhūto so bhagavā nadiṃ taritukāmo nadītīraṃ upāgami.

170. “Siddhattha at that time” means: at that time, when I went to the ford, the Blessed One Siddhattha—the foremost individual, the eldest and best among all beings, self-become, self-arisen, having become a Buddha—that Blessed One, wishing to cross the river, approached the riverbank.

172. Pettikaṃ visayaṃ mayhanti mayhaṃ pitupitāmahādīhi paramparānītaṃ, yadidaṃ sampattasampattamahānubhāvānaṃ taraṇanti attho.

172. “My paternal domain” means: my domain, handed down in succession by my father, grandfather, and so on. The meaning is: this is the crossing place for those of great power who have arrived.

173. Mama [V 2.0041] uggajjanaṃ sutvāti mayhaṃ uggajjanaṃ ārādhanaṃ sutvā mahāmuni bhagavā abhiruhīti sambandho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

173. “Having heard my call” means: having heard my call, my invitation, the Great Sage, the Blessed One, ascended—this is the connection. The rest is clear in meaning.

Uttiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uttiya is concluded.

9. Ekañjalikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekañjalika

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇantiādikaṃ āyasmato ekañjalikattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto ratanattaye pasanno piṇḍāya carantaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso añjaliṃ paggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto sabbattha pūjanīyo hutvā ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā [P 0.0350] imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne kule nibbattitvā sāsane pasīditvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Pubbe katapuññavasena ekañjalikattheroti pākaṭo.

9. The Apadāna of the Venerable Ekañjalika begins with the words 'Golden-hued.' He too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating, in various existences, merits that support liberation, was reborn in a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, he gained faith in the Three Jewels. Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī walking for alms, with a mind full of faith, he raised his hands in reverence and stood still. Through that meritorious deed, while transmigrating among gods and humans, he was honored everywhere and experienced both kinds of success. At the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn into a wealthy family. Gaining faith in the Teaching, he went forth, developed insight, and was established in Arahantship. Due to the merit made in the past, he became known as the Elder Ekañjalika.

180. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā taṃ hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya disvā udānavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento suvaṇṇavaṇṇantiādimāha. Vipassiṃ satthavāhagganti vāṇije kantārā vahati tāretīti satthavāho[M 2.0046]. Vāḷakantārā coḷakantārā dubbhikkhakantārā nirudakakantārā yakkhakantārā appabhakkhakantārā ca tāreti uttāreti patāreti nittāreti khemantabhūmiṃ pāpetīti attho. Ko so? Vāṇijajeṭṭhako. Satthavāhasadisattā ayampi bhagavā satthavāho. Tathā hi so tividhaṃ bodhiṃ patthayante katapuññasambhāre satte jātikantārā jarākantārā byādhikantārā maraṇakantārā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsakantārā ca sabbasmā saṃsārakantārā ca tāreti uttāreti patāreti nittāreti nibbānathalaṃ pāpetīti attho. Satthavāho ca so aggo seṭṭho padhāno cāti satthavāhaggo, taṃ satthavāhaggaṃ vipassiṃ sambuddhanti sambandho. Naravaraṃ vināyakanti narānaṃ antare asithilaparakkamoti naravīro, taṃ. Visesena katapuññasambhāre satte neti nibbānapuraṃ pāpetīti vināyako, taṃ.

Recalling his past deeds and seeing them as clearly as an āmalaka fruit on the palm of his hand, out of inspired utterance he declared his former life story, beginning with the words, 'Golden-hued.' As for 'Vipassī, the supreme caravan leader': one who leads merchants through the wilderness is a caravan leader (satthavāha). The meaning is that he leads them across, brings them out, guides them through, and delivers them from the wilderness of wild beasts, the wilderness of robbers, the wilderness of famine, the waterless wilderness, the wilderness of yakkhas, and the wilderness of scarce food, bringing them to a land of safety. Who is that? The chief of the merchants. Because he is like a caravan leader, this Blessed One is also a caravan leader. For he leads beings who have accumulated the requisites of merit and aspire to the threefold enlightenment; he leads them across, brings them out, guides them through, and delivers them from the wilderness of birth, the wilderness of aging, the wilderness of sickness, the wilderness of death, the wilderness of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and from the entire wilderness of saṃsāra, bringing them to the ground of Nibbāna. He is a caravan leader and he is supreme, the best, the foremost; thus he is the 'supreme caravan leader' (satthavāhagga). 'That supreme caravan leader, Vipassī, the Fully Enlightened One'—this is the connection. As for 'the supreme man, the guide' (naravaraṃ vināyakaṃ): among men, he is a hero (naravīra) because of his unslacking effort. He is a guide (vināyaka) because he specifically leads beings who have accumulated the requisites of merit to the city of Nibbāna.

181. Adantadamanaṃ tādinti rāgadosamohādikilesasampayuttattā kāyavacīmanodvārehi adante satte dametīti adantadamano, taṃ. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu akampiyatādiguṇayuttoti tādī, taṃ. Mahāvādiṃ mahāmatinti sakasamayaparasamayavādīnaṃ antare attanā samadhikapuggalavirahitattā mahāvādī[V 2.0042], mahatī pathavisamānā merusamānā ca mati yassa so mahāmati, taṃ mahāvādiṃ mahāmatiṃ sambuddhanti iminā tulyādhikaraṇaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

180. “The tamer of the untamed, the steadfast one” means: he tames beings who are untamed through the doors of body, speech, and mind due to their being associated with defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, he is the tamer of the untamed. “Steadfast” means: endowed with the quality of being unshaken by the agreeable and disagreeable; therefore, he is steadfast. “The great proponent, the great-minded” means: because there is no individual superior or equal to him among proponents of his own and others’ doctrines, he is the great proponent; he whose wisdom is great, like the earth or Mount Meru, is the great-minded. That 'great proponent, great-minded' is in apposition with 'the Fully Awakened One.' The rest is easily understood.

Ekañjalikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

181. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekañjalika is concluded.

10. Khomadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Khomadāyaka

Nagare bandhumatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato khomadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vayappatto sāsane abhippasanno ratanattayamāmako vipassissa bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso khomadussena pūjaṃ akāsi. So tadeva mūlaṃ katvā yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā tato devaloke nibbatto. Chasu [P 0.0351] devesu aparāparaṃ dibbasukhaṃ [M 2.0047] anubhavitvā tato cavitvā manussaloke cakkavattiādianekavidhamanussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā paripākagate puññasambhāre imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vayappatto satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Katapuññanāmena khomadāyakattheroti pākaṭo.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Khomadāyaka begins with the words, 'In the city of Bandhumatī.' He too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating, in various existences, merits that support liberation, was reborn in a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having come of age, with deep faith in the Teaching and devotion to the Three Jewels, he listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī. With a mind full of faith, he made an offering of linen cloth. Taking that as his foundation, he performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life and was reborn in a celestial world. Having repeatedly experienced divine bliss in the six celestial realms, he passed away from there and experienced various human fortunes in the human world, such as that of a wheel-turning monarch. When his store of merit had ripened, at the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn into a good family. Having come of age, he heard the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, gained faith, went forth, developed insight, and in no long time attained Arahantship. He became known as the Elder Khomadāyaka, named after his meritorious deed.

184. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ dassento nagare bandhumatiyātiādimāha. Tattha bandhu vuccati ñātako, te bandhū yasmiṃ nagare aññamaññaṃ saṅghaṭitā vasanti, taṃ nagaraṃ “bandhumatī”ti vuccati. Ropemi bījasampadanti dānasīlādipuññabījasampattiṃ ropemi paṭṭhapemīti attho.

184. Recollecting his past deeds, he became joyful and, wishing to show the Apadāna of his past conduct, spoke the verse beginning with, 'In the city of Bandhumatī.' Therein, 'bandhu' is called a relative. The city where those relatives live together, associated with one another, is called 'Bandhumatī.' The meaning of 'I plant the abundance of seed' is 'I plant, I establish the abundance of the seed of merit, such as generosity and virtue'.

Khomadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of Khomadāyaka Thera is concluded.

Tatiyassa subhūtivaggassa vaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the third Subhūti Vagga is concluded.

Catubhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Four Recitation Sections is concluded.

4. Kuṇḍadhānavaggo

4. The Chapter on Kuṇḍadhāna

1. Kuṇḍadhānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna

Sattāhaṃ [V 2.0043] paṭisallīnantiādikaṃ āyasmato kuṇḍadhānattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto vuttanayena bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā tadanurūpaṃ puññaṃ karonto vicari. So ekadivasaṃ padumuttarassa bhagavato nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhāya nisinnassa manosilācuṇṇapiñjaraṃ mahantaṃ kadaliphalakaṇṇikaṃ upanesi, taṃ bhagavā paṭiggahetvā paribhuñji. So tena puññakammena ekādasakkhattuṃ devesu devarajjaṃ kāresi. Catuvīsativāre ca rājā ahosi cakkavattī.

4. The Apadāna of the Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna Thera begins with, 'For seven days, being in seclusion.' He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a supporting condition for liberation in various existences, was reborn into a family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having approached the Blessed One in the manner described and listened to the Dhamma, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who take the first ticket. Aspiring for that eminent position, he went about performing meritorious deeds appropriate to it. One day, he brought a large cluster of bananas, reddish-yellow like realgar powder, to the Blessed One Padumuttara who had arisen from the attainment of cessation and was seated. The Blessed One accepted and partook of it. By that meritorious deed, he exercised the sovereignty of the devas among the devas eleven times, and twenty-four times he was a wheel-turning monarch.

So [M 2.0048] evaṃ aparāparaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapabuddhakāle bhummadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Dīghāyukabuddhānañca nāma na anvaddhamāsiko uposatho hoti. Tathā hi vipassissa bhagavato chabbassantare chabbassantare uposatho ahosi, kassapadasabalo pana chaṭṭhe chaṭṭhe māse pātimokkhaṃ osāresi, tassa pātimokkhassa osāraṇakāle disāvāsikā dve sahāyakā bhikkhū “uposathaṃ karissāmā”ti gacchanti. Ayaṃ bhummadevatā cintesi – “imesaṃ dvinnaṃ [P 0.0352] bhikkhūnaṃ metti ativiya daḷhā, kiṃ nu kho bhedake sati bhijjeyya, na bhijjeyyā”ti. Tesaṃ okāsaṃ olokayamānā tesaṃ avidūre gacchati.

1. Thus, having performed meritorious deeds again and again, while wandering among devas and humans, he was reborn as an earth deity in the time of the Buddha Kassapa. Now, for Buddhas with long life spans, the Uposatha is not held every half-month. Indeed, for the Blessed One Vipassī, the Uposatha was held at intervals of six years, while Kassapa, the one of Ten Powers, recited the Pātimokkha every sixth month. At the time of that Pātimokkha recitation, two companion monks dwelling in different regions were journeying, thinking, 'We will perform the Uposatha.' This earth deity thought: 'The friendship between these two monks is exceedingly strong. If there were a cause for division, would it break or not?' Looking for an opportunity, the deity went near them.

Atheko thero ekassa hatthe pattacīvaraṃ datvā sarīravaḷañjanatthaṃ udakaphāsukaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā dhotahatthapādo hutvā gumbasamīpato nikkhamati. Bhummadevatā tassa therassa pacchato pacchato uttamarūpā itthī hutvā kese vidhunitvā saṃvidhāya bandhantī viya piṭṭhiyaṃ paṃsuṃ puñchamānā viya sāṭakaṃ saṃvidhāya nivāsayamānā viya ca hutvā therassa padānupadikā hutvā gumbato nikkhantā[V 2.0044]. Ekamante ṭhito sahāyakatthero taṃ kāraṇaṃ disvāva domanassajāto “naṭṭho dāni me iminā bhikkhunā saddhiṃ dīgharattānugato sineho, sacāhaṃ evaṃvidhabhāvaṃ jāneyyaṃ, ettakaṃ kālaṃ iminā saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ na kareyya”nti cintetvā āgacchantaṃyeva naṃ “gaṇhāhāvuso, tuyhaṃ pattacīvaraṃ, tādisena pāpena saddhiṃ ekamaggena na gacchāmī”ti āha. Taṃ kathaṃ sutvā tassa lajjibhikkhuno hadayaṃ tikhiṇasattiṃ gahetvā viddhaṃ viya ahosi. Tato naṃ āha – “āvuso, kinnāmetaṃ vadasi, ahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ dukkaṭamattampi āpattiṃ na jānāmi, tvaṃ pana maṃ ajja ‘pāpo’ti vadasi, kiṃ te diṭṭhanti, kiṃ aññena diṭṭhena, kiṃ tvaṃ evaṃvidhena alaṅkatapaṭiyattena mātugāmena saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne hutvā nikkhanto”ti? “Natthetaṃ, āvuso, mayhaṃ, nāhaṃ evarūpaṃ mātugāmaṃ passāmī”ti tassa yāvatatiyaṃ kathentassāpi itaro thero kathaṃ asaddahitvā attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃyeva bhūtattaṃ katvā gaṇhanto tena saddhiṃ ekamaggena agantvā aññena maggena satthu santikaṃ gato. Itaropi bhikkhu aññena maggena satthu santikaṃyeva gato.

Then one elder, having given his bowl and robe into the hand of the other, went to a place with suitable water to tend to his body. Having washed his hands and feet, he came out from near a thicket. The earth deity, taking the form of a woman of supreme beauty, followed right behind that elder. As if shaking out her hair, arranging it, and tying it up; as if wiping dust from his back; and as if arranging and putting on her lower garment, she followed in the elder's footsteps and came out from the thicket. The companion elder, standing to one side, saw this and at once became distressed, thinking, 'Now my long-standing affection for this monk is destroyed! If I had known of such a character, I would not have placed my trust in him for so long.' Seeing him approaching, he said: 'Take your bowl and robe, friend. I will not go on the same path with such a wicked person.' Hearing these words, the heart of that conscientious monk was as if pierced by a sharp spear. Then he said to him: 'Friend, what is this you say? For so long I have not been aware of an offense even as minor as a dukkaṭa, yet today you call me "wicked." What have you seen?' The other replied: 'What need is there of seeing anything else? Were you not coming out from the same place together with such an adorned and arrayed woman?' 'That is not so for me, friend. I do not see such a woman.' But even though he said this up to the third time, the other elder did not believe his words. Taking what he himself had seen as the truth, he would not go with him on the same path, but went to the Teacher's presence by another way. The other monk also went to the Teacher's presence by another way.

Tato [M 2.0049] bhikkhusaṅghassa uposathāgāraṃ pavisanavelāya so bhikkhu taṃ bhikkhuṃ uposathagge disvā sañjānitvā “imasmiṃ uposathagge evarūpo nāma pāpabhikkhu atthi, nāhaṃ tena saddhiṃ uposathaṃ karissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā bahi aṭṭhāsi. Atha bhummadevatā “bhāriyaṃ mayā kammaṃ kata”nti mahallakaupāsakavaṇṇena tassa santikaṃ gantvā – “kasmā, bhante, ayyo imasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito”ti āha. “Upāsaka, imaṃ uposathaggaṃ eko pāpabhikkhu paviṭṭho, ‘ahaṃ tena saddhiṃ uposathaṃ na karomī’ti bahi ṭhitomhī”ti. “Bhante, mā evaṃ gaṇhatha, parisuddhasīlo esa bhikkhu, tumhehi diṭṭhamātugāmo nāma ahaṃ. Mayā tumhākaṃ vīmaṃsanatthāya [P 0.0353] ‘daḷhā nu kho imesaṃ therānaṃ metti, no daḷhā’ti bhijjanābhijjanabhāvaṃ olokentena taṃ kammaṃ kata”nti. “Ko pana tvaṃ, sappurisā”ti? “Ahaṃ ekā bhummadevatā, bhante”ti. Devaputto kathentoyeva dibbānubhāvena ṭhatvā therassa pādamūle patitvā “mayhaṃ, bhante, khamatha, therassa eso doso natthi, uposathaṃ karothā”ti theraṃ yācitvā uposathaggaṃ pavesesi. So thero uposathaṃ tāva ekaṭṭhāne akāsi. Mittasanthavavasena pana puna tena saddhiṃ na ekaṭṭhāne vasi. Imassa therassa dosaṃ na kathesi. Aparabhāge cuditakatthero pana vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Then, at the time when the community of monks was entering the Uposatha hall, that monk saw the other monk in the Uposatha hall, recognized him, and thought, 'In this Uposatha hall, there is a wicked monk of such a kind. I will not perform the Uposatha with him.' So he left and stood outside. Then a terrestrial deity, realizing, 'A grave deed has been done by me,' approached him in the guise of an elderly lay devotee and said, 'Venerable sir, why does the noble one stand in this place?' 'Lay devotee, a wicked monk has entered this Uposatha hall. Thinking, "I will not perform the Uposatha with him," I am standing outside.' 'Venerable sir, do not take it thus. This monk is of pure virtue. I am the woman you saw. That deed was done by me for the purpose of testing you, observing whether the friendship of these elders was firm or not, whether it would break or not break.' 'But who are you, good sir?' 'I am a terrestrial deity, venerable sir.' As the son of a deva was speaking, he stood there by his divine power, fell at the elder's feet, and pleaded, 'Forgive me, venerable sir. There is no fault in that elder. Please perform the Uposatha.' Having thus requested of the elder, he led him into the Uposatha hall. That elder then performed the Uposatha in one place. However, on account of their friendly acquaintance, he did not again dwell with him in the same place. The fault of this elder is not related here. In a later time, the elder who had been accused, undertaking the practice of insight meditation, attained Arahantship.

Bhummadevatā tassa kammassa nissandena ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ apāyato na muccittha. Sace pana kālena kālaṃ manussattaṃ āgacchati, aññena yena kenaci kato doso tasseva upari patati. So amhākaṃ bhagavato uppannakāle sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, dhānamāṇavotissa nāmaṃ [V 2.0045] akaṃsu. So vayappatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā mahallakakāle satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho sāsane pabbaji. Tassa upasampannadivasato paṭṭhāya ekā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā itthī tasmiṃ gāmaṃ pavisante saddhiṃyeva pavisati, nikkhamante nikkhamati, vihāraṃ pavisantepi saddhiṃ pavisati, tiṭṭhantepi tiṭṭhatīti evaṃ niccānubandhā paññāyati. Thero taṃ na passati. Tassa pana purimakammassa nissandena sā aññesaṃ upaṭṭhāsi.

As a result of that kamma, the terrestrial deity was not freed from the woeful states for an entire Buddha-interval. And if, from time to time, he came to a human existence, any fault committed by another would fall upon him. During the time of our Blessed One's arising, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī, and they gave him the name Dhānamāṇava. Having come of age, he learned the three Vedas. In his old age, after hearing the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith and went forth in the Dispensation. From the very day of his higher ordination, a certain beautifully adorned woman would enter the village together with him whenever he entered, leave when he left, enter the monastery together with him when he entered, and stand when he stood—thus she was perceived as constantly following him. The elder did not see her, but as a result of his former kamma, she appeared to others.

Gāme [M 2.0050] yāgubhikkhaṃ dadamānā itthiyo, “bhante, ayaṃ eko yāguuḷuṅko tumhākaṃ, eko imissā amhākaṃ sahāyikāyā”ti parihāsaṃ karonti. Therassa mahatī vihesā hoti. Vihāragatampi naṃ sāmaṇerā ceva daharabhikkhū ca parivāretvā “dhāno koṇḍo jāto”ti parihāsaṃ karonti. Athassa teneva kāraṇena kuṇḍadhāno theroti nāmaṃ jātaṃ. So uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya tehi kariyamānaṃ keḷiṃ sahituṃ asakkonto ummādaṃ gahetvā “tumhe koṇḍā, tumhākaṃ upajjhāyo koṇḍo, ācariyo koṇḍo”ti vadati. Atha naṃ satthu ārocesuṃ – “kuṇḍadhāno, bhante, daharasāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ evaṃ pharusavācaṃ vadatī”ti. Satthā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, dhāna, daharasāmaṇerehi saddhiṃ pharusavācaṃ vadasī”ti pucchi. Tena “saccaṃ bhagavā”ti vutte – “kasmā evaṃ vadasī”ti āha. “Bhante, nibaddhaṃ vihesaṃ sahituṃ asakkonto evaṃ kathemī”ti[P 0.0354]. “Tvaṃ pubbe katakammaṃ yāvajjadivasā jīrāpetuṃ na sakkosi, puna evaṃ pharusavācaṃ mā vada bhikkhū”ti vatvā āha –

In the village, women giving alms of rice-gruel would say in jest, 'Venerable sir, this one ladle of gruel is for you, and one is for this friend of ours.' The elder felt great vexation. Even when he went to the monastery, the novices and young monks would surround him and mock him, saying, 'Dhāna has become a reprobate!' For that very reason, he became known by the name Elder Kuṇḍadhāna. Rising up again and again, unable to endure the sport they were making of him, he flew into a rage and said, 'You are reprobates! Your preceptor is a reprobate! Your teacher is a reprobate!' Then they reported him to the Teacher, saying, 'Venerable sir, Kuṇḍadhāna speaks such harsh words to the young novices.' The Teacher had him summoned and asked, 'Dhāna, is it true that you speak harsh words to the young novices?' When he said, 'It is true, Blessed One,' the Teacher asked, 'Why do you speak thus?' 'Venerable sir, I spoke thus because I was unable to endure the constant harassment.' The Teacher said, 'You have been unable to wear out the kamma you made in the past, even up to this day. Do not again speak such harsh words to the monks.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

“Māvoca pharusaṃ kañci, vuttā paṭivadeyyu taṃ;

Dukkhā hi sārambhakathā, paṭidaṇḍā phuseyyu taṃ.

Speak harshly to no one; those thus addressed may retort. Contentious speech is painful, and retribution may befall you.

“Sace neresi attānaṃ, kaṃso upahato yathā;

Esa pattosi nibbānaṃ, sārambho te na vijjatī”ti. (dha. pa. 133-134) –

If you keep yourself silent like a cracked bronze gong, you have already reached Nibbāna; no contention is found in you.

Imañca pana tassa therassa mātugāmena saddhiṃ vicaraṇabhāvaṃ kosalaraññopi kathayiṃsu. Rājā “gacchatha, bhaṇe, naṃ vīmaṃsathā”ti pesetvā sayampi mandeneva parivārena saddhiṃ therassa santikaṃ gantvā ekamante olokento aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thero sūcikammaṃ karonto nisinno hoti. Sāpi itthī avidūre ṭhāne ṭhitā viya paññāyati.

Furthermore, they told the king of Kosala about this elder's state of associating with a woman. The king, having sent men with the command, 'Go, sirs, and investigate him,' also went himself with but a small retinue to the elder's presence and stood to one side, observing. At that moment, the elder was seated, doing needlework. And that woman also appeared, as if standing in a place not far away.

Rājā [V 2.0046] taṃ disvā “atthi taṃ kāraṇa”nti tassā ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Sā tasmiṃ āgacchante therassa vasanapaṇṇasālaṃ paviṭṭhā viya ahosi. Rājāpi tāya saddhiṃ eva paṇṇasālāyaṃ pavisitvā sabbattha olokento adisvā “nāyaṃ mātugāmo, therassa eko kammavipāko”ti saññaṃ katvā paṭhamaṃ therassa samīpena gacchantopi theraṃ avanditvā tassa kāraṇassa abhūtabhāvaṃ ñatvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā theraṃ vanditvā ekamante [M 2.0051] nisinno “kacci, bhante, piṇḍakena na kilamathā”ti pucchi. Thero “vaṭṭati, mahārājā”ti āha. “Jānāmahaṃ, bhante, ayyassa kathaṃ, evarūpenupakkilesena saddhiṃ carantānaṃ tumhākaṃ ke nāma pasīdissanti, ito paṭṭhāya vo katthaci gamanakiccaṃ natthi. Ahaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahissāmi, tumhe yonisomanasikāre mā pamajjitthā”ti vatvā nibaddhabhikkhaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Thero rājānaṃ upatthambhakaṃ labhitvā bhojanasappāyena ekaggacitto hutvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tato paṭṭhāya sā itthī antaradhāyi.

The king, seeing her, thought, 'There must be a reason for this,' and went to the place where she was standing. As he approached, she seemed to enter the elder's leaf hut for dwelling. The king also entered the leaf hut with her, and looking everywhere but not seeing her, he perceived, 'This is no woman, but a karmic result of the elder.' At first, though passing near the elder, he did not pay homage. But having understood the unreality of that matter, he came out of the leaf hut, paid homage to the elder, and sitting to one side, asked, 'Venerable sir, are you not wearied by the alms-food?' The elder replied, 'It is sufficient, great king.' 'Venerable sir, I know your situation. How can anyone have faith in you while you associate with such a defilement? From now on, you have no need to go anywhere. I will provide you with the four requisites. Do not be heedless in wise attention.' Having spoken thus, he established a regular offering of alms-food. The elder, having obtained the king as a supporter, with his mind made one-pointed through suitable food, developed insight and attained arahantship. From that time onward, the woman disappeared.

Tadā mahāsubhaddā ugganagare micchādiṭṭhikule vasamānā “satthā maṃ anukampatū”ti uposathaṅgaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nirāmagandhā hutvā uparipāsādatale ṭhitā “imāni pupphāni antare aṭṭhatvā dasabalassa matthake vitānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhantu, dasabalo imāya saññāya sve pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatū”ti saccakiriyaṃ katvā aṭṭha sumanapupphamuṭṭhiyo vissajjesi. Pupphāni gantvā dhammadesanāvelāya satthu matthake vitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Satthā taṃ sumanapupphavitānaṃ disvā citteneva subhaddāya bhikkhaṃ adhivāsetvā punadivase aruṇe uṭṭhite [P 0.0355] ānandattheraṃ āha – “ānanda, mayaṃ ajja dūraṃ bhikkhācāraṃ gamissāma, puthujjanānaṃ adatvā ariyānaṃyeva salākaṃ dehī”ti. Thero bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi – “āvuso, satthā ajja dūraṃ bhikkhācāraṃ gamissati. Puthujjanā mā gaṇhantu, ariyāva salākaṃ gaṇhantū”ti. Kuṇḍadhānatthero – “āharāvuso, salāka”nti paṭhamaṃyeva hatthaṃ pasāresi. Ānando “satthā tādisānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ salākaṃ na dāpeti, ariyānaṃyeva dāpetī”ti vitakkaṃ uppādetvā gantvā satthu ārocesi. Satthā “āharāpentassa salākaṃ dehī”ti āha. Thero cintesi – “sace kuṇḍadhānassa salākā dātuṃ na yuttā, atha satthā paṭibāheyya, bhavissati ettha kāraṇa”nti “kuṇḍadhānassa salākaṃ dassāmī”ti gamanaṃ abhinīhari. Kuṇḍadhāno tassa purāgamanā eva abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā iddhiyā ākāse ṭhatvā “āharāvuso ānanda, satthā maṃ jānāti, mādisaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantaṃ na satthā vāretī”ti hatthaṃ pasāretvā salākaṃ gaṇhi. Satthā taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā theraṃ imasmiṃ sāsane paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Yasmā [M 2.0052] ayaṃ thero rājānaṃ upatthambhaṃ labhitvā sappāyāhārapaṭilābhena [V 2.0047] samāhitacitto vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto upanissayasampannatāya chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Evaṃbhūtassāpi imassa therassa guṇe ajānantā ye puthujjanā bhikkhū “ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ salākaṃ gaṇhati, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti vimatiṃ uppādenti. Tesaṃ taṃ vimatividhamanatthaṃ thero ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā aññāpadesena aññaṃ byākaronto “pañca chinde”ti gāthaṃ abhāsi.

At that time, Mahāsubhaddā, dwelling in a family of wrong views in the city of Ugga, undertook the Uposatha precepts, thinking, 'May the Teacher have compassion on me.' Becoming free from the scent of the worldly, she stood on the upper terrace of the palace and made an act of truth, saying: 'May these flowers, without stopping in between, form a canopy over the head of the Ten-Powered One and remain there. By this sign, may the Ten-Powered One, together with five hundred monks, accept my offering of alms-food tomorrow.' Having made this act of truth, she released eight handfuls of jasmine flowers. The flowers went and, at the time of the Dhamma discourse, formed a canopy over the Teacher’s head and remained there. The Teacher, seeing that jasmine flower canopy, consented by mind to Subhaddā’s alms-offering. The next day at the break of dawn, he said to the Venerable Ānanda, 'Ānanda, today we will go on a long alms-round. Do not give the tokens to the ordinary monks; give them only to the noble ones.' The elder announced to the monks: 'Venerable sirs, today the Teacher will go on a long alms-round. Let the ordinary monks not take the tokens; let only the noble ones take the tokens.' The Venerable Kuṇḍadhāna was the very first to extend his hand, saying, 'Bring the token, venerable sir.' Ānanda, thinking, 'The Teacher does not have tokens given to such monks; he has them given only to the noble ones,' went and informed the Teacher. The Teacher said, 'Give the token to him who is asking for it.' The elder reflected, 'If it were not proper to give the token to Kuṇḍadhāna, the Teacher would have forbidden it. There must be a reason for this.' He then set out to give the token to Kuṇḍadhāna. But even before his arrival, Kuṇḍadhāna entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for the higher knowledges, and standing in the air by his psychic power, said, 'Bring it, Venerable Ānanda. The Teacher knows me. The Teacher does not prevent a monk such as I from taking the first token.' Extending his hand, he took the token. The Teacher, making this the occasion, placed the elder in the foremost position among those who take the first token in this Dispensation. For this elder, having received the king's support and obtained suitable food, with a concentrated mind, while practicing the work of insight, became one possessed of the six higher knowledges due to the perfection of his supporting conditions. Yet, there were ordinary monks who, not knowing the qualities of this elder, even though he was such a one, gave rise to doubt, thinking, 'This one takes the first token. What can this be?' To dispel that doubt of theirs, the elder rose into the sky, displayed a marvel of psychic power, and while declaring his final knowledge by way of an allusion, spoke the verse beginning, 'Cut off five.'

1. Evaṃ so pūritapuññasambhārānurūpena arahā hutvā pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sattāhaṃ paṭisallīnantiādimāha. Tattha satthāhaṃ sattadivasaṃ nirodhasamāpattivihārena paṭisallīnaṃ vivekabhūtanti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

1. Thus, having become an Arahant in accordance with the accumulation of his merit, and having attained the foremost position, recalling his past deeds, he declared his former course of conduct with joy, saying, 'For seven days I dwelt in seclusion,' and so on. Therein, 'for seven days I dwelt in seclusion' means he remained secluded for seven days in the abiding of the attainment of cessation. The rest is of clear meaning.

Kuṇḍadhānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna is complete.

2. Sāgatattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Sāgata

Sobhito nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato sāgatattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato [P 0.0356] kāle ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto nāmena sobhito nāma hutvā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ sākkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ padako veyyākaraṇo lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo. So ekadivasaṃ padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasiriyā sobhamānaṃ uyyānadvārena gacchantaṃ disvā atīva pasannamānaso anekehi upāyehi anekehi guṇavaṇṇehi thomanaṃ akāsi. Bhagavā tassa thomanaṃ sutvā “anāgate gotamassa bhagavato sāsane sāgato nāma sāvako bhavissatī”ti byākaraṇaṃ adāsi. So tato paṭṭhāya puññāni karonto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto. Kappasatasahassadevamanussesu ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto. Tassa mātāpitaro [M 2.0053] somanassaṃ vaḍḍhento sujāto āgatoti sāgatoti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So sāsane pasīditvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patto.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Sāgata Thera, beginning with 'Sobhito nāma nāmena.' This one too, having established a foundation of merit under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a supporting condition for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born in a brahmin family, having attained mastery in all arts. Known by the name Sobhito, he became a master of the three Vedas, along with the Nighaṇḍu, Keṭubha, and the divisions of phonetics, with the Itihāsa as the fifth; he was a reciter of the Pada text, a grammarian, and flawless in the Lokāyata and the marks of a great man. One day, seeing the Blessed One Padumuttara—resplendent with the glory of the thirty-two marks of a great man—passing through the garden gate, his mind became exceedingly serene.
