He praised him with many methods and with many descriptions of his virtues. Hearing his praise, the Blessed One gave a prediction: 'In the future, during the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama, there will be a disciple named Sāgata.' From then on, performing meritorious deeds and living out his lifespan, he passed away and was reborn in the deva world. After experiencing the twofold prosperities of devas and humans for one hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in a family household at the arising of this Buddha. His parents, increasing their joy, named him Sāgata, thinking, 'A well-born one has come.' Having gained faith in the Dispensation, he went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship.

17. Evaṃ so puññasambhārānurūpena pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto [V 2.0048] pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sobhito nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Tattha tadā puññasambhārassa paripūraṇasamaye nāmena sobhito nāma brāhmaṇo ahosinti sambandho.

17. Thus, having attained the fruit of arahantship in accordance with his accumulation of merit, he recollected his past deeds and, filled with joy, proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'Sobhito nāma nāmena.' Here, the connection is to be understood thus: at that time, when the accumulation of merit was fulfilled, there was a brahmin named Sobhito.

21. Vipathā uddharitvānāti viruddhapathā kumaggā, uppathā vā uddharitvā apanetvā. Pathaṃ ācikkhaseti, bhante, sabbaññu tuvaṃ pathaṃ sappurisamaggaṃ nibbānādhigamanupāyaṃ ācikkhase kathesi desesi vibhaji uttāniṃ akāsīti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

21. 'Having lifted from the wrong paths' means: having lifted up from and removed the opposing paths, the bad paths, or the wrong paths. 'You show the path' means: 'Venerable sir, All-Knowing One, you show the path—the path of good people, the means for attaining Nibbāna—you told of it, taught it, analyzed it, and made it manifest.' This is the meaning. The rest is clear in meaning.

Sāgatattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sāgata is concluded.

3. Mahākaccānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākaccāna

Padumuttaranāthassātiādikaṃ āyasmato kaccānattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle gahapatimahāsālakulagehe nibbattetvā vuddhippatto ekadivasaṃ satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ [P 0.0357] disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento dānādīni puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle vijjādharo hutvā ākāsena gacchanto satthāraṃ ekasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nisinnaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kaṇikārapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kaccāna, beginning with 'Padumuttaranāthassa.' This one too, having established a foundation of merit under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences as a supporting condition for liberation, was born in the household of a wealthy householder during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara and reached maturity. One day, while listening to the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among those who analyze in detail the meaning of what was spoken concisely. Aspiring for that same position himself, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and wandered among devas and humans. In the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he became a knowledge-holder and, while traveling through the sky, saw the Teacher seated in a forest grove. With a serene mind, he made an offering with kaṇikāra flowers.

So tena puññakammena aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva parivattetvā kassapadasabalassa kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ kulaghare nibbattitvā parinibbute bhagavati suvaṇṇacetiyakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ dasasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇiṭṭhakāya pūjaṃ katvā “bhagavā mayhaṃ nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne sarīraṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ hotū”ti pattharaṃ akāsi. Tato yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu [M 2.0054] saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ujjeniyaṃ rañño caṇḍapajjotassa purohitassa gehe nibbatti, tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase mātāpitaro “amhākaṃ putto suvaṇṇavaṇṇo attano nāmaṃ gahetvā āgato”ti kañcanamāṇavotveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vuddhimanvāya tayo vede uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena purohitaṭṭhānaṃ labhi. So gottavasena kaccānoti paññāyittha.

Through that meritorious deed, being reborn again and again only in happy destinations, during the time of Kassapa of the ten powers, he was born into a family of good standing in Bārāṇasī. After the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, at the place where a golden cetiya was being built, he made an offering of a golden brick worth ten thousand and made this aspiration: 'Venerable Sir, in whatever place I am reborn, may my body have a golden complexion.' Thereafter, having performed wholesome deeds for as long as he lived and having wandered among devas and humans for one Buddha-interval, at the arising of this Buddha, he was born in Ujjenī in the house of the chaplain to King Caṇḍapajjota. On his naming day, his parents thought, 'Our son has a golden complexion; he has come having taken his own name,' and so they named him Kañcanamāṇava. Upon reaching maturity, he learned the three Vedas, and on the passing of his father, he received the position of chaplain. By his clan name, he was known as Kaccāna.

Rājā caṇḍapajjoto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā, “ācariya, tvaṃ tattha gantvā satthāraṃ idhānehī”ti [V 2.0049] pesesi. So attaṭṭhamo satthu santikaṃ upagato. Tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi. Desanāpariyosāne so sattahi janehi saddhiṃ sahapaṭisambhidāhi arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Atha satthā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Te tāvadeva dvaṅgulamattakesamassukā iddhimayapattacīvaradharā vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya ahesuṃ. Evaṃ thero sadatthaṃ nipphādetvā, “bhante, rājā pajjoto tumhākaṃ pāde vandituṃ dhammañca sotuṃ icchatī”ti satthu ārocesi. Satthā “tvaṃyeva bhikkhu tattha gaccha, tayi gatepi rājā pasīdissatī”ti āha. Thero attaṭṭhamo tattha gantvā rājānaṃ pasādetvā avantīsu sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā puna satthu santikameva gato.

King Caṇḍapajjota, hearing of the Buddha's arising, sent him, saying: 'Teacher, go there and bring the Teacher here.' He, as the eighth, approached the Teacher. The Teacher taught them the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, he, together with the seven others, was established in arahantship with the analytical knowledges. Then the Teacher stretched out his hand, saying, 'Come, monks.' At that very moment, they became like elders of sixty years' standing, with hair and beard two fingers' breadth long, bearing robes and bowls created by psychic power. Thus, the elder, having accomplished his own welfare, informed the Teacher: 'Venerable sir, King Pajjota wishes to pay homage at your feet and to hear the Dhamma.' The Teacher said: 'You yourself go there, monk. When you have gone, the king will gain faith.' The elder, as the eighth, went there, inspired faith in the king, established the Dispensation in the Avanti country, and then returned to the Teacher.

31. Evaṃ so pattaarahattaphalo “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākaccāno”ti (a. ni. 1.188, 197) etadaggaṭṭhānaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaranāthassātiādimāha. Tattha padumaṃ nāma cetiyanti padumehi chāditattā vā padumākārehi katattā vā bhagavato vasanagandhakuṭivihārova pūjanīyabhāvena cetiyaṃ, yathā “gotamakacetiyaṃ, āḷavakacetiya”nti vutte tesaṃ yakkhānaṃ nivasanaṭṭhānaṃ pūjanīyaṭṭhānattā [P 0.0358] cetiyanti vuccati, evamidaṃ bhagavato vasanaṭṭhānaṃ cetiyanti vuccati, na dhātunidhāyakacetiyanti veditabbaṃ. Na hi aparinibbutassa bhagavato sarīradhātūnaṃ abhāvā dhātucetiyaṃ akari. Silāsanaṃ kārayitvāti tassā padumanāmikāya gandhakuṭiyā pupphādhāratthāya heṭṭhā phalikamayaṃ silāsanaṃ kāretvā. Suvaṇṇenābhilepayinti taṃ silāsanaṃ jambonadasuvaṇṇena abhivisesena lepayiṃ chādesinti attho.

3. Thus, having attained the fruit of arahantship, and having reached the foremost position—‘Monks, among my disciples who explain in detail the meaning of what has been stated briefly, Mahākaccāna is the foremost’—he, recollecting his past deeds, proclaimed his former conduct, speaking verses beginning with, ‘To the Lord Padumuttara...’ Therein, ‘a shrine named Paduma’ means that the Blessed One’s dwelling, the fragrant hut-monastery, is itself a shrine on account of being a place of veneration, either because it was covered with lotuses or because it was made in the shape of a lotus. Just as when ‘the Gotamaka shrine’ or ‘the Āḷavaka shrine’ is mentioned, the dwelling place of those yakkhas is called a shrine because it is a place of veneration, so too this dwelling place of the Blessed One is called a shrine. It should be understood that this is not a shrine for the enshrinement of relics. Indeed, he did not make a relic-shrine, due to the absence of the Blessed One’s bodily relics, as he had not yet attained final Nibbāna. ‘Having had a stone seat made’ means having had a crystal stone seat made beneath that fragrant hut named Paduma for the purpose of holding flowers. ‘I anointed it with gold’ means I especially anointed that stone seat with gold from the Jambu river; that is, I covered it.

32. Ratanāmayaṃ [M 2.0055] sattahi ratanehi kataṃ chattaṃ paggayha muddhani dhāretvā vāḷabījaniñca setapavaracāmariñca paggayha buddhassa abhiropayiṃ. Lokabandhussa tādinoti sakalalokabandhusadisassa tādiguṇasamaṅgissa buddhassa dhāresinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

1. ‘A jeweled parasol,’ made of seven kinds of gems, I raised and held over his head; and raising a yak-tail fan and an excellent white chowrie, I offered them to the Buddha. ‘For the Kinsman of the World, the Such-one’ means I held them for the Buddha, who was like a kinsman to the whole world and was endowed with the quality of being ‘Such.’ The rest has an obvious meaning.

Mahākaccānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

9. The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākaccāna is concluded.

4. Kāḷudāyittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kāḷudāyī

Padumuttarabuddhassātiādikaṃ āyasmato kāḷudāyittherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro [V 2.0050] tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ kulappasādakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā tajjaṃ abhinīhāraṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthesi.

10. The Apadāna of the Venerable Kāḷudāyī begins with the words, ‘Of the Buddha Padumuttara...’ He also, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that would serve as a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in a family household in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher place a certain monk in the foremost position among monks who inspire faith in families. Seeing this, he made an aspiration for that same attainment and longed for that position.

So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bodhisattassa mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase kapilavatthusmiṃyeva amaccagehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, bodhisattena saddhiṃ ekadivasaṃyeva jātoti taṃ divasaṃyeva naṃ dukūlacumbaṭake nipajjāpetvā bodhisattassa upaṭṭhānatthāya nayiṃsu. Bodhisattena hi saddhiṃ bodhirukkho, rāhulamātā, cattāro nidhī, ārohanahatthī, assakaṇḍako, ānando, channo, kāḷudāyīti ime satta ekadivase jātattā sahajātā nāma ahesuṃ. Athassa nāmaggahaṇadivase sakalanagarassa udaggacittadivase jātattā udāyitveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Thokaṃ kāḷadhātukattā pana kāḷudāyīti paññāyittha. So bodhisattena saddhiṃ kumārakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vuddhiṃ agamāsi.

4. He, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering among gods and humans, took rebirth in a minister’s household in Kapilavatthu itself on the very day that our Bodhisatta took conception in his mother’s womb. He was born on the very same day as the Bodhisatta, and on that day they laid him on a fine cloth and brought him to attend upon the Bodhisatta. Indeed, along with the Bodhisatta, the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four great treasures, the state elephant, the horse Kaṇḍaka, Ānanda, Channa, and Kāḷudāyī—these seven were born on the same day and were thus called the ‘Co-natals.’ Then, on his naming day, because it was a day of great joy for the entire city, they gave him the name Udāyī. However, because he was of a slightly dark complexion, he became known as Kāḷudāyī. Playing children’s games with the Bodhisatta, he grew to maturity.

Aparabhāge lokanāthe mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā anukkamena sabbaññutaṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakke rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane viharante suddhodanamahārājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā [P 0.0359] purisasahassaparivāraṃ ekaṃ [M 2.0056] amaccaṃ “puttaṃ me idhānehī”ti pesesi. So dhammadesanāvelāyaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ sutvā saparivāro arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha ne satthā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Sabbe taṅkhaṇaññeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya ahesuṃ. Arahattappattito paṭṭhāya pana ariyā majjhattāva honti. Tasmā raññā pahitasāsanaṃ dasabalassa na kathesi. Rājā “neva gato āgacchati, na sāsanaṃ suyyatī”ti aparaṃ amaccaṃ purisasahassehi pesesi. Tasmimpi tathā paṭipanne aparampi pesesīti evaṃ navahi purisasahassehi saddhiṃ nava amacce pesesi. Sabbe arahattaṃ patvā tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

Later, when the Lord of the World, having gone forth in the Great Renunciation and gradually attained omniscience, setting in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, was dwelling near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, King Suddhodana heard of this event. He sent a minister with a retinue of a thousand men, saying, “Bring my son here.” Arriving at the time of the Dhamma discourse, he stood at the edge of the assembly, heard the Dhamma, and together with his retinue attained arahantship. Then the Teacher stretched out his hand, saying, “Come, monks.” Instantly, they all had robes and bowls created by psychic power, appearing like elders of sixty rainy seasons. From the moment of attaining arahantship, however, the noble ones are always neutral. Therefore, he did not convey the king’s message to the One with Ten Powers. The king, thinking, “The one who went does not return, nor is any message heard,” sent another minister with a thousand men. When the same happened to him, he sent yet another. In this way, he sent nine ministers with nine thousand men. All attained arahantship and remained silent.

Atha rājā cintesi – “ettakā janā mayi sinehābhāvena dasabalassa idhāgamanatthāya na kiñci kathayiṃsu, ayaṃ kho udāyi dasabalena samavayo, sahapaṃsukīḷiko, mayi ca sineho atthi, imaṃ pesessāmī”ti taṃ pakkosāpetvā, “tāta, tvaṃ purisasahassaparivāro rājagahaṃ gantvā dasabalaṃ idhānehī”ti vatvā pesesi. So pana gacchanto “sacāhaṃ, deva, pabbajituṃ labhissāmi, evāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ idhānessāmī”ti vatvā “yaṃ kiñci katvā mama puttaṃ dassehī”ti vutto rājagahaṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanavelāyaṃ parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ sutvā saparivāro [V 2.0051] arahattaṃ patvā ehibhikkhubhāve patiṭṭhāsi. Arahattaṃ pana patvā “na tāvāyaṃ dasabalassa kulanagaraṃ gantuṃ kālo, vasante pana upagate pupphite vanasaṇḍe haritatiṇasañchannāya bhūmiyā gamanakālo bhavissatī”ti kālaṃ paṭimānento vasante sampatte satthu kulanagaraṃ gantuṃ gamanamaggavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇento –

Then the king thought: “So many people, lacking affection for me, have said nothing to bring the One with Ten Powers here. But this Udāyī is of the same age as the One with Ten Powers, a childhood playmate, and he has affection for me. I will send him.” Having summoned him, he said, “My dear, go to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the One with Ten Powers here,” and sent him off. But Udāyī, before departing, said, “If, Your Majesty, I am able to receive the going forth, only then will I bring the Blessed One here.” And being told by the king, “By whatever means, show me my son,” he went to Rājagaha. Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he heard the Dhamma and, together with his retinue, attained arahantship and was established in the state of an ehi-bhikkhu. Having attained arahantship, however, he thought, “It is not yet time for the One with Ten Powers to go to his ancestral city. But when spring arrives, when the groves are in bloom and the ground is covered with fresh green grass, that will be the time to go.” Waiting for the right time, when spring arrived, he praised the beauty of the path for the journey to the Teacher’s ancestral city, saying:

“Aṅgārino dāni dumā bhadante, phalesino chadanaṃ vippahāya;

Te accimantova pabhāsayanti, samayo mahāvīra bhāgī rathānaṃ.

“Now, venerable sir, the trees are like glowing embers; having shed their foliage, they seek to bear fruit. They blaze as if with flame. O Great Hero, it is time for your kinsmen, the Sakyans.”

“Dumāni phullāni manoramāni, samantato sabbadisā pavanti;

Pattaṃ pahāya phalamāsasānā, kālo ito pakkamanāya vīra.

“The trees, delightful and in full bloom, waft their fragrance in every direction. Having shed their leaves, they await their fruit. O Hero, it is time to depart from here.”

“Nevātisītaṃ [M 2.0057][P 0.0360] na panātiuṇhaṃ, sukhā utu addhaniyā bhadante;

Passantu taṃ sākiyā koḷiyā ca, pacchāmukhaṃ rohiniyaṃ tarantaṃ.

“It is neither too cold nor too hot; the season is pleasant for a journey, venerable sir. Let the Sakyans and the Koliyans see you crossing the Rohinī river, facing west.”

“Āsāya kasate khettaṃ, bījaṃ āsāya vappati;

Āsāya vāṇijā yanti, samuddaṃ dhanahārakā;

Yāya āsāya tiṭṭhāmi, sā me āsā samijjhatu. (theragā. 527-530);

“With hope the farmer plows the field, with hope he sows the seed; with hope the merchants, seeking wealth, travel across the sea. The hope on which I stand—may that hope of mine be fulfilled.”

“Nātisītaṃ nātiuṇhaṃ, nātidubbhikkhachātakaṃ;

Saddalā haritā bhūmi, esa kālo mahāmuni. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.225);

“It is not too cold, nor is it too hot; there is no famine or want. The earth is green with fresh grass; this is the time, O Great Sage.”

“Punappunañceva vapanti bījaṃ, punappunaṃ vassati devarājā;

Punappunaṃ khettaṃ kasanti kassakā, punappunaṃ dhaññamupeti raṭṭhaṃ.

“Again and again they sow the seed; again and again the King of Devas sends the rain. Again and again the farmers plow the field; again and again the kingdom obtains grain.”

“Punappunaṃ yācanakā caranti, punappunaṃ dānappatī dadanti;

Punappunaṃ dānappatī daditvā, punappunaṃ saggamupenti ṭhānaṃ.

“Again and again the mendicants wander; again and again the patrons give. Having given again and again, the patrons go again and again to a heavenly state.”

“Vīro [V 2.0052] have sattayugaṃ puneti, yasmiṃ kule jāyati bhūripañño;

Maññāmahaṃ sakkati devadevo, tayā hi jāto muni saccanāmo.

“A hero of great wisdom, indeed, purifies seven generations in the family where he is born. I consider you, O Sakyan, the God of gods! For through you I have been born a sage, true to the name.”

“Suddhodano nāma pitā mahesino, buddhassa mātā pana māyanāmā;

Yā bodhisattaṃ parihariya kucchinā, kāyassa bhedā tidivamhi modati.

“Suddhodana was the name of the Great Seer’s father, and the Buddha’s mother was named Māyā. Having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, at the breaking up of the body, she rejoices in the heaven of the Thirty-three.”

“Sā gotamī kālakatā ito cutā, dibbehi kāmehi samaṅgibhūtā;

Sā modati kāmaguṇehi pañcahi, parivāritā devagaṇehi tehī”ti. (theragā. 531-535);

“That Gotamī, having passed away and fallen from this world, is endowed with divine sensual pleasures. Surrounded by those hosts of devas, she rejoices in the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

Imā [M 2.0058] gāthā abhāsi. Tattha aṅgārinoti aṅgārāni viyāti aṅgārāni. Aṅgārāni rattapavāḷavaṇṇāni rukkhānaṃ pupphaphalāni, tāni etesaṃ santīti [P 0.0361] aṅgārino, abhilohitakusumakisalayehi aṅgāravuṭṭhisamparikiṇṇā viyāti attho. Dānīti imasmiṃ kāle. Dumāti rukkhā. Bhadanteti bhaddaṃ ante etassāti, “bhadante”ti ekassa da-kārassa lopaṃ katvā vuccati. Guṇavisesayutto, guṇavisesayuttānañca aggabhūto satthā. Tasmā, bhadanteti satthu ālapanameva, paccattavacanañcetaṃ ekārantaṃ “sugate paṭikamme sukhe dukkhe jīve”tiādīsu viya. Idha pana sambodhanaṭṭhe daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ, “bhadanteti ālapana”nti. “Bhaddasaddena samānatthaṃ padantarameka”nti keci. Phalāni esantīti phalesino. Acetanepi hi sacetanakiriyaṃ āha. Evaṃ therena yācito bhagavā tattha gamane bahūnaṃ visesādhigamanaṃ disvā vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto rājagahato aturitacārikāvasena kapilavatthugāmimaggaṃ paṭipajji. Thero iddhiyā kapilavatthuṃ gantvā rañño purato ākāse ṭhitova adiṭṭhapubbavesaṃ disvā raññā “kosi tva”nti pucchito “amaccaputtaṃ tayā bhagavato santikaṃ pesitaṃ maṃ na jānāsi, tvaṃ evaṃ pana jānāhī”ti dassento –

He spoke these verses. Therein, `aṅgārino` means 'like embers.' The flowers and fruits of the trees are like embers, red as coral. Because these belong to them, they are called `aṅgārino`, meaning they are as if strewn with a shower of embers amidst very red blossoms and young leaves. `Dāni` means 'at this time.' `Dumā` means 'trees.' `Bhadante` is formed from `bhaddaṃ ante etassāti` by eliding one `da-kāra`. It refers to the Teacher, who is endowed with special qualities and is the foremost among those endowed with special qualities. Therefore, `bhadante` is an address to the Teacher. It is a nominative singular ending in 'e', used as a vocative, as in such cases as `sugate`, `paṭikamme`, `sukhe`, `dukkhe`, and `jīve`. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of a vocative address. Thus it is said, '`bhadante` is an address.' Some say it is another word with the same meaning as `bhadda`. `Phalesino` means 'they seek fruits.' For here an action of a sentient being is ascribed to a non-sentient thing. Thus requested by the elder, the Blessed One, seeing that many would attain special realization if he went there, set out from Rājagaha, surrounded by twenty thousand destroyers of the cankers, and took the road to Kapilavatthu, journeying at a measured pace. The elder went to Kapilavatthu by his psychic power and stood in the air before the king. Seeing a form he had never seen before, the king asked, 'Who are you?' Being so asked, the elder, indicating, 'Do you not recognize me, the minister's son whom you sent to the Blessed One? You should know it thus,' said:

“Buddhassa puttomhi asayhasāhino, aṅgīrasassappaṭimassa tādino;

Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsi sakka, dhammena me gotama ayyakosī”ti. (theragā. 536) –

“I am a son of the Buddha, the endurer of the unendurable, of Aṅgīrasa, the Incomparable, the steadfast one. You, O Sakka, are the father of my Father; O Gotama, through the Dhamma, you are my grandfather.” (Theragāthā 536)

Gāthamāha.

He spoke the verse.

Tattha [V 2.0053] buddhassa puttomhīti sabbaññubuddhassa orassa putto amhi. Asayhasāhinoti abhisambodhito pubbe ṭhapetvā mahābodhisattaṃ aññehi sahituṃ vahituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā asayhassa sakalassa bodhisambhārassa mahākāruṇikādhikārassa ca sahanato vahanato, tato parampi aññehi sahituṃ abhibhavituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā asayhānaṃ pañcannaṃ mārānaṃ sahanato abhibhavanato, āsayānusayacaritādhimuttiādivibhāgāvabodhanena yathārahaṃ veneyyānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi anusāsanīsaṅkhātassa aññehi asayhassa buddhakiccassa [M 2.0059] sahanato, tattha vā sādhukāribhāvato asayhasāhino. Aṅgīrasassāti aṅgīkatasīlādisampattikassa. Aṅgamaṅgehi niccharaṇakaobhāsassāti apare. Keci pana “aṅgīraso, siddhatthoti dve nāmāni pitarāyeva gahitānī”ti vadanti. Appaṭimassāti anūpamassa. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu tādilakkhaṇappattiyā [P 0.0362] tādino. Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsīti ariyajātivasena mayhaṃ pitu sammāsambuddhassa lokavohārena tvaṃ pitā asi. Sakkāti jātivasena rājānaṃ ālapati. Dhammenāti sabhāvena ariyajāti lokiyajātīti dvinnaṃ jātīnaṃ sabhāvasamodhānena. Gotamāti rājānaṃ gottena ālapati. Ayyakosīti pitāmaho asi. Ettha ca “buddhassa puttomhī”tiādiṃ vadanto thero aññaṃ byākāsi.

Therein, 'I am a son of the Buddha' means: I am the true-born son of the Omniscient Buddha. 'Of the endurer of the unendurable': because, before his full enlightenment, he endured and bore the entire accumulation for enlightenment and the aspiration of great compassion, which was unendurable and unsupportable for any other than the Great Bodhisatta; and because, after that, he endured and overcame the five Māras, who are unendurable and unconquerable by others; and because he endured the Buddha's task, called 'instruction,' which is unendurable by others, whereby he teaches the disciples according to their needs through his understanding of the divisions of their inclinations, latent tendencies, characters, dispositions, and so on, for their benefit in this life, in the next, and in the ultimate sense; or else, because of his excellence in performing these tasks, he is the endurer of the unendurable. 'Of Aṅgīrasa': of one who has undertaken the accomplishment of virtue and so forth. Others say it means 'of one whose radiance issues from his every limb.' Some, however, say that 'Aṅgīrasa' and 'Siddhattha' are two names given by his father. 'Of the Incomparable': of one who is without equal. 'Of the steadfast one': of one who has attained the characteristic of steadfastness amidst the agreeable and disagreeable. 'You are the father of my Father': by way of noble birth, you are, in worldly convention, the father of my Father, the Perfectly Enlightened One. 'O Sakka': he addresses the king by his lineage. 'Through the Dhamma': by nature, through the harmonious combination of the two births, the noble birth and the worldly birth. 'O Gotama': he addresses the king by his clan name. 'You are my grandfather': you are my grandfather. And here, the elder, in saying, 'I am a son of the Buddha,' and so forth, was making an indirect declaration of his identity.

Evaṃ pana attānaṃ jānāpetvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhena raññā mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā attano paṭiyāditassa nānaggarasabhojanassa pattaṃ pūretvā dinne gamanākāraṃ dassesi. “Kasmā, bhante, gantukāmattha, bhuñjathā”ti ca vutte, “satthu santikaṃ gantvā bhuñjissāmī”ti. “Kahaṃ pana satthā”ti? “Vīsatisahassabhikkhuparivāro tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya maggaṃ paṭipanno”ti. “Tumhe imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjatha, aññaṃ bhagavato harissatha. Yāva ca mama putto imaṃ nagaraṃ sampāpuṇāti, tāvassa ito piṇḍapātaṃ harathā”ti vutte thero bhattakiccaṃ katvā rañño parisāya ca dhammaṃ kathetvā satthu āgamanato puretarameva sakalarājanivesanaṃ ratanattaye abhippasannaṃ karonto sabbesaṃ passantānaṃyeva satthu āharitabbabhattapuṇṇaṃ pattaṃ ākāse vissajjetvā sayampi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā piṇḍapātaṃ upanāmetvā satthu hatthe ṭhapesi. Satthā taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñji. Evaṃ saṭṭhiyojanamagge divase divase yojanaṃ gacchantassa bhagavato rājagehatoyeva piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Atha naṃ bhagavā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ pituno sakalanivesanaṃ pasādetī”ti “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ kulappasādakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yadidaṃ kāḷudāyī”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 225) kulappasādakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

Having thus made himself known, the elder was seated on a magnificent couch by the delighted and overjoyed king. When the king had filled a bowl with various delicious foods prepared for himself and given it to him, the elder showed signs of wishing to leave. When asked, 'Why, venerable sir, do you wish to go? Please eat,' he replied, 'I will go to the Teacher's presence and eat.' 'But where is the Teacher?' 'He is on his way to see you, accompanied by twenty thousand monks.' When the king said, 'You eat this almsfood. And until my son arrives in this city, you are to bring almsfood from here for him,' the elder, having finished his meal and taught the Dhamma to the king and his assembly, made the entire royal household deeply devoted to the Triple Gem even before the Teacher's arrival. Then, before the very eyes of all, he released the bowl filled with food that was to be brought to the Teacher into the sky and, rising into the air himself, he presented the almsfood, placing it in the Teacher's hands. The Teacher partook of that almsfood. In this way, as the Blessed One traveled one yojana each day along the sixty-yojana road, the elder brought almsfood from the royal palace and gave it to him. Then the Blessed One, considering, 'This one inspires faith in my father's entire household,' placed him in the foremost position among those who inspire faith in families, declaring: 'Monks, foremost among my disciples, the monks who inspire faith in families, is this Kāḷudāyī.'

48-9. Evaṃ so katapuññasambhārānurūpena arahattaṃ patvā pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ [V 2.0054] saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ [M 2.0060] pakāsento padumuttarassa buddhassātiādimāha. Addhānaṃ paṭipannassāti apararaṭṭhaṃ gamanatthāya dūramaggaṃ paṭipajjantassa. Carato cārikaṃ tadāti antomaṇḍalaṃ majjhemaṇḍalaṃ bahimaṇḍalanti tīṇi maṇḍalāni tadā cārikaṃ carato carantassa padumuttarabuddhassa bhagavato suphullaṃ suṭṭhu phullaṃ pabodhitaṃ gayha gahetvā na kevalameva padumaṃ, uppalañca mallikaṃ vikasitaṃ ahaṃ gayha ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā pūresinti sambandho. Paramannaṃ gahetvānāti paramaṃ uttamaṃ seṭṭhaṃ madhuraṃ sabbasupakkaṃ sāliodanaṃ gahetvā satthuno adāsiṃ bhojesinti attho.

48-49. Thus, having attained arahantship in accordance with his accumulation of merit, and having reached the foremost position, he, remembering his past deeds, joyfully revealed the story of his past conduct, beginning with 'To the Buddha Padumuttara...' and so forth. 'To one proceeding on a long journey' means to one proceeding on a distant path for the purpose of going to another country. 'To one wandering on tour at that time' means: at that time, while the Blessed One, the Buddha Padumuttara, was wandering on tour in the three regions—the inner region, the middle region, and the outer region—I took a fully bloomed, splendidly opened, awakened lotus. The connection is that I took not only a lotus, but also a blossoming blue water lily and jasmine, and holding them with both hands, I made an offering. 'Having taken the finest food' means: having taken the supreme, excellent, foremost, sweet, fully cooked rice, I gave it to the Teacher and fed him.

97. Sakyānaṃ [P 0.0363] nandijananoti sakyarājakulānaṃ bhagavato ñātīnaṃ ārohapariṇāharūpayobbanavacanālapanasampattiyā nandaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ janento uppādento. Ñātibandhu bhavissatīti ñāto pākaṭo bandhu bhavissati. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

97. 'Bringing joy to the Sakyans' means bringing forth and generating joy and delight in the Sakyan royal families, the Blessed One's relatives, by means of their attainment of stature, proportion, beauty, youth, speech, and eloquence. 'He will be a kinsman' means he will be a known and renowned kinsman. The rest is easily understood.

Kāḷudāyittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kāḷudāyī is complete.

5. Mogharājattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mogharāja

Atthadassī tu bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato mogharājattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ ākaṅkhanto paṇidhānaṃ katvā tattha tattha bhave puññāni karonto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle puna brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato ekadivasaṃ atthadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ rathiyaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā sirasi añjaliṃ katvā “yāvatā rūpino satthā”tiādīhi chahi gāthāhi abhitthavitvā bhājanaṃ pūretvā madhuṃ upanesi. Satthā taṃ paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapabhagavato kāle kaṭṭhavāhanassa nāma rañño amacco hutvā nibbatto tena satthu ānayanatthāya [M 2.0061] pesito satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vīsativassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ katvā tato cuto ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ sugatīsuyeva parivattento imasmiṃ buddhuppāde brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā mogharājāti laddhanāmo bāvarīyabrāhmaṇassa [V 2.0055] santike uggahitasippo saṃvegajāto tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tāpasasahassaparivāro ajitādīhi saddhiṃ satthu santikaṃ pesito tesaṃ pannarasamo hutvā pañhaṃ pucchitvā vissajjanapariyosāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahattaṃ pana patvā satthalūkhaṃ suttalūkhaṃ rajanalūkhanti visesena tividhenapi lūkhena samannāgataṃ paṃsukūlaṃ dhāresi. Tena naṃ satthā lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

Beginning with 'Atthadassī, the Blessed One,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Mogharāja. He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that served as a condition for liberation in various existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the Teacher’s presence, he saw the Teacher placing a certain monk in the foremost position among those who wore coarse robes. Desiring that eminent position, he made a resolution and performed meritorious deeds in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn again in a brahmin family and attained proficiency in the brahmins' sciences and arts. One day, seeing the Blessed One Atthadassī walking on the street surrounded by the Sangha of monks, with a mind full of faith, he paid homage with the five-point prostration, placed his joined hands on his head, and extolled him with six verses beginning, “As far as there are teachers with form…” Having filled a vessel, he offered honey. The Teacher accepted it and gave a blessing of appreciation. Through that meritorious deed, while wandering through the round of rebirths among devas and humans, he was reborn during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa as a minister to a king named Kaṭṭhavāhana. Sent by that king to bring the Teacher, he went to the Teacher’s presence, listened to the Dhamma, and, having gained faith, went forth. He practiced the ascetic's duties for twenty thousand years. Passing away from there, he spent one Buddha-interval revolving only in happy destinations. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a brahmin family and received the name Mogharāja. Having learned the arts under the brahmin Bāvarī, he became filled with spiritual urgency, undertook the ascetic life, and had a following of a thousand ascetics. He was sent with Ajita and others to the Teacher’s presence, and being the fifteenth among them, he asked a question. At the conclusion of the answer, he attained arahantship. Having attained arahantship, he wore rag-robes that were specifically coarse in three ways: coarse in material, coarse in thread, and coarse in dye. For this reason, the Teacher placed him in the foremost position among those who wore coarse robes.

64. Evaṃ [P 0.0364] so paṇidhānānurūpena arahattaphalaṃ patvā attano pubbasambhāraṃ disvā pubbakammāpadānaṃ pakāsento atthadassī tu bhagavātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthameva.

64. Thus, having attained the fruit of arahantship in accordance with his aspiration, and seeing his past accumulation of merit, he declared this account of his past deeds, beginning with 'Atthadassī, the Blessed One.' All of this has a clear meaning.

73. Puṭakaṃ pūrayitvānāti puṭakaṃ vuccati vārakaṃ, ghaṭaṃ vā. Aneḷakaṃ niddosaṃ makkhikaṇḍavirahitaṃ khuddamadhunā ghaṭaṃ pūretvā taṃ ubhohi hatthehi paggayha pakārena ādarena gahetvā mahesino bhagavato upanesinti sambandho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

73. 'Having filled a container…' A 'container' (puṭaka) refers to a vessel (vāraka) or a pot (ghaṭa). The connection is as follows: having filled a pot with honey from small bees that was pure, flawless, and free from bee larvae, and lifting it with both hands, taking it with care and respect, he offered it to the Great Sage, the Blessed One. The rest is easily understood.

Mogharājattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mogharāja is complete.

6. Adhimuttattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Adhimutta

Nibbute lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato adhimuttattherassa apadānaṃ (theragā. aṭṭha. 2.adhimuttattheragāthāvaṇṇanā). Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassimhi lokanāthe parinibbute ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto ratanattaye pasanno bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā ucchūhi maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā pariyosāne santipadaṃ paṇidhesi. So tato cuto devesu ca manussesu ca ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto sāsane pasīditvā saddhāya patiṭṭhitattā adhimuttattheroti pākaṭo.

Beginning with 'When the Leader of the World had attained Nibbāna,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Adhimutta (Theragāthā Commentary 2, Commentary on the Verses of Elder Adhimutta). He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that served as a condition for liberation in various existences, was reborn in a certain good family after the World-Leader Atthadassī had attained final Nibbāna. With faith in the Triple Gem, he invited the community of monks, had a pavilion made with sugar cane, held a great almsgiving, and at its conclusion, he aspired for the state of peace. Passing away from there, he experienced the prosperities of both devas and humans. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a good family, gained faith in the teaching, and, because he was established in faith, he became known as the Elder Adhimutta.

84. Evaṃ [M 2.0062] katasambhāravasena arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

84. Thus, having attained arahantship by the power of his accumulated merit, recollecting his past deeds, and with joy arisen in him, he declared his former course of conduct, beginning with 'When the Leader of the World had attained Nibbāna.' All of this has a clear meaning.

Adhimuttattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Adhimutta is complete.

7. Lasuṇadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Lasuṇadāyaka

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ [V 2.0056] āyasmato lasuṇadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Esopāyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ disvā gehaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantaṃ nissāya vane vasanto bahūni lasuṇāni ropetvā tadeva vanamūlaphalañca khādanto vihāsi. So bahūni lasuṇāni kājenādāya manussapathaṃ āharitvā pasanno dānaṃ datvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa bhesajjatthāya datvā gacchati. Evaṃ so yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā teneva puññabalena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiṃ anubhavitvā kamena imasmiṃ buddhuppāde uppanno paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ [P 0.0365] vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto pubbakammavasena lasuṇadāyakattheroti pākaṭo.

Beginning with 'Not far from the Himalayas,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Lasuṇadāyaka. This venerable one, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that served as a basis for liberation in various existences, was reborn in a certain family household during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having attained discernment and seeing the peril in the household life, he abandoned his home and went forth into the ascetic life. Dwelling in the forest, relying on the Himalayas, he planted many garlic plants and subsisted by eating that very garlic, as well as forest roots and fruits. Taking many garlic bulbs in a basket, he brought them to a path frequented by humans and, with a serene mind, gave them as a gift for medicinal purposes to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, and then went on his way. Thus, having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, by the power of that merit he wandered through the round of rebirths among devas and humans, experiencing prosperity in both realms. In due course, at the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn, and having gained faith, he went forth. Developing insight, he attained arahantship in no long time. On account of his past karma, he became known as the Elder Lasuṇadāyaka.

89. Attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Tattha himālayapabbatassa pariyosāne manussānaṃ sañcaraṇaṭṭhāne yadā vipassī bhagavā udapādi, tadā ahaṃ tāpaso ahosinti sambandho. Lasuṇaṃ upajīvāmīti rattalasuṇaṃ ropetvā tadeva gocaraṃ katvā jīvikaṃ kappemīti attho. Tena vuttaṃ “lasuṇaṃ mayhabhojana”nti.

89. Recalling his own past karma, and with joy arisen, proclaiming the apadāna of his former conduct, he spoke, beginning with 'Not far from the Himalayas.' Therein, the connection is as follows: 'At the end of the Himalaya mountain, in a place frequented by humans, when the Blessed One Vipassī arose, at that time I was an ascetic.' As for 'I subsist on garlic,' the meaning is: 'Having planted red garlic and made that very thing my resort for sustenance, I maintained my livelihood.' Therefore it was said: 'Garlic was my food.'

90. Khāriyo pūrayitvānāti tāpasabhājanāni lasuṇena pūrayitvā kājenādāya saṅghārāmaṃ saṅghassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ hemantādīsu tīsu kālesu saṅghassa catūhi iriyāpathehi vasanavihāraṃ agacchiṃ agamāsinti attho. Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittenāti ahaṃ santuṭṭho somanassayuttacittena saṅghassa lasuṇaṃ adāsinti attho.

90. As for 'Having filled the carrying-baskets': the meaning is, having filled the ascetic's containers with garlic and taken them with a carrying-pole, I went to the monastery, the dwelling place of the Sangha, a residence suitable for living in the four postures during the three seasons beginning with winter. As for 'Glad, with a gladdened mind': the meaning is, I, being content, with a mind endowed with joy, gave the garlic to the Sangha.

91. Vipassissa…pe… [M 2.0063] niratassahanti narānaṃ aggassa seṭṭhassa assa vipassissa bhagavato sāsane nirato nissesena rato ahanti sambandho. Saṅghassa…pe… modahanti ahaṃ saṅghassa lasuṇadānaṃ datvā saggamhi suṭṭhu aggasmiṃ devaloke āyukappaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāno modiṃ, santuṭṭho bhavāmīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

91. As for 'Of Vipassī... I was devoted': the connection is, 'I was devoted, completely dedicated, to the teaching of this Blessed One Vipassī, the foremost, the best of men.' As for 'To the Sangha... I rejoiced': the meaning is, 'Having given the gift of garlic to the Sangha, I rejoiced in heaven, in the excellent, supreme celestial world, experiencing divine prosperity for a life-aeon; I became content.' The rest is easily understood.

Lasuṇadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Lasuṇadāyaka is concluded.

8. Āyāgadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Āyāgadāyaka.

Nibbute [V 2.0057] lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato āyāgadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato parinibbutakāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto sāsane pasanno vaḍḍhakīnaṃ mūlaṃ datvā atimanoharaṃ dīghaṃ bhojanasālaṃ kārāpetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā paṇītenāhārena bhojetvā mahādānaṃ datvā cittaṃ pasādesi. So yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesuyeva saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā ghaṭento vāyamanto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā na cirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Pubbe katapuññavasena āyāgattheroti pākaṭo.

Beginning with 'When the World-Protector had attained Nibbāna,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Āyāgadāyaka. This one also, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that served as a basis for liberation in various existences, was reborn in a certain family household at the time of the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One Sikhi. With a serene mind towards the teaching, he gave payment to carpenters and had a very delightful, long dining hall built. Having invited the community of monks, fed them with excellent food, and given a great gift, he gladdened his mind. Having performed meritorious deeds for as long as he lived, he wandered only among devas and humans, experiencing prosperity in both realms. At the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn in a family household, and having gained faith, he went forth. Striving and endeavoring, he developed insight and in no long time attained arahantship. On account of the merit he had made previously, he became known as the Elder of the Long Hall (Āyāgatthera).

94. Evaṃ so katapuññasambhāravasena arahattaṃ patvā attanā pubbe katakusalakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Tattha nibbuteti vadataṃ “mayaṃ buddhā”ti vadantānaṃ antare vare [P 0.0366] uttame sikhimhi bhagavati parinibbuteti attho. Haṭṭho haṭṭhena cittenāti saddhatāya haṭṭhapahaṭṭho somanassayuttacittatāya pahaṭṭhena cittena uttamaṃ thūpaṃ seṭṭhaṃ cetiyaṃ avandiṃ paṇāmayinti attho.

94. Thus he, having attained arahantship on account of his accumulation of merit, recalled the skilled karma he had previously performed himself, and with joy arisen, proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'When the World-Protector had attained Nibbāna.' Therein, as for 'had attained Nibbāna': the meaning is that the Blessed One Sikhi—the choice, the supreme one among those who declare 'We are Buddhas'—had attained Parinibbāna. As for 'Glad, with a gladdened mind': the meaning is, being glad and very glad on account of faith, with a mind gladdened due to being endowed with joy, 'I paid homage to the supreme stūpa, the excellent shrine.'

95. Vaḍḍhakīhi kathāpetvāti “bhojanasālāya pamāṇaṃ kittaka”nti pamāṇaṃ kathāpetvāti attho. Mūlaṃ datvānahaṃ tadāti tadā tasmiṃ kāle ahaṃ kammakaraṇatthāya tesaṃ vaḍḍhakīnaṃ mūlaṃ datvā āyāgaṃ [M 2.0064] āyataṃ dīghaṃ bhojanasālaṃ ahaṃ santuṭṭho somanassacittena kārapesahaṃ kārāpesiṃ ahanti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

95. As for 'Having had the carpenters state': the meaning is, having had the measurements stated by asking, 'What is the measurement of the dining hall?' As for 'Having given the payment then, I': the meaning is, 'At that time, having given payment to those carpenters for the purpose of performing the work, I, being content and with a joyful mind, had a long, extended dining hall built; I had it constructed.' The rest is easily understood.

97. Āyāgassa idaṃ phalanti bhojanasāladānassa idaṃ vipākanti attho.

97. As for 'This is the fruit of the long hall': the meaning is, 'This is the result of the gift of the dining hall.'

Āyāgadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Āyāgadāyaka is concluded.

9. Dhammacakkikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Dhammacakkika.

Siddhatthassa bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato dhammacakkikattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu [V 2.0058] katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto puttadārehi vaḍḍhito vibhavasampanno mahābhogo, so ratanattaye pasanno saddhājāto dhammasabhāyaṃ dhammāsanassa piṭṭhito ratanamayaṃ dhammacakkaṃ kāretvā pūjesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu nibbattaṭṭhānesu sakkasampattiṃ cakkavattisampattiñca anubhavitvā kamena imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe uppanno vibhavasampanno sañjātasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā pubbe katakusalanāmasadisanāmena dhammacakkikattheroti pākaṭo jāto ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Dhammacakkika, beginning with 'Siddhatthassa bhagavato.' He too, having made a resolution under past Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a supporting condition for the rolling back of the round of rebirths in various existences, was reborn in a certain family at the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having reached maturity and flourished with sons and wives, he was endowed with wealth and great possessions. He, pleased with the Triple Gem and with faith arisen, had a Dhamma-wheel made of jewels constructed behind the Dhamma-seat in the Dhamma-hall and offered it. Through that meritorious deed, in his places of rebirth among devas and humans, he experienced the fortune of Sakka and the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch. Gradually, during this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a certain family, endowed with wealth. With faith arisen, he went forth, developed insight, and not long after attained Arahantship. He became renowned as the Elder Dhammacakkika, a name corresponding to the wholesome deed performed in the past.

102. So puññasambhārānurūpena pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā jātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento siddhatthassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Sīhāsanassa sammukhāti sīhassa bhagavato nisinnassa sammukhā buddhāsanassa abhimukhaṭṭhāneti attho, dhammacakkaṃ me ṭhapitanti mayā dhammacakkākārena ubhato sīharūpaṃ dassetvā majjhe ādāsasadisaṃ kāretvā kataṃ dhammacakkaṃ ṭhapitaṃ pūjitaṃ. Kiṃ bhūtaṃ? Viññūhi medhāvīhi “atīva sundara”nti vaṇṇitaṃ thomitaṃ sukataṃ dhammacakkanti sambandho.

102. He, having attained the fruit of Arahantship in accordance with his accumulation of merit, with joy arisen, recollected his past deeds and, to declare his former course of conduct, spoke, beginning with 'Siddhatthassa bhagavato.' 'In front of the lion-seat' means in front of the Blessed One, the lion, who was seated; that is, in a place facing the Buddha's seat. 'The Dhamma-wheel was established by me' means: a Dhamma-wheel made by me in the shape of a Dhamma-wheel, showing a lion-figure on both sides and having made the center like a mirror, was established and offered. Of what sort? It was praised and extolled by the wise and intelligent as 'exceedingly beautiful'; a well-made Dhamma-wheel—this is the connection.

103. Cāruvaṇṇova [M 2.0065] sobhāmīti suvaṇṇavaṇṇo iva sobhāmi virocāmīti [P 0.0367] attho. “Catuvaṇṇehi sobhāmī”tipi pāṭho, tassa khattiyabrāhmaṇavessasuddajātisaṅkhātehi catūhi vaṇṇehi sobhāmi virocāmīti attho. Sayoggabalavāhanoti suvaṇṇasivikādīhi yoggehi ca senāpatimahāmattādīhi sevakehi balehi ca hatthiassarathasaṅkhātehi vāhanehi ca sahitoti attho. Bahujjanā bahavo manussā anuyantā mamānuvattantā niccaṃ niccakālaṃ parivārentīti sambandho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

103. 'I shine with a beautiful complexion' means: I shine, I gleam, as if with a golden complexion. There is also the reading 'I shine with the four classes'; its meaning is: I shine, I gleam, with the four classes designated as nobles, brahmins, merchants, and serfs. 'With vehicles, forces, and mounts' means: accompanied by conveyances such as golden palanquins, by forces with attendants such as generals and great ministers, and by mounts designated as elephants, horses, and chariots. 'Many people, following, always surround me'—this is the connection. The rest is easily understood.

Dhammacakkikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhammacakkika is concluded.

10. Kapparukkhiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kapparukkhiya

Siddhatthassa bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato kapparukkhiyattherassa apadānaṃ (theragā. aṭṭha. 2.576). Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tesu tesu bhavesu nibbānādhigamūpāyabhūtāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto mahaddhano mahābhogo [V 2.0059] satthari pasanno sattahi ratanehi vicittaṃ suvaṇṇamayaṃ kapparukkhaṃ kāretvā siddhatthassa bhagavato cetiyassa sammukhe ṭhapetvā pūjesi. So evarūpaṃ puññaṃ katvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto kamena imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā ratanattaye pasanno dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho satthu ārādhetvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā pubbe katakusalanāmena kapparukkhiyattheroti pākaṭo ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kapparukkhiya, beginning with 'Siddhatthassa bhagavato.' He too, having made a resolution under past Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a means for the attainment of Nibbāna in various existences, was born into a family endowed with wealth at the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Being of great wealth and great possessions, and pleased with the Teacher, he had a golden wishing-tree, variegated with seven kinds of jewels, constructed and, placing it before the shrine of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he offered it. Having performed such a merit and lived for the extent of his lifespan, after passing away from there, he wandered only in happy destinations. Gradually, during this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a certain family. Having reached discretion and established a household, he was pleased with the Triple Gem. Having heard the Dhamma and acquired faith, he pleased the Teacher and went forth. Not long after, he attained Arahantship. By the name of the wholesome deed performed in the past, he became renowned as the Elder Kapparukkhiya.

108. So evaṃ pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento siddhatthassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Thūpaseṭṭhassa sammukhāti seṭṭhassa uttamassa dhātunihitathūpassa cetiyassa sammukhaṭṭhāne vicittadusse anekavaṇṇehi visamena visadisena cittena manohare cinapaṭṭasomārapaṭṭādike dusse[M 2.0066]. Lagetvā olaggetvā kapparukkhaṃ ṭhapesiṃ ahaṃ patiṭṭhapesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

108. Thus, having attained the fruit of Arahantship, he recollected his past deeds and, by way of joy, to declare his former course of conduct, spoke, beginning with 'Siddhatthassa bhagavato.' 'Before the foremost stūpa' means: in a place facing the shrine, the foremost, supreme stūpa in which relics were enshrined. 'With variegated cloths' means: with delightful cloths of many colors, of various and dissimilar patterns, such as Chinese silk, Somāra silk, and so on. 'Having attached and hung them, I set up the wishing-tree' means: I established it. The rest has a plain meaning.

Kapparukkhiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kapparukkhiya is concluded.

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Fourth Chapter is concluded.

5. Upālivaggo

5. The Upāli Chapter

1. Bhāgineyyupālittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhāgineyyupāli

Khīṇāsavasahassehītiādikaṃ [V 2.0060] āyasmato upālittherassa bhāgineyyupālittherassa apadānaṃ. Eso hi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro [P 0.0368] tasmiṃ tasmiṃ bhave puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ disvā gehaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcābhiññāaṭṭhasamāpattilābhī hutvā himavante vāsaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ samaye padumuttaro bhagavā vivekakāmo himavantaṃ pāvisi. Tāpaso bhagavantaṃ puṇṇacandamiva virocamānaṃ dūratova disvā pasannamānaso ajinacammaṃ aṃse katvā añjaliṃ paggayha vanditvā ṭhitakova dasanakhasamodhānañjaliṃ sirasi patiṭṭhapetvā anekāhi upamāhi anekehi thutivacanehi bhagavantaṃ thomesi. Taṃ sutvā bhagavā – “ayaṃ tāpaso anāgate gotamassa nāma bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā vinaye tikhiṇapaññānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti byākaraṇamadāsi. So yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbatti. Tato cuto devamanussesu saṃsaranto sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthunagare upālittherassa bhāgineyyo hutvā nibbatti. So kamena vuddhippatto mātulassa upālittherasa santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. So attano ācariyassa samīpe vasitattā vinayapañhe tikhiṇañāṇo ahosi. Atha bhagavā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayapañhe tikhiṇapaññānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yadidaṃ bhāgineyyupālī”ti taṃ etadaggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Bhāgineyyupāli, the nephew of the Elder Upāli, beginning with 'With a thousand Arahants...' Indeed, this elder, having made his resolve under former Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a certain family. Having come of age and seeing the danger in household life, he renounced his home and went forth as an ascetic. Having gained the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments, he took up residence in the Himālaya. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, desiring seclusion, entered the Himālaya. The ascetic, seeing the Blessed One from afar shining like the full moon, with a mind full of faith, placed a deerskin on his shoulder, raised his joined palms in homage, and stood still. Then, placing his joined hands with the ten fingertips together upon his head, he praised the Blessed One with many similes and many words of praise. Hearing this, the Blessed One made a declaration: 'In the future, this ascetic will go forth in the Dispensation of the Blessed One named Gotama and will become the foremost among the monks sharp in wisdom regarding the Vinaya.' Having lived for his full lifespan, with his jhāna undiminished, he was reborn in the Brahma world. Passing away from there and wandering among gods and humans, he experienced various states of fortune. During this Buddha's advent, he was born in the city of Kapilavatthu as the nephew of the Elder Upāli. Having gradually grown up, he went forth in the presence of his maternal uncle, the Elder Upāli, received a meditation subject, developed insight, and before long became an Arahant. Because he lived near his teacher, he became sharp in knowledge regarding questions on the Vinaya. Then the Blessed One declared: 'Monks, among my disciples, the monks who are sharp in wisdom regarding questions on the Vinaya, the foremost is this Bhāgineyyupāli.' Thus, he placed him in that foremost position.

1. So [M 2.0067] evaṃ etadaggaṭṭhānaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento khīṇāsavasahassehītiādimāha. Tattha ā samantato yāvabhavaggā savanti pavattantīti āsavā. Kāmāsavādayo cattāro āsavā, te khīṇā sositā visositā viddhaṃsitā yehi teti khīṇāsavā, teyeva sahassā khīṇāsavasahassā, tehi khīṇāsavasahassehi[V 2.0061]. Pareto parivuto lokanāyako lokassa nibbānapāpanako vivekaṃ anuyutto paṭisallituṃ ekībhavituṃ gacchateti sambandho.

1. Having thus attained that foremost position, recollecting his own past deeds, and with joy arisen, he proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'With a thousand whose taints are destroyed...' Herein, 'āsavā' are so called because they flow and proceed from all sides up to the apex of existence. The four taints, such as the taint of sensual desire, are the `āsavā`. Those by whom these are destroyed, dried up, completely dried up, and demolished are the `khīṇāsavā`. A thousand of these very `khīṇāsavā` are `khīṇāsavasahassā`. The connection is as follows: 'The Leader of the World, who leads the world to Nibbāna, surrounded by those thousand whose taints are destroyed, devoted to seclusion, goes to be in solitude, to be alone.'

2. Ajinena nivatthohanti ahaṃ ajinamigacammena paṭicchanno, ajinacammavasanoti attho. Tidaṇḍaparidhārakoti kuṇḍikaṭṭhapanatthāya tidaṇḍaṃ gahetvā dhārentoti attho. Bhikkhusaṅghena paribyūḷhaṃ parivāritaṃ lokanāyakaṃ addasanti sambandho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

2. 'Clothed in deerskin' means 'I was covered with a deerskin hide,' that is, 'wearing a deerskin.' 'Bearing a three-pronged staff' means 'carrying a three-pronged staff for the purpose of placing the water pot.' The connection is: 'I saw the Leader of the World, well-surrounded and attended by the community of monks.' The remainder is self-evident.

Bhāgineyyupālittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhāgineyyupāli is complete.

2. Soṇakoḷivisattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Soṇakoḷivisa.

Anomadassissa [P 0.0369] muninotiādikaṃ āyasmato koḷivisattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto anomadassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vayappatto puttadārehi vaḍḍhito vibhavasampanno bhagavato caṅkamanatthāya sobhanaṃ caṅkamaṃ kāretvā sudhāparikammaṃ kāretvā ādāsatalamiva samaṃ vijjotamānaṃ katvā dīpadhūpapupphādīhi sajjetvā bhagavato niyyādetvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītenāhārena pūjesi. So evaṃ yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā tato cavitvā devaloke nibbatto. Tattha pāḷiyā vuttanayena dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā antarā okkākakulappasutoti taṃ sabbaṃ pāḷiyā vuttānusārena veditabbaṃ. Pacchimabhave pana koliyarājavaṃse jāto vayappatto koṭiagghanakassa kaṇṇapiḷandhanassa dhāritattā koṭikaṇṇoti, kuṭikaṇṇoti ca pākaṭo ahosi. So bhagavati pasanno [M 2.0068] dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

“To the sage Anomadassī” and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Koḷivisa Thera. He too, having made his resolve in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a foundation for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was born into a certain family, reached maturity, flourished with sons and wives, and became prosperous. He had a beautiful walking path constructed for the Blessed One, had it plastered with whitewash, made it smooth and shining like a mirror, adorned it with lamps, incense, flowers, and so forth, and offered it to the Blessed One. He then honored the Sangha headed by the Buddha with choice food. Having performed such meritorious deeds throughout his life, he passed away and was reborn in the deva world. There, he enjoyed divine bliss as stated in the Pāli text, and in the interim, he was born into the Okkāka royal lineage—all this should be understood in accordance with what is stated in the Pāli text. In his last existence, he was born into the Koliyan royal lineage, reached maturity, and became known as Koṭikaṇṇa or Kuṭikaṇṇa, because he wore earrings worth a koṭi. With faith in the Blessed One, he heard the Dhamma, and having acquired confidence, went forth, developed insight, and before long attained arahantship.

25. So arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento anomadassissa muninotiādimāha. Tattha anomadassissāti anomaṃ alāmakaṃ sundaraṃ dassanaṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitattā byāmappabhāmaṇḍalopasobhitattā ārohapariṇāhena samannāgatattā ca dassanīyaṃ sarīraṃ yassa bhagavato so anomadassī, tassa anomadassissa muninoti attho. Tādinoti iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu akampiyasabhāvassa. Sudhāya lepanaṃ katvāti [V 2.0062] sudhāya avalittaṃ katvā dīpadhūpapupphadhajapaṭākādīhi ca alaṅkataṃ caṅkamaṃ kārayiṃ akāsinti attho. Sesagāthānaṃ attho pāḷiyā anusārena suviññeyyova.

25. Having become an arahant, recollecting his past deeds and filled with joy, he declared his former conduct in the Apadāna beginning “To the sage Anomadassī.” Herein, “Anomadassī” means the Blessed One whose body was beautiful to behold—adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, radiant with a halo of a fathom’s span, and endowed with perfect height and proportion—thus he is Anomadassī; the meaning is 'to that sage Anomadassī.' “Such a one” refers to one whose nature is unshaken by desirable or undesirable things. “Having plastered it with whitewash” means 'I had the walking path plastered with whitewash and adorned with lamps, incense, flowers, banners, flags, and so forth.' The meaning of the remaining verses is easily understood in accordance with the Pāli.

35. Parivārasampattidhanasampattisaṅkhātaṃ yasaṃ dhāretīti yasodharo, sabbe ete sattasattaticakkavattirājāno yasodharanāmena ekanāmakāti sambandho.

35. “He bears fame (yasaṃ dhāreti), which is reckoned as the perfection of retinue and the perfection of wealth”—thus he is Yasodhara. The connection is that all these seventy-seven wheel-turning kings shared the single name Yasodhara.

52. Aṅgīrasoti aṅgato sarīrato niggatā rasmi yassa so aṅgīraso, chandadosamohabhayāgatīhi vā pāpācāravasena vā caturāpāyaṃ na gacchatīti nāgo, mahanto pūjito ca so nāgo ceti mahānāgo. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

52. “Aṅgīrasa” means one from whose limbs (aṅga), that is, from his body, rays (rasmi) have issued; thus he is Aṅgīrasa. “Nāga” means one who does not go (na gacchati) to the four states of misery due to the wrong paths of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear, or on account of evil conduct. And since that Nāga is great (mahanto) and revered (pūjito), he is Mahānāga. The rest is self-evident in meaning.

Koḷivisattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Koṭikaṇṇa is complete.

3. Kāḷigodhāputtabhaddiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhaddiya, Son of Kāḷigodhā

Padumuttarasambuddhantiādikaṃ āyasmato bhaddiyassa kāḷigodhāputtattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto [P 0.0370] padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhippatto puttadārehi vaḍḍhito nagaravāsino puññāni karonte disvā sayampi puññāni kātukāmo [M 2.0069] buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā thūlapaṭalikādianekāni mahārahāni sayanāni paññāpetvā tattha nisinne bhagavati sasaṅghe paṇītenāhārena bhojetvā mahādānaṃ adāsi. So evaṃ yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā aparabhāge imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kāḷigodhāya nāma deviyā putto hutvā nibbatti. So viññutaṃ patto ārohapariṇāhahatthapādarūpasampattiyā bhaddattā ca kāḷigodhāya deviyā puttattā ca bhaddiyo kāḷigodhāputtoti pākaṭo. Satthari pasīditvā mātāpitaro ārādhetvā pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Bhaddiya, son of Kāḷigodhā, begins with “Padumuttara, the Fully Enlightened One” and so forth. This venerable one too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a family endowed with wealth, grew up, and prospered with sons and wives. Seeing the townspeople performing meritorious deeds, he too wished to do so. He invited the community of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head, prepared many valuable seats, such as thickly padded ones, and having seated the Blessed One with the Saṅgha there, served them with choice food and offered a great donation. Having performed such meritorious deeds throughout his life, he experienced both divine and human prosperity. In a later existence, during the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn as the son of a queen named Kāḷigodhā. Having attained maturity, he became known as Bhaddiya Kāḷigodhāputta on account of his auspicious nature, the perfection of his form, hands, and feet in height and proportion, and because he was the son of Queen Kāḷigodhā. Having gained faith in the Teacher and obtained his parents’ permission, he went forth and soon became an arahant.

54. So arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttarasambuddhantiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Mettacittanti mijjati sinehati nandati sabbasatteti mettā, mettāya sahagataṃ cittaṃ mettacittaṃ, taṃ yassa bhagavato atthīti mettacitto, taṃ mettacittaṃ. Mahāmuninti sakalabhikkhūnaṃ mahantattā mahāmuni, taṃ padumuttaraṃ sambuddhanti [V 2.0063] sambandho. Janatā sabbāti sabbo janakāyo, sabbanagaravāsinoti attho. Sabbalokagganāyakanti sakalalokassa aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ nibbānassa nayanato pāpanato nāyakaṃ padumuttarasambuddhaṃ janatā upeti samīpaṃ gacchatīti sambandho.

54. Having become an arahant, recalling his past deeds and filled with joy, he declared the Apadāna of his former conduct beginning with “Padumuttara, the Fully Enlightened One.” Its meaning is as explained below. Regarding `mettacittaṃ`: `mettā` is so called because it is affectionate towards, cherishes, and delights in all beings. A mind accompanied by `mettā` is a `mettacitta`. The Blessed One who possesses this is `mettacitto`; the phrase refers to him, the one with a mind of loving-kindness. Regarding `mahāmuniṃ`: because he is great among all the bhikkhus, he is a `mahāmuni`; the connection is to be made with “that Great Sage, Padumuttara, the Fully Enlightened One.” Regarding `janatā sabbā`: this means the entire populace, that is, all the townspeople. Regarding `sabbalokagganāyakaṃ`: the leader of the entire world, who leads and brings them to the supreme, the best, which is Nibbāna. The connection is: “the people approach (`upeti`) Padumuttara, the Fully Enlightened One.”

55. Sattukañca baddhakañcāti baddhasattuabaddhasattusaṅkhātaṃ āmisaṃ. Atha vā bhattapūpakhajjabhojjayāguādayo yāvakālikattā āmisaṃ pānabhojanañca gahetvā puññakkhette anuttare satthuno dadantīti sambandho.

55. Regarding `sattukañca baddhakañca`: this refers to material offerings reckoned as bound `sattu` and unbound `sattu`. Alternatively, the connection is: taking food and drink—such as cooked rice, cakes, hard food, soft food, gruel, and so forth—which are material offerings allowable for a limited time, they give them to the Teacher, the unsurpassed field of merit.

58. Āsanaṃ buddhayuttakanti buddhayoggaṃ buddhārahaṃ buddhānucchavikaṃ sattaratanamayaṃ āsananti attho. Sesaṃ nayānuyogena suviññeyyamevāti.

58. Regarding `āsanaṃ buddhayuttakaṃ` (a seat suitable for the Buddha): the meaning is a seat that is `buddhayogga` (fit for the Buddha), `buddhāraha` (worthy of the Buddha), `buddhānucchavika` (befitting the Buddha), a seat made of the seven precious substances. The rest is easily understood by applying the method.

Kāḷigodhāputtabhaddiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kāḷigodhāputta Bhaddiya is complete.

4. Sanniṭṭhāpakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka

Araññe [M 2.0070] kuṭikaṃ katvātiādikaṃ āyasmato sanniṭṭhāpakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharabandhanena [P 0.0371] baddho gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ disvā vatthukāmakilesakāme pahāya himavantassa avidūre pabbatantare araññavāsaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ kāle padumuttaro bhagavā vivekakāmatāya taṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha so tāpaso bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā nisīdanatthāya tiṇasantharaṃ paññāpetvā adāsi. Tattha nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ anekehi madhurehi tiṇḍukādīhi phalāphalehi santappesi. So tena puññakammena tato cuto devesu ca manussesu ca aparāparaṃ saṃsaranto dve sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto saddhāsampanno pabbajito vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. Khuragge arahattaphalappattiyaṃ viya nirussāheneva santipadasaṅkhāte nibbāne suṭṭhu ṭhitattā sanniṭṭhāpakattheroti pākaṭo.

“Having built a hut in the forest,” and so forth—this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka. He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, and accumulating merits here and there as conditions for release in successive lives, was born into a family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having come of age, he was bound by household ties. Seeing the danger in household life, he abandoned material sensual pleasures and defilement-born sensual pleasures, and took up residence in a forest in a mountain region not far from the Himalayas. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, desiring solitude, arrived at that place. Then that ascetic, seeing the Blessed One, with a joyful mind, paid homage and prepared a grass mat for him to sit on. Seated there, he satisfied the Blessed One with various sweet fruits such as tiṇḍuka and others. Through that meritorious deed, after passing away from there, he wandered on repeatedly through the realms of gods and humans, experiencing two kinds of prosperity. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a certain family, endowed with faith, went forth, developed insight, and before long became an Arahant. Because he was firmly established in Nibbāna, the state of peace, as effortlessly as one attains the fruit of Arahantship on a razor’s edge, he became known as the Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka.

70. Arahā pana hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento araññe kuṭikaṃ katvātiādimāha. Tattha araññeti sīhabyagghādīnaṃ bhayena manussā ettha [V 2.0064] na rajjanti na ramanti na allīyantīti araññaṃ, tasmiṃ araññe. Kuṭikanti tiṇacchadanakuṭikaṃ katvā pabbatantare vasāmi vāsaṃ kappesinti attho. Lābhena ca alābhena ca yasena ca ayasena ca santuṭṭho vihāsinti sambandho.

70. Having become an Arahant, recalling his past deeds, and filled with joy, revealing the account of his former conduct, he began, saying, “Having made a hut in the forest,” and so forth. Here, `araññe` (in the forest) means a place where people do not become attached, do not delight, and do not cling due to fear of lions, tigers, and so forth; thus, it is a forest. And `kuṭikaṃ` (a hut) means having made a grass-roofed hut; the meaning is “I dwelt in a mountain crevice, establishing my dwelling.” The connection is that he dwelt content with gain and non-gain, with fame and disrepute.

72. Jalajuttamanāmakanti jale jātaṃ jalajaṃ, padumaṃ, jalajaṃ uttamaṃ jalajuttamaṃ, jalajuttamena samānaṃ nāmaṃ yassa so jalajuttamanāmako, taṃ jalajuttamanāmakaṃ buddhanti attho. Sesaṃ pāḷinayānuyogena suviññeyyamevāti.

72. Regarding `jalajuttamanāmakaṃ`: `jalajaṃ` means ‘born in water’ (`jale jātaṃ`), that is, a lotus. `jalajuttamaṃ` is the ‘supreme water-born,’ that is, the supreme lotus. `jalajuttamanāmako` is he whose name is like the supreme lotus. The meaning is ‘that Buddha, who has a name like the supreme lotus.’ The rest is easily understood by applying the method of the Pāli.

Sanniṭṭhāpakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sanniṭṭhāpaka is complete.

5. Pañcahatthiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcahatthiya

Sumedho [M 2.0071] nāma sambuddhotiādikaṃ āyasmato pañcahatthiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā ratanattaye pasanno vihāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye pañcauppalahatthāni ānesuṃ. So tehi pañcauppalahatthehi vīthiyaṃ caramānaṃ sumedhaṃ bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. Tāni gantvā ākāse vitānaṃ hutvā chāyaṃ kurumānāni tathāgateneva saddhiṃ gacchiṃsu. So taṃ disvā somanassajāto pītiyā phuṭṭhasarīro yāvajīvaṃ tadeva puññaṃ anussaritvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto saddhājāto pabbajitvā [P 0.0372] vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. Katakusalanāmena pañcahatthiyattheroti pākaṭo.

The words beginning, 'Sumedha by name, a Fully Enlightened One,' are the Apadāna of the Venerable Pañcahatthiya Thera. He too, having made a foundation under former Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a supporting condition for turning away from the round of rebirths in various existences, was born into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having reached maturity, he dwelt with faith in the Three Jewels. At that time, they brought five handfuls of water lilies. With those five handfuls of water lilies, he worshipped the Blessed One Sumedha, who was walking along the road. Those flowers went and, having become a canopy in the sky and providing shade, they proceeded together with the Tathāgata. Seeing that, with joy arisen and his body suffused with rapture, he recollected that very merit for as long as he lived. Having passed away from there, he was reborn in the deva world. Wandering on and on, in this Buddha-era he was born into a certain family, reached maturity, and with faith arisen, went forth. Having developed insight, he became an Arahant before long. By the name of the meritorious deed he had performed, he became known as Pañcahatthiya Thera.

77. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā paccakkhato paññāya diṭṭhapubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sumedho nāma sambuddhotiādimāha. Tattha sumedhoti sundarā medhā catusaccapaṭivedhapaṭisambhidādayo paññā yassa so bhagavā sumedho sambuddho antarāpaṇe antaravīthiyaṃ gacchatīti sambandho. Okkhittacakkhūti adhokhittacakkhu. Mitabhāṇīti pamāṇaṃ ñatvā bhaṇanasīlo, pamāṇaṃ jānitvā dhammaṃ desesīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

77. He, recollecting his past deed and revealing the Apadāna of his former conduct, which he had seen directly with wisdom, spoke the words beginning, 'Sumedha by name, a Fully Enlightened One.' Therein, 'Sumedha' means: he is the Blessed One Sumedha because he possesses beautiful (`sundarā`) wisdom (`medhā`), that is, the wisdom of the penetration of the Four Truths, the analytical knowledges, and so forth. The connection is: 'The Fully Enlightened One walks in the market, in the inner street.' 'With eyes cast down' (`okkhittacakkhu`) means with eyes directed downwards. 'Moderate in speech' (`mitabhāṇī`) means he is accustomed to speaking having known the measure; the meaning is that he taught the Dhamma having known the proper measure. The rest is indeed easily understood.

Pañcahatthiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcahatthiya is complete.

6. Padumacchadaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Padumacchadaniya

Nibbute [V 2.0065] lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato padumacchadaniyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katapuññasambhāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto ratanattaye pasanno parinibbutassa vipassissa bhagavato citakaṃ padumapupphehi pūjesi. So teneva [M 2.0072] cittappasādena yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto dibbasampattiṃ manussasampattiñcāti dve sampattiyo anekakkhattuṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ amhākaṃ sammāsambuddhakāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthari pasīditvā sāsane pabbajito ghaṭento vāyamanto nacirasseva arahā ahosi. Tassa rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānādīsu tattha tattha viharantassa vihāro padumapupphehi chādīyati, tena so padumacchadaniyattheroti pākaṭo.

The words beginning, 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna,' are the Apadāna of the Venerable Padumacchadaniya Thera. He too, having accumulated a store of merit under former Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a supporting condition for turning away from the round of rebirths in various existences, was born into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity and gained faith in the Three Jewels, he worshipped the funeral pyre of the Blessed One Vipassī, who had attained Parinibbāna, with lotus flowers. Through that very confidence of mind, having lived for his full lifespan, he passed away from there and, wandering only in happy destinations, experienced the two prosperities—divine prosperity and human prosperity—many times. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a certain family, reached maturity, gained faith in the Teacher, and went forth into the Dispensation. Striving and making effort, he became an Arahant before long. For him, while dwelling here and there in his places for the night, places for the day, and so forth, his dwelling was covered with lotus flowers. Therefore, he became known as Padumacchadaniya Thera.

83. Attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassavasena pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Tattha nibbuteti khandhaparinibbānena parinibbute satthari, vipassissa sammāsambuddhassa sarīre citamāniyamāne citake āropite suphullaṃ padumakalāpaṃ ahaṃ gahetvā citakaṃ āropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.
