Mahantaṃ sīlakkhandhādikaṃ esati gavesatīti mahesī, taṃ mahesiṃ buddhaṃ. Visesena kilesakhandhamārādayo māre jitavāti vijitāvī, taṃ vijitāvinaṃ sambuddhaṃ. Suvaṇṇassa vaṇṇo iva vaṇṇo yassa sambuddhassa so suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, taṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ disvā ko nāma satto nappasīdatīti.

And so on. This brahmin, due to a common turn of phrase, says 'usabha,' and so on, where 'āsabha' should be said. 'Varo' means one who is to be chosen, who is to be desired. Because of his exertion of effort over many hundreds of thousands of aeons, he is a hero (vīro). Because he seeks and searches for the great mass of virtues, such as the aggregate of morality, he is the great seer (mahesī); that great seer is the Buddha. Because he has especially conquered the Māras—such as the Māra of defilements and the Māra of the aggregates—he is the conqueror (vijitāvī); that conqueror is the Perfectly Enlightened One. The color of that Perfectly Enlightened One is like the color of gold; thus, he is the golden-coloured one (suvaṇṇavaṇṇo). Having seen that golden-coloured Perfectly Enlightened One, what being would not be filled with faith?

Parappasādakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Parappasādaka is complete.

5. Bhisadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Bhisadāyaka

Vessabhū [M 2.0092] nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato bhisadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vessabhussa bhagavato kāle himavantasmiṃ hatthiyoniyaṃ nibbatto tasmiṃ paṭivasati. Tasmiṃ samaye vessabhū bhagavā vivekakāmo himavantamagamāsi. Taṃ disvā so hatthināgo pasannamānaso bhisamuḷālaṃ [P 0.0389] gahetvā bhagavantaṃ bhojesi. So tena puññakammena hatthiyonito cuto devaloke uppajjitvā tattha cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussattamāgato manussesu cakkavattisampattiādayo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde mahābhoge aññatarasmiṃ kule nibbatto pubbavāsanābalena satthari pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi, so pubbe katakusalanāmena bhisadāyakattheroti pākaṭo.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Bhisadāyaka begins with 'Vessabhū by name,' and so on. He too, having established a foundation under previous Buddhas and accumulating meritorious deeds that serve as a basis for liberation in various existences, was born into the elephant species in the Himalayas during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū and dwelt there. At that time, the Blessed One Vessabhū, desiring seclusion, went to the Himalayas. Seeing him, that great elephant, with a serene mind, took a lotus stalk and root and served it to the Blessed One. Through that meritorious deed, he passed away from the elephant species and arose in the world of the devas. There, having experienced the six kinds of sensual-sphere prosperity, he came to human existence. Among humans, having experienced the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch and so on, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was born into a certain family of great wealth. Through the power of his former conditioning, he gained faith in the Teacher, went forth, and before long became an Arahant. He became known as the Elder Bhisadāyaka, a name derived from his wholesome deed performed in the past.

29. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā pubbacaritāpadānaṃ dassento vessabhū nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Tattha vessabhūti vessaṃ bhunāti atikkamatīti vessabhū. Atha vā vesse vāṇijakamme vā kāmarāgādike vā kusalādikamme vā vatthukāmakilesakāme vā bhunāti abhibhavatīti [V 2.0085] vessabhū, so nāmena vessabhū nāma bhagavā. Isīnaṃ tatiyo ahūti kusaladhamme esati gavesatīti isi, “vipassī, sikhī, vessabhū”ti vuttattā tatiyo isi tatiyo bhagavā ahu ahosīti attho. Kānanaṃ vanamoggayhāti kānanasaṅkhātaṃ vanaṃ ogayha ogahetvā pāvisīti attho.

29. Recalling his past deed and showing the apadāna of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Vessabhū by name.' Therein, 'Vessabhū' means one who overcomes (`bhunāti`) the merchant class (`vessaṃ`). Or, he is Vessabhū because he overcomes (`bhunāti abhibhavati`) the merchant class or trade (`vesse vāṇijakamme`), sensual passions and the like (`kāmarāgādike`), wholesome actions and the like (`kusalādikamme`), or object-desires and defilement-desires (`vatthukāmakilesakāme`). That Blessed One was Vessabhū by name. As for 'he was the third of the seers,' one is a seer (`isi`) because one seeks (`esati`) and searches for (`gavesati`) wholesome states. Because it is said, 'Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū,' he was the third seer, the third Blessed One; this is the meaning. As for 'having entered the forest wilderness,' it means having plunged into and entered the forest known as a wilderness; this is the meaning.

30. Bhisamuḷālaṃ gaṇhitvāti dvipadacatuppadānaṃ chātakaṃ bhisati hiṃsati vināsetīti bhisaṃ, ko so? Padumakando, bhisañca muḷālañca bhisamuḷālaṃ, taṃ bhisamuḷālaṃ gahetvāti attho.

30. As for 'having taken a lotus stalk and root': that which harms (`bhisati`), injures (`hiṃsati`), or destroys (`vināseti`) the hunger (`chātakaṃ`) of two-footed and four-footed beings is a `bhisa`. What is that? The lotus tuber (`padumakando`). `Bhisa` and `muḷāla` (lotus stalk) make `bhisamuḷāla`. 'Having taken that `bhisamuḷāla`' is the meaning.

31. Karena ca parāmaṭṭhoti taṃ mayā dinnadānaṃ, vessabhūvarabuddhinā uttamabuddhinā vessabhunā karena hatthatalena parāmaṭṭho katasamphasso ahosi. Sukhāhaṃ nābhijānāmi, samaṃ tena kutottarinti tena sukhena [M 2.0093] samaṃ sukhaṃ nābhijānāmi, tato uttariṃ tato paraṃ tato adhikaṃ sukhaṃ kutoti attho. Sesaṃ nayānusārena suviññeyyanti.

31. As for 'and it was touched by his hand': that gift given by me was touched—contact was made—by the hand (`karena`), the palm (`hatthatalena`), of Vessabhū, the excellent Buddha (`varabuddhinā`), the one of supreme wisdom (`uttamabuddhinā`). As for 'I know no happiness equal to that; whence one more sublime?': the meaning is, 'I do not know a happiness equal to that happiness; where could there be a happiness that is more sublime (`uttariṃ`), beyond (`paraṃ`), or greater (`adhikaṃ`) than that?' The rest is to be easily understood according to this method.

Bhisadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Bhisadāyaka is complete.

6. Sucintitattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Sucintita

Giriduggacaro āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato sucintitattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle himavantappadese nesādakule uppanno migasūkarādayo vadhitvā khādanto viharati. Tadā lokanātho lokānuggahaṃ sattānuddayatañca paṭicca himavantamagamāsi. Tadā so nesādo bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso attano khādanatthāya ānītaṃ varamadhuramaṃsaṃ adāsi. Paṭiggahesi bhagavā tassānukampāya, taṃ bhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So teneva puññena [P 0.0390] teneva somanassena tato cuto sugatīsu saṃsaranto cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu cakkavattisampattiādayo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

'I was a wanderer in the mountain fortress,' and so on, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sucintita. He too, having established a foundation under previous Buddhas and accumulating meritorious deeds that serve as a basis for liberation in various existences, was born into a hunter's family in the Himalayan region during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. He lived by killing and eating deer, boars, and other animals. At that time, the Protector of the World, out of consideration for the welfare of the world and compassion for beings, went to the Himalayas. Then that hunter, upon seeing the Blessed One, with a serene mind, gave the excellent, sweet meat he had brought for his own consumption. The Blessed One accepted it out of compassion for him. Having eaten it and spoken words of appreciation, he departed. Through that very merit and that very joy, he passed away from that state and, wandering through fortunate destinations, experienced the six kinds of sensual-sphere prosperity. Among humans, having experienced the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch and so on, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was born into a good family, gained faith in the Teacher, went forth, and before long became an Arahant.

36. Catupaṭisambhidāpañcābhiññādibhedaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto [V 2.0086] pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento giriduggacaro āsintiādimāha. Girati saddaṃ karotīti giri, ko so? Silāpaṃsumayapabbato, duṭṭhu dukkhena gamanīyaṃ duggaṃ, girīhi duggaṃ giriduggaṃ, duggamoti attho. Tasmiṃ giridugge pabbatantare caro caraṇasīlo āsiṃ ahosiṃ. Abhijātova kesarīti abhi visesena jāto nibbatto kesarīva kesarasīho iva giriduggasmiṃ carāmīti attho.

36. Having attained the divisions of the four analytical knowledges, the five higher knowledges, and so on, he recalled his past deed. Filled with joy, and proclaiming the apadāna of his former conduct, he spoke the verse beginning with 'I was a wanderer in the mountain fortress.' A `giri` (mountain) is so called because it 'swallows' (`girati`) or 'makes a sound' (`saddaṃ karoti`). What is that? A mountain made of rock and soil. A `dugga` is a place that is very difficult to travel to. A place made difficult by mountains is a `giridugga` (mountain fortress); 'difficult to access' is the meaning. In that mountain fortress, among the mountains, 'I was a wanderer,' meaning I had the habit of wandering. As for 'like a well-born lion (`kesarī`)': 'well-born' means specially born. 'Like a `kesarī`' means like a maned lion. The meaning is: 'I wander in the mountain fortress like a maned lion.'

40. Giriduggaṃ pavisiṃ ahanti ahaṃ tadā tena maṃsadānena pītisomanassajāto pabbatantaraṃ pāvisiṃ. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

40. As for 'I entered the mountain fortress': at that time, filled with rapture and joy on account of that gift of meat, I entered the mountain's interior. The meaning of the rest is self-evident.

Sucintitattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Sucintita is complete.

7. Vatthadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Vatthadāyaka

Pakkhijāto [M 2.0094] tadā āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato vatthadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle supaṇṇayoniyaṃ nibbatto gandhamādanapabbataṃ gacchantaṃ atthadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā māṇavakavaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā mahagghaṃ dibbavatthaṃ ādāya bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. Sopi bhagavā paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So teneva somanassena vītināmetvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto tattha aparāparaṃ saṃsaranto puññāni anubhavitvā tato manussesu manussasampattinti sabbattha mahagghaṃ vatthābharaṇaṃ laddhaṃ, tato uppannuppannabhave vatthacchāyāya gatagataṭṭhāne vasanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva chaḷabhiññappattakhīṇāsavo ahosi, pubbe katapuññanāmena vatthadāyakattheroti pākaṭo.

“I was then born as a bird”—thus begins the Apadāna of the Venerable Vatthadāyaka Thera. He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation in various existences, was reborn in the garuḍa species during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. Seeing the Blessed One Atthadassī traveling to Gandhamādana Mountain, with a mind full of faith, he abandoned his garuḍa form and created the appearance of a young man. Taking a precious divine garment, he offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One accepted it, expressed his appreciation, and departed. Having passed his time with that same joy and lived for the extent of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn in the deva realm. Wandering from one existence to the next, he experienced the fruits of his merits. Then, reborn among humans, he experienced human prosperity; everywhere he obtained precious garments and ornaments. Thereafter, in every life he was born into, he dwelt wherever he went with an abundance of cloth. During this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a certain family, and upon reaching maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher and went forth. Not long after, he attained the six higher knowledges and became an Arahant with the cankers destroyed. He became known as the Elder Vatthadāyaka, named for his past meritorious deed.

45. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento pakkhijāto tadā āsintiādimāha. Tattha pakkhijātoti pakkhandati upalavati sakuṇo etenāti pakkhaṃ, pakkhamassa atthīti pakkhī, pakkhiyoniyaṃ jāto nibbattoti attho. Supaṇṇoti sundaraṃ paṇṇaṃ pattaṃ yassa so supaṇṇo, vātaggāhasuvaṇṇavaṇṇajalamānapattamahābhāroti [P 0.0391][V 2.0087] attho. Garuḷādhipoti nāge gaṇhanatthāya garuṃ bhāraṃ pāsāṇaṃ giḷantīti garuḷā, garuḷānaṃ adhipo rājāti garuḷādhipo, virajaṃ buddhaṃ addasāhanti sambandho.

45. Recalling his past deeds and filled with joy, he revealed his Apadāna of former conduct, beginning with, “I was then born as a bird.” Therein, “born as a bird” means: that by which a bird flies and soars is a wing (pakkha); one who has a wing is a bird (pakkhī); the meaning is one born and arisen in the bird species. “Supaṇṇa” means one who has beautiful (sundaraṃ) wings (paṇṇa). “Garuḷādhipa” means: they are called garuḷas because they swallow heavy (garu) stones as a weight in order to seize nāgas; the lord and king of the garuḷas is a garuḷādhipa. The connection is: “I saw the dustless Buddha.”

Vatthadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vatthadāyaka, the Giver of Cloth, is complete.

8. Ambadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Venerable Ambadāyaka Thera.

Anomadassī bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato ambadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto anomadassissa bhagavato kāle vānarayoniyaṃ [M 2.0095] nibbatto himavante kapirājā hutvā paṭivasati. Tasmiṃ samaye anomadassī bhagavā tassānukampāya himavantamagamāsi. Atha so kapirājā bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sumadhuraṃ ambaphalaṃ khuddamadhunā adāsi. Atha bhagavā tassa passantasseva taṃ sabbaṃ paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. Atha so somanassasampannahadayo teneva pītisomanassena yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ tattha dibbasukhamanubhavitvā manussesu ca manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto satthari pasīditvā pabbajitvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiññappatto ahosi. Pubbapuññanāmena ambadāyakattheroti pākaṭo.

“The Blessed One Anomadassī,” etc.—this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Ambadāyaka Thera. He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation in various existences, was reborn in the monkey species during the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī. He lived in the Himalayas, having become the king of monkeys. At that time, the Blessed One Anomadassī, out of compassion for him, went to the Himalayas. Then that monkey-king, seeing the Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, offered him a very sweet mango fruit together with a little wild honey. Then the Blessed One, while he watched, consumed it all, expressed his appreciation, and departed. Then, with a heart full of joy, he lived for the extent of his lifespan with that same rapture and joy and, passing away from there, was reborn in the deva realm. There, from one existence to the next, he experienced divine happiness, and among humans, he experienced human prosperity. During this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a wealthy family, gained faith in the Teacher, went forth and, not long after, attained the six higher knowledges. He became known as the Elder Ambadāyaka, named for his past meritorious deed.

53. So aparabhāge attanā katakusalabījaṃ disvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento anomadassī bhagavātiādimāha. Mettāya aphari loke, appamāṇe nirūpadhīti so bhagavā sabbaloke appamāṇe satte “sukhī hontū”tiādinā nirupadhi upadhivirahitaṃ katvā mettāya mettacittena aphari patthari vaḍḍhesīti attho.

53. Then, in a later time, seeing the wholesome seed he himself had planted and filled with joy, he revealed his Apadāna of former conduct, beginning with, “The Blessed One Anomadassī,” etc. As to the verse, “With loving-kindness he pervaded the world, boundless and free from defilement”: the meaning is that the Blessed One, with such thoughts as “May they be happy,” pervaded, spread, and extended loving-kindness with a mind of mettā towards the boundless beings in all the world, doing so in a way that was free from defilement (nirupadhi). That is the meaning.

54. Kapi ahaṃ tadā āsinti tadā tassāgamanakāle kapirājā ahosinti attho.

54. “I was a monkey then.” At that time, at the time of his arrival, I was the monkey king—that is the meaning.

Ambadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ambadāyaka is complete.

9. Sumanattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Sumana

Sumano [V 2.0088] nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato sumanattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle mālākārassa kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya saddhājāto bhagavati pasannamānaso sumanamālāmuṭṭhiyo gahetvā ubhohi [P 0.0392] hatthehi pūjesi. So tena puññena devamanussesu dve sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya puttadārehi vaḍḍhitvā sumananāmena [M 2.0096] pākaṭo satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

“By name, Sumana”—thus begins the Apadāna of the Venerable Sumana Thera. He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas and accumulating merits conducive to liberation in various existences, was reborn in the family of a garland-maker during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity, faith arose in him and, with a mind full of faith in the Blessed One, he took handfuls of jasmine flowers and worshipped with both hands. Through that merit, he experienced the two kinds of prosperity among devas and humans. During this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn into a certain family. Having reached maturity and prospered with a wife and children, he became known by the name Sumana. Having gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and, not long after, became an Arahant.

62. So arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sumano nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Sundaraṃ manaṃ cittaṃ yassa so sumano. Saddhāpasādabahumānena yutto nāmena sumano nāma mālākāro tadā ahaṃ ahosiṃ.

62. Having become an Arahant, recollecting his past deeds and filled with joy, he revealed his Apadāna of former conduct, beginning with the words, “By name, Sumana.” “Sumana” is one whose mind (mana, citta) is beautiful (sundaraṃ). Endowed with faith, confidence, and great respect, at that time I was a garland-maker named Sumana.

63. Sikhino lokabandhunoti sikhā muddhā kāsatīti sikhī. Atha vā sampayuttasampayoge khādati viddhaṃsetīti sikhī, kā sā? Aggisikhā, aggisikhā viya sikhāya dippanato sikhī. Yathā aggisikhā jotati pākaṭā hoti, sikhī pattatiṇakaṭṭhapalāsādike dahati, evamayampi bhagavā nīlapītādiraṃsīhi jotati sakalalokasannivāse pākaṭo hoti. Sakasantānagatasabbakilese soseti viddhaṃseti jhāpetīti vohāranāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ, tassa sikhino. Sakalalokassa bandhuñātakoti lokabandhu, tassa sikhino lokabandhuno bhagavato sumanapupphaṃ abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.

63. Regarding "Sikhino lokabandhuno": He is called Sikhī because his crest (sikhā), his head (muddhā), shines (kāsati). Or alternatively, he is called Sikhī because he consumes (khādati) and destroys (viddhaṃseti) that which is connected and associated. What is that like? A flame of fire (aggisikhā). Like a flame of fire, he is called Sikhī because he shines with a crest. Just as a flame of fire shines and becomes manifest, and a flame burns leaves, grass, wood, palāsa leaves, and so on, so too does this Blessed One shine with blue, yellow, and other rays, and becomes renowned in the entire assembly of the world. He dries up, destroys, and burns all the defilements that have arisen in his own continuum. Thus, this is a conventional name, a functional name, an appellation. Of that Sikhī. He is the kinsman and relative of the entire world, thus he is the Kinsman of the World (lokabandhu). The meaning is: "I offered and worshipped the Blessed One Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World, with a sumana flower."

Sumanattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Sumana is concluded.

10. Pupphacaṅkoṭiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Pupphacaṅkoṭiya

Abhītarūpaṃ sīhaṃ vātiādikaṃ āyasmato pupphacaṅkoṭiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto mahāvibhavasampanno satthari pasīditvā pasannākāraṃ dassento suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ anojapupphamocinitvā caṅkoṭakaṃ pūretvā bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā “bhagavā[V 2.0089], imassa nissandena nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne suvaṇṇavaṇṇo pūjanīyo hutvā nibbānaṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti patthanamakāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu nibbatto sabbattha pūjito [M 2.0097] suvaṇṇavaṇṇo abhirūpo ahosi. So aparabhāge imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Pupphacaṅkoṭiya begins with "Abhītarūpaṃ sīhaṃ vā..." ("Like a lion, fearless in form..."). He also, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences that served as a basis for liberation from the cycle of rebirth, was reborn in a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity and become endowed with great wealth, he gained faith in the Teacher. Wishing to show his devotion, he gathered golden-colored anojā flowers, filled a basket, and worshipped the Blessed One, making this aspiration: "O Blessed One, by the fruit of this deed, in every place I am reborn, may I be of golden hue, worthy of veneration, and may I attain Nibbāna." Through that meritorious deed, he was reborn among devas and humans, and was everywhere venerated, of golden hue, and exceedingly handsome. In a later time, during this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a prosperous family. Having reached maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher, went forth, developed insight, and before long became an Arahant.

68-9. So [P 0.0393] pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento abhītarūpaṃ sīhaṃ vātiādimāha. Tattha sīhanti dvipadacatuppadādayo satte abhibhavati ajjhottharatīti sīho, abhītarūpo abhītasabhāvo, taṃ abhītarūpaṃ sīhaṃ iva nisinnaṃ pūjesinti sambandho. Pakkhīnaṃ aggaṃ garuḷarājaṃ iva pavaraṃ uttamaṃ byaggharājaṃ iva abhi visesena jātaṃ sabbasīhānaṃ visesaṃ kesarasīhaṃ iva tilokassa saraṇaṃ sikhiṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ. Kiṃ bhūtaṃ? Anejaṃ nikkilesaṃ khandhamārādīhi aparājitaṃ nisinnaṃ sikhinti sambandho. Māraṇānagganti sabbakilesānaṃ māraṇe sosane viddhaṃsane aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ kilese mārentānaṃ paccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ vijjamānānampi tesaṃ agganti attho. Bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhataṃ parivāritaṃ parivāretvā nisinnaṃ sikhinti sambandho.

He, having attained the fruit of Arahantship, recollecting his past deeds and being filled with joy, proclaimed the apadāna of his past conduct, speaking the verses beginning with "Abhītarūpaṃ sīhaṃ vā..." Therein, "sīha" (lion) means a being who overcomes (abhibhavati) and overwhelms (ajjhottharati) other beings, two-footed, four-footed, and so on. "Abhītarūpa" means one whose nature is fearless. The connection is to be understood as: "I worshipped him who was seated like a fearless lion." Like the garuḷa king, foremost among birds; like the excellent, supreme tiger king; like the mane-lion, especially distinguished among all lions, was Sikhī, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the refuge of the three worlds. What was he like? Unwavering (anejaṃ), stainless (nikkilesaṃ), unconquered by the Māra of the aggregates and so on. The connection is made to Sikhī, who was seated. "Māraṇānaggaṃ" means foremost (aggaṃ) and best (seṭṭhaṃ) in the killing (māraṇe), drying up (sosane), and destroying (viddhaṃsane) of all defilements. The meaning is that he is foremost among the Paccekabuddhas and the disciples of the Buddha who destroy defilements, even while they exist. The connection is made to Sikhī, who was seated, placed at the fore and surrounded by the community of monks.

70. Caṅkoṭake ṭhapetvānāti uttamaṃ anojapupphaṃ karaṇḍake pūretvā sikhīsambuddhaṃ seṭṭhaṃ samokiriṃ pūjesinti attho.

70. "Caṅkoṭake ṭhapetvāna" ("Having placed in a basket") means: having filled a basket (karaṇḍake) with the finest anojā flowers, I scattered them over and worshipped (samokiriṃ pūjesiṃ) the supreme Perfectly Enlightened One, Sikhī. This is the meaning.

Pupphacaṅkoṭiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Pupphacaṅkoṭiya is concluded.

Sattamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the seventh chapter is concluded.

8. Nāgasamālavaggo

8. The Nāgasamāla Chapter

1. Nāgasamālattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Nāgasamāla

Āpāṭaliṃ [V 2.0090] ahaṃ pupphantiādikaṃ āyasmato nāgasamālattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tathārūpasajjanasaṃsaggassa [M 2.0098] alābhena satthari dharamānakāle dassanasavanapūjākammamakaritvā parinibbutakāle tassa bhagavato sārīrikadhātuṃ nidahitvā katacetiyamhi cittaṃ pasādetvā pāṭalipupphaṃ pūjetvā somanassaṃ uppādetvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā teneva somanassena tato kālaṃ kato tusitādīsu chasu devalokesu sukhamanubhavitvā aparabhāge manussesu manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto nāgarukkhapallavakomaḷasadisasarīrattā nāgasamāloti mātāpitūhi katanāmadheyyo bhagavati pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Nāgasamāla begins with "Āpāṭaliṃ ahaṃ pupphaṃ..." ("An āpāṭali flower I..."). He also, having made his resolve under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences that served as a basis for liberation from the cycle of rebirth, was reborn in a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity, he established a household life. However, due to not obtaining the association of such virtuous people, he did not perform the acts of seeing, hearing, and worshipping while the Teacher was still living. After the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, he aroused faith in his heart towards the cetiya that had been built enshrining the bodily relics of that Blessed One. Having worshipped it with a pāṭali flower and given rise to joy, he remained for the extent of his lifespan and, with that same joy, passed away from that existence. After experiencing happiness in the six deva worlds, including Tusita, and in a later time enjoying human prosperity among humans, he was reborn into a family during this Buddha-dispensation. Having reached maturity, he was given the name Nāgasamāla by his parents because his body was as tender as a young shoot of a nāga tree. With a mind full of faith in the Blessed One, he went forth and before long became an Arahant.

1. So [P 0.0394] pacchā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento āpāṭaliṃ ahaṃ pupphantiādimāha. Tattha āpāṭalinti ā samantato, ādarena vā pāṭalipupphaṃ gahetvā ahaṃ thūpamhi abhiropesiṃ pūjesinti attho. Ujjhitaṃ sumahāpatheti sabbanagaravāsīnaṃ vandanapūjanatthāya mahāpathe nagaramajjhe vīthiyaṃ ujjhitaṃ uṭṭhāpitaṃ, iṭṭhakakammasudhākammādīhi nipphāditanti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca suviññeyyamevāti.

1. Afterwards, recollecting his past deeds and being filled with joy, he proclaimed the apadāna of his past conduct, speaking the verses beginning with "Āpāṭaliṃ ahaṃ pupphaṃ..." Therein, "āpāṭaliṃ" means: having taken a pāṭali flower either from all around (ā samantato) or with great respect (ādarena), "I offered it at the thūpa and worshipped." This is the meaning. "Ujjhitaṃ sumahāpathe" ("Set up on a great highway") means: it was set up (ujjhitaṃ/uṭṭhāpitaṃ) on a great road, on a street in the middle of the city, for the veneration and worship of all the city-dwellers; it was completed with brickwork, plasterwork, and so on. This is the meaning. The rest is easily understood, both because the method has been explained below and because its meaning is plain.

Nāgasamālattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Nāgasamāla is concluded.

2. Padasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Padasaññaka

Akkantañca padaṃ disvātiādikaṃ āyasmato padasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu [V 2.0091] katādhikāro uppannuppannabhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ saddhāsampanne upāsakagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto ratanattaye pasanno bhagavatā tassa anukampāya dassitaṃ padacetiyaṃ disvā pasanno lomahaṭṭhajāto vandanapūjanādibahumānamakāsi. So teneva sukhette sukatena puññena tato cuto sagge nibbatto tattha dibbasukhamanubhavitvā aparabhāge manussesu jāto manussasampattiṃ sabbamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampannakule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya saddhājāto [M 2.0099] pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi, purākatapuññanāmena padasaññakattheroti pākaṭo.

“Seeing a footprint…” and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Padasaññaka. He too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a foundation for liberation in successive lives, was born in the time of the Blessed One Tissa in the house of a faithful lay devotee. Having reached maturity, he became devoted to the Triple Gem. Seeing the footprint shrine shown by the Blessed One out of compassion for him, he was filled with faith, his hair stood on end, and he paid great respect with veneration and offerings. Through that merit, well-made in a good field, after passing away from there, he was reborn in heaven. Having experienced divine happiness there, in a later period he was born among humans. Having experienced all human prosperity, in this Buddha’s dispensation he was born into a wealthy family. Upon reaching maturity and developing faith, he went forth and before long became an arahant. He became known as the Elder Padasaññaka on account of his past merit.

5. So ekadivasaṃ attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento akkantañca padaṃ disvātiādimāha. Tattha akkantanti akkamitaṃ dassitaṃ. Sabbabuddhānaṃ sabbadā caturaṅgulopariyeva gamanaṃ, ayaṃ pana tassa saddhāsampannataṃ ñatvā “eso imaṃ passatū”ti padacetiyaṃ dassesi, tasmā so tasmiṃ pasīditvā vandanapūjanādisakkāramakāsīti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

5. One day, recalling his past deeds and revealing the Apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke, beginning with “Seeing the footprint which had been stepped upon…”. Therein, 'stepped upon' means 'shown'. The walking of all Buddhas is always just four finger-breadths above the ground, but this Buddha, knowing his accomplishment in faith, showed the footprint shrine, thinking, “Let this one see this.” Therefore, being pleased with it, he paid respect with veneration and offerings; this is the meaning. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Padasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Padasaññaka is concluded.

3. Buddhasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Cīvarasaññaka

Dumagge paṃsukūlikantiādikaṃ āyasmato buddhasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe [P 0.0395] nibbatto vuddhippatto saddhājāto dumagge laggitaṃ bhagavato paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ disvā pasannamānaso “arahaddhaja”nti cintetvā vandanapūjanādisakkāramakāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussasampattimanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto saddhājāto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

“The rag-robe on the treetop…” and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Cīvarasaññaka. He too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a foundation for liberation in various existences, was born in the time of the Blessed One Tissa into a certain family. Having reached maturity and developed faith, seeing the Blessed One's rag-robe hanging on a treetop, with a gladdened mind, he thought, “It is the banner of Arahantship,” and paid respect with veneration and offerings. Through that meritorious deed, he experienced the prosperity of gods and humans. In this Buddha’s dispensation, born into a wealthy family, he developed faith, went forth, and before long became an Arahant.

9. So pattaarahattādhigamo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento dumagge paṃsukūlikantiādimāha. Tattha dhunāti kampatīti dumo. Duhati pūreti ākāsatalanti vā dumo, dumassa aggo koṭīti dumaggo, tasmiṃ dumagge. Paṃsumiva paṭikkūlabhāvaṃ amanuññabhāvaṃ ulati gacchatīti paṃsukūlaṃ, paṃsukūlameva paṃsukūlikaṃ, satthuno [V 2.0092] paṃsukūlaṃ dumagge laggitaṃ disvā ahaṃ añjaliṃ paggahetvā taṃ paṃsukūlaṃ avandiṃ paṇāmamakāsinti attho. Tanti nipātamattaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

9. Having attained the realization of Arahantship, he recalled his past deeds, and filled with joy, he revealed the Apadāna of his past conduct, saying, “The rag-robe on the treetop…” and so forth. Therein, a tree is a 'duma' because it 'shakes' (dhunāti) or 'trembles' (kampati). Or, it is a 'duma' because it 'fills' (duhati pūreti) the expanse of the sky. The 'treetop' (dumagga) is the 'top' (agga) or 'tip' (koṭi) of the tree; thus, 'on the treetop' (tasmiṃ dumagge). A 'rag-robe' (paṃsukūla) is so called because it 'goes to' (ulati gacchati) a state of being 'repulsive' (paṭikkūlabhāva) and 'disagreeable' (amanuññabhāva) 'like dust' (paṃsumiva). 'Paṃsukūlikaṃ' is the same as 'paṃsukūlaṃ'. The meaning is: 'Seeing the Teacher’s rag-robe hanging on the treetop, I raised my joined hands and venerated that rag-robe, paying homage to it.' The word 'taṃ' is merely a particle. The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Buddhasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Cīvarasaññaka is concluded.

4. Bhisāluvadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhisāluvadāyaka.

Kānanaṃ [M 2.0100] vanamoggayhātiādikaṃ āyasmato bhisāluvadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle himavantassa samīpe araññāvāse vasanto vanamūlaphalāhāro vivekavasenāgataṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pañcabhisāluve adāsi. Bhagavā tassa cittaṃ pasādetuṃ passantasseva paribhuñji. So tena cittappasādena kālaṃ katvā tusitādīsu sampattimanubhavitvā pacchā manussasampattiñca anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vibhavasampattiṃ patto taṃ pahāya sāsane pabbajito nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

“Having entered the forest, the wilderness…” and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Bhisāluvadāyaka. He too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a foundation for liberation in various existences, was born in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Dwelling in a forest residence near the Himālaya, subsisting on the roots and fruits of the forest, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī who had come seeking solitude. With a gladdened mind, he gave five lotus stalks. The Blessed One, in order to gladden his mind, consumed them in his presence. Through that mental confidence, when he died, he experienced prosperity in the Tusita realm and others. Afterwards, having also experienced human prosperity, in this Buddha’s dispensation he was born into a certain family. Having attained great wealth, he abandoned it and went forth in the Dispensation, and before long, he attained Arahantship.

13. So tato attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento kānanaṃ vanamoggayhātiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Vasāmi vipine ahanti vivekavāso ahaṃ vasāmīti sambandho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

13. Thereafter, recalling his past deeds, he became filled with joy and, revealing the Apadāna of his past conduct, spoke the verse beginning with “Having entered the forest, the wilderness…”. The meaning of that is as has been stated. The phrase 'I dwell in the forest' is to be construed as 'I, a dweller in solitude, dwell.' The rest has a clear meaning.

Bhisāluvadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhisāluvadāyaka is concluded.

Chaṭṭhabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sixth Recitation Section is concluded.

5. Ekasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekasaññaka.

Khaṇḍo [P 0.0396] nāmāsi nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato ekasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto ratanattaye pasannamānaso tassa satthuno khaṇḍaṃ nāma aggasāvakaṃ bhikkhāya caramānaṃ disvā saddahitvā piṇḍapātamadāsi. So tena puññakammena [V 2.0093] devamanussasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ piṇḍapātassa saññaṃ manasikaritvā paṭiladdhavisesattā ekasaññakattheroti pākaṭo.

“His name was Khaṇḍa…” and so forth is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ekasaññaka. He too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a foundation for liberation in various existences, was born in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī into a certain family. Having reached maturity, with a mind devoted to the Triple Gem, he saw that Teacher’s chief disciple named Khaṇḍa wandering for alms. Filled with faith, he gave him almsfood. Through that meritorious deed, he experienced divine and human prosperity. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a family in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, gained faith, went forth, and before long became an Arahant. Because he had attained special qualities by bringing to mind the perception of the almsfood, he became known as the Elder Ekasaññaka.

18. So [M 2.0101] aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento khaṇḍo nāmāsi nāmenātiādimāha. Tattha tassa aggasāvakattherassa kilesānaṃ khaṇḍitattā khaṇḍoti nāmaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

18. In a later time, recollecting his own past deed, he became joyful and, wishing to reveal the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning with, 'His name was Khaṇḍa.' Therein, that chief disciple elder received the name 'Khaṇḍa' because of his having cut off the defilements. The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.

Ekasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekasaññaka is concluded.

6. Tiṇasantharadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tiṇasantharadāyaka

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato tiṇasantharadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto buddhuppādato pageva uppannattā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantassa avidūre ekaṃ saraṃ nissāya paṭivasati. Tasmiṃ samaye tisso bhagavā tassānukampāya ākāsena agamāsi. Atha kho so tāpaso ākāsato oruyha ṭhitaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso tiṇaṃ lāyitvā tiṇasantharaṃ katvā nisīdāpetvā bahumānādarena pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā paṭikuṭiko hutvā pakkāmi. So yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cavitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto anekavidhasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Tiṇasantharadāyaka begins with 'Not far from the Himālaya.' He too, having made a resolve under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences that were a supporting condition for liberation, was born into a certain family in the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Having been born even before the arising of the Buddha, he abandoned the household life, went forth into the ascetic life, and dwelt depending on a certain lake not far from the Himālaya. At that time, the Blessed One Tissa, out of compassion for him, traveled through the sky. Then that ascetic, seeing the Blessed One who had descended from the sky and was standing there, with a gladdened mind, cut grass, made a grass mat, had him sit down, and having paid homage with great respect and reverence with the five-point prostration, he departed. He remained for his lifespan, and having passed away from there, while wandering among gods and humans and experiencing various kinds of prosperity, in this Buddha-era he was born into a certain family. Having reached maturity and gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and in no long time became an Arahant.

22. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Mahājātassaroti ettha pana saranti ettha pānīyatthikā dvipadacatuppadādayo sattāti saraṃ, atha vā saranti ettha nadīkandarādayoti saraṃ, mahanto [P 0.0397] ca so sayameva jātattā saro ceti mahājātassaro. Anotattachaddantadahādayo viya apākaṭanāmattā “mahājātassaro”ti vuttoti daṭṭhabbo. Satapattehi [V 2.0094] sañchannoti ekekasmiṃ pupphe satasatapattānaṃ vasena satapatto, satapattasetapadumehi [M 2.0102] sañchanno gahanībhūtoti attho. Nānāsakuṇamālayoti aneke haṃsakukkuṭakukkuhadeṇḍibhādayo ekato kuṇanti saddaṃ karontīti sakuṇāti laddhanāmānaṃ pakkhīnaṃ ālayo ādhārabhūtoti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

22. In a later time, recollecting his own past deed, he became joyful and, wishing to reveal the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning with, 'Not far from the Himālaya.' The meaning of that is as stated previously. Regarding 'Mahājātassara,' it is a 'sara' (lake) because beings desiring water, such as bipeds and quadrupeds, go (saranti) there. Or, it is a 'sara' because rivers, ravines, and so forth flow (saranti) there. And because it is great (mahā) and is a lake (sara) that arose by itself (jāta), it is a Mahājātassara. It should be understood that it is called 'Mahājātassara' because its name is not well-known, unlike lakes such as Anotatta and Chaddanta. 'Covered with hundred-petaled lotuses' (satapattehi sañchanno) means: a 'satapatta' has a hundred petals on each flower; the meaning is that it was densely covered with hundred-petaled white lotuses. 'The abode of various birds' (nānāsakuṇamālayo) means: it was the abode, the support, for birds (pakkhīnaṃ) who get the name 'sakuṇa' because many of them—swans, junglefowl, cuckoos, herons, and so on—cry out (kuṇanti) and make sounds together. The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.

Tiṇasantharadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tiṇasantharadāyaka is concluded.

7. Sūcidāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sūcidāyaka

Tiṃsakappasahassamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato sūcidāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya bhagavato cīvarakammaṃ kātuṃ pañca sūciyo adāsi. So tena puññena devamanussesu puññamanubhavitvā vicaranto uppannuppannabhave tikkhapañño hutvā pākaṭo imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya satthari pasīditvā pabbajanto tikkhapaññatāya khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sūcidāyaka begins with 'Thirty thousand eons ago.' He too, having made a resolve under previous Victorious Ones, accumulating merits in various existences that were a supporting condition for liberation, was born into a certain family in the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having reached maturity, he gave five needles for the sake of the Blessed One's robe-work. Through that merit, while wandering among gods and humans experiencing the fruit of that merit, he became renowned in every life for his keen wisdom. In this Buddha-era, he was born into a certain family, and having reached maturity and gained faith in the Teacher, while going forth, due to his keen wisdom, he attained Arahantship at the very razor's edge.

30. So aparabhāge puññaṃ paccavekkhanto taṃ disvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento tiṃsakappasahassamhītiādimāha. Antarantaraṃ panettha suviññeyyameva.

30. In a later time, while reflecting on his merit, he saw it and became joyful. Wishing to reveal the Apadāna of his former conduct, he spoke the verses beginning with, 'Thirty thousand eons ago.' The intervening passages here are easily understood.

31. Pañcasūcī mayā dinnāti ettha sūcati chiddaṃ karoti vijjhatīti sūci, pañcamattā sūcī pañcasūcī mayā dinnāti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

31. Regarding the phrase 'Five needles were given by me,' a 'sūci' (needle) is so called because it pierces (sūcati), makes a hole (chiddaṃ karoti), and penetrates (vijjhati). The meaning is, 'Five needles were given by me.' The remainder is easily understood.

Sūcidāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sūcidāyaka is concluded.

8. Pāṭalipupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pāṭalipupphiya

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhantiādikaṃ āyasmato pāṭalipupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ [M 2.0103] kulagehe seṭṭhiputto hutvā nibbatto vuddhippatto kusalākusalaññū satthari pasīditvā pāṭalipupphaṃ gahetvā satthu pūjesi. So tena puññena bahudhā [V 2.0095] sukhasampattiyo anubhavanto devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya satthari pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pāṭalipupphiya begins with 'The golden-hued Sambuddha.' He too, having made a resolve under previous supreme Victors, accumulating merits in various existences that were a supporting condition for liberation, was born as the son of a wealthy merchant in a certain family in the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Having reached maturity and come to know the wholesome and unwholesome, he gained faith in the Teacher, took a Pāṭali flower, and worshipped the Teacher. Through that merit, while wandering among gods and humans experiencing manifold blissful attainments, in this Buddha-era he was born into a family, and having reached maturity and gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth and in no long time became an Arahant.

36. So aparabhāge [P 0.0398] attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sambuddhantiādimāha. Tattha antarāpaṇeti ā samantato hiraññasuvaṇṇādikaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ paṇenti vikkiṇanti pattharanti etthāti āpaṇaṃ, āpaṇassa antaraṃ vīthīti antarāpaṇaṃ, tasmiṃ antarāpaṇe. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ kañcanagghiyasaṃkāsaṃ dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇaṃ sambuddhaṃ disvā pāṭalipupphaṃ pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

36. In a later time, recollecting his own past deed, he became joyful and, wishing to reveal the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning with, 'The golden-hued Sambuddha.' Therein, regarding 'in the marketplace street' (antarāpaṇe): a place where goods such as silver and gold are traded, sold, and displayed all around is an 'āpaṇa' (marketplace). The middle (antaraṃ) of the marketplace is a street (vīthī); thus 'antarāpaṇa.' The meaning is: 'In that marketplace street, having seen the Sambuddha—golden-hued, like refined gold, endowed with the thirty-two excellent marks—I worshipped him with a Pāṭali flower.' The remainder is clear in meaning everywhere.

Pāṭalipupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pāṭalipupphiya is concluded.

9. Ṭhitañjaliyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ṭhitañjaliya

Migaluddo pure āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato ṭhitañjaliyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tatthuppannabhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle purākatena ekena kammacchiddena nesādayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto migasūkarādayo māretvā nesādakammena araññe vāsaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ samaye tisso bhagavā tassānukampāya himavantaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇehi asītānubyañjanabyāmappabhāhi ca jalamānaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā somanassajāto paṇāmaṃ katvā gantvā paṇṇasanthare nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe devo gajjanto asani pati, tato maraṇasamaye buddhamanussaritvā punañjalimakāsi. So tena puññena sukhette katakusalattā akusalavipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā sagge nibbatto kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu manussasampattiyo ca anubhavitvā aparabhāge imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya purākatavāsanāya satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Elder Ṭhitañjaliya begins with “Migaluddo pure āsi” (Long ago, I was a hunter). This elder, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits as a support for liberation in various existences, in the time of the Blessed One Tissa, due to a past karmic obstruction, was reborn in a hunter’s family. Having gained intelligence, killing deer, boars, and other animals, he made his living in the forest by hunting. At that time, the Blessed One Tissa, out of compassion for him, went to the Himalayas. Seeing the Blessed One blazing with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and a fathom-long aura, he became joyful, paid homage, and went to sit on a leaf-covered seat. At that moment, as the sky thundered, a thunderbolt struck. At the time of death, remembering the Buddha, he rejoined his hands in reverence. By that merit, having done good deeds in a good field (of merit), and having blocked the fruition of unwholesome deeds, he was reborn in heaven. After enjoying sense-sphere pleasures and human prosperity among humans, in a later birth, during the appearance of this Buddha, he was born into a certain family. Growing up, due to past inclinations, he developed faith in the Teacher, went forth, and before long became an arahant.

42. So [M 2.0104] tato paraṃ attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento migaluddo pure āsintiādimāha. Tattha migaluddoti migānaṃ māraṇaṃ upagacchatīti migaluddo. Miganti sīghaṃ vātavegena gacchanti dhāvantīti migā, tesaṃ migānaṃ māraṇe luddo dāruṇo lobhīti migaluddo. So ahaṃ pure bhagavato dassanasamaye migaluddo āsiṃ ahosinti attho[V 2.0096]. Araññe kānaneti arati gacchati migasamūho etthāti araññaṃ, atha vā ā samantato rajjanti tattha vivekābhiratā buddhapaccekabuddhādayo [P 0.0399] mahāsārappattā sappurisāti araññaṃ. Kā kucchitākārena vā bhayānakākārena vā nadanti saddaṃ karonti, ānanti vindantīti vā kānanaṃ, tasmiṃ araññe kānane migaluddo pure āsinti sambandho. Tattha addasaṃ sambuddhanti tattha tasmiṃ araññe upagataṃ sambuddhaṃ addasaṃ addakkhinti attho. Dassanaṃ pure ahosi avidūre, tasmā manodvārānusārena cakkhuviññāṇaṃ purecārikaṃ kāyaviññāṇasamaṅgiṃ pāpeti appetīti attho.

42. Then, recollecting his past deeds with joy, he revealed his former life story and said, “Migaluddo pure āsi” (Long ago, I was a hunter). Here, ‘migaludda’ means one who brings about the death of deer. “Migā” (deer) are those that go swiftly with the speed of the wind, that run; and “ludda” (hunter) refers to one who is cruel and greedy in killing those deer. Thus, the meaning is, “I was a deer hunter in the past at the time of the Blessed One’s appearance.” Regarding “araññe kānane” (in the forest grove): “arañña” (forest) is where a herd of deer goes without delight, or alternatively, it is called a forest because good persons who delight in seclusion, such as Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, who have attained great essence, are delighted all around there. “Kānana” (grove) is where (animals) make sounds in a wretched or fearful manner, or where they find enjoyment (ānanti). The connection is, 'I was a deer hunter in that forest grove in the past.' Regarding “Tattha addasaṃ Sambuddhaṃ” (There I saw the Fully Awakened One): the meaning is, 'In that forest, I saw the Fully Awakened One who had arrived.' The sight occurred nearby before, so through the mind-door, eye-consciousness went first and brought about association with body-consciousness—this is the meaning.

44. Tato me asanīpātoti ā samantato sananto gajjanto patatīti asani, asaniyā pāto patanaṃ asanīpāto, devadaṇḍoti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

44. Regarding “Tato me asanīpāto” (Then a thunderbolt struck me)—‘asani’ (thunderbolt) is that which, sounding and roaring from all sides, falls; and ‘pāto’ (strike) means its fall, hence ‘asanīpāto’ (thunderbolt strike), meaning the devas’ weapon. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

Ṭhitañjaliyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ṭhitañjaliya is complete.

10. Tipadumiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tipadumiya.

Padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato tipadumiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatiyaṃ mālākārakulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto mālākārakammaṃ katvā vasanto ekadivasaṃ anekavidhāni jalajathalajapupphāni gahetvā rañño santikaṃ gantukāmo evaṃ cintesi – “rājā imāni tāva pupphāni disvā pasanno sahassaṃ vā dhanaṃ gāmādikaṃ vā dadeyya, lokanāthaṃ pana pūjetvā nibbānāmatadhanaṃ labhāmi, kiṃ me etesu sundara”nti tena “bhagavantaṃ [M 2.0105] pūjetvā saggamokkhasampattiyo nipphādetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā vaṇṇavantaṃ atīva rattapupphattayaṃ gahetvā pūjesi. Tāni gantvā ākāsaṃ chādetvā pattharitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Nagaravāsino acchariyabbhutacittajātā celukkhepasahassāni pavattayiṃsu. Taṃ disvā bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsi. So tena puññena devamanussesu sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde gahapatikule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya satthari pasīditvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Tipadumiya, beginning with “Padumuttaro nāma jino.” This one too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits as the foundation for liberation in various existences, was born in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in Haṃsavatī, in the family of garland-makers. Having grown up, he engaged in the work of making garlands. One day, having gathered various kinds of flowers—water-born and land-born—he intended to go to the king’s presence and thought thus: “The king, seeing these flowers, might be pleased and give a thousand coins or a village, etc. But by worshipping the Lord of the World, I would obtain the wealth of Nibbāna. What use are these beautiful things to me?” Thinking thus, “It is fitting to worship the Blessed One and thereby achieve the attainments of heaven and liberation,” he took three very beautiful red flowers and offered them. Those flowers, having gone up, covered the sky and spread out, and remained there. The city-dwellers, their minds filled with wonder and amazement, raised thousands of cloths in acclamation. Seeing this, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation. By that merit, he enjoyed prosperity among gods and humans, and in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born in a householder’s family. Growing up, he gained faith in the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and having obtained faith, he went forth. Not long after, he became an arahant.

48. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro [V 2.0097] nāma jinotiādimāha. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttova. Sabbadhammāna pāragūti sabbesaṃ navalokuttaradhammānaṃ pāraṃ nibbānaṃ gato paccakkhaṃ katoti attho. Danto dantaparivutoti sayaṃ kāyavācādīhi [P 0.0400] danto etadagge ṭhapitehi sāvakehi parivutoti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha sambandhavasena uttānatthamevāti.

48. Recollecting his past deeds, filled with joy, he revealed his Apadāna of former conduct, saying, “Padumuttara, the Victorious One,” etc. Its meaning is as stated before. “Gone beyond all phenomena” means he has gone to Nibbāna, the beyond of all nine supramundane dhammas, and directly realized it. “Tamed, surrounded by the tamed” means he himself is tamed in body, speech, etc., and is surrounded by disciples who are established as foremost in being tamed. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere by connection.

Tipadumiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tipadumiya is complete.

Aṭṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the eighth section is complete.

9. Timiravaggo

9. The Darkness Chapter

1. Timirapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Timirapupphiya.

Candabhāgānadītīretiādikaṃ [V 2.0098] āyasmato timirapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā candabhāgāya nadiyā samīpe vasati, vivekakāmatāya himavantaṃ gantvā nisinnaṃ siddhatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā vanditvā tassa guṇaṃ pasīditvā timirapupphaṃ gahetvā pūjesi. So tena puññena devesu ca manussesu ca [M 2.0106] sampattimanubhavanto saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Timirapupphiya, beginning with “On the bank of the Candabhāgā River.” What is the origin? This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a basis for liberation in various existences, was born in the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha in a certain family. Having reached maturity and established himself in household life, while living he saw the danger in sensual pleasures, abandoned his home life, and took up the ascetic life of a recluse. He dwelt near the Candabhāgā River. Desiring solitude, he went to the Himālaya. There, seeing the Blessed One Siddhattha seated, he paid homage and, gaining faith in his virtues, took a timira flower and offered it. Through that merit, experiencing fortune among gods and humans while wandering in saṃsāra, in this Buddha-era he was born in a certain family. Having reached maturity and gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth, and before long became an arahant.

1. So aparabhāge pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento candabhāgānadītīretiādimāha. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttova. Anubhotaṃ vajāmahanti gaṅgāya āsanne vasanabhāvena sabbattha rammabhāvena gaṅgāto heṭṭhā sotānusārena ahaṃ vajāmi gacchāmi tattha tattha vasāmīti attho. Nisinnaṃ samaṇaṃ disvāti samitapāpattā sositapāpattā samaṇasaṅkhātaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ disvāti attho.

1. In a later time, recalling his past deed, he became filled with joy and, wishing to declare the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke the words beginning with “On the bank of the Candabhāgā River.” Its meaning is as stated below. As for ‘I travel downstream’: because of dwelling near the Gaṅgā, and because of the pleasantness everywhere, I travel downstream from the Gaṅgā, following the current; I go, I proceed, I dwell in various places—this is the meaning. As for ‘Seeing the seated recluse’: it means seeing the Fully Enlightened One, known as a recluse (samaṇa) because his evil has been calmed (samita) and dried up.

2. Evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadāti ayaṃ bhagavā sayaṃ tiṇṇo sabbasatte tārayissati saṃsārato uttāreti sayaṃ kāyadvārādīhi damito ayaṃ bhagavā pare dameti.

2. As for ‘Thus I thought at that time’: ‘This Blessed One, having himself crossed over, will lead all beings across; he brings them out of saṃsāra. Having himself been tamed through the doors of body and so on, this Blessed One tames others.’

3. Sayaṃ assattho assāsampatto, kilesapariḷāhato mutto sabbasatte assāseti, santabhāvaṃ āpāpeti. Sayaṃ santo santakāyacitto paresaṃ santakāyacittaṃ pāpeti. Sayaṃ mutto saṃsārato muccito pare saṃsārato mocayissati. So ayaṃ bhagavā sayaṃ nibbuto kilesaggīhi nibbuto paresampi kilesaggīhi nibbāpessatīti ahaṃ tadā evaṃ cintesinti attho.

3. ‘He himself is comforted, having attained consolation, freed from the torment of defilements, he comforts all beings, causing them to reach a state of peace. He himself is peaceful, with a peaceful body and mind, and he causes others to attain a peaceful body and mind. He himself is liberated, freed from saṃsāra, and will liberate others from saṃsāra. This Blessed One, himself extinguished from the fires of defilements, will also extinguish the fires of defilements for others.’ The meaning is: ‘Thus I thought at that time.’

4. Gahetvā timirapupphanti sakalaṃ vanantaṃ nīlakāḷaraṃsīhi andhakāraṃ viya kurumānaṃ khāyatīti [V 2.0099] timiraṃ pupphaṃ taṃ gahetvā kaṇṇikāvaṇṭaṃ gahetvā matthake sīsassa upari ākāse okiriṃ pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

4. As for ‘Taking the timira flower’: it is called a timira flower because it appears as if making the entire forest dark with its blue-black rays. Taking that flower and its stalk, I scattered it in the sky above my head and offered it—this is the meaning. The rest is clear in meaning.

Timirapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Timirapupphiya is complete.

2. Gatasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Gatasaññaka

Jātiyā [P 0.0401] sattavassohantiādikaṃ āyasmato gatasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ [M 2.0107] kulagehe nibbatto purākatavāsanāvasena saddhājāto sattavassikakāleyeva pabbajito bhagavato paṇāmakaraṇeneva pākaṭo ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ atīva nīlamaṇippabhāni naṅgalakasitaṭṭhāne uṭṭhitasattapupphāni gahetvā ākāse pūjesi. So yāvatāyukaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Gatasaññaka, beginning with “I was seven years of age.” This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a basis for liberation in various existences, was born in the time of the Blessed One Tissa in a certain family. Due to the influence of past conditioning, faith arose in him, and he went forth at the age of seven. He became famous just by paying homage to the Blessed One. One day, he took seven flowers that had sprung up in a plowed field, which were exceedingly radiant like blue sapphires, and offered them in the sky. Having practiced the duties of a recluse for as long as he lived, he wandered among gods and humans due to that merit. In this Buddha-era, he was born in a certain family, reached maturity, gained faith in the Teacher, went forth, and soon became an arahant.

10. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento jātiyā sattavassohantiādimāha. Tattha jātiyā sattavassoti mātugabbhato nikkhantakālato paṭṭhāya paripuṇṇasattavassikoti attho. Pabbajiṃ anagāriyanti agārassa hitaṃ āgāriyaṃ kasivāṇijjādikammaṃ natthi āgāriyanti anagāriyaṃ, buddhasāsane pabbajiṃ ahanti attho.

10. In a later time, recalling his own past deed, he became filled with joy and, wishing to declare the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke the words beginning with “I was seven years of age.” Therein, “seven years of age” means that from the time he came out of his mother’s womb, he was a full seven years old. As for ‘I went forth into homelessness (anagāriyaṃ)’: that which is for the benefit of the house (agāra) is household life (āgāriyaṃ), namely, work such as farming and trade. Where there is no such household life, that is homelessness (anagāriyaṃ). The meaning is: ‘I went forth in the Buddha’s dispensation.’

12. Sugatānugataṃ magganti buddhena gataṃ maggaṃ. Atha vā sugatena desitaṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipattipūraṇavasena haṭṭhamānaso tuṭṭhacitto pūjetvāti sambandho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

12. As for ‘The path followed by the Sugata’: it means the path traveled by the Buddha. Alternatively, the connection is: with a delighted mind and a joyful heart on account of fulfilling the practice in accordance with the Dhamma taught by the Sugata, he offered. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Gatasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Gatasaññaka is complete.

3. Nipannañjalikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Apadāna of the Elder Nipannañjalika

Rukkhamūle [V 2.0100] nisinnohantiādikaṃ āyasmato nipannañjalikattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto pabbajitvā rukkhamūlikaṅgaṃ pūrayamāno araññe viharati. Tasmiṃ samaye kharo ābādho uppajji, tena pīḷito paramakāruññappatto ahosi. Tadā bhagavā tassa kāruññena tattha agamāsi. Atha so nipannakova uṭṭhituṃ asakkonto sirasi añjaliṃ katvā bhagavato paṇāmaṃ akāsi. So tato cuto tusitabhavane uppanno tattha sampattimanubhavitvā evaṃ cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā [M 2.0108] imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi, purākatapuññavasena nipannañjalikattheroti pākaṭo.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Nipannañjalika, beginning with “I was seated at the foot of a tree.” This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a basis for liberation in many existences, was born in a family in the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Having reached maturity, he went forth and, while fulfilling the ascetic practice of dwelling at the foot of a tree, he lived in the forest. At that time, a severe illness arose, and afflicted by it, he came to be in a most pitiable state. Then the Blessed One, out of compassion for him, went there. Then he, lying down and unable to rise, made the añjali gesture on his head and paid homage to the Blessed One. Passing away from there, he arose in the Tusita heaven. Having experienced the fortune there, and thus having experienced the fortunes of the six sense-sphere heavens, in this Buddha-era he was born in a certain family. Having reached maturity and gained faith in the Teacher, he went forth, and before long became an arahant. Due to his past merit, he became known as the Elder Nipannañjalika.

16. So aparabhāge attano puññasampattiyo oloketvā somanassajāto [P 0.0402] pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento rukkhamūle nisinnohantiādimāha. Tattha ruhati paṭiruhati uddhamuddhaṃ ārohatīti rukkho, tassa rukkhassa mūle samīpeti attho. Byādhito paramena cāti paramena adhikena kharena kakkhaḷena byādhinā rogena byādhito, byādhinā ahaṃ samannāgatoti attho. Paramakāruññappattomhīti paramaṃ adhikaṃ kāruññaṃ dīnabhāvaṃ dukkhitabhāvaṃ pattomhi araññe kānaneti sambandho.

16. In a later period, having reflected upon his own meritorious attainments and become joyful, he, wishing to proclaim the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke, beginning with the words, 'I was seated at the foot of a tree' (`rukkhamūle nisinno'haṃ`). Therein, 'tree' (`rukkho`) is so called because it grows (`ruhati`), grows again (`paṭiruhati`), and ascends (`ārohati`) higher and higher. 'At the foot of the tree' (`rukkhassa mūle`) means near it; this is the meaning. 'Afflicted by an extreme [disease]' (`byādhito paramena ca`) means afflicted (`byādhito`) by an extreme (`paramena`), that is, superior (`adhikena`), harsh (`kharena`), and rough (`kakkhaḷena`) disease (`byādhinā`), that is, illness (`rogena`); 'I was possessed by disease' is the meaning. 'I had attained a state of extreme wretchedness' (`paramakāruññappattomhi`) means I had attained (`patto'mhi`) an extreme (`paramaṃ`), that is, superior (`adhikaṃ`), state of wretchedness (`kāruññaṃ`), a pitiable state (`dīnabhāvaṃ`), a state of suffering (`dukkhitabhāvaṃ`). The connection is with 'in the wilderness, in the forest' (`araññe kānane`).

20. Pañcevāsuṃ mahāsikhāti sirasi piḷandhanatthena sikhā vuccati cūḷā. Maṇīti jotamānaṃ makuṭaṃ tassa atthīti sikho, cakkavattino ekanāmakā pañceva cakkavattino āsuṃ ahesunti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

20. Regarding 'There were five with great crests' (`pañcevāsuṃ mahāsikhā`): A topknot (`cūḷā`) is called a crest (`sikhā`) because it is an ornament (`piḷandhana`) on the head (`sirasi`). He is `Sikho` because he has a shining (`jotamānaṃ`) crown (`makuṭaṃ`) with a jewel (`maṇi`). The meaning is that there were (`āsuṃ`, `ahesuṃ`) five universal monarchs (`cakkavattino`) of the same name (`ekanāmakā`). The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Nipannañjalikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nipannañjalika is concluded.

4. Adhopupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Adhopupphiya

Abhibhū nāma so bhikkhūtiādikaṃ āyasmato adhopupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato [V 2.0101] kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā aparabhāge kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā taṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcābhiññāaṭṭhasamāpattilābhī iddhīsu ca vasībhāvaṃ patvā himavantasmiṃ paṭivasati. Tassa sikhissa bhagavato abhibhū nāma aggasāvako vivekābhirato himavantamagamāsi. Atha so tāpaso taṃ aggasāvakattheraṃ disvā therassa ṭhitapabbataṃ āruhanto pabbatassa heṭṭhātalato sugandhāni vaṇṇasampannāni satta pupphāni gahetvā pūjesi. Atha so thero tassānumodanamakāsi. Sopi tāpaso sakassamaṃ agamāsi. Tattha ekena ajagarena pīḷito aparabhāge aparihīnajjhāno [M 2.0109] teneva upaddavena upadduto kālaṃ katvā brahmalokaparāyano hutvā brahmasampattiṃ chakāmāvacarasampattiñca anubhavitvā manussesu manussasampattiyo ca khepetvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. So aparabhāge attano katapuññanāmena adhopupphiyattheroti pākaṭo.

The Apadāna of the venerable Adhopupphiya begins with the words, 'That monk named Abhibhū.' He also, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merits in many existences, was reborn in a family home in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity and established a household, in a later period, seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he abandoned it and went forth into the life of a seer. Having gained the five supernormal knowledges and the eight meditative attainments, and having reached mastery in the spiritual powers, he resided in the Himālaya. The Blessed One Sikhī's chief disciple named Abhibhū, who delighted in seclusion, went to the Himālaya. Then that ascetic, seeing the chief disciple elder, while ascending the mountain where the elder was standing, took seven fragrant and well-colored flowers from the base of the mountain and made an offering. Then the elder expressed his appreciation to him. That ascetic also went to his own hermitage. There, being crushed by a python, he later, with undiminished jhāna, being afflicted by that very affliction, passed away and was destined for the Brahma-world. Having experienced the fortune of the Brahma-world and the fortune of the six sensual spheres, and having exhausted human fortunes among humans, during this Buddha's appearance he was reborn in a certain family home. Having reached maturity, hearing the Blessed One's Dhamma, with a confident mind, he went forth and in no long time became an Arahant. In a later period, he became famous by the name of his meritorious deed as the Elder Adhopupphiya.

22. So ekadivasaṃ attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento abhibhū nāma so bhikkhūtiādimāha. Tattha sīlasamādhīhi pare abhibhavatīti abhibhū, khandhamārādimāre [P 0.0403] abhibhavati ajjhottharatīti vā abhibhū, sasantānaparasantānagatakilese abhibhavati viheseti viddhaṃsetīti vā abhibhū. Bhikkhanasīlo yācanasīloti bhikkhu, chinnabhinnapaṭadharoti vā bhikkhu. Abhibhū nāma aggasāvako so bhikkhūti attho, sikhissa bhagavato aggasāvakoti sambandho.

22. One day, recalling his past deed and becoming joyful, he, wishing to proclaim the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke, beginning with the words, 'That monk named Abhibhū.' Therein, he is 'Abhibhū' because he overcomes (`abhibhavati`) others by means of virtue and concentration. Or, he is 'Abhibhū' because he overcomes (`abhibhavati`) and overwhelms (`ajjhottharati`) the Māras of the aggregates and so forth. Or, he is 'Abhibhū' because he overcomes (`abhibhavati`), harasses (`viheseti`), and demolishes (`viddhaṃseti`) the defilements that have arisen in his own mental continuum and in the mental continua of others. He is a 'bhikkhu' because he is of a nature to beg (`bhikkhanasīlo`), of a nature to ask (`yācanasīlo`). Or, he is a 'bhikkhu' because he is a wearer of cut and torn cloth (`chinnabhinnapaṭadharo`). The meaning is: 'That monk was the chief disciple named Abhibhū.' The connection is: 'the chief disciple of the Blessed One Sikhī'.

27. Ajagaro maṃ pīḷesīti tathārūpaṃ sīlasampannaṃ jhānasampannaṃ tāpasaṃ pubbe katapāpena verena ca mahanto ajagarasappo pīḷesi. So teneva upaddavena upadduto aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo āsi. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

27. Regarding 'A python crushed me' (`ajagaro maṃ pīḷesi`): A great python (`mahanto ajagarasappo`) crushed (`pīḷesi`) such a virtuous (`sīlasampannaṃ`) and meditative (`jhānasampannaṃ`) ascetic (`tāpasaṃ`) because of enmity (`verena`) from an evil deed done previously (`pubbe katapāpena`). He, being afflicted (`upadduto`) by that very affliction (`teneva upaddavena`), with undiminished jhāna (`aparihīnajjhāno`), passed away (`kālaṃ katvā`) and was destined for the Brahma-world (`brahmalokaparāyaṇo āsi`). The rest has a clear meaning everywhere.

Adhopupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Adhopupphiya is concluded.

5. Raṃsisaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṃsisaññaka

Pabbate himavantamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato raṃsisaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tesu tesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa [V 2.0102] bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā ajinacammadharo himavantamhi vāsaṃ kappesi. Tasmiṃ samaye vipassī bhagavā himavantamagamāsi. Atha so tāpaso tamupagataṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā tassa bhagavato [M 2.0110] sarīrato nikkhantachabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsīsu pasīditvā añjaliṃ paggayha pañcaṅgena namakkāramakāsi. So teneva puññena ito cuto tusitādīsu dibbasampattiyo anubhavitvā aparabhāge manussasampattiyo ca anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tatthādīnavaṃ disvā gehaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the venerable Raṃsisaññaka begins with the words, 'On the Himavant mountain.' He also, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated merits in those various existences, was reborn in a family home in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity and established a household, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures, abandoned the household life, and went forth into the ascetic life. As a wearer of an antelope hide, he took up residence in the Himālaya. At that time, the Blessed One Vipassī went to the Himālaya. Then that ascetic, seeing the Blessed One who had come there, became confident in the six-colored Buddha-rays emanating from the Blessed One's body, raised his joined hands, and paid homage with the five points. By that same merit, having passed away from here, he experienced divine fortunes in the Tusita and other realms, and in a later period also experienced human fortunes. During this Buddha's appearance, he was reborn in a family home. Having reached maturity and established a household, seeing the danger in that, he abandoned the home, went forth, and in no long time became an Arahant.

30. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento pabbate himavantamhītiādimāha. Tattha pabbateti pakārena brūhati vaḍḍhetīti pabbato, himo assa atthīti himavanto, himavanto ca so pabbato cāti himavantapabbato. Himavantapabbateti vattabbe gāthāvacanasukhatthaṃ “pabbate himavantamhī”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmiṃ himavantamhi pabbate vāsaṃ kappesiṃ pure ahanti sambandho. Sesaṃ sabbattha nayānusārena uttānamevāti.

30. In a later period, recalling his past deed and becoming joyful, he, wishing to proclaim the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke, beginning with the words, 'On the Himavant mountain.' Therein, it is a 'mountain' (`pabbato`) because it grows (`brūhati`) or increases (`vaḍḍhati`) in a particular way. It is 'Himavant' because 'it has snow' (`himo assa atthi`). It is the Himavant mountain because it is both Himavant and a mountain. When 'on the Himavant mountain' (`himavantapabbate`) should be said, for the sake of metrical ease in the verse, it is said 'on the mountain, in the Himavant' (`pabbate himavantamhi`). The connection is: 'Formerly, I made my dwelling on that Himavant mountain.' The rest has a clear meaning everywhere according to the method.

Raṃsisaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṃsisaññaka is concluded.

6. Dutiyaraṃsisaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Second Elder Raṃsisaññaka

Pabbate [P 0.0404] himavantamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato dutiyaraṃsisaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katakusalo uppannuppannabhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto phussassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tattha dosaṃ disvā taṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantapabbate vasanto vākacīranivasano vivekasukhena viharati. Tasmiṃ samaye so phussaṃ bhagavantaṃ taṃ padesaṃ sampattaṃ disvā tassa sarīrato nikkhantachabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo ito cito vidhāvantiyo daṇḍadīpikānikkhantavipphurantamiva disvā tasmiṃ pasanno añjaliṃ paggahetvā vanditvā cittaṃ pasādetvā teneva pītisomanassena kālaṃ katvā tusitādīsu nibbatto tattha cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo ca anubhavitvā aparabhāge manussasampattiyo [V 2.0103] ca [M 2.0111] anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto pubbavāsanāvasena pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Dutiyaraṃsisaññaka Thera, beginning with 'On the Himavanta mountain.' He too, having performed wholesome deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits that are a supporting condition for liberation in each successive existence, was born into a family during the time of the Blessed One Phussa. Having reached maturity, he established a household, and seeing the danger therein, he abandoned it and went forth into the ascetic life. Dwelling on the Himavanta mountain, clad in bark garments, he lived with the bliss of seclusion.
