Gaining understanding, he went forth in the Teacher’s dispensation and soon became an arahant.

31. So pacchā sakakammaṃ saritvā taṃ tathato ñatvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento [V 2.0123] varuṇo nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Tattha yadā ahaṃ sambodhanatthāya buddhaṃ bodhiñca pūjesiṃ, tadā varuṇo nāma devarājā ahosinti sambandho.

31. Later, recollecting his own deeds and truly knowing them, he became joyful and, revealing the Apadāna of his former conduct, he spoke beginning with 'Varuṇa by name.' Here, the connection is: 'When I honored the Buddha and the Bodhi tree for the sake of enlightenment, at that time I was the deva king named Varuṇa.'

34. Dharaṇīruhapādapanti ettha rukkhalatāpabbatasattharatanādayo dhāretīti dharaṇī, tasmiṃ ruhati patiṭṭhahatīti dharaṇīruho. Pādena pivatīti pādapo, siñcitasiñcitodakaṃ pādena mūlena pivati rukkhakkhandhasākhāviṭapehi āporasaṃ patthariyatīti attho, taṃ dharaṇīruhapādapaṃ bodhirukkhanti sambandho.

34. Regarding the term 'Dharaṇīruhapādapa,' here, that which sustains trees, creepers, mountains, bedding, jewels, and so forth is 'dharaṇī' (earth); that which grows and is established in it is 'dharaṇīruha' (earth-rooted). That which drinks with its foot is 'pādapa,' meaning it drinks the sprinkled water with its foot, its root, and spreads moisture through its trunk, branches, and foliage. The connection is with that 'dharaṇīruhapādapa,' the Bodhi tree.

35. Sakakammābhiraddhoti attano kusalakammena abhiraddho pasanno uttame bodhimhi pasannoti sambandho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

35. The phrase 'pleased by one's own kamma' (sakakammābhiraddho) means pleased by one's own wholesome kamma, confident; the connection is 'confident in the supreme enlightenment.' The rest is clear throughout.

Ekāsaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekāsaniya is concluded.

5. Suvaṇṇapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Suvaṇṇapupphiya

Vipassī [M 2.0132] nāma bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato suvaṇṇapupphiyattherassa [P 0.0421] apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ ṭhāne bhūmaṭṭhakadevaputto hutvā nibbatto tassa bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso catūhi suvaṇṇapupphehi pūjesi. Tāni pupphāni ākāse suvaṇṇavitānaṃ hutvā chādesuṃ, suvaṇṇapabhā ca buddhassa sarīrapabhā ca ekato hutvā mahāobhāso ahosi. So atirekataraṃ pasanno sakabhavanaṃ gatopi saratiyeva. So tena puññakammena tusitabhavanādisugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Suvaṇṇapupphiya, beginning with 'There was a Blessed One named Vipassī,' is as follows: He too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Jinas, accumulating merits that served as a basis for liberation in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn as an earth-dwelling deity in a certain place. Hearing the Dhamma from that Blessed One, his mind became serene, and he worshipped with four golden flowers. Those flowers became a golden canopy in the sky and provided shade, and their golden radiance, merging with the Buddha’s bodily aura, created a great brilliance. Exceedingly pleased, even after returning to his own abode, he kept remembering. Through the merit of that deed, he wandered through happy destinies such as the Tusita heaven, enjoying divine prosperity. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a good family. Having attained maturity, he listened to the Teacher’s discourse, devoted himself to the Dispensation, went forth, and soon became an Arahant.

40. So aparabhāge pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento vipassī nāma bhagavātiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

40. Later, recalling his past deeds, he was filled with joy and, declaring the Apadāna of his former conduct, began with 'There was a Blessed One named Vipassī...' The meaning of that is as stated in the text that follows.

44. Pāmojjaṃ janayitvānāti balavapītiṃ uppādetvā “pāmojjaṃ āmodanā pamodanā hāso [V 2.0124] pahāso vitti odagyaṃ attamanatā cittassā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 9, 86; mahāni. 1) viya attamanatā sakabhāvaṃ uppādetvāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

44. 'Generating joy' means producing strong delight, generating a state of mental contentment—as in passages like 'joy, rejoicing, delight, laughter, mirth, satisfaction, elation, and happiness of mind' (Dhs. 9, 86; Mahāni. 1)—that is its own nature. The rest is clear everywhere.

Suvaṇṇapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Suvaṇṇapupphiya is concluded.

6. Citakapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Citakapūjaka

Vasāmi rājāyatanetiādikaṃ āyasmato citakapūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tato paraṃ uppannuppannabhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle rājāyatanarukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatto antarantarā devatāhi saddhiṃ dhammaṃ [M 2.0133] sutvā pasanno bhagavati parinibbute saparivāro gandhadīpadhūpapupphabheriādīni gāhāpetvā bhagavato āḷahanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā dīpādīni pūjetvā anekehi tūriyehi anekehi vāditehi taṃ pūjesi. Tato paṭṭhāya sakabhavanaṃ upaviṭṭhopi bhagavantameva saritvā sammukhā viya vandati. So teneva puññena tena cittappasādena rājāyatanato kālaṃ kato tusitādīsu nibbatto dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato manussesu manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto bhagavati uppannacittappasādo bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

This is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Citakapūjaka, beginning with 'I dwelt at Rājāyatana...' He too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, thereafter, in successive rebirths, he accumulated merits that served as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was reborn as a tree deity of the Rājāyatana tree. From time to time, hearing the Dhamma together with other deities, he became serene. When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he, together with his retinue, had offerings such as perfumes, lamps, incense, flowers, and drums brought. He went to the Blessed One’s cremation site, worshipped with lamps and other items, and honored him with various musical instruments and music. From then on, even while residing in his own abode, he would recollect the Blessed One and pay homage as if in his presence. By that merit and purity of mind, when he passed away from the Rājāyatana, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven and other divine realms, enjoying divine prosperity; thereafter, among humans, he experienced human prosperity. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a noble family. Having attained maturity, he developed faith in the Blessed One, went forth into the Blessed One’s Dispensation, and soon became an Arahant.

49. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento vasāmi rājāyatanetiādimāha. Rājāyataneti [P 0.0422] devarājūnaṃ āyatanaṃ rājāyatanaṃ, tassa rukkhassa nāmadheyyo vā. Parinibbute bhagavatīti parisamantato kiñci anavasesetvā khandhaparinibbānakāle parinibbānasamaye parinibbānappattassa sikhino lokabandhunoti sambandho.

49. Then, later, recalling his past deeds and filled with joy, he revealed the Apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'I dwelt at Rājāyatana...' 'Rājāyatana' is the abode of the kings of gods, or it is the name of that tree. 'When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna' refers to the connection with Sikhī, the Kinsman of the World, who had attained Nibbāna at the time of the Nibbāna of the aggregates, leaving nothing whatsoever remaining around him, at the moment of final Nibbāna.

50. Citakaṃ agamāsahanti candanāgarudevadārukappūratakkolādisugandhadārūhi citaṃ rāsigatanti citaṃ, citameva citakaṃ, buddhagāravena citakaṃ pūjanatthāya citakassa samīpaṃ ahaṃ agamāsinti attho. Tattha gantvā katakiccaṃ dassento tūriyaṃ tattha vādetvātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

50. 'I approached the pyre' means that the pyre was piled up with fragrant woods such as sandalwood, aloe, divine cedar, camphor, and takkola, arranged in a heap; the pyre is indeed a pyre. Out of reverence for the Buddha, I approached the pyre for the purpose of honoring it. Describing the deed he performed after going there, he said, 'having played musical instruments there,' and so on. All of that is easily understood.

Citakapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Citakapūjaka is concluded.

7. Buddhasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Buddhasaññaka

Yadā [V 2.0125] vipassī lokaggotiādikaṃ āyasmato buddhasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ bhūmaṭṭhakavimāne devaputto hutvā nibbatti. Tadā vipassī bhagavā āyusaṅkhāraṃ vossajji. Atha sakaladasasahassilokadhātu sasāgarapabbatā pakampittha. Tadā tassa devaputtassa bhavanampi kampittha. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so devaputto [M 2.0134] saṃsayajāto – “kiṃ nu kho pathavīkampāya nibbattī”ti cintetvā buddhassa āyusaṅkhāravossajjabhāvaṃ ñatvā mahāsokaṃ domanassaṃ uppādesi. Tadā vessavaṇo mahārājā āgantvā “mā cintayitthā”ti assāsesi. So devaputto tato cuto tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

This is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Buddhasaññaka, beginning with 'When Vipassī, the World-Leader...' He too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits that served as a basis for liberation in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn as a deity in an earth-dwelling celestial mansion. Then the Blessed One Vipassī relinquished his life-span. At that moment, the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, with its oceans and mountains, trembled. Then that deity’s mansion also trembled. At that moment, that deity, filled with doubt, thought, 'What could be the cause of this earthquake?' and upon realizing that the Buddha had relinquished his life-span, he was overcome with great sorrow and distress. Then the Great King Vessavaṇa came and consoled him, saying, 'Do not be concerned.' That deity, having passed away from there, wandered through the realms of devas and humans due to that merit. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a noble family. Having attained maturity, he renounced household life, went forth, and soon became an Arahant.

57. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento yadā vipassī lokaggotiādimāha. Āyusaṅkhāramossajjīti ā samantato yunoti pāleti satteti āyu, āyussa saṅkhāro rāsibhāvo āyusaṅkhāro, taṃ āyusaṅkhāraṃ ossajji pariccaji jahāsīti attho. Tasmiṃ āyusaṅkhāravossajjane. Jalamekhalāsāgarodakamekhalāsahitā sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷapathavī kampitthāti sambandho.

57. Later, recalling his past deeds, he was filled with joy and proclaimed the Apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'When Vipassī, the World-Leader...' 'Relinquished his life-span' means: 'āyu' is that which unites, maintains, and attaches beings all around; 'āyusaṅkhāro' is the formation or aggregation of 'āyu'; he relinquished, abandoned, and discarded that life-span. At the moment of relinquishing the life-span, the entire ten-thousandfold world-system, together with the earth girt by the ocean, trembled—this is the connection.

58. Otataṃ vitthataṃ mayhanti mayhaṃ bhavanaṃ otataṃ vitthataṃ cittaṃ vicittaṃ suci suparisuddhaṃ cittaṃ anekehi [P 0.0423] sattahi ratanehi vicittaṃ sobhamānaṃ pakampittha pakārena kampitthāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

58. 'My (mansion), spread out and extensive' means my dwelling was spread out and extensive, variegated and decorated, pure and very pure, adorned and made beautiful with many of the seven kinds of jewels, and radiant; and it trembled in a special way. The rest is clear everywhere.

Buddhasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Buddhasaññaka is concluded.

8. Maggasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maggasaññaka.

Padumuttarabuddhassātiādikaṃ āyasmato maggasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tato oraṃ tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle himavante devaputto hutvā nibbatto araññaṃ gantvā maggamūḷhānaṃ maggaṃ [V 2.0126] gavesantānaṃ tassa sāvakānaṃ bhojetvā maggaṃ ācikkhi. So tena puññena devamanussasampattimanubhavitvā uppannuppannabhave sabbattha amūḷho saññavā ahosi. Atha imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāse anallīno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Maggasaññaka begins with 'Of the Buddha Padumuttara...' This venerable one, too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences conducive to liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn as a devaputta in the Himalayas. Going into a forest, he fed the disciples of that Buddha who were lost and seeking the way, and showed them the path. By that merit, he experienced divine and human prosperity, and in each successive rebirth, he was never confused and was mindful. Then, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a respectable family, reached maturity, and without being attached to household life, he went forth and soon became an arahant.

66. So [M 2.0135] aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttarabuddhassātiādimāha. Sāvakā vanacārinoti bhagavato vuttavacanaṃ sammā ādarena suṇantīti sāvakā, atha vā bhagavato desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā saddhammaṃ suṇantīti sāvakā. Vanacārino vane vicaraṇakā sāvakā vippanaṭṭhā maggamūḷhā mahāaraññe andhāva cakkhuvirahitāva anusuyyare vicarantīti sambandho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

66. Later, recalling his past deeds, he was filled with joy and, beginning with “Padumuttarabuddhassa,” declared his former conduct in the Apadāna. Regarding the phrase “Sāvakā vanacārino” (Disciples who wander in the forest): “Sāvakā” (disciples) refers to those who listen to the Blessed One’s spoken words with proper reverence, or alternatively, those who, following the Blessed One’s teaching, direct their wisdom and listen to the true Dhamma. “Vanacārino” (forest-wanderers) refers to disciples who wander in the forest, lost and bewildered as to the path in the great forest, like the blind without eyes, wandering about aimlessly—this is the connection. The rest is clear throughout.

Maggasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maggasaññaka is concluded.

9. Paccupaṭṭhānasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Paccupaṭṭhānasaññaka

Atthadassimhi sugatetiādikaṃ āyasmato paccupaṭṭhānasaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbatto bhagavati dharamāne dassanassa aladdhattā pacchā parinibbute mahāsokappatto vihāsi. Tadā hissa bhagavato sāgato nāma aggasāvako anusāsanto bhagavato sārīrikadhātupūjā bhagavati dharamāne katapūjā viya cittappasādavasā mahapphalaṃ bhavatī”ti vatvā “thūpaṃ karohī”ti niyojito thūpaṃ kāresi, taṃ pūjetvā tato cuto devamanussesu sakkacakkavattisampattimanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ [P 0.0424] patto satthari pasīditvā pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Paccupaṭṭhānasaññaka begins with “Atthadassimhi sugate,” etc. This venerable one, too, having made his resolution in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was reborn in the yaksha realm. Unable to see the Blessed One while he was alive, he was overcome with great sorrow after the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna. At that time, the Blessed One's chief disciple named Sāgata, instructing him, said, “The worship of the Blessed One’s bodily relics, through the power of a serene mind, brings great fruit, just as worship done while the Blessed One was alive.” Urged to “Build a stupa,” he had a stupa built and worshipped it. After passing away from there, he experienced the prosperity of Sakka and of a universal monarch among gods and humans. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a certain family in Sāvatthī, attained understanding, gained faith in the Teacher, went forth, and soon became an arahant.

72. So aparabhāge attano puññakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento atthadassimhi sugatetiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Yakkhayoniṃ upapajjinti ettha pana attano sakāsaṃ sampattasampatte khādantā yanti gacchantīti yakkhā, yakkhānaṃ yoni jātīti yakkhayoni, yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbattoti attho.

72. Then, later on, recollecting his own meritorious deeds, filled with joy, he declared his former conduct in the Apadāna, beginning with “Atthadassimhi sugate,” etc. That has already been explained below. But regarding the phrase “Yakkhayoniṃ upapajjiṃ” (I was reborn in the yaksha realm): here, “yakkhā” means those who go about eating whoever comes into their presence; “yakkhayoni” means the birth-origin of yakshas; the meaning is: being reborn in the yaksha realm.

73. Dulladdhaṃ [V 2.0127] vata me āsīti me mayā laddhayasaṃ dulladdhaṃ, buddhabhūtassa satthuno sakkāraṃ akatattā virādhetvā laddhanti attho. Duppabhātanti duṭṭhu [M 2.0136] pabhātaṃ rattiyā pabhātakaraṇaṃ, mayhaṃ na suṭṭhuṃ pabhātanti attho. Duruṭṭhitanti duuṭṭhitaṃ, sūriyassa uggamanaṃ mayhaṃ duuggamananti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

73. Regarding “Dulladdhaṃ vata me āsi” (Ill-obtained indeed was it for me): this means that the honor I obtained was ill-obtained because, having failed to pay respect to the Teacher who had become the Buddha, I obtained it by having missed that opportunity. Regarding “Duppabhātaṃ” (ill-dawned): this means the night’s breaking was an ill dawning; that is, the dawn was not good for me. Regarding “Duruṭṭhitaṃ” (ill-risen): this means an ill rising; the sun’s rising was an ill rising for me. The rest is clear throughout.

Paccupaṭṭhānasaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Paccupaṭṭhānasaññaka is concluded.

10. Jātipūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Jātipūjaka

Jāyaṃ tassa vipassissātiādikaṃ āyasmato jātipūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto nakkhattapāṭhakehi vipassibodhisattassa vuttalakkhaṇanimittaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ kira kumāro buddho hutvā sakalalokassa aggo seṭṭho sutvā sabbasatte saṃsārato uddharissatī”ti sutvā taṃ bhagavantaṃ kumārakāleyeva buddhassa viya mahāpūjamakāsi. Pacchā kamena kumārakālaṃ rājakumārakālaṃ rajjakālanti kālattayamatikkamma buddhe jātepi mahāpūjaṃ katvā tato cuto tusitādīsu nibbatto dibbasukhamanubhavitvā pacchā manussesu cakkavattādimanussasukhamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto sattaṭṭhavassakāleyeva bhagavati pasanno pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Jātipūjaka begins with “Jāyaṃ tassa vipassissa,” etc. This venerable one, too, having made his resolution in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn into a certain family. Having attained understanding, he heard the marks and characteristics spoken of by the astrologers for the Bodhisatta Vipassī. Having heard, “This prince, it is said, will become the Buddha, and having become the supreme and foremost of all the world, he will liberate all beings from saṃsāra,” he paid great homage to that Blessed One even in his childhood, as if he were the Buddha. Later, having passed through the three stages of time—childhood, princehood, and kingship—even after the Buddha arose, he made great offerings. After passing away from there, he was reborn in Tusita and other divine realms, experiencing divine bliss. Later, among humans, he experienced the happiness of a universal monarch and other human happiness. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was born into a certain family, and at the age of seven or eight, having gained faith in the Blessed One, he went forth. Developing insight, he soon became an arahant.

82. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento jāyaṃ tassa vipassissātiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

82. Then, later on, recollecting his past deeds, filled with joy, he declared his former conduct in the Apadāna, beginning with “Jāyaṃ tassa vipassissa,” etc. That has the meaning already stated below.

84. Nemittānaṃ suṇitvānāti ettha nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ sukhadukkhappattihetuṃ jānantīti nemittā, tesaṃ nemittānaṃ nakkhattapāṭhakānaṃ [P 0.0425] vacanaṃ suṇitvāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

84. Regarding “Nemittānaṃ suṇitvāna” (Having heard the omen-readers): here, “nemittā” (omen-readers) are those who know the sign, the cause, the reason for the attainment of happiness and suffering. The meaning is: having heard the words of those omen-readers, the reciters of constellations. The rest is clear throughout.

Jātipūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Jātipūjaka is concluded.

Dvādasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Twelfth Chapter is concluded.

13. Sereyyavaggo

13. The Sereyya Chapter

1. Sereyyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sereyyaka

Ajjhāyako [M 2.0137][V 2.0128] mantadharotiādikaṃ āyasmato sereyyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tato paresu attabhāvasahassesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṃ gantvā itihāsādisakalabrāhmaṇadhammesu koṭippatto ekasmiṃ divase abbhokāse saparivāro ṭhito bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sereyyapupphaṃ gahetvā ākāse khipanto pūjesi. Tāni pupphāni ākāse vitānaṃ hutvā sattāhaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā antaradhāyiṃsu. So taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā atīva pasannamānaso teneva pītisomanassena kālaṃ katvā tusitādīsu nibbatto tattha dibbasukhamanubhavitvā tato manussasukhamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā pubbavāsanābalena satthari pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sereyyaka begins with “Ajjhāyako mantadharo,” etc. He too, having made his resolution in the presence of former supreme Jinas, accumulated merits conducive to liberation in thousands of subsequent existences. In the time of Vipassī, the Blessed One, he was born into a brahmin family. Having attained maturity, he mastered the three Vedas and reached the pinnacle in all brahminical traditions, including history and so on. One day, while standing in the open air with his entourage, he saw the Blessed One and, with a serene mind, took a sereyyaka flower and offered it by throwing it into the sky. Those flowers formed a canopy in the sky and remained for seven days, after which they disappeared. Seeing this marvel, his mind became exceedingly serene, and with that same joy and happiness, he passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven and other such realms, experiencing divine happiness. Then, experiencing human happiness, in this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a certain family. Having attained maturity, through the power of his past tendencies, he developed faith in the Teacher, went forth, and not long after became an arahant.

1. So aparabhāge purākatakusalaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento ajjhāyako mantadharotiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva.

1. Later, recalling his past wholesome kamma, he was filled with happiness and, revealing the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke, beginning with 'The reciter of sacred texts, the bearer of mantras,' and so on. That meaning is as stated previously.

3. Sereyyakaṃ gahetvānāti sirise bhavaṃ jātipupphaṃ sereyyaṃ, sereyyameva sereyyakaṃ, taṃ sereyyakaṃ gahetvānāti sambandho. Bhagavati pasanno jātisumanamakuḷacampakādīni pupphāni patiṭṭhapetvā pūjetuṃ kālaṃ natthitāya tattha sampattaṃ taṃ sereyyakaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

3. Regarding 'taking the sereyyaka flower': sereyya is a jāti flower born in the sirisa tree; sereyya itself is sereyyaka. The connection is 'taking that sereyyaka flower.' Being devoted to the Blessed One, he wished to establish and honor with jasmine buds, campaka, and other flowers, but since there was no time for that, he took that sereyyaka flower which was present there and offered it. This is the meaning. The rest is clear everywhere.

Sereyyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sereyyaka is concluded.

2. Pupphathūpiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pupphathūpiya

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ [M 2.0138] āyasmato pupphathūpiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassibuddhassa bhagavato kāle [V 2.0129] brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā sakasippe nipphattiṃ patto tattha sāraṃ apassanto gehaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā attanā sahagatehi pañcasissasahassehi saddhiṃ pañcābhiññā aṭṭha [P 0.0426] samāpattiyo nibbattetvā kukkuranāmapabbatasamīpe paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā paṭivasati. Tadā buddhuppādabhāvaṃ sutvā sissehi saha buddhassa santikaṃ gantukāmo kenaci byādhinā pīḷito paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā sissasantikā buddhassānubhāvaṃ lakkhaṇañca sutvā pasannamānaso himavantato campakāsokatilakakeṭakādyaneke pupphe āharāpetvā thūpaṃ katvā buddhaṃ viya pūjetvā kālaṃ katvā brahmalokūpago ahosi. Atha te sissā tassa āḷahanaṃ katvā buddhasantikaṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Atha bhagavā buddhacakkhunā oloketvā anāgataṃsañāṇena pākaṭīkaraṇamakāsi. So aparabhāge imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto pubbavāsanābalena satthari pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pupphathūpiya begins with 'Not far from the Himālaya,' and so on. He too, having made a resolution in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulated merits conducive to liberation in various existences. During the time of Vipassī, the Blessed One, he was born into a brahmin family. Having attained maturity and reached proficiency in his own craft, yet seeing no essence there, he left home and entered the Himālaya. There, together with five thousand disciples who accompanied him, he produced the five supernormal knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. He had a leaf hut built near the mountain named Kukkura and resided there. Hearing of the arising of the Buddha, he wished to go with his disciples to the presence of the Buddha, but afflicted by some illness, he entered the leaf hut. Hearing from his disciples about the Buddha’s power and characteristics, his mind became serene. He had many flowers—campaka, asoka, tilaka, ketaka, and others—brought from the Himālaya, made a stupa, and worshipped it as if it were the Buddha. Having passed away, he went to the Brahma world. Then those disciples performed his cremation and, going to the Buddha, reported that event. Then the Blessed One, surveying with the Buddha-eye, made it manifest with his knowledge of the future. He later, in this Buddha-dispensation, was born into a family in Sāvatthī. Having attained maturity, through the power of his past tendencies, he developed faith in the Teacher, went forth, and not long after became an arahant.

10. Atha so attano pubbakusalaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Kukkuro nāma pabbatoti pabbatassa sikharaṃ kukkurākārena sunakhākārena saṇṭhitattā “kukkurapabbato”ti saṅkhyaṃ gato, tassa samīpe paṇṇasālaṃ katvā pañcatāpasasahassehi saha vasamānoti attho. Nayānusārena sesaṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

10. Then, recalling his past wholesome kamma, he was filled with happiness and, revealing the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke, beginning with 'Not far from the Himālaya,' and so on. That meaning is as stated previously. Regarding 'the mountain called Kukkura': the peak of the mountain, being shaped like a dog, was designated 'Kukkura Mountain.' The meaning is that he built a leaf-hut near it and lived together with five thousand ascetics. According to the method of interpretation, the rest is all clear in meaning.

Pupphathūpiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pupphathūpiya is concluded.

3. Pāyasadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pāyasadāyaka

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddhotiādikaṃ āyasmato pāyasadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ [M 2.0139] vibhavasampanne kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto hatthiassadhanadhaññasattaratanādivibhavasampanno saddhāsampanno kammaphalaṃ saddahitvā sahassamattā suvaṇṇapātiyo kāretvā tasmiṃ khīrapāyasasahassassa pūretvā tā sabbā gāhāpetvā simbalivanaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye vipassī bhagavā chabbaṇṇaraṃsiyo vissajjetvā ākāse caṅkamaṃ māpetvā caṅkamati. So pana seṭṭhi taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā atīva pasanno pātiyo ṭhapetvā vanditvā ārocesi paṭiggahaṇāya. Atha bhagavā anukampaṃ upādāya paṭiggahesi, paṭiggahetvā ca pana tassa [V 2.0130] somanussuppādanatthaṃ sahassamattehi bhikkhusaṅghehi saddhiṃ paribhuñji, tadavasesaṃ anekasahassabhikkhū paribhuñjiṃsu. So tena puññena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde [P 0.0427] kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto saddhājāto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pāyasadāyaka begins with 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One of golden hue,' and so on. He too, having made a resolution in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulated merits conducive to liberation in various existences. During the time of Vipassī, the Blessed One, he was born into a prosperous family home. Having attained maturity, while living the household life, he became endowed with prosperity consisting of elephants, horses, wealth, grain, and the seven treasures, and was endowed with faith. Having faith in the fruits of kamma, he had a thousand golden bowls made, filled them with a thousand portions of milk-rice, had them all taken, and went to the Simbalī forest. At that time, Vipassī, the Blessed One, was emitting six-colored rays and, having created a walkway in the sky, was walking back and forth. Seeing this marvel, that wealthy man was exceedingly serene. He set down the bowls, paid homage, and announced his wish for them to be accepted. Then the Blessed One, out of compassion, accepted them. Having accepted them, to bring about his happiness, he partook of the meal together with a thousand monks. The remainder was partaken of by many thousands of monks. Through that merit, he wandered only in happy destinations. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn into a family home. Having attained maturity, faith arose in him, he went forth, and not long after became an arahant.

26. So aparabhāge attano kusalaṃ paccavekkhamāno taṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddhotiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

26. Later, reflecting on his own wholesome kamma and recalling it, he was filled with happiness and, revealing the Apadāna of his former conduct, spoke, beginning with 'The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One of golden hue,' and so on. That has been stated previously.

28. Caṅkamaṃ susamārūḷhoti cadinanto padavikkhepaṃ karonto kamati gacchatīti caṅkamaṃ, caṅkamassa padavikkhepassa ādhārabhūtapathavipadeso caṅkamaṃ nāmāti attho, etaṃ caṅkamaṃsu visesena ārūḷhoti sambandho. Ambare anilāyaneti varīyati chādiyati anenāti varaṃ, na baranti ambaraṃ, setavatthasadisaṃ ākāsanti attho. Natthi nilīyanaṃ gopanaṃ etthāti anilaṃ, ā samantato yanti gacchanti anena iddhimantoti āyanaṃ, anilañca taṃ āyanañceti anilāyanaṃ, tasmiṃ ambare anilāyane caṅkamaṃ māpayinti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

28. Regarding 'well-ascended upon the walkway': 'caṅkama' means 'one walks, making movements of the feet, going back and forth.' The meaning is that the part of the path that serves as the basis for the movement of the feet of one walking back and forth is called 'caṅkama.' The connection is 'especially ascended upon this walkway.' Regarding 'in the sky, without a hiding place': 'vara' means that by which something is covered or hidden. 'Ambara' means that which does not cover, meaning the sky, like a white cloth. 'Anila' means there is no concealment or hiding there. 'Āyana' means that by which the powerful go everywhere. 'Anila' and that 'āyana' is 'anilāyana.' The meaning is that he had a walkway constructed in that sky, which is without a hiding place. The rest is clear everywhere.

Pāyasadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pāyasadāyaka is concluded.

4. Gandhodakiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gandhodakiya

Nisajja pāsādavaretiādikaṃ āyasmato gandhodakiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave nibbānūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassībhagavato kāle seṭṭhikule nibbatto [M 2.0140] viññutaṃ patvā mahaddhano mahābhogo dibbasukhamanubhavanto viya manussasukhamanubhavanto ekasmiṃ divase pāsādavare nisinno hoti. Tadā bhagavā suvaṇṇamahāmeru viya vīthiyā vicarati, taṃ vicaramānaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso gantvā vanditvā sugandhodakena bhagavantaṃ osiñcamāno pūjesi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsena anallīno satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Gandhodakiya Thera, beginning with 'Seated on a splendid terrace,' etc. This elder, too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences as a support for Nibbāna, was born during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī in a banker's family. Having come of age, he was of great wealth and property, experiencing human happiness as if it were divine bliss. One day, while seated on a splendid terrace, he saw the Blessed One walking along the street like a golden Mount Meru. With a confident mind, he approached, paid homage, and honored the Blessed One by sprinkling him with fragrant water. As a result of that merit, he wandered through saṃsāra among devas and humans. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a certain family household. Having come of age and being unattached to the household life, he went forth in the Teacher’s presence, took up a meditation subject, developed insight, and before long became an arahant.

35. So aparabhāge attano pubbakusalaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nisajja pāsādavaretiādimāha. Tattha pāsādoti pasādaṃ somanassaṃ janeti uppādetīti pāsādo[V 2.0131], mālākammacittakammasuvaṇṇakammādyanekavicittaṃ disvā tattha paviṭṭhānaṃ janānaṃ pasādaṃ janayatīti attho. Pāsādo [P 0.0428] ca so patthetabbaṭṭhena varo cāti pāsādavaro, tasmiṃ pāsādavare nisajja nisīditvā vipassiṃ jinavaraṃ addasanti sambandho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

35. Later, recalling his past wholesome deeds, he became joyful and, revealing the apadāna of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning with 'Seated on a splendid terrace.' Here, 'pāsāda' means it generates confidence and joy. Seeing the various decorations such as garlands, paintings, and gold work, it generates confidence in those who enter—that is the meaning. And 'pāsādavaro' means a splendid palace, in that it is to be desired. 'Seated on that splendid terrace, I saw Vipassī, the excellent Victor'—this is the connection. The rest is clear everywhere.

Gandhodakiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gandhodakiya is complete.

5. Sammukhāthavikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sammukhāthavika

Jāyamāne vipassimhītiādikaṃ āyasmato sammukhāthavikattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto sattavassikakāleyeva sakasippe nipphattiṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto vipassimhi bodhisatte uppanne sabbabuddhānaṃ lakkhaṇāni vedattaye dissamānāni tāni rājappamukhassa janakāyassa vipassībodhisattassa lakkhaṇañca buddhabhāvañca byākaritvā janānaṃ mānasaṃ nibbāpesi, anekāni ca thutivacanāni nivedesi. So tena kusalakammena cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavattisampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto saddhājāto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi. Katakusalanāmena sammukhāthavikattheroti pākaṭo.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Sammukhāthavika Thera, beginning with 'When Vipassī was being born.' He, too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas and accumulating merits here and there in existence as a support for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. At the age of seven, having mastered his craft, he settled into household life. When the Bodhisatta Vipassī was born, he explained the marks of all Buddhas found in the three Vedas, and specifically the marks and future Buddhahood of the Bodhisatta Vipassī, to the assembly of people led by the king. He thereby pacified their minds and proclaimed many words of praise. Through that wholesome deed, he experienced the six kinds of sensual-sphere prosperity and, among humans, the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a family household, came of age, and, having gained faith, went forth and before long became an arahant. He became renowned as the Elder Sammukhāthavika, named for the wholesome deed he had performed.

41. So [M 2.0141] attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento jāyamāne vipassimhītiādimāha. Vipassimhi sammāsambuddhe jāyamāne uppajjamāne mātukucchito nikkhante ahaṃ pātubhūtaṃ nimittaṃ kāraṇaṃ buddhabhāvassa hetuṃ byākariṃ kathesiṃ, anekāni acchariyāni pākaṭāni akāsinti attho. Sesaṃ vuttanayānusārena suviññeyyamevāti.

41. Recollecting his past kamma and becoming joyful, he proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct by uttering the verses beginning with 'When Vipassī was being born.' The meaning is: 'When the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, Vipassī, was being born, arising, emerging from his mother’s womb, I explained the manifested sign, the cause, and the reason for his Buddhahood, and I made manifest many wonders.' The rest is easily understood in accordance with the method already stated.

Sammukhāthavikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sammukhāthavika is complete.

6. Kusumāsaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kusumāsaniya

Nagare dhaññavatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato kusumāsaniyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa [V 2.0132] bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto mahaddhano mahābhogo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṃ gato brāhmaṇasippesu koṭippatto sakaparasamayakusalo mātāpitaro pūjetukāmo pañca uppalakalāpe attano samīpe ṭhapetvā nisinno bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā nīlapītādighanabuddharasmiyo [P 0.0429] ca disvā pasannamānaso āsanaṃ paññāpetvā tattha tāni pupphāni santharitvā bhagavantaṃ tattha nisīdāpetvā sakaghare mātu atthāya paṭiyattāni sabbāni khādanīyabhojanīyāni gahetvā saparivāraṃ bhagavantaṃ sahatthena santappento bhojesi. Bhojanāvasāne ekaṃ uppalahatthaṃ adāsi. Tena somanassajāto patthanaṃ akāsi. Bhagavāpi anumodanaṃ katvā pakāmi. So tena puññena devamanussesu dve sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto bhogayasehi vaḍḍhito kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Kusumāsaniya Thera, beginning with 'In the city of Dhaññavatī.' He, too, having made his resolve under former excellent Jinas and accumulating merits in various existences as a support for liberation, was born in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having come of age, he was very wealthy and prosperous, had mastered the three Vedas, had reached the pinnacle of the brahminical arts, and was an expert in his own and others' tenets. Desiring to honor his parents, he sat down after placing five clusters of water lilies beside himself. Seeing the Blessed One Vipassī approaching surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus, and also seeing the dense, blue, yellow, and other-colored rays of the Buddha, with a confident mind he prepared a seat, spread those flowers on it, and had the Blessed One sit there. Then, taking all the hard and soft food that had been prepared in his house for his mother, he served and satisfied the Blessed One and his retinue with his own hands. At the end of the meal, he gave him a handful of water lilies. Filled with joy by this, he made an aspiration. The Blessed One, after expressing his appreciation, departed. Through that merit, he experienced the two kinds of prosperity among devas and humans. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born in Sāvatthī into a family endowed with wealth. Having come of age and grown in wealth and fame, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures, abandoned the household life, went forth, and before long became an arahant.

65. So aparabhāge pubbe katakusalaṃ pubbenivāsañāṇena saritvā somanassappatto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nagare dhaññavatiyātiādimāha. Dhaññānaṃ puññavantānaṃ khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatimahāsālānaṃ anekesaṃ kulānaṃ ākarattā dhaññavatī, atha vā muttāmaṇiādisattaratanānaṃ [M 2.0142] sattavidhadhaññānaṃ upabhogaparibhogānaṃ ākarattā dhaññavatī, atha vā dhaññānaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhakhīṇāsavānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ārāmavihārādīnaṃ ākarattā dhaññavatī, tassā dhaññavatiyā. Nagaranti patthenti ettha upabhogaparibhogatthikā janāti nagaraṃ, na gacchatīti vā nagaṃ, rājayuvarājamahāmattādīnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ. Nagaṃ rāti ādadāti gaṇhātīti nagaraṃ, rājādīnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānasamūhabhūtaṃ pākāraparikhādīhi parikkhittaṃ paricchinnaṭṭhānaṃ nagaraṃ nāmāti attho. Nagare yadā ahaṃ vipassissa bhagavato santike byākaraṇaṃ alabhiṃ, tadā tasmiṃ dhaññavatiyā nagare brāhmaṇo ahosinti sambandho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

65. Later, recalling with the knowledge of past lives the wholesome deeds he had done previously, he attained joy and proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'In the city of Dhaññavatī.' Dhaññavatī is so called because it was a source for many families of fortunate and meritorious khattiyas, brahmins, and eminent householders; or because it was a source for the enjoyment and use of the seven kinds of gems, such as pearls and jewels, and of the seven kinds of grain; or because it was a source of dwelling places—parks, monasteries, etc.—for the fortunate ones: Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and arahants. Of Dhaññavatī. A 'nagara' (city) is so called because people who desire enjoyment and use seek ('patthenti') it. Or 'naga' means 'it does not go' ('na gacchati'), the dwelling place of kings, crown princes, and chief ministers. It is called 'nagara' because it takes ('rāti, ādadāti') the 'naga'; the meaning is that a place that is a collection of dwellings for kings and others, enclosed by walls, moats, etc., is called a 'nagara.' The connection is: 'When I received the prediction in the presence of the Blessed One Vipassī, at that time I was a brahmin in that city of Dhaññavatī.' The rest is clear everywhere.

Kusumāsaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kusumāsaniya is complete.

7. Phaladāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Phaladāyaka

Ajjhāyako mantadharotiādikaṃ āyasmato phaladāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā vedattayādisakasippesu pārappatto anekesaṃ brāhmaṇasahassāniṃ [V 2.0133] pāmokkho ācariyo sakasippānaṃ pariyosānaṃ adisvā tattha ca sāraṃ apassanto [P 0.0430] gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantassa avidūre assamaṃ kāretvā saha sissehi vāsaṃ kappesi, tasmiṃ samaye padumuttaro bhagavā bhikkhāya caramāno tassānukampāya taṃ padesaṃ sampāpuṇi. Tāpaso bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso attano atthāya puṭake nikkhipitvā rukkhagge laggitāni madhurāni padumaphalāni madhunā saha adāsi. Bhagavā tassa somanassuppādanatthaṃ passantasseva paribhuñjitvā ākāse ṭhito phaladānānisaṃsaṃ kathetvā pakkāmi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Phaladāyaka begins, 'A reciter, a bearer of mantras…' He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits over many existences as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a brahmin family, attained understanding, and became proficient in the three Vedas and other arts. As the foremost teacher, the ācariya, of many thousands of brahmins, not seeing the culmination of his own arts and failing to perceive their essence, he renounced the household life and went forth into the ascetic life. Having established a hermitage not far from the Himālaya, he lived there with his disciples. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, while wandering for alms, arrived in that area out of compassion for him. The ascetic, seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind, took sweet lotus fruits that were in a container hanging on a tree and gave them together with honey. To arouse joy in him, the Blessed One partook of the offering in his presence and, standing in the air, expounded the benefits of the gift of fruit before departing.

75. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto sattavassikoyeva arahattaṃ patvā pubbe katakusalakammaṃ [M 2.0143] saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento ajjhāyako mantadharotiādimāha. Tattha ajjheti cintetīti ajjhāyi, ajjhāyiyeva ajjhāyako. Ettha hi akāro “paṭisedhe vuddhitabbhāve…pe… akāro virahappake”ti evaṃ vuttesu dasasu atthesu tabbhāve vattati. Sissānaṃ savanadhāraṇādivasena hitaṃ ajjheti cinteti sajjhāyaṃ karotīti ajjhāyako, cintakoti attho. Ācariyassa santike uggahitaṃ sabbaṃ mantaṃ manena dhāreti pavattetīti mantadharo. Tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragūti vedaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, vedena veditabbā bujjhitabbāti vedā, iruvedayajuvedasāmavedasaṅkhātā tayo ganthā, tesaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṃ pariyosānaṃ koṭiṃ gato pattoti pāragū. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti

75. Through that merit, wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of good fortune, in this Buddha-dispensation he was born into a wealthy family. At the age of only seven, he attained arahantship. Remembering his past wholesome kamma, he became filled with joy and revealed the Apadāna of his former conduct, declaring, 'A reciter, a bearer of mantras,' and so forth. Herein, 'ajjhāyī' means one who reflects or contemplates; 'ajjhāyaka' is simply 'ajjhāyī.' The suffix '-ka' here is used in the sense of 'possessing that quality,' which is one of ten meanings given for it. He reflects on and recites what is for the welfare of his disciples by way of listening and memorizing—thus, he is a 'reciter,' meaning one who contemplates. 'Mantadharo' means one who retains in mind and transmits all the mantras learned from his teacher. 'Tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū' means one who has gone to the far shore of the three Vedas. 'Veda' means knowledge; those things that are to be known or understood through knowledge are the Vedas, namely the three collections known as the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. One who has gone to their far shore, their culmination, their limit, is a 'pāragū.' The rest is evident.

Phaladāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Phaladāyaka is concluded.

8. Ñāṇasaññikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ñāṇasaññika

Pabbate himavantamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato ñāṇasaññikattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tasmiṃ tasmiṃ uppannuppanne bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantassa avidūre pabbatantare paṇṇasālaṃ [P 0.0431] kāretvā pañcābhiññāaṭṭhasamāpattiyo nibbattetvā [V 2.0134] vasanto ekadivasaṃ parisuddhaṃ paṇḍaraṃ pulinatalaṃ disvā “īdisā parisuddhā buddhā, īdisaṃva parisuddhaṃ buddhañāṇa”nti buddhañca tassa ñāṇañca anussari thomesi ca.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ñāṇasaññika begins, 'On the Himavant mountain…' He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that are a basis for liberation in his various existences, was born into a family home during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, he renounced the household life and went forth into the ascetic life. Dwelling in a leaf-hut he had built in a mountain cleft not far from the Himālaya, he developed the five direct knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. One day, seeing a pure white sandbank, he reflected, 'So pure are the Buddhas, and just so pure is the Buddha-knowledge!' Thus he recollected and praised the Buddha and his knowledge.

84. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā sāsane pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto pubbe katapuññaṃ anussaritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento “pabbate himavantamhī”tiādimāha. Pulinaṃ sobhanaṃ disvāti paripuṇṇakataṃ viya pulākārena parisodhitākārena pavattaṃ ṭhitanti pulinaṃ, sobhanaṃ [M 2.0144] vālukaṃ disvā seṭṭhaṃ buddhaṃ anussarinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

84. Through that merit, wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of good fortune, in this Buddha-dispensation he was born into a family. Having attained understanding, he went forth into the Teaching and before long attained arahantship. Recollecting the merit he had made in the past, he became joyful and declared the Apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with, 'On the Himavant mountain…' Regarding the verse phrase 'seeing the beautiful sandbank,' this means seeing the beautiful sand—'pulinaṃ' being so called because it appears as if perfectly made and purified by winnowing—and thereby recollecting the supreme Buddha. The rest is easily understood.

Ñāṇasaññikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ñāṇasaññika is concluded.

9. Gaṇṭhipupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gaṇṭhipupphiya

Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddhotiādikaṃ āyasmato gaṇṭhipupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekāsu jātīsu katapuññasañcayo vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto upabhogaparibhogehi anūno ekadivasaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ sagaṇaṃ disvā pasannamānaso lājāpañcamehi pupphehi pūjesi. So teneva cittappasādena yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato devaloke nibbatto dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā aparabhāge manussesu manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto saddhājāto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Gaṇṭhipupphiya begins, 'Golden-hued is the Perfectly Enlightened One…' He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, had accumulated a store of merit in many lives. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was born in a certain family, not lacking in possessions for use and enjoyment. One day, seeing the Blessed One Vipassī with his retinue, his mind became confident, and he honored him with flowers, with parched grain as the fifth. Through that very confidence of mind, having lived out his lifespan, he was reborn in the deva world. After experiencing divine good fortune, and later human good fortune among humans, in this Buddha-dispensation he was born into a certain family. When faith arose in him, he went forth, and before long attained arahantship.

91. So ekadivasaṃ pubbe katapuññaṃ saritvā somanassajāto “iminā kusalenāhaṃ nibbānaṃ patto”ti pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sambuddhotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

91. One day, recollecting the merit he had made in the past, he became joyful and declared the Apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'Golden-hued is the Perfectly Enlightened One,' and proclaiming, 'Through this wholesome deed, I have attained Nibbāna.' All this is clear in meaning for the reason already stated.

Gaṇṭhipupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gaṇṭhipupphiya is concluded.

10. Padumapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Padumapūjaka Thera

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ [V 2.0135] āyasmato padumapūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā sakasippe nipphattiṃ patvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto buddhuppattito puretaraṃ [P 0.0432] uppannattā ovādānusāsanaṃ alabhitvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantassa avidūre gotamakaṃ [M 2.0145] nāma pabbataṃ nissāya assamaṃ kāretvā pañcābhiññā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā jhānasukheneva vihāsi. Tadā padumuttaro bhagavā buddho hutvā satte saṃsārato uddharanto tassānukampāya himavantaṃ agamāsi. Tāpaso bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sakasisse samānetvā tehi padumapupphāni āharāpetvā pūjesi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto saddho pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

Beginning with 'Not far from the Himālaya,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Padumapūjaka Thera. He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences that are a supporting condition for liberation. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a brahmin family. Having attained maturity and achieved mastery in his own craft, yet not seeing the essence in it, and because he was born before the arising of a Buddha, he did not receive guidance and instruction. Abandoning the household life, he went forth into the ascetic life of a sage. Not far from the Himālaya, he settled near a mountain called Gotamaka, built a hermitage, and developed the five direct knowledges and the eight attainments. He dwelt in the bliss of jhāna. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, having become a Buddha and while liberating beings from saṃsāra, approached the Himālaya out of compassion for him. The ascetic, seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind, gathered his disciples, had them bring lotus flowers, and made an offering. Through that merit, he wandered among devas and humans, experiencing both kinds of good fortune. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a family in Sāvatthī. With faith and confidence, he went forth and before long became an arahant.

97. So attano puññakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Gotamo nāma pabbatoti anekesaṃ yakkhadevatānaṃ āvāsabhāvena adhiṭṭhānavasena gotamassa bhavanattā gotamoti pākaṭo ahosi. Pavattati tiṭṭhatīti pabbato. Nāgarukkhehi sañchannoti ruhati tiṭṭhatīti rukkho. Atha vā pathaviṃ khananto uddhaṃ ruhatīti rukkho, nānā anekappakārā campakakappūranāgaagarucandanādayo rukkhāti nānārukkhā, tehi nānārukkhehi sañchanno parikiṇṇo gotamo pabbatoti sambandho. Mahābhūtagaṇālayoti bhavanti jāyanti uppajjanti vaḍḍhanti cāti bhūtā, mahantā ca te bhūtā cāti mahābhūtā, mahābhūtānaṃ gaṇo samūhoti mahābhūtagaṇo, mahābhūtagaṇassa ālayo patiṭṭhāti mahābhūtagaṇālayo.

97. Recollecting his own meritorious deed, he became joyful and, proclaiming the Apadāna of his past conduct, spoke beginning with 'Not far from the Himālaya.' Herein, 'a mountain named Gotama': because it was the dwelling place and residence of many yakkhas and devatās, and because it was the abode of Gotama, it became known as 'Gotama.' 'It proceeds and stands, thus it is a mountain.' Regarding 'covered with various trees': 'It grows and stands, thus it is a tree.' Or, 'digging into the earth, it grows upwards, thus it is a tree.' 'Various trees' are trees of many kinds, such as campaka, kappūra, nāga, agaru, candana, and so on. The connection is: the Gotama mountain is covered and surrounded by these various trees. Regarding 'the abode of the host of great beings': 'They are, are born, arise, and grow, thus they are beings.' And those beings are great, thus they are 'great beings.' A group or collection of great beings is a 'host of great beings.' The abode or establishment for the host of great beings is 'the abode of the host of great beings.'

98. Vemajjhamhi ca tassāsīti tassa gotamassa pabbatassa vemajjhe abbhantare assamo abhinimmito nipphādito katoti attho. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti.

98. Regarding 'And in the middle of that there was': the meaning is that in the middle, in the interior, of that Gotama mountain, a hermitage was created, produced, and made. The rest is clear in meaning.

Padumapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of Padumapūjaka Thera is finished.

Terasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter is finished.

14. Sobhitavaggo

14. The Sobhita Chapter

1. Sobhitattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Sobhita Thera

Padumuttaro [M 2.0146][V 2.0136] nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato sobhitattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā ekadivasaṃ [P 0.0433] satthārā dhamme desiyamāne somanassena pasannamānaso nānappakārehi thomesi. So teneva somanassena kālaṃ katvā devesu nibbatto tattha dibbasukhaṃ anubhavitvā manussesu ca manussasukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto sattavassikova pabbajitvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño arahā ahosi.

Beginning with 'Padumuttara named the Conqueror,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Sobhita Thera. He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences that are a supporting condition for liberation. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a certain family. Having reached maturity and established a household, one day, while the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma, with a joyful and confident mind he praised him with various kinds of praises. Having passed away with that very joy, he was reborn among the devas. Having experienced divine happiness there and human happiness among humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation he was reborn in a family in Sāvatthī. He went forth at the age of seven and before long became an arahant with the six direct knowledges.

1. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā suviññeyyamevāti.

1. In a later time, recalling his own past deed, he became joyful and, proclaiming the Apadāna of his past conduct, spoke beginning with 'Padumuttara named the Conqueror.' All of that is easily understood as it follows the method stated above.

Sobhitattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of Sobhita Thera is finished.

2. Sudassanattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Sudassana Thera

Vitthatāya nadītīretiādikaṃ āyasmato sudassanattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave katapuññūpacayo sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto vitthatāya nāma gaṅgāya samīpe pilakkhuphalitaṃ pariyesanto tassā tīre nisinnaṃ jalamānaaggisikhaṃ iva sikhiṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ disvā pasannamānaso ketakīpupphaṃ vaṇṭeneva chinditvā pūjento evamāha – “bhante, yena ñāṇena tvaṃ evaṃ mahānubhāvo sabbaññubuddho jāto, taṃ ñāṇaṃ ahaṃ pūjemī”ti. Atha bhagavā anumodanamakāsi. So tena puññena devamanussesu jāto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto satthari pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

Beginning with 'On the bank of the broad river,' this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Sudassana Thera. He too, having made his aspiration under previous excellent Conquerors and having accumulated merit in various existences, was reborn in a good family in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having reached maturity and established a household, while living there and searching for pilakkhu fruit near the river Ganges named Vitthatā, he saw the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Sikhī seated on its bank, blazing like a mass of fire. With a confident mind, he plucked a ketakī flower together with its stalk and, making an offering, said: 'Venerable Sir, I worship that knowledge by which you, of such great power, have become an All-Knowing Buddha.' Then the Blessed One expressed his appreciation. Through that merit, having been born among devas and humans and having experienced both kinds of good fortune, in this Buddha’s dispensation he was reborn in a good family. Having gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth and before long became an arahant.

10. [M 2.0147] So [V 2.0137] attano katakusalaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento vitthatāya nadītīretiādimāha. Tattha vitthatāyāti vittharati pattharati vitthiṇṇā hotīti vitthatā, nadanti saddaṃ karonti itā gatā pavattāti nadī, nadiṃ tarantā etaṃ patvā tiṇṇā nāma hontīti tīraṃ, tassā vitthatāya nadiyā tīre tīrasamīpeti attho. Ketakiṃ pupphitaṃ disvāti kucchitākārena gaṇhantānaṃ hatthaṃ kaṇḍako chindati vijjhatīti ketaṃ, ketassa esā ketakīpupphaṃ, taṃ disvā vaṇṭaṃ chinditvāti sambandho.

10. Recollecting his own wholesome deed, he became joyful and, proclaiming the Apadāna of his past conduct, spoke beginning with 'On the bank of the broad river.' Therein, regarding 'broad': it spreads out, it extends, it becomes wide, thus it is 'broad.' Regarding 'river': they roar, make a sound, go, move, proceed, thus it is a 'river.' Regarding 'bank': those crossing a river, having reached this, are said to be 'crossed over,' thus it is the 'bank.' The meaning is 'on the bank of that broad river,' that is, near the bank. Regarding 'seeing a ketakī flower in bloom': because for those who grasp it in a contemptible way, a thorn cuts or pierces the hand, it is 'ketaṃ.' This flower is of the keta, thus it is a 'ketakī flower.' The phrase 'having seen it' is connected with 'plucked the stalk.'

11. Sikhino lokabandhunoti sikhī vuccati aggi, sikhīsadisā nīlapītādibhedā jalamānā chabbaṇṇaghanaraṃsiyo yassa so sikhī, lokassa sakalalokattayassa bandhu ñātakoti lokabandhu, tassa sikhino lokabandhuno ketakīpupphaṃ [P 0.0434] vaṇṭe chinditvā pūjesinti sambandho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

11. Regarding 'of Sikhī, the kinsman of the world': 'Sikhī' is said to be fire. He whose solid six-hued rays, blazing with distinctions of blue, yellow, and so on, are like a fire-crest, he is 'Sikhī.' 'Kinsman of the world' means a kinsman, a relative, of the world, of the entire triple world. The connection is: 'I worshipped that Sikhī, the kinsman of the world, by plucking a ketakī flower at the stalk.' The rest is clear in meaning.

Sudassanattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of Sudassana Thera is finished.

3. Candanapūjanakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Candanapūjanaka

Candabhāgānadītīretiādikaṃ āyasmato candanapūjanakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle himavante candabhāgānadiyā samīpe kinnarayoniyaṃ nibbatto pupphabhakkho pupphanivasano candanaagaruādīsu gandhavibhūsito himavante bhummadevatā viya uyyānakīḷajalakīḷādianekasukhaṃ anubhavanto vāsaṃ kappesi. Tadā atthadassī bhagavā tassānukampāya himavantaṃ gantvā ākāsato oruyha saṅghāṭiṃ paññāpetvā nisīdi. So kinnaro taṃ bhagavantaṃ vijjotamānaṃ tattha nisinnaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sugandhacandanena pūjesi. Tassa bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Candanapūjanaka begins with the words: 'On the bank of the river Candabhāgā…' This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation from the round, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī in the womb of a kinnara near the Candabhāgā river in the Himālaya. Eating flowers, clothed in flowers, and adorned with the fragrance of sandalwood, aloeswood, and so on, he dwelt in the Himālaya enjoying many pleasures such as garden sports and water sports, like a terrestrial deity. Then the Blessed One Atthadassī, out of compassion for him, went to the Himālaya, descended from the sky, spread out his outer robe, and sat down. That kinnara, seeing the Blessed One seated there, shining brightly, with a confident mind worshipped him with fragrant sandalwood. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation.

17. So tena puññena tena somanassena yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu cakkavattirajjapadesarajjasampattiyo anubhavitvā [M 2.0148] imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento candabhāgānadītīretiādimāha. Tattha candaṃ manaṃ ruciṃ ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā viya jātoti cando. Candamaṇḍalena pasannanimmalodakena ubhosu passesu muttādalasadisasantharadhavalapulinatalena [V 2.0138] ca samannāgatattā candena bhāgā sadisāti candabhāgā, tassā candabhāgāya nadiyā tīre samīpeti attho. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā suviññeyyamevāti.

17. By that merit and that joy, having lived out his full lifespan, he passed away and was reborn in a deva world. After successively experiencing the six kinds of sensual-sphere fortune, he enjoyed among humans the fortunes of a wheel-turning monarch and of regional kings. In this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a good family, attained understanding, went forth, and soon reached arahantship. Recalling his past deeds and filled with joy, he declared his past life story, beginning with: 'On the bank of the river Candabhāgā…' Herein, `cando` (moon) is so called because it is born as if knowing the mind's delight and disposition. The river is called `Candabhāgā` because it is similar (`sadisā`) in part (`bhāgā`) to the moon (`candena`), being endowed with clear, pure water and, on both banks, with white sandy expanses spread out like strings of pearls. The meaning is 'on the bank of that river Candabhāgā,' that is, near the bank. The rest is all easy to understand in the way already stated.

Candanapūjanakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Candanapūjanaka is complete.

Aṭṭhamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Eighth Recitation Section is complete.

4. Pupphacchadaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pupphacchadaniya

Sunando nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato pupphacchadaniyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā sakasippesu nipphattiṃ patto mahābhogo mahāyaso dānābhirato ahosi. Ekadivasaṃ so “sakalajambudīpe ime yācakā nāma ‘ahaṃ dānaṃ na laddhosmī’ti [P 0.0435] vattuṃ mā labhantū”ti mahādānaṃ sajjesi. Tadā padumuttaro bhagavā saparivāro ākāsena gacchati. Brāhmaṇo taṃ disvā pasannacitto sakasisse pakkosāpetvā pupphāni āharāpetvā ākāse ukkhipitvā pūjesi. Tāni sakalanagaraṃ chādetvā satta divasāni aṭṭhaṃsu.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pupphacchadaniya begins with the words: 'Sunanda was my name...' This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating over many existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation from the round, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a brahmin family. Having attained understanding and reached perfection in his own crafts, he was of great wealth and fame, and delighted in giving. One day, resolving, 'Let no beggar in all of Jambudīpa have occasion to say, "I did not receive a gift,"' he arranged a great giving. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara was traveling through the sky with his assembly. Seeing him, the brahmin, with a confident mind, had his pupils summoned, had flowers brought, and tossing them into the sky, he paid homage. Those flowers covered the entire city and remained for seven days.

26. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu sukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto saddhājāto pabbajitvā khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sunando nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā suviññeyyamevāti.

26. Through that meritorious deed, having experienced happiness among devas and humans, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a family in Sāvatthī. When faith arose in him, he went forth and attained arahantship at the very razor's edge. Recalling his own past kamma, with gladness arisen, he declared his past life story, beginning with the words: 'Sunanda was my name...' That is easy to understand in the way already stated.

Pupphacchadaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pupphacchadaniya is complete.

5. Rahosaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rahosaññaka

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ [M 2.0149] āyasmato rahosaññakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto ekasmiṃ buddhasuññakāle majjhimadese brāhmaṇakule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya sakasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto kevalaṃ udaraṃ pūretvā kodhamadamānādayo akusaleyeva disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ [V 2.0139] pabbajitvā anekatāpasasataparivāro vasabhapabbatasamīpe assamaṃ māpetvā tīṇi vassasahassāni himavanteyeva vasamāno “ahaṃ ettakānaṃ sissānaṃ ācariyoti sammato garuṭṭhāniyo garukātabbo vandanīyo, ācariyo me natthī”ti domanassappatto te sabbe sisse sannipātetvā buddhānaṃ abhāve nibbānādhigamābhāvaṃ pakāsetvā sayaṃ ekako raho vivekaṭṭhāneva nisinno buddhassa sammukhā nisinno viya buddhasaññaṃ manasi karitvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā sālāyaṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbatti.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Rahosaññaka begins with the words: 'Not far from the Himālaya…' This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation from the round, was reborn in a brahmin family in the Middle Country during an interval when there was no Buddha. Having grown up and reached perfection in his own crafts, but seeing no essence in them—seeing only the filling of the belly and unwholesome states such as anger, intoxication, and conceit—he abandoned the household life, entered the Himālaya, and went forth into the ascetic life. With a retinue of many hundreds of ascetics, he had a hermitage built near Mount Vasabha. Dwelling in the Himālaya for three thousand years, he became afflicted with grief, thinking: 'I am regarded as the teacher of so many disciples, esteemed, to be respected, to be venerated, yet I myself have no teacher.' Gathering all his disciples, he explained that in the absence of Buddhas, there is no attainment of Nibbāna. Then, sitting alone by himself in a secluded place, as if sitting in the presence of a Buddha, he brought to mind the perception of a Buddha and generated rapture with the Buddha as its object. Sitting cross-legged in his hall, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma-world.

34. So tattha jhānasukhena ciraṃ vasitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto kāmesu anallīno sattavassiko pabbajitvā khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ patvā chaḷabhiñño hutvā pubbenivāsañāṇena attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Vasabho nāma pabbatoti himavantapabbataṃ vinā sesapabbatānaṃ uccatarabhāvena seṭṭhatarabhāvena vasabhoti saṅkhaṃ gato pabbatoti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

34. Having dwelt there for a long time with the bliss of jhāna, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a good family. Unattached to sensual pleasures, he went forth at the age of seven and attained arahantship at the very razor's edge. Having become one with the six direct knowledges, he recalled his own past kamma with the knowledge of recollection of past lives. With gladness arisen, he declared his past life story, beginning with the words: 'Not far from the Himālaya…' The phrase 'the mountain named Vasabha' means a mountain known as 'Vasabha' (Chief) because, apart from the Himālaya mountain, it is higher and more excellent than the other mountains. The rest has a plain meaning everywhere.

Rahosaññakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rahosaññaka is complete.

6. Campakapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Campakapupphiya

Kaṇikāraṃva [P 0.0436] jotantantiādikaṃ āyasmato campakapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vessabhussa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule [M 2.0150] nibbatto vuddhippatto sakasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vanantare vasanto vessabhuṃ bhagavantaṃ uddissa sissehi ānītehi campakapupphehi pūjesi. Bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsi. So teneva kusalena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā pubbavāsanābalena gharāvāse anallīno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Campakapupphiya begins with the words: 'Shining like a kaṇikāra tree…' He too, having laid a foundation of merit under previous Buddhas and accumulating in his various existences wholesome deeds that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū. Having come of age and attained proficiency in his own crafts, he saw no essence therein and renounced the household life. He went forth into the ascetic life and, while dwelling in the forest, he paid homage to the Blessed One Vessabhū with campaka flowers brought by his disciples. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation. Through that wholesome deed, wandering on through saṃsāra among devas and humans, he experienced both kinds of good fortune. During this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a good family. Having reached maturity, by the power of his past dispositions he was unattached to the household life. He went forth, and not long afterwards he became an arahant.

41. So aparabhāge attano pubbapuññakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento kaṇikāraṃva jotantantiādimāha. Tattha kaṇikāranti sakalapattapalāsāni paribhajja pātetvā pupphagahaṇasamaye kaṇṇikābaddho hutvā pupphamakuḷānaṃ gahaṇato kaṇṇikākārena pakatoti kaṇikāro, “kaṇṇikāro”ti vattabbe niruttinayena ekassa pubba ṇa-kārassa lopaṃ katvā “kaṇikāra”nti [V 2.0140] vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Taṃ pupphitaṃ kaṇikārarukkhaṃ iva jotantaṃ buddhaṃ addasanti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

41. Subsequently, recalling his past meritorious action, he was filled with mental gladness and, disclosing the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning with: 'Shining like a kaṇikāra tree…' Herein, kaṇikāra: it is called a kaṇikāra because, having shed and dropped all its leaves and foliage, at the time of flowering it becomes bound with ear-ornaments, so to speak, and is known for its ear-ornament shape due to the taking up of its flower buds. It should be understood that although one should say kaṇṇikāra, by etymological rule, kaṇikāra is said after eliding the preceding letter 'ṇ'. The meaning is: 'I saw the Buddha shining like that flowering kaṇikāra tree.' The rest has a plain meaning.

Campakapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Campakapupphiya is concluded.

7. Atthasandassakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Atthasandassaka

Visālamāḷe āsīnotiādikaṃ āyasmato atthasandassakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu attabhāvesu katapuññūpacayo padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya sakasippesu nipphattiṃ patto tattha sāraṃ apassanto gehaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ gantvā ramaṇīye ṭhāne paṇṇasālaṃ katvā paṭivasati, tadā sattānukampāya himavantamāgataṃ padumuttarabhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pañcaṅgasamannāgato vanditvā thutivacanehi thomesi. So tena puññena yāvatāyukaṃ katvā kālaṅkatvā brahmalokūpago ahosi. So aparabhāge imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Atthasandassaka begins with the words: 'Seated in a great hall…' He too, having laid a foundation of merit under previous Buddhas and having an accumulation of merit from many existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having come of age and attained proficiency in his own crafts, he saw no essence therein, renounced his home, and went to the Himālaya. There, in a delightful place, he built a leaf-hut and resided. Then, when the Blessed One Padumuttara came to the Himālaya out of compassion for beings, he saw him and, with a confident mind, paid homage with the five-limbed prostration and extolled him with words of praise. Through that merit, having lived for the full extent of his lifespan, he passed away and arose in the Brahma-world. Subsequently, during this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn in a good family. Having reached maturity, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, gained faith, went forth, and attained arahantship.

47. So [M 2.0151] attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento visālamāḷe āsīnotiādimāha. Tattha [P 0.0437] visālamāḷeti visālaṃ patthaṭaṃ vitthiṇṇaṃ mahantaṃ māḷaṃ visālamāḷaṃ, tasmiṃ visālamāḷe āsīno nisinno ahaṃ lokanāyakaṃ addasanti sambandho. Tesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

47. Recalling his past deeds and filled with mental gladness, disclosing the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning with: 'Seated in a great hall…' Herein, in a great hall: a great hall is a hall that is great because it is wide, spread out, and extensive. The connection is: 'Seated, sitting in that great hall, I saw the Leader of the World.' The meaning of these verses is easily understood.

Atthasandassakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Atthasandassaka is concluded.

8. Ekapasādaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekapasādaniya

Nārado iti me nāmantiādikaṃ āyasmato ekapasādaniyattherassa apadānaṃ.
