Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekāsu jātīsu katakusalo atthadassissa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto kesavoti pākaṭo hutvā viññutaṃ patvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā vasanto ekadivasaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso añjaliṃ paggayha ativiya pītisomanassajāto pakkāmi. So yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā teneva somanassena kālaṃ katvā devesu nibbatto tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā manussesu uppanno tattha sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde aññatarasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto satthari pasīditvā pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ekapasādaniya begins with the words: 'My name was Nārada…' He too, having laid a foundation of merit under previous Buddhas and having done wholesome deeds in many births, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. He became known as Kesava. Having reached maturity, he renounced the household life and went forth. While dwelling as a recluse, one day he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse and, with a confident mind, he raised his hands in reverential salutation and departed, filled with extreme joy and mental gladness. Having remained for the full extent of his lifespan, he passed away with that same mental gladness and was reborn among the devas. There he experienced divine good fortune. Then, being reborn among humans, he experienced worldly good fortune. During this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn into a certain good family. Having come of age, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth, and not long afterwards he became an arahant.

55. So [V 2.0141] aparabhāge attano katakusalakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nārado iti me nāmantiādimāha. Tattha nāradoti jātivasena suddhasarīrattā natthi rajo dhūli malaṃ etassāti nārado, ja-kārassa da-kāraṃ katvā nāradoti kuladattikaṃ nāmaṃ. Kesavoti kisavacchagotte jātattā kesavo nāradakesavo iti maṃ janā vidū jānantīti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

55. Subsequently, recalling the wholesome action he had done, he was filled with mental gladness and, disclosing the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning with: 'My name was Nārada…' Herein, Nārada: because of the purity of his body by birth, 'there is no dust (rajo), dirt (dhūli), or stain (malaṃ) in him,' thus he is Nārada. By making the letter 'da' for the letter 'ja', Nārada is the family-given name. As to Kesava: because he was born in the Kisavaccha clan, he was Kesava. The meaning is: 'People knew me as Nārada-Kesava.' The rest is evident.

Ekapasādaniyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekapasādaniya is concluded.

9. Sālapupphadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sālapupphadāyaka

Migarājā [M 2.0152] tadā āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato sālapupphadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave katakusalasañcayo kenaci kammacchiddena himavante sīhayoniyaṃ nibbatto anekasīhaparivāro vihāsi. Tadā sikhī bhagavā tassānukampāya himavantaṃ agamāsi. Sīho taṃ upagataṃ disvā pasannamānaso sākhābhaṅgena sakaṇṇikasālapupphaṃ gahetvā pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa anumodanaṃ akāsi.

The verses beginning 'Migarājā tadā āsiṃ' are the Apadāna of the Venerable Sālapupphadāyaka. He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulated a store of merit in various existences, due to some flaw in his kamma was reborn in the womb of a lion in the Himālaya and dwelt there surrounded by a retinue of many lions. Then the Blessed One Sikhī, out of compassion for him, went to the Himālaya. Seeing him approach, the lion, with a confident mind, took a sāla flower with its stalk by breaking off a branch and paid homage to him. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation.

60. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthari pasanno pabbajitvā arahattaṃ patto attano pubbakammaṃ [P 0.0438] saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento migarājā tadā āsintiādimāha. Tattha maraṇaṃ gacchantīti migā, atha vā ghāsaṃ magganti gavesantīti migā, migānaṃ rājā migarājā. Sakalacatuppadānaṃ rājabhāve satipi gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ mige ādiṃ katvā migarājāti vuttaṃ. Yadā bhagavantaṃ disvā sapupphaṃ sālasākhaṃ bhañjitvā pūjesiṃ, tadā ahaṃ migarājā ahosinti attho.

60. As a result of that merit, wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of success, during the advent of this Buddha he was reborn in a certain family. Having reached maturity, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth, and attained arahantship. Remembering his own past kamma, filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his former conduct, saying: 'I was then the king of beasts,' and so on. Herein, 'miga' means 'they go to their death,' or 'they seek or search for fodder.' The king of beasts is 'migarājā.' Although he was king of all quadrupeds, for the sake of metrical convenience, he is called 'migarājā,' taking 'miga' as the primary term. The meaning is: 'When, having seen the Blessed One, I broke off a flowering sāla branch and paid homage, at that time I was the king of beasts.'

62. Sakosaṃ pupphamāharinti sakaṇṇikaṃ sālapupphaṃ āhariṃ pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

62. 'I brought a flower with its sheath' means: I brought a sāla flower with its stalk and paid homage. The rest has an obvious meaning.

Sālapupphadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sālapupphadāyaka is finished.

10. Piyālaphaladāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Piyālaphaladāyaka

Parodhako [V 2.0142] tadā āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato piyālaphaladāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle nesādakule nibbatto himavante ekasmiṃ pabbhāre mige vadhitvā jīvikaṃ kappetvā vasati. Tasmiṃ kāle tattha gataṃ sikhiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso sāyaṃ pātaṃ namassamāno kañci deyyadhammaṃ apassanto madhurāni [M 2.0153] piyālaphalāni uccinitvā adāsi. Bhagavā tāni paribhuñji. So nesādo buddhārammaṇāya pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭṭhasarīro pāpakamme virattacitto mūlaphalāhāro nacirasseva kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatti.

'I was then a hunter,' and so on, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Piyālaphaladāyaka. He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences that are a support for liberation, was reborn in a hunter's family in the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. He lived on a mountain slope in the Himālaya, making his living by killing beasts. At that time, seeing the Blessed One Sikhī who had gone there, with a confident mind he paid homage in the morning and evening. Not seeing any other gift to offer, he picked sweet piyāla fruits and gave them. The Blessed One consumed them. That hunter, his body constantly pervaded by joy with the Buddha as its object, his mind detached from evil deeds, subsisting on roots and fruits, soon passed away and was reborn in the deva world.

66. So tattha dibbasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu ca anekavidhasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde gahapatikule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tattha anabhirato gehaṃ pahāya satthu santike pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto attano kataphaladānakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento parodhako tadā āsintiādimāha. Tattha yadā ahaṃ piyālaphalaṃ datvā cittaṃ pasādesiṃ, tadā ahaṃ parodhako āsinti sambandho. Parodhakoti parasattarodhako vihesako. “Pararodhako”ti vattabbe pubbassa ra-kārassa lopaṃ katvā “parodhako”ti vuttaṃ.

66. Having enjoyed divine felicities there and various kinds of success among humans, during the advent of this Buddha he was reborn in a householder's family. Having reached maturity, he established a household, but not delighting in it, he abandoned the home life and went forth in the Teacher's presence. Developing insight, he soon attained arahantship. Remembering his own kamma of giving the fruit, filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his former conduct, saying: 'I was then a hunter,' and so on. Herein, the connection is: 'When I gave the piyāla fruit and made my mind confident, at that time I was a hunter.' 'Parodhako' means one who obstructs and harasses other beings. When 'pararodhako' should be said, the initial 'ra' is elided and it is said as 'parodhako.'

69. Paricāriṃ vināyakanti taṃ nibbānapāpakaṃ satthāraṃ, “bhante[P 0.0439], imaṃ phalaṃ paribhuñjathā”ti pavāriṃ nimantesiṃ ārādhesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

69. 'I served the leader' refers to that Teacher who leads to Nibbāna. The meaning is: I invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please consume this fruit,' and thus I gratified him. The rest is easy to understand.

Piyālaphaladāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Piyālaphaladāyaka is finished.

Cuddasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Fourteenth Chapter is finished.

15. Chattavaggo

15. The Umbrella Chapter

1. Atichattiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Atichattiya

Parinibbute [V 2.0143] bhagavatītiādikaṃ āyasmato atichattiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto dharamānassa bhagavato adiṭṭhattā parinibbutakāle “aho mama parihānī”ti cintetvā “mama jātiṃ saphalaṃ karissāmī”ti katasanniṭṭhāno chattādhichattaṃ kāretvā tassa bhagavato sarīradhātuṃ nihitadhātugabbhaṃ pūjesi. Aparabhāge pupphacchattaṃ kāretvā tameva dhātugabbhaṃ [M 2.0154] pūjesi. So teneva puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde gahapatikule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthari pasanno pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vāyamanto nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

'When the Blessed One had passed into Parinibbāna,' and so on, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Atichattiya. He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences as a support for liberation, was reborn in a certain family in the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. Since he had not seen the Blessed One while he was still living, at the time of the Parinibbāna he thought, 'Alas, my loss!' and having made the resolution, 'I will make my birth fruitful,' he had a tiered umbrella made and paid homage to the relic chamber in which the bodily relics of that Blessed One were deposited. Later, having had a flower-umbrella made, he paid homage to that same relic chamber. By that same merit, wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of success, during the advent of this Buddha he was reborn in a householder's family. Having reached maturity, he gained confidence in the Teacher, went forth, took up a meditation subject, and by striving, soon attained arahantship.

1. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento parinibbute bhagavatītiādimāha. Tattha chattātichattanti chādiyati saṃvariyati ātapādinti chattaṃ, chattassa atichattaṃ chattassa upari katachattaṃ chattātichattaṃ, chattassa uparūpari chattanti attho. Thūpamhi abhiropayinti thūpiyati rāsikarīyatīti thūpo, atha vā thūpati thirabhāvena vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjamāno patiṭṭhātīti thūpo, tasmiṃ thūpamhi mayā kāritaṃ chattaṃ uparūpari ṭhapanavasena abhi visesena āropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.

1. Remembering his own past kamma, filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his former conduct, saying: 'When the Blessed One had passed into Parinibbāna,' and so on. Herein, 'chattātichattaṃ': a 'chatta' (umbrella) is so called because it shades and covers from the sun. 'Atichattaṃ' is an umbrella placed over an umbrella; 'chattātichattaṃ' means an umbrella over an umbrella, that is, umbrellas one above the other. 'I placed upon the stūpa': a 'thūpa' (stūpa) is so called because it is heaped up, made into a pile; or, it stands firmly, attaining growth, increase, and expansion. The meaning is: 'By way of placing it on top, I especially placed the umbrella I had made upon that stūpa and thus paid homage.'

2. Pupphacchadanaṃ katvānāti vikasitehi sugandhehi anekehi phupphehi chadanaṃ chattupari vitānaṃ katvā pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

2. 'Having made a flower-covering' means: having made a covering—a canopy—over the umbrella with many fragrant, blossomed flowers, I paid homage. The rest has an obvious meaning everywhere.

Atichattiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Atichattiya is finished.

2. Thambhāropakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Thambhāropaka

Nibbute [V 2.0144] lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato thambhāropakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto dhammadassissa bhagavato [P 0.0440] kāle kulagehe nibbatto saddho pasanno parinibbute bhagavati tassa bhagavato dhātugabbhamāḷake thambhaṃ nikhanitvā dhajaṃ āropesi. Bahūni jātisumanapupphāni ganthitvā nisseṇiyā ārohitvā pūjesi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Thambhāropaka begins with the words, 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna…' This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a family household during the time of the Blessed One Dhammadassī. Being faithful and confident, after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna, he planted a pillar in the enclosure of that Blessed One's relic chamber and raised a banner. Stringing many jasmine flowers, he climbed a ladder and paid homage.

5. So yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā kālaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā sabbattha pūjito imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto daharakālato pabhuti pūjanīyo sāsane baddhasaddho pabbajitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patto [M 2.0155] attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Tattha nibbute lokanāthamhīti sakalalokassa nāthe padhānabhūte paṭisaraṇe ca satthari khandhaparinibbānena nibbute nibbutadīpasikhā viya adassanaṃ gateti attho. Dhammadassīnarāsabheti catusaccadhammaṃ passatīti dhammadassī, atha vā satipaṭṭhānādike sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhamme dassanasīlo passanasīloti dhammadassī, narānaṃ āsabho pavaro uttamoti narāsabho, dhammadassī ca so narāsabho ceti dhammadassīnarāsabho, tasmiṃ dhammadassīnarāsabhe. Āropesiṃ dhajaṃ thambhanti cetiyamāḷake thambhaṃ nikhanitvā tattha dhajaṃ āropesiṃ bandhitvā ṭhapesinti attho.

5. Having lived for the full extent of his lifespan, he passed away. Wandering among gods and humans, experiencing both kinds of good fortune and being honored everywhere, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a certain family household. From his youth, being worthy of honor and having firm faith in the Teaching, he went forth and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Remembering his past kamma, he became joyful and declared the apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna…' Herein, 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna' means that when the Teacher—the chief and refuge of the entire world—had attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna of the aggregates, he passed from sight like an extinguished lamp. 'Dhammadassī, the bull among men': he is called Dhammadassī because he sees the Four Noble Truths, or because he is accustomed to seeing and observing the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, such as the establishments of mindfulness. 'A bull among men' means the foremost and supreme among men. Thus, he is Dhammadassī and a bull among men, hence 'Dhammadassī, the bull among men.' 'I raised a banner on the pillar' means: having planted a pillar in the cetiya enclosure, I raised and fastened a banner there.

6. Nisseṇiṃ māpayitvānāti nissāya taṃ iṇanti gacchanti ārohanti uparīti nisseṇi, taṃ nisseṇiṃ māpayitvā kāretvā bandhitvā thūpaseṭṭhaṃ samāruhinti sambandho. Jātipupphaṃ gahetvānāti jāyamānameva janānaṃ sundaraṃ manaṃ karotīti jātisumanaṃ, jātisumanameva pupphaṃ “jātisumanapuppha”nti vattabbe gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ sumanasaddassa lopaṃ katvā “jātipuppha”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ jātisumanapupphaṃ gahetvā ganthitvā thūpamhi āropayiṃ, āropetvā pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

6. Regarding 'Having had a ladder made': a ladder (nisseṇi) is so called because, relying on it, one goes or ascends upwards. The connection is: 'having had that ladder made, constructed, and fastened, I climbed the excellent stupa.' Regarding 'Taking jasmine flowers': jasmine (jātisumana) is so called because as soon as it is born it makes people's minds beautiful. Although it should be said 'jātisumanapuppha' (jasmine flower), for the sake of metrical convenience the word 'sumana' is elided and it is said 'jātipuppha.' The meaning is: 'Taking those jasmine flowers and stringing them, I placed them on the stupa; having placed them, I paid homage.' The rest is easy to understand.

Thambhāropakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Thambhāropaka is complete.

3. Vedikārakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vedikāraka

Nibbute [V 2.0145] lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato vedikārakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto piyadassissa bhagavato kāle vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā nibbute satthari pasanno tassa cetiye valayaṃ kāresi, sattahi ratanehi paripūretvā mahāpūjaṃ kāresi. So [P 0.0441] tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto anekesu jātisatasahassesu pūjanīyo mahaddhano mahābhogo ubhayasukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vibhavasampanno pabbajitvā vāyamanto nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Vedikāraka begins with the words, 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna…' This one, too, having made his aspiration under the former supreme Jinas and accumulating merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn into a prosperous family during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī. Having reached maturity and established a household, with a confident mind when the Teacher had attained Nibbāna, he had a railing made for his cetiya. Filling it with the seven kinds of gems, he made a great offering. By that merit, wandering among gods and humans for many hundreds of thousands of births, he was worthy of honor, possessed great wealth and great property, and experienced both kinds of happiness. During this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a family household, became prosperous, went forth, and by striving, soon became an Arahant.

10. So [M 2.0156] ekadivasaṃ attano pubbe katakusalaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Piyadassīnaruttameti piyaṃ somanassākāraṃ dassanaṃ yassa so piyadassī, ārohapariṇāhadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītānubyañjanabyāmappabhāmaṇḍalehi sādhu mahājanappasādaṃ janayanākāradassanoti attho. Narānaṃ uttamoti naruttamo, piyadassī ca so naruttamo ceti piyadassīnaruttamo, tasmiṃ piyadassīnaruttame nibbute dhātugabbhamhi muttavediṃ ahaṃ akāsinti sambandho. Pupphādhāratthāya pariyosāne vedikāvalayaṃ akāsinti attho.

10. One day, remembering the wholesome deeds he had done in the past, he became joyful and, in order to reveal the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning, 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna…' Its meaning is as stated above. Regarding 'Piyadassī, the supreme among men': he is Piyadassī because his appearance is pleasing, generating gladness in the great populace, being well-endowed with height and girth, the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-wide aura. He is the supreme among men (naruttamo) because he is the best of men. He is Piyadassī and he is the supreme among men, thus 'Piyadassī, the supreme among men.' The connection is: 'When that Piyadassī, the supreme among men, had attained Nibbāna, I made a pearl railing at the relic chamber.' The meaning is that he made a circular railing at the end for the purpose of holding flowers.

11. Maṇīhi parivāretvāti maṇati jotati pabhāsatīti maṇi, atha vā janānaṃ manaṃ pūrento somanassaṃ karonto ito gato pavattoti maṇi, jātiraṅgamaṇiveḷuriyamaṇiādīhi anekehi maṇīhi katavedikāvalayaṃ parivāretvā uttamaṃ mahāpūjaṃ akāsinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

11. Regarding 'Having surrounded it with gems': a gem (maṇi) is so called because it shines, glows, and illuminates; or, it is so called because it fills people's minds, creating joy. The meaning is: 'Having surrounded the circular railing made of many gems—such as jāti-gems, raṅga-gems, veḷuriya-gems, and so on—he made a supreme, great offering.' The rest has a plain meaning.

Vedikārakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vedikāraka is complete.

4. Saparivāriyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Saparivāriya

Padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato saparivāriyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekāsu jātīsu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato [V 2.0146] kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto mahaddhano mahābhogo ahosi. Atha padumuttare bhagavati parinibbute mahājano tassa dhātuṃ nidahitvā mahantaṃ cetiyaṃ kāretvā pūjesi. Tasmiṃ kāle ayaṃ upāsako tassupari candanasārena cetiyagharaṃ karitvā mahāpūjaṃ akāsi. So teneva puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya kusalaṃ katvā saddhāya sāsane pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Saparivāriya Thera begins with the words, 'Padumuttara, the Victor…' He too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, and in numerous births accumulated merits that serve as a basis for liberation. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a good family and, having reached maturity, became very wealthy and prosperous. Then, when the Blessed One Padumuttara attained final Nibbāna, the great populace enshrined his relics, had a great cetiya built, and paid homage to it. At that time, this lay follower had a shrine-house of sandalwood built over it and made a great offering. By that very merit, transmigrating among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of good fortune, in this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a certain family. Having come of age and done what is wholesome, he went forth in the Dispensation out of faith and before long became an arahant.

15-8. So [M 2.0157] aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Tattha [P 0.0442] omattanti lāmakabhāvaṃ nīcabhāvaṃ dukkhitabhāvaṃ vā na passāmi na jānāmi, na diṭṭhapubbo mayā nīcabhāvoti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

15-8. Later, recollecting his own past kamma and becoming joyful, he proclaimed the apadāna of his past conduct, speaking the verses beginning, 'Padumuttara, the Victor…' Herein, omattaṃ means a wretched, low, or miserable state. The meaning is: 'I do not see, I do not know; a lowly state has never been seen by me.' The rest is clear.

Saparivāriyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Saparivāriya is finished.

5. Umāpupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Umāpupphiya

Nibbute lokamahitetiādikaṃ āyasmato umāpupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto nibbutassa bhagavato cetiyamahe vattamāne indanīlamaṇivaṇṇaṃ umāpupphaṃ gahetvā pūjesi. So tena puññena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto dibbamānusasampattiyo anubhavitvā uppannuppannabhave bahulaṃ nīlavaṇṇo jātisampanno vibhavasampanno ahosi. So imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā saddhājāto pabbajito nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Umāpupphiya Thera begins with the words, 'When the one revered by the world had attained Nibbāna…' He too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and in various existences accumulated merits that serve as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born into a good family. Having come of age, he established a household and was living there. While a great festival for the cetiya of the Blessed One who had attained Parinibbāna was taking place, he took an umā flower the color of sapphire and offered it in worship. By that merit, transmigrating only in happy destinations, he experienced divine and human good fortune. In each successive existence he was often of a dark-blue complexion, endowed with high birth and great wealth. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a wealthy family, and having reached maturity, he was inspired by faith and went forth. Before long he attained arahantship.

21. So pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokamahitetiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha lokamahiteti lokehi mahito pūjitoti lokamahito, tasmiṃ lokamahite siddhatthamhi bhagavati parinibbuteti sambandho. Āhutīnaṃpaṭiggaheti āhutino vuccanti pūjāsakkārā, tesaṃ āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ arahatīti āhutīnaṃpaṭiggaho, aluttakitantasamāso, tasmiṃ āhutīnaṃpaṭiggahe bhagavati parinibbuteti attho.

21. Recollecting his past kamma, he became joyful and, proclaiming the apadāna of his past conduct, spoke the verses beginning, 'When the one revered by the world had attained Nibbāna…' Herein, lokamahite means revered and worshipped by the worlds; thus lokamahito. The connection is: 'when the Blessed One Siddhattha, revered by the world, had attained Parinibbāna.' Āhutīnaṃpaṭiggahe: āhutiyo are said to be offerings and honors. He is worthy to receive those offerings, thus he is āhutīnaṃpaṭiggaho, a recipient of offerings. This is an unelided compound ending in a kṛt suffix. The meaning is: 'when the Blessed One, the recipient of offerings, had attained Parinibbāna.'

22. Umāpupphanti [V 2.0147] uddhamuddhaṃ nīlapabhaṃ muñcamānaṃ pupphati vikasatīti umāpupphaṃ, taṃ umāpupphaṃ gahetvā cetiye pūjaṃ akāsinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

22. Umāpupphaṃ: it blooms, emitting a blue radiance upwards; thus it is an umāpupphaṃ. The meaning is: 'Taking that umā flower, he made an offering at the cetiya.' The rest has a clear meaning.

Umāpupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Umāpupphiya is finished.

6. Anulepadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Anulepadāyaka

Anomadassīmuninotiādikaṃ [M 2.0158] āyasmato anulepadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto anomadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto mahaddhano mahābhogo tassa bhagavato bodhirukkhassa vedikāvalayaṃ kāretvā sudhākammañca kāretvā vālukasantharaṇaṃ daddaḷhamānaṃ rajatavimānamiva kāresi. So tena puññena sukhappatto uppannuppannabhave rajatavimānarajatageharajatapāsādesu [P 0.0443] sukhamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthari pasanno pabbajitvā vipassanamanuyutto nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Anulepadāyaka Thera begins with the words, 'The sage Anomadassī…' He too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and in various existences accumulated merits that serve as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was reborn in a good family and was very wealthy and prosperous. He had a railing built around that Blessed One's Bodhi tree, had plasterwork done, and had sand spread so that it shone like a silver celestial mansion. By that merit, having attained happiness, in successive existences he experienced bliss in silver celestial mansions, silver houses, and silver palaces. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a good family, and having reached maturity, he gained faith in the Teacher, went forth, applied himself to insight meditation, and before long became an arahant.

26. So aparabhāge “kiṃ nu kho kusalaṃ katvā mayā ayaṃ viseso adhigato”ti pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena paṭipāṭiyā anussaritvā pubbe katakusalaṃ jānitvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento anomadassīmuninotiādimāha. Tattha anomaṃ alāmakaṃ dassanaṃ dassanīyaṃ sarīraṃ yassa so anomadassī, dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītānubyañjanabyāmappabhāsamujjalavirājitasarīrattā sundaradassanoti attho. Sudhāya piṇḍaṃ datvānāti bodhighare vedikāvalayaṃ kāretvā sakale bodhighare sudhālepanaṃ katvāti attho. Pāṇikammaṃ akāsahanti sārakaṭṭhena phalakapāṇiyo katvā tāhi pāṇīhi maṭṭhakammaṃ akāsinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

26. Later, reflecting, 'By doing what wholesome kamma have I attained this distinction?' he recollected his past abodes in sequence with the knowledge of recollection of past abodes. Knowing the wholesome kamma he had done in the past, he became joyful and, revealing the apadāna of his past conduct, spoke the verses beginning, 'The sage Anomadassī…' Herein, Anomadassī means one whose sight is faultless, whose body is lovely to see, because his body shines and is resplendent with the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor characteristics, and the fathom-long halo; the meaning is 'beautiful to see.' 'Sudhāya piṇḍaṃ datvāna' means: having had a railing built at the Bodhi-tree shrine and having had the entire Bodhi-tree shrine coated with plaster. This is the meaning. 'Pāṇikammaṃ akāsaṃ' means: having made polishing boards from heartwood, with those boards I did the burnishing work. This is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.

Anulepadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Anulepadāyaka is concluded.

7. Maggadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maggadāyaka

Uttaritvāna nadikantiādikaṃ āyasmato maggadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu [V 2.0148] katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu nibbānādhigamatthāya puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle lokasammate kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ ekaṃ nadiṃ uttaritvā vanantaraṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso “idāni mayā bhagavato maggaṃ samaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā kudālañca piṭakañca [M 2.0159] ādāya bhagavato gamanamaggaṃ samaṃ katvā vālukaṃ okiritvā bhagavato pāde vanditvā, “bhante, iminā maggālaṅkārakaraṇena nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne pūjanīyo bhaveyyaṃ, nibbānañca pāpuṇeyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Bhagavā “yathādhippāyaṃ samijjhatū”ti anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi.

The story beginning 'Having crossed the river' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Maggadāyaka. He too, having made a foundation of merit under former Jinas, accumulating merits for the attainment of Nibbāna through many existences, was reborn in a family esteemed in the world during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having come of age and living the household life, one day he saw the Blessed One crossing a river and going into a forest, and with a serene mind he thought: 'Now it is fitting for me to make the path for the Blessed One smooth.' Taking a hoe and a basket, he leveled the path for the Blessed One, scattered sand on it, and worshipped at the Blessed One’s feet. He then made an aspiration: 'Venerable sir, by this act of adorning the path, may I be worthy of honor wherever I am reborn, and may I attain Nibbāna.' The Blessed One said, 'May your wish be fulfilled,' and after expressing his appreciation, he departed.

32-3. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto sabbattha pūjito ahosi. Imasmiṃ pana buddhuppāde pākaṭe ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto satthari pasanno pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ paccakkhato ñatvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento uttaritvāna nadikantiādimāha. Tattha nadati saddaṃ karoti gacchatīti nadī, nadīyeva nadikā, taṃ nadikaṃ uttaritvā atikkamitvāti attho. Kudālapiṭakamādāyāti [P 0.0444] ku vuccati pathavī, taṃ vidālane padālane chindane alanti kudālaṃ, piṭakaṃ vuccati paṃsuvālikādivāhakaṃ, tālapaṇṇavettalatādīhi katabhājanaṃ, kudālañca piṭakañca kudālapiṭakaṃ, taṃ ādāya gahetvāti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Through that merit, as he wandered through saṃsāra among devas and humans, he was honored everywhere. When this Buddha-dispensation appeared, he was reborn in a certain family, and having gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth. Having developed insight, he soon attained arahantship. Having known his own past kamma directly, he became joyful, and to reveal the story of his past conduct, he recited the verses beginning 'Having crossed the river.' Here, nadī is so called because it makes a sound (nadati) or because it flows (gacchati); nadikā is simply a river. 'Uttaritvā' means having crossed over it. As to 'kudālapiṭakamādāya': 'ku' means earth; that which is able (alaṃ) to break up (vidālane), break apart (padālane), or cut (chindane) it is a 'kudāla', a hoe. A 'piṭaka' is a carrier for things like soil and sand, a container made from palm leaves, reeds, vines, and so on. 'Kudālapiṭakaṃ' is both the hoe and the basket. 'Ādāya' means having taken it. The rest has an obvious meaning.

Maggadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maggadāyaka is concluded.

8. Phalakadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Phalakadāyaka

Yānakāro pure āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato phalakadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu attabhāvesu katapuññasambhāro siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle vaḍḍhakikule nibbatto ratanattaye pasanno candanena ālambanaphalakaṃ katvā bhagavato adāsi. Bhagavā tassānumodanaṃ akāsi.

The story beginning 'Formerly I was a cart-maker' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Phalakadāyaka. He too, having made a foundation of merit under former Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit in many existences, was reborn into a carpenter's family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. With confidence in the Triple Gem, he made a support-plank of sandalwood and gave it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation.

37. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto sabbattha kāle cittasukhapīṇito ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sañjātappasādo pabbajitvā vāyamanto nacirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ [V 2.0149] patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento [M 2.0160] yānakāro pure āsintiādimāha. Tattha yānakāroti yanti etena icchiticchitaṭṭhānanti yānaṃ, taṃ karotīti yānakāro, pure buddhadassanasamaye ahaṃ yānakāro āsiṃ ahosinti attho. Candanaṃ phalakaṃ katvāti candati pariḷāhaṃ vūpasametīti candanaṃ. Atha vā candanti sugandhavāsanatthaṃ sarīraṃ vilimpanti etenāti candanaṃ, taṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ katvā. Lokabandhunoti sakalalokassa bandhu ñātibhūtoti lokabandhu, tassa lokabandhuno satthussa adāsinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

37. By that merit, as he wandered through saṃsāra among devas and humans, he was always suffused with mental happiness and experienced both kinds of good fortune. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a good family, and having attained discernment, he heard the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma. When confidence arose in him, he went forth, and by striving, he soon attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Remembering his own past kamma, he became joyful, and to reveal the story of his past conduct, he recited the verses beginning 'Formerly I was a cart-maker.' Here, as to 'yānakāro': a 'yāna' is that by which one goes (yanti) to whatever place one wishes; one who makes (karoti) that is a 'yānakāro', a cart-maker. The meaning is: 'Formerly, at the time I saw the Buddha, I was a cart-maker.' As to 'having made a sandalwood plank': 'candana' is so called because it soothes (candati) burning heat (pariḷāhaṃ). Or, because people anoint (vilimpanti) their bodies with it for its fragrance, it is called 'candana'. This he made into a support-plank. As to 'of the Kinsman of the World': he is the kinsman (bandhu), the relative, of the entire world, thus he is the Kinsman of the World. The meaning is that he gave it to that Kinsman of the World, the Teacher. The rest is easy to understand.

Phalakadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Phalakadāyaka is concluded.

9. Vaṭaṃsakiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vaṭaṃsakiya

Sumedho nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato vaṭaṃsakiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimamunindesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tattha ādīnavaṃ disvā gehaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā mahāvane vihāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye sumedho bhagavā vivekakāmatāya taṃ vanaṃ sampāpuṇi. Atha so tāpaso bhagavantaṃ [P 0.0445] disvā pasannamānaso vikasitaṃ saḷalapupphaṃ gahetvā vaṭaṃsakākārena ganthetvā bhagavato pādamūle ṭhapetvā pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa cittappasādatthāya anumodanamakāsi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne kule jāto vuddhimanvāya saddho pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The story beginning 'By name he was Sumedha' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Vaṭaṃsakiya. He too, having made a foundation of merit under former Sages, accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having attained discernment and established a household, he saw the danger in it, and abandoning his home, he went forth into the ascetic life and dwelt in a great forest. At that time, the Blessed One Sumedha, desiring seclusion, came to that forest. Then that ascetic, seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind took a blossoming salala flower, wove it into the shape of a diadem, placed it at the Blessed One's feet, and worshipped. To inspire confidence in his mind, the Blessed One expressed his appreciation. By that merit, as he wandered through saṃsāra among devas and humans, he experienced both kinds of good fortune. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a prosperous family, and upon coming of age, full of faith and confidence, he went forth and soon became an Arahant.

43. So aparabhāge pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sumedho nāma nāmenātiādi vuttaṃ. Vivekamanubrūhantoti janākiṇṇataṃ pahāya janavivekaṃ cittavivekañca anubrūhanto vaḍḍhento bahulīkaronto mahāvanaṃ ajjhogāhi pāvisīti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

43. Later, remembering his past kamma, he became joyful, and to illuminate the story of his past conduct, he recited the verses beginning 'By name he was Sumedha.' As for 'developing seclusion': the meaning is that, having abandoned places crowded with people, he was developing, augmenting, and cultivating both physical seclusion and mental seclusion when he plunged into, that is, entered, the great forest. The rest has an obvious meaning.

Vaṭaṃsakiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vaṭaṃsakiya is concluded.

10. Pallaṅkadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka

Sumedhassa [M 2.0161][V 2.0150] bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato pallaṅkadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu nibbānādhigamatthāya katapuññūpacayo sumedhassa bhagavato kāle gahapatikule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya mahābhogasampanno satthari pasīditvā dhammaṃ sutvā tassa satthuno sattaratanamayaṃ pallaṅkaṃ kāretvā mahantaṃ pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto sabbattha pūjito ahosi. So anukkamena imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā pubbe katapuññanāmena pallaṅkadāyakattheroti pākaṭo ahosi. Heṭṭhā viya uparipi pubbe katapuññanāmena therānaṃ nāmāni evameva veditabbāni.

The Apadāna of the venerable Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka begins with the words 'Of the Blessed One Sumedha.' This one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit in many existences for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, was reborn in a householder family in the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having reached maturity and become possessed of great wealth, he gained faith in the Teacher. After hearing the Dhamma, he had a couch made of the seven kinds of gems for that Teacher and made a great offering. Through that merit, while wandering on among devas and humans, he was honored everywhere. Gradually, during this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a prosperous family. Having reached maturity and established a household, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, gained faith, went forth, and not long afterwards attained arahantship. He became renowned under the name Pallaṅkadāyaka, derived from his past meritorious deed. The names of the elders, both in the preceding and subsequent sections, should be understood in this same way, as being derived from their past meritorious deeds.

47. So ekadivasaṃ attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sumedhassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Pallaṅko hi mayā dinnoti pallaṅkaṃ ūrubaddhāsanaṃ katvā yattha upavīsanti nisīdanti, so pallaṅkoti vuccati, so pallaṅko sattaratanamayo mayā dinno pūjitoti attho. Sauttarasapacchadoti saha uttaracchadena saha pacchadena sauttarasapacchado, uparivitānaṃ bandhitvā āsanaṃ uttamavatthehi acchādetvāti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

47. One day, recalling his past kamma, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning: 'Of the Blessed One Sumedha…' 'For a couch was given by me': a couch (pallaṅka) is a seat for sitting cross-legged; that is what is called a couch. The meaning is: that couch, made of the seven kinds of gems, was given by me and honored. 'With a canopy and a coverlet': this means with an upper cover and with a coverlet. The meaning is: having fastened a canopy above and having covered the seat with excellent cloths. The rest is clear.

Pallaṅkadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pallaṅkadāyaka is completed.

Pannarasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Fifteenth Chapter is completed.

16. Bandhujīvakavaggo

16. The Bandhujīvaka Chapter

1. Bandhujīvakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bandhujīvaka

Candaṃva [P 0.0446][V 2.0151] vimalaṃ suddhantiādikaṃ āyasmato bandhujīvakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto [M 2.0162] viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto sikhissa bhagavato rūpakāyasampattiṃ disvā pasannamānaso bandhujīvakapupphāni gahetvā bhagavato pādamūle pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa cittappasādavaḍḍhanatthāya anumodanamakāsi. So yāvatāyutaṃ ṭhatvā teneva puññena devaloke nibbatto cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavattiādisampattiyo anubhavitvā imassa amhākaṃ sammāsambuddhassa uppannakāle gahapatikule nibbatto rūpaggayasaggappatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saddhājāto gehaṃ pahāya pabbajito arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The Apadāna of the venerable Elder Bandhujīvaka begins with the words 'Like the moon, immaculate and pure…' This venerable one, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas, accumulated in various existences merits that serve as a basis for turning away from the round. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was born into a good family. Having reached maturity and established a household, while living there he saw the perfection of the Blessed One Sikhī's physical form and, with a confident mind, he took bandhujīvaka flowers and offered them at the Blessed One's feet. The Blessed One gave a blessing in order to increase his mental confidence. He lived for the full lifespan and by that merit was reborn in the deva world. Having experienced the felicities of the six sense-sphere heavens, and among humans the felicities of a universal monarch and so on, at the time of the arising of our Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, he was reborn in a householder's family. Having attained the pinnacle of beauty and fame, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, and faith arose in him. He went forth from the household life and attained arahantship.

1. So pubbenivāsañāṇena pubbe katakusalakammaṃ anussaritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhantiādimāha. Tattha candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhanti abbhā, mahikā, dhumo, rajo, rāhūti imehi upakkilesamalehi vimuttaṃ candaṃ iva diyaḍḍhasahassupakkilesamalānaṃ pahīnattā vimalaṃ nikkilesattā suddhaṃ pasannaṃ sikhiṃ sambuddhanti sambandho. Kilesakaddamānaṃ abhāvena anāvilaṃ. Nandībhavasaṅkhātāya balavasnehāya parisamantato khīṇattā nandībhavaparikkhīṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ loketi lokattayato tiṇṇaṃ uttiṇṇaṃ atikkantaṃ. Visattikanti visattikaṃ vuccati taṇhā, nittaṇhanti attho.

1. Recollecting his past wholesome kamma by means of the knowledge of recollection of past lives, he became filled with joy and, proclaiming the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning: 'Like the moon, immaculate and pure…' Herein, 'like the moon, immaculate and pure': just as the moon is free from such blemishes of defilement as clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu, so the Buddha is immaculate (vimala) because he has abandoned the fifteen hundred blemishes of defilement, and pure (suddha) and clear (pasanna) because he is without defilements. The connection is with Sikhī the Sambuddha. Because of the absence of the mud of defilements, he is 'untroubled' (anāvila). Because the strong attachment called 'delight in existence' has been completely destroyed, he is 'one whose delight in existence is exhausted' (nandībhavaparikkhīṇa). 'Having crossed the three worlds' means he has crossed over, gone beyond the triple world. 'Unattached' (visattika): 'attachment' is a term for craving (taṇhā); the meaning is 'without craving'.

2. Nibbāpayantaṃ janatanti dhammavassaṃ vassanto janataṃ janasamūhaṃ kilesapariḷāhābhāvena nibbāpayantaṃ vūpasamentaṃ. Sayaṃ saṃsārato tiṇṇaṃ, sabbasatte saṃsārato tārayantaṃ atikkamentaṃ catunnaṃ saccānaṃ munanato jānanato muniṃ sikhiṃ sambuddhanti sambandho. Vanasmiṃ jhāyamānanti ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇūpanijjhānehi jhāyantaṃ cintentaṃ cittena bhāventaṃ vanamajjheti attho. Ekaggaṃ [V 2.0152] ekaggacittaṃ susamāhitaṃ suṭṭhu ārammaṇe āhitaṃ ṭhapitacittaṃ sikhiṃ muniṃ disvāti sambandho.

2. “Extinguishing the populace” means: raining down the rain of the Dhamma, he extinguishes, he pacifies the populace, the multitude of people, by the absence of the fever of defilements. “Himself crossed over from saṃsāra, he ferries all beings across saṃsāra,” leading them beyond it. Because he comprehends, because he knows the four truths, he is a “sage” (muni). The connection is with Sikhī the Sambuddha. “Meditating in the forest” means: meditating by means of absorption upon the object and absorption upon the characteristics, thinking, developing with the mind in the midst of the forest, is the meaning. “One-pointed” (ekaggaṃ) means with a one-pointed mind. “Well-concentrated” (susamāhitaṃ) means with the mind well-placed, established on its object. The connection is: “having seen the sage Sikhī.”

3. Bandhujīvakapupphānīti bandhūnaṃ ñātīnaṃ jīvakaṃ jīvitanissayaṃ hadayamaṃsalohitaṃ bandhujīvakaṃ hadayamaṃsalohitasamānavaṇṇaṃ pupphaṃ bandhujīvakapupphaṃ gahetvā sikhino lokabandhuno pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

3. “Bandhujīvaka flowers”: a bandhujīvaka is that which is life-giving (jīvaka) to relatives (bandhu), a support for life, the heart, flesh, and blood; a bandhujīvaka flower is a flower of the same color as heart, flesh, and blood. The meaning is: “Taking the bandhujīvaka flower, I worshipped Sikhī, the kinsman of the world.” The rest has an obvious meaning.

Bandhujīvakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bandhujīvaka is completed.

2. Tambapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tambapupphiya

Parakammāyane [M 2.0163][P 0.0447] yuttotiādikaṃ āyasmato tambapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi āyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto piyadassissa bhagavato kāle kenaci pure katena akusalakammena duggatakule nibbatto vuddhippatto paresaṃ kammaṃ katvā bhatiyā jīvikaṃ kappesi. So evaṃ dukkhena vasanto paresaṃ aparādhaṃ katvā maraṇabhayena palāyitvā vanaṃ pāvisi. Tattha gataṭṭhāne pāṭalibodhiṃ disvā vanditvā sammajjitvā ekasmiṃ rukkhe tambavaṇṇaṃ pupphaṃ disvā taṃ sabbaṃ kaṇṇike ocinitvā bodhipūjaṃ akāsi. Tattha cittaṃ pasādetvā vanditvā pallaṅkamābhujitvā nisīdi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe te manussā padānupadikaṃ anubandhitvā tattha agamaṃsu. So te disvā bodhiṃ āvajjentova palāyitvā bhayānake gīriduggapapāte patitvā mari.

“Engaged in the work of others,” and so on, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Tambapupphiya. This venerable one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a destitute family during the time of the Blessed One Piyadassī due to some unwholesome kamma he had done previously. Having come of age, he earned his living by working for others for wages. Living thus in hardship, having committed an offense against others, he fled in fear of death and entered the forest. There, at the place he had gone, seeing a Pāṭali Bodhi tree, he paid homage to it and swept the area. Seeing a copper-colored flower on a tree, he gathered all its blossoms from the stalks and made an offering to the Bodhi tree. Having clarified his mind there, he paid homage and sat down with his legs crossed. At that moment, those people, following his tracks, arrived there. Seeing them, while still reflecting on the Bodhi tree, he fled and, falling into a frightening, impassable mountain precipice, he died.

7. So bodhipūjāya anussaritattā teneva pītisomanassena tāvatiṃsādīsu upapanno cha kāmāvacarasampattiṃ anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavattiādisampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne kule nibbatto vuddhippatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento parakammāyane yuttotiādimāha. Tattha paresaṃ kammāni parakammāni, parakammānaṃ āyane karaṇe vāhane dhāraṇe yutto yojito ahosinti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

7. Because he recollected his offering to the Bodhi tree, with that very rapture and mental joy he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and other such realms. After experiencing the good fortune of the six sense-sphere heavens and, among humans, the good fortune of a wheel-turning monarch and so on, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a family endowed with wealth. Having come of age, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, and with a confident mind, he went forth. Not long afterwards he became an arahant. Remembering his own past kamma, he became filled with mental joy and, in order to reveal the story of his past deeds, he spoke the verses beginning with, “Engaged in the work of others.” Herein, ‘parakammāni’ means the work of others. ‘Parakammāyane yutto’ means: he was engaged in the undertaking, doing, carrying on, and maintaining of the work of others. This is the meaning. The rest is evident.

Tambapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tambapupphiya is completed.

3. Vīthisammajjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vīthisammajjaka

Udentaṃ [V 2.0153] sataraṃsiṃ vātiādikaṃ āyasmato vīthisammajjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu jātisatesu katapuññasañcayo sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto nagaravāsīhi saddhiṃ vīthiṃ sajjetvā nīyamānaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vīthiṃ samaṃ katvā dhajaṃ tattha ussāpesi.

“Like the rising hundred-rayed one,” and so on, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Vīthisammajjaka. This venerable one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit over many hundreds of births, was born in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. While living the household life, together with the townspeople, he prepared a street, and seeing the Blessed One being led along it, with a confident mind he leveled the street and raised a banner there.

15. So [M 2.0164] teneva puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho bahumānahadayo pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ anussaranto paccakkhato jānitvā pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento udentaṃ sataraṃsiṃ vātiādimāha. Tattha [P 0.0448] udentaṃ uggacchantaṃ sataraṃsiṃ satapabhaṃ. Sataraṃsīti desanāsīsamattaṃ, anekasatasahassapabhaṃ sūriyaṃ ivāti attho. Pītaraṃsiṃva bhāṇumanti pītaraṃsiṃ saṃkucitapabhaṃ bhāṇumaṃ pabhāvantaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ iva sambuddhaṃ disvāti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

15. Through that same merit, wandering through the round of rebirths among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of good fortune, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a certain family. Having reached the age of discretion, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, gained faith, and with a heart full of respect, went forth. Having received the higher ordination, not long afterwards he became an arahant. Remembering his own past kamma and knowing it directly, in order to reveal the story of his past deeds, he spoke the verses beginning with, “Like the rising hundred-rayed one.” Herein, ‘udentaṃ’ means rising; ‘sataraṃsiṃ’ means hundred-rayed, having a hundred splendors. “Hundred-rayed” is just the heading of the discourse; the meaning is “like the sun with its many hundreds of thousands of rays.” The phrase ‘pītaraṃsiṃva bhāṇumaṃ’ means: having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One who was like the radiant moon-disk, with its yellow rays and soft splendor. The rest is easy to understand.

Vīthisammajjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vīthisammajjaka is completed.

4. Kakkārupupphapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kakkārupupphapūjaka

Devaputto ahaṃ santotiādikaṃ āyasmato kakkārupupphapūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave katapuññasañcayo sikhissa bhagavato kāle bhummaṭṭhakadevaputto hutvā nibbatto sikhiṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ disvā dibbakakkārupupphaṃ gahetvā pūjesi.

“I, being a devaputta,” and so on, is the Apadāna of the Venerable Kakkārupupphapūjaka. This venerable one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated a store of merit in various existences, was reborn as a terrestrial devaputta during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Seeing the Perfectly Enlightened One Sikhī, he took a divine kakkāru flower and made an offering.

21. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ekatiṃsakappabbhantare ubhayasukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya satthari pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ paccakkhato ñatvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento devaputto ahaṃ santotiādimāha. Tattha dibbanti kīḷanti pañcahi dibbehi kāmaguṇehīti devā, devānaṃ putto, devo eva vā putto devaputto, ahaṃ devaputto [V 2.0154] santo vijjamāno dibbaṃ kakkārupupphaṃ paggayha pakārena, gahetvā sikhissa bhagavato abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

21. Through that merit, wandering through the round of rebirths among devas and humans for an interval of thirty-one aeons and experiencing both kinds of happiness, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a good family in Sāvatthī. Having come of age and gained confidence in the Teacher, he went forth, and not long afterwards he became an arahant. Directly knowing his own past kamma, he became filled with mental joy and, in order to reveal the story of his past deeds, he spoke the verses beginning with, “I, being a devaputta.” Herein, devas are so called because they sport and play with the five divine cords of sensual pleasure. A ‘devaputta’ is a son of the devas, or a son who is himself a deva. The meaning is: “I, being a devaputta, took a divine kakkāru flower and, holding it up in a special way, placed it upon the Blessed One Sikhī as an offering.” The rest has a plain meaning.

Kakkārupupphapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kakkārupupphapūjaka is concluded.

5. Mandāravapupphapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mandāravapupphapūjaka

Devaputto [M 2.0165] ahaṃ santotiādikaṃ āyasmato mandāravapupphapūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle bhummaṭṭhakadevaputto hutvā nibbatto sikhiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso dibbamandāravapupphehi pūjesi.

"Being a son of a deva," and so on—this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Mandāravapupphapūjaka Thera. This elder too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as conditions conducive to liberation. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, he was reborn as a deva of the earth realm. Seeing the Blessed One Sikhī, with a mind full of faith, he worshipped Him with divine mandārava flowers.

25. So tena puññenātiādikaṃ sabbaṃ anantarattherassa apadānavaṇṇanāya vuttanayeneva veditabbanti.

25. "So tena puññenāti," and so forth—everything should be understood in the same way as described in the commentary on the Apadāna of the immediately preceding elder.

Mandāravapupphapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mandāravapupphapūjaka is complete.

6. Kadambapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kadambapupphiya

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato kadambapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sammāsambuddhasuññe loke ekasmiṃ [P 0.0449] kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ vasanto tattha ādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantasamīpe kukkuṭe nāma pabbate assamaṃ katvā vihāsi. So tattha satta paccekabuddhe disvā pasannamānaso pupphitaṃ kadambapupphaṃ ocinitvā te paccekabuddhe pūjesi. Tepi “icchitaṃ patthita”ntiādinā anumodanaṃ akaṃsu.

"Not far from the Himalayas," and so on—this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Kadambapupphiya Thera. This venerable one too, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Conquerors, accumulated merits in various existences conducive to emancipation. In a world devoid of a Sammāsambuddha, he was born into a certain family. Growing up and seeing the drawbacks of household life, he abandoned it and took up the ascetic life. Dwelling near the Himalayas on a mountain named Kukkuṭa, he made a hermitage and lived there. There, seeing seven Paccekabuddhas, with a mind full of faith, he gathered blooming kadamba flowers and offered them to those Paccekabuddhas. They, in turn, gave their approval, saying, "May your wishes be fulfilled."

30. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento [V 2.0155] himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Taṃ vuttatthameva. Kukkuṭo nāma pabbatoti tassa ubhosu passesu kukkuṭacūḷākārena pabbatakūṭānaṃ vijjamānattā kukkuṭoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Pakārena tiro hutvā patiṭṭhahatīti pabbato. Tamhi pabbatapādamhīti tasmiṃ pabbatasamīpe. Satta buddhā vasantīti satta paccekabuddhā tasmiṃ kukkuṭapabbatapāde paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasantīti attho.

30. By that merit, wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of prosperity, in this Buddha's dispensation, he was born in a respectable family in Sāvatthī. Growing up, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, acquired faith, and went forth. Before long, he became an arahant. Recalling his past deeds and filled with joy, he revealed his former conduct in this Apadāna, beginning with "Not far from the Himalayas." The meaning is as stated. It is called Kukkuṭa Mountain because peaks resembling a rooster's crest exist on both sides of it. It is called a mountain (pabbato) because it stands firmly, as if hidden from view. "At the foot of that mountain" means near that mountain. "Seven Buddhas dwelled there" means seven Paccekabuddhas lived in a leaf-hut at the foot of Kukkuṭa Mountain.

31. Dīparājaṃva [M 2.0166] uggatanti dīpānaṃ rājā dīparājā, sabbesaṃ dīpānaṃ jalamānānaṃ tārakānaṃ rājā candoti attho. Atha vā sabbesu jambudīpapubbavidehaaparagoyānauttarakurusaṅkhātesu catūsu dīpesu dvisahassaparittadīpesu ca rājā ālokapharaṇato cando dīparājāti vuccati, taṃ nabhe uggataṃ candaṃ iva pupphitaṃ phullitaṃ kadambarukkhaṃ disvā tato pupphaṃ ocinitvā ubhohi hatthehi paggayha pakārena gahetvā satta paccekabuddhe samokiriṃ suṭṭhu okiriṃ, ādarena pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

31. "Like the rising of the king of lights"—the moon is the king of lights, meaning the king of all shining stars. Alternatively, the moon is called the king of continents (dīpa) because it spreads light over all four continents—Jambudīpa, Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, and Uttarakuru—and the two thousand minor islands. Seeing the kadamba tree in full bloom like the moon risen in the sky, he plucked its flowers, raised them with both hands, took them with care, and scattered them over the seven Paccekabuddhas, scattering them well, meaning he worshipped them with reverence. The rest is of clear meaning.

Kadambapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kadambapupphiya is complete.

7. Tiṇasūlakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tiṇasūlaka

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato tiṇasūlakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimajinavaresu katapuññasambhāro uppannuppannabhave kusalāni upacinanto sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tattha dosaṃ disvā taṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vasanto himavantasamīpe bhūtagaṇe nāma pabbate vasantaṃ ekataṃ vivekamanubrūhantaṃ sikhiṃ sambuddhaṃ disvā pasannamānaso tiṇasūlapupphaṃ gahetvā pādamūle pūjesi. Buddhopi tassa anumodanaṃ akāsi.

"Not far from the Himalayas," and so on—this is the Apadāna of the Venerable Tiṇasūlaka Thera. This elder, having accumulated a wealth of merit under former Conquerors, accumulating skillful deeds in each and every existence, was born in a family home during the time of the Blessed Sikhī. Establishing a household, seeing the faults in it, and abandoning it, he went forth into the ascetic life. While dwelling near the Himalayas, on a mountain named Bhūtagaṇa, he saw the Fully Enlightened One Sikhī cultivating solitude and, with a mind full of faith, took a tiṇasūla flower and honored him at his feet. The Buddha also approved of his offering.

35. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampanne [P 0.0450] ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya sāsane pasanno pabbajitvā upanissayasampannattā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassappatto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Bhūtagaṇo nāma pabbatoti bhūtagaṇānaṃ devayakkhasamūhānaṃ āvāsabhūtattā bhavanasadisattā avirūḷhabhāvena pavattattā [V 2.0156] ca bhūtagaṇo nāma pabbato, tasmiṃ eko adutiyo jino jitamāro buddho vasate dibbabrahmaariyairiyāpathavihārehi viharatīti attho.

35. Through that merit, wandering among gods and humans, experiencing both kinds of prosperity, in this Buddha-era, he was born in Sāvatthī, in a family endowed with wealth. Growing up and becoming devoted to the Teaching, he went forth, and due to his well-established support, soon attained Arahantship. Recollecting his former deeds and filled with joy, he declared the story of his former conduct, beginning with "Not far from the Himalayas..." The mountain called Bhūtagaṇa is so named due to its being a dwelling place for hosts of spirits and yakkhas, its resemblance to a dwelling, and its undisturbed nature due to lack of overgrowth. Therein dwells the Jina, the Buddha, the One without a second, the conqueror of Māra, living in divine, brahmā-like, and noble deportment.

36. Ekūnasatasahassaṃ[M 2.0167], kappaṃ na vinipātikoti tena tiṇasūlapupphapūjākaraṇaphalena nirantaraṃ ekūnasatasahassakappānaṃ avinipātako caturāpāyavinimutto saggasampattibhavameva upapannoti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

36. "For ninety-nine thousand aeons, I did not fall away." Due to the merit of offering the tiṇasūla flower, he was continuously free from the four woeful states for ninety-nine thousand aeons, and was only reborn in states of heavenly attainment. The rest is easily understood.

Tiṇasūlakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tiṇasūlaka is complete.

8. Nāgapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nāgapupphiya

Suvaccho nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato nāgapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimajinanisabhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarabhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto vuddhippatto vedattayādīsu sakasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā tattha sāraṃ adisvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānasamāpattisukhena vītināmesi. Tasmiṃ samaye padumuttaro bhagavā tassānukampāya tattha agamāsi. So tāpaso taṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā lakkhaṇasatthesu chekattā bhagavato lakkhaṇarūpasampattiyā pasanno vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Ākāsato anotiṇṇattā pūjāsakkāre akateyeva ākāseneva pakkāmi. Atha so tāpaso sasisso nāgapupphaṃ ocinitvā tena pupphena bhagavato gatadisābhāgamaggaṃ pūjesi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Nāgapupphiya Thera, beginning with “Suvaccho nāma nāmena,” is as follows. This elder, too, having established his aspiration in the presence of previous chief Jinas, accumulating in various existences merits that would serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having come of age and attained proficiency in his own crafts, including the three Vedas, but not seeing any essence in them, he entered the Himālaya. Having gone forth into the ascetic life, he passed his time in the bliss of the jhānas and attainments. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara, out of compassion for him, went there. Seeing the Blessed One, the ascetic, being an expert in the science of marks, was inspired by the perfection of the Blessed One's marks and form. He paid homage and stood with his hands raised in reverence. As the Blessed One had not descended from the sky, he departed by way of the sky itself before any offerings or honors were made. Then that ascetic, together with his disciple, gathered nāga flowers and with those flowers honored the path in the direction the Blessed One had gone.

39. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavanto sabbattha pūjito imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya saddhāsampanno pabbajitvā vattapaṭipattiyā sāsanaṃ sobhayamāno nacirasseva arahā hutvā “kena nu kho kusalakammena mayā ayaṃ lokuttarasampatti laddhā”ti atītakammaṃ saranto pubbakammaṃ paccakkhato ñatvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento suvaccho nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Tattha vacchagotte jātattā vaccho, sundaro ca so vaccho ceti suvaccho. Nāmena suvaccho nāma brāhmaṇo mantapāragū vedattayādisakalamantasatthe [P 0.0451] koṭippattoti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

39. As a result of that merit, he wandered among gods and humans, experiencing both kinds of success and being honored everywhere. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a family home in Sāvatthī. Having come of age, endowed with faith, he went forth. Adorning the Dispensation by his practice of the duties, he soon became an arahant. Reflecting, “By what wholesome kamma have I obtained this supramundane attainment?” he recollected his past kamma. Having known his former deed directly, he became glad at heart and, to reveal the apadāna of his past conduct, he uttered the verses beginning: “By name I was Suvaccha.” Herein, because he was born in the Vaccha clan, he was Vaccha; and since that Vaccha was handsome, he was Suvaccha. “By name I was Suvaccha, a brahmin, a master of mantras” means he had reached the pinnacle in the entire science of mantras, including the three Vedas. The rest has a plain meaning in accordance with the method stated below.

Nāgapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of Nāgapupphiya Thera is concluded.

9. Punnāgapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Punnāgapupphiya Thera

Kānanaṃ [M 2.0168][V 2.0157] vanamogayhātiādikaṃ āyasmato punnāgapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto phussassa bhagavato kāle nesādakule nibbatto mahāvanaṃ paviṭṭho tattha supupphitapunnāgapupphaṃ disvā hetusampannattā buddhārammaṇapītivasena bhagavantaṃ saritvā taṃ pupphaṃ saha kaṇṇikāhi ocinitvā vālukāhi cetiyaṃ katvā pūjesi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Punnāgapupphiya Thera, beginning with “Kānanaṃ vanamogayha,” is as follows. This elder, too, having established his aspiration in the presence of previous excellent Jinas, accumulating in various existences merits that would serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a hunter's family in the time of the Blessed One Phussa. Having entered a great forest, he saw a fully blossomed punnāga flower. Being endowed with the right conditions, with rapture that had the Buddha as its object, he recollected the Blessed One. He picked that flower together with its pericarp, made a cetiya out of sand, and made an offering.

46. So tena puññena dvenavutikappe nirantaraṃ devamanussasampattiyoyeva anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampanne kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya pubbavāsanābalena sāsane pasanno pabbajitvā vāyamanto nacirasseva arahā hutvā pubbe katakusalaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento kānanaṃ vanamogayhātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttattā uttānatthamevāti.

46. As a result of that merit, for ninety-two aeons he continuously experienced only the good fortune of gods and humans. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a wealthy family in Sāvatthī. Having come of age, inspired by the power of his past dispositions, he gained faith in the Dispensation and went forth. Striving, he soon became an arahant. Recollecting his past wholesome kamma, he became glad at heart and, to reveal the apadāna of his past conduct, he uttered the verses beginning: “Having plunged into the grove, the wood…” All of this has a plain meaning in accordance with what has been stated below.

Punnāgapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of Punnāgapupphiya Thera is concluded.

10. Kumudadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Kumudadāyaka Thera

Himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato kumudadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle himavantassa āsanne mahante jātassare kukuttho nāma pakkhī hutvā nibbatto kenaci akusalena pakkhī samānopi pubbe katasambhārena buddhisampanno puññāpuññesu cheko sīlavā pāṇagocarato paṭivirato ahosi. Tasmiṃ samaye padumuttaro bhagavā ākāsenāgantvā tassa samīpe caṅkamati. Atha so sakuṇo bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannacitto kumudapupphaṃ ḍaṃsitvā bhagavato pādamūle pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa somanassuppādanatthaṃ paṭiggahetvā anumodanamakāsi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Kumudadāyaka Thera, beginning with “Not far from the Himālaya,” is as follows. This elder, too, having established his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating in many existences merits that would serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara as a bird named Kukuttha in a large natural lake near the Himālaya. Although he was a bird because of some unwholesome kamma, due to provisions made in the past he was endowed with intelligence, skilled in distinguishing merit from demerit, virtuous, and abstained from preying on living beings. At that time, the Blessed One Padumuttara came through the sky and was practicing walking meditation near him. Then that bird, seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind, took a kumuda flower in its beak and offered it at the Blessed One's feet. In order to give rise to gladness in him, the Blessed One accepted it and expressed his appreciation.

51. So [M 2.0169] tena puññena devamanussesu ubhayasampattisukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ aññatarasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya mahaddhano mahābhogo ratanattaye pasanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ paccakkhato ñatvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Padumuppalasañchannoti [P 0.0452][V 2.0158] ettha satapattehi sampuṇṇo setapadumo ca tīṇi nīlarattasetuppalāni ca padumuppalāni tehi sañchanno gahanībhūto sampuṇṇo mahājātassaro ahūti sambandho. Puṇḍarīkasamotthaṭoti puṇḍarīkehi rattapadumehi otthaṭo sampuṇṇoti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

51. As a result of that merit, having experienced the happiness of both divine and human success, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in a certain family in Sāvatthī. Having come of age, he was very wealthy and affluent. Having gained confidence in the Three Jewels and heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he acquired faith, went forth, and soon became an arahant. Having known his past kamma directly, he became glad at heart and, to reveal the apadāna of his past conduct, he uttered the verses beginning: “Not far from the Himālaya…” Herein, regarding “covered with lotuses and water lilies”: the connection is that the great natural lake was covered, dense, and filled with these—hundred-petaled white lotuses and the three kinds of water lilies: blue, red, and white. Regarding “strewn with puṇḍarīka lotuses”: this means it was strewn and filled with red lotuses, which are puṇḍarīkas. The rest is easily understood.

Kumudadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of Kumudadāyaka Thera is concluded.

Soḷasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Sixteenth Chapter is concluded.

17. Supāricariyavaggo

17. The Supāricariya Chapter

1. Supāricariyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Supāricariya Thera

Padumo [V 2.0159] nāma nāmenātiādikaṃ āyasmato supāricariyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimamunipuṅgavesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle yakkhayoniyaṃ nibbatto himavati yakkhasamāgamaṃ gato bhagavato devayakkhagandhabbanāgānaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso ubho hatthe ābhujitvā apphoṭesi namassi ca. So tena puññena tato cuto upari devaloke uppanno tattha dibbasukhaṃ anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavatiādisampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ gahapatikule nibbatto aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo ratanattaye pasanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saddhājāto pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Supāricariyatthera begins with the words, 'My name was Paduma…' This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous foremost sages and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn as a yakkha in the Himalayas during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having gone to an assembly of yakkhas, he heard the Blessed One's discourse on the Dhamma to devas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and nāgas. With a mind full of faith, he clapped his hands and paid homage. By that merit, after passing away from there, he was reborn in a higher deva world, where he experienced divine bliss. Then, among humans, he experienced the fortune of a wheel-turning monarch and other kinds of prosperity. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a householder family in Sāvatthī, prosperous, wealthy, and affluent. With confidence in the Three Jewels, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, and with faith arisen, he went forth. Not long afterwards, he attained arahantship.

1. So ekadivasaṃ attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumo nāma nāmenātiādimāha. Tattha [M 2.0170] padumoti yassa pādanikkhepasamaye pathaviṃ bhinditvā padumaṃ uggantvā pādatalaṃ sampaṭicchati, tena saññāṇena so bhagavā padumoti saṅkhaṃ gato, idha padumuttaro bhagavā adhippeto. So bhagavā pavanā vasanavihārā abhinikkhamma vanamajjhaṃ pavisitvā dhammaṃ desetīti sambandho.

1. One day, recalling his past kamma and becoming joyful, he declared the apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with the words, 'My name was Paduma…' Herein, 'Paduma' is so called because when he took a step, a lotus, having split the earth, would rise up and receive the sole of his foot. By that sign, that Blessed One came to be known as 'Paduma.' Here, the Blessed One Padumuttara is intended. The connection is this: 'That Blessed One, having gone forth from his dwelling in the forest, entered the middle of the forest and taught the Dhamma.'

Yakkhānaṃ samayoti devānaṃ samāgamo āsi ahosīti attho. Ajjhāpekkhiṃsu tāvadeti tasmiṃ desanākāle adhiapekkhiṃsu, visesena passanasīlā ahesunti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

'An assembly of yakkhas' means there was a gathering of devas. 'They were watching attentively' means that at the time of the discourse they were looking on; the meaning is that they were especially disposed to seeing. The rest is clear.

Supāricariyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Supāricariya is complete.

2. Kaṇaverapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇaverapupphiya

Siddhattho [V 2.0160] nāma bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato kaṇaverapupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle suddakule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya [P 0.0453] rañño antepurapālako ahosi. Tasmiṃ samaye siddhattho bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto rājavīthiṃ paṭipajji. Atha so antepurapālako caramānaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso hutvā kaṇaverapupphena bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. So tena puññena sugatisampattiyoyeva anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbattitvā vuddhippatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Kaṇaverapupphiyatthera begins with the words, 'The Blessed One named Siddhattha…' This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, was reborn in a śūdra family during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha. Having reached maturity, he became a guard of the king's inner quarters. At that time, the Blessed One Siddhattha, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, was walking along the royal road. Then that palace guard, seeing the Blessed One walking by, with a mind full of faith honored the Blessed One with a kaṇavera flower and stood paying homage.
