By that merit, he experienced only fortunate rebirths. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a certain family, and having reached maturity, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, gained faith, went forth, and not long afterwards became an arahant.

7. So pattaaggaphalo pubbe katakusalaṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento siddhattho nāma bhagavātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttattā uttānatthamevāti.

7. He, having reached the ultimate fruit, recalled the wholesome deeds he had done in the past, and becoming joyful, declared the apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with the words, 'The Blessed One named Siddhattha…' Since all this has been explained before, its meaning is plain.

Kaṇaverapupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇaverapupphiya is complete.

3. Khajjakadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Khajjakadāyaka

Tissassa kho bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato khajjakadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle [M 2.0171] suddakule nibbatto bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso ambajambuādimanekaṃ madhuraphalāphalaṃ nāḷikeraṃ pūvakhajjakañca adāsi. Bhagavā tassa pasādavaḍḍhanatthāya passantasseva paribhuñji. So tena puññena sugatisampattiyoyeva anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sañjātasaddho pasādabahumāno pabbajitvā vattapaṭipattiyā sāsanaṃ sobhento sīlālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Khajjakadāyakatthera begins with the words, 'Of the Blessed One Tissa…' This one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Jinas and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a śūdra family during the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Seeing the Blessed One, with a mind full of faith, he gave many kinds of sweet fruits such as mangoes and rose-apples, as well as coconuts and sweetmeats. In order to increase his faith, the Blessed One partook of them while he was looking on. By that merit, having experienced only the good fortune of happy destinations, in this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in a good family home in Sāvatthī. Having reached discernment, he heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, and with faith and great reverence arisen, he went forth. Adorning the Dispensation by his practice of the observances, embellished with the ornament of virtue, he not long afterwards attained arahantship.

13. So pubbakammaṃ saranto “pubbe mayā sukhette kusalaṃ kataṃ sundara”nti somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento tissassa kho bhagavatotiādimāha. Tattha tissopi bhavasampattiyo dadamāno jātoti mātāpitūhi katanāmavasena tisso. Atha vā tīhi [V 2.0161] saraṇagamanehi assāsento ovadanto hetusampannapuggale saggamokkhadvaye patiṭṭhāpento buddho jātoti tisso. Samāpattiguṇādīhi bhagehi yuttoti bhagavā, tassa tissassa bhagavato pubbe ahaṃ phalaṃ adāsinti sambandho. Nāḷikerañca pādāsinti nāḷikākārena pavattaṃ phalaṃ nāḷikeraṃ, tañca phalaṃ adāsinti attho. Khajjakaṃ abhisammatanti khāditabbaṃ khajjakaṃ abhi visesena madhusakkarādīhi sammissaṃ [P 0.0454] katvā nipphāditaṃ sundaraṃ madhuranti sammataṃ ñātaṃ abhisammataṃ khajjakañca adāsinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

13. Recalling his past kamma and becoming joyful, thinking, 'In the past I did a beautiful wholesome deed in a good field,' he declared the apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with the words, 'Of the Blessed One Tissa…' Herein, he was named Tissa by his parents because he was born granting the blessings of existence. Or, he is Tissa because as a Buddha he was born to console and instruct by means of the three refuges, establishing in the twofold way of heaven and liberation those persons who are endowed with the right conditions. 'Bhagavā' is one who is endowed with the shares (bhāga) of the qualities of the attainments and so on. The connection is: 'Formerly I gave a fruit to that Blessed One, Tissa.' 'And I gave a coconut' means: a coconut (nāḷikera) is a fruit that has the shape of a tube (nāḷikā); the meaning is that he gave that fruit. 'An approved sweetmeat' means: a sweetmeat (khajjaka) is something to be eaten; 'approved' (abhisammata) means it is considered and known to be excellent and sweet, having been specially prepared by mixing it with honey, sugar, and so on; the meaning is that he also gave this sweetmeat. The rest is easy to understand.

Khajjakadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Khajjakadāyaka is complete.

4. Desapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Desapūjaka

Atthadassī tu bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato desapūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya saddho pasanno buddhamāmako dhammamāmako saṅghamāmako ahosi. Tadā atthadassī bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto cando viya sūriyo viya ca ākāsena gacchati. So upāsako bhagavato gatadisābhāgaṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjento añjaliṃ paggayha namassamāno aṭṭhāsi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Desapūjaka begins with the words, 'The Blessed One Atthadassī…' This elder, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī, he was born into a good family; having come of age, he was faithful and confident, devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. At that time, the Blessed One Atthadassī, surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, traveled through the sky like the moon and the sun. That lay follower, worshipping with perfumes and garlands the direction in which the Blessed One had gone, stood paying homage with his hands raised in reverential salutation.

18. So [M 2.0172] tena puññena devaloke nibbatto saggasampattiṃ anubhavitvā manussesu ca manussasampattiṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhippatto upabhogaparibhogasampanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso gharāvāse anallīno pabbajitvā vattasampanno nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento atthadassī tu bhagavātiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Anilañjaseti “maggo pantho patho pajjo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyana”nti (cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 101) pariyāyassa vuttattā anilassa vātassa añjasaṃ gamanamaggoti anilañjasaṃ, tasmiṃ anilañjase, ākāseti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

18. Through that merit, he was reborn in the deva world and experienced celestial bliss, and among humans he experienced human prosperity. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a certain family, attained maturity, and was endowed with wealth for use and enjoyment. Hearing the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma, with a confident mind, and not clinging to the household life, he went forth. Accomplished in his duties, he soon attained arahantship. Recollecting his past deeds and filled with joy, he revealed his former conduct in the Apadāna, beginning with 'The Blessed One Atthadassī…' The meaning of that is as has been stated. Anilañjase: since it is said in the Cūḷaniddesa (Pārāyanatthutigāthāniddesa 101) that 'magga, pantha, patho, pajjo, añjasaṃ, vaṭumāyana' are synonyms for path, anilañjasa means the direct path of the wind; thus anilañjase means 'in the path of the wind,' that is, 'in space.' The rest is clear in meaning.

Desapūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Desapūjaka is complete.

5. Kaṇikārachattiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇikārachattiya

Vessabhū [V 2.0162] nāma sambuddhotiādikaṃ āyasmato kaṇikārachattiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vessabhussa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto saddhāsampanno ahosi. Tasmiṃ samaye vessabhū bhagavā vivekakāmo mahāvanaṃ pavisitvā nisīdi. Atha sopi upāsako kenacideva karaṇīyena tattha gantvā bhagavantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ viya jalamānaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kaṇikārapupphaṃ ocinitvā chattaṃ katvā bhagavato nisinnaṭṭhāne vitānaṃ katvā pūjesi, taṃ bhagavato ānubhāvena sattāhaṃ amilātaṃ hutvā tatheva aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavāpi phalasamāpattiṃ nirodhasamāpattiñca samāpajjitvā vihāsi[P 0.0455], so taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā somanassajāto bhagavantaṃ vanditvā añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā samāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā vihārameva agamāsi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Kaṇikārachattiya begins with the words, 'A Sambuddha named Vessabhū…' This elder, too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, he was born into a good family, reached maturity, and became endowed with faith. At that time, the Blessed One Vessabhū, desiring seclusion, entered a great forest and sat down. Then this lay follower, having gone there for some reason, saw the Blessed One seated, blazing like a mass of fire. With a confident mind, he gathered kaṇikāra flowers, made a canopy of them, and paid homage by placing it as a covering above the Blessed One's seat. By the spiritual power of the Blessed One, it remained unfaded for seven days, just as it was. The Blessed One entered and abided in the attainment of fruition and the attainment of cessation. Seeing this marvel, the lay follower was filled with joy, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood with his hands raised in reverential salutation. The Blessed One, emerging from the attainment, went to the monastery.

23. So tena puññena devamanussesu sampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya saddhāsampanno satthu [M 2.0173] dhammadesanaṃ sutvā gharāvāse anallīno pabbajitvā vattapaṭipattiyā jinasāsanaṃ sobhento nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento vessabhū nāma sambuddhotiādimāha. Tattha vessabhūti vesse vessajane bhunāti abhibhavatīti vessabhū. Atha vā vesse pañcavidhamāre abhibhunāti ajjhottharatīti vessabhū. Sāmaṃyeva bujjhitā saccānīti sambuddho, nāmena vessabhū nāma sambuddhoti attho. Divāvihārāya munīti dibbati pakāseti taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ pākaṭaṃ karotīti divā. Sūriyuggamanato paṭṭhāya yāva atthaṅgamo, tāva paricchinnakālo, viharaṇaṃ catūhi iriyāpathehi pavattanaṃ vihāro, divāya vihāro divāvihāro, tassa divāvihārāya lokajeṭṭho narāsabho buddhamuni mahāvanaṃ ogāhitvā pavisitvāti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

23. Through that merit, having experienced prosperity among gods and humans, in this Buddha-era he was born into a good family in Sāvatthī. Growing up and becoming endowed with faith, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, and being unattached to the household life, he went forth. Adorning the Victor’s Dispensation with his practice and conduct, he soon became an arahant. Recollecting his past deeds and filled with joy, he declared the account of his past conduct, beginning with 'A Sambuddha named Vessabhū…' Herein, Vessabhū means 'he who overcomes the Vessa people' or 'he who completely overcomes the fivefold Māra.' Sambuddho means 'one who has awakened to the truths by himself.' Thus the meaning is 'the Sambuddha named Vessabhū.' As for 'divāvihārāya munī': 'divā' is so called because it shines and illuminates, making things manifest; it is the period of time from sunrise until sunset. 'Vihāra' is abiding, the carrying on in the four postures. The abiding of the day is 'divāvihāra'. The meaning of the full phrase is: 'for the daytime abiding, the world's chief, the bull among men, the Buddha-sage, plunged into and entered the great forest.' The rest is clear in meaning.

Kaṇikārachattiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇikārachattiya is complete.

6. Sappidāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sappidāyaka

Phusso [V 2.0163] nāmātha bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato sappidāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto phussassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto ahosi. Tadā bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto vīthiyaṃ caramāno tassa upāsakassa gehadvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Atha so upāsako bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso vanditvā pattapūraṃ sappitelaṃ adāsi, bhagavā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So teneva somanassena yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto tena puññena devaloke uppanno tattha dibbasukhaṃ anubhavitvā manussesu ca nibbatto uppannuppannabhave sappitelamadhuphāṇitādimadhurāhārasamaṅgī sukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhippatto saddho buddhisampanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā vattasampanno nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Elder Sappidāyaka, which begins, 'The Blessed One named Phussa…' He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating merits that serve as a basis for liberation over many existences, was reborn in a good family in the time of the Blessed One Phussa. Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, while walking along the street, arrived at the door of that lay follower’s house. Seeing the Blessed One, the lay follower, with a confident mind, paid homage and gave a bowlful of ghee and oil. The Blessed One gave his blessing and departed. With that very gladness, he lived for the rest of his life and, after passing away from there, was reborn in the deva world on account of that merit. There he experienced divine happiness. And being reborn among humans, in existence after existence he experienced happiness, endowed with sweet foods such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses. During the advent of this Buddha, he was reborn in a family in Sāvatthī. Having come of age, he was faithful and endowed with wisdom. Having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, with a confident mind he went forth. Accomplished in the observances, before long he became an arahant.

28. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā jātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento phusso nāmātha bhagavātiādimāha. Tattha phussoti [M 2.0174][P 0.0456] phussanakkhattayogena jātattā mātāpitūhi katanāmadheyyena phusso. Atha vā nibbānaṃ phusi passi sacchi akāsīti phusso. Atha vā samatiṃsapāramitāsattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhamme sakale ca tepiṭake pariyattidhamme phusi passi aññāsīti phusso. Bhaggavā bhagyavā yuttotiādipuññakoṭṭhāsasamaṅgitāya bhagavā. Āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahoti āhutino vuccanti pūjāsakkārā, tesaṃ āhutīnaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ arahatīti āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho. Mahājanaṃ nibbāpento vīro phusso nāma bhagavā vīthiyaṃ atha tadā gacchateti sambandho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

28. Then, recollecting his own past deeds, with gladness arisen, he declared the apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with, 'The Blessed One named Phussa…' Herein, 'Phussa' means that because he was born in conjunction with the Phussa constellation, his parents gave him the name Phussa. Alternatively, because he touched, saw, and directly realized Nibbāna, he was called Phussa. Or else, because he touched, saw, and understood the thirty perfections, the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, and all the scriptural teachings of the Tipiṭaka, he was called Phussa. 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) means he was endowed with a store of merit, being fortunate, accomplished, and so on. 'Receiver of offerings' (āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho) means that 'offerings' (āhutino) are honors and venerations, and he was worthy to receive such offerings; thus he is called the 'receiver of offerings.' The connection is: 'The hero Phussa, the Blessed One, calming the great populace, was then walking along the street.' The rest is evident.

Sappidāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the apadāna of the Elder Sappidāyaka is complete.

7. Yūthikāpupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Yūthikāpupphiya

Candabhāgānadītīretiādikaṃ āyasmato yūthikāpupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi āyasmā purimamunindesu katādhikāro anekesu ca jātisatesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto phussasseva bhagavato kāle suddakule nibbatto vuddhippatto candabhāgāya nadiyā tīre [V 2.0164] kenacideva karaṇīyena anusotaṃ caramāno phussaṃ bhagavantaṃ nhāyitukāmaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ viya jalamānaṃ disvā somanassajāto tattha jātaṃ yūthikāpupphaṃ ocinitvā bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa anumodanamakāsi.

The apadāna of the Elder Yūthikāpupphiya, which begins, 'On the bank of the river Candabhāgā…' This venerable one, too, having made his aspiration under previous Chief Sages and having accumulated merits that serve as a basis for liberation over many hundreds of births, was reborn in a commoner's family in the time of the Blessed One Phussa. Having come of age, while traveling downstream along the bank of the Candabhāgā river on some business, he saw the Blessed One Phussa, who wished to bathe, blazing like a mass of fire. With gladness arisen, he plucked a yūthikā flower that was growing there and honored the Blessed One with it. The Blessed One gave his approval.

33. So tattha tena puññakoṭṭhāsena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā vattapaṭipattiyā sāsanaṃ sobhento nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento candabhāgānadītīretiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

33. On account of that share of merit, wandering in saṃsāra among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of good fortune, during this Buddha's advent he was reborn in a good family. Having come of age and heard the Blessed One's discourse on the Dhamma, with a confident mind he went forth. Adorning the Dispensation with the practice of the observances, he became an arahant before long. Then, recalling his past kamma, with gladness arisen, he declared the apadāna of his past conduct, speaking the verses that begin, 'On the bank of the river Candabhāgā…' All of that has a plain meaning.

Yūthikāpupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the apadāna of the Elder Yūthikāpupphiya is complete.

8. Dussadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dussadāyaka

Tivarāyaṃ [M 2.0175] pure rammetiādikaṃ āyasmato dussadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle rājakule nibbatto vuddhippattakāle yuvarājabhāvaṃ patvā pākaṭo ekaṃ janapadaṃ labhitvā tatrādhipatibhūto sakalajanapadavāsino dānapiyavacanaatthacariyāsamānatthatāsaṅkhātehi catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgaṇhāti. Tasmiṃ samaye siddhattho bhagavā taṃ janapadaṃ sampāpuṇi. Atha so yuvarājā paṇṇākāraṃ [P 0.0457] labhitvā tattha sukhumavatthena bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. Bhagavā taṃ vatthaṃ hatthena parāmasitvā ākāsaṃ pakkhandi. Tampi vatthaṃ bhagavantameva anubandhi. Atha so yuvarājā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā atīva pasanno añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavato sampattasampattaṭṭhāne sabbe janā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutacittā añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhaṃsu. Bhagavā vihārameva agamāsi. Yuvarājā teneva kusalakammena tato cuto devaloke uppanno tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā manussesu cakkavattiādisampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā ratanattaye pasanno bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vāyamanto nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Elder Dussadāyaka begins, 'In the delightful city of Tivarā…' This venerable one, having made his aspiration under previous supreme Jinas, accumulated merits that serve as a basis for liberation in various existences. During the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born into a royal family. When he came of age, he attained the position of crown prince and became renowned. Having obtained a certain country and become its ruler, he supported all its inhabitants with the four bases of sympathy: generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. At that time, the Blessed One Siddhattha arrived in that country. The crown prince, having received a tribute, honored the Blessed One with a fine cloth. The Blessed One touched the cloth with his hand and ascended into the sky. That cloth followed the Blessed One. Seeing this marvel, the crown prince was exceedingly pleased and stood with his hands raised in reverence. In every place the Blessed One went, all the people, witnessing this wonder, were amazed and astonished and stood with their hands raised in reverence. The Blessed One then went to the monastery. On account of that wholesome kamma, the crown prince passed away from there and was reborn in the deva world, where he enjoyed divine fortune. After experiencing the fortunes of a wheel-turning monarch and other such fortunes in the human world, he was reborn in a wealthy family during this Buddha's advent. Having attained discernment, he established a household life and developed confidence in the Three Jewels. After hearing the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma and gaining faith, he went forth. Striving diligently, before long he became an arahant.

38. So [V 2.0165] ekadivasaṃ attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento tivarāyaṃ pure rammetiādimāha. Tattha tivaranāmake nagare ramaṇīye ahaṃ rājaputto hutvā siddhatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ vatthena pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

38. One day, recalling his own past kamma, with gladness arisen, he declared the apadāna of his past conduct, speaking the verses that begin, 'In the delightful city of Tivarā…' The meaning here is: 'In the delightful city named Tivarā, I, being a prince, honored the Blessed One Siddhattha with a cloth.' The rest is easily understood.

Dussadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the apadāna of the Elder Dussadāyaka is complete.

9. Samādapakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Samādapaka

Nagare bandhumatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato samādapakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhānaṃ santike katakusalasambhāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato [M 2.0176] kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā puññāni karonto vasamāno saddho pasanno bahū upāsake sannipātetvā gaṇajeṭṭhako hutvā “māḷakaṃ karissāmā”ti te sabbe samādapetvā ekaṃ māḷakaṃ samaṃ kāretvā paṇḍarapulinaṃ okiritvā bhagavato niyyādesi. So tena puññena devaloke uppanno cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavattiādisampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto bhagavati pasanno dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso saddhājāto pabbajitvā sīlasampanno vattasampanno nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

“In the city of Bandhumatī,” etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Samādapaka. This elder, having accumulated a wealth of merit in the presence of past Buddhas, and accumulating meritorious deeds that were a basis for liberation through many existences, was reborn in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity and established a household, he lived performing meritorious deeds, full of faith and confidence. Having gathered many lay followers and becoming their leader, he incited them all, saying, “Let us make a māḷaka.” He had a level māḷaka built, spread white sand over it, and dedicated it to the Blessed One. Through that merit, he was reborn in the deva world, enjoyed the good fortune of the six heavens of the sensual sphere, and in the human world, experienced the good fortune of a wheel-turning monarch and so on. In this Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn in a good family, attained discernment, and gained confidence in the Blessed One. Having heard the Dhamma, his mind became confident and faith arose in him. He went forth, became accomplished in virtue and the observances, and before long attained arahantship.

44. So aparabhāge attano katakusalaṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nagare bandhumatiyātiādimāha. Tattha bandhanti ñātigottādivasena ekasambandhā honti sakalanagaravāsinoti bandhū, bandhū etasmiṃ vijjantīti bandhumatī, tassā bandhumatiyā [P 0.0458] nāma nagare mahāpūgagaṇo upāsakasamūho ahosīti attho. Māḷaṃ kassāma saṅghassāti ettha māti gaṇhāti sampattasampattajanānaṃ cittanti māḷaṃ, atha vā sampattayatigaṇānaṃ cittassa vivekakaraṇe alanti māḷaṃ, māḷameva māḷakaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghassa phāsuvihāratthāya māḷakaṃ karissāmāti attho. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

44. Later, reflecting on his own meritorious deeds, he became joyful and, revealing the apadāna of his past conduct, began with “In the city of Bandhumatī.” Herein, `bandhū` are those who are bound together, being interconnected by way of kinship, clan, and so on; thus all the city-dwellers are relatives. `Bandhumatī` is so called because it possesses relatives. The meaning is that in that city named Bandhumatī, there was a great multitude, a group of lay followers. Regarding “Let us make a pavilion (`māḷaṃ`) for the Saṅgha”: `māḷaṃ` is so called because it captivates (`gaṇhāti`) the minds of the people who have arrived; or, it is sufficient (`alaṃ`) for bringing seclusion to the minds of the group of ascetics who have arrived. `Māḷaka` is the same as `māḷaṃ`. The meaning is: “We will make a pavilion for the comfortable abiding of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.” The rest is evident.

Samādapakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Samādapaka is finished.

10. Pañcaṅguliyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcaṅguliya

Tisso [V 2.0166] nāmāsi bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato pañcaṅguliyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāre tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto tissassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vibhavasampanno saddho pasanno vīthito vihāraṃ paṭipannaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā jātisumanādianekāni sugandhapupphāni candanādīni ca vilepanāni gāhāpetvā vihāraṃ gato pupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā vilepanehi bhagavato sarīre pañcaṅgulikaṃ katvā vanditvā pakkāmi.

“The Blessed One was named Tissa,” etc., is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Pañcaṅguliya. This one too, having made his resolve under past Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that served as a basis for liberation, was born into a certain family in the time of the Blessed One Tissa. Having reached maturity and established a household, he became prosperous, faithful, and confident. Seeing the Blessed One proceeding from the street to the monastery, he had various fragrant flowers such as jasmine and sumana, and anointing substances such as sandalwood paste brought. He went to the monastery, honored the Blessed One with the flowers, made a five-fingered mark on the Blessed One's body with the anointing paste, paid homage, and departed.

50. So [M 2.0177] tena puññena devamanussesu ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbattitvā vuddhimanvāya satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā pubbakammaṃ saranto paccakkhato ñatvā “imaṃ nāma kusalakammaṃ katvā īdisaṃ lokuttarasampattiṃ pattomhī”ti pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento tisso nāmāsi bhagavātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

50. Through that merit, having experienced good fortune among both devas and humans, he was reborn in this Buddha-dispensation into a prosperous family. Having reached maturity, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching and, with a confident mind, went forth. He cultivated insight and soon became an arahant. Recalling his past deeds and knowing them directly—“Having done such a skillful deed, I have attained such supramundane fortune”—he declared the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with “The Blessed One's name was Tissa.” All this has a plain meaning.

Pañcaṅguliyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pañcaṅguliya is finished.

Sattarasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Seventeenth Chapter is finished.

18. Kumudavaggo

18. The Kumuda Chapter

1. Kumudamāliyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kumudamāliya

Pabbate [V 2.0167] himavantamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato kumudamāliyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto atthadassissa bhagavato kāle himavantapabbatasamīpe jātassarassa āsanne rakkhaso hutvā nibbatto atthadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ tattha upagataṃ disvā pasannamānaso kumudapupphāni ocinitvā bhagavantaṃ pūjesi. Bhagavā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

“On the Himālaya mountain,” etc., is the apadāna of the venerable Elder Kumudamāliya. This elder too, having made his resolve under former Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that served as a basis for liberation, was reborn as a rakshasa near Lake Jātasara in the vicinity of the Himālaya mountain during the time of the Blessed One Atthadassī. Seeing the Blessed One Atthadassī arrive there, with a confident mind he plucked kumuda flowers and honored the Blessed One. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation and departed.

1. So tena puññena tato cavitvā devalokaṃ upapanno cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo [P 0.0459] anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavattiādisampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto ratanattaye pasanno pabbajitvā vāyamanto brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento pabbate himavantamhītiādimāha. Tattha tatthajo rakkhaso āsinti tasmiṃ jātassarasamīpe jāto nibbatto rakkhaso pararudhiramaṃsakhādako niddayo ghorarūpo bhayānakasabhāvo mahābalo mahāthāmo kakkhaḷo yakkho āsiṃ ahosinti attho.

1. Through that merit, he passed away from there and was reborn in the deva world. After experiencing the good fortune of the six heavens of the sensual sphere and, among humans, the good fortune of a wheel-turning monarch and so on, he was reborn in a good family during this Buddha's dispensation. Having reached maturity, he gained confidence in the Three Jewels, went forth, and while striving, attained arahantship, the culmination of the holy life. Recalling his past deeds and with joy arisen, he declared the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning, “On the Himālaya mountain,” etc. Therein, “I was a rakshasa born there” means: I was born, I arose near Lake Jātasara as a rakshasa—one who eats the blood and flesh of others, merciless, of dreadful appearance, of terrifying nature, of great strength, of great power, a harsh yakkha.

Kumudaṃ [M 2.0178] pupphate tatthāti tasmiṃ mahāsare sūriyaraṃsiyā abhāve sati sāyanhe makuḷitaṃ kuñcitākārena nippabhaṃ avaṇṇaṃ hotīti “kumuda”nti laddhanāmaṃ pupphaṃ pupphate vikasatīti attho. Cakkamattāni jāyareti tāni pupphāni rathacakkapamāṇāni hutvā jāyantīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

Regarding “The kumuda blooms there”: the meaning is that in that great lake, the flower named 'kumuda' blooms, that is, it opens up. It is so named because in the evening, in the absence of the sun's rays, what was formerly budded, contracted, lustreless, and colorless, now blooms. Regarding “They are the size of wheels”: the meaning is that those flowers grow to the size of chariot wheels. The rest is easily understood.

Kumudamāliyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kumudamāliya is finished.

2. Nisseṇidāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nisseṇidāyaka

Koṇḍaññassa [V 2.0168] bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato nisseṇidāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro anekāsu jātīsu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto koṇḍaññassa bhagavato kāle vaḍḍhakikule nibbatto saddho pasanno bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso bhagavato vasanapāsādassārohanatthāya sārakaṭṭhamayaṃ nisseṇiṃ katvā ussāpetvā ṭhapesi. Bhagavā tassa pasādasaṃvaḍḍhanatthāya passantasseva uparipāsādaṃ āruhi. So atīva pasanno teneva pītisomanassena kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatto tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā manussesu jāyamāno nisseṇidānanissandena uccakule nibbatto manussasukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saddhājāto pabbajito nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Nisseṇidāyaka begins: 'Of the Blessed One Koṇḍañña…' This one too, having made his aspiration under former supreme Jinas and accumulating in many births merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was born into a carpenter’s family at the time of the Blessed One Koṇḍañña. Faithful and confident, having heard the Blessed One’s Dhamma discourse, with a confident mind, he made a ladder of heartwood for the Blessed One’s ascent to his dwelling mansion and set it up. To increase his confidence, the Blessed One ascended to the upper mansion while he was watching. Exceedingly confident, with that joy and happiness he passed away and was reborn in the deva world. Having enjoyed divine fortune there, when born among humans, as a result of his gift of the ladder he was reborn into a high family and experienced human happiness. During this Buddha-arising, he was born into a certain family, and having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, faith arose in him and he went forth. Not long after, he became an arahant.

9. So attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento koṇḍaññassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Tattha koṇḍaññassāti kucchito hutvā ḍeti pavattatīti koṇḍo, lāmakasatto, koṇḍato aññoti koṇḍañño, alāmako uttamapurisoti attho. Atha vā brāhmaṇagottesu koṇḍaññagotte uppannattā “koṇḍañño”ti [P 0.0460] gottavasena tassa nāmaṃ, tassa koṇḍaññassa. Sesaṃ pākaṭamevāti.

9. Recollecting his past deeds, with joy arisen, he disclosed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with: 'Of the Blessed One Koṇḍañña…' Therein, regarding 'of Koṇḍañña': one who, being contemptible, struts about is a 'koṇḍa,' a base being. One who is other than a 'koṇḍa' is a 'koṇḍañña,' meaning one who is not base, a supreme person. Alternatively, since he was born in the Koṇḍañña clan among the brahmin clans, 'Koṇḍañña' was his name by way of his clan; thus 'of that Koṇḍañña.' The rest is self-evident.

Nisseṇidāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nisseṇidāyaka is concluded.

3. Rattipupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rattipupphiya

Migaluddo [M 2.0179] pure āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato rattipupphiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle nesādakule uppanno migavadhāya araññe vicaramāno tassa kāruññena araññe caramānaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pupphitaṃ rattikaṃ nāma pupphaṃ kuṭajapupphañca saha vaṇṭena ocinitvā somanassacittena pūjesi. Bhagavā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Rattipupphiya begins: 'I was formerly a deer-hunter…' This one too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was born into a hunter’s family at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. While wandering in the forest to hunt deer, he saw the Blessed One Vipassī wandering in the forest out of compassion. With a confident mind, he plucked a blooming rattika flower and a kuṭaja flower, together with their stalks, and offered them with a joyful mind. The Blessed One gave his approval and departed.

13. So teneva puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto ratanattaye pasanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ [V 2.0169] disvā pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā “nesādabhūtena mayā katakusalaṃ sundara”nti somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento migaluddo pure āsintiādimāha. Tattha migānaṃ luddo sāhasiko mārakoti migaluddo, migesu vā luddo lobhīti migaluddo, nesādo āsiṃ pureti attho.

13. By that very merit, wandering in saṃsāra among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of fortune, during this Buddha-arising he was reborn in a good family. Having reached maturity, he became confident in the Triple Gem. After hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he went forth and not long after attained arahantship. Recalling his past deeds, with joy arisen, he declared: 'The wholesome deed I did as a hunter was beautiful!' Thus, disclosing the apadāna of his former conduct, he spoke, beginning with: 'I was formerly a deer-hunter…' Therein, 'deer-hunter' (migaluddo) means one who is cruel, violent, and a killer of deer, or one who is cruel and greedy for deer. The meaning is: 'I was formerly a hunter.'

14. Rattikaṃ pupphitaṃ disvāti padumapupphādīni anekāni pupphāni sūriyaraṃsisamphassena divā pupphanti rattiyaṃ makuḷitāni honti. Jātisumanamallikādīni anekāni pupphāni pana rattiyaṃ pupphanti no divā. Tasmā rattiyaṃ pupphanato rattipupphanāmakāni anekāni sugandhapupphāni ca kuṭajapupphāni ca gahetvā pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

14. Regarding 'Having seen a rattika flower blooming': Many flowers, such as lotuses, bloom by day through contact with the sun’s rays and are closed at night. But many flowers, such as jasmine, sumana, and mallikā, bloom at night, not by day. Therefore, the meaning is that he took many fragrant flowers that are called night-bloomers because they bloom at night, as well as kuṭaja flowers, and offered them in worship. The rest is self-evident.

Rattipupphiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rattipupphiya is concluded.

4. Udapānadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Udapānadāyaka

Vipassino bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato udapānadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimamunivaresu katādhikāro anekesu bhavesu katapuññasañcayo vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe [M 2.0180] nibbatto vuddhippatto “pānīyadānaṃ mayā dātabbaṃ, tañca nirantaraṃ katvā pavattetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā ekaṃ kūpaṃ khanāpetvā udakasampattakāle iṭṭhakāhi cināpetvā thiraṃ katvā tattha uṭṭhitena udakena puṇṇaṃ taṃ udapānaṃ vipassissa bhagavato niyyādesi. Bhagavā pānīyadānānisaṃsadīpakaṃ anumodanaṃ akāsi[P 0.0461]. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne pokkharaṇīudapānapānīyādisampanno sukhamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya saddho pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Udapānadāyaka begins: 'Of the Blessed One Vipassī…' This elder too, having made his aspiration under former supreme sages and accumulated a store of merit over many existences, was born into a good family at the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, he thought: 'I should give the gift of drinking water, and it is proper to do so continuously.' He had a well dug, and when water was reached, he had it lined with bricks to make it firm. Having filled that well with the water that arose there, he dedicated it to the Blessed One Vipassī. The Blessed One gave a blessing that illuminated the benefits of giving drinking water. By that merit, wandering in saṃsāra among devas and humans, in every place he was reborn he was endowed with lotus ponds, wells, and drinking water, and experienced happiness. During this Buddha-arising, he was reborn in a certain family. Having reached maturity, faithful and confident, he went forth and not long after became an arahant.

18. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento vipassino bhagavatotiādimāha. Tattha udapāno kato mayāti udakaṃ pivanti etthāti udapāno, kūpapokkharaṇītaḷākānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. So udapāno kūpo vipassissa bhagavato atthāya kato khanitoti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

18. In a later time, recalling his past deeds, with joy arisen, he disclosed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with: 'Of the Blessed One Vipassī…' Therein, regarding 'A well was made by me': a place where they drink water (udakaṃ pivanti) is a 'well' (udapāna); this is a term for wells, lotus ponds, and tanks. The meaning is that this well, this pit, was made and dug for the sake of the Blessed One Vipassī. The rest has a plain meaning.

Udapānadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Udapānadāyaka is concluded.

5. Sīhāsanadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka

Nibbute [V 2.0170] lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato sīhāsanadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave nibbānādhigamatthāya katapuññūpacayo padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle gahapatikule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā ratanattaye pasanno tasmiṃ bhagavati parinibbute sattahi ratanehi khacitaṃ sīhāsanaṃ kārāpetvā bodhirukkhaṃ pūjesi, bahūhi mālāgandhadhūpehi ca pūjesi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka begins with the words, 'When the Protector of the World had attained Nibbāna…' This elder, too, had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and had accumulated a store of merit in various existences for the sake of attaining Nibbāna. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a householder’s family. Having reached maturity and heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, he gained faith in the Triple Gem. When that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, he had a lion seat inlaid with the seven kinds of gems made and venerated the Bodhi tree. He also venerated it with many garlands, perfumes, and incense.

21. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā sabbattha pūjito imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto vuddhippatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso ñātivaggaṃ pahāya pabbajito nacirasseva arahā hutvā [M 2.0181] pubbūpacitakusalasambhāraṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Tattha sīhāsanamadāsahanti sīharūpahiraññasuvaṇṇaratanehi khacitaṃ āsanaṃ sīhāsanaṃ, sīhassa vā abhītassa bhagavato nisinnārahaṃ, sīhaṃ vā seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ āsananti sīhāsanaṃ, taṃ ahaṃ adāsiṃ, bodhirukkhaṃ pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

21. Through that merit, wandering among devas and humans, he experienced both kinds of good fortune and was honored everywhere. In this Buddha-arising, he was reborn in a family of good standing in Sāvatthī. Having grown up and while living the household life, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse. With a confident mind, he abandoned his circle of relatives, went forth, and before long became an arahant. Recalling his store of wholesome karma accumulated in the past, and with gladness arisen, he disclosed the apadāna of his former deeds, speaking the verses beginning with, 'When the Protector of the World was extinguished…' Herein, 'I gave a lion seat' means a seat inlaid with figures of lions, silver, gold, and gems; or a seat worthy for the Blessed One, who is fearless like a lion, to sit upon; or a 'lion' seat, that is, a best and supreme seat. 'That I gave' means 'I venerated the Bodhi tree.' The rest is easy to understand.

Sīhāsanadāyakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīhāsanadāyaka is concluded.

6. Maggadattikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maggadattika

Anomadassī bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato maggadattikattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto anomadassissa [P 0.0462] bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vuddhimanvāya gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto anomadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ ākāse caṅkamantaṃ pāduddhāre pāduddhāracaṅkamanaṭṭhāne pupphānaṃ vikiraṇaṃ acchariyañca disvā pasannamānaso pupphāni ākāse ukkhipi, tāni vitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Maggadattika begins with the words, 'The Blessed One Anomadassī…' This venerable one, too, had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and had accumulated in various existences meritorious deeds that are a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Anomadassī, he was reborn in a family of good standing. Having grown up and established a household, while living there he saw the Blessed One Anomadassī practicing walking meditation in the sky. Seeing the amazing scattering of flowers at the place of his walking meditation with each lifting of his feet, with a confident mind he tossed flowers into the air. They formed a canopy and remained there.

26. So tena puññena sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto sabbattha pūjito sukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto kamena yobbaññaṃ pāpuṇitvā saddhājāto pabbajitvā vattasampanno [V 2.0171] nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto caṅkamanassa pūjitattā maggadattikattheroti pākaṭo. So pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento anomadassī bhagavātiādimāha. Diṭṭhadhammasukhatthāyāti imasmiṃ attabhāve caṅkamanena sarīrasallahukādisukhaṃ paṭiccāti attho. Abbhokāsamhi caṅkamīti abbhokāse aṅgaṇaṭṭhāne caṅkami, padavikkhepaṃ padasañcāraṃ akāsīti attho.

26. By that merit, wandering only in happy destinations, he was honored everywhere and experienced happiness. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a certain family and, having gradually reached youth, faith arose in him and he went forth. Accomplished in the observances, he soon attained arahantship. Because he had honored the walking meditation, he became known as the Elder Maggadattika. Remembering his past kamma, with gladness arisen, he disclosed the apadāna of his former deeds by speaking the verses beginning, 'The Blessed One Anomadassī…' 'For the sake of happiness in this very life' means: on account of the happiness of bodily lightness and so on from walking meditation in this very life. 'He walked in the open' means he practiced walking meditation in an open space, a courtyard; that is, he took steps, he moved his feet.

Uddhate pāde pupphānīti caṅkamantena pāde uddhate padumuppalādīni pupphāni pathavito uggantvā caṅkame vikiriṃsūti attho. Sobhaṃ muddhani tiṭṭhareti buddhassa [M 2.0182] muddhani sīse sobhayamānā tāni tiṭṭhantīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

'When the foot was lifted, flowers' means that when he was practicing walking meditation and lifted his foot, lotuses, blue water lilies, and other flowers rose up from the earth and scattered on the walking path. 'They stood adorning his head' means that they remained there, beautifying the Buddha's head, his crown. The rest is easy to understand.

Maggadattikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maggadattika is completed.

7. Ekadīpiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekadīpiya

Padumuttarassa muninotiādikaṃ āyasmato ekadīpiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimajinaseṭṭhesu katakusalasambhāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle gahapatikule nibbatto vuddhippatto saddho pasanno bhagavato salalamahābodhimhi ekapadīpaṃ pūjesi, thāvaraṃ katvā niccamekapadīpapūjanatthāya telavaṭṭaṃ paṭṭhapesi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto sabbattha jalamāno pasannacakkhuko ubhayasukhamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampanne ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patto ratanattaye pasanno pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ patto dīpapūjāya laddhavisesādhigamattā ekadīpiyattheroti pākaṭo.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Ekadīpiya begins with the words, 'Of the sage Padumuttara…' This venerable one, too, had accumulated a store of wholesome kamma under the foremost Conquerors of the past and had accumulated in various existences meritorious deeds that are a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in a householder’s family. Having grown up, faithful and confident, he offered a single lamp at the Blessed One’s great Salala Bodhi tree. Making it a permanent offering, he established a supply of oil and wicks for the constant veneration with a single lamp. Through that merit, wandering among devas and humans, he was radiant everywhere, had clear vision, and experienced happiness in both spheres. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was reborn in a prosperous family in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he gained faith in the Triple Gem, went forth, and soon attained arahantship. Because he had gained a special attainment through his lamp offering, he became known as the Elder Ekadīpiya.

30. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttarassa muninotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

30. Later, remembering his own past kamma, with gladness arisen, he disclosed the apadāna of his former deeds by speaking the verses beginning, 'Of the sage Padumuttara…' All of that has a plain meaning.

Ekadīpiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ekadīpiya is completed.

8. Maṇipūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maṇipūjaka

Orena [P 0.0463][V 2.0172] himavantassātiādikaṃ āyasmato maṇipūjakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā tatthādīnavaṃ disvā gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantaorabhāge ekissā nadiyā samīpe paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā vasanto vivekakāmatāya tassānukampāya ca tattha upagataṃ padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso maṇipallaṅkaṃ [M 2.0183] bhagavato pūjesi. Bhagavā tassa pasādavaḍḍhanatthāya tattha nisīdi. So bhiyyosomattāya pasanno nibbānādhigamatthāya patthanaṃ akāsi. Bhagavā anumodanaṃ vatvā pakkāmi. So tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto sabbattha pūjito sukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampanne kule nibbatto gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekadivasaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Elder Maṇipūjaka, beginning with the words, 'On this side of the Himālaya…' This elder, having laid his foundation under previous Buddhas and accumulated merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation, was born into a certain family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having established a household, he saw the danger in it, and abandoning the household life, he went forth into the ascetic life. While dwelling in a leaf-hut he had made near a river on this side of the Himālaya, out of a desire for seclusion, he saw the Blessed One Padumuttara who had approached there out of compassion for him. With a confident mind, he offered a jeweled seat to the Blessed One. The Blessed One sat on it in order to increase his confidence. Being even more joyful and confident, he made an aspiration for the attainment of Nibbāna. The Blessed One expressed his appreciation and departed. Through that merit, he wandered among devas and humans, being honored everywhere and experiencing happiness. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a prosperous family in Sāvatthī. While living the household life, one day he heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith, and went forth. Not long afterwards, he became an arahant.

34. So ekadivasaṃ attanā katakusalaṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento orena himavantassātiādimāha. Tattha orenāti himavantassa aparaṃ bhāgaṃ vihāya orena, bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, orasmiṃ disābhāgeti attho. Nadikā sampavattathāti apākaṭanāmadheyyā ekā nadī saṃsuṭṭhu pavattānī vahānī sandamānā ahosīti attho. Tassā cānupakhettamhīti tassā nadiyā anupakhettamhi tīrasamīpeti attho. Sayambhū vasate tadāti yadā ahaṃ maṇipallaṅkaṃ pūjesiṃ, tadā anācariyako hutvā sayameva buddhabhūto bhagavā vasate viharatīti attho.

34. One day, recalling the wholesome deed he himself had done, with joy arisen in him, he disclosed the apadāna of his former conduct, speaking the verses beginning: 'On this side of the Himālaya…' Herein, orena means on this side, leaving aside the further part of the Himālaya; the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative, meaning 'in the region on this side.' Nadikā sampavattathā means a river of an obscure name flowed, that is, it was streaming and flowing along very well. Tassā cānupakhettamhīti means in the area along that river, that is, near its bank. Sayambhū vasate tadā means that when I worshipped the jeweled seat, the Blessed One, the Self-become One, who had become a Buddha by himself without a teacher, was dwelling, was abiding there.

35. Maṇiṃ paggayha pallaṅkanti maṇinti cittaṃ ārādheti somanassaṃ karotīti maṇi, atha vā māti pamāṇaṃ karoti ābharaṇanti maṇi, atha vā marantāpi rājayuvarājādayo taṃ na pariccajanti tadatthāya saṅgāmaṃ karontīti maṇi, taṃ maṇiṃ maṇimayaṃ pallaṅkaṃ manoramaṃ sādhu cittaṃ suṭṭhu vicittaṃ paggayha gahetvā buddhaseṭṭhassa abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

35. Regarding Maṇiṃ paggayha pallaṅkaṃ (Having raised up a jeweled seat): A maṇi (jewel) is so called because it pleases the mind (cittaṃ ārādheti) and brings joy (somanassaṃ karoti); or because it sets the standard (māti) for ornaments; or because kings, crown princes, and others do not relinquish it even when dying but wage war for its sake. The meaning is: 'Having taken up and raised that jewel—that is, a jeweled seat that was delightful, fine, beautiful, and well-adorned—I presented it to the Chief of Buddhas; that is, I worshipped him.' The rest is all of plain meaning.

Maṇipūjakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Maṇipūjaka is finished.

9. Tikicchakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tikicchaka

Nagare [V 2.0173] bandhumatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato tikicchakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampāyasmā purimajinavaresu katādhikāro [P 0.0464] tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle bandhumatīnagare vejjakule nibbatto bahussuto susikkhito vejjakamme cheko [M 2.0184] bahū rogino tikicchanto vipassissa bhagavato upaṭṭhākassa asokanāmattherassa rogaṃ tikicchi. So tena puññena devamanussesu aparāparaṃ sukhaṃ anubhavanto nibbattanibbattabhave arogo dīghāyuko suvaṇṇavaṇṇasarīro ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Tikicchaka, beginning with the words, 'In the city of Bandhumatī…' This venerable one, having laid his foundation under former supreme Conquerors and accumulated merits in various existences that serve as a basis for liberation, was born into a physician’s family in the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Being very learned, well-trained, and expert in the medical art, he treated many sick people and cured a disease of the elder named Asoka, the attendant of the Blessed One Vipassī. Through that merit, experiencing successive happiness among devas and humans, in whatever existence he was reborn he was free from disease, long-lived, and had a body the color of gold.

39. So imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ gahapatikule nibbatto vuddhimanvāya sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto arogo sukhito vibhavasampanno ratanattaye pasanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho gharāvāsaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nagare bandhumatiyātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

39. In this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into a householder’s family in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he attained proficiency in all crafts; he was healthy, happy, and prosperous. Confident in the Triple Gem, he listened to the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, gained faith, renounced the household life, and went forth. Not long afterwards, he became an arahant. Recalling his past deeds, with joy arisen in him, he disclosed the apadāna of his former conduct, speaking the verses beginning: 'In the city of Bandhumatī…' All of this is of plain meaning, in the way stated previously.

Tikicchakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tikicchaka is finished.

10. Saṅghupaṭṭhākattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Saṅghupaṭṭhāka

Vessabhumhi bhagavatītiādikaṃ āyasmato saṅghupaṭṭhākattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katakusalasambhāro anekesu bhavesu vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vessabhussa bhagavato kāle tassārāmikassa putto hutvā nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā saddho pasanno vihāresu ārāmikakammaṃ karonto sakkaccaṃ saṅghaṃ upaṭṭhāsi. So teneva kusalakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ gahapatikule nibbatto vuddhippatto vibhavasampanno sukhappatto pākaṭo satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sāsane pasanno pabbajitvā vattasampanno sāsanaṃ sobhayamāno vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento nacirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patto chaḷabhiñño pubbe katakusalakammavasena saṅghupaṭṭhākattheroti pākaṭo ahosi.

The apadāna of the Venerable Saṅghupaṭṭhāka, beginning with the words, 'When Vessabhū was the Blessed One…' This elder, too, having amassed a store of wholesome merit under past Buddhas and accumulated merits in many existences that serve as a basis for liberation, was born as the son of a monastery attendant during the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū. Having reached discernment, being faithful and confident, he respectfully attended on the Saṅgha while performing the duties of a monastery attendant. By that wholesome deed, while wandering among devas and humans and experiencing both kinds of success, in this Buddha-dispensation he was born into a householder’s family in Sāvatthī. Having reached maturity, he was prosperous, happy, and renowned. Hearing the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma and becoming confident in the Teaching, he went forth. Accomplished in the observances and illuminating the Teaching, he developed insight and not long afterwards attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. He became a possessor of the six supernormal knowledges. By the power of the wholesome kamma he had done in the past, he became renowned as the Elder Saṅghupaṭṭhāka (the Saṅgha-Attendant).

45. So [V 2.0174] ekadivasaṃ “pubbe mayā kiṃ nāma kammaṃ katvā ayaṃ lokuttarasampatti laddhā”ti attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā paccakkhato jānitvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pākaṭaṃ karonto vessabhumhi bhagavatītiādimāha. Tattha ahosārāmiko ahanti ahaṃ [M 2.0185] vessabhussa bhagavato sāsane ārāmiko ahosinti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthattā ca suviññeyyamevāti.

45. One day, reflecting on his past kamma, thinking, 'By doing what kamma in the past have I gained this supramundane attainment?' and having known it directly for himself, with joy arisen in him, he made the apadāna of his former conduct manifest, speaking the verses beginning: 'When Vessabhū was the Blessed One…' Herein, `ahosiṃ ārāmiko ahaṃ` means: 'I was a monastery attendant in the teaching of the Blessed One Vessabhū.' The rest is easily knowable because the method has been stated previously and because its meaning is plain.

Saṅghupaṭṭhākattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Saṅghupaṭṭhāka is finished.

Aṭṭhārasamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Eighteenth Chapter is finished.

19. Kuṭajapupphiyavaggo

19. The Kuṭajapupphiya Chapter

1-10. Kuṭajapupphiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Kuṭajapupphiya and others.

Ito [P 0.0465][V 2.0175] parampi ekūnavīsatimavagge āgatānaṃ imesaṃ kuṭajapupphiyattherādīnaṃ dasannaṃ therānaṃ apubbaṃ natthi. Tesañhi therānaṃ purimabuddhānaṃ santike katapuññasambhārānaṃ vasena pākaṭanāmāni ceva nivāsanagarādīni ca heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva veditabbānīti taṃ sabbaṃ apadānaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

From here onward, in the nineteenth chapter, there is nothing new regarding the Apadānas of these ten elders, beginning with the Elder Kuṭajapupphiya. For these elders, due to the accumulation of merit made in the presence of previous Buddhas, both their well-known names and their places of residence, cities, and so on, should be understood in the same way as previously stated. Thus, the entire Apadāna is easily understood.

Ekūnavīsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Nineteenth Chapter is finished.

20. Tamālapupphiyavaggo

20. The Tamālapupphiya Chapter

1-10. Tamālapupphiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Tamālapupphiya and others.

Vīsatime [V 2.0176] vagge paṭhamattherāpadānaṃ uttānameva.

In the twentieth chapter, the Apadāna of the first elder is clear in meaning.

6. Dutiyattherāpadāne yaṃ dāyavāsiko isīti isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vane vasanabhāvena dāyavāsiko isīti saṅkhaṃ gato, attano anukampāya taṃ vanaṃ upagatassa siddhatthassa satthuno vasanamaṇḍapacchādanatthāya yaṃ tiṇaṃ, taṃ lāyati chindatīti attho. Dabbachadanaṃ katvā anekehi khuddakadaṇḍakehi maṇḍapaṃ katvā taṃ tiṇena chādetvā siddhatthassa bhagavato ahaṃ adāsiṃ pūjesinti attho.

6. In the Apadāna of the second elder, regarding 'a sage dwelling in the grove': having gone forth as a sage and living in the forest, he came to be known as 'a sage dwelling in the grove.' For the Teacher Siddhattha who had approached that forest out of compassion for him, for the purpose of covering a dwelling pavilion, `lāyati` means `chindati`, 'he cuts' the grass. The meaning is: 'Having made a pavilion with many small sticks and covered it with grass, I gave it to the Blessed One Siddhattha, honoring him.'

8. Sattāhaṃ dhārayuṃ tatthāti taṃ maṇḍapaṃ tattha ṭhitā devamanussā sattāhaṃ nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisinnassa satthuno dhārayuṃ dhāresunti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

8. Regarding 'For seven days they held it there': the meaning is that the gods and humans who were present there sustained the pavilion for seven days for the Teacher who was seated, having entered the attainment of cessation. The rest is clear in meaning.

Tatiyattherassa [M 2.0186] apadāne khaṇḍaphulliyattheroti ettha khaṇḍanti kaṭṭhānaṃ jiṇṇattā chinnabhinnaṭṭhānaṃ, phullanti kaṭṭhānaṃ jiṇṇaṭṭhāne kaṇṇakitamahicchattakādipupphanaṃ, khaṇḍañca phullañca khaṇḍaphullāni, khaṇḍaphullānaṃ paṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ punappunaṃ thirakaraṇanti khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Imassa pana therassa sambhārapūraṇakāle phussassa bhagavato cetiye chinnabhinnaṭṭhāne sudhāpiṇḍaṃ makkhetvā thirakaraṇaṃ khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇaṃ nāma. Tasmā so khaṇḍaphulliyo theroti pākaṭo ahosi. Tatiyaṃ.

In the Apadāna of the third elder, the Elder Khaṇḍaphulliya: here, 'khaṇḍa' refers to the broken and split parts of wood due to its age; 'phulla' refers to the blooming of flowers such as kaṇṇikā and mahicchattaka on the aged parts of the wood; 'khaṇḍaphulla' are the broken parts and the flowers; and 'khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇa' means repeatedly repairing and reinforcing them. At the time of fulfilling his accumulations, this elder applied plaster to the broken parts of the shrine of the Blessed One Phussa, reinforcing them—this was called 'khaṇḍaphullapaṭisaṅkharaṇa.' Therefore, he became known as the Elder Khaṇḍaphulliya. Third.

17. Catutthattherassāpadāne rañño baddhacaro ahanti rañño paricārako kammakārako ahosinti attho.

17. In the Apadāna of the fourth elder, 'I was a bound follower of the king' means 'I was an attendant and worker for the king.'

19. Jalajuttamanāminoti [P 0.0466] jale udake jātaṃ jalajaṃ, kiṃ taṃ padumaṃ, padumena samānanāmattā [V 2.0177] padumuttarassa bhagavatoti attho. Uttamapadumanāmassa bhagavatoti vā attho. Catutthaṃ.

19. Regarding 'one named after the best of the water-born': `jalaja` means born in water. What is that? The lotus (`paduma`). Because his name was the same as the lotus, the meaning refers to the Blessed One Padumuttara. Or, the meaning is 'the Blessed One named the Supreme Lotus.' Fourth.

Pañcamaṃ uttānatthameva.

The fifth is clear in meaning.

28. Chaṭṭhe nagare dvāravatiyāti mahādvāravātapānakavāṭaphalakāhi vatipākāraṭṭālagopurakaddamodakaparikhāhi ca sampannaṃ nagaranti dvāravatīnagaraṃ, dvāraṃ vatiñca padhānaṃ katvā nagarassa upalakkhitattā “dvāravatī nagara”nti voharantīti nagare dvāravatiyāti vuttaṃ. Mālāvaccho pupphārāmo mama ahosīti attho.

28. In the sixth, regarding 'in the city of Dvāravatī': the city called Dvāravatī was a city well-equipped with large gates, windows, door panels, walls, ramparts, watchtowers, gate towers, and moats of mud and water. Because it was characterized by its prominent gate (dvāra) and wall (vati), it was called 'Dvāravatī Nagara.' Thus it is said, 'in the city of Dvāravatī.' The meaning is: 'The flower park Mālāvaccha was mine.'

31. Te kisalayāti te asokapallavā. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

31. Regarding 'those shoots': this means shoots of the asoka tree. Sixth.

Sattamaṭṭhamanavamāni uttānatthāneva. Dasamepi apubbaṃ natthīti.

The seventh, eighth, and ninth are clear in meaning. In the tenth, too, there is nothing new.

Vīsatimavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twentieth chapter is concluded.

21-23. Kaṇikārapupphiyādivaggo

21-23. The Chapter on Kaṇikārapupphiya and Others

1-30. Kaṇikārapupphiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-30. The Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Kaṇikārapupphiya and others.

Ito [V 2.0178] paraṃ sabbattha anuttānapadavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Ekavīsatime bāvīsatime tevīsatime ca vagge sabbesaṃ therānaṃ sayaṃkatena puññena laddhanāmāni, katapuññānañca nānattaṃ tesaṃ byākaraṇadāyakānaṃ buddhānaṃ nāmāni [M 2.0187] vasitanagarāni ca heṭṭhā vuttanayattā sabbānipi uttānāneva. Apadānagāthānamattho ca nayānuyogena suviññeyyoyevāti.

From here onward, we will provide a commentary on all terms that are not clear. In the twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-third chapters, the names of all the elders were acquired through merit they themselves made; the diversity of their merit, the names of the Buddhas who gave the prediction, and the cities where they resided are all clear, according to the method explained previously. The meaning of the Apadāna verses is also easily understood by applying the proper method.

24. Udakāsanavaggo

24. The Udakāsana Chapter

1-10.Udakāsanadāyakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadānas of the Elder Udakāsanadāyaka and others.

Catuvīsatime [V 2.0179] vagge paṭhamadutiyāpadānāni uttānāneva.

In the twenty-fourth chapter, the first and second Apadānas are clear in meaning.

9. Tatiyāpadāne aruṇavatiyā nagareti ā samantato ālokaṃ karonto uṇati uggacchatīti aruṇo, so tasmiṃ vijjatīti aruṇavatī, tasmiṃ nagare ālokaṃ karonto sūriyo uggacchatīti attho. Sesanagaresupi sūriyuggamane vijjamānepi visesavacanaṃ sabbacatuppadānaṃ [P 0.0467] mahiyaṃ sayanepi sati mahiyaṃ sayatīti mahiṃsoti vacanaṃ viya rūḷhivasena vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Atha vā pākārapāsādahammiyādīsu suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādisattaratanapabhāhi aruṇuggamanaṃ viya pabhāvatī aruṇavatī nāma, tasmiṃ aruṇavatiyā nagare, pūpiko pūpavikkayena jīvikaṃ kappento ahosinti attho.

9. In the third Apadāna, regarding 'in the city of Aruṇavatī': `aruṇa` (dawn) is so called because it rises (`uṇati uggacchati`), spreading light all around; a place where this exists is `aruṇavatī`. The meaning is that in that city, the sun rises spreading light. Although the sun rises in other cities too, this specific term is used conventionally, just as the word `mahiṃsa` (buffalo) is used, even though all four-footed creatures lie on the earth (`mahiyaṃ sayati`). Or else, Aruṇavatī is so named because its walls, palaces, mansions, and so on, shine with the radiance of the seven kinds of gems—gold, silver, jewels, pearls, etc.—like the rising of the dawn. The meaning is: 'In that city of Aruṇavatī, I was a cake-seller, making a living by selling cakes.'

14. Catutthāpadāne tivarāyaṃ pure rammeti tīhi pākārehi parivāritā parikkhittāti tivarā, khajjabhojjādiupabhogavatthābharaṇādinaccagītādīhi ramaṇīyanti rammaṃ, tasmiṃ tivarāyaṃ pure nagare ramme naḷakāro ahaṃ ahosinti sambandho.

14. In the fourth Apadāna, regarding 'in the delightful city of Tivarā': `tivarā` means surrounded and enclosed by three ramparts; `rammaṃ` means delightful with enjoyments such as hard and soft foods, consumer goods, ornaments, dancing, and singing. The connection is: 'In that delightful city of Tivarā, I was a reed-worker.'

Pañcamāpadānaṃ uttānatthameva.

The fifth Apadāna is clear in meaning.

23. Chaṭṭhāpadāne vaṇṇakāro ahaṃ tadāti nīlapītarattādivaṇṇavasena vatthāni karoti rañjetīti vaṇṇakāro. Vattharajako hutvā cetiye vatthehi acchādanasamaye nānāvaṇṇehi dussāni rañjesinti attho.

23. In the sixth Apadāna, regarding 'I was a dyer then': a `vaṇṇakāro` is one who works on cloths with colors such as blue, yellow, and red, that is, he dyes them. The meaning is: 'Having been a cloth-dyer, at the time of covering the shrine with cloths, I dyed fabrics with various colors.'

27. Sattamāpadāne piyālaṃ pupphitaṃ disvāti supupphitaṃ piyālarukkhaṃ disvā. Gatamagge khipiṃ [V 2.0180] ahanti ahaṃ migaluddo nesādo hutvā piyālapupphaṃ ocinitvā buddhassa gatamagge khipiṃ pūjesinti attho.

27. In the seventh Apadāna, regarding 'Having seen the piyāla in bloom': this means having seen a piyāla tree in full bloom. Regarding 'I scattered them on the path he had gone': the meaning is, 'I, having been a deer-hunter and trapper, plucked piyāla flowers and scattered them on the path the Buddha had gone, as an offering.'

30. Aṭṭhamāpadāne [M 2.0188] sake sippe apatthaddhoti attano takkabyākaraṇādisippasmiṃ apatthaddho patiṭṭhito cheko ahaṃ kānanaṃ agamaṃ gato sambuddhaṃ yantaṃ disvānāti vanantare gacchantaṃ vipassiṃ sambuddhaṃ passitvā. Ambayāgaṃ adāsahanti ahaṃ ambadānaṃ adāsinti attho.

30. In the eighth Apadāna, regarding 'unwavering in my own craft': this means I was unwavering, established, and skilled in my own craft of logic, grammar, and so on. 'I went to the forest.' Regarding 'having seen the Self-Enlightened One going': this means having seen the Self-Enlightened One Vipassī going in the forest. Regarding 'I gave a mango offering': the meaning is, 'I gave a gift of mangoes.'

33. Navamāpadāne jagatī kāritā mayhanti atthadassissa bhagavato sarīradhātunidhāpitacetiye jagati chinnabhinnaālindapupphādhānasaṅkhātā jagati mayā kāritā kārāpitāti attho.

33. In the ninth Apadāna, regarding 'A terrace was caused to be made by me': the meaning is, 'A terrace—that is, what had been a broken and ruined veranda and flower-receptacle—was caused to be made by me at the shrine where the bodily relics of the Blessed One Atthadassī were enshrined.'

Dasamāpadānaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

The tenth Apadāna is clear in meaning.

Catuvīsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter is concluded.

25. Tuvaradāyakavaggo

25. The Tuvaradāyaka Chapter

1-10. Tuvaradāyakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Tuvaradāyaka.

1. Pañcavīsatime [P 0.0468][V 2.0181] vagge paṭhamāpadāne bharitvā tuvaramādāyāti tuvaraaṭṭhiṃ muggakalayasadisaṃ tuvaraṭṭhiṃ bhajjitvā pupphetvā bhājanena ādāya saṅghassa vanamajjhogāhakassa adadiṃ adāsinti attho.

1. In the twenty-fifth chapter, in the first Apadāna, regarding the phrase 'having filled and taken tuvara': this means having roasted tuvara seeds—seeds similar to mung beans and kalāya beans—and caused them to pop, I took them in a vessel and gave them to the Sangha, which had entered into the middle of the forest. This is the meaning of 'I gave'.

4-5. Dutiyāpadāne dhanuṃ advejjhaṃ katvānāti migādīnaṃ māraṇatthāya dhanuṃ sannayhitvā caramāno kesaraṃ ogataṃ disvāti supupphitaṃ khuddakasaraṃ disvā buddhassa abhiropesinti ahaṃ cittaṃ pasādetvā vanaṃ sampattassa tissassa bhagavato abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.

4-5. In the second Apadāna, 'having made the bow unerring' means wandering about with a bow strung for the purpose of killing deer and other animals. 'Having seen a kesara that had gone down' means having seen a small, well-flowered lake. 'I will offer it to the Buddha' means: having gladdened my mind, I offered it to the Blessed One Tissa, who had arrived in the forest; that is, I paid homage. This is the meaning.

9-10. Tatiyāpadāne jalakukkuṭoti jātassare caramānakukkuṭo. Tuṇḍena kesariṃ gayhāti padumapupphaṃ mukhatuṇḍena ḍaṃsitvā ākāsena gacchantassa tissassa bhagavato abhiropesiṃ pūjesinti attho.

9-10. In the third Apadāna, 'a water-cock' means a cock moving about on a natural lake. 'Having taken a kesara with its beak' means having grasped a lotus flower with its beak-tip, I offered it to the Blessed One Tissa, who was traveling through the sky; that is, I paid homage. This is the meaning.

14. Catutthāpadāne viravapupphamādāyāti vividhaṃ ravati saddaṃ karotīti viravaṃ, saddakaraṇavelāyaṃ vikasanato “virava”nti laddhanāmaṃ pupphasamūhaṃ ādāya gahetvā siddhatthassa buddhassa abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.

14. In the fourth Apadāna, regarding 'having taken virava flowers': 'virava' is so called because it makes various sounds. Having taken a collection of flowers that obtained the name 'virava' because they blossom at the time of making sound, I offered them to the Buddha Siddhattha; that is, I paid homage. This is the meaning.

17. Pañcamāpadāne kuṭigopakoti senāsanapālako. Kālena kālaṃ dhūpesinti sampattasampattakālānukāle dhūpesiṃ, dhūpena sugandhaṃ akāsinti [M 2.0189] attho. Siddhatthassa bhagavato gandhakuṭikālānusāridhūpena dhūpesiṃ vāsesinti attho.

17. In the fifth Apadāna, 'a hut-guardian' means a guardian of the lodging. 'I fumigated from time to time' means I fumigated at each appropriate time as it arrived, making it fragrant with incense. The meaning is that I fumigated, that is, perfumed, the fragrant chamber of the Blessed One Siddhattha with incense appropriate to the time.

Chaṭṭhasattamāpadānāni uttānatthāneva.

The sixth and seventh Apadānas are clear in meaning.

27. Aṭṭhamāpadāne [V 2.0182] satta sattalipupphānīti sattalisaṅkhātāni, satta pupphāni sīsenādāya vessabhussa bhagavato abhiropesiṃ pūjesinti attho.

27. In the eighth Apadāna, 'seven sattali flowers' means: having taken on my head seven flowers called sattali, I offered them to the Blessed One Vessabhū; that is, I paid homage. This is the meaning.

31. Navamāpadāne bimbijālakapupphānīti rattaṅkuravakapupphāni siddhatthassa bhagavato pūjesinti attho.

31. In the ninth Apadāna, 'bimbijālaka flowers' means red kuravaka flowers. The meaning is that I paid homage to the Blessed One Siddhattha with them.

35. Dasamāpadāne uddālakaṃ gahetvānāti jātassare vihaṅgasobbhe jātaṃ uddālakapupphaṃ ocinitvā kakusandhassa bhagavato pūjesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

35. In the tenth Apadāna, 'having taken the uddālaka' means: having picked an uddālaka flower that grew in a natural lake, in a pool frequented by birds, I paid homage to the Blessed One Kakusandha. This is the meaning. The rest is indeed easy to understand.

Pañcavīsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-fifth chapter is completed.

26. Thomakavaggo

26. The Thomaka Chapter

1-10. Thomakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Thomaka.

Chabbīsatime [P 0.0469][V 2.0183] vagge paṭhamāpadānaṃ uttānameva.

In the twenty-sixth chapter, the first Apadāna is straightforward in meaning.

5-6. Dutiyāpadāne vijahitvā devavaṇṇanti devatā sarīraṃ vijahitvā chaḍḍetvā, manussasarīraṃ nimminitvāti attho. Adhikāraṃ kattukāmoti adhikakiriyaṃ puññasambhāraṃ kattukāmo devaro nāma ahaṃ devarājā bhariyāya saha buddhaseṭṭhassa sāsane sādaratāya idha imasmiṃ manussaloke āgamiṃ āgatoti attho. Tassa bhikkhā mayā dinnāti padumuttarassa bhagavato yo nāmena devalo nāma sāvako ahosi, tassa sāvakassa mayā vippasannena cetasā bhikkhā dinnā piṇḍapāto dinnoti attho.

5-6. In the second Apadāna, 'having abandoned the divine form' means having abandoned, having discarded the divine body, and having created a human body. This is the meaning. 'Desiring to make a foundation' means desiring to perform a superior action, an accumulation of merit. The meaning is: I, a deva king named Devaro, came here to this human world together with my wife out of respect for the teaching of the best of Buddhas. 'Alms were given by me to him' means: with a confident mind, I gave alms, that is, almsfood, to that disciple named Devala, who was a disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara. This is the meaning.

9-10. Tatiyāpadāne ānando nāma sambuddhoti ānandaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ jananato ānando nāma paccekabuddhoti attho. Amanussamhi kānaneti amanussapariggahe kānane mahāaraññe parinibbāyi anupādisesanibbānadhātuyā [M 2.0190] antaradhāyi, adassanaṃ agamāsīti attho. Sarīraṃ tattha jhāpesinti ahaṃ devalokā idhāgantvā tassa bhagavato sarīraṃ tattha araññe jhāpesiṃ dahanaṃ akāsinti attho.

9-10. In the third Apadāna, 'the Sambuddha named Ānanda' means he was a Paccekabuddha named Ānanda because he generated bliss and contentment. This is the meaning. 'In a non-human forest' means in a great wilderness possessed by non-humans. The meaning is: he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining; he vanished, he went to invisibility. 'I had his body cremated there' means: having come here from the deva world, I had the body of that Blessed One cremated in that forest; I performed the cremation. This is the meaning.

Catutthapañcamāpadānāni uttānāneva.

The fourth and fifth Apadānas are straightforward in meaning.

20. Chaṭṭhāpadāne ahosiṃ candano nāmāti nāmena paṇṇattivasena candano nāma. Sambuddhassatrajoti paccekasambuddhabhūtato pubbe tassa atrajo putto ahaṃ. Ekopāhano mayā dinnoti ekaṃ upāhanayugaṃ mayā dinnaṃ. Bodhiṃ sampajja me tuvanti tena upāhanayugena me mayhaṃ sāvakabodhiṃ tuvaṃ sampajja nipphādehīti attho.

20. In the sixth Apadāna, 'I was named Candana' means I was known by the name Candana by way of designation. 'Son of the Sambuddha' means I was his son before he became a Paccekasambuddha. 'One sandal was given by me' means a single pair of sandals was given by me. 'Attain enlightenment for me' means: by means of that pair of sandals, may you accomplish, may you bring to fulfillment, the enlightenment of a disciple for me. This is the meaning.

23-24. Sattamāpadāne [V 2.0184] mañjarikaṃ karitvānāti mañjeṭṭhipupphaṃ haritacaṅkoṭakaṃ gahetvā rathiyaṃ vīthiyā paṭipajjiṃ ahaṃ tathā paṭipannova bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhataṃ bhikkhusaṅghena parivutaṃ samaṇānaggaṃ samaṇānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ addasanti sambandho. Buddhassa abhiropayinti disvā ca pana taṃ pupphaṃ ubhohi hatthehi paggayha ukkhipitvā buddhassa phussassa bhagavato abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.

23-24. In the seventh Apadāna, 'having made a cluster' means having taken a mañjeṭṭhi flower in a green basket. The connection is as follows: 'I entered the street, the road.' As I was proceeding thus, I saw the Fully Enlightened One—the chief of ascetics, the best among monks, placed at the head of the Sangha of bhikkhus and surrounded by them. 'I offered it to the Buddha' means: having seen him, I raised that flower with both hands and offered it to the Buddha, the Blessed One Phussa; that is, I paid homage. This is the meaning.

28-29. Aṭṭhamāpadāne aloṇapaṇṇabhakkhomhīti khīrapaṇṇādīni uñchācariyāya āharitvā loṇavirahitāni paṇṇāni pacitvā bhakkhāmi, aloṇapaṇṇabhakkho [P 0.0470] amhi bhavāmīti attho. Niyamesu ca saṃvutoti niyamasaññitesu pāṇātipātāveramaṇiādīsu niccapañcasīlesu saṃvuto pihitoti attho. Pātarāse anuppatteti purebhattakāle anuppatte. Siddhattho upagacchi manti mama samīpaṃ siddhattho bhagavā upagañchi sampāpuṇi. Tāhaṃ buddhassa pādāsinti ahaṃ taṃ aloṇapaṇṇaṃ tassa buddhassa adāsinti attho.

28-29. In the eighth Apadāna, 'I am one who eats unsalted leaves' means: having gathered milk-leaves and so on by gleaning, I cook the leaves without salt and eat them; I am one who eats unsalted leaves.
