This is the meaning. 'And restrained in the observances' means restrained in the permanent five precepts, such as abstention from destroying living beings, which are called 'observances.' This is the meaning. 'When the morning meal arrived' means when the forenoon mealtime arrived. 'Siddhattha approached me' means the Blessed One Siddhattha approached, drew near to me. 'I gave that to the Buddha' means I gave those unsalted leaves to that Buddha. This is the meaning.

Navamāpadānaṃ uttānameva.

The ninth Apadāna is straightforward in meaning.

37-38. Dasamāpadāne sikhinaṃ sikhinaṃ yathāti sarīrato nikkhantachabbaṇṇaraṃsīhi obhāsayantaṃ jalantaṃ sikhīnaṃ sikhībhagavantaṃ sikhīnaṃ yathā jalamānaaggikkhandhaṃ viya. Aggajaṃ pupphamādāyāti aggajanāmakaṃ pupphaṃ gahetvā buddhassa sikhissa bhagavato abhiropayiṃ pūjesinti attho.

37-38. In the tenth Apadāna, 'like the crested one' means the Blessed One Sikhī, who is crested, illuminating and blazing with the six-colored rays issuing from his body, like a blazing mass of fire. 'Having taken the Aggaja flower' means: having taken the flower named Aggaja, I offered it to the Buddha, the Blessed One Sikhī; that is, I paid homage. This is the meaning.

Chabbīsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-sixth chapter is completed.

27. Padumukkhipavaggo

27. The Padumukkhipa Chapter

1-10. Ākāsukkhipiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Ākāsukkhipiya.

1-2. Sattavīsatime [M 2.0191][V 2.0185] vagge paṭhamāpadāne jalajagge duve gayhāti jale udake jāte agge uppalādayo dve pupphe gahetvā buddhassa samīpaṃ gantvā ekaṃ pupphaṃ pādesu nikkhipiṃ pūjesiṃ, ekaṃ pupphaṃ ākāse khipinti attho.

1-2. In the first Apadāna of the twenty-seventh chapter, 'Having taken two excellent water-born ones' means: having taken two excellent flowers born in the water, such as water lilies, I went near the Buddha, placed one flower at his feet and paid homage, and threw one flower into the sky. This is the meaning.

Dutiyāpadānaṃ pākaṭameva.

The second Apadāna is indeed clear.

10. Tatiyāpadāne bodhiyā pādaputtameti uttame bodhipādape. Aḍḍhacandaṃ mayā dinnanti tasmiṃ bodhimūle aḍḍhacandākārena mayā anekapupphāni pūjitānīti attho. Dharaṇīruhapādapeti rukkhapabbataratanādayo dhāretīti dharaṇī, pathavī, dharaṇiyā ruhati patiṭṭhahatīti dharaṇīruho, pādasaṅkhātena mūlena udakaṃ pivati khandhaviṭapādīsu patthariyatīti pādapo, dharaṇīruho ca so pādapo ceti dharaṇīruhapādapo, tasmiṃ dharaṇīruhapādape pupphaṃ mayā pūjitanti attho.

10. In the third Apadāna, 'the supreme tree of awakening' refers to the excellent Bodhi tree. 'A half-moon was given by me' means: at the root of that Bodhi tree, I paid homage with many flowers in the shape of a half-moon. This is the meaning. 'At the earth-growing tree': The earth (`pathavī`) is called `dharaṇī` because it holds (`dhāreti`) things like trees, mountains, and jewels. A `dharaṇīruha` is so called because it grows (`ruhati`) established on the earth. A `pādapa` is so called because it drinks (`pivati`) water with its root, which is called a 'foot' (`pāda`), and spreads it through its trunk, branches, and so on. It is an earth-grower and a tree, thus it is a `dharaṇīruhapādapo`, an 'earth-growing tree.' The meaning is: I paid homage with a flower at that earth-growing tree.

Catutthāpadānaṃ uttānatthameva.

The fourth Apadāna is self-explanatory.

18-19. Pañcamāpadāne himavantassāvidūreti himavantassa āsanne. Romaso nāma pabbatoti rukkhalatāgumbābhāvā kevalaṃ dabbatiṇādisañchannattā romaso nāma pabbato ahosi. Tamhi pabbatapādamhīti [P 0.0471] tasmiṃ pabbatapariyante. Samaṇo bhāvitindriyoti samitapāpo vūpasantakileso samaṇo vaḍḍhitaindriyo, rakkhitacakkhundriyādiindriyoti attho. Atha vā vaḍḍhitaindriyo vaḍḍhitasaddhindriyādiindriyoti attho. Tassa samaṇassa ahaṃ biḷāliāluve gahetvā adāsinti attho.

18-19. In the fifth Apadāna, 'not far from the Himālaya' means near the Himālaya. 'A mountain named Romasa': there was a mountain named Romasa because, being devoid of trees, creepers, and bushes, it was covered only with dabba grass and the like. 'At the foot of that mountain' means at the edge of that mountain. 'A recluse with developed faculties' means a recluse (`samaṇa`) who has quelled evil and whose defilements are appeased, one with developed faculties; that is, one whose faculties, such as the eye-faculty, are guarded. Or else, 'with developed faculties' means one whose faculties, such as the faculty of faith, are developed. The meaning is: having taken cat-tail rushes, I gave them to that recluse.

Chaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamanavamadasamāpadānāni uttānatthānevāti.

The sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth Apadānas have straightforward meanings.

Sattavīsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-seventh chapter is complete.

28. Suvaṇṇabibbohanavaggo

28. The Suvaṇṇabibbohana Chapter

1-10. Suvaṇṇabibbohaniyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Suvaṇṇabibbohaniya.

Aṭṭhavīsatime [V 2.0186] vagge paṭhamāpadānaṃ uttānameva.

The first Apadāna in the twenty-eighth chapter is straightforward.

5. Dutiyāpadāne manomayena kāyenāti yathā cittavasena pavattakāyenāti attho.

5. In the second Apadāna, 'with a mind-made body' means with a body that operates in accordance with the mind. This is the meaning.

10. Tatiyāpadāne [M 2.0192] mahāsamuddaṃ nissāyāti mahāsāgarāsanne ṭhitassa pabbatassa antare pabbataleṇeti attho. Siddhattho bhagavā vivekakāmatāya vasati paṭivasatīti attho. Paccuggantvānakāsahanti ahaṃ tassa bhagavato paṭiuggantvā samīpaṃ gantvā vandanādipuññaṃ akāsinti attho. Caṅkoṭakamadāsahanti siddhatthassa bhagavato ahaṃ pupphabharitaṃ caṅkoṭakaṃ kadambaṃ adāsiṃ pūjesinti attho.

10. In the third Apadāna, 'relying on the great ocean' means in a mountain cave within a mountain situated near the great ocean. This is the meaning. 'The Blessed One Siddhattha dwells' means he dwelt and resided there out of a desire for seclusion. This is the meaning. 'Having gone out to meet him, I did' means: having gone out to meet that Blessed One and having approached him, I performed meritorious deeds such as paying homage. This is the meaning. 'I gave a caṅkoṭaka' means: I gave a caṅkoṭaka, a kadamba branch full of flowers, to the Blessed One Siddhattha and paid homage. This is the meaning.

14. Catutthāpadāne akakkasacittassāthāti apharusacittassa, atha-saddo padapūraṇe.

14. In the fourth Apadāna, 'of one with a non-harsh mind' (akakkasacittassa) means of one with a non-rough mind (apharusacittassa); the word 'atha' is a metrical expletive.

19. Pañcamāpadāne udumbare vasantassāti udumbararukkhamūle rukkhacchāyāya vasantassa tissassa bhagavato. Niyate paṇṇasanthareti niyāmite paṭibaddhe paṇṇasanthare sākhābhaṅgāsane nisinnassa. Vutthokāso mayā dinnoti vivittokāse maṇḍapadvārādīhi pihitokāso mayā dinno sampāditoti attho.

19. In the fifth Apadāna, 'of one dwelling at the udumbara' means of the Blessed One Tissa, who was dwelling at the root of an udumbara tree in its shade. 'On a fixed leaf-bed' means of one sitting on a seat of broken branches, on a fixed and prepared leaf-bed. 'A secluded space was given by me' means: a secluded space, one enclosed by the door of a pavilion and so on, was given, was provided by me. This is the meaning.

24. Chaṭṭhāpadāne potthadānaṃ mayā dinnanti potthavaṭṭiṃ potthachalliṃ tāḷetvā kataṃ sāṭakaṃ visamaṃ gophāsukena ghaṃsitvā nimmitaṃ suttaṃ gahetvā kantitvā tena suttena nisīdanatthāya vā bhūmattharaṇatthāya vā sāṭakaṃ vāyāpetvā taṃ sāṭakaṃ mayā ratanattayassa dinnanti attho.

24. In the sixth Apadāna, 'A gift of pottha was given by me' means: having taken thread that was produced by beating a roll of bark or bark-rind and rubbing the uneven material with a cow's rib, and having spun it, and then having had a cloth woven with that thread for use either as a sitting-cloth or as a ground-covering—that cloth was given by me to the Triple Gem. This is the meaning.

27. Sattamāpadāne candabhāgānadītīreti candabhāgāya nāma nadiyā tīrato, nissakke bhummavacanaṃ[V 2.0187]. Anusotanti sotassa anu heṭṭhāgaṅgaṃ [P 0.0472] vajāmi gacchāmi ahanti attho. Satta māluvapupphāni, citamāropayiṃ ahanti ahaṃ māluvapupphāni satta pattāni gahetvā citake vālukarāsimhi vālukāhi thūpaṃ katvā pūjesinti attho.

27. In the seventh Apadāna, 'on the bank of the river Candabhāgā' means from the bank of the river named Candabhāgā; this is the locative case used in an ablative sense. 'Downstream' means: 'I go along the stream, downstream.' This is the meaning. 'Seven māluvā flowers, I placed on the pyre' means: 'Having taken seven māluvā flowers, I paid homage by making a stūpa with sand on a heap of sand, a sand-pyre.' This is the meaning.

31-32. Aṭṭhamāpadāne mahāsindhu sudassanāti sundaradassanasundarodakadhavalapulinopasobhitattā suṭṭhu manoharā mahāsindhu nāma vārinadī ahosi. Tattha tissaṃ sindhuvārinadiyaṃ sappabhāsaṃ pabhāya sahitaṃ sudassanaṃ sundararūpaṃ paramopasame yuttaṃ uttame upasame yuttaṃ samaṅgībhūtaṃ vītarāgaṃ ahaṃ addasanti attho. Disvāhaṃ vimhitāsayoti [M 2.0193] “evarūpaṃ bhayānakaṃ himavantaṃ kathaṃ sampatto”ti vimhitaajjhāsayo acchariyabbhutacittoti attho. Āluvaṃ tassa pādāsinti tassa arahato ahaṃ pasannamānaso āluvakandaṃ pādāsiṃ ādarena adāsinti attho.

31-32. In the eighth Apadāna, 'the great Sindhu, fair to see': the great river named Sindhu was exceedingly charming because it was adorned with beautiful sights, lovely water, and white sandbanks. The meaning is: 'There, in that river Sindhu, I saw Tissa, radiant and endowed with splendor, fair to see and of beautiful form, yoked to supreme peace, endowed with the highest tranquility, accomplished, and free from lust.' 'Having seen him, I was astonished' means my mind was amazed and filled with wonder, thinking: 'How did he reach such a fearsome Himālaya?' This is the meaning. 'I gave him an edible root' means: 'With a confident mind, I respectfully gave an edible root (āluvakanda) to that Arahant.' This is the meaning.

Navamadasamāpadānāni uttānānevāti.

The ninth and tenth Apadānas are simple.

Aṭṭhavīsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the twenty-eighth chapter is complete.

29. Paṇṇadāyakavaggo

29. The Chapter of the Leaf-Giver

1-10. Paṇṇadāyakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Paṇṇadāyaka.

1-2. Ekūnatiṃsatime [V 2.0188] vagge paṭhamāpadāne paṇṇabhojanabhojanoti khīrapaṇṇādibhojanassa bhuñjanatthāya paṇṇasālāya nisinno amhi bhavāmīti attho. Upaviṭṭhañca maṃ santanti paṇṇasālāyaṃ upaviṭṭhaṃ santaṃ vijjamānaṃ maṃ. Upāgacchi mahāisīti mahante sīlādikhandhe esanato mahāisi. Lokapajjoto lokapadīpo siddhattho bhagavā upagacchi, mama samīpaṃ agamāsīti attho. Nisinnassa paṇṇasanthareti upagantvā paṇṇasanthare nisinnassa khādanatthāya seditaṃ paṇṇaṃ mayā dinnanti sambandho.

1-2. In the first Apadāna of the twenty-ninth chapter, 'paṇṇabhojanabhojano' means: 'I was seated in a leaf-hut for the purpose of eating food such as milk-leaves.' 'Upaviṭṭhañca maṃ santaṃ' means: 'I, being present, was seated in the leaf-hut.' 'Upāgacchi mahāisi' means 'the great sage approached'. A great sage (mahāisi) is one who seeks the great aggregates of virtue and so on. The Light of the World, the Lamp of the World, the Blessed One Siddhattha, approached, meaning he came near me. 'Nisinnassa paṇṇasanthare' is connected thus: having approached, I gave cooked leaves for eating to him who was seated on a spread of leaves.

5-7. Dutiyāpadāne sinerusamasantoso dharaṇīsamasādiso siddhattho bhagavāti sambandho. Vuṭṭhahitvā samādhimhāti nirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā visuṃ hutvāti attho. Bhikkhāya mamupaṭṭhitoti bhikkhācāravelāya “ajja mama yo koci kiñci dānaṃ dadāti, tassa mahapphala”nti cintetvā nisinnassa mama santikaṃ samīpaṃ upaṭṭhito samīpamāgatoti attho. Harītakaṃ…pe… phārusakaphalāni cāti evaṃ sabbaṃ taṃ phalaṃ sabbalokānukampino tassa siddhatthassa mahesissa mayā vippasannena cetasā dinnanti attho.

5-7. In the second Apadāna, the connection is: 'The Blessed One Siddhattha, as tranquil as Sineru, similar to the earth.' 'Vuṭṭhahitvā samādhimhā' means having arisen from the attainment of cessation, that is, having stood apart. 'Bhikkhāya mamupaṭṭhito' means that at the time of the alms-round, thinking, 'Today, whoever gives me any gift will receive great fruit,' he approached me where I was seated; that is, he came near to me. 'Harītakaṃ…pe… phārusakaphalāni ca' means that all those fruits were given by me with a confident mind to that great sage Siddhattha, the one compassionate to all the world; this is the meaning.

11-12. Tatiyāpadāne [P 0.0473] sīhaṃ yathā vanacaranti vane caramānaṃ sīharājaṃ iva caramānaṃ siddhatthaṃ bhagavantanti sambandho. Nisabhājāniyaṃ yathāti vasabho, nisabho, visabho, āsabhoti cattāro gavajeṭṭhakā. Tesu gavasatassa jeṭṭhako vasabho, gavasahassassa jeṭṭhako nisabho, gavasatasahassassa jeṭṭhako visabho, gavakoṭisatasahassassa [M 2.0194] jeṭṭhako āsabho. Idha pana āsabho “nisabho”ti vutto, ājānīyaṃ abhītaṃ niccalaṃ usabharājaṃ ivāti attho. Kakudhaṃ vilasantaṃvāti pupphapallavehi sobhamānaṃ kakudharukkhaṃ iva narāsabhaṃ narānaṃ āsabhaṃ uttamaṃ āgacchantaṃ siddhatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā saddhāya sampayuttattā vippasannena cetasā paccuggamanaṃ akāsinti attho.

11-12. In the third Apadāna, 'sīhaṃ yathā vanacaraṃ' is connected thus: the Blessed One Siddhattha wandered like a lion-king roaming in the forest. 'Nisabhājāniyaṃ yathā' refers to four types of foremost bulls: vasabha, nisabha, visabha, and āsabha. Among them, vasabha is the foremost of a hundred cattle, nisabha of a thousand, visabha of a hundred thousand, and āsabha of a hundred thousand crores. Here, however, āsabha is referred to as 'nisabha.' This means 'like a fearless, unwavering bull-king of noble breed.' 'Kakudhaṃ vilasantaṃva' means: 'Seeing the Blessed One Siddhattha, the bull among men, approaching like a kakudha tree resplendent with flowers and shoots, and being filled with faith, I went forth to meet him with a confident mind'; this is the meaning.

Catutthāpadānādīni dasamāvasānāni suviññeyyānevāti.

The Apadānas from the fourth to the tenth are indeed easy to understand.

Ekūnatiṃsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Twenty-ninth Chapter is complete.

30. Citakapūjakavaggo

30. The Chapter of the Pyre-Worshipper

1-10. Citakapūjakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder who Worshipped a Pyre and others.

1-2. Tiṃsatime [V 2.0189] vagge paṭhamāpadāne āhutiṃ yiṭṭhukāmohanti pūjāsakkāraṃ kāretukāmo ahaṃ. Nānāpupphaṃ samānayinti nānā anekavidhaṃ campakasalalādipupphaṃ saṃ suṭṭhu ānayiṃ, rāsiṃ akāsinti attho. Sikhino lokabandhunoti sakalalokattayabandhussa ñātakassa sikhissa bhagavato parinibbutassa citakaṃ āḷāhanacitakaṃ dārurāsiṃ jalantaṃ ādittaṃ disvā tañca mayā rāsīkataṃ pupphaṃ okiriṃ pūjesinti attho.

1-2. In the first apadāna of the thirtieth chapter, 'āhutiṃ yiṭṭhukāmohaṃ' means: 'I was desirous of making an offering and paying homage.' 'Nānāpupphaṃ samānayiṃ' means: 'I brought various kinds of flowers—such as campaka and salala—and made a heap.' 'Sikhino lokabandhuno' means: 'Seeing the blazing cremation pyre—a pile of wood—of the Blessed One Sikhi, the Kinsman of the World, who had attained final Nibbāna, I scattered the heap of flowers I had gathered; that is, I worshipped.'

6-7. Dutiyāpadāne ajinuttaravāsanoti ajinamigacammaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā nivāsino acchādanoti attho. Abhiññā pañca nibbattāti iddhividhādayo pañca abhiññāyo pañca ñāṇāni nibbattā uppāditā nipphāditā. Candassa parimajjakoti candamaṇḍalassa samantato majjako, phuṭṭho ahosinti attho. Vipassiṃ lokapajjotanti sakalalokattaye padīpasadisaṃ vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ mama santikaṃ abhigataṃ visesena sampattaṃ āgataṃ. Disvā pāricchattakapupphānīti devalokato pāricchattakapupphāni āharitvā vipassissa satthuno matthake chattākārena ahaṃ dhāresinti attho.

6-7. In the second apadāna, 'ajinuttaravāsano' means one who wears a deer-hide as an upper robe; that is, a covering. 'Abhiññā pañca nibbattā' means the five higher knowledges—the five knowledges beginning with the kinds of psychic power—were produced and accomplished. 'Candassa parimajjako' means a polisher all around the lunar orb; that is, I touched it. 'Vipassiṃ lokapajjotaṃ' means the Blessed One Vipassi, like a lamp in the entire triple world, had come near me, had specially arrived. 'Disvā pāricchattakapupphāni' means: 'Having brought coral-tree flowers from the world of the devas, I held them like a parasol over the head of the Teacher Vipassi.'

11-13. Tatiyāpadāne putto mama pabbajitoti mayhaṃ putto saddhāya pabbajito. Kāsāyavasano tadāti tasmiṃ pabbajitakāle kāsāyanivattho[P 0.0474], na bāhirakapabbajjāya pabbajitoti attho. So [M 2.0195] ca buddhattaṃ sampattoti so mayhaṃ putto catūsu buddhesu sāvakabuddhabhāvaṃ saṃ suṭṭhu patto, arahattaṃ pattoti attho. Nibbuto lokapūjitoti sakalalokehi katasakkāro khandhaparinibbānena parinibbutoti attho. Vicinanto sakaṃ puttanti ahaṃ tassa gatadesaṃ pucchitvā sakaṃ puttaṃ vicinanto pacchato agamaṃ, anugato asmīti attho. Nibbutassa mahantassāti mahantehi sīlakkhandhādīhi yuttattā mahantassa tassa mama puttassa arahato ādahanaṭṭhāne citakaṃ citakaṭṭhānaṃ ahaṃ agamāsinti attho. Paggayha añjaliṃ tatthāti tasmiṃ ādahanaṭṭhāne [V 2.0190] añjaliṃ dasaṅgulisamodhānaṃ paggahetvā sirasi katvā ahaṃ citakaṃ dahanadārurāsiṃ vanditvā paṇāmaṃ katvā setacchattañca paggayhāti na kevalameva vanditvā dhavalacchattañca paggayha ukkhipitvā ahaṃ āropesiṃ patiṭṭhapesinti attho.

11-13. In the third apadāna, 'putto mama pabbajito' means my son went forth out of faith. 'Kāsāyavasano tadā' means at that time he was robed in saffron; that is, he did not go forth into an external sect. 'So ca buddhattaṃ sampatto' means my son fully attained the state of a disciple-buddha; that is, he attained arahantship. 'Nibbuto lokapūjito' means he was revered by the entire world and attained final Nibbāna through the extinguishing of the aggregates. 'Vicinanto sakaṃ puttaṃ' means I inquired about his destination and followed behind, searching for my own son. 'Nibbutassa mahantassa' means I went to the cremation site, the place of the pyre, for that great one, my son, the arahant endowed with great qualities like the aggregate of virtue. 'Paggayha añjaliṃ tattha' means at that cremation site, I raised my joined palms to my head, paid homage to the pyre of burning wood, and not only that, but also lifted up and erected a white parasol.

17-18. Catutthāpadāne anuggatamhi ādicceti sūriye anuggate anuṭṭhite paccūsakāleti attho. Pasādo vipulo ahūti rogapīḷitassa mayhaṃ cittappasādo vipulo atireko buddhānussaraṇena ahu ahosi. Mahesino buddhaseṭṭhassa lokamhi pātubhāvo pākaṭabhāvo ahosīti sambandho. Ghosamassosahaṃ tatthāti tasmiṃ pātubhāve sati “ahaṃ gilāno buddho uppanno”ti ghosaṃ assosiṃ. Na ca passāmi taṃ jinanti taṃ jitapañcamāraṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ na passāmi, bāḷhagilānattā gantvā passituṃ na sakkomīti attho. Maraṇañca anuppattoti maraṇāsannakālaṃ anuppatto, āsannamaraṇo hutvāti attho. Buddhasaññamanussarinti buddhotināmaṃ anussariṃ, buddhārammaṇaṃ manasi akāsinti attho.

17-18. In the fourth apadāna, 'anuggatamhi ādicce' means before sunrise, at the time of dawn, when the sun has not yet risen. 'Pasādo vipulo ahū' means that for me, afflicted by illness, a great and extraordinary confidence of mind arose due to the recollection of the Buddha. The connection is with 'mahesino...': 'The manifestation, the appearance in the world of the Great Sage, the Supreme Buddha, took place.' 'Ghosamassosahaṃ tattha' means: 'At the time of that manifestation, I heard the announcement, "A Buddha has arisen." I myself was sick.' 'Na ca passāmi taṃ jinaṃ' means: 'I do not see that Victor, the Perfectly Enlightened One who has conquered the five Māras; because of my severe illness, I am unable to go and see him.' 'Maraṇañca anuppatto' means: 'I have approached the time of death; that is, having become near death.' 'Buddhasaññamanussariṃ' means: 'I recollected the perception of the Buddha, making the Buddha the object of my mind.'

21-23. Pañcamāpadāne ārāmadvārā nikkhammāti ārāmadvārato saṅghassa nikkhamanadvāramaggehi attho. Gosīsaṃ santhataṃ mayāti tasmiṃ nikkhamanadvāramagge “bhagavato bhikkhusaṅghassa ca pādā mā kaddamaṃ akkamantū”ti akkamanatthāya gosīsaṭṭhiṃ mayā santharitanti attho. Anubhomi sakaṃ kammanti attano gosīsaattharaṇakammassa balena ājānīyā vātajavā sindhavā sīghavāhanādīni vipākaphalāni anubhomīti attho. Aho [M 2.0196][P 0.0475] kāraṃ paramakāranti sukhette saṅghe mayā suṭṭhu kataṃ kāraṃ appakampi kiccaṃ mahapphaladānato paramakāraṃ uttamakiccaṃ aho vimhayanti attho. Yathā tiṇadosādivirahitesu khettesu vappitaṃ sālibījaṃ mahapphalaṃ deti, evameva rāgadosādidosarahite parisuddhakāyavacīsamācāre saṅghakhette gosīsaattharaṇakammaṃ mayā kataṃ, idaṃ mahapphalaṃ detīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na aññaṃ kalamagghatīti aññaṃ bāhirasāsane kataṃ kammaṃ saṅghe katassa kārassa pūjāsakkārassa kalaṃ soḷasiṃ kalaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ na agghatīti sambandho.

21-23. In the fifth apadāna, 'ārāmadvārā nikkhammā' means by the path at the monastery gate from which the Sangha exits. 'Gosīsaṃ santhataṃ mayā' means that on that exit path, I spread sandalwood powder, thinking, 'May the feet of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus not tread on mud.' 'Anubhomi sakaṃ kammaṃ' means: 'By the power of my own kamma of spreading sandalwood powder, I experience its results, such as thoroughbred horses, Sindh horses, and other fast vehicles.' 'Aho kāraṃ paramakāraṃ' means: 'Ah, what a supreme deed is the deed I did so well in the fertile field of the Sangha! Even if a small act, it is a supreme act because it yields a great fruit.' This expresses wonder. Just as rice seeds sown in fields free from weeds and other faults yield a great harvest, so too the kamma of spreading sandalwood powder done by me in the field of the Sangha—which is pure in bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, and free from the faults of greed, hatred, and delusion—yields a great fruit. 'Na aññaṃ kalamagghati' is connected thus: 'No other deed done in an external teaching is worth a sixteenth part of the deed of offering and homage done to the Sangha.'

Chaṭṭhasattamaṭṭhamanavamadasamāpadānāni uttānānevāti.

The sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth apadānas are indeed clear.

Tiṃsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Thirtieth Chapter is complete.

31. Padumakesaravaggo

31. The Lotus Stamen Chapter

1-10. Padumakesariyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Padumakesariya and others

1-2. Ekatiṃsatime [V 2.0191] vagge paṭhamāpadāne isisaṅghe ahaṃ pubbeti ahaṃ pubbe bodhisambhārapūraṇakāle isisaṅghe paccekabuddhaisisamūhe tesaṃ samīpe himavantapabbate mātaṅgahatthikule vāraṇo caṇḍahatthī ahosinti sambandho. Manussādayo vāretīti vāraṇo, atha vā vācāya ravati koñcanādaṃ nadatīti vāraṇo. Mahesīnaṃ pasādenāti paccekabuddhamahesīnaṃ pasādena. Paccekajinaseṭṭhesu, dhutarāgesu tādisūti lokadhammehi niccalesu paccekabuddhesu padmakesaraṃ padumareṇuṃ okiriṃ avasiñcinti sambandho.

1-2. In the thirty-first chapter, the first apadāna, concerning 'in the community of seers, I in the past': In the past, during the time of fulfilling the accumulations for enlightenment, I was in a community of seers, a group of Paccekabuddha seers. Near them, on the Himālaya mountain, I was a fierce elephant, a vāraṇa, in the Mātaṅga elephant family—this is the connection. 'Vāraṇa' is one who wards off humans and others; or, alternatively, one who roars with his voice, making a sound like a crane's cry. 'Through the grace of the great seers' refers to the grace of the great Paccekabuddha seers. 'Among the foremost Paccekajinas, those who have shaken off passion, such ones' means among the Paccekabuddhas who are unshaken by worldly conditions, I scattered lotus filaments and sprinkled lotus pollen—this is the connection.

Dutiyatatiyāpadānāni uttānāni.

The second and third apadānas are straightforward.

13-16. Catutthāpadāne mahābodhimaho ahūti vipassissa bhagavato catumaggañāṇādhārabhāvato “bodhī”ti laddhanāmassa rukkhassa pūjā ahosīti attho. Rukkhaṭṭhasseva sambuddhoti assa bodhipūjāsamaye sannipatitassa mahājanassa sambuddho lokajeṭṭho narāsabho rukkhaṭṭho iva rukkhe ṭhito viya paññāyatīti attho. Bhagavā tamhi samayeti tasmiṃ bodhipūjākaraṇakāle bhagavā bhikkhusaṅghapurakkhato bhikkhusaṅghena parivuto. Vācāsabhimudīrayanti mudusiliṭṭhamadhurauttamaghosaṃ udīrayaṃ kathayanto nicchārento catusaccaṃ pakāsesi, desesīti attho. Saṃkhittena [M 2.0197] ca desentoti veneyyapuggalajjhāsayānurūpena desento saṃkhittena ca vitthārena ca desayīti attho. Vivaṭṭacchadoti rāgo [P 0.0476] chadanaṃ, doso chadanaṃ, moho chadanaṃ, sabbakilesā chadanā”ti evaṃ vuttā chadanā vivaṭā ugghāṭitā viddhaṃsitā anenāti vivaṭṭacchado, sambuddho. Taṃ mahājanaṃ desanāvasena nibbāpesi pariḷāhaṃ vūpasamesīti attho. Tassāhaṃ dhammaṃ sutvānāti tassa bhagavato desentassa dhammaṃ sutvā.

13-16. In the fourth apadāna, 'a great festival for the great Bodhi occurred' means that a festival was held for the tree that had received the name 'Bodhi' because it was the basis for the knowledge of the four paths of the Blessed One Vipassī. 'The Enlightened One as if at the tree' means that at the time of the Bodhi festival, to the great crowd that had gathered, the Enlightened One, the foremost in the world, the bull among men, appeared as if standing at the tree, as if stationed in the tree. 'The Blessed One at that time' means that during the occasion of performing the Bodhi festival, the Blessed One was attended by the Saṅgha of monks and surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. 'Uttering a sublime voice' means uttering, speaking, emitting a soft, smooth, sweet, supreme sound, he proclaimed the four truths, he taught them. 'Teaching concisely' means that teaching in accordance with the dispositions of the individuals to be trained, he taught both concisely and in detail. 'With covering unveiled' means: lust is a covering, hatred is a covering, delusion is a covering, all defilements are coverings—the coverings thus spoken of have been unveiled, opened up, and destroyed by him; thus he is the Enlightened One 'with covering unveiled.' By means of his teaching, he extinguished that great crowd, meaning he pacified their fever. 'Having heard his Dhamma' means having heard the Dhamma from that Blessed One as he was teaching.

20. Pañcamāpadāne [V 2.0192] phalahattho apekkhavāti vipassiṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā madhurāni phalāni gahetvā apekkhavā aturito saṇikaṃ assamaṃ gañchinti attho.

20. In the fifth apadāna, 'holding fruits, expectant'—having seen the Blessed One Vipassī, he took sweet fruits and, with anticipation, unhurriedly went to the hermitage; this is the meaning.

Chaṭṭhasattamāpadānāni uttānāneva.

The sixth and seventh apadānas are straightforward.

40. Aṭṭhamāpadāne niṭṭhite navakamme cāti sīmāya navakamme niṭṭhaṃ gate sati. Anulepamadāsahanti anupacchā sudhālepaṃ adāsiṃ, sudhāya lepāpesinti attho.

40. In the eighth apadāna, 'and when the new work was completed' means when the new construction on the boundary was finished. 'I gave a coating of plaster' means: I afterwards gave a coating of lime plaster, that is, I had it plastered with lime.

Navamadasamāpadānāni uttānāniyevāti.

The ninth and tenth apadānas are indeed clear.

Ekatiṃsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the thirty-first chapter is complete.

32. Ārakkhadāyakavaggo

32. The Chapter of the Giver of Protection

1-10. Ārakkhadāyakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Ārakkhadāyaka and others

Bāttiṃsatimavagge [V 2.0193] paṭhamadutiyatatiyāpadānāni suviññeyyāneva.

In the thirty-second chapter, the first, second, and third apadānas are indeed easy to understand.

16. Catutthāpadāne jalajaggehi okirinti jalajehi uttamehi uppalapadumādīhi pupphehi okiriṃ pūjesinti attho.

16. In the fourth apadāna, 'I scattered with the best of water-born flowers' means: I scattered and worshipped with the best water-born flowers, such as blue water lilies, lotuses, and so on; this is the meaning.

Pañcamāpadānaṃ uttānameva.

The fifth apadāna is self-explanatory.

26-27. Chaṭṭhāpadāne cetiyaṃ uttamaṃ nāma, sikhino lokabandhunoti sakalalokattayassa bandhuno ñātakassa sikhissa bhagavato uttamaṃ cetiyaṃ. Irīṇe janasañcaravirahite vane manussānaṃ kolāhalavirahite mahāaraññe ahosīti sambandho. Andhāhiṇḍāmahaṃ tadāti tasmiṃ kāle vane maggamūḷhabhāvena andho, na cakkhunā [M 2.0198] andho, ahaṃ āhiṇḍāmi maggaṃ pariyesāmīti attho. Pavanā nikkhamantenāti mahāvanato nikkhamantena mayā sīhāsanaṃ uttamāsanaṃ, sīhassa vā bhagavato āsanaṃ diṭṭhanti attho. Ekaṃsaṃ añjaliṃ katvāti ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvāti attho. Santhaviṃ lokanāyakanti sakalalokattayanayaṃ taṃ nibbānaṃ pāpentaṃ thomitaṃ thutiṃ akāsinti attho.

26-27. In the sixth apadāna, 'a supreme shrine by name, of Sikhi, the Kinsman of the World' means the supreme shrine of the Blessed One Sikhi, the kinsman and relative of the entire triple world. The connection is: 'In a desolate place... it was' means in a forest devoid of human traffic, in a great wilderness free from the clamor of people. 'Blind, I wandered then' means: at that time, in the forest, being blind from having lost my way, not blind in the eyes, I wandered seeking the path. 'Emerging from the wood' means: as I was emerging from the great forest, the lion-seat was seen by me—the supreme seat, or the seat of the lion, the Blessed One. 'Having made the añjali with one shoulder bare' means: having arranged my upper robe over one shoulder and placed my hands in reverence on my head. 'I praised the Leader of the World' means: I praised, I offered a eulogy, to him who leads the entire triple world to Nibbāna.

34. Sattamāpadāne [P 0.0477] sudassano mahāvīroti sundaradassano dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasampannasarīrattā manoharadassano mahāvīriyo siddhattho bhagavāti sambandho. Vasatigharamuttameti uttame vihāre vasatīti attho.

34. In the seventh apadāna, the phrase 'of good appearance, the great hero' is connected thus: the Blessed One Siddhattha was beautiful to see, delightful to behold, because his body was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, and he was of great energy. 'The supreme dwelling house' means he dwells in the most excellent monastery; this is the meaning.

Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāpadānāni uttānānevāti.

The eighth, ninth, and tenth apadānas are indeed clear.

Bāttiṃsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the thirty-second chapter is complete.

33. Umāpupphiyavaggo

33. The Umāpupphiya Chapter

1-10. Umāpupphiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-10. Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Umāpupphiya

Tettiṃsatime [V 2.0194] vagge paṭhamadutiyatatiyacatutthapañcamachaṭṭhāpadānāni uttānāniyeva.

In the thirty-third chapter, the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth apadānas are straightforward.

55. Sattamāpadāne samayaṃ agamāsahanti samūhaṃ samāgamaṭṭhānaṃ ahaṃ agamāsinti attho.

55. In the seventh apadāna, the phrase 'samayaṃ agamāsaṃ' means: 'I went to the assembly,' that is, 'I went to the place of gathering.'

62. Abbudanirabbudānīti “pakoṭisatasahassānaṃ sataṃ abbudaṃ, abbudasatasahassānaṃ sataṃ nirabbuda”nti vuttattā āyunā abbudanirabbudāni gatamahāāyuvantā manujādhipā cakkavattino khattiyā aṭṭha aṭṭha hutvā kappānaṃ pañcavīsasahassamhi āsiṃsu ahesunti attho. Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāpadānāni pākaṭānevāti.

62. Regarding 'abbudanirabbudāni': Because it is said, 'A hundred hundred-thousands of pakoṭis is an abbuda; a hundred hundred-thousands of abbudas is a nirabbuda,' the meaning is: because of their lifespan, those long-lived human lords, wheel-turning khattiyas, having lived for abbudas and nirabbudas, existed—there were eight of them—during twenty-five thousand kappas. The eighth, ninth, and tenth apadānas are indeed clear.

Tettiṃsatimavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the thirty-third chapter is finished.

34-38. Gandhodakādivaggo

34-38. The Chapter on Gandhodaka and Others

1-50. Gandhadhūpiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1-50. Commentary on the Apadānas beginning with that of the Elder Gandhadhūpiya

Catutiṃsatimavaggapañcatiṃsatimavaggachattiṃsatimavaggasattatiṃsatimavaggaaṭṭhatiṃsatimavaggā [M 2.0199][V 2.0195] uttānatthāyeva.

The thirty-fourth, thirty-fifth, thirty-sixth, thirty-seventh, and thirty-eighth chapters are all clear in meaning.

Ekūnacattālīsamavaggepi paṭhamāpadānādīni aṭṭhamāpadānantāni uttānānevāti.

In the thirty-ninth chapter, too, the apadānas from the first up to the eighth are indeed straightforward.

39. Avaṭaphalavaggo

39. The Avaṭaphala Chapter

9. Soṇakoṭivīsattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Soṇa Koṭivīsa

Navamāpadāne [V 2.0196] pana vipassino pāvacanetiādikaṃ āyasmato soṇassa koṭivīsattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle mahāvibhave seṭṭhikule nibbatto vuddhippatto seṭṭhi hutvā upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso [P 0.0478] bhagavato caṅkamanaṭṭhāne sudhāya parikammaṃ kāretvā ekañca leṇaṃ kāretvā nānāvirāgavatthehi leṇabhūmiyā santharitvā upari vitānañca katvā cātuddisassa saṅghassa niyyādetvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā paṇidhānaṃ akāsi. Satthā anumodanaṃ akāsi. So tena kusalakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ kappe parinibbute kassapadasabale anuppanne amhākaṃ bhagavati bārāṇasiyaṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto gaṅgātīre paṇṇasālaṃ karitvā vasantaṃ ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ temāsaṃ catūhi paccayehi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahi. Paccekabuddho vuṭṭhavasso paripuṇṇaparikkhāro gandhamādanameva agamāsi. Sopi kulaputto yāvajīvaṃ tattha puññāni katvā tato cavitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle campānagare aggaseṭṭhissa gehe paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa paṭisandhiggahaṇakālato paṭṭhāya seṭṭhissa mahābhogakkhandho abhivaḍḍhi. Tassa mātukucchito nikkhamanadivase sakalanagare mahālābhasakkārasammāno ahosi, tassa pubbe paccekabuddhassa satasahassagghanikarattakambalapariccāgena suvaṇṇavaṇṇo sukhumālataro ca attabhāvo ahosi, tenassa soṇoti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So [M 2.0200] mahatā parivārena abhivaḍḍhi. Tassa hatthapādatalāni bandhujīvakapupphavaṇṇāni ahesuṃ, tesaṃ satavāraṃ vihatakappāsaṃ viya mudusamphasso ahosi. Pādatalesu maṇikuṇḍalāvaṭṭavaṇṇalomāni jāyiṃsu. Vayappattassa tassa tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavike tayo pāsāde kārāpetvā nāṭakitthiyo upaṭṭhāpesuṃ. So tattha mahatiṃ sampattiṃ anubhavanto devakumāro viya paṭivasati.

Now, in the ninth apadāna, the one beginning 'In Vipassī's dispensation...' is the apadāna of the Venerable Elder Soṇa Koṭivīsa. This elder, too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that are a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī in a treasurer's family of great wealth. Having come of age and become a treasurer, he went to the monastery with other lay followers, heard the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma, and with a confident mind, had the surface of the Blessed One's walking path prepared with plaster. He also had a cave dwelling built, had its floor strewn with cloths of various colors, and had a canopy set up overhead. Having dedicated it to the Sangha of the four directions, he gave a great offering for seven days and made an aspiration. The Teacher gave his approval. By that wholesome kamma, wandering through transmigrations among devas and humans and experiencing the twofold success, in this kappa, after the Parinibbāna of Kassapa of the Ten Powers but before our Blessed One arose, he was reborn in a clansman's house in Bārāṇasī. Having reached maturity, he built a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges and for three months respectfully attended with the four requisites upon a certain paccekabuddha who was dwelling there. Having completed the rains-residence, his requisites complete, the paccekabuddha went to Gandhamādana mountain. That clansman, having made merit there for as long as he lived, passed away from there and wandered through transmigrations among devas and humans. In the time of our Blessed One, he took conception in the house of the chief treasurer in Campā. From the time he took conception, the treasurer's great mass of wealth increased. On the day he emerged from his mother's womb, there was great gain, honor, and respect in the entire city. Because of his previous gift of a red blanket worth a hundred thousand to the paccekabuddha, his physical frame was gold-colored and extremely delicate. For that reason, they gave him the name Soṇa. He grew up with a great retinue. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were the color of the bandhujīvaka flower, and their touch was as soft as cotton carded a hundred times. On the soles of his feet, hairs grew in whorls the color of jeweled earrings. When he came of age, they had three mansions built for him suitable for the three seasons and provided him with dancing women. Dwelling there, enjoying great prosperity, he lived like a young deva.

Atha amhākaṃ bhagavati sabbaññutaṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakke rājagahaṃ upanissāya viharante bimbisāraraññā pakkosāpito tehi asītiyā gāmikasahassehi saddhiṃ rājagahaṃ āgato satthu [V 2.0197] santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā laddhūpasampado satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā janasaṃsaggapariharaṇatthaṃ [P 0.0479] sītavane vihāsi. So tattha vasanto “mama sarīraṃ sukhumālaṃ, na ca sakkā sukheneva sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ, kāyaṃ kilametvāpi samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāya padhānamanuyuñjanto pādatalesu phoṭesu uṭṭhitesupi vedanaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā daḷhaṃ vīriyaṃ karonto accāraddhavīriyatāya visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto “evaṃ ahaṃ vāyamantopi maggaphalāni nibbattetuṃ na sakkomi, kiṃ me pabbajjāya, hīnāyāvattitvā bhoge ca bhuñjāmi, puññāni ca karissāmī”ti cintesi. Atha satthā tassa cittācāraṃ ñatvā tattha gantvā vīṇopamovādena (mahāva. 243) ovaditvā vīriyasamatāyojanavidhiṃ dassento kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā gijjhakūṭaṃ gato. Soṇopi kho satthu santikā ovādaṃ labhitvā vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

Then, when our Blessed One had attained perfect enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, while he was dwelling near Rājagaha, Soṇa was summoned by King Bimbisāra. He went to Rājagaha with eighty thousand village headmen, approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. Having obtained his parents' permission, he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One and received the higher ordination. Taking a meditation subject from the Teacher, he dwelled in the Cool Wood to avoid contact with people. While dwelling there, he thought: 'My body is delicate, and happiness cannot be attained through happiness. It is proper to practice the ascetic's duties even by wearying the body.' Having undertaken only standing and walking meditation, he strove diligently. Though blisters arose on the soles of his feet, he looked on at the feeling with equanimity and made a firm effort. But because his energy was overly strenuous, he was unable to produce a special attainment. He thought: 'Though I am striving in this way, I cannot produce the paths and fruits. What is the use of this going forth for me? I will return to the lower life, enjoy my wealth, and make merit.' Then the Teacher, knowing the trend of his thought, went there and exhorted him with the simile of the lute (Mv 243), showing him the method of applying balanced energy. Having clarified his meditation subject, the Teacher went to the Vulture Peak. Having received the Teacher's exhortation, Soṇa applied balanced energy, roused insight, and became established in arahantship.

49. So arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento vipassino pāvacanetiādimāha. Tattha vipassīti visesena, vividhaṃ vā passatīti vipassī. Pāvacaneti pakārena vuccatīti pāvacanaṃ, piṭakattayaṃ. Tassa vipassino tasmiṃ pāvacaneti attho. Leṇanti linante nilīyante etthāti leṇaṃ vihāraṃ. Bandhumārājadhāniyāti bandhanti kulaparamparāya vasena aññamaññaṃ sambajjhantīti bandhū, ñātakā. Te ettha paṭivasantīti bandhumā, bandhu assa atthīti [M 2.0201] vā bandhumā. Rājūnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānanti rājadhānī, bandhumā ca sā rājadhānī ceti bandhumārājadhānī, tassā bandhumārājadhāniyā, leṇaṃ mayā katanti sambandho. Sesamettha uttānatthamevāti.

49. Having become an Arahant, recollecting his own past kamma and filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his former life, beginning with the words, 'In Vipassī's dispensation…' Herein, `vipassī` means 'one who sees distinctly' or 'one who sees in various ways.' `Pāvacana` (dispensation) means that which is spoken in a special way, that is, the Tipiṭaka. The meaning is: 'in the dispensation of that Vipassī.' `Leṇa` (shelter) is a place where one hides or takes refuge, that is, a monastery. Regarding 'the royal capital of Bandhumā': `Bandhū` are relatives, so called because they are mutually connected by family lineage. Because they dwell there, it is called `Bandhumā`, or because it has relatives, it is `Bandhumā`. A `rājadhānī` is the dwelling place of kings. `Bandhumā` and that `rājadhānī` together is `Bandhumārājadhānī`. The connection is: 'a shelter was made by me in the royal capital of Bandhumā.' The rest here is straightforward in meaning.

Soṇakoṭivīsattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Soṇa Koṭivīsa is complete.

10. Pubbakammapilotikabuddhaapadānavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pubbakammapilotika.

64. Dasamāpadāne anotattasarāsanneti pabbatakūṭehi paṭicchannattā candimasūriyānaṃ santāpehi otattaṃ uṇhaṃ udakaṃ ettha natthīti anotatto. Saranti gacchanti pabhavanti sandanti etasmā mahānadiyoti saro. Sīhamukhādīhi nikkhantā mahānadiyo tikkhattuṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nikkhantanikkhantadisābhāgena saranti gacchantīti attho. Anotatto ca so saro [V 2.0198] cāti anotattasaro[P 0.0480]. Tassa āsannaṃ samīpaṭṭhānanti anotattasarāsannaṃ, tasmiṃ anotattasarāsanne, samīpeti attho. Ramaṇīyeti devadānavagandhabbakinnaroragabuddhapaccekabuddhādīhi ramitabbaṃ allīyitabbanti ramaṇīyaṃ, tasmiṃ ramaṇīye. Silātaleti ekagghanapabbatasilātaleti attho. Nānāratanapajjoteti padumarāgaveḷuriyādinānāanekehi ratanehi pajjote pakārena jotamāne. Nānāgandhavanantareti nānappakārehi candanāgarukappūratamālatilakāsokanāgapunnāgaketakādīhi anekehi sugandhapupphehi gahanībhūtavanantare silātaleti sambandho.

64. In the tenth Apadāna, 'near Anotattasara': because it is covered by mountain peaks, the water there is not heated by the heat of the sun and moon, hence it is called Anotatta. Because great rivers flow, go forth, originate, and stream from it, it is called a lake (sara). The meaning is that the great rivers, emerging from sources such as the mouths of lions, having circumambulated it three times, flow forth in the direction of their emergence. Anotatta and that lake together form Anotattasara. Its proximity means a nearby place—thus, 'near Anotattasara,' meaning nearby. 'Delightful' means it is a place to be delighted in and resorted to by devas, dānavas, gandhabbas, kinnaras, uragas, Buddhas, and Paccekabuddhas. 'On the rocky plateau' means on a single, solid mountain plateau. 'Illuminated by various jewels' means shining brightly with many diverse gems such as ruby, beryl, and others. 'Among fragrant groves of diverse scents'—the connection is to 'on the rocky plateau'—means amidst dense forests filled with various kinds of fragrant flowers such as sandalwood, agarwood, camphor, tamāla, tilaka, aśoka, nāga, punnāga, and ketaka.

65. Guṇamahantatāya saṅkhyāmahantatāya ca mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena, pareto parivuto lokanāyako lokattayasāmisammāsambuddho tattha silāsane nisinno attano pubbāni kammāni byākarī visesena pākaṭamakāsīti attho. Sesamettha heṭṭhā buddhāpadāne (apa. thera 1.1.1 ādayo) vuttattā uttānatthattā ca suviññeyyameva. Buddhāpadāne antogadhampi idhāpadāne kusalākusalaṃ kammasaṃsūcakattā vaggasaṅgahavasena dhammasaṅgāhakattherā saṅgāyiṃsūti.

65. Due to the greatness of virtues and the vastness of numbers, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikkhus, the Leader of the World, the Master of the Three Worlds, the Perfectly Enlightened One, seated there on the stone seat, declared his past deeds, making them especially manifest—this is the meaning. The rest here, as stated before in the Buddhāpadāna (Ap. Thera 1.1.1, etc.), is easily understood because its meaning is plain. Even what is included within the Buddhāpadāna, the elder compilers of the Dhamma recited here in this Apadāna by way of chapter collection because it is indicative of wholesome and unwholesome kamma.

Pubbakammapilotikabuddhaapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Pubbakammapilotika Apadāna of the Buddha is complete.

Ekūnacattālīsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the thirty-ninth chapter is complete.

40. Pilindavacchavaggo

40. The Pilindavaccha Chapter

1. Pilindavacchattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pilindavaccha

Cattālīsamavagge [M 2.0202][V 2.0199] apadāne nagare haṃsavatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato pilindavacchattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare dovārikakule nibbatto mahaddhano mahābhogo ahosi. So koṭisannicitadhanarāsiṃ oloketvā raho nisinno “imaṃ sabbadhanaṃ mayā sammā gahetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā “buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbaparikkhāradānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā chattasatasahassaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaparibhogaparikkhārānipi satasahassavasena kāretvā padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Evaṃ sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā pariyosānadivase nibbānādhigamaṃ patthetvā yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā [P 0.0481] jīvitapariyosāne devaloke nibbatto cha kāmāvacare dibbasampattiyo anubhavitvā manussesu ca cakkavattiādisampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde brāhmaṇakule nibbatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto gottavasena pilindavacchoti pākaṭo ahosi.

In the fortieth chapter of the Apadāna, the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Pilindavaccha begins with 'In the city of Haṃsavatī,' and so forth. He too, having performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas, accumulating merits here and there as a supporting condition for liberation, was, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, born into a gatekeeper's family in the city of Haṃsavatī and was very wealthy and prosperous. Observing his vast heap of wealth, he sat in seclusion and thought, 'It is fitting for me to make good use of this entire wealth before I go.' Resolving, 'It is fitting to give a gift of all requisites to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha,' he had one hundred thousand parasols made as the first item, and all other requisites for use also by the hundred thousand. He then invited the Blessed One Padumuttara and gave a great gift to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Having given gifts thus for seven days, on the final day he aspired for the attainment of Nibbāna. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, at the end of his life, he was reborn in a deva world. There, he enjoyed divine bliss in the six desire-sphere heavens. Later, among humans, he experienced the fortunes of a wheel-turning monarch and so forth. In this Buddha-era, he was reborn into a brahmin family and attained proficiency in all skills. By his clan name, he became known as Pilindavaccha.

1. So ekadivasaṃ satthu santike dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā nacirasseva arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto udānavasena taṃ pakāsento nagare haṃsavatiyātiādimāha. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttova. Āsiṃ dovāriko ahanti ahaṃ haṃsavatīnagare rañño gehadvāre dvārapālako āsiṃ ahosinti attho. Akkhobhaṃ amitaṃ bhoganti rañño vallabhattā aññehi khobhetuṃ cāletuṃ asakkuṇeyyaṃ amitaṃ aparimāṇabhogaṃ dhanaṃ mama ghare sannicitaṃ rāsīkataṃ ahosīti attho.

1. One day, after hearing a Dhamma discourse from the Teacher, having gained faith, he went forth, and soon became an arahant. Recalling his past deeds, he was filled with joy and proclaimed this in an inspired utterance, beginning with 'In the city of Haṃsavatī,' and so forth. Its meaning has been stated before. 'I was a gatekeeper' means I was a gatekeeper at the king’s palace in the city of Haṃsavatī. 'Unshakeable, immeasurable wealth' means that due to being a favorite of the king, my immeasurable, boundless wealth, which could not be disturbed or shaken by others, was heaped up and accumulated in my house.

3. Bahū medhigatā bhogāti anekā bhogā me mayā adhigatā pattā paṭiladdhāti attho[V 2.0200]. Satthavāsiādīnaṃ parikkhārānaṃ nāmāni nayānuyogena suviññeyyāni. Parikkhāradānānisaṃsāni ca suviññeyyānevāti.

3. 'Many riches were acquired by me' means that numerous riches were acquired, attained, and obtained by me. The names of the requisites of a caravan-dweller and others should be well understood by applying the proper method. And the benefits of giving requisites should also be well understood.

Pilindavacchattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Pilindavaccha is complete.

Dutiyatatiyacatutthapañcamāpadānāni uttānānevāti.

The second, third, fourth, and fifth Apadānas are indeed straightforward.

6. Bākulattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bākula

Chaṭṭhāpadāne [M 2.0203] himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ bākulattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayaṃ kira thero atīte ito kappasatasahassādhikassa asaṅkhyeyyassa matthake anomadassissa bhagavato uppattito puretarameva brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā tattha sāraṃ apassanto “samparāyikatthaṃ gavesissāmī”ti isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pabbatapāde viharanto pañcābhiññāaṭṭhasamāpattīnaṃ lābhī hutvā viharanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhito satthu vātābādhe uppanne araññato bhesajjāni ānetvā taṃ vūpasametvā taṃ puññaṃ ārogyatthāya pariṇāmetvā tato cuto brahmaloke nibbatto ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto padumuttarabuddhakāle haṃsavatīnagare ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā [P 0.0482] satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ appābādhānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayaṃ taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ ākaṅkhanto paṇidhānaṃ katvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalakammaṃ upacinitvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto vipassissa bhagavato uppattito puretarameva bandhumatīnagare brāhmaṇakule nibbatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto tattha sāraṃ apassanto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā jhānābhiññālābhī hutvā pabbatapāde vasanto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ tiṇapupphakaroge uppanne taṃ vūpasametvā tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto brahmaloke nibbattitvā tato ekanavutikappe devamanussesu saṃsaranto kassapassa bhagavato kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekaṃ jiṇṇaṃ vinassamānaṃ mahāvihāraṃ disvā tattha uposathāgārādikaṃ sabbaṃ āvasathaṃ kārāpetvā tattha bhikkhusaṅghassa sabbaṃ bhesajjaṃ paṭiyādetvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato uppattito puretarameva kosambiyaṃ seṭṭhikule nibbatti.

The sixth apadāna is that of the Elder Bākula, which begins: 'Not far from the Himālaya…' It seems that in the past, at the head of an incalculable aeon more than one hundred thousand aeons ago from the present, even before the arising of the Blessed One Anomadassī, this elder was reborn in a brahmin family. Having come of age, he mastered the three Vedas, but seeing no essence in them, he thought, 'I will seek what pertains to the future life,' and went forth into the ascetic life of a seer. Dwelling at the foot of a mountain, he became a possessor of the five direct knowledges and the eight attainments. Hearing of the arising of a Buddha, he went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and became established in the refuges. When a wind-illness arose in the Teacher, he brought medicines from the forest and pacified it, dedicating that merit for the sake of health. Passing away from there, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. For one incalculable aeon he wandered among devas and humans. During the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, he was reborn in a certain family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having reached understanding, he listened to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse. Seeing the Teacher establish a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those with few illnesses, he himself aspired to that position and made a resolution. For the rest of his life he accumulated wholesome kamma and wandered only in good destinations. Even before the arising of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a brahmin family in the city of Bandhumatī. Having achieved perfection in all crafts, but seeing no essence in them, he went forth into the ascetic life of a seer and became a possessor of the jhānas and direct knowledges. Dwelling at the foot of a mountain, he heard of the arising of a Buddha, went to the Teacher, and became established in the refuges. When an illness from grass and flowers arose among the bhikkhus, he pacified it. Having remained there for the extent of his lifespan, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Brahma-world. Then, for ninety-one aeons, he wandered among devas and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in a family household in Bārāṇasī. While living the household life, he saw a great monastery that was old and decaying. He had the entire residence built there, including the Uposatha hall, and provided all kinds of medicine for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Having done wholesome deeds for the rest of his life, he wandered among devas and humans for one Buddha-interval. Even before the arising of our Blessed One, he was reborn in a treasurer's family in Kosambī.

So [V 2.0201] mātukucchito nikkhamitvā dhātīhi arogabhāvāya yamunāyaṃ nhāpiyamāno tāsaṃ hatthato muccitvā macchena gilito ahosi. Kevaṭṭā taṃ macchaṃ jālāya gahetvā bārāṇasiyaṃ seṭṭhibhariyāya vikkiṇiṃsu. Sā taṃ gahetvā phālayamānā pubbe katapuññaphalena arogaṃ [M 2.0204] dārakaṃ disvā “putto me laddho”ti gahetvā posesi. So janakehi mātāpitūhi taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā āgantvā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ putto, detha no putta”nti anuyoge kate raññā “ubhayesampi sādhāraṇo hotū”ti dvinnaṃ kulānaṃ dāyādabhāvena vinicchayaṃ katvā ṭhapitattā bākuloti laddhanāmo vayappatto mahāsampattiṃ anubhavanto dvīsu seṭṭhikulesu ekekasmiṃ chamāsaṃ chamāsaṃ vasati. Te attano vāre sampatte nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ bandhitvā tatrūpari ratanamaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā pañcaṅgikatūriye nipphādetvā kumāraṃ tattha nisīdāpetvā ubhayanagaramajjhaṭṭhānaṃ gaṅgāya āgacchanti, aparaseṭṭhimanussāpi evameva sajjetvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā kumāraṃ tattha āropetvā gacchanti. So evaṃ vaḍḍhamāno āsītiko hutvā ubhayaseṭṭhiputtoti pākaṭo. Satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā sattāhaṃ vāyamanto aṭṭhame divase saha paṭisambhidāya arahattaṃ [P 0.0483] pāpuṇi.

Having come out from his mother’s womb, while he was being bathed in the Yamunā river by his nurses for the sake of his health, he slipped from their hands and was swallowed by a fish. Fishermen caught that fish with a net and sold it to the treasurer’s wife in Bārāṇasī. When she cut it open, as a result of his previously done merit, she saw the unharmed boy and, thinking, 'I have gotten a son,' she took him and raised him. When his birth parents heard about this event, they came and made a claim: 'This is our son. Give us our son!' The king made a decision: 'Let him be common to both.' Since he was established as the heir of two families, he received the name Bākula. Having come of age and enjoying great fortune, he lived for six months in each of the two treasurer’s families. When their turn came, they would lash boats together into a raft, have a jeweled pavilion made on top of it, have the five kinds of musical instruments played, and, having seated the boy there, they would come along the Ganges to a place midway between the two cities. The people of the other treasurer would also prepare in the same way, go to that place, take the boy on board, and depart. Growing up in this way, he became eighty years old and was famous as 'the son of both treasurers.' He went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and, having gained faith, went forth. Striving for seven days, on the eighth day he attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

386. So arahā hutvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento himavantassāvidūretiādimāha. Tassattho heṭṭhā vuttova. Apadānapāḷiatthopi suviññeyyova. So arahattaṃ patvā vimuttisukhena viharanto saṭṭhivassasatāyuko hutvā parinibbāyīti.

386. Having become an Arahant, he recalled his own past kamma and, filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his previous conduct, beginning with: 'Not far from the Himālaya…' Its meaning is as stated above. The meaning of the Apadāna Pāli is also very easy to understand. Having attained arahantship, he dwelled in the bliss of liberation, and after living for one hundred and sixty years, he attained final Nibbāna.

Bākulattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bākula is finished.

7. Girimānandattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Girimānanda.

Sattamāpadāne bhariyā me kālaṅkatātiādikaṃ āyasmato girimānandattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vayappatto gharāvāsaṃ saṇṭhapetvā vasanto attano bhariyāya ca putte ca kālaṅkate sokasallasamappito araññaṃ pavisitvā pavattaphalabhojano rukkhamūle vihāsi. Tadā sumedho bhagavā tassānukampāya tattha gantvā dhammaṃ desetvā sokasallaṃ abbūḷhesi[V 2.0202]. So dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso sugandhapupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjetvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā sirasi añjaliṃ katvā abhitthavi.

In the seventh Apadāna, beginning with 'My wife has died,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Girimānanda. He too, having performed meritorious deeds under former Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences as a condition for liberation, was reborn in a respectable family during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha. Having reached maturity, he established a household and lived there. When his wife and children died, afflicted by the dart of sorrow, he entered the forest, eating fallen fruit, and lived at the foot of a tree. Then, the Blessed One Sumedha, out of compassion for him, went there, taught the Dhamma, and extracted the dart of sorrow. Hearing the Dhamma, his mind became serene. He honored the Blessed One with fragrant flowers, venerated him with the five-point prostration, placed his joined hands on his head, and praised him.

So [M 2.0205] tena puññena devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayattha sukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe bimbisārarañño purohitassa putto hutvā nibbatti, girimānandotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patvā satthu rājagahāgamane buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto katipayaṃ divasaṃ gāmakāvāse vasitvā satthāraṃ vandituṃ rājagahaṃ agamāsi. Bimbisāramahārājā tassa āgamanaṃ sutvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “idheva, bhante, vasatha, ahaṃ catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahāmī”ti sampavāretvā gatopi bahukiccattā taṃ na sari. “Thero abbhokāseyeva vasatī”ti. Devatā therassa temanabhayena vassadhāraṃ vāresuṃ. Rājā avassanakāraṇaṃ upadhāretvā ñatvā therassa kuṭikaṃ kārāpesi. Thero kuṭikāyaṃ vasanto senāsanasappāyalābhena cittasamādhānaṃ labhitvā vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Through that merit, wandering among gods and humans, he experienced happiness in both realms. In this arising of a Buddha, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of King Bimbisāra’s chaplain, and his name was Girimānanda. Upon reaching maturity, when the Teacher came to Rājagaha, he witnessed the Buddha’s power, gained faith, and went forth. Practicing the duties of a recluse, he stayed in a village dwelling for a few days before going to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher. King Bimbisāra, hearing of his arrival, approached him and invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, dwell right here; I shall provide the four requisites.' But, having departed, due to his many duties, the king did not remember him. The Elder was dwelling in the open air. The deities, fearing the Elder would get wet, held back the rain. The king, investigating the reason for the lack of rain, understood and had a hut built for the Elder. Dwelling in the hut, the Elder gained mental concentration through obtaining suitable lodging, applied balanced effort, diligently developed insight, and attained arahantship.

419. So arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento bhariyā me kālaṅkatātiādimāha. Taṃ bhagavato nivedanañca bhagavatā katānusāsanañca maggaṃ phalādhigamāpadānañca pāṭhānusārena suviññeyyamevāti.

419. Having attained arahantship, recollecting his past deeds and becoming joyful, he declared the account of his former conduct, beginning with 'My wife has died'. That report to the Blessed One, the instruction given by the Blessed One, and the account of the attainment of the path and fruit are easily understood according to the text.

Girimānandattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Girimānanda is concluded.

Aṭṭhamanavamadasamāpadānāni [P 0.0484] uttānatthānevāti.

The eighth, ninth, and tenth Apadānas are clear in meaning.

Cattālīsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Chapter of the Forties is concluded.

41. Metteyyavaggo

41. The Metteyya Chapter

1. Tissametteyyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Tissametteyya

1. Ekacattālīsame [V 2.0203] vagge paṭhamāpadāne pabbhārakūṭaṃ nissāyātiādikaṃ tissametteyyattherassa apadānaṃ. Tattha tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā padumuttarassa bhagavato ajinacammaṃ nisīdanatthāya dinnameva nānaṃ. Sesaṃ apadānapāḷiyā suviññeyyamevāti.

1. In the first Apadāna of the forty-first chapter, beginning with 'relying on Pabbhārakūṭa', is the Apadāna of the Elder Tissametteyya. There, having gone forth into the ascetic life, the distinction is that he gave a deer hide to the Blessed One Padumuttara for the purpose of a seat. The rest is easily understood from the Apadāna text itself.

2. Puṇṇakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Puṇṇaka

29. Dutiyāpadāne [M 2.0206] pabbhārakūṭaṃ nissāyātiādikaṃ āyasmato puṇṇakattherassa apadānaṃ. Tattha himavante yakkhasenāpati hutvā parinibbutassa paccekabuddhassa āḷahanakaraṇameva nānattaṃ. Sesaṃ pāṭhānusārena suviññeyyameva.

29. In the second Apadāna, beginning with 'relying on Pabbhārakūṭa', is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇaka. There, having been a yaksha commander in the Himalayas, the distinction is only the performing of the cremation for a Paccekabuddha who had attained final Nibbāna. The rest is easily understood according to the text.

45. Tatiyāpadāne himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato mettaguttherassa apadānaṃ. Tattha himavantasamīpe asokapabbate so tāpaso hutvā paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasanto sumedhasambuddhaṃ disvā pattaṃ gahetvā sappipūraṇaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ puññaphalāni ca suviññeyyāneva. Apadānagāthānaṃ attho ca pākaṭoyeva.

45. In the third Apadāna, beginning with 'not far from the Himalayas', is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Mettagū. There, having become an ascetic on Mount Asoka near the Himalayas and dwelling in a leaf-hut, the distinction was that, having seen the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Sumedha, he took a bowl and filled it with ghee. The rest and the fruits of merit are easily understood. The meaning of the Apadāna verses is also clear.

72. Catutthāpadāne gaṅgā bhāgīrathī nāmātiādikaṃ āyasmato dhotakattherassa apadānaṃ. Tatrāpi brāhmaṇo hutvā bhāgīrathīgaṅgāya taramāne bhikkhū disvā pasannamānaso setuṃ kārāpetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niyyāditabhāvoyeva viseso. Puññaphalaparidīpanagāthānaṃ attho nayānusārena suviññeyyova.

72. In the fourth Apadāna, beginning with 'the river Gaṅgā, named Bhāgīrathī', is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Dhotaka. There too, having been a brahmin, he saw monks crossing the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā and, with a pleased mind, had a bridge built and dedicated it to the community of monks headed by the Buddha—this is the distinction. The meaning of the verses that illuminate the fruits of merit is easily understood according to the method.

100. Pañcamāpadāne himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato upasivattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto gharāvāsaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā [V 2.0204] himavante padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā tiṇasantharaṃ santharitvā tattha nisinnassa bhagavato sālapupphapūjaṃ akāsīti ayaṃ viseso, sesamuttānameva.

100. In the fifth Apadāna, beginning with 'not far from the Himalayas', is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Upasiva. He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences as a supporting condition for liberation, was born in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, he renounced the household life and went forth into the ascetic life. Seeing the Blessed One Padumuttara in the Himalayas, he spread a grass mat and made an offering of sāla flowers to the Blessed One seated there—this is the distinction. The rest is clear.

161. Chaṭṭhāpadāne migaluddo pure āsintiādikaṃ āyasmato nandakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato [P 0.0485] kāle karavikasakuṇo hutvā madhurakūjitaṃ karonto satthāraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. Aparabhāge mayūro hutvā aññatarassa paccekabuddhassa vasanaguhādvāre pasannamānaso divasassa tikkhattuṃ madhurena vassitaṃ vassi. Evaṃ tattha tattha bhave puññāni katvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sāvatthiyaṃ kulagehe nibbatto nandakoti laddhanāmo satthu santike dhammaṃ [M 2.0207] sutvā pabbajitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento migaluddo pure āsintiādimāha. Tattha paccekabuddhassa maṇḍapaṃ katvā padumapupphehi chadanameva viseso.

161. In the sixth Apadāna, beginning with 'I was a hunter in the past', is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Nandaka. It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was a karavika bird and, singing sweetly, circumambulated the Teacher. Later, he became a peacock and, with a pleased mind, called out sweetly three times a day at the entrance to the dwelling cave of a certain Paccekabuddha. Having thus performed meritorious deeds in various existences, he was reborn in a good family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One, was given the name Nandaka, and having heard the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, went forth, developed insight, and attained arahantship. Later, recalling his past deeds and becoming joyful, he declared the account of his former conduct, beginning with 'I was a hunter in the past'. The distinction here was making a pavilion for the Paccekabuddha and covering it with lotus flowers.

183. Sattamāpadāne pabbhārakūṭaṃ nissāyātiādikaṃ āyasmato hemakattherassa apadānaṃ. Tatthāpi isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante vasanto piyadassiṃ bhagavantaṃ upagataṃ disvā ratanamayaṃ pīṭhaṃ attharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Tattha nisinnassa kumbhamattaṃ jambuphalaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Bhagavā tassa cittappasādatthāya taṃ phalaṃ paribhuñji. Ettakameva viseso.

183. In the seventh Apadāna, beginning with 'relying on Pabbhāra Peak', is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Hemaka. Here too, having gone forth into the ascetic life and dwelling in the Himalayas, seeing the Blessed One Piyadassī approaching, he prepared a jeweled seat and stood by. To him, seated there, he brought a jambu fruit the size of a pot and gave it. The Blessed One, for the sake of the confidence in his mind, partook of that fruit. This much alone was the distinction.

224. Aṭṭhamāpadāne rājāsi vijayo nāmātiādikaṃ āyasmato todeyyattherassa apadānaṃ. Tattha rājāsi vijayo nāmāti daharakālato paṭṭhāya sabbasaṅgāmesu jinato, catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ rañjanato allīyanato vijayo nāma rājā ahosīti attho. Ketumatīpuruttameti ketu vuccanti dhajapaṭākā. Atha vā nagarasobhanatthāya nagaramajjhe ussāpitaratanatoraṇāni, te ketū niccaṃ ussāpitā sobhayamānā assā atthīti ketumatī. Pūreti dhanadhaññehi sabbajanānaṃ mananti puraṃ. Ketumatī ca sā purañca seṭṭhaṭṭhena uttamañceti ketumatīpuruttamaṃ, tasmiṃ ketumatīpuruttame. Sūro vikkamasampannoti abhīto vīriyasampanno vijayo nāma rājā ajjhāvasīti sambandho. Itthaṃ [P 0.0486] bhūtaṃ purañca sabbavatthuvāhanañca chaḍḍetvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vasanto sumedhabhagavantaṃ disvā somanassaṃ uppādetvā candanena pūjākaraṇameva viseso.

224. In the eighth Apadāna, beginning with 'King Vijaya by name,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Todeyya. Here, 'King Vijaya by name' means that from his youth, being victorious in all battles, and delighting the people with the four bases of sympathy, thus winning them over, he was called King Vijaya. 'The excellent city of Ketumatī'—'ketu' means banners or flags. Alternatively, for the city’s splendor, jeweled arches were erected in the city center; because these banners were always raised and adorned, it was called Ketumatī. It fills the minds of all people with wealth and grain, hence 'puraṃ' (city). And because it is Ketumatī and also excellent in being the foremost city, it is 'Ketumatīpuruttama'; in that excellent city of Ketumatī. 'A hero endowed with vigor'—the connection is that King Vijaya, fearless and full of energy, dwelt there. Thus, having abandoned such a city and all possessions and vehicles, he entered the Himalayas, went forth into the ascetic life, and while dwelling there, seeing the Blessed Sumedha, he generated joy and made an offering of sandalwood—this was the distinction.

276. Navamāpadāne nagare haṃsavatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato jatukaṇṇittherassa apadānaṃ[V 2.0205]. Tattha seṭṭhiputto hutvā suvaṇṇapāsāde vasanabhāvo ca pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samaṅgī hutvā vasanabhāvo ca sabbadesavāsīnaṃ sabbasippaviññūnañca āgantvā sevanabhāvo ca viseso.

276. In the ninth Apadāna, beginning with 'In the city of Haṃsavatī,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Jatukaṇṇi. Therein, the distinction is that he was the son of a wealthy merchant, living in a golden palace, endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasures, and that people from all countries, skilled in all arts, came and attended upon him.

330. Dasamāpadāne himavantassāvidūretiādikaṃ āyasmato udenattherassa apadānaṃ. Tattha himavantasamīpe padumapabbataṃ nissāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ [M 2.0208] pabbajitvā vasantena padumuttarassa bhagavato padumapupphaṃ gahetvā pūjitabhāvova viseso. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

330. In the tenth Apadāna, beginning with 'not far from the Himalayas,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Udena. There, near the Himalayas, relying on Paduma Mountain, he went forth into the ascetic life and lived. The distinction was that he took a lotus flower and offered it to the Blessed One Padumuttara. The rest is clear everywhere.

Ekacattālīsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Forty-first Chapter is concluded.

42. Bhaddālivaggo

42. The Bhaddāli Chapter

1-10. Bhaddālittheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1–10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Bhaddāli and Others

Bācattālīsamavagge [V 2.0206] paṭhamāpadānañca dutiyāpadānañca tatiyāpadānañca nayānusārena suviññeyyameva.

In the forty-second chapter, the first, second, and third Apadānas are easily understood according to the method.

106. Catutthāpadāne nagare bandhumatiyātiādikaṃ āyasmato madhumaṃsadāyakattherassa apadānaṃ. Tattha sūkarikoti sūkaramaṃsaṃ vikkiṇitvā jīvikaṃ kappento. Ukkoṭakaṃ randhayitvāti pihakapapphāsamaṃsaṃ pacitvā madhumaṃsamhi okiriṃ pakkhipiṃ. Tena maṃsena pattaṃ pūretvā bhikkhusaṅghassa datvā tena puññakammena imasmiṃ buddhuppāde arahattaṃ pāpuṇinti attho.

106. In the fourth Apadāna, beginning with 'In the city of Bandhumatī,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Madhumaṃsadāyaka Thera. Here, 'sūkariko' means one who makes a living by selling pork. 'Having cooked ukkoṭakaṃ' means having cooked the flesh of the spleen and lungs and mixed it into honey-meat. The meaning is that by filling a bowl with that meat and giving it to the Saṅgha of monks, through that meritorious act, he attained arahantship in this Buddha's dispensation.

Nāgapallavattherassa pañcamāpadānampi ekadīpiyattherassa chaṭṭhāpadānampi ucchaṅgapupphiyattherassa sattamāpadānampi yāgudāyakattherassa aṭṭhamāpadānampi patthodanadāyakattherassa navamāpadānampi mañcadāyakattherassa dasamāpadānampi sabbaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

The fifth Apadāna of the Elder Nāgapallava, the sixth Apadāna of the Elder Ekadīpiya, the seventh Apadāna of the Elder Ucchaṅgapupphiya, the eighth Apadāna of the Elder Yāgudāyaka, the ninth Apadāna of the Elder Patthodanadāyaka, and the tenth Apadāna of the Elder Mañcadāyaka—all these are easily understood.

Bācattālīsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Forty-second Chapter is concluded.

43-48. Sakiṃsammajjakādivaggo

43–48. The Chapter on Sakiṃsammajjaka and Others

1-60. Sakiṃsammajjakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1–60. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Sakiṃsammajjaka and Others

Tecattālīsamavagge [P 0.0487][V 2.0207] sabbatherāpadānāni uttānāneva. Kevalaṃ therānaṃ nāmanānattaṃ puññanānattañca viseso.

In the forty-third chapter, all the Apadānas of the Elders are straightforward. The only distinction is the variety of the Elders' names and the variety of their meritorious deeds.

Catucattālīsame vaggepi sabbāni apadānāni pākaṭāneva. Kevalaṃ puññanānattaṃ phalanānattañca viseso.

In the forty-fourth chapter, all the Apadānas are also clearly evident. The only distinction is the variety of merit and the variety of its fruits.

1. Pañcacattālīsamavagge paṭhamāpadāne kakusandho mahāvīrotiādikaṃ āyasmato vibhīṭakamiñjiyattherassa apadānaṃ.

1. In the forty-fifth chapter, the first Apadāna, beginning with 'Kakusandha, the great hero,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Vibhīṭakamiñjiya Thera.

2. Tattha [M 2.0209] bījamiñjamadāsahanti vibhīṭakaphalāni phāletvā bījāni miñjāni gahetvā madhusakkarāhi yojetvā kakusandhassa bhagavato adāsinti attho. Dutiyāpadānādīni sabbāni suviññeyyāneva, therānaṃ nāmanānattādīnipi pāṭhānusārena veditabbāni.

2. Here, 'I gave the seeds and pith' means having split the vibhīṭaka fruits, taken the seeds and pith, mixed them with honey and sugar, and offered them to the Blessed One Kakusandha. The second Apadāna and others are all easily understood, and the various names of the Elders and so forth should be known according to the text.

1. Chacattālīsame vagge paṭhamāpadāne jagatiṃ kārayiṃ ahanti uttamabodhirukkhassa samantato āḷindaṃ ahaṃ kārayinti attho. Sesāni dutiyāpadānādīni sabbānipi uttānāneva.

1. In the forty-sixth chapter, in the first Apadāna, 'I caused a platform to be made' means 'I caused a terrace to be made all around the supreme Bodhi tree.' The remaining Apadānas, from the second onwards, are all straightforward.

Sattacattālīsame vagge paṭhamāpadānādīni pāḷianusārena suviññeyyāneva.

In the forty-seventh chapter, the first Apadāna and others are easily understood according to the Pāli text.

Aṭṭhacattālīsame vagge paṭhamadutiyāpadānāni uttānāneva.

In the forty-eighth chapter, the first and second Apadānas are straightforward.

30. Tatiyāpadāne kosiyo nāma bhagavāti kosiyagotte jātattā kosiyo nāma paccekabuddhoti [V 2.0208] attho. Cittakūṭeti cittakūṭakelāsakūṭasānukūṭādīsu anotattadahaṃ paṭicchādetvā ṭhitapabbatakūṭesu nānāratanaosadhādīhi vicitte cittakūṭapabbate so paccekabuddho vasīti attho.

30. In the third Apadāna, 'Kosiya by name, the Blessed One' means the Paccekabuddha was named Kosiya because he was born in the Kosiya clan. 'Cittakūṭa' means that Paccekabuddha dwelt on Mount Cittakūṭa, which is variegated with various gems, medicinal herbs, and so forth, among the mountain peaks such as Cittakūṭa, Kelāsa, and Sānukūṭa, which stand concealing Lake Anotatta.

Catutthapañcamāpadānāni uttānāneva.

The fourth and fifth Apadānas are straightforward.

56. Chaṭṭhāpadāne kusaṭṭhakamadāsahanti pakkhikabhattauposathikabhattadhurabhattasalākabhattādīsu kusapaṇṇavasena dātabbaṃ aṭṭhasalākabhattaṃ ahaṃ adāsinti attho.

56. In the sixth Apadāna, 'I gave the kusaṭṭhaka' means 'I gave eight ticket-meals (such as the fortnightly meal, observance day meal, regular meal, ticket meal, and so forth) to be distributed by means of kusa grass stalks.'

61. Sattamāpadāne sobhito nāma sambuddhoti ārohapariṇāhadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇabyāmappabhādīhi sobhamānasarīrattā sobhito nāma sammāsambuddhoti attho.

61. In the seventh Apadāna, 'Sobhita by name, the Fully Enlightened One' means the Sammāsambuddha was named Sobhita because his body was resplendent with height, breadth, the thirty-two marks of a great man, a fathom-wide radiance, and so forth.

66. Aṭṭhamāpadāne [P 0.0488] takkarāyaṃ vasī tadāti taṃ dasapuññakiriyavatthuṃ karontā janā paṭivasanti etthāti takkarā, rājadhānī. Tissaṃ takkarāyaṃ, tadā vasīti attho.

66. In the eighth Apadāna, 'At that time, I dwelt in Takkarā' means Takkarā was a royal capital where people lived performing the ten bases of meritorious deeds. The meaning is, 'I dwelt in that Takkarā at that time.'

72. Navamāpadāne [M 2.0210] pānadhiṃ sukataṃ gayhāti upāhanayugaṃ sundarākārena nipphāditaṃ gahetvāti attho. Dasamāpadānaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

72. In the ninth Apadāna, 'Taking well-made footwear' means taking a pair of sandals beautifully crafted. The tenth Apadāna is easily understood.

Aṭṭhacattālīsamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Forty-eighth Chapter is concluded.

49. Paṃsukūlavaggo

49. The Rag-Robe Chapter

1-10. Paṃsukūlasaññakattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1–10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Paṃsukūlasaññaka and Others.

Ekūnapaññāsamavagge [V 2.0209] paṭhamāpadānaṃ suviññeyyameva.

In the forty-ninth chapter, the first Apadāna is easily understood.

14. Dutiyāpadāne adhiccuppattikā buddhāti adhiccena akāraṇena uppattikā sayambhūtā, aññehi devabrahmamārādīhi upadesadāyakehi rahitā sayambhūñāṇena uppannā jātā pātubhūtāti attho.

14. In the second Apadāna, 'Buddhas who arise spontaneously' means they arise without a cause, self-arisen, without teachers such as devas, Brahmās, Māra, and so forth, born, arisen, and manifested through their self-originating knowledge. This is the meaning.

16. Odumbarikapupphaṃ vāti udumbararukkhe pupphaṃ dullabhaṃ dullabhuppattikaṃ iva. Candamhi sasakaṃ yathāti candamaṇḍale sasalekhāya rūpaṃ dullabhaṃ yathā. Vāyasānaṃ yathā khīranti kākānaṃ niccaṃ rattindivaṃ khuddāpīḷitabhāvena khīraṃ dullabhaṃ yathā, evaṃ dullabhaṃ lokanāyakaṃ caturāsaṅkhyeyyaṃ vā aṭṭhāsaṅkhyeyyaṃ vā soḷasāsaṅkhyeyyaṃ vā kappasatasahassaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā buddhabhāvato dullabho lokanāyakoti attho.

16. 'Like an Udumbara flower' means that a flower on an Udumbara tree is rare, like a rare occurrence. 'Like a hare on the moon' means that just as the image of a hare in the disc of the moon is rare. 'Like milk for crows' means that just as milk is rare for crows, who are constantly afflicted by hunger day and night. Similarly, a leader of the world is rare. The meaning is that a leader of the world is difficult to attain on account of Buddhahood, having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kalpas, or eight incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kalpas, or sixteen incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand kalpas.
