30. Tatiyāpadāne madhuṃ bhisehi savatīti pokkharamadhupadumakesarehi savati paggharati. Khīraṃ sappiṃ muḷālibhīti khīrañca sappirasañca padumamuḷālehi savati paggharati. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ mama santakaṃ buddho paṭiggaṇhatūti attho.

30. In the third Apadāna, 'Honey flows from the lotus stalks' means it flows and drips from the honey of the lotuses and the lotus filaments. 'Milk and ghee from the lotus roots' means milk and the essence of ghee flow and drip from the lotus roots. Therefore, the meaning is, 'May the Buddha accept both of these, which are my property.'

Catutthapañcamachaṭṭhāpadānāni uttānāneva.

The fourth, fifth, and sixth Apadānas are straightforward.

119. Sattamāpadāne cattālīsadijāpi cāti dvikkhattuṃ jātāti dijā. Kumāravaye uṭṭhitadantānaṃ patitattā puna uṭṭhitadantā dijā, te ca dantā. Byākaraṇañca heṭṭhā nidānakathāyaṃ vuttameva.

119. In the seventh Apadāna, regarding 'and forty teeth also': 'twice-born' (dijā) means born twice. Because the teeth that erupt in childhood fall out, the teeth that erupt again are 'twice-born' (dijā), and these are the teeth. The explanation has already been given below in the introductory story.

Aṭṭhamāpadānaṃ uttānamevāti.

The eighth Apadāna is straightforward.

171. Navamāpadāne [P 0.0489] tadāhaṃ māṇavo āsinti yadā sumedhapaṇḍito dīpaṅkarabhagavato santikā byākaraṇaṃ labhi, tadā ahaṃ megho nāma brāhmaṇamāṇavo [M 2.0211] hutvā sumedhatāpasena saha isipabbajjaṃ [V 2.0210] pabbajitvā sikkhāpadesu sikkhito kenaci pāpasahāyena saṃsaṭṭho saṃsaggadosena pāpavitakkādivasaṃ gato mātughātakammavasena narake aggijālādidukkhamanubhavitvā tato cuto samudde timiṅgalamahāmaccho hutvā nibbatto, samuddamajjhe gacchantaṃ mahānāvaṃ gilitukāmo gato. Disvā maṃ vāṇijā bhītā “aho gotamo bhagavā”ti saddamakaṃsu. Atha mahāmaccho pubbavāsanāvasena buddhagāravaṃ uppādetvā tato cuto sāvatthiyaṃ vibhavasampanne brāhmaṇakule nibbatto saddho pasanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā divasassa tikkhattuṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā saramāno vandati. Tadā bhagavā “ciraṃ dhammarucī”ti maṃ āha.

171. In the ninth Apadāna, 'At that time, I was a young man' means that when the wise Sumedha received the prediction from the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, I, a young brahmin named Megha, having gone forth into the ascetic life with the ascetic Sumedha, was trained in the training rules. But, having associated with an evil companion, through the fault of that association I came under the sway of evil thoughts and so forth, and on account of the kamma of killing my mother, I experienced the suffering of hellfire and other pains in hell. After passing away from there, I was reborn as a great Timiṅgala fish in the ocean. While moving through the middle of the ocean, I went with the desire to swallow a large ship. Seeing me, the terrified merchants cried out, 'Ah, Gotama, the Blessed One!' Then, due to the influence of past habitations, the great fish developed reverence for the Buddha. After passing away from that state, I was reborn in a prosperous brahmin family in Sāvatthī. With faith and confidence, having heard the Teacher’s discourse on the Dhamma, I went forth and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Remembering this, I would go to attend upon him three times a day and pay homage. Then the Blessed One said to me, 'For a long time you have had delight in the Dhamma, Dhammaruci.'

184. Atha so thero “suciraṃ satapuññalakkhaṇa”ntiādīhi gāthāhi thomesi. Bhante, satapuññalakkhaṇadhara gotama. Patipubbena visuddhapaccayanti pubbe dīpaṅkarapādamūle paripuṇṇapāramīpaccayasambhāro suṭṭhu ciraṃ kālaṃ mayā na diṭṭho asīti attho. Ahamajjasupekkhananti ajja imasmiṃ divase ahaṃ supekkhanaṃ sundaradassanaṃ, sundaradiṭṭhaṃ vā nirupamaṃ viggahaṃ upamārahitasarīraṃ gotamaṃ vata ekantena passāmi dakkhāmīti attho.

184. Then that elder praised him with verses beginning, 'For a long time, the mark of a hundred merits.' 'Venerable sir, Gotama, bearer of the mark of a hundred merits.' 'Through the gradual purification of conditions' means that the accumulation of conditions for the complete perfections was not seen by me for a very long time previously at the feet of Dīpaṅkara. This is the meaning. 'Today I have a good sight' means that today, on this very day, I certainly see, I will behold Gotama, of beautiful appearance or of beautiful sight, the incomparable form, the body without comparison. This is the meaning.

185-186. Suciraṃ vihatatamo mayāti visesena hatatamo viddhaṃsitamoho tvaṃ mayāpi suṭṭhu ciraṃ thomitoti attho. Sucirakkhena nadī visositāti esā taṇhānadī sundararakkhena gopanena visesena sositā, abhabbuppattikatā tayāti attho. Suciraṃ amalaṃ visodhitanti suṭṭhu ciraṃ dīghena addhunā amalaṃ nibbānaṃ visesena sodhitaṃ, suṭṭhu kataṃ adhigataṃ tayāti attho. Nayanaṃ ñāṇamayaṃ mahāmune. Cirakālasamaṅgitoti mahāmune mahāsamaṇa ñāṇamayaṃ nayanaṃ dibbacakkhuṃ cirakālaṃ samadhigato sampatto tvanti attho. Avinaṭṭho punarantaranti ahaṃ puna antaraṃ antarābhave majjhe parinaṭṭho [P 0.0490] parihīno ahosinti attho. Punarajjasamāgato tayāti ajja imasmiṃ kāle tayā saddhiṃ punapi samāgato ekībhūto saha vasāmīti attho. Na hi nassanti katāni gotamāti gotama sabbaññubuddha, tayā saddhiṃ katāni samāgamādīni [M 2.0212] na hi nassanti yāva khandhaparinibbānā na vinā bhavissantīti attho. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti.

185–186. 'For a long time, darkness has been dispelled by me' means: the meaning is that you, whose darkness has been especially struck, whose delusion has been shattered, have also been praised by me for a very long time. 'The river has been dried up by long protection' means: the meaning is that this river of craving has been especially dried up by you through excellent protection and guarding, made incapable of arising again. 'For a long time, the stainless has been purified' means: the meaning is that for a very long time, over a long path, the stainless Nibbāna has been especially purified, well-accomplished, and attained by you. 'O great sage, the eye of wisdom, possessed for a long time' means: the meaning is, O great sage, great ascetic, you have for a long time fully attained and reached the eye made of knowledge, the divine eye. 'Not lost again in between' means: the meaning is that I was again lost and diminished in the middle, in an intermediate existence. 'Reunited with you today' means: the meaning is that today, at this time, I have come together with you again, become one, and dwell together with you. 'Indeed, the deeds done are not lost, O Gotama' means: the meaning is, O Gotama, All-Knowing Buddha, the deeds done with you, such as meeting, do not perish; they will not be destroyed until the final passing away of the aggregates. The rest is straightforward.

Dhammaruciyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dhammaruci is concluded.

Dasamāpadānaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

The tenth Apadāna is easily understood.

Ekūnapaññāsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the forty-ninth chapter is concluded.

50-53. Kiṅkaṇipupphādivaggo

50–53. The Chapter on the Kiṅkaṇi Flower and So Forth

1-40. Kiṅkaṇipupphiyattheraapadānādivaṇṇanā

1–40. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kiṅkaṇipupphiya and So Forth

Paññāsamavagge [V 2.0211] ca ekapaññāsamavagge ca dvepaññāsamavagge ca tepaññāsamavagge ca sabbāni apadānāni uttānānevāti.

In the fiftieth chapter, the fifty-first chapter, the fifty-second chapter, and the fifty-third chapter, all the Apadānas are straightforward.

54. Kaccāyanavaggo

54. The Kaccāyana Chapter

1. Mahākaccāyanattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākaccāyana

Catupaññāsamavagge [V 2.0212] paṭhamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato mahākaccāyanattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle gahapatimahāsālakule nibbattitvā vuddhippatto ekadivasaṃ satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthārā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapiyamānaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento paṇidhānaṃ katvā dānādīni puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle vijjādharo hutvā ākāsena gacchanto ekasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kaṇikārapupphehi pūjaṃ akāsi.

In the first Apadāna of the fifty-fourth chapter, the Apadāna of the Venerable Mahākaccāyana begins with "Padumuttara, the Victorious One," and so forth. This one, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences as supportive conditions for the rolling back of saṃsāra. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn into a great family of wealthy householders and, having grown up, one day listened to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. Seeing a monk being placed by the Teacher in the foremost position among those who explain in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief, he himself aspired for that same position. Making a resolution, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and wandered among gods and humans. During the time of the Blessed One Sumedha, he became a knowledge-holder and, while traveling through the sky, saw the Blessed One seated in a forest grove. With a joyful mind, he offered worship with kaṇikāra flowers.

So tena puññena aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva parivattento kassapadasabalassa kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ kulagehe nibbattitvā parinibbute bhagavati suvaṇṇacetiyakammaṭṭhāne satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇiṭṭhakāya pūjaṃ katvā “imassa nissandena nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne sarīraṃ me suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ hotū”ti [M 2.0213] patthanaṃ akāsi. Tato yāvajīvaṃ kusalakammaṃ katvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devamanussesu saṃsaritvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde ujjeniyaṃ rañño caṇḍapajjotassa purohitagehe nibbatti, tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase mātā “mayhaṃ [P 0.0491] putto suvaṇṇavaṇṇo, attano nāmaṃ gahetvā āgato”ti kañcanamāṇavotveva nāmaṃ akāsi. So vuddhimanvāya tayo vede uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena purohitaṭṭhānaṃ labhi. So gottavasena kaccāyanoti paññāyittha. Atha rājā caṇḍapajjoto buddhuppādaṃ sutvā, “ācariya, tumhe tattha gantvā satthāraṃ idhānethā”ti pesesi. So attaṭṭhamo satthu santikaṃ upagato tassa satthā dhammaṃ desesi, desanāpariyosāne sattahi janehi saddhiṃ saha paṭisambhidāhi arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

By that merit, he was reborn again and again in happy destinies. At the time of Kassapa, the One of Ten Powers, he was born in a family home in Bārāṇasī. After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, he made an offering of a golden brick worth a hundred thousand at the site of the golden stupa's construction, aspiring: "By the result of this, may my body be golden-colored wherever I am reborn." Then, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, he wandered among devas and humans for one Buddha-interval. In this Buddha’s time, he was born in the household of King Caṇḍapajjota’s chaplain in Ujjenī. On his naming day, his mother said, "My son is golden-colored; he has come bearing his own name," and thus named him Kañcanamāṇava. Growing up, he mastered the three Vedas and, upon his father’s death, attained the position of chaplain. By lineage, he became known as Kaccāyana. Then, King Caṇḍapajjota, hearing of the Buddha’s appearance, sent him, saying, "Teacher, go there and bring the Teacher here." He, with seven others, went to the Teacher. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, together with seven others, he was established in arahantship along with the analytical knowledges.

1. So evaṃ pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ [V 2.0213] pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Atha satthā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Te tāvadeva dvaṅgulamattakesamassuiddhimayapattacīvaradharā vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya ahesuṃ. Evaṃ thero sadatthaṃ nipphādetvā, “bhante, rājā pajjoto tumhākaṃ pāde vandituṃ dhammañca sotuṃ icchatī”ti ārocesi. Satthā “tvaṃyeva, kaccāna, tattha gaccha, tayi gate rājā pasīdissatī”ti āha. Thero satthu āṇāya attaṭṭhamo tattha gantvā rājānaṃ pasādetvā avantīsu sāsanaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā puna satthu santikameva āgato. Attano pubbapatthanāvasena kaccāyanappakaraṇaṃ mahāniruttippakaraṇaṃ nettippakaraṇanti pakaraṇattayaṃ saṅghamajjhe byākāsi. Atha santuṭṭhena bhagavatā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ vibhajantānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākaccāno”ti (a. ni. 1.188, 197) etadaggaṭṭhāne ṭhapito aggaphalasukhena vihāsīti.

1. Thus, having attained the fruit of arahantship and recalling his past deeds, filled with joy, he proclaimed his Apadāna of past deeds, saying, "The Victor named Padumuttara," and so forth. The meaning of this is as stated before. Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, "Come, monks." Instantly, they became like elders of sixty years' standing, with hair and beards two fingers in length, wearing robes and carrying bowls created by psychic power. Having thus accomplished his own welfare, the elder reported, "Venerable sir, King Pajjota wishes to pay homage at your feet and to hear the Dhamma." The Teacher replied, "You go there yourself, Kaccāna. When you go, the king will be pleased." The elder, following the Teacher's instruction, went there with seven others, pleased the king, established the Dispensation in Avanti, and then returned to the Teacher's presence. In accordance with his former aspiration, he expounded three treatises—the Kaccāyana Treatise, the Mahānirutti Treatise, and the Netti Treatise—in the midst of the Sangha. Then, the satisfied Blessed One declared, "Monks, among my disciples who explain in detail the meaning of what has been stated briefly, Mahākaccāna is the foremost." (A. Ni. 1.188, 197) Thus, he was established in the foremost position and dwelt in the bliss of the highest fruit.

Mahākaccāyanattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākaccāyana is complete.

2. Vakkalittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vakkali

Dutiyāpadāne [M 2.0214] ito satasahassamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato vakkalittherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi thero purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthu santikaṃ gacchantehi upāsakehi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ suṇanto satthārā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ [P 0.0492] saddhādhimuttānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapitaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā paṇidhānaṃ akāsi. Satthā tassa anantarāyaṃ disvā byākari.

In the second Apadāna, beginning with "a hundred thousand aeons hence," is the Apadāna of the Venerable Vakkali. This elder, having performed meritorious deeds in the presence of previous Supreme Conquerors, accumulated merits in various existences as supportive conditions for the rolling back of saṃsāra. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having reached discernment, he went to the monastery with lay devotees who were visiting the Teacher. Standing at the edge of the assembly, he listened to the Dhamma. Seeing the Teacher place one monk in the foremost position among those liberated by faith, he himself aspired for that same position. After offering a great alms-giving to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha for seven days, he made his aspiration. The Teacher, seeing no obstruction for him, made a declaration.

So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti, tassa vakkalīti nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Tattha kalīti aparādhatilakāḷakādidosassa adhivacanaṃ. Niddhantasuvaṇṇapiṇḍasadisatāya apagato byapagato kali doso assāti va-kārāgamaṃ katvā vakkalīti vuccati. So vuddhippatto tayo vede uggaṇhitvā brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gato, satthāraṃ disvā rūpakāyasampattidassanena atitto satthārā saddhiṃyeva vicarati. “Agāramajjhe vasanto niccakālaṃ satthu dassanaṃ na labhissāmī”ti [V 2.0214] satthu santike pabbajitvā ṭhapetvā bhojanakālaṃ sarīrakiccakālañca sesakāle yattha ṭhitena sakkā dasabalaṃ passituṃ, tattha ṭhito aññaṃ kiccaṃ pahāya bhagavantaṃ olokentoyeva viharati. Satthā tassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamento bahukālaṃ tasmiṃ rūpadassaneneva vicarante kiñci avatvā punekadivasaṃ – “kiṃ te, vakkali, iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena? Yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passati; yo maṃ passati, so dhammaṃ passati. Dhammañhi, vakkali, passanto maṃ passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87) āha. Satthari evaṃ vadantepi thero satthu dassanaṃ pahāya aññattha gantuṃ na sakkoti. Tato satthā, “nāyaṃ bhikkhu saṃvegaṃ alabhitvā bujjhissatī”ti vassūpanāyikadivase – “apehi, vakkalī”ti theraṃ paṇāmesi. So satthārā paṇāmito satthu sammukhe ṭhātuṃ asakkonto – “kiṃ mayhaṃ jīvitena, yohaṃ satthāraṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhāmī”ti gijjhakūṭe pabbate papātaṭṭhānaṃ [M 2.0215] abhiruhi? Satthā tassa taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā – “ayaṃ bhikkhu mama santikā assāsaṃ alabhanto maggaphalānaṃ upanissayaṃ nāseyyā”ti attānaṃ dassetvā obhāsaṃ vissajjento –

Having done good deeds throughout his life, wandering among gods and humans, he was born in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī during the time of our Blessed One. They named him Vakkali. Here, "kali" is a term for a fault, such as a blemish or a dark spot of an offense. Because his fault was removed and gone, like a lump of refined gold, they added the prefix "va-" and called him Vakkali. Having grown up, he mastered the three Vedas and became accomplished in the brahminical arts. Upon seeing the Teacher, he was insatiate with the sight of the Teacher’s beautiful physical form and followed him constantly. Thinking, "Living in a household, I will not always get to see the Teacher," he went forth in the Teacher’s presence. Except during meal times and times for bodily needs, he spent all his time standing wherever he could see the Ten-Powered One, abandoning other duties and simply gazing at the Blessed One. The Teacher, waiting for the maturing of his knowledge, for a long time said nothing while he spent his time merely beholding his form. Then one day he said: "What good is it to you, Vakkali, to see this foul body? Whoever sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me; whoever sees me, sees the Dhamma. For in seeing the Dhamma, Vakkali, one sees me" (SN 3.87). Even when the Teacher spoke thus, the elder could not bring himself to abandon the sight of the Teacher and go elsewhere. Then the Teacher, thinking, "This monk will not awaken without gaining a sense of urgency," dismissed the elder on the day of the commencement of the rains-residence, saying, "Go away, Vakkali." Dismissed by the Teacher and unable to stand in his presence, he thought, "What use is life to me if I cannot see the Teacher?" and climbed to a precipice on Vulture Peak. Knowing what had occurred, the Teacher thought, "This monk, not finding solace from me, might destroy the supporting condition for the path and fruits," and so revealed himself, emitting a radiance—

“Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane;

Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 381) –

"A monk full of joy, serene in the Buddha's teaching, may attain the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of formations."

Gāthaṃ vatvā “ehi, vakkalī”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.381) hatthaṃ pasāresi. Thero “dasabalo me diṭṭho, ‘ehī’ti avhāyanampi laddha”nti balavapītisomanassaṃ uppādetvā “kuto gacchāmī”ti attano gamanabhāvaṃ ajānitvāva satthu sammukhe [P 0.0493] ākāse pakkhanditvā paṭhamena pādena pabbate ṭhitoyeva satthārā vuttagāthāyo āvajjento ākāseyeva pītiṃ vikkhambhetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇīti aṅguttaraṭṭhakathāyaṃ (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.208) dhammapadavaṇṇanāyañca (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.381 vakkalittheravatthu) āgataṃ.

Having spoken the verse, he extended his hand, saying, "Come, Vakkali." The elder, thinking, "I have seen the Ten-Powered One, and I have even received the call 'Come,'" gave rise to strong rapture and joy. Without even knowing where he was going, he leapt into the air in the presence of the Teacher. While his first foot was still on the mountain, he reflected on the verses spoken by the Teacher. Then, overcoming his rapture in mid-air, he attained arahantship along with the analytical knowledges. This is told in the Aṅguttara Commentary (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.208) and the Dhammapada Commentary (Dhp. Aṭṭha. 2.381, the story of Venerable Vakkali).

Idha pana evaṃ veditabbaṃ – “kiṃ te, vakkalī”tiādinā satthārā ovadito gijjhakūṭe viharanto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi, tassa saddhāya balavabhāvato eva vipassanā vīthiṃ na otarati? Bhagavā taṃ ñatvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā adāsi. So puna vipassanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ nāsakkhiyeva. Athassa āhāravekallena vātābādho uppajji, taṃ vātābādhena pīḷiyamānaṃ ñatvā bhagavā tattha gantvā pucchanto –

Here, however, it should be understood thus: When admonished by the Teacher with the words, "What is it to you, Vakkali?" and so on, while dwelling on Vulture Peak, he established insight meditation. But due to the strength of his faith, his insight did not enter the path. The Blessed One, knowing this, purified the meditation subject and gave it to him. Yet again, he was unable to bring his insight to its culmination. Then, due to a lack of food, a wind ailment arose in him. Knowing he was afflicted by this wind ailment, the Blessed One went there and asked:

“Vātarogābhinīto [V 2.0215] tvaṃ, viharaṃ kānane vane;

Paviddhagocare lūkhe, kathaṃ bhikkhu karissasī”ti. (theragā. 350) –

“Afflicted by a wind disease, dwelling in the forest, in a remote and rough alms-resort, how will you manage, bhikkhu?”

Āha. Taṃ sutvā thero –

He said this. Hearing it, the Elder replied:

“Pītisukhena vipulena, pharamāno samussayaṃ;

Lūkhampi abhisambhonto, viharissāmi kānane.

“Pervading my whole body with abundant rapture and bliss, I will dwell in the forest, enduring even the rough conditions.

“Bhāvento satipaṭṭhāne, indriyāni balāni ca;

Bojjhaṅgāni ca bhāvento, viharissāmi kānane.

“Developing the establishments of mindfulness, the faculties and the powers, and developing the factors of enlightenment, I will dwell in the forest.

“Āraddhavīriye pahitatte, niccaṃ daḷhaparakkame;

Samagge sahite disvā, viharissāmi kānane.

“With energy aroused and mind directed, always of firm exertion, seeing myself united and harmonious, I will dwell in the forest.

“Anussaranto [M 2.0216] sambuddhaṃ, aggaṃ dantaṃ samāhitaṃ;

Atandito rattindivaṃ, viharissāmi kānane”ti. (theragā. 351-354) –

“Recollecting the Perfectly Enlightened One—supreme, tamed, and composed—unwearied day and night, I will dwell in the forest.”

Catasso gāthāyo abhāsi. Tāsaṃ attho theragāthāvaṇṇanāyaṃ (theragā. aṭṭha. 2.351-354) vuttoyeva. Evaṃ thero vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

He spoke these four verses. Their meaning is explained in the Theragāthā Commentary (Theragā. Aṭṭha. 2.351-354). Thus, the Elder, having diligently applied himself to insight, attained arahantship.

28. So arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento ito satasahassamhītiādimāha. Tattha itoti kakusandhādīnaṃ uppannabhaddakappato heṭṭhā kappasatasahassamatthaketi attho.

28. Having attained arahantship, recollecting his past deeds, and filled with joy, he revealed his former conduct, saying, “A hundred thousand eons from now…” and so on. Here, “from now” means a hundred thousand eons prior to this auspicious eon in which Kakusandha and others arose.

29. Padumākāravadanoti supupphitapadumasassirīkamukho. Padumapattakkhoti setapadumapupphapaṇṇasadisaakkhīti attho.

29. “With a face like a lotus” means a face with the beauty of a fully blossomed lotus. “With eyes like lotus petals” means eyes resembling the petals of a white lotus flower.

30. Padumuttaragandhovāti padumagandhamukhoti attho.

30. “With the supreme fragrance of a lotus” means his mouth was fragrant with the scent of a lotus.

31. Andhānaṃ [P 0.0494] nayanūpamoti cakkhuvirahitānaṃ sattānaṃ nayanasadiso, dhammadesanāya sabbasattānaṃ [V 2.0216] paññācakkhādicakkhudāyakoti attho. Santavesoti santasabhāvo santairiyāpatho. Guṇanidhīti guṇānaṃ nidhi, sabbaguṇagaṇānaṃ nidhānaṭṭhānabhūtoti attho. Karuṇāmatiākaroti sādhūnaṃ cittakampanasaṅkhātāya karuṇāya ca atthānatthaminanaparicchinnamatiyā ca ākaro ādhārabhūto.

31. “An eye for the blind” means he is like an eye for beings deprived of sight; that is, through his teaching of the Dhamma, he is a giver of eyes, such as the eye of wisdom, to all beings. “Of peaceful demeanor” means having a peaceful nature and peaceful deportment. “A treasury of virtues” means a treasury of virtues, being the repository for all collections of virtues. “A source of compassion and wisdom” means he is a foundation for compassion—described as the trembling of the hearts of the good—and for wisdom, which discerns benefit and harm.

32. Brahmāsurasuraccitoti brahmehi ca asurehi ca devehi ca accito pūjitoti attho.

32. “Revered by Brahmās, Asuras, and Devas” means he is worshipped by Brahmās, Asuras, and devas.

33. Madhurena rutena cāti karavīkarutamadhurena saddena sakalaṃ janaṃ rañjayantīti sambandho. Santhavī sāvakaṃ sakanti attano sāvakaṃ madhuradhammadesanāya santhavī, thutiṃ akāsīti attho.

33. “With a sweet voice” refers to delighting all people with a sound as sweet as the call of the karavīka bird. “He praised his disciple” means he praised his own disciple with a sweet Dhamma teaching; that is, he offered praise.

34. Saddhādhimuttoti saddahanasaddhāya sāsane adhimutto patiṭṭhitoti attho. Mama dassanalālasoti mayhaṃ dassane byāvaṭo tapparo.

34. “Devoted through faith” means firmly established in the Dispensation through trusting faith. “Eager to see me” means he was occupied and devoted to seeing me.

35. Taṃ [M 2.0217] ṭhānamabhirocayinti taṃ saddhādhimuttaṭṭhānantaraṃ abhirocayiṃ, icchiṃ patthesinti attho.

35. “I delighted in that position” means I delighted in, desired, and aspired to that state of devotion through faith.

40. Pītamaṭṭhanivāsananti siliṭṭhasuvaṇṇavaṇṇavatthe nivatthanti attho. Hemayaññopacitaṅganti suvaṇṇapāmaṅgalaggitagattanti attho.

40. “Clothed in yellow undergarments” means dressed in garments the color of burnished gold. “With a body built up with gold” means his body was covered with golden auspicious marks.

47-48. Nonītasukhumālaṃ manti navanītamiva mudutaluṇahatthapādaṃ. Jātapallavakomalanti asokapallavapattakomalamiva mudukanti attho. Pisācībhayatajjitāti tadā evaṃbhūtaṃ kumāraṃ maṃ aññā pisācī ekā rakkhasī bhayena tajjesi bhiṃsāpesīti attho. Tadā mahesissa sammāsambuddhassa pādamūle maṃ sāyesuṃ nipajjāpesuṃ. Dīnamānasā bhītacittā mama mātāpitaro imaṃ dārakaṃ te dadāma, imassa saraṇaṃ patiṭṭhā hotu nātha nāyakāti sambandho.

47-48. “Soft as fresh butter” means having hands and feet as tender as freshly churned butter. “Delicate as a young leaf” means as soft as the tender leaf of an ashoka tree. “Terrified by the fear of a goblin” means at that time, another goblin, a certain ogress, frightened and terrified me, such a child, with fear. Then, at the feet of the Great Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, they laid me down. With distressed minds and frightened hearts, my parents said, “We give this child to you; O Protector, O Leader, be a refuge and a foundation for this child!”

49. Tadā paṭiggahi so manti so bhagavā tadā tasmiṃ mama mātuyā dinnakāle jālinā jālayuttena saṅkhālakena cakkalakkhaṇādīhi [P 0.0495] lakkhitena mudukomalapāṇinā mudukena visuddhena hatthatalena maṃ aggahesīti attho.

49. “Then he accepted me” means that at that time, when my mother offered me, the Blessed One received me with his hand—webbed, marked with the wheel and other signs, soft and delicate—and with his soft, pure palm he took hold of me.

52. Sabbapāramisambhūtanti [V 2.0217] sabbehi dānapāramitādīhi sambhūtaṃ jātaṃ. Nīlakkhinayanaṃ varaṃ puññasambhārajaṃ uttamanīlaakkhivantaṃ. Sabbasubhākiṇṇaṃ sabbena subhena vaṇṇena saṇṭhānena ākiṇṇaṃ gahanībhūtaṃ rūpaṃ bhagavato hatthapādasīsādirūpaṃ disvāti attho, tittiṃ apatto viharāmi ahanti sambandho.

52. “Born from all perfections” means produced, born from all the perfections, such as the perfection of generosity. “With excellent dark eyes” means having supreme dark eyes, born from the accumulation of merit. “Adorned with all beauties” means the Blessed One’s form—his hands, feet, head, and other features—was filled and dense with every beautiful color and shape. The connection is: ‘Seeing this, I dwell without attaining satisfaction.’

61. Tadā maṃ caraṇantagoti tasmiṃ mayhaṃ arahattaṃ pattakāle sīlādipannarasannaṃ caraṇadhammānaṃ antago, pariyosānappatto paripūrakārīti attho. “Maraṇantago”tipi pāṭho. Tassa maraṇassa antaṃ nibbānaṃ pattoti attho. Saddhādhimuttānaṃ aggaṃ paññapesīti sambandho. Atha satthā bhikkhusaṅghamajjhe nisinno “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ saddhādhimuttānaṃ yadidaṃ, vakkalī”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 208) maṃ etadaggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

61. At that time, I was called “Caraṇantago,” because when I attained arahantship, I had reached the end of the fifteen qualities of conduct, such as virtue—meaning I had reached the limit, attained the culmination, and was their fulfiller. There is also a variant reading, “Maraṇantago,” meaning that one has reached the end of death, which is Nibbāna. The connection is: ‘He declared me foremost among those devoted through faith.’ Then, the Teacher, seated amidst the community of bhikkhus, declared, “Monks, among my disciples devoted to faith, Vakkali is the foremost” (A. Ni. 1.198, 208), thus establishing me in that foremost position. The rest is easily understood.

Vakkalittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vakkali is complete.

3. Mahākappinattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākappina

Padumuttaro [M 2.0218] nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato kappinattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā satthu santike dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthārā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ovādakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapitaṃ disvā adhikārakammaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthesi.

The Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kappina begins with 'Padumuttara, the Victorious.' He too, having made a resolve in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits conducive to the cessation of rebirth in various existences, was born in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having attained maturity and listening to the Dhamma discourse in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher place one monk in the foremost position among those who give exhortation. Having made an act of aspiration, he aspired to that same position.

So tattha yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto bārāṇasito avidūre ekasmiṃ pesakāragāme jeṭṭhapesakāragehe nibbatto tadā sahassamattā paccekabuddhā himavante aṭṭha māse vasitvā vassike cattāro māse janapade vasanti. Te ekavāraṃ bārāṇasiyā avidūre otaritvā “senāsanaṃ karaṇatthāya hatthakammaṃ yācathā”ti rañño santikaṃ aṭṭha paccekabuddhe pahiṇiṃsu. Tadā pana rañño vappamaṅgalaṃ ahosi. So “paccekabuddhā [P 0.0496] kira āgatā”ti sutvā nikkhamitvā āgatakāraṇaṃ pucchitvā “ajja, bhante, okāso natthi sve amhākaṃ vappamaṅgalaṃ[V 2.0218], tatiyadivase karissāmā”ti vatvā paccekabuddhe animantetvāva pāvisi. Paccekabuddhā “aññaṃ gāmaṃ pavisissāmā”ti pakkamiṃsu.

So, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life and wandering among gods and humans, he was reborn in the house of the chief weaver in a weaver's village not far from Bārāṇasī. At that time, about a thousand Paccekabuddhas, having spent eight months in the Himalayas, dwelled in the countryside for the four months of the rainy season. They descended once near Bārāṇasī and sent eight Paccekabuddhas to the king, saying, 'Seek manual labor for the purpose of preparing a dwelling.' At that time, the king was holding a ploughing festival. Hearing that the Paccekabuddhas had arrived, he went out, inquired about their purpose, and said, 'Today, Venerables, there is no opportunity. Tomorrow is our ploughing festival; we will attend to it on the third day.' Having spoken thus, he entered without inviting the Paccekabuddhas. The Paccekabuddhas thought, 'We shall enter another village,' and departed.

Tasmiṃ samaye jeṭṭhapesakārassa bhariyā kenacideva karaṇīyena bārāṇasiṃ gacchantī te paccekabuddhe disvā vanditvā, “kiṃ, bhante, avelāya ayyā āgatā”ti pucchi. Te ādito paṭṭhāya kathesuṃ. Taṃ sutvā saddhāsampannā buddhisampannā itthī “sve, bhante, amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantesi. “Bahukā mayaṃ, bhaginī”ti. “Kittakā, bhante”ti? “Sahassamattā, bhaginī”ti. “Bhante, imasmiṃ no gāme sahassamattā vasimhā, ekeko ekekassa bhikkhaṃ dassati, bhikkhaṃ adhivāsetha, ahameva vo vasanaṭṭhānaṃ kārāpessāmī”ti āha. Paccekabuddhā adhivāsesuṃ.

At that time, the wife of the chief weaver, while going to Bārāṇasī for some business, saw the Paccekabuddhas. She paid homage to them and asked, 'Venerables, why have you come at this untimely hour?' They explained everything from the beginning. Hearing this, the woman, endowed with faith and wisdom, invited them, saying, 'Venerables, please accept alms from us tomorrow.' They replied, 'We are many, sister.' 'How many, Venerables?' 'About a thousand, sister.' She said, 'Venerables, in this village of ours there are about a thousand inhabitants. Each one will give alms to one. Please accept the alms. I myself will arrange a dwelling place for you.' The Paccekabuddhas consented.

Sā gāmaṃ pavisitvā ugghosesi – “ammatātā, ahaṃ sahassamatte paccekabuddhe disvā nimantesiṃ, ayyānaṃ nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ saṃvidahatha, yāgubhattādīni sampādethā”ti gāmamajjhe maṇḍapaṃ kārāpetvā āsanāni paññāpetvā punadivase paccekabuddhe nisīdāpetvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisitvā bhattakiccapariyosāne tasmiṃ gāme sabbā itthiyo [M 2.0219] ādāya tāhi saddhiṃ paccekabuddhe vanditvā temāsaṃ vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gaṇhitvā puna gāme ugghosesi – “ammatātā, ekekakulato ekekapuriso vāsipharasuādīni gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā dabbasambhāre āharitvā ayyānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ karotū”ti. Gāmavāsino tassāyeva vacanaṃ sutvā ekeko ekekaṃ katvā saddhiṃ rattidivāṭṭhānehi paṇṇasālasahassaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā attano attano paṇṇasālāyaṃ upagataṃ paccekabuddhaṃ “ahaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmi, ahaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti vatvā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Sā vassaṃvuṭṭhakāle “attano attano paṇṇasālāya vassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ paccekabuddhānaṃ cīvarasāṭake sajjethā”ti samādapetvā ekekassa sahassa sahassamūlaṃ cīvaraṃ dāpesi. Paccekabuddhā vuṭṭhavassā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Gāmavāsinopi idaṃ puññakammaṃ katvā tato cuto tāvatiṃsadevaloke nibbattitvā gaṇadevatā nāma ahesuṃ.

She entered the village and announced: 'Dear mothers and fathers, I have seen about a thousand Paccekabuddhas and invited them. Prepare seats for the noble ones and arrange for rice porridge and other food.' In the middle of the village, she had a pavilion built and seats arranged. The next day, she seated the Paccekabuddhas and served them with exquisite hard and soft food. When the meal was finished, she gathered all the women of the village and, after paying respects to the Paccekabuddhas with them, made a pledge to provide them with a dwelling for the three months. Then she announced again in the village: 'Dear mothers and fathers, let one man from each household, taking axes, adzes, and other tools, enter the forest, gather materials, and build a dwelling place for the noble ones.' The villagers, hearing her words, each one building one, completed a thousand leaf-huts with day and night quarters. They then attended to the Paccekabuddha who had come to their respective leaf-hut, saying, 'I will attend to you respectfully,' and served them devotedly. At the end of the rains-retreat, she instructed them, saying, 'Prepare robes and garments for the Paccekabuddhas who have completed the rains-retreat in your respective leaf-huts.' She arranged for each to be given a robe worth a thousand. The Paccekabuddhas, having completed their rains-retreat, gave their blessings and departed. The villagers, having performed this meritorious deed, passed away from there and were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, becoming deities known as the Gaṇadevatā.

Te tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā kassapasammāsambuddhakāle kuṭumbikagehesu nibbattiṃsu. Pubbe jeṭṭhakapesakāro jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikassa putto ahosi. Bhariyāpissa ekassa jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikassa dhītā ahosi. Sesānaṃ bhariyāyo sesakuṭumbikānaṃ dhītaro [P 0.0497] ahesuṃ, tā sabbāpi vayappattā parakulaṃ gacchantiyo tesaṃ tesaṃyeva gehāni agamaṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ vihāre dhammassavane saṅghuṭṭhe “satthā dhammaṃ desessatī”ti sutvā te sabbepi kuṭumbikā “dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti [V 2.0219] bhariyāhi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ agamaṃsu. Tesaṃ vihāramajjhaṃ paviṭṭhakkhaṇe vassaṃ vassi. Yesaṃ kulūpakā vā ñātisāmaṇerādayo vā atthi, te tesaṃ pariveṇādīni pavisiṃsu. Te pana tathārūpānaṃ natthitāya katthaci pavisituṃ avisahantā vihāramajjheyeva aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha ne jeṭṭhakakuṭumbiko āha – “passatha, bho, amhākaṃ vippakāraṃ, kulaputtehi nāma ettakena lajjituṃ yutta”nti. “Ayya, kiṃ karomā”ti? “Mayaṃ vissāsikaṭṭhānassa abhāvena imaṃ vippakāraṃ pattā, sabbe dhanaṃ saṃharitvā pariveṇaṃ karissāmā”ti. “Sādhu, ayyā”ti jeṭṭhako sahassaṃ adāsi. Sesā pañca pañca satāni. Itthiyo aḍḍhateyyāni aḍḍhateyyāni satāni. Te taṃ dhanaṃ āharitvā sahassakūṭāgāraparivāraṃ satthu vasanatthāya mahāpariveṇaṃ nāma [M 2.0220] kārāpesuṃ. Navakammassa mahantatāya dhane appahonte pubbe dinnadhanato puna upaḍḍhūpaḍḍhaṃ adaṃsu. Niṭṭhite pariveṇe vihāramahaṃ karontā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānaṃ cīvarāni sajjayiṃsu.

Having enjoyed divine bliss there, they were reborn in the households of householders during the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The one who was formerly the chief weaver was reborn as the son of the chief householder. His wife was the daughter of a certain chief householder. The wives of the others were the daughters of the other householders, and when they all came of age and went to their husbands' families, they went to those very homes. Then one day, when a Dhamma talk was announced at the monastery, 'The Teacher will teach the Dhamma,' all those householders, thinking, 'We will listen to the Dhamma,' went to the monastery with their wives. At the moment they entered the monastery, it began to rain. Those who had family attendants or novice relatives entered their residences. But the others, having no such connections and being unable to enter anywhere, remained standing in the middle of the monastery. Then the chief householder said to them, 'Behold, friends, our predicament! It is not fitting for sons of good families to be shamed in this way.' 'What shall we do, sir?' they asked. 'Because we lack a familiar place, we have met with this predicament; let us all collect wealth and build a residence.' 'Very well, sir,' they agreed. The eldest gave a thousand; the others, five hundred each; and the women, two hundred and fifty each. Bringing that wealth together, they had a great residence built called Mahāpariveṇa, surrounded by a thousand pinnacled buildings, for the Teacher to reside in. Because the construction project was so great, when the funds proved insufficient, they again gave half of what they had previously given. When the residence was completed, holding a great monastery festival, they gave great alms for seven days to the Saṅgha of monks with the Buddha at its head, and prepared robes for twenty thousand monks.

Jeṭṭhakakuṭumbikassa pana bhariyā attano paññāya ṭhitā ahaṃ tehi samakaṃ akatvā atirekataraṃ katvā “satthāraṃ pūjessāmī”ti anojapupphavaṇṇena sahassamūlena sāṭakena saddhiṃ anojapupphacaṅkoṭakaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ anojapupphehi pūjetvā taṃ sāṭakaṃ satthu pādamūle ṭhapetvā, “bhante, nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne anojapupphavaṇṇaṃyeva me sarīraṃ hotu, anojātveva ca nāmaṃ hotū”ti patthanaṃ akāsi. Satthā “evaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ akāsi. Te sabbepi yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cutā devaloke nibbattiṃsu. Te imasmiṃ buddhuppāde devalokā cavitvā jeṭṭhako kukkuṭavatīnagare rājakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto mahākappinarājā nāma ahosi. Sesā amaccakulesu nibbattiṃsu. Jeṭṭhakassa bhariyā maddaraṭṭhe sākalanagare rājakule nibbatti anojapupphavaṇṇamevassā sarīraṃ ahosi, tena anojātvevassā nāmaṃ akaṃsu, sā vayappattā mahākappinarañño gehaṃ gantvā anojādevīti pākaṭā ahosi.

The wife of the chief householder, however, acting on her own wisdom, thought, 'I will not act equally with them, but will do something more to honor the Teacher.' Taking an Anojā flower basket along with a cloth of Anojā flower color worth a thousand, she honored the Teacher with Anojā flowers and placed that cloth at the Teacher’s feet. She made this aspiration: 'Venerable sir, wherever I am reborn, may my body always be the color of Anojā flowers, and may my name always be Anojā.' The Teacher gave his blessing, saying, 'So be it.' All of them lived out their full lifespans and, after passing away from there, were reborn in the heavenly realm. In this Buddha-era, they passed away from the heavenly world. The chief was reborn in the royal family of Kukkuṭavatī city and, upon reaching maturity, became the great King Kappina. The others were reborn in the families of ministers. The chief’s wife was reborn in the royal family of Sākala city in the Madda country. Her body was indeed the color of Anojā flowers, for which reason they named her Anojā. When she came of age, she went to the household of King Mahākappina and became known as Queen Anojā.

Sesitthiyopi amaccakulesu nibbattitvā vayappattā tesaṃyeva amaccaputtānaṃ [P 0.0498] gehāni agamaṃsu. Te sabbepi rañño sampattisadisaṃ sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu. Yadā hi rājā alaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā vicarati, tadāpi te tatheva vicaranti. Tasmiṃ assena vā rathena vā vicarante tepi tatheva vicaranti. Evaṃ te ekato hutvā katānaṃ puññānaṃ balena ekatova sampattiṃ anubhaviṃsu. Rañño pana vālo, vālavāhano, puppho, pupphavāhano, supattoti pañceva assā honti. Tesu rājā supattaṃ assaṃ sayaṃ ārohati, itare cattāro asse assārohānaṃ sāsanāharaṇatthāya adāsi. Rājā te pātova bhojetvā “gacchatha[V 2.0220], bhaṇe, dve vā tīṇi vā yojanāni āhiṇḍitvā buddhassa vā dhammassa vā saṅghassa vā uppannabhāvaṃ sutvā mayhaṃ sukhasāsanaṃ [M 2.0221] ārocethā”ti pesesi. Te catūhi dvārehi nikkhamitvā dve tīṇi yojanāni āhiṇḍitvā kiñci sāsanaṃ alabhitvāva paccāgamiṃsu.

The remaining women also, having been reborn in the families of ministers and having come of age, went to the houses of those very sons of ministers. They all enjoyed a prosperity similar to that of the king. For when the king, adorned with ornaments, mounted an elephant and traveled about, they too traveled in the same way. When he traveled by horse or by chariot, they did likewise. Thus, by the power of the merit they had made together, they enjoyed prosperity together. Now, the king had five horses: Vāla, Vālavāhana, Puppha, Pupphavāhana, and Supatta. Among them, the king himself rode the horse Supatta, while he gave the other four horses to his horsemen for carrying messages. The king fed them early in the morning and sent them off, saying, 'Go, sirs, wander two or three yojanas, and if you hear of the arising of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, report the good news to me.' They went out through the four gates, wandered two or three yojanas, but having obtained no message, they returned.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā supattaṃ āruhitvā amaccasahassaparivuto uyyānaṃ gacchanto kilantarūpe pañcasatamatte vāṇijake nagaraṃ pavisante disvā “ime addhānakilantā, addho imesaṃ santikā ekaṃ bhaddakaṃ sāsanaṃ sossāmī”ti te pakkosāpetvā “kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, ito vīsatiyojanasatamatthake sāvatthi nāma nagaraṃ, tato āgatamhā”ti. “Atthi pana vo dese kiñci sāsanaṃ uppanna”nti. “Deva, aññaṃ kiñci natthi, sammāsambuddho uppanno”ti. Rājā tāvadeva balavapītiyā phuṭṭhasarīro kiñci sallakkhetuṃ asakkonto muhuttaṃ vītināmetvā pana, “tātā, kiṃ vadethā”ti pucchi. “Buddho, deva, uppanno”ti. Rājā dutiyampi tatiyampi tatheva vītināmetvā catutthavāre “kiṃ vadetha, tātā”ti pucchitvā “buddho uppanno”ti vutte, “tātā, sukhasāsanasavanāya satasahassaṃ vo dammī”ti vatvā “aparampi kiñci sāsanaṃ atthi, tātā”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, dhammo uppanno”ti. Rājā tampi sutvā purimanayeneva tayo vāre vītināmetvā catutthavāre “dhammo uppanno”ti vutte – “idhāpi vo satasahassaṃ dammī”ti vatvā “aparampi kiñci sāsanaṃ atthi, tātā”ti pucchi. “Atthi, deva, saṅgho uppanno”ti. Rājā tampi sutvā tatheva tayo vāre vītināmetvā catutthavāre “saṅgho uppanno”ti vutte – “idhāpi vo satasahassaṃ dammī”ti vatvā amaccasahassaṃ oloketvā, “tātā, kiṃ karissāmā”ti pucchi. “Deva, tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Ahaṃ, tātā, ‘buddho uppanno dhammo uppanno saṅgho uppanno’ti sutvā na puna nivattissāmi, bhagavantaṃ uddissa gantvā tassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. “Mayampi, deva, tumhehi saddhiṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. Rājā suvaṇṇapaṭṭe [P 0.0499] akkharāni likhāpetvā vāṇijakānaṃ datvā “imaṃ anojāya nāma deviyā detha, sā tumhākaṃ tīṇi satasahassāni dassati, evañca pana naṃ vadeyyātha ‘raññā kira te issariyaṃ vissaṭṭhaṃ, yathāsukhaṃ sampattiṃ paribhuñjāhī’ti, sace pana ‘vo rājā kaha’nti pucchati, ‘satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajissāmī’ti vatvā gatoti āroceyyāthā”ti āha. Amaccāpi attano attano bhariyānaṃ tatheva [M 2.0222] sāsanaṃ pahiṇiṃsu. Rājā vāṇijake uyyojetvā assaṃ abhiruyha amaccasahassaparivuto taṃkhaṇaññeva nikkhami.

Then one day, the king, having mounted Supatta and surrounded by a thousand ministers, was going to the park when he saw about five hundred merchants with weary forms entering the city. Thinking, 'These men are tired from their journey; surely I will hear some good news from them,' he had them summoned and asked: 'Whence have you come?' 'Your Majesty, there is a city named Sāvatthī one hundred and twenty yojanas from here. We have come from there.' 'Has any news arisen in your country?' 'Your Majesty, there is nothing else, but a Perfectly Enlightened One has arisen.' The king’s body was immediately suffused with powerful joy, and being unable to comprehend anything, he let a moment pass, and then asked: 'My dears, what did you say?' 'A Buddha has arisen, Your Majesty.' The king let a second and a third time pass in the same way, and on the fourth occasion he asked, 'What did you say, my dears?' When they said, 'A Buddha has arisen,' he said, 'My dears, for hearing this happy news I give you a hundred thousand.' Then he asked, 'Is there any other news, my dears?' 'There is, Your Majesty, the Dhamma has arisen.' Hearing this too, the king let three times pass in the same way as before, and on the fourth occasion, when they said, 'The Dhamma has arisen,' he said, 'For this too I give you a hundred thousand.' And he asked, 'Is there any other news, my dears?' 'There is, Your Majesty, the Saṅgha has arisen.' Hearing this too, he let three times pass in the same way, and on the fourth occasion, when they said, 'The Saṅgha has arisen,' he said, 'For this too I give you a hundred thousand.' Then, looking at his thousand ministers, he asked, 'My dears, what shall we do?' 'Your Majesty, what will you do?' 'My dears, having heard, "A Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma has arisen, the Saṅgha has arisen," I will not turn back. I will go with the Blessed One as my destination and go forth in his presence.' 'We too, Your Majesty, will go forth with you.' The king had letters inscribed on a golden plate and gave it to the merchants, saying: 'Give this to the queen named Anojā. She will give you three hundred thousand. And you should tell her this: "The king has relinquished his sovereignty to you. Enjoy your fortune as you please." But if she asks, "Where is your king?" you should report: "He has gone, saying, ‘I will go forth with the Teacher as my destination.’"' The ministers also sent the same message to their own wives. The king sent the merchants on their way, mounted his horse, and, surrounded by his thousand ministers, he departed at that very moment.

Satthāpi taṃdivasaṃ paccūsakāle lokaṃ volokento mahākappinarājānaṃ saparivāraṃ disvā “ayaṃ [V 2.0221] mahākappino vāṇijakānaṃ santikā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ uppannabhāvaṃ sutvā tesaṃ vacanaṃ tīhi satasahassehi pūjetvā rajjaṃ pahāya amaccasahassaparivuto maṃ uddissa pabbajitukāmo sve nikkhamissati, so saparivāro saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇissati, paccuggamanaṃ karissāmī”ti punadivase cakkavattī viya khuddakagāmabhojakaṃ rājānaṃ paccuggacchanto sayameva pattacīvaramādāya vīsayojanasataṃ maggaṃ paccuggantvā candabhāgāya nadiyā tīre nigrodharukkhamūle chabbaṇṇabuddharasmiyo vissajjetvā nisīdi. Rājāpi āgacchanto ekaṃ nadiṃ patvā “kā nāmāya”nti pucchi. “Aparacchā nāma, devā”ti. “Kimassā parimāṇaṃ, tātā”ti? “Gambhīrato gāvutaṃ, puthulato dve gāvutāni, devā”ti. “Atthi panettha nāvā vā uḷumpo vā”ti? “Natthi, devā”ti. “Nāvādīni olokente amhe jāti jaraṃ upaneti, jarā maraṇaṃ. Ahaṃ nibbematiko hutvā tīṇi ratanāni uddissa nikkhanto, tesaṃ me ānubhāvena ‘idaṃ udakaṃ udakaṃ viya mā hotū’ti ratanattayassa guṇaṃ āvajjetvā ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho’”ti buddhaguṇaṃ anussaranto saparivāro assasahassena udakapiṭṭhe pakkhandi. Sindhavā piṭṭhipāsāṇe viya pakkhandiṃsu. Khurānaṃ aggaṭṭhāneva temiṃsu.

On that day, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw the great King Kappina with his retinue and thought: "This King Kappina, having heard from merchants about the arising of the Three Jewels and having honored their words with three hundred thousand, will renounce his kingdom and, surrounded by a thousand ministers, set out tomorrow to go forth for my sake. He and his retinue will attain arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. I will go to meet him." The next day, like a universal monarch going to meet a petty king, the Teacher himself took his bowl and robe, went one hundred and twenty yojanas to meet him, and sat down at the foot of a banyan tree on the bank of the Candabhāgā River, emitting the six-colored Buddha-rays. As the king was approaching, he came to a river and asked, "What is the name of this river?" "It is called Aparacchā, lord." "What are its dimensions, sirs?" "In depth, one gāvuta; in width, two gāvutas, lord." "Is there a boat or a raft here?" "There is not, lord." "While we look for a boat and such, birth brings on old age, and old age brings on death. I have set out without hesitation for the sake of the Three Jewels. By their power, may this water not be as water." Reflecting on the qualities of the Triple Gem, he recollected the qualities of the Buddha, thinking: "Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One," and with his retinue and a thousand horses, he plunged onto the surface of the water. The Sindhu horses moved on it as if on a stone slab. Only the tips of their hooves got wet.

So taṃ uttaritvā purato gacchanto aparampi nadiṃ disvā “ayaṃ kā nāmā”ti pucchi. “Nīlavāhā nāma, devā”ti. “Kimassā parimāṇa”nti? “Gambhīratopi puthulatopi aḍḍhayojanaṃ, devā”ti. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Taṃ pana nadiṃ disvā “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo”ti dhammānussatiṃ anussaranto pakkhandi. Tampi atikkamitvā gacchanto aparampi nadiṃ disvā “ayaṃ kā nāmā”ti pucchi. “Candabhāgā [P 0.0500] nāma, devā”ti. “Kimassā parimāṇa”nti? “Gambhīratopi puthulatopi yojanaṃ, devā”ti. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Taṃ pana nadiṃ disvā “suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”ti saṅghānussatiṃ anussaranto [M 2.0223] pakkhandi. Tampi nadiṃ atikkamitvā gacchanto satthu sarīrato nikkhantā chabbaṇṇabuddharasmiyo nigrodharukkhassa sākhāviṭapapalāsāni obhāsayamānā disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ obhāso neva candassa, na sūriyassa, na devamārabrāhmaṇasupaṇṇanāgānaṃ aññatarassa, addhā ahaṃ satthāraṃ uddissa āgacchanto sammāsambuddhena diṭṭho bhavissāmī”ti. So tāvadeva assapiṭṭhito otaritvā onatasarīro rasmiyānusārena satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā manosilārase nimujjanto viya buddharasmīnaṃ anto pāvisi. So satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi saddhiṃ amaccasahassena. Satthā tesaṃ anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Desanāpariyosāne saparivāro rājā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

Having crossed it, as he proceeded forward, he saw another river and asked, "What is this river called?" "It is called the Nīlavāhā, lord." "What are its dimensions?" "It is half a yojana in both depth and width, lord." The rest was as before. Upon seeing that river, he plunged in while recollecting the Dhamma: "Well expounded is the Dhamma by the Blessed One." Having crossed that too and proceeding further, he saw another river and asked, "What is this river called?" "It is called the Candabhāgā, lord." "What are its dimensions?" "It is a yojana in both depth and width, lord." The rest was as before. Upon seeing that river, he plunged in while recollecting the Saṅgha: "Well-practiced is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples." Having crossed that river too and proceeding, he saw the six-colored Buddha-rays emanating from the Teacher's body, illuminating the branches, twigs, and leaves of the banyan tree. He thought: "This radiance is not that of the moon, nor the sun, nor of any deva, Māra, Brahmā, garuḍa, or nāga. Surely, as I come for the sake of the Teacher, I must have been seen by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One." He immediately dismounted from his horse, bowed his body, and, following the rays, approached the Teacher and entered into the midst of the Buddha-rays as if plunging into a pool of red arsenic paste. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he sat down to one side along with his thousand ministers. The Teacher gave them a graduated discourse. At the end of the discourse, the king together with his retinue was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Atha [V 2.0222] sabbe uṭṭhahitvā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Satthā “āgamissati nu kho imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ iddhimayapattacīvara”nti upadhārento “ime kulaputtā paccekabuddhasahassānaṃ cīvarasahassaṃ adaṃsu, kassapabuddhakāle vīsatiyā bhikkhusahassānaṃ vīsaticīvarasahassānipi adaṃsu, anacchariyaṃ imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ iddhimayapattacīvarāgamana”nti ñatvā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā “etha, bhikkhavo, caratha brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāyā”ti āha. Te tāvadeva aṭṭhaparikkhāradharā vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya hutvā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā paccorohitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

Then they all rose up and requested the going forth. The Teacher, considering, "Will a bowl and robes created by psychic power come to these clansmen?" and knowing, "These clansmen gave a thousand robes to a thousand paccekabuddhas, and in the time of the Buddha Kassapa they also gave twenty thousand robes to twenty thousand bhikkhus—it is no wonder that a bowl and robes created by psychic power will come to these clansmen," extended his right hand and said, "Come, bhikkhus, lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering." Instantly, they became bearers of the eight requisites, appearing like elders of sixty years' standing. They rose up into the air, descended, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side.

Te pana vāṇijakā rājagehaṃ gantvā deviyā raññā pahitasāsanaṃ ārocetvā deviyā “āgacchantū”ti vutte pavisitvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha ne devī pucchi – “tātā, kiṃkāraṇā āgatatthā”ti? “Mayaṃ raññā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ pesitā, tīṇi kira no satasahassāni dethā”ti. “Bahuṃ, bhaṇe, bhaṇatha, kiṃ tumhehi rañño santike kataṃ, kismiṃ vo rājā pasanno ettakaṃ dhanaṃ dāpetī”ti? “Devi, na aññaṃ kiñci kataṃ, ekaṃ pana sāsanaṃ ārocayimhā”ti. “Sakkā pana, tātā, mayhampi taṃ ārocetu”nti. “Sakkā, devī”ti suvaṇṇabhiṅgārena mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā “devi, buddho loke uppanno”ti. Sāpi taṃ sutvā pītiyā phuṭṭhasarīrā tikkhattuṃ kiñci asallakkhetvā catutthavāre “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā “kiṃ, tātā, imasmiṃ pade raññā dinna”nti[P 0.0501]? “Satasahassaṃ, devī”ti. “Tātā, ananucchavikaṃ raññā kataṃ evarūpaṃ sāsanaṃ [M 2.0224] sutvā tumhākaṃ satasahassadadamānena, ahaṃ vo mama duggatapaṇṇākāre tīṇi satasahassāni dammi. Aparaṃ kiñci tumhehi ārocita”nti? Te idañca idañcāti itarānipi dve sāsanāni ārocesuṃ. Devī purimanayeneva tayo tayo vāre asallakkhetvā catutthacatutthavāre tīṇi tīṇi satasahassāni adāsi. Evaṃ te sabbāni dvādasasatasahassāni labhiṃsu.

Then the merchants went to the royal palace and announced to the queen the message sent by the king. When the queen said, “Come in,” they entered and stood to one side. Then the queen asked them, “Sirs, for what reason have you come?” “We have been sent to you by the king with the message: ‘Give us three hundred thousand.’” “Sirs, you speak of a great amount. What have you done for the king? Why is the king so pleased with you that he is having so much wealth given to you?” “Your Majesty, we have done nothing else, but we announced one piece of news.” “Sirs, can you announce that news to me as well?” “Certainly, Your Majesty.” They rinsed their mouths with a golden pitcher and said, “Your Majesty, a Buddha has arisen in the world.” Upon hearing this, her body was suffused with rapture. Three times she did not register it, but on the fourth time, hearing “a Buddha has arisen,” she asked, “Sirs, what did the king give for this phrase?” “A hundred thousand, Your Majesty.” “Sirs, it was unbecoming of the king, having heard such news, to give you a hundred thousand. I shall give you three hundred thousand as a humble gift from me. Have you announced anything else?” They then announced the other two pieces of news as well. In the same way as before, the queen did not register it three times for each, but on the fourth time for each, she gave them three hundred thousand. Thus, they received a total of twelve hundred thousand.

Atha ne devī pucchi – “rājā kahaṃ, tātā”ti? “Devi, rājā ‘satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajissāmī’ti vatvā gato”ti. “Mayhaṃ tena kiṃ sāsanaṃ dinna”nti? “Sabbaṃ kira issariyaṃ tumhākaṃ vissaṭṭhaṃ, ‘tumhe kira yathāsukhaṃ sampattiṃ anubhavathā’”ti. “Amaccā pana kuhiṃ, tātā”ti? “Tepi raññā saddhiṃ ‘pabbajissāmā’ti gatā, devī”ti. Sā tesaṃ bhariyāyo pakkosāpetvā, “ammā, tumhākaṃ sāmikā raññā saddhiṃ ‘pabbajissāmā’ti gatā, tumhe kiṃ karissathā”ti? “Kiṃ pana tehi amhākaṃ sāsanaṃ pahitaṃ, devī”ti? “Tehi kira attano sampatti tumhākaṃ vissaṭṭhā ‘tumhe kira sampattiṃ yathāsukhaṃ paribhuñjathā’”ti. “Tumhe pana, devi, kiṃ [V 2.0223] karissathā”ti? “Amhākaṃ so tāva rājā magge ṭhito tīhi satasahassehi tīṇi ratanāni pūjetvā kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya sampattiṃ pahāya ‘pabbajissāmī’ti nikkhanto, mayāpi tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā tāni navahi satasahassehi pūjitāni, na kho panesā sampatti nāma raññoyeva dukkhā, mayhampi dukkhā eva. Ko raññā chaḍḍitakheḷapiṇḍaṃ jaṇṇukehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā mukhena gaṇhissati, na mayhaṃ sampattiyā attho, satthāraṃ uddissa pabbajissāmī”ti. “Devi, mayampi tumhehi saddhiṃ pabbajissāmā”ti. “Sace sakkotha, sādhū”ti. “Sakkoma, devī”ti. Tena hi “ethā”ti rathasahassaṃ yojāpetvā rathaṃ āruyha tāhi saddhiṃ nikkhamitvā antarāmagge paṭhamaṃ nadiṃ disvā yathā raññā paṭhamaṃ pucchitā, tatheva pucchitvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “raññā gatamaggaṃ olokethā”ti vatvā “sindhavānaṃ padavalañjaṃ na passāmā”ti vutte rājā “tīṇi ratanāni uddissa nikkhantosmī”ti saccakiriyaṃ karitvā tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe anussaritvā gato bhavissati[P 0.0502], ahampi tīṇi ratanāni uddissa nikkhantā, tesaṃ me ānubhāvena “idaṃ udakaṃ udakaṃ viya mā hotū”ti tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe anussarantī rathasahassaṃ [M 2.0225] pesesi. Udakaṃ piṭṭhipāsāṇasadisaṃ ahosi, cakkānaṃ aggaṭṭhāneva temiṃsu. Eteneva upāyena itarā dvepi nadiyo uttariṃsu.

Then the queen asked them, "Sirs, where is the king?" "Your Majesty, the king has gone, saying, ‘I will go forth for the sake of the Teacher.’" "What message did he give for me?" "He has relinquished all sovereignty to you, saying, ‘You may enjoy your fortune as you please.’" "And where are the ministers, sirs?" "They too have gone with the king, saying, ‘We will go forth,’ Your Majesty." She then had their wives summoned and asked, "Ladies, your husbands have gone with the king, saying, ‘We will go forth.’ What will you do?" "What message did they send for us, Your Majesty?" "They have relinquished their own fortune to you, saying, ‘You may enjoy your fortune as you please.’" "And what will you do, Your Majesty?" "Our king, while still on the road, honored the Three Jewels with three hundred thousand, and then, abandoning his fortune like a lump of spittle, he set out, saying, ‘I will go forth.’ Having heard the news of the Three Jewels, I too honored them with nine hundred thousand. This so-called fortune is not suffering only for the king; it is suffering for me as well. Who would get down on their knees and pick up with their mouth a lump of spittle spat out by the king? I have no use for this fortune. I will go forth for the sake of the Teacher." "Your Majesty, we too will go forth with you." "If you are able, that is good." "We are able, Your Majesty." "Then come." She had a thousand chariots yoked, mounted a chariot, and set out with them. On the way, she saw the first river and asked about it just as the king had done. Having heard the whole story, she said, "Look for the path the king took." When they said, "We do not see the tracks of the Sindhu horses," she thought, "The king must have gone by making an asseveration of truth, saying, ‘I have set out for the sake of the Three Jewels,’ and by recollecting their qualities. I too have set out for the sake of the Three Jewels. By their power, may this water not be like water." Recollecting the qualities of the Three Jewels, she sent the thousand chariots forward. The water became like a stone slab, and only the rims of the wheels got wet. By this same method, they crossed the other two rivers as well.

Satthā tāsaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā yathā tā attano santike nisinne sāmike bhikkhū na passanti, tathā adhiṭṭhāsi. Devīpi āgacchantī satthu sarīrato nikkhantā rasmiyo disvā tatheva cintetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā, vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā pucchi – “bhante, mahākappino rājā tumhe uddissa nikkhamitvā gato, kahaṃ nu kho so, amhākaṃ taṃ dassethā”ti. “Nisīdatha tāva, idheva naṃ passissathā”ti. Tā sabbāpi haṭṭhatuṭṭhā “idheva kira nisinnā sāmike no passissāmā”ti nisīdiṃsu. Satthā anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Anojādevī desanāpariyosāne tāhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Mahākappino thero tāsaṃ desiyamānaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saparivāro saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā tāsaṃ te bhikkhū dassesi. Tāsañhi āgatakkhaṇeyeva attano sāmike kāsāvadhare muṇḍasīse disvā cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na bhaveyya, maggaphalaṃ nibbattetuṃ sakkā na bhaveyya. Tasmā acalasaddhāya patiṭṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya tāsaṃ te bhikkhū arahattappatte dassesi. Tāpi te disvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā, “bhante, tumhākaṃ pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakappatta”nti vatvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu.

The Teacher, knowing of their arrival, made a determination so that they would not see their husbands, the bhikkhus, who were seated near him. The queen, upon arriving and seeing the rays emanating from the Teacher's body, thought in the same way, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and, standing to one side, asked: “Venerable Sir, King Mahākappina has gone forth on account of you. Where might he be? Please show him to us.” “First sit down; you will see him right here.” Delighted, they all sat down, thinking: “It seems we will see our husbands while seated right here.” The Teacher then gave a graduated discourse. At the conclusion of the discourse, Queen Anojā, together with the other women, attained the fruit of stream-entry. Hearing the Dhamma discourse being delivered to them, the Elder Mahākappina, along with his retinue, attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. At that moment, the Teacher showed them those bhikkhus. For if, at the very moment of their arrival, they had seen their husbands wearing ochre robes and with shaven heads, their minds would not have become concentrated, and they would not have been able to realize the path and fruit. Therefore, it was only after their faith had become unshakable and well established that he showed them those bhikkhus who had attained arahantship. Seeing them, they too paid homage with the five-point prostration and said: “Venerable Sirs, the task of your going forth has reached its consummation.” Then, having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side and requested to go forth.

Evaṃ vutte satthā uppalavaṇṇāya theriyā āgamanaṃ cintesi. Sā satthu cintitakkhaṇeyeva ākāsenāgantvā [V 2.0224] tā sabbā itthiyo gahetvā ākāsena bhikkhunupassayaṃ netvā pabbājesi. Tā sabbā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthā bhikkhusahassaṃ ādāya ākāsena jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Tatra sudaṃ āyasmā mahākappino rattiṭṭhānādīsu “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udānento vicarati. Bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ – “bhante, mahākappino ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’nti udānaṃ udānento vicarati, attano rajjasukhaṃ ārabbha udāneti maññe”ti. Satthā taṃ pakkosāpetvā – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, kappina, kāmasukhaṃ ārabbha udānaṃ udānesī”ti? “Bhagavā me, bhante, taṃ ārabbha udānabhāvaṃ vā aññaṃ ārabbha udānabhāvaṃ vā jānātī”ti. Atha satthā – “na, bhikkhave, mama putto kāmasukhaṃ rajjasukhaṃ ārabbha udānaṃ udāneti, puttassa [M 2.0226] pana me dhammaṃ carato dhammapīti nāma uppajjati, so amatamahānibbānaṃ [P 0.0503] ārabbha evaṃ udānaṃ udānesī”ti anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

When this was said, the Teacher thought of the arrival of the Therī Uppalavaṇṇā. At the very moment the Teacher thought of her, she came through the air, took all those women, and led them through the air to the bhikkhunīs’ quarters, where she gave them the going forth. Before long, they all attained arahantship. The Teacher, taking the thousand bhikkhus, went through the air to Jetavana. There, the Venerable Mahākappina was wandering about in his day and night quarters uttering the inspired utterance: “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!” The bhikkhus reported this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, Mahākappina is wandering about uttering the inspired utterance, ‘Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!’ We think he utters it with reference to his own royal happiness.” The Teacher had him summoned and asked: “Is it true, Kappina, that you utter this inspired utterance with reference to sensual happiness?” “Venerable Sir, the Blessed One knows whether I utter it with reference to that or with reference to something else.” Then the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, my son does not utter this inspired utterance with reference to sensual happiness or royal happiness. But for my son who is practicing the Dhamma, a rapture in the Dhamma arises. It is with reference to the deathless, great Nibbāna that he utters this inspired utterance.” Connecting the story, while teaching the Dhamma he spoke this verse:

“Dhammapīti sukhaṃ seti, vippasannena cetasā;

Ariyappavedite dhamme, sadā ramati paṇḍito”ti. (dha. pa. 79);

He who drinks the Dhamma lives happily with a tranquil mind. The wise one ever delights in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.

Athekadivasaṃ satthā bhikkhū āmantesi – “kacci, bhikkhave, kappino bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desetī”ti? “Appossukko, bhante, diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāraṃ anuyutto viharati, ovādamattampi na detī”ti. Satthā theraṃ pakkosāpetvā – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, kappina, antevāsikānaṃ ovādamattampi na desī”ti? “Saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, mā evaṃ akāsi, ajja paṭṭhāya upagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desehī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti thero bhagavato vacanaṃ sirasā sampaṭicchitvā ekovādeneva samaṇasahassaṃ arahatte patiṭṭhāpesi. Tena naṃ satthā paṭipāṭiyā attano sāvake ṭhānantare ṭhapento “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhuovādakānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākappino”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 231) etadagge ṭhapesi.

Then one day the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, does Kappina teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus?” “Venerable Sir, he is not zealous. He dwells committed to the blissful abiding in the here and now; he does not give even a word of instruction.” The Teacher had the elder summoned and asked: “Is it true, Kappina, that you do not give even a word of instruction to your resident pupils?” “It is true, Blessed One.” “Brahmin, do not act like that. From today onwards, teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus who approach you.” “Very well, Venerable Sir,” the elder replied, and he accepted the Blessed One’s word by bowing his head. With a single exhortation, he established a thousand samaṇas in arahantship. For this reason, the Teacher, when placing his disciples in their respective foremost positions, declared: ‘Bhikkhus, the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are exhorters of bhikkhus is Mahākappina’ (AN 1.24), and placed him in that foremost position.

66. Evaṃ thero pattaarahattaphalo attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Udito ajaṭākāseti sakalākāse udito uṭṭhito pākaṭabhūto. Saradambare saradakāle ākāse ravīva sūriyo ivāti attho.

66. Thus the elder, having attained the fruit of arahantship, recollecting his former deeds, with gladdened mind, and disclosing the story of his former conduct, spoke the verses beginning: ‘The Victor named Padumuttara….’ The phrase ‘udito ajaṭākāse’ (arisen in the clear sky) means: arisen, risen, become manifest in the entire sky. The phrase ‘saradambare ravīva’ (like the sun in the autumn sky) means: like the sun in the sky in the autumn season. This is the meaning.

70. Akkhadasso tadā āsinti tasmiṃ padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle sāradassī hitadassī ācariyo pākaṭo ahosinti attho.

70. The phrase ‘akkhadasso tadā āsiṃ’ (I was then a teacher) means: at the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, I was a well-known teacher, a seer of the essential, a seer of what is beneficial. This is the meaning.

71. Sāvakassa [V 2.0225] katāvinoti tassa bhagavato me manaṃ mama cittaṃ, tappayantassa tosayantassa sāvakassa ovādakassa guṇaṃ pakāsayato aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentassa katāvino sātaccakiccayuttassa vacanaṃ sutvāti sambandho.

71. Regarding the phrase ‘sāvakassa katāvino’ (of the disciple who has done his duty): the connection is with ‘having heard the words.’ That is, having heard the words of that Blessed One who, by proclaiming the virtue of the disciple—the exhorter who had done his duty and was dedicated to the task of perseverance—and by placing him in the foremost position, was satisfying and pleasing my mind.

73. Haṃsasamabhāgoti [M 2.0227] haṃsasadisagāmi. Haṃsadundubhinissanoti haṃsaravo dundubhibherisaddasadisavacano “etaṃ mahāmattaṃ passatha, bhikkhavo”ti āhāti sambandho.

73. The phrase ‘haṃsasamabhāgo’ (with the gait of a swan) means: one who walks like a swan. The phrase ‘haṃsadundubhinissano’ (with the voice of a swan and a drum) means: one whose voice is like the cry of a swan and the sound of a kettledrum or war-drum. The connection is with the words: ‘Bhikkhus, look at this great minister!’

74. Samuggatatanūruhanti suṭṭhu uggatalomaṃ uddhaggalomaṃ, udagyamanaṃ vā. Jīmūtavaṇṇanti muttaphalasamānavaṇṇaṃ sundarasarīrapabhanti [P 0.0504] attho. Pīṇaṃsanti paripuṇṇaṃ aṃsaṃ. Pasannanayanānananti pasannaakkhipasannamukhanti attho.

74. The phrase ‘samuggatatanūruhaṃ’ (with body hair growing upwards) means: with well-grown hair, with hair standing on end, or rising up. The phrase ‘jīmūtavaṇṇaṃ’ (with the color of a cloud) means: having a color like a pearl, with a beautiful bodily radiance. This is the meaning. The phrase ‘pīṇaṃsaṃ’ (with full shoulders) means: with perfectly full shoulders. The phrase ‘pasannanayanānanaṃ’ (with clear eyes and face) means: with clear eyes and a clear face. This is the meaning.

75. Katāvinoti katādhikārassa etadagge ṭhitassa bhikkhuno ṭhānaṃ so eso muditāya pahaṭṭhacittatāya patthetīti sambandho.

75. Regarding ‘katāvino’ (of one who has done his duty): the connection is that he aspires, with joy and a gladdened mind, to the position of that bhikkhu who has made the requisite conditions and stands in that foremost position.

81. Sataso anusāsiyāti dhammena samena vacanena kāraṇavasena anusāsitvāti attho. Bārāṇasiyamāsanneti bārāṇasiyā samīpe pesakāragāme. Jāto keniyajātiyanti tantavāyajātiyā pesakārakule jātoti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

81. The phrase ‘sataso anusāsiya’ (having instructed hundreds) means: having instructed by means of the Dhamma, with balanced speech, and by way of reason. This is the meaning. The phrase ‘bārāṇasiyamāsanne’ (near Bārāṇasī) means: in a weavers’ village near Bārāṇasī. The phrase ‘jāto keniyajātiyaṃ’ (born into the Keniya clan) means: born into a weaver clan, in a weaver’s family. This is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.

Mahākappinattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Chronicle of the Elder Mahākappina is concluded.

4. Dabbamallaputtattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Dabbamallaputta

Catutthāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato dabbamallaputtattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare seṭṭhiputto hutvā jāto vibhavasampanno ahosi, satthari pasanno satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā pasannamānaso buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā sattāhaccayena bhagavato pādamūle nipatitvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ patthesi. Bhagavāpissa samijjhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā byākāsi. So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā tato cuto tusitādīsu devesu dibbasampattiṃ anubhavitvā tato cuto [V 2.0226] vipassissa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto asappurisasaṃsaggena tassa sāvakaṃ bhikkhuṃ arahāti jānantopi abbhūtena abbhācikkhi. Tasseva sāvakānaṃ khīrasalākabhattaṃ adāsi. So yāvatāyukaṃ [M 2.0228] puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā kassapadasabalassa kāle kulagehe nibbatto osānakāle sāsane pabbajito parinibbute bhagavati sakalaloke kolāhale jāte satta bhikkhavo pabbajito paccantajanapade vanamajjhe ekaṃ pabbataṃ abhiruhitvā “jīvitāsā orohantu nirālayā nisīdantū”ti nisseṇiṃ pātesuṃ. Tesaṃ ovādadāyako jeṭṭhakatthero satthāhabbhantare arahā ahosi. Tadanantaratthero anāgāmī, itare pañca parisuddhasīlā tato cutā devaloke nibbattā. Tattha ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ dibbasukhaṃ anubhavitvā [P 0.0505] imasmiṃ buddhuppāde pukkusāti (ma. ni. 3.342), sabhiyo (su. ni. sabhiyasutta), bāhiyo (udā. 10), kumārakassapoti (ma. ni. 1.249) ime cattāro tattha tattha nibbattiṃsu. Ayaṃ pana mallaraṭṭhe anupiyanagare nibbatti. Tasmiṃ mātukucchito anikkhanteyeva mātā kālamakāsi, atheko tassā sarīraṃ jhāpanatthāya citakasmiṃ āropetvā kumāraṃ dabbantare patitaṃ gahetvā jaggāpesi. Dabbe patitattā dabbo mallaputtoti pākaṭo ahosi. Aparabhāge pubbasambhāravasena pabbaji, so kammaṭṭhānamanuyutto nacirasseva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

In the fourth Apadāna, the story of the Venerable Elder Dabbamallaputta, beginning with “the Victor Padumuttara,” is told. This one too, having performed wholesome deeds in the presence of former Buddhas, accumulating merits here and there as a basis for the turning away from existence, was born in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī as the son of a wealthy merchant, endowed with prosperity. Having faith in the Teacher, he listened to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse. Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu as the foremost in assigning lodgings, his mind filled with faith, he invited the bhikkhu Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and offered a great almsgiving for seven days. After seven days, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and aspired for that position. The Blessed One, knowing that his wish would be fulfilled, prophesied it. Having done wholesome deeds throughout his life, after passing away, he experienced divine bliss among the devas in Tusita and other realms. Then, passing from there, he was reborn in a certain family in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Due to association with unwholesome people, even though he knew that monk, a disciple of his, was an arahant, he made a false accusation against him. He also gave milk-ticket meals to the disciples of that arahant. Having performed wholesome deeds for his entire lifespan, wandering among devas and humans, experiencing both kinds of prosperity, he was reborn in a noble family during the time of Kassapa, the possessor of ten powers. In his later years, he went forth in the dispensation. After the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, when there was an uproar throughout the world, seven bhikkhus who had gone forth, dwelling in a remote region, climbed a mountain in the midst of a forest. They cast down a ladder, saying, “Let those who desire to live descend; let those without attachment sit.” Their advisor, the senior elder, became an arahant within seven days. The next elder was a non-returner, and the other five were of purified virtue. After passing away from there, they were reborn in the deva realm. There, having experienced divine happiness for one Buddha-interval, in this Buddha’s dispensation, they were reborn as Pukkusāti (MN 3.342), Sabhiya (SN, Sabhiyasutta), Bāhiya (Udāna 10), and Kumāra Kassapa (MN 1.249)—these four in various places. This one, however, was born in the city of Anupiya in the Malla country. While he was still in his mother’s womb, his mother died. Someone, after placing her body on the pyre for cremation, rescued the boy who had fallen among the wood and raised him. Because he fell among the wood (dabba), he became known as Dabba the Mallian’s son. Later, due to past preparations, he went forth. Devoted to his meditation subject, he soon attained arahantship together with the discriminations.

Atha naṃ satthā majjhattabhāvena ānubhāvasampannabhāvena ca bhikkhūnaṃ senāsanaṃ paññāpane bhattuddesane ca niyojesi. Sabbo ca bhikkhusaṅgho taṃ samannesi. Taṃ vinayakhandhake (cūḷava. 189-190) āgatameva. Aparabhāge thero ekassa varasalākadāyakassa salākabhattaṃ mettiyabhūmajakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ uddisi. Te haṭṭhatuṭṭhā “sve mayhaṃ muggaghatamadhumissakabhattaṃ bhuñjissāmā”ti ussāhajātā ahesuṃ. So pana upāsako tesaṃ vārappattabhāvaṃ sutvā dāsiṃ āṇāpesi – “ye, je, bhikkhū sve idha āgamissanti, te kaṇājakena bilaṅgadutiyena parivisāhī”ti. Sāpi tatheva te bhikkhū āgate koṭṭhakapamukhe nisīdāpetvā bhojesi. Te bhikkhū anattamanā kopena taṭataṭāyantā there āghātaṃ bandhitvā “madhurabhattadāyakaṃ amhākaṃ amadhurabhattaṃ dāpetuṃ esova niyojesī”ti dukkhī dummanā nisīdiṃsu. Atha te mettiyā nāma bhikkhunī “kiṃ, bhante, dummanā”ti pucchi. Te, “bhagini, kiṃ amhe dabbena [M 2.0229] mallaputtena viheṭhiyamāne ajjhupekkhasī”ti āhaṃsu. “Kiṃ, bhante, mayā sakkā kātu”nti? “Tassa dosaṃ āropehī”ti. Sā tattha tattha therassa abhūtāropanaṃ akāsi. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Atha bhagavā dabbaṃ mallaputtaṃ pakkosāpetvā – “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ, dabba, mettiyāya bhikkhuniyā vippakāramakāsī”ti pucchi. “Yathā maṃ, bhante, bhagavā jānātī”ti. “Na kho, dabba[V 2.0227], dabbā evaṃ nibbeṭhenti, kārakabhāvaṃ vā akārakabhāvaṃ vā vadehī”ti. “Akārako ahaṃ, bhante”ti. Bhagavā – “mettiyaṃ bhikkhuniṃ nāsetvā te bhikkhū anuyuñjathā”ti āha. Upālittherappamukhā [P 0.0506] bhikkhū taṃ bhikkhuniṃ uppabbājetvā mettiyabhūmajake bhikkhū anuyuñjitvā tehi “amhehi niyojitā sā bhikkhunī”ti vutte bhagavato ekamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā mettiyabhūmajakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ amūlakasaṅghādisesaṃ paññapesi.

Then the Teacher, by his impartiality and powerful influence, appointed him to assign lodgings and allocate meals among the bhikkhus. The entire bhikkhu Saṅgha approved of this. This is recorded in the Vinaya, Cūḷavagga 189-190. Later, the Elder designated the meal-ticket from a certain excellent ticket-giver to the Mettiya and Bhūmajaka bhikkhus.
