Delighted and excited, they thought, “Tomorrow we will enjoy a meal of mung beans, ghee, and honey.” However, when that lay follower heard of their turn, he instructed his female servant, “Those bhikkhus who come here tomorrow, serve them with broken rice accompanied by sour gruel.” Accordingly, when those bhikkhus arrived, she made them sit at the entrance of the storeroom and fed them. Displeased and seething with anger, the bhikkhus harbored resentment toward the Elder, thinking, “It was he who arranged for the donor of sweet food to have us given unsweet food.” They sat there miserable and dejected. Then a nun named Mettiya asked, “Venerable sirs, why are you dejected?” They replied, “Sister, why do you remain indifferent while we are being harmed by Dabba the Mallian’s son?” “What can I do, venerable sirs?” she asked. “Accuse him of wrongdoing,” they said. So she made unfounded accusations against the Elder here and there. Hearing this, the bhikkhus reported it to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One had Dabba the Mallian’s son summoned and asked, “Dabba, is it true that you harmed the nun Mettiya?” “As the Blessed One knows me,” he replied. “Dabba, the innocent do not equivocate like that; declare whether you did it or not,” the Blessed One said. “I did not do it, Lord,” he replied. The Blessed One said, “After expelling the nun Mettiya, you should question those bhikkhus.” The bhikkhus, headed by the Elder Upāli, expelled that nun and questioned the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka bhikkhus. When they said, “We instructed that nun,” they reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then promulgated the groundless Saṅghādisesa offense for the Mettiya-Bhūmajaka bhikkhus.

Tena ca samayena dabbatthero bhikkhūnaṃ senāsanaṃ paññāpento veḷuvanavihārassa sāmantā aṭṭhārasamahāvihāre sabhāge bhikkhū pesento rattibhāge andhakāre aṅguliyā padīpaṃ jāletvā tenevālokena aniddhimante bhikkhū pesesi. Evaṃ therassa senāsanapaññāpanabhattuddesanakicce pākaṭe jāte satthā ariyagaṇamajjhe dabbattheraṃ ṭhānantare ṭhapento “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ senāsanapaññāpakānaṃ yadidaṃ dabbo mallaputto”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 214) etadagge ṭhapesi.

At that time, Elder Dabba was assigning lodgings to the bhikkhus. Around the Bamboo Grove Monastery, he sent bhikkhus to their respective quarters in eighteen great monasteries. During the night, in the darkness, he lit a lamp with his finger and by that light sent bhikkhus who lacked psychic power. When this duty of assigning lodgings and allocating meals became well-known, the Teacher, placing Elder Dabba in a special position among the assembly of noble ones, declared, “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who are assigners of lodgings, Dabba the Mallian’s son is foremost.” Thus, he established him in that foremost position.

108. Thero attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttatthameva. Ito ekanavute kappe vipassī nāma nāyako loke uppajjīti sambandho.

108. The Elder, recalling his past deeds, became joyful and, revealing his past conduct, uttered the verse beginning “There was a Victor named Padumuttara.” All of that has the same meaning as previously stated. The connection is: “Ninety-one eons ago, a leader named Vipassī arose in the world.”

125. Duṭṭhacittoti dūsitacitto asādhusaṅgamena apasannacittoti attho. Upavadiṃ sāvakaṃ tassāti tassa bhagavato khīṇāsavaṃ sāvakaṃ upavadiṃ, upari abhūtaṃ vacanaṃ āropesiṃ, abbhakkhānaṃ akāsinti attho.

125. “With a corrupted mind” means having a mind defiled by association with unwholesome people, meaning a mind lacking faith. “I falsely accused his disciple” means I falsely accused that disciple of the Blessed One, a perfected one, meaning I imputed untrue speech, I slandered him. That is the meaning.

132. Dundubhiyoti [M 2.0230] dunduṃ iti saddāyanato dundubhisaṅkhātā bheriyo. Nādayiṃsūti saddaṃ kariṃsu. Samantato asaniyoti sabbadisābhāgato asane vināsane niyuttoti asaniyo, devadaṇḍā bhayāvahā phaliṃsūti sambandho.

132. `Dundubhiyo` means drums, so called because they make the sound 'dunduṃ.' `Nādayiṃsu` means they made a sound. `Samantato asaniyo` means: from all directions, terrifying divine rods, which are thunderbolts (`asaniyo`) appointed for destruction, fell. This is the connection.

133. Ukkā patiṃsu nabhasāti ākāsato aggikkhandhā ca patiṃsūti attho. Dhūmaketu ca dissatīti dhūmarājisahito aggikkhandho ca dissati paññāyatīti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

133. `Ukkā patiṃsu nabhasā` means that masses of fire fell from the sky. `Dhūmaketu ca dissati` means that a mass of fire accompanied by a trail of smoke was seen, became apparent. The rest is easily understood.

Dabbamallaputtattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Dabba Mallaputta is completed.

5. Kumārakassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kumārakassapa

Pañcamāpadāne [V 2.0228] ito satasahassamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato kumārakassapattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayaṃ kira padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā ekadivasaṃ satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ cittakathikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento [P 0.0507] paṇidhānaṃ katvā tadanurūpāni puññāni karonto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā kassapassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto tassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ katvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto dibbasukhaṃ mānusasukhañca anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe ekissā seṭṭhidhītāya kucchimhi nibbatto. Sā kira kumārikākāleyeva pabbajitukāmā mātāpitaro yācitvā pabbajjaṃ alabhamānā patikulaṃ gantvā gabbhaṃ gaṇhitvā taṃ ajānitvā “sāmikaṃ ārādhetvā pabbajjaṃ anujānāpessāmī”ti cintesi. Sā sāmikaṃ ārādhentī, ayyaputta –

In the fifth Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Venerable Kumārakassapa, which begins: “A hundred thousand eons ago….” It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was born into a brahmin family. Having attained understanding, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, he saw the Teacher establishing a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who give variegated discourses. Aspiring to that same position himself, he made a resolution and performed meritorious deeds in accordance with it. After living out his lifespan, he passed away from there and wandered among gods and humans, experiencing the good fortune of both realms. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn into a good family. Having gone forth in that Blessed One’s Dispensation and practiced the duties of a recluse, he continued wandering only in happy destinations, enjoying divine and human happiness. During this Buddha-era, he was conceived in the womb of a certain banker's daughter in Rājagaha. It is said that this girl, while still a maiden, desired to go forth. Having asked her parents for permission but not receiving it, she went to her husband’s family and became pregnant. Unaware of this, she thought: “I will please my husband and then get his permission to go forth.” While pleasing her husband, she said: “My lord…”

“Sace imassa kāyassa, anto bāhirako siyā;

Daṇḍaṃ nūna gahetvāna, kāke soṇe nivāraye”ti. (visuddhi. 1.122) –

“If the inside of this body were on the outside, one would surely have to take a stick to ward off the crows and dogs.” (Visuddhimagga 1.122)

Ādinā sarīrassa dosaṃ dassentī taṃ ārādhesi.

By showing the faultiness of the body with such verses as the preceding one, she won him over.

Sā [M 2.0231] sāmikena anuññātā gabbhinibhāvaṃ ajānantī devadattapakkhiyāsu bhikkhunīsu pabbaji. Tassā gabbhinibhāvaṃ disvā bhikkhuniyo devadattaṃ pucchiṃsu. So “assamaṇī”ti āha. Sā “nāhaṃ devadattaṃ uddissa pabbajitā, bhagavantaṃ uddissa pabbajitā”ti bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā dasabalaṃ pucchi. Satthā upālittheraṃ paṭicchāpesi. Thero sāvatthinagaravāsīni kulāni visākhañca upāsikaṃ pakkosāpetvā sarājikāya parisāya taṃ vinicchinanto “pure laddho gabbho, arogā pabbajjā”ti āha. Taṃ sutvā satthā “sādhu suvinicchitaṃ upālinā adhikaraṇa”nti therassa sādhukāraṃ adāsi.

Having been permitted by her husband, and not knowing she was pregnant, she went forth among the bhikkhunīs of Devadatta’s faction. When her pregnancy became apparent, the bhikkhunīs asked Devadatta. He said: “She is no recluse.” She said: “I did not go forth on account of Devadatta; I went forth on account of the Blessed One,” and she went to the Blessed One and asked the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher had the Elder Upāli investigate the matter. The elder had the families residing in Sāvatthi and the female lay follower Visākhā summoned, and while judging the case in an assembly that included the king, he declared: “The conception occurred before she went forth; the going forth is valid.” Hearing this, the Teacher said: “Good! The legal case has been well decided by Upāli,” and he gave his approval to the elder.

Sā bhikkhunī suvaṇṇabimbasadisaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Taṃ rājā pasenadi kosalo “dārakapariharaṇaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ palibodho”ti dhātīnaṃ dāpetvā posāpesi, kassapotissa nāmaṃ kariṃsu[V 2.0229]. Aparabhāge alaṅkaritvā satthu santikaṃ netvā pabbājesi. Kumārakāle pabbajitattā pana bhagavatā “kassapaṃ pakkosatha, idaṃ phalaṃ vā khādanīyaṃ vā kassapassa dethā”ti vutte “katarakassapassā”ti “kumārakassapassā”ti evaṃ gahitanāmattā raññā posāvanīyaputtattā ca vuddhakālepi kumārakassapotveva paññāyittha.

That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking, “Caring for a child is an obstruction for bhikkhunīs,” had him given to wet nurses to be raised. They named him Kassapa. Later, after adorning him, they brought him to the Teacher and had him go forth. Since he had gone forth as a boy, whenever the Blessed One said, “Summon Kassapa; give this fruit or food to Kassapa,” and someone asked, “To which Kassapa?” the reply would be, “To Kumārakassapa (the boy Kassapa).” Thus, because he acquired this name and because he was the king’s foster son, even in his old age he was known as Kumārakassapa.

So pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya vipassanāya kammaṃ karoti, buddhavacanañca uggaṇhāti. Atha tena saddhiṃ pabbatamatthake samaṇadhammaṃ katvā anāgāmī hutvā suddhāvāse nibbattamahābrahmā “vipassanāya mukhaṃ dassetvā [P 0.0508] maggaphaluppattiyā upāyaṃ karissāmī”ti pañcadasapañhe abhisaṅkharitvā andhavane vasantassa therassa “ime pañhe satthāraṃ puccheyyāsī”ti ācikkhi. Tato so te pañhe bhagavantaṃ pucchi. Bhagavāpissa vissajjesi. Thero bhagavatā kathitaniyāmeneva te uggaṇhitvā vipassanaṃ gabbhaṃ gāhāpetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

From the time he went forth, he undertook the practice of insight and learned the word of the Buddha. Now, a certain Great Brahmā, who in a past life had practiced the recluse’s duties with him on a mountain peak, become a non-returner, and been reborn in the Pure Abodes, thought: “I will show him the entrance to insight and create a means for him to attain the path and fruit.” He formulated fifteen questions and instructed the elder, who was dwelling in Andhavana, to ask the Teacher these questions. Then the elder asked the Blessed One these questions, and the Blessed One answered them for him. The elder, having learned them according to the method explained by the Blessed One, made insight take hold and attained arahantship.

150. So arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento ito satasahassamhītiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayañca uttānatthañca, taṃ sabbaṃ na vaṇṇayissāma. Anuttānapadameva vaṇṇayissāma.

150. Having attained arahantship, he recalled his past deeds and, filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with: “A hundred thousand aeons from now….” Here, we will not comment on what has been explained below and is of clear meaning. We will comment only on the passages that are not obvious.

169. Āpannasattā me mātāti mayhaṃ mātā garugabbhā gabbhinī pasutāsannagabbhāti attho.

169. `Āpannasattā me mātā` means: my mother was pregnant, that is, heavy with child, with a womb close to giving birth. That is the meaning.

173. Vammikasadisaṃ [M 2.0232] kāyanti sarīraṃ nāma vammikasadisaṃ yathā vammiko ito cito ca chiddāvachiddo gharagoḷikaupacikādīnaṃ āsayo, evameva ayaṃ kāyo navachiddo dhuvassavoti buddhena bhagavatā desitaṃ pakāsitaṃ taṃ sutvā me cittaṃ āsave aggahetvā asesetvā kilesato vimucci, arahatte patiṭṭhāsīti attho. Aparabhāge tattha tattha bhikkhūnaṃ vicittadhammakathikabhāvaṃ sutvā satthā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cittakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ kumārakassapo”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 217) etadagge ṭhapesīti.

173. `Vammikasadisaṃ kāyaṃ`: the body is like an anthill. Just as an anthill is pierced through and through, a resort for house lizards, termites, and other creatures, so too this body has nine openings and is constantly oozing. This was taught and explained by the Buddha, the Blessed One. Hearing this, my mind, without grasping the taints, was utterly liberated from the defilements and became established in arahantship. This is the meaning. Later, hearing that bhikkhus in various places were speakers of variegated Dhamma talks, the Teacher declared: “Bhikkhus, foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are speakers of variegated talks is Kumārakassapa” (AN 1.209, 217), and he placed him in that foremost position.

Kumārakassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kumārakassapa is completed.

6. Bāhiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bāhiya

Chaṭṭhāpadāne [V 2.0230] ito satasahassamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato bāhiyassa dārucīriyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto brāhmaṇasippesu nipphattiṃ gantvā vedaṅgesu anavayo ekadivasaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto pasannamānaso satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ khippābhiññānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ pattukāmo sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā sattāhassa accayena bhagavato pādamūle nipanno “bhagavā, bhante, ito sattame divase yaṃ bhikkhuṃ khippābhiññānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi, so viya ahampi anāgate ekassa buddhassa sāsane khippābhiññānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi[P 0.0509]. Bhagavā anāgataṃsañāṇena oloketvā samijjhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “anāgate gotamassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā khippābhiññānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti byākāsi. So yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto tattha cha kāmāvacarasampattiyo anubhavitvā puna manussesu cakkavattiādisampattiyo anekakappakoṭisatesu anubhavitvā kassapassa bhagavato kāle ekasmiṃ kule nibbatto, bhagavati parinibbute pabbajito yadā sāsane osakkamāne satta bhikkhū catunnaṃ parisānaṃ ajjhācāraṃ [M 2.0233] disvā saṃvegappattā araññaṃ pavisitvā “yāva sāsanassa antaradhānaṃ na hoti, tāva attano patiṭṭhaṃ karissāmā”ti suvaṇṇacetiyaṃ vanditvā tattha araññe ekaṃ pabbataṃ disvā “jīvitasālayā nivattantu, nirālayā imaṃ pabbataṃ abhiruhantū”ti nisseṇiṃ bandhitvā sabbe taṃ pabbataṃ abhiruyha nisseṇiṃ pātetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kariṃsu. Tesu saṅghatthero ekarattātikkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So anotattadahe nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā uttarakuruto piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā te bhikkhū āha – “āvuso, imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjathā”ti. Te āhaṃsu – “kiṃ, bhante, amhehi evaṃ katikā katā ‘yo paṭhamaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, tenābhataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ avasesā paribhuñjantū’”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Tena hi sace mayampi tumhe viya visesaṃ nibbattessāma, sayaṃ āharitvā bhuñjissāmā”ti na icchiṃsu.

In the sixth Apadāna, beginning 'A hundred thousand kappas ago,' is the Apadāna of the Venerable Bāhiya Dārucīriya Thera. He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating meritorious deeds that served as a basis for liberation in various existences, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having mastered the brahminical arts and become proficient in the Vedāṅgas, one day he went to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, and with a gladdened mind, saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhu as foremost in quick direct knowledge. Desiring that position, for seven days he gave a great offering to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. After seven days, he prostrated himself at the Blessed One’s feet and made this aspiration: 'Venerable sir, just as the Blessed One seven days ago appointed a bhikkhu as foremost in quick direct knowledge, so too may I, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, become foremost in quick direct knowledge.' The Blessed One, looking into the future with his knowledge of the future and seeing that his aspiration would be fulfilled, made this prediction: 'In the future, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Gotama, having gone forth, you will become foremost in quick direct knowledge.' Having performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life, he passed away and was reborn in a deva world. There he enjoyed the six kinds of sense-sphere fortune, and then for many hundreds of thousands of crores of kappas he experienced the fortunes of a wheel-turning monarch and so on among humans. During the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was reborn in a certain family. After the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, he went forth. When the dispensation was declining, seven bhikkhus, seeing the misconduct of the four assemblies, were filled with a sense of spiritual urgency and entered the forest, thinking: 'Before the dispensation disappears, we will establish ourselves.' After paying homage to the golden cetiya, they saw a mountain in the forest and resolved: 'Let those who cling to life turn back; let those free from attachment ascend this mountain.' Having made a ladder, they all climbed the mountain, cast down the ladder, and practiced the ascetic’s duties. Among them, the Saṅghatthera attained arahantship after one night. Having chewed a tooth-stick of nāga creeper from Lake Anotatta and rinsed his mouth, he brought almsfood from Uttarakuru and said to those bhikkhus: 'Friends, eat this almsfood.' They replied: 'What, venerable sir? Did we make an agreement that, "Whoever attains arahantship first shall bring almsfood, and the rest shall partake of it"?' 'No, friends.' 'Then, if we too attain a special attainment like you, we shall bring our own almsfood and eat it.' Thus, they declined.

Dutiyadivase dutiyatthero anāgāmī hutvā tatheva piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā itare nimantesi. Te evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ panāvuso, katikā katā, ‘mahātherena ābhataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ abhuñjitvā anutherena ābhataṃ bhuñjissāmā’”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”ti. “Evaṃ sante tumhe [V 2.0231] viya mayampi visesaṃ nibbattetvā attano attano purisakārena bhuñjituṃ sakkontā bhuñjissāmā”ti na icchiṃsu. Tesu arahattappattatthero parinibbāyi, dutiyo anāgāmī brahmaloke nibbatti, itare pañca visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkontā sussitvā sattame divase kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattiṃsu. Tattha dibbasukhaṃ anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde tato cavitvā manussesu nibbattiṃsu. Tesu eko pukkusāti rājā ahosi, eko gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ kumārakassapo, eko bāhiyo dārucīriyo, eko dabbo mallaputto, eko sabhiyo paribbājakoti. Tesu [P 0.0510] ayaṃ bāhiyo dārucīriyo suppārakapaṭṭane vāṇijakule nibbatto vāṇijakamme nipphattiṃ gato mahaddhano mahābhogo, so suvaṇṇabhūmiṃ gacchantehi vāṇijehi saddhiṃ nāvamāruyha videsaṃ gacchanto katipāhaṃ gantvā bhinnāya nāvāya sesesu macchakacchapabhakkhesu jātesu ekoyeva avasiṭṭho ekaṃ phalakaṃ gahetvā vāyamanto sattame divase suppārakapaṭṭanatīraṃ okkami. Tassa nivāsanapārupanaṃ natthi, so aññaṃ kiñci apassanto sukkhakaṭṭhadaṇḍake vākehi [M 2.0234] paliveṭhetvā nivāsetvā pārupitvā ca devakulato kapālaṃ gahetvā suppārakapaṭṭanaṃ agamāsi. Manussā taṃ disvā yāgubhattādīni datvā “ayaṃ eko arahā”ti sambhāvesuṃ. So vatthesu upanītesu “sacāhaṃ nivāsemi, pārupāmi vā, lābhasakkāro me parihāyissatī”ti tāni paṭikkhipitvā dārucīrāneva parihari.

On the second day, the second elder, having become a non-returner, similarly brought almsfood and invited the others. They said: 'But, friend, was an agreement made that "having not eaten the almsfood brought by the chief elder, we will eat that brought by the next elder"?' 'No, friend.' 'In that case, if we too, like you, can produce a special attainment, we will eat by our own personal effort.' Thus they refused. Among them, the elder who had attained arahantship attained parinibbāna; the second, the non-returner, was reborn in the Brahmā world; the other five, unable to produce a special attainment, wasted away and died on the seventh day, and were reborn in a deva world. There they experienced divine bliss, and at the time of this Buddha-arising, they passed away from there and were reborn among humans. Among them, one became King Pukkusāti; one, Kumārakassapa in the country of Gandhāra at Takkasilā; one, Bāhiya Dārucīriya; one, Dabba Mallaputta; and one, the wanderer Sabhiya. Of these, this Bāhiya Dārucīriya was born into a merchant family in the port of Suppāraka. Having become accomplished in the business of a merchant, he was very wealthy, with great possessions. He boarded a ship with merchants going to Suvaṇṇabhūmi to travel abroad. After they had traveled for some days, the ship broke apart. While the rest became food for fish and turtles, he alone was left. Grasping a plank and striving, on the seventh day he came ashore at the port of Suppāraka. He had nothing for a lower or upper garment. Seeing nothing else, he wrapped dry sticks and bark around himself as a lower and upper garment. Taking a bowl from a devas' shrine, he went to Suppāraka. People saw him and, thinking, 'This is an arahant,' gave him rice-gruel, cooked rice, and other things. When clothes were brought to him, he thought, 'If I wear these, my gain and honor will decline,' so he rejected them and continued to wear only the bark-cloth.

Athassa “arahā, arahā”ti bahūhi sambhāviyamānassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “ye keci loke arahanto vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannā, ahaṃ tesaṃ aññataro”ti so tena niyāmena kuhanakammena jīvikaṃ kappeti.

Then, as he was being honored by many with the words, 'An arahant, an arahant!' a reflection arose in his mind thus: 'Of those in the world who are arahants or have entered upon the path to arahantship, I am one.' In this way, he made his living by deceitful practice.

Kassapadasabalassa sāsane sattasu janesu pabbataṃ āruyha samaṇadhammaṃ karontesu eko anāgāmī hutvā suddhāvāsabrahmaloke nibbattitvā attano brahmasampattiṃ olokento āgataṭṭhānaṃ āvajjento pabbatamāruyha samaṇadhammaṃ karaṇaṭṭhānaṃ disvā sesānaṃ nibbattanaṭṭhānaṃ āvajjento ekassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ itaresañca pañcannaṃ kāmāvacaradevaloke nibbattabhāvaṃ ñatvā te kālānukālaṃ āvajjesi “imasmiṃ pana kāle kahaṃ nu kho te”ti āvajjento dārucīriyaṃ suppārakapaṭṭanaṃ nissāya kuhanakammena jīvitaṃ kappentaṃ disvā “naṭṭho vatāyaṃ bālo, pubbe samaṇadhammaṃ karonto atiukkaṭṭhabhāvena arahatāpi ābhataṃ piṇḍapātaṃ aparibhuñjitvā idāni udarahetu anārahāva samāno arahattaṃ paṭijānitvā lokaṃ vañcento vicarati, dasabalassa uppannabhāvaṃ na jānāti, gacchāmi naṃ saṃvejetvā buddhuppādaṃ jānāpessāmī”ti khaṇeneva brahmalokato otaritvā suppārakapaṭṭane rattibhāgasamanantare dārucīriyassa sammukhe pāturahosi. So [V 2.0232] attano vasanaṭṭhāne obhāsaṃ disvā bahi nikkhamitvā mahābrahmānaṃ disvā añjaliṃ paggayha “ke tumhe”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ tumhākaṃ porāṇakasahāyo anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā brahmaloke nibbatto, amhākaṃ sabbajeṭṭhako arahā hutvā parinibbuto, tumhe pana pañcajanā [P 0.0511] devaloke nibbattā. Svāhaṃ dāni taṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kuhanakammena jīvikaṃ kappentaṃ disvā damituṃ āgato”ti vatvā idaṃ kāraṇaṃ āha – “neva kho tvaṃ, bāhiya, arahā nāpi arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpanno, sāpi te paṭipadā natthi, yāya tvaṃ arahā vā assa arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpanno”ti. Athassa satthu uppannabhāvaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ vasanabhāvañca [M 2.0235] ācikkhitvā “satthu santikaṃ gacchā”ti taṃ uyyojetvā brahmalokameva agamāsi.

In the dispensation of Kassapa of the Ten Powers, while seven persons were practicing the ascetic’s duties after climbing a mountain, one became a non-returner and was reborn in a Suddhāvāsa Brahmā world. Surveying his own Brahmā-attainment, he reflected on the place he had come from. Seeing the mountain where they had practiced the ascetic’s duties, he then reflected on the rebirth-destinations of the others. Knowing that one had attained parinibbāna and the other five had been reborn in a sense-sphere devaloka, from time to time he would reflect on them. Reflecting, 'Where might they be at this time?' he saw Dārucīriya living near the port of Suppāraka, making his living by deceitful practice. 'Alas, this fool is lost! Formerly, when practicing the ascetic’s duties with extreme austerity, he would not even partake of almsfood brought by an arahant, but now, for his belly’s sake, though not an arahant, he claims to be an arahant and goes about deceiving the world. He does not know that one with the Ten Powers has arisen. I will go and stir a sense of urgency in him and let him know of the Buddha's appearance.' Instantly descending from the Brahmā world, he appeared before Dārucīriya in the port of Suppāraka just after the night had passed. Seeing a light in his dwelling, Dārucīriya came out, and upon seeing the great Brahmā, he raised his joined palms in homage and asked, 'Who are you?' 'I am your former companion who attained the fruit of non-returning and was reborn in the Brahmā world. Our eldest became an arahant and attained parinibbāna, while you five were reborn in a deva world. Now, seeing you making a living by deceitful practice in this place, I have come to tame you.' Then he stated the reason: 'You are not an arahant, Bāhiya, nor have you entered upon the path to arahantship. You do not even have the practice by which you could be an arahant or could enter upon the path to arahantship.' Then, informing him of the Teacher's arising and of his residence in Sāvatthī, he urged him, 'Go to the Teacher,' and returned to the Brahmā world.

Bāhiyo pana ākāse ṭhatvā kathentaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ oloketvā cintesi – “aho bhāriyaṃ kammaṃ mayā kataṃ, anarahaṃ arahā ahanti cintesiṃ, ayañca maṃ ‘na tvaṃ arahā, nāpi arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannāsī’ti vadati, atthi nu kho loke añño arahā”ti. Atha naṃ pucchi – “atha ke carahi sadevake loke arahanto vā arahattamaggaṃ vā samāpannā”ti. Athassa devatā ācikkhi – “atthi, bāhiya, uttaresu janapadesu sāvatthi nāma nagaraṃ, tattha so bhagavā etarahi viharati arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. So hi, bāhiya, bhagavā arahā ceva arahattāya ca dhammaṃ desesī”ti. Bāhiyo rattibhāge devatāya kathaṃ sutvā saṃviggamānaso taṃkhaṇaṃyeva suppārakā nikkhamitvā ekarattivāsena sāvatthiṃ agamāsi, gacchanto ca pana devatānubhāvena buddhānubhāvena ca vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ atikkamitvā sāvatthiṃ anuppatto, tasmiṃ khaṇe satthā sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho hoti. So jetavanaṃ pavisitvā abbhokāse caṅkamante sambahule bhikkhū pucchi – “kuhiṃ etarahi satthā”ti? Bhikkhū “sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti vatvā “tvaṃ pana kuto āgatosī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Suppārakā āgatomhī”ti. “Kadā nikkhantosī”ti? “Hiyyo sāyanhasamaye nikkhantomhī”ti. “Dūratopi āgato, nisīda tāva pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā thokaṃ vissamāhi, āgatakāle satthāraṃ dakkhissatī”ti āhaṃsu. “Ahaṃ, bhante, satthu vā attano vā jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, katthaci aṭṭhatvā anisīditvā ekaratteneva vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ āgato, satthāraṃ passitvāva vissamissāmī”ti āha. So evaṃ vatvā taramānarūpo sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā bhagavantaṃ anopamāya buddhasiriyā carantaṃ disvā “cirassaṃ vata me gotamo sammāsambuddho diṭṭho”ti diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya [P 0.0512] onatasarīro gantvā antaravīthiyaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā gopphakesu daḷhaṃ gahetvā evamāha – “desetu, bhante bhagavā, dhammaṃ, desetu [V 2.0233] sugato dhammaṃ, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “akālo kho tāva, bāhiya, antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhamhā piṇḍāyā”ti paṭikkhipi.

Then Bāhiya, looking at the great Brahmā who was speaking while standing in the sky, thought: 'Oh, what a grave deed I have done! Though not an Arahant, I considered myself an Arahant. And this one tells me, "You are not an Arahant, nor have you even entered upon the path to Arahantship." Is there, then, another Arahant in the world?' Then he asked him: 'Who, then, in this world with its devas are Arahants or have entered upon the path to Arahantship?' Then the deity told him: 'There is, Bāhiya, in the northern districts a city named Sāvatthī. The Blessed One is now dwelling there, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. For he, Bāhiya, the Blessed One, is an Arahant and he teaches the Dhamma for the attainment of Arahantship.' Hearing the deity's words in the night, Bāhiya, his mind stirred with a sense of urgency, departed from Suppāraka at that very moment and reached Sāvatthī in a single night's journey. As he went, by the power of the deity and the power of the Buddha, he traversed a path of one hundred and twenty yojanas and arrived at Sāvatthī. At that moment, the Teacher had entered Sāvatthī for alms-food. Bāhiya entered the Jeta Grove and, seeing many bhikkhus walking in the open, asked: 'Where is the Teacher now?' The bhikkhus replied: 'He has entered Sāvatthī for alms-food.' Then they asked him: 'But where have you come from?' 'I have come from Suppāraka.' 'When did you depart?' 'I departed yesterday evening.' They said: 'You have come from afar. First sit down, wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest for a while. You will see the Teacher when he returns.' He replied: 'Venerable sirs, I do not know what dangers to life there may be for the Teacher or for myself. Having come a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night without stopping or sitting anywhere, I will rest only after I have seen the Teacher.' Having said this, he hurriedly entered Sāvatthī and saw the Blessed One walking with incomparable Buddha-splendor. He thought: 'After a long time, I have finally seen Gotama, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One!' From the place where he first saw him, he approached with his body bowed. In the middle of the street, he prostrated himself with the five-point prostration, firmly grasped the Blessed One's ankles, and said: 'Teach the Dhamma, Blessed One! Teach the Dhamma, Sublime One! It will be for my long-term welfare and happiness.' Then the Teacher refused him, saying: 'This is not the time, Bāhiya. We have entered among the houses for alms-food.'

Taṃ [M 2.0236] sutvā bāhiyo, “bhante, saṃsāre saṃsarantena kabaḷīkārāhāro na aladdhapubbo, tumhākaṃ vā mayhaṃ vā jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, desetu me, bhante bhagavā, dhammaṃ, desetu sugato dhamma”nti puna yāci. Satthā dutiyampi tatheva paṭikkhipi. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “imassa diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā nirantaraṃ ajjhotthaṭaṃ hoti, balavapītivego dhammaṃ sutvāpi na sakkhissati paṭivijjhituṃ, majjhattupekkhāya tāva tiṭṭhatu, ekaratteneva vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ āgatassapi cassa daratho balavā sopi tāva paṭippassambhatū”ti. Tasmā dvikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā tatiyaṃ yācito antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitova “tasmātiha te, bāhiya, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ, diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissatī”tiādinā (udā. 10) nayena anekapariyāyena dhammaṃ desesi. So satthu dhammaṃ suṇantoyeva sabbāsave khepetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Hearing this, Bāhiya pleaded again: 'Venerable sir, while wandering in saṃsāra, physical food has not been unobtainable, but I do not know what dangers to life there may be for you or for me. Teach me the Dhamma, Blessed One! Teach me the Dhamma, Sublime One!' The Teacher refused him a second time in the same way. For it occurred to him: 'From the moment this man saw me, his entire body has been pervaded by rapture without interruption. With such a powerful surge of rapture, he will not be able to penetrate the Dhamma even if he hears it. Let him first become established in equanimity. Moreover, having come one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night, his fatigue is strong; let that, too, be calmed.' Therefore, having refused him twice, when he was asked a third time, the Teacher stood right there in the street and taught him the Dhamma in various ways, beginning with the words (Ud. 1.10): 'Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train yourself thus: In the seen, there will be only what is seen…' While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, he eradicated all the taints and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

178. So arahattaṃ pattakkhaṇeyeva pubbakammaṃ saritvā sañjātasomanasso pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento ito satasahassamhītiādimāha. Taṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva. Anuttānapadavaṇṇanameva karissāma.

178. At the very moment of attaining Arahantship, he recalled his past kamma and, with joy arisen, he declared the story of his past conduct, beginning with the words: 'A hundred thousand aeons ago…' Since its method has been stated above, the meaning is plain. We will provide a commentary only on the terms that are not plain.

181. Hasanaṃ paccavekkhaṇanti paripuṇṇasomanassajātaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ, komāravaṇṇaṃ atikomalanti attho.

181. `Hasanaṃ paccavekkhaṇaṃ` means reflection born of complete mental gladness. `Komāravaṇṇaṃ` means extremely delicate, like the complexion of a youth; this is the meaning.

182. Hemayaññopacitaṅganti suvaṇṇasuttayaññopacitasuttaavayavaṃ sarīraṃ dehanti attho. Palambabimbatamboṭṭhanti olambitabimbaphalasadisaṃ rattavaṇṇaṃ oṭṭhadvayasamannāgatanti attho. Setatiṇhasamaṃ dijanti sunisitatikhiṇaayalohaghaṃsanena ghaṃsitvā samaṃ kataṃ viya samadantanti attho.

182. 'With limbs built up by gold and sacrifice' means a body, a frame, whose limbs are adorned with golden threads and sacrificial threads. 'With red lips like a dangling bimba fruit' means endowed with a pair of red-colored lips resembling a dangling bimba fruit. 'With white, sharp, and even teeth' means with even teeth, as if made even by being polished with a well-sharpened, keen iron file.

183. Pītisamphullitānananti pītiyā suṭṭhu phullitaṃ vikasitaṃ ānanaṃ mukhaṃ ādāsatalasadisamukhavantanti attho.

183. 'A face blossomed with rapture' means a face, a countenance, fully blossomed and opened up by rapture, possessing a face like the surface of a mirror; this is the meaning.

184. Khippābhiññassa bhikkhunoti khippaṃ desanāya samugghāṭitakkhaṇeyeva abhivisesena ñātuṃ samatthassa bhikkhunoti attho.

184. 'Of the bhikkhu of quick direct knowledge' means: of the bhikkhu who is capable of knowing with special distinction at the very moment the teaching is expounded; this is the meaning.

186. Saggaṃ [P 0.0513][V 2.0234] agaṃ sabhavanaṃ yathāti attano gehaṃ viya saggaṃ lokaṃ agamāsinti attho.

186. 'I went to heaven as to my own home' means: I went to the heavenly world as if to my own house; this is the meaning.

196. Na [M 2.0237] tvaṃ upāyamaggaññūti tvaṃ nibbānādhigamūpāyabhūtamaggaññū na ahosīti attho.

196. 'You do not know the path of the means' means: you were not one who knew the path that is the means for attaining Nibbāna; this is the meaning.

200. Satthuno sadā jinanti sadā sabbakālaṃ jinaṃ jinanto parājitakopo satthuno sammāsambuddhassa vimalānanaṃ ādāsatalasadisamukhaṃ passissāmi passituṃ nikkhamāmīti yojanā. Dije apucchiṃ kuhiṃ lokanandanoti kuhiṃ ṭhāne lokapasādakaro satthāti dije brāhmaṇe ahaṃ bhikkhū apucchinti attho.

200. The construction for 'Always the Teacher's... the Conqueror's' is: 'Always, at all times, I, who am conquering and have defeated anger, will see the stainless face of the Teacher, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, a face like the surface of a mirror. I am setting out to see it.' 'I asked the twice-born, "Where is the delighter of the world?"' means: I asked the twice-born—that is, the brahmins, meaning the bhikkhus—'In what place is the Teacher, who inspires faith in the world?'; this is the meaning.

201. Sasova khippaṃ munidassanussukoti munidassane tathāgatadassane ussuko ussāhajāto saso iva khippaṃ pāpuṇātīti attho.

201. “Like a hare, swift and eager to see the Sage” means: eager and zealous to see the Sage, that is, to see the Tathāgata, one arrives swiftly like a hare; this is the meaning.

202. Tuvaṭaṃ gantvāti sīghaṃ gantvā. Piṇḍatthaṃ apihāgidhanti piṇḍapātaṃ paṭicca apihaṃ apagatapihaṃ agidhaṃ nittaṇhaṃ.

202. “Having gone quickly” means having gone swiftly. “For alms, without longing or greed” means, in regard to alms-food, being without longing, with longing departed, without greed, and without craving.

203. Alolakkhanti ito cito ca anolokayamānaṃ uttame sāvatthinagare piṇḍāya vicarantaṃ adakkhinti sambandho. Sirīnilayasaṅkāsanti siriyā lakkhaṇānubyañjanasobhāya nilayaṃ saṅkāsaṃ jalamānatoraṇasadisaṃ. Ravidittiharānananti vijjotamānasūriyamaṇḍalaṃ viya vijjotamānamukhamaṇḍalaṃ.

203. “Not looking about”: the connection is “I saw him, not looking here and there, wandering for alms-food in the excellent city of Sāvatthī.” “Like an abode of splendor” means an abode of splendor, that is, of the beauty of the major and minor marks, resembling a blazing archway. “With a face captivating like the radiant sun” means with a radiant facial orb like the radiant solar orb.

204. Kupathe vippanaṭṭhassāti kucchitapathe sopaddavamagge mūḷhassa micchāpaṭipannassa me saraṇaṃ hohi patiṭṭhā hohi. Gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati.

204. “For one lost on a wrong path”: for me, who am lost on a contemptible path, a perilous road, who am deluded and practicing wrongly, be my refuge, be my support. “O Gotama”: he addresses the Blessed One by his clan name.

218. Na tattha sukkā jotantīti sukkapabhāsampannā jotamānaosadhitārakādayo na jotanti nappabhāsanti. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. So evaṃ pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsetvā tāvadeva ca bhagavantaṃ pabbajjaṃ yāci. “Paripuṇṇaṃ te pattacīvara”nti ca puṭṭho “na paripuṇṇa”nti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “tena hi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesāhī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. So kira vīsativassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ karonto “bhikkhunā nāma attanā paccaye labhitvā aññaṃ anoloketvā [V 2.0235] sayameva paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā ekabhikkhussāpi pattena vā cīvarena vā saṅgahaṃ nākāsi, “na tenassa [M 2.0238] iddhimayaṃ pattacīvaraṃ uppajjissatī”ti ñatvā bhagavā ehibhikkhubhāvena pabbajjaṃ nādāsi. Tampi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesamānameva saṅkāraṭṭhānato coḷakkhaṇḍāni saṃkaḍḍhentaṃ pubbaveriko amanusso ekissā taruṇavacchāya gāviyā sarīre adhimuccitvā vāmaūrumhi paharitvā [P 0.0514] jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Satthā piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco sambahulehi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ nikkhamanto bāhiyassa sarīraṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne patitaṃ disvā “gaṇhatha, bhikkhave, etaṃ bāhiyaṃ dārucīriyanti ekasmiṃ gehadvāre ṭhatvā mañcakaṃ āharāpetvā imaṃ sarīraṃ nagaradvārato nīharitvā jhāpetvā dhātuyo gahetvā thūpaṃ karothā”ti bhikkhū āṇāpesi.

218. “The bright ones do not shine there” means that the shining medicinal herbs, stars, and so on, endowed with white radiance, do not shine or give light there. The rest has a plain meaning. Having thus declared the story of his past conduct, he immediately asked the Blessed One for the going forth. When asked, “Are your bowl and robes complete?” he replied, “They are not complete.” Then the Teacher said, “In that case, search for a bowl and robes,” and departed. It is said that while practicing the ascetic's duties for twenty thousand years, he had declared, “A bhikkhu should obtain his own requisites and use them by himself without looking to another,” and thus he had never helped even a single bhikkhu with a bowl or robes. Knowing that for this reason a bowl and robes created by psychic power would not arise for him, the Blessed One did not grant him the going forth with the “Come, bhikkhu” formula. While that same Bāhiya was searching for a bowl and robes, pulling scraps of cloth from a rubbish heap, a non-human being who was a former enemy took possession of the body of a young heifer, struck him on the left thigh, and brought him to the end of his life. The Teacher, having returned from his alms round and finished his meal, was departing with many bhikkhus when he saw Bāhiya's body lying on a rubbish heap. He instructed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, take up Bāhiya Dārucīriya. Having a bier brought from a certain house, carry this body out of the city gate, cremate it, collect the relics, and build a stūpa for them.”

Te bhikkhū dhātuṃ mahāpathe thūpaṃ kāretvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā attano katakammaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tato saṅghamajjhe kathā udapādi – “tathāgato bhikkhusaṅghena sarīrajhāpanakiccaṃ kāresi, dhātuyo ca gāhāpetvā cetiyaṃ kārāpesi, kataramaggo nu kho tena samadhigato, sāmaṇero nu kho so, bhikkhu nu kho”ti. Satthā taṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā “patiṭṭhito, bhikkhave, bāhiyo dārucīriyo arahatto”ti upari dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍheti. Tassa parinibbutabhāvañca ācikkhitvā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ khippābhiññānaṃ yadidaṃ bāhiyo dārucīriyo”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 216) etadagge ṭhapesi.

Those bhikkhus, having had a stūpa for the relics built on the main road, approached the Teacher and reported what they had done. Then a discussion arose in the midst of the Saṅgha: “The Tathāgata had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus perform the cremation rites for the body, and after having the relics collected, he had a shrine built. What path did he attain? Was he a novice, or a full bhikkhu?” The Teacher, making that the occasion for an utterance, said: “Bhikkhus, Bāhiya Dārucīriya is established in arahantship,” and he elaborated on this Dhamma teaching. And having explained that he had attained final Nibbāna, he placed him in the foremost position, saying: “Bhikkhus, the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples in regard to quick direct knowledge is Bāhiya Dārucīriya.”

Atha naṃ bhikkhū pucchiṃsu – “tumhe, bhante, ‘bāhiyo dārucīriyo arahattaṃ patto’ti vadetha, kadā so arahattaṃ patto”ti? “Mama dhammaṃ sutakāle, bhikkhave”ti. “Kadā panassa, bhante, tumhehi dhammo kathito”ti? “Bhikkhāya carantena antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitenā”ti. “Appamattako, bhante, tumhehi antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvā kathitadhammo; kathaṃ so tāvattakena visesaṃ nibbattesī”ti? Atha ne satthā, “bhikkhave, mama dhammaṃ ‘appaṃ’ vā ‘bahuṃ vā’ti mā cintayittha. Anekānipi hi anatthapadasaṃhitāni gāthāsahassāni na seyyo, atthanissitaṃ pana ekampi gāthāpadaṃ seyyo”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the bhikkhus asked him: “Venerable sir, you say that Bāhiya Dārucīriya attained arahantship. When did he attain it?” “At the time he heard my Dhamma, bhikkhus.” “But when, venerable sir, was the Dhamma taught to him by you?” “While I was on my alms-round, standing in the middle of the street.” “Venerable sir, the Dhamma taught by you while standing in the middle of the street was so very brief. How did he bring about a special attainment with just that much?” Then the Teacher said to them: “Bhikkhus, do not think of my Dhamma as ‘little’ or ‘much.’ For even a thousand verses composed of meaningless words are not as good as a single meaningful line of a verse.” Having said this, he connected the story to the teaching and, while teaching the Dhamma, spoke this verse:

“Sahassamapi ce gāthā, anatthapadasaṃhitā;

Ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammatī”ti. (dha. pa. 101) –

“Though a thousand verses are composed of meaningless words, better is one line of a verse, hearing which one becomes pacified.”

Desanāpariyosāne [M 2.0239][V 2.0236] caturāsītiyā pāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosīti.

At the conclusion of the discourse, the penetration of the Dhamma occurred to eighty-four thousand beings.

Bāhiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bāhiya is complete.

7. Mahākoṭṭhikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika

Sattamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato mahākoṭṭhikattherassa apadānaṃ. Kā uppatti? Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare mahābhogakule [P 0.0515] nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto mātāpitūnaṃ accayena kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā gharāvāsaṃ vasanto ekadivasaṃ padumuttarassa bhagavato dhammadesanākāle haṃsavatīnagaravāsino gandhamālādihatthe yena buddho yena dhammo yena saṅgho, tanninne tappoṇe tappabbhāre gacchante disvā tehi saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā “ayaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggo, yaṃnūnāhampi ekassa buddhassa sāsane ayaṃ viya paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti cintetvā satthu desanāpariyosāne vuṭṭhitāya parisāya bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, sve mayhaṃ gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantesi. Satthā adhivāsesi. So bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā sakanivesanaṃ gantvā sabbarattiṃ buddhassa ca bhikkhusaṅghassa ca nisajjaṭṭhānaṃ gandhamālādīhi alaṅkaritvā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā tassā rattiyā accayena sakanivesane bhikkhusatasahassaparivāraṃ satthāraṃ vividhayāgukhajjakaparivāraṃ sasūpabyañjanaṃ gandhasālibhojanaṃ bhojāpetvā bhattakiccapariyosāne cintesi – “mahantaṃ kho ahaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthemi, na pana yuttaṃ mayā ekadivasameva dānaṃ datvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthetuṃ, anupaṭipāṭiyā sattāhaṃ dānaṃ datvā patthessāmī”ti. So teneva niyāmena sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā bhattakiccapariyosāne dussakoṭṭhāgāraṃ vivarāpetvā uttamaṃ ticīvarappahonakaṃ sukhumavatthaṃ buddhassa pādamūle ṭhapetvā bhikkhusatasahassassa ca ticīvaraṃ datvā tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “bhante, yo so bhikkhu tumhehi ito sattame divasamatthake [M 2.0240] paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapito, ahampi so bhikkhu viya anāgate uppajjanakassa buddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti satthu pādamūle nipajjitvā patthanaṃ akāsi. Satthā tassa samijjhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “anāgate ito kappasatasahassamatthake gotamo nāma buddho loke uppajjissati, tassa sāsane tava patthanā samijjhissatī”ti [V 2.0237] byākāsi. So tattha yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā tato cuto devasampattiṃ anubhavitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu paribbhami.

In the seventh Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika, beginning with 'The Victor named Padumuttara.' What is its origin? This one too, having made his resolve under previous Buddhas and accumulating in successive existences merits that are a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī. Having reached maturity, after his parents passed away, he took over the family and lived as a householder. One day, during a Dhamma discourse by the Blessed One Padumuttara, he saw the citizens of Haṃsavatī with perfumes and garlands in their hands, heading toward the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, inclined, sloping, and bending toward them. He approached the Blessed One along with them. Seeing the Teacher establish a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those who had attained the analytical knowledges, he thought: 'This one is the foremost in this Dispensation among those who have attained the analytical knowledges. Surely I too, in the dispensation of a future Buddha, should become the foremost among those who attain the analytical knowledges, just like him!' At the conclusion of the Teacher's discourse, when the assembly had risen, he approached the Blessed One and invited him: 'Venerable Sir, tomorrow please accept a meal at my house.' The Teacher consented. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him, he went to his own residence. All night long he had the seating for the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus adorned with perfumes, garlands, and so on, and had staple and non-staple foods prepared. At the end of that night, in his own residence, he served the Teacher and his retinue of one hundred thousand bhikkhus with food made of fragrant rice, accompanied by various kinds of gruel and hard foods, with curries and condiments. At the end of the meal, he thought: 'I aspire for a great position. It is not proper for me to aspire for that position after giving alms for only a single day. I will give alms for seven days in succession and then make my aspiration.' So, in that same way, he gave a great offering for seven days. At the end of the meal, he had his cloth storeroom opened, placed the finest delicate cloth sufficient for a triple robe at the Buddha’s feet, and also gave a triple robe to each of the one hundred thousand bhikkhus. Then he approached the Tathāgata, prostrated himself at the Teacher’s feet, and made his aspiration: 'Venerable Sir, just as that bhikkhu was established by you seven days ago in the foremost position among those who have attained the analytical knowledges, so may I too, in the dispensation of a Buddha who will arise in the future, go forth and become the foremost among those who attain the analytical knowledges.' The Teacher, knowing that his aspiration would succeed, made a prediction: 'In the future, one hundred thousand eons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise in the world. In his dispensation your aspiration will be fulfilled.' Having performed meritorious deeds there for the rest of his life, he passed away from that existence, experienced divine fortune, and wandered on among gods and humans.

Evaṃ so devamanussesu saṃsaranto tattha tattha bhave puññañāṇasambhāre sambharanto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālakule [P 0.0516] nibbatti, koṭṭhikotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Kasmā mātuyā vā ayyakapayyakādīnaṃ vā nāmaṃ aggahetvā evaṃ nāmaṃ kariṃsūti ce? Attano paññavantatāya vedaṅgesu satakkaparatakkesu sanighaṇḍukeṭubhesu sākkharappabhedesu sakalabyākaraṇesu ca chekabhāvena ca diṭṭhadiṭṭhe jane mukhasattīhi koṭṭhento pakkoṭṭhento vitudanto vicaratīti anvatthanāmaṃ kariṃsūti veditabbaṃ. So vayappatto tayo vede uggahetvā brāhmaṇasippe nipphattiṃ patto ekadivasaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā upasampannakālato paṭṭhāya vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā paṭisambhidāsu ciṇṇavasī hutvā abhīto mahāthere upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchantopi dasabalaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭisambhidāsuyeva pañhaṃ pucchi. Evamayaṃ thero tattha katādhikāratāya tattha ciṇṇavasībhāvena ca paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggo jāto. Atha naṃ satthā mahāvedallasuttaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi, “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ paṭisambhidāppattānaṃ yadidaṃ mahākoṭṭhiko”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 218).

Thus, wandering on in saṃsāra among gods and humans, accumulating stores of merit and knowledge in successive existences, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in Sāvatthī in a brahmin family of great wealth. They gave him the name Koṭṭhika. If it is asked why they gave him such a name, not taking one from his mother or from his grandparents and other ancestors, it should be understood that they gave him a name that fit his character because, being very intelligent and skilled in the Vedāṅgas, in logic and counter-logic, in etymology and lexicography, in phonology and all the grammars, he would go about striking, pecking, and piercing the people he met with the spears of his mouth. Having come of age, he mastered the three Vedas and achieved perfection in the brahminical arts. One day he went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. Having gone forth and from the time of his higher ordination, he worked at insight meditation and attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Having become a master of the analytical knowledges, he would fearlessly approach the great elders and ask them questions, and he would also approach the Possessor of the Ten Powers and ask questions specifically on the analytical knowledges. Thus this elder, on account of the resolve he had made and his mastery in this area, became the foremost of those who had attained the analytical knowledges. Then the Teacher, making the Mahāvedalla Sutta the occasion, placed him in the foremost position among those who had attained the analytical knowledges, declaring: 'Bhikkhus, the foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who have attained the analytical knowledges is Mahākoṭṭhika.'

221. So aparena samayena vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthameva.

221. At a later time, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he became filled with joy, and in order to make known the story of his past life, he spoke the verses beginning, 'The Victor named Padumuttara…' The meaning of all this is plain in the way explained above.

Itthaṃ [M 2.0241] sudamāyasmā mahākoṭṭhikoti ettha sudanti nidassane nipāto. Āyasmāti gāravādhivacanaṃ, yathā taṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallānoti.

In the phrase 'Itthaṃ sudamāyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko' ('Thus indeed the venerable Mahākoṭṭhika'), the word 'sudaṃ' is a particle of illustration. 'Āyasmā' is an expression of respect, as in 'the venerable Mahāmoggallāna'.

Mahākoṭṭhikattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika is complete.

8. Uruvelakassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uruvelakassapa

Aṭṭhamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato uruvelakassapattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi [V 2.0238] purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto vayappatto satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ mahāparivārānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento mahādānaṃ datvā paṇidhānaṃ akāsi. Bhagavā cassa anantarāyataṃ [P 0.0517] disvā “anāgate gotamabuddhassa sāsane mahāparivārānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti byākāsi. So tattha yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā tato cavitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito dvenavutikappamatthake phussassa bhagavato vemātikakaniṭṭhabhātā hutvā nibbatto, aññepissa dve kaniṭṭhabhātaro ahesuṃ. Te tayo buddhappamukhabhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā paramāya pūjāya pūjetvā yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bhagavato uppattito puretarameva bārāṇasiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule tayo bhātaro hutvā nibbattā gottavasena tayopi kassapāti evaṃ nāmakā ahesuṃ. Te tayo vayappattā tayo vede uggaṇhiṃsu. Tesaṃ jeṭṭhabhātikassa pañcamāṇavakasatāni parivārā, majjhimassa tīṇi, kaniṭṭhassa dve, te attano ganthesu sāraṃ olokentā diṭṭhadhammikameva atthaṃ disvā pabbajjaṃ rocesuṃ. Tesu jeṭṭhabhātā attano parivārena saddhiṃ uruvelaṃ gantvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā uruvelakassapo nāma jāto, majjhimo gaṅgānadīvaṅke pabbajito nadīkassapo nāma jāto, kaniṭṭho gayāsīse pabbajito gayākassapo nāma jāto. Evaṃ tesu isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tattha tattha vasantesu bahūnaṃ divasānaṃ accayena amhākaṃ bodhisatto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā [M 2.0242] paṭividdhasabbaññutaññāṇo anukkamena dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā pañcavaggiyatthere arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā yasakulaputtappamukhe pañcapaññāsajane sahāyake vinetvā saṭṭhi arahante “caratha, bhikkhave, cārika”nti (mahāva. 32) vissajjetvā tiṃsabhaddavaggiye vinetvā uruvelakassapassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vasanatthāya agyāgāraṃ pavisitvā tattha gatanāgadamanādīhi aḍḍhuḍḍhasahassehi pāṭihāriyehi uruvelakassapaṃ saparivāraṃ vinetvā pabbājesi. Tassa pabbajjāvidhānañca iddhipāṭihāriyakaraṇañca sabbaṃ nadīkassapassa apadānaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āvi bhavissati. Tassa pabbajitabhāvaṃ sutvā itarepi dve bhātaro saparisā āgantvā satthu santike pabbajiṃsu. Sabbeva te iddhimayapattacīvaradharā ehibhikkhukā ahesuṃ. Satthā taṃ samaṇasahassaṃ ādāya gayāsīsaṃ gantvā piṭṭhipāsāṇe nisinno ādittapariyāyadesanāya (mahāva. 54) te sabbe arahatte patiṭṭhāpesi.

The eighth apadāna, beginning with 'The Victor named Padumuttara,' is the apadāna of the Venerable Elder Uruvelakassapa. He too, having performed deeds of merit under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome kamma in various existences as a foundation for liberation, was born into a family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having come of age, he heard the Dhamma from the Teacher. Seeing the Teacher place a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those with a great retinue, he himself aspired to that same position. He made a great offering and formed a resolution. The Blessed One, foreseeing his future without obstruction, declared: 'In the future, during the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama, he will become the foremost among those with a great retinue.' Having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life there, he passed away and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Ninety-two eons ago from now, he was reborn as the youngest step-brother of the Blessed One Phussa. He had two other younger brothers as well. The three of them invited the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and honored them with the highest offerings. Having performed wholesome deeds throughout their lives, they wandered among devas and humans. Even before the arising of our Blessed One, they were reborn in a brahmin family in Bārāṇasī as three brothers, all bearing the name Kassapa by clan. When they came of age, the three studied the three Vedas. The eldest brother had a retinue of five hundred young men, the middle brother three hundred, and the youngest two hundred. Reflecting on the essence of their studies and seeing only worldly benefit in them, they all desired to go forth. Among them, the eldest brother, along with his retinue, went to Uruvela, took up the ascetic life, and became known as Uruvelakassapa. The middle brother went forth on the banks of the Ganges River and became known as Nadīkassapa. The youngest took up the ascetic life at Gayāsīsa and became known as Gayākassapa. Thus, while they were dwelling here and there, having gone forth as ascetics, after many days had passed, our Bodhisatta undertook the Great Renunciation, penetrated omniscient knowledge, gradually set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, established the group of five elders in Arahantship, and trained the fifty-five companions led by the noble son Yasa. Sending out sixty Arahants with the words, 'Go forth, bhikkhus, on your journey,' he then trained the thirty Bhaddavaggiya monks. He went to the dwelling place of Uruvelakassapa and entered the fire-temple to stay. There, through various miracles such as taming the fierce Nāga and other miracles numbering one and a half thousand, he converted Uruvelakassapa and his retinue and ordained them. The details of his ordination and the display of miraculous powers will be fully explained in the Apadāna Commentary of Nadīkassapa. Hearing of his ordination, the other two brothers arrived with their followers and went forth in the presence of the Teacher. All of them, possessing robes and bowls created by psychic power, became bhikkhus through the 'Come, bhikkhu' invitation. The Teacher, taking that assembly of a thousand ascetics, went to Gayāsīsa. Seated on the slope of a rock, he delivered the 'Fire Sermon' and established them all in Arahantship.

251. So evaṃ arahattaṃ patvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Anuttānapadameva [P 0.0518] vaṇṇayissāma.

251. Having thus attained Arahantship, filled with joy, revealing the apadāna of his past conduct, he spoke the verses beginning with 'The Victor named Padumuttara.' We shall explain only the verses that are not clear.

268. So [V 2.0239] ca sabbaṃ tamaṃ hantvāti so phusso bhagavā rāgadosamohādikilesandhakāraṃ viddhaṃsetvā. Vijaṭetvā mahājaṭanti taṇhāmānādīhi diyaḍḍhasahassehi kilesagaṇehi mahābyākulaṃ jaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā padāletvā phāletvāti attho. Sadevakaṃ devalokasahitaṃ sakalaṃ lokasannivāsaṃtappayanto santappayanto pīṇento amataṃ vuṭṭhiṃ mahānibbānavuṭṭhidhāraṃ vassate paggharāpetīti yojanā.

268. So ca sabbaṃ tamaṃ hantvāti: 'Having destroyed all that darkness' means that the Blessed One Phussa dispelled the darkness of defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion. Vijaṭetvā mahājaṭanti: 'Having unraveled the great tangle' means having unraveled, split, and shattered the great tangle, which was exceedingly confused by the multitude of one and a half thousand defilements such as craving and conceit. Sadevakaṃ devalokasahitaṃ sakalaṃ lokasannivāsaṃtappayanto santappayanto pīṇento amataṃ vuṭṭhiṃ mahānibbānavuṭṭhidhāraṃ vassate paggharāpetīti yojanā: 'Bringing contentment to the world with its devas' means delighting and satisfying the entire world, including the deva-world, showering and causing to flow the rain of immortality, the stream of the great rain of Nibbāna. This is the connection.

269. Tadā hi bārāṇasiyanti “bārasa manussā”tiādīsu viya bārasa dvādasarāsī hutvā purā, himavantato isayo ca paccekamunisaṅkhātā isayo ca gandhamādanato ākāsenāgantvā ettha gacchanti otaranti pavisantīti bārāṇasī, atha vā sammāsambuddhasaṅkhātānaṃ anekasatasahassānaṃ dhammacakkapavattanatthāya otaraṭṭhānaṃ nagaraṃ liṅgavipallāsaṃ katvā itthiliṅgavasena bārāṇasīti vuccati, tissaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ.

269. Tadā hi bārāṇasiyanti: 'At that time, in Bārāṇasī'—just as in phrases like 'twelve people,' [it is so called because] in the past there were twelve groups, and sages from the Himalayas and sages known as Paccekamunis from Gandhamādana, having come through the sky, would go, descend, and enter here—hence Bārāṇasī. Alternatively, it is the city, the place of descent for the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma by countless hundreds of thousands of those reckoned as Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones. Having made a gender reversal, it is called Bārāṇasī in the feminine form. Tissaṃ bārāṇasiyaṃ: 'in that Bārāṇasī'.

273. Nikkhittasatthaṃ [M 2.0243] paccantanti chaḍḍitasatthaṃ pātitaāvudhaṃ paccantajanapadaṃ nibbisevanaṃ katvā punarupaccatanti punarapi taṃ nagaraṃ upecca upagamma sampattāti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

273. Nikkhittasatthaṃ paccantanti: 'Having laid down arms in the borderlands' means having abandoned weapons, having discarded arms, and having made the borderlands free from oppression. Punarupaccatanti: 'he returned again' means having approached, gone to, and arrived back at that city. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti: The rest is easily understood.

Uruvelakassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uruvelakassapa is concluded.

9. Rādhattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rādha

296. Navamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato rādhattherassa apadānaṃ. Taṃ sabbaṃ pāṭhānusārena nayānucintanena viññūhi suviññeyyameva. Kevalaṃ puññanānattamevāti.

296. In the ninth Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Rādha, beginning with 'The Victor named Padumuttara.' All of that should be easily understood by the wise in accordance with the text and by means of reflective contemplation. It is simply a diversity of merit.

Rādhattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Rādha is concluded.

Dasamaṃ mogharājattheraapadānaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

The tenth Apadāna, that of the Elder Mogharāja, is indeed easy to understand.

Catupaññāsamavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Fifty-fourth Chapter is concluded.

55. Bhaddiyavaggo

55. The Bhaddiya Chapter

1. Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya

Pañcapaññāsamavagge [P 0.0519][V 2.0240] paṭhamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare mahābhogakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto satthu dhammaṃ suṇanto nisinno satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ mañjussarānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā sayampi taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthento buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sappisakkharādimadhurarasasammissaṃ mahādānaṃ datvā “ahampi, bhante, anāgate ayaṃ bhikkhu viya ekassa buddhassa sāsane mañjussarānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti paṇidhānaṃ akāsi. Bhagavā tassa anantarāyaṃ disvā byākaritvā pakkāmi.

In the first Apadāna of the Fifty-fifth Chapter is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya, beginning with 'The Victor named Padumuttara.' He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merit that serves as a basis for turning away from the round, was reborn in a family of great wealth in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, while sitting and listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, he saw the Teacher establishing a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those with a melodious voice. Desiring that high position for himself, he gave a great gift, mixed with sweet flavors such as ghee and sugar, to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. He then made the aspiration: 'Venerable sir, in the future, in the dispensation of a certain Buddha, may I too, like this bhikkhu, become the foremost among those with a melodious voice.' The Blessed One, seeing that there was no obstacle for him, made a prediction and departed.

So [M 2.0244] yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā phussabhagavato kāle citrakokilo hutvā nibbatto rājuyyānato madhuraṃ ambaphalaṃ tuṇḍenādāya gacchanto satthāraṃ disvā pasannamānaso “dassāmi buddhassā”ti cittaṃ uppādesi. Satthā tassa cittācāraṃ ñatvā pattaṃ gahetvā nisīdi. Kokilo dasabalassa patte ambapakkaṃ ṭhapesi. Satthā tassa somanassuppādanatthaṃ tassa passantasseva taṃ paribhuñji. Atha so kokilo pasannamānaso teneva pītisukhena sattāhaṃ vītināmesi. Teneva puññakammena uppannuppannabhave mañjussaro ahosi. Kassapasammāsambuddhakāle vaḍḍhakikule nibbattetvā jeṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī hutvā pākaṭo ahosi. Parinibbute bhagavati tassa sarīradhātuyo nidahituṃ sattayojanappamāṇe thūpe āraddhe so āha – “yojanāvaṭṭaṃ yojanubbedhaṃ karomā”ti. Te sabbe tassa vacane aṭṭhaṃsu. Iti appamāṇassa buddhassa orappamāṇaṃ cetiyaṃ kāresi, tena kammena nibbattaṭṭhāne aññehi hīnappamāṇo ahosi. So amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā atirassatāya ca suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya sundarasarīratāya ca lakuṇḍakabhaddiyoti paññāyittha. So aparabhāge satthu dhammadesanaṃ [V 2.0241] sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā bahussuto dhammakathiko hutvā madhurena sarena paresaṃ dhammaṃ kathesi.

Having performed meritorious deeds for the remainder of his life, he wandered among devas and humans, experiencing both kinds of good fortune. During the time of the Blessed One Phussa, he was reborn as a painted cuckoo. While taking a sweet mango from the king's park in his beak, he saw the Teacher and, with a confident mind, the thought arose: 'I will give this to the Buddha.' The Teacher, knowing the state of his mind, took his bowl and sat down. The cuckoo placed the ripe mango in the bowl of the One with Ten Powers. In order to arouse joy in him, the Teacher consumed it as he watched. Then that cuckoo, with a confident mind, passed seven days in that same rapture and happiness. Because of that meritorious kamma, in every future existence he had a melodious voice. During the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa, he was reborn in a carpenter's family and became famous as the chief carpenter. When the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna, as they began to build a stūpa seven yojanas in size to enshrine his bodily relics, he said: 'Let us make it one yojana in circumference and one yojana in height.' They all abided by his word. Thus he had a cetiya of limited measure built for the immeasurable Buddha. By that kamma, in the places where he was reborn, he was of inferior stature to others. During the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn in a good family and became known as Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya on account of his very short stature and his beautiful body, which was like a golden image. Later, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he gained faith and went forth. He became learned, a Dhamma speaker, and taught the Dhamma to others with a sweet voice.

Athekasmiṃ ussavadivase ekena brāhmaṇena saddhiṃ rathena gacchantī ekā gaṇikā theraṃ disvā dantavidaṃsakaṃ hasi. Thero tassā dantaṭṭhike nimittaṃ gahetvā jhānaṃ uppādetvā taṃ pādakaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anāgāmī ahosi, so abhiṇhaṃ kāyagatāya satiyā viharanto ekadivasaṃ [P 0.0520] āyasmatā dhammasenāpatinā ovadiyamāno anusāsiyamāno arahatte patiṭṭhahi. Ekacce bhikkhū ca sāmaṇerā ca tassa arahattappattabhāvaṃ ajānanto kaṇṇesu gahetvā kaḍḍhanti, sīse bāhāya hatthapādādīsu vā gahetvā cāletvā kīḷantā viheṭhesuṃ. Atha bhagavā sutvā – “mā, bhikkhave, mama puttaṃ viheṭhethā”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya taṃ “arahā”ti jānitvā na viheṭhesuṃ.

Then on a certain festival day, a courtesan who was traveling in a chariot with a certain brahmin saw the elder and laughed, displaying her teeth. The elder, taking the bones of her teeth as his object, developed jhāna, and making that the basis, he cultivated insight and became a non-returner. He dwelt constantly with mindfulness directed to the body. One day, being advised and instructed by the Venerable General of the Dhamma, he became established in arahantship. Some bhikkhus and novices, not knowing that he had attained arahantship, would harass him playfully, grabbing and pulling his ears, or taking hold of his head, arms, hands, feet, and so on, and shaking him. Then the Blessed One heard of this and said: 'Bhikkhus, do not harass my son.' From then on, knowing he was an arahant, they did not harass him.

12. So [M 2.0245] arahā hutvā sañjātasomanasso attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Mañjunābhinikūjahanti madhurena pemaniyena sarena abhinikūjiṃ saddaṃ nicchāresiṃ ahanti attho. Sesamettha suviññeyyamevāti.

12. Having become an arahant, with joy arisen in him, he declared the story of his own past deeds, beginning with: 'The Victor named Padumuttara.' The meaning of 'I warbled melodiously' is: I emitted a sound with a sweet and lovely voice. The rest here is indeed easy to understand.

Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya is concluded.

2. Kaṅkhārevatattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata

34. Dutiyāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato kaṅkhārevatattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto, taṃ sabbaṃ pāṭhānusārena suviññeyyamevāti.

34. In the second Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Kaṅkhārevata, beginning with “The Victor named Padumuttara.” He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merits in various existences as a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. All this is easily understood according to the text.

Kaṅkhārevatattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata is concluded.

3. Sīvalittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīvali

Tatiyāpadāne [V 2.0242] padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato sīvalittherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto heṭṭhā vuttanayena vihāraṃ gantvā parisāya pariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ lābhīnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā “mayāpi anāgate evarūpena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dasabalaṃ nimantetvā sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhasaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā, “bhante, iminā adhikārakammena na aññaṃ sampattiṃ patthemi, anāgate pana ekassa buddhassa sāsane ahampi tumhehi so etadagge ṭhapitabhikkhu viya lābhīnaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ akāsi. Satthā tassa anantarāyataṃ disvā “ayaṃ te patthanā anāgate gotamassa buddhassa santike samijjhissatī”ti byākaritvā pakkāmi. So kulaputto yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā vipassissa [M 2.0246] bhagavato [P 0.0521] kāle bandhumatīnagarato avidūre ekasmiṃ gāmake nibbatti, tasmiṃ samaye bandhumatīnagaravāsino raññā saddhiṃ sākacchitvā dasabalassa dānaṃ adaṃsu.

In the third Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Sīvali, beginning with “The Victor named Padumuttara.” He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merits here and there in various existences as a supporting condition for liberation, was born in a good family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. As previously described, he went to the monastery, stood at the edge of the assembly, and listened to the Dhamma. Seeing the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among recipients of requisites, he thought: “In the future, may I too become like this.” He invited the Ten-Powered One and for seven days gave a great offering of alms to the Sangha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. He made an aspiration: “Venerable Sir, by this foundational act of merit, I do not aspire for any other attainment. But in the future, in the dispensation of a Buddha, may I too, like that bhikkhu appointed by you to this pre-eminent position, become the foremost among recipients of requisites.” The Teacher, seeing that he was without obstacles, declared: “This aspiration of yours will be fulfilled in the future in the presence of the Buddha Gotama,” and then departed. That clansman, having performed wholesome deeds throughout his life, experienced both divine and human prosperity. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he was reborn in a village not far from the city of Bandhumatī. At that time, the inhabitants of Bandhumatī, after consulting with the king, were giving alms to the Ten-Powered One.

Ekadivasaṃ sabbe ekato hutvā dānaṃ dentā “kiṃ nu kho amhākaṃ dānagge natthī”ti (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.207; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.59 sīvalittheragāthāvaṇṇanā) olokentā madhuñca guḷadadhiñca nāddasaṃsu. Te “yato kutoci āharissāmā”ti janapadato nagarapavisanamaggesu purise ṭhapesuṃ. Tadā esa kulaputto attano gāmato guḷadadhivārakaṃ gahetvā “kiñcideva āharissāmī”ti nagaraṃ gacchanto “mukhaṃ dhovitvā dhotahatthapādo pavisissāmī”ti phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ olokento naṅgalasīsappamāṇaṃ nimmakkhikadaṇḍakamadhuṃ disvā “puññena me idaṃ uppanna”nti gahetvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Nāgarehi ṭhapitapuriso taṃ disvā, “mārisa, kassa imaṃ harasī”ti pucchi. “Na kassaci, sāmi, vikkāyikaṃ me ida”nti. “Tena hi imaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ gahetvā etaṃ madhuñca guḷadadhiñca dehī”ti.

One day, when all had gathered to give alms, they looked around and wondered, “What is lacking among our offerings?” They did not see honey and curd with molasses. They thought, “We shall bring these from wherever we can,” and stationed men on the roads leading into the city from the countryside. At that time, this clansman, taking a pot of curd with molasses from his village and thinking, “I will bring something,” was going to the city. He thought, “I will wash my face and enter with clean hands and feet.” While looking for a suitable spot, he saw a piece of stick-honey the size of a ploughshare, free of flies. Thinking, “This has arisen for me through merit,” he took it and entered the city. The man stationed by the city-dwellers saw him and asked, “Friend, for whom are you carrying this?” “For no one, sir, it is for sale,” he replied. “Then take this kahāpaṇa and give me this honey and the curd with molasses.”

So cintesi – “idaṃ me na bahuṃ agghati, ayañca ekappahāreneva bahuṃ deti, vīmaṃsissāmī”ti. Tato naṃ āha – “nāhaṃ ekakahāpaṇena demī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ dve kahāpaṇe gahetvā dehī”ti. “Dvīhipi na demī”ti. Etenupāyena vaḍḍhetvā yāva sahassaṃ pāpuṇi, so cintesi – “atiañchituṃ na vaṭṭati, hotu tāva iminā kattabbakammaṃ pucchissāmī”ti[V 2.0243]. Atha naṃ āha – “na idaṃ bahuagghanakaṃ, tvaṃ pana bahuṃ desi, kena kammena idaṃ gaṇhasī”ti. “Idha, bho, nagaravāsino raññā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhitvā vipassisammāsambuddhassa dānaṃ dentā idaṃ dvayaṃ dānagge apassantā maṃ pariyesāpenti. Sace idaṃ dvayaṃ na labhissanti, nāgarānaṃ parājayo bhavissati. Tasmā sahassaṃ datvā gaṇhāmī”ti. “Kiṃ panetaṃ nāgarānaṃ eva vaṭṭati, udāhu aññesampi dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Yassa kassaci dātuṃ avāritameta”nti. “Atthi pana koci nāgarānaṃ dāne ekadivasaṃ sahassaṃ dātā”ti? “Natthi, sammā”ti. “Imesaṃ me dvinnaṃ sahassagghanakabhāvaṃ jānāsī”ti? “Āma, jānāmī”ti. “Tena hi gaccha, nāgarānaṃ ārocehi – ‘eko puriso imāni dve mūlena na deti, tumhehi saddhiṃ sahattheneva dātukāmo, tumhe imesaṃ dvinnaṃ kāraṇā nibbitakkā hothā”ti. “Tvaṃ imasmiṃ dāne jeṭṭhakabhāgassa [M 2.0247] kāyasakkhī hohī”ti vatvā gato. So pana kulaputto gāmato paribbayatthaṃ gahitakahāpaṇena pañcakaṭukaṃ gahetvā cuṇṇaṃ katvā [P 0.0522] dadhito kañciyaṃ vāhetvā tattha madhupaṭalaṃ pīḷetvā pañcakaṭukacuṇṇena yojetvā paduminipatte pakkhipitvā taṃ saṃvidahitvā ādāya dasabalassa avidūre nisīdi. Mahājanehi āhariyamānassa sakkārassa antare attano pattavāraṃ olokento okāsaṃ ñatvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā, “bhante, ayaṃ me duggatasakkāro, imaṃ me anukampaṃ paṭicca paṭiggaṇhathā”ti. Satthā tassānukampaṃ paṭicca catumahārājehi dattiyena selamayapattena taṃ paṭiggahetvā yathā aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyā bhikkhusatasahassassa diyyamānaṃ na khīyati, evaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi.

He thought: “This is not worth much, but this man offers a lot at once. I will test him.” Then he said to him: “I will not give it for one kahāpaṇa.” “If so, take two kahāpaṇas and give it.” “I will not give it for two either.” In this way, the price was increased until it reached a thousand. He thought: “It is not right to be too grasping. For now, I will ask what this is for.” Then he said to him: “This is not very valuable, yet you offer a lot. For what purpose are you acquiring it?” “Here, friend, the city-dwellers are competing with the king in giving alms to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Vipassī. Not seeing this pair of items for the offering, they have sent me to search. If they do not obtain this pair, the city-dwellers will be defeated. Therefore, I am acquiring it by offering a thousand.” “Is this only for the city-dwellers, or is it permissible to give to others as well?” “It is not restricted; anyone may give.” “Is there anyone among the city-dwellers who gives a thousand for a single day's alms?” “No, friend.” “Do you realize that these two items of mine are worth a thousand?” “Yes, I realize it.” “Then go and inform the city-dwellers: ‘A certain man will not give these two for a price; he wants to give them himself in partnership with you. You need not worry about these two items.’ You shall be a personal witness to my receiving the principal share in this offering.” Having said this, the man left. That clansman, however, with a kahāpaṇa he had brought from his village for expenses, bought the five pungent spices and ground them to a powder. He then strained the whey from the curd, squeezed the honeycomb into it, mixed in the spice powder, placed the mixture on a lotus leaf, and having prepared it thus, he took it and sat down not far from the Ten-Powered One. Watching for his turn among the offerings being brought by the great crowd, he saw his opportunity and went to the Teacher, saying: “Venerable sir, this is my humble offering. Please accept it out of compassion for me.” The Teacher, out of compassion for him, accepted it in the stone bowl given by the Four Great Kings and made a determination that it would not be exhausted even when served to sixty-eight hundred thousand bhikkhus.

So kulaputto niṭṭhitabhattakiccaṃ bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno āha – “diṭṭho me, bhante bhagavā, ajja bandhumatīnagaravāsīhi tumhākaṃ sakkāro āhariyamāno, ahampi imassa nissandena nibbattanibbattabhave lābhaggayasaggappatto bhaveyya”nti. Satthā “evaṃ hotu kulaputtā”ti vatvā tassa ca nagaravāsīnañca bhattānumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So kulaputto yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde suppavāsāya rājadhītuyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa paṭisandhiggahaṇakālato paṭṭhāya sāyaṃ pātañca pañcapaṇṇākārasatāni suppavāsāya upanīyanti. Athassa sā puññavīmaṃsanatthaṃ hatthena bījapacchiṃ phusāpentī aṭṭhāsi. Ekekabījato salākasataṃ salākasahassampi niggacchati, ekekakarīsakhettato paṇṇāsampi saṭṭhipi sakaṭapamāṇāni uppajjanti. Koṭṭhapūraṇakālepissā koṭṭhadvāraṃ hatthena phusantiyā rājadhītāya puññena gaṇhantānaṃ gahitagahitaṃ puna pūrati.
