Paripuṇṇabhattakumbhitopi “rājadhītāya puñña”nti vatvā yassa kassaci dentā naṃ yāva na ukkaḍḍhanti, na tāva bhattaṃ khīyati. Dārake kucchigateyeva satta vassāni atikkamiṃsu.

When the Blessed One had finished his meal, that clansman paid homage to him and, sitting to one side, said: “Venerable sir, today I have seen the honor being paid to you by the inhabitants of the city of Bandhumatī. Through the fruit of this deed, in whatever existence I am reborn, may I attain the pinnacle of gain and the summit of honor!” The Teacher replied, “So be it, clansman,” and after giving the blessing for the meal, he departed. That clansman performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life and, wandering through saṃsāra among gods and humans, at the time of this Buddha's appearance, he took conception in the womb of the princess Suppavāsā. From the time he was conceived, five hundred portions of tribute were brought to Suppavāsā every morning and evening. Then, to test his merit, she stood touching a seed basket with her hand. From each single seed, a hundred or even a thousand stalks would sprout. From each karīsa of field, fifty or sixty cartloads of produce would arise. Even at the time of filling the granary, when the princess touched the granary door with her hand, through the princess's merit, whatever was taken out was instantly replenished. Even from a full pot of rice, if anyone, when giving some out, said, “This is by the princess's merit,” the rice would not be exhausted so long as they did not move the pot. Seven years passed while the boy was in the womb.

Gabbhe [V 2.0244] pana paripakke sattāhaṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhosi. Sā sāmikaṃ āmantetvā – “pure maraṇā jīvamānā dānaṃ dassāmī”ti satthu santikaṃ [M 2.0248] pesesi – “gaccha, sāmi, imaṃ pavattiṃ satthu ārocetvā satthāraṃ nimantehi, yañca satthā vadati, taṃ sādhukaṃ upalakkhetvā āgantvā mayhaṃ kathehī”ti. So gantvā tassā sāsanaṃ satthu ārocesi – “satthu bhante, koḷiyadhītā pāde vandatī”ti. Satthā tassā anukampaṃ paṭicca – “sukhinī hotu suppavāsā koḷiyadhītā arogā, arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyatū”ti āha. So taṃ sutvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā attano gāmābhimukho [P 0.0523] pāyāsi. Tassa pure āgamanāyeva suppavāsāya kucchito dhammakaraṇato udakaṃ viya gabbho nikkhami, parivāretvā nisinnajano assumukho rodituṃ āraddho haṭṭhatuṭṭhova tassā sāmikassa tuṭṭhisāsanaṃ ārocetuṃ agamāsi. So tesaṃ iṅgitaṃ disvā – “dasabalena kathitakathā nipphannā bhavissati maññe”ti cintesi. So āgantvā satthu kathaṃ rājadhītāya kathesi. Rājadhītā tayā nimantitaṃ jīvabhattameva maṅgalabhattaṃ bhavissati, gaccha sattāhaṃ dasabalaṃ nimantehīti. So tathā akāsi. Sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ pavattayiṃsu. So dārako ñātīnaṃ santattacittaṃ nibbāpento sītalabhāvaṃ kurumāno jātoti, sīvalitveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So satta vassāni gabbhe vasitattā jātakālato paṭṭhāya sabbakammakkhamo ahosi. Dhammasenāpati sāriputtatthero sattame divase tena saddhiṃ kathāsallāpamakāsi. Satthāpi imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

When the fetus was fully matured, she endured great suffering for seven days. She addressed her husband: “My lord, before I die, while I am still alive, I wish to give alms.” She sent him to the Teacher with this message: “Go, my lord, inform the Teacher of this matter and invite him. Whatever the Teacher says, take careful note of it, and come back and tell me.” He went and conveyed her message to the Teacher, saying: “Venerable sir, the Koliyan daughter pays homage at the Teacher’s feet.” Out of compassion for her, the Teacher said: “May Suppavāsā the Koliyan daughter be happy and healthy; may she, being healthy, give birth to a healthy son.” Hearing this, the husband paid homage to the Blessed One and set off toward his village. Even before he arrived, the child came forth from Suppavāsā’s womb as easily as water from a water pot. The people sitting around her, who had been weeping with tearful faces, were now filled with joy and delight and went to give the joyful news to her husband. Seeing their gestures, he thought: “I suppose the words spoken by the Possessor of the Ten Powers have come to pass.” He returned and told the Teacher’s words to the princess. The princess said: “The meal for the living for which you invited him will itself be an auspicious meal. Go and invite the Possessor of the Ten Powers for seven days.” He did so. For seven days, they gave a great offering of alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Because the boy was born extinguishing the burning hearts of his relatives and making them cool, they gave him the name Sīvali. Having remained in the womb for seven years, from the time of his birth he was capable of all tasks. On the seventh day, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, engaged in conversation with him. The Teacher then recited this verse:

“Yomaṃ palipathaṃ duggaṃ, saṃsāraṃ mohamaccagā;

Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato jhāyī, anejo akathaṃkathī;

Anupādāya nibbuto, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 414; su. ni. 643);

“One who has overcome this quagmire, this difficult path, the round of existence, and delusion; who has crossed over and gone to the far shore; who is meditative, desireless, and free from doubt; who is extinguished through non-clinging—him I call a brahmin.”

Atha naṃ thero evamāha – “kiṃ pana tayā evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavitvā pabbajituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? “Labhanto pabbajeyyaṃ, bhante”ti. Suppavāsā taṃ therena saddhiṃ kathentaṃ disvā – “kiṃ nu kho me putto dhammasenāpatinā kathetī”ti theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi – “mayhaṃ putto tumhehi saddhiṃ kiṃ katheti, bhante”ti? Attanā anubhuttagabbhavāsadukkhaṃ kathetvā – “tumhehi anuññāto pabbajissāmī”ti vadatīti. “Sādhu bhante, pabbājetha na”nti. Thero taṃ vihāraṃ netvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ datvā pabbājento, “sīvali[M 2.0249], tuyhaṃ aññena ovādena kammaṃ natthi, tayā satta vassāni anubhuttadukkhameva paccavekkhāhī”ti. “Bhante, pabbajjāyeva tumhākaṃ bhāro, yaṃ pana mayā sakkā kātuṃ, tamahaṃ jānissāmī”ti. So pana paṭhamakesavaṭṭiyā [V 2.0245] oropitakkhaṇeyeva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, dutiyāya oropitakkhaṇe sakadāgāmiphale, tatiyāya anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Sabbesaṃyeva kesānaṃ oropanañca arahattaphalasacchikiriyā ca apure apacchā ahosi.

Then the elder said to him: “Having endured such suffering, is it not proper for you to go forth?” “If I get the opportunity, venerable sir, I would go forth.” Seeing her son conversing with the elder, Suppavāsā thought, “What is my son discussing with the General of the Dhamma?” She approached the elder and asked: “Venerable sir, what is my son discussing with you?” The elder replied: “He recounted the suffering he endured in the womb and says, ‘If permitted by you, I will go forth.’” “Very well, venerable sir, please ordain him.” The elder took him to the monastery, gave him the meditation subject on the five parts of the body, and while ordaining him, said: “Sīvali, you have no need for any other instruction. Simply reflect on the suffering you have endured for seven years.” “Venerable sir, the ordination is your responsibility. As for what I am able to do, I myself will know.” At the very moment the first lock of his hair was being shaved off, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. At the moment the second was being shaved, he was established in the fruit of once-returning. At the moment the third was being shaved, he was established in the fruit of non-returning. The completion of the shaving of all his hair and the realization of the fruit of arahantship occurred simultaneously.

Atha [P 0.0524] bhikkhusaṅghe kathā udapādi – “aho evaṃ puññavāpi thero sattamāsādhikāni satta saṃvaccharāni mātugabbhe vasitvā satta divasāni mūḷhagabbhe vasī”ti. Satthā āgantvā – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā – “imāya nāmā”ti vutte – “na, bhikkhave, iminā kulaputtena imāya jātiyā katakamma”nti vatvā atītaṃ āharitvā atīte, bhikkhave, buddhuppādato puretarameva esa kulaputto bārāṇasiyaṃ rājakule nibbatto, pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya vibhavasampanno pākaṭo ahosi. Tadā eko paccantarājā “rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti āgantvā nagaraṃ uparundhitvā khandhāvāraṃ kāretvā vihāsi. Atha rājā mātuyā saddhiṃ samānacchando hutvā sattāhaṃ khandhāvāranagare catūsu disāsu dvāraṃ pidhāpesi, nikkhamantānaṃ pavisantānañca dvāramūḷhaṃ ahosi. Atha migadāyavihāre paccekabuddhā ugghosesuṃ. Rājā sutvā dvāraṃ vivarāpesīti. Paccantarājāpi palāyi. So tena kammavipākena narakādīsu dukkhamanubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājakule nibbattopi mātuyā saddhiṃ imaṃ evarūpaṃ dukkhamanubhavi. Tassa pana pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya bhikkhusaṅghassa cattāro paccayā yadicchakaṃ uppajjanti. Evaṃ ettha vatthu samuṭṭhitaṃ.

Then a discussion arose in the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: “Alas, though so meritorious, the elder dwelt in his mother’s womb for seven years and seven months, and for seven days he was in an obstructed womb.” The Teacher came and asked: “For what discussion are you now assembled, bhikkhus?” When they told him, “For this one,” he said: “Bhikkhus, the kamma for this was not done by this clansman in this life.” He then related a story of the past. “In the past, bhikkhus, long before the arising of a Buddha, this clansman was born into the royal family of Bārāṇasī. After his father’s death, he was established in the kingship and became famous and prosperous. At that time, a border king came to seize the kingdom, besieged the city, and set up an encampment. Then the king, in agreement with his mother, had the gates of the fortified city closed on all four sides for seven days. Those trying to leave and enter found the gates blocked. Then, in the Migadāya monastery, Paccekabuddhas made a proclamation. Hearing it, the king had the gates opened. The border king fled. As a result of that kamma, after experiencing suffering in hell and other woeful states, even though born into a royal family in this Buddha-era, he experienced such suffering along with his mother. However, from the time of his going forth, the four requisites have arisen for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus whenever wished. Thus this story arose.”

Aparabhāge satthā sāvatthiṃ agamāsi. Thero bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā, “bhante, mayhaṃ puññabalaṃ vīmaṃsissāmi, pañcabhikkhusatāni dethā”ti. “Gaṇha, sīvalī”ti. So pañcasate bhikkhū gahetvā himavantābhimukhaṃ gacchanto aṭavimaggaṃ gacchati. Tassa paṭhamaṃ diṭṭhanigrodhe adhivatthā devatā satta divasāni dānaṃ adāsi. Iti so –

Later, the Teacher went to Sāvatthī. The elder paid homage to the Blessed One and said: “Venerable sir, I wish to test the power of my merit. Please give me five hundred bhikkhus.” “Take them, Sīvalī.” Taking the five hundred bhikkhus, he set out towards the Himālaya, traveling along a forest path. A devatā dwelling in the first banyan tree he saw gave them alms for seven days. Thus he—

“Nigrodhaṃ paṭhamaṃ passi, dutiyaṃ paṇḍavapabbataṃ;

Tatiyaṃ aciravatiyaṃ, catutthaṃ varasāgaraṃ.

“First he saw the banyan tree, second the Paṇḍava Mountain; third the Aciravatī River, fourth the excellent ocean.

“Pañcamaṃ [M 2.0250] himavantaṃ so, chaṭṭhaṃ chaddantupāgami;

Sattamaṃ gandhamādanaṃ, aṭṭhamaṃ atha revata”nti. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.207; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.59 sīvalittheragāthāvaṇṇanā) –

Fifth, he went to the Himālaya; sixth, he approached Chaddanta; seventh, to Gandhamādana; and eighth, then, to Revata.”

Sabbaṭṭhānesu [V 2.0246] satta satta divasāneva dānaṃ adaṃsu. Gandhamādanapabbate pana nāgadattadevarājā sattasu divasesu ekadivasaṃ khīrapiṇḍapātaṃ adāsi, ekadivasaṃ sappipiṇḍapātaṃ adāsi. Atha naṃ [P 0.0525] bhikkhusaṅgho āha – “āvuso, imassa devarañño neva dhenuyo duyhamānā paññāyanti, na dadhinimmathanaṃ, kuto te, devarāja, idaṃ uppajjatī”ti? “Bhante, kassapadasabalassa kāle khīrasalākabhattadānassetaṃ phala”nti devarājā āha.

In all these places, they were given alms for seven days each. On Gandhamādana Mountain, however, the deva-king Nāgadatta gave an alms-meal of milk-rice on one of the seven days, and an alms-meal of ghee on another. Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhus asked him: “Friend, for this deva-king, we see no cows being milked nor any churning of curds. From where, O deva-king, does this arise for you?” The deva-king replied: “Venerable sirs, this is the fruit of an offering of ticket-food with milk made in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Possessor of the Ten Powers.”

Aparabhāge satthā khadiravaniyarevatattherassa paccuggamanaṃ akāsi. Kathaṃ? Athāyasmā sāriputto satthāraṃ āha – “bhante, mayhaṃ kira kaniṭṭhabhātā revato pabbajito, so abhirameyya vā na vā, gantvā naṃ passissāmī”ti. Bhagavā revatassa āraddhavipassakabhāvaṃ ñatvā dve vāre paṭikkhipitvā tatiyavāre yācito arahattappattabhāvaṃ ñatvā – sāriputta, ahampi gamissāmi bhikkhūnaṃ ārocehīti. Thero bhikkhū sannipātāpetvā – “āvuso, satthā cārikaṃ caritukāmo, gantukāmā āgacchantū”ti sabbesaṃyeva ārocesi. Dasabalassa cārikatthāya gamanakāle ohiyyamānakabhikkhū nāma appakā honti, “satthu suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ sarīraṃ passissāma, madhuradhammakathaṃ vā suṇissāmā”ti yebhuyyena gantukāmā bahutarāva honti. Iti satthā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro “revataṃ passissāmā”ti nikkhanto.

Later, the Teacher went out to meet the Elder Revata of the Acacia Wood. How so? The Venerable Sāriputta said to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, my younger brother Revata, it seems, has gone forth. I will go and see him, whether he is delighting in the holy life or not.” The Blessed One, knowing that Revata had undertaken the development of insight, refused him twice. But when asked a third time, knowing that he had attained arahantship, he said: “Sāriputta, I too will go. Inform the bhikkhus.” The elder had the bhikkhus assembled and announced: “Friends, the Teacher wishes to go on a wandering. Let those who wish to go, come.” When the Possessor of the Ten Powers sets out on a wandering, there are few bhikkhus who stay behind; for the most part, the majority wish to go, thinking: “We will see the Teacher’s golden-hued body and hear his sweet Dhamma talk.” Thus the Teacher, surrounded by a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, set out, thinking: “We will see Revata.”

Athekasmiṃ padese ānandatthero dvedhāpathaṃ patvā bhagavantaṃ pucchi – “bhante, imasmiṃ ṭhāne dvedhāpatho, kataramaggena bhikkhusaṅgho gacchatū”ti? “Kataramaggo, ānanda, ujuko”ti? “Bhante, ujumaggo tiṃsayojaniko amanussapatho. Parihāramaggo pana saṭṭhiyojaniko khemo subhikkho”ti. “Ānanda, sīvali, amhehi saddhiṃ āgato”ti? “Āma, bhante, āgato”ti. “Tena hi saṅgho ujumaggameva gacchatu, sīvalissa puññaṃ vīmaṃsissāmā”ti. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro sīvalittherassa puññavīmaṃsanatthaṃ tiṃsayojanamaggaṃ abhiruhi (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.203).

Then, at a certain place, the Venerable Ānanda came to a fork in the road and asked the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, at this place the road divides. By which path should the Saṅgha of bhikkhus go?” “Ānanda, which is the direct path?” “Venerable sir, the direct path is thirty yojanas long and is a path of non-humans. The roundabout path, however, is sixty yojanas long, safe, and with abundant almsfood.” “Ānanda, has Sīvali come with us?” “Yes, venerable sir, he has come.” “In that case, let the Saṅgha take the direct path. We shall test Sīvali’s merit.” The Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, took the thirty-yojana path in order to test the Elder Sīvali’s merit.

Maggaṃ [M 2.0251] abhiruhanaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya devasaṅgho yojane yojane ṭhāne nagaraṃ māpetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa vasanatthāya vihāre paṭiyādesi. Devaputtā raññā pesitakammakārā viya hutvā yāgukhajjakādīni gahetvā – “kahaṃ, ayyo sīvalī”ti pucchantā gacchanti. Thero sakkārasammānaṃ gāhāpetvā satthu santikaṃ gacchati. Satthā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ paribhuñji. Imināva niyāmena satthā sakkāraṃ anubhavanto devasikaṃ yojanaparamaṃ gantvā tiṃsayojanikaṃ kantāraṃ atikkamma khadiravaniyarevatattherassa [P 0.0526] vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patto, thero satthu āgamanaṃ ñatvā attano [V 2.0247] vasanaṭṭhāne buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa pahonakavihāre dasabalassa gandhakuṭiṃ rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni ca iddhiyā māpetvā tathāgatassa paccuggamanaṃ gato. Satthā alaṅkatapaṭiyattena maggena vihāraṃ pāvisi. Atha tathāgate gandhakuṭiṃ paviṭṭhe bhikkhū vassaggena pattasenāsanāni pavisiṃsu. Devatā “akālo āhārassā”ti aṭṭhavidhaṃ pānakaṃ āhariṃsu. Satthā saṅghena saddhiṃ pānakaṃ pivi. Iminā niyāmeneva tathāgatassa sakkārasammānaṃ anubhavantasseva addhamāso atikkanto.

Starting from the place where the path ascended, the assembly of devas, at every yojana, created a city and prepared monasteries for the residence of the Bhikkhu Sangha headed by the Buddha. The devas, like workers dispatched by a king, took rice gruel and other edibles and went about asking, “Where is the Venerable Sīvalī?” The Elder, having been presented with the offerings and honors, went to the Teacher. The Teacher partook of the meal together with the Bhikkhu Sangha. In this very manner, while the Teacher enjoyed the honors, traveling at most a yojana each day, he crossed the thirty-yojana wilderness and reached the dwelling place of the Elder Revata of Khadiravaniya. The Elder, aware of the Teacher’s arrival, by his psychic power created in his own dwelling place a monastery sufficient for the Bhikkhu Sangha headed by the Buddha, a fragrant chamber for the Ten-Powered One, and places for abiding by day and by night, and he went forth to welcome the Tathāgata. The Teacher entered the monastery along the adorned and prepared path. Then, when the Tathāgata had entered the fragrant chamber, the monks entered the lodgings assigned to them according to seniority. The deities, thinking, “It is not the time for a meal,” brought eight kinds of beverages. The Teacher drank the beverage together with the Sangha. In this very manner, while the Tathāgata was enjoying the offerings and honors, half a month passed.

Athekacce ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhū ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nisīditvā kathaṃ uppādayiṃsu – “dasabalo ‘mayhaṃ aggasāvakassa kaniṭṭhabhātā’ti vatvā evarūpaṃ navakammikaṃ bhikkhuṃ passituṃ āgato, imassa vihārassa santike jetavanavihāro vā veḷuvanavihārādayo vā kiṃ karissanti? Ayampi bhikkhu evarūpassa navakammassa kārako, kiṃ nāma samaṇadhammaṃ karissatī”ti? Atha satthā cintesi – “mayi idha ciraṃ vasante idaṃ ṭhānaṃ ākiṇṇaṃ bhavissati, āraññakā nāma bhikkhū pavivekatthikā honti, revatassa phāsuvihāro na bhavissatī”ti. Tato therassa divāṭṭhānaṃ gato. Theropi ekakova caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya pāsāṇaphalake nisinno satthāraṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā paccuggantvā vandi.

Then some discontented monks, sitting in one place, started a conversation: “The Ten-Powered One, saying, ‘He is my chief disciple’s younger brother,’ has come to see a monk undertaking such construction work. What can the Jetavana Monastery or the Veḷuvana Monastery and others do in comparison to this monastery? This monk, too, is a doer of such new work—what duties of a recluse will he perform?” Then the Teacher thought: “If I stay here long, this place will become crowded. Forest-dwelling monks seek solitude; Revata’s comfortable abiding will be disturbed.” So he went to the elder’s daytime quarters. The elder was sitting alone on a stone slab, leaning against a support panel at the end of the walking path. Seeing the Teacher approaching from afar, he went to meet him and paid homage.

Atha naṃ satthā pucchi – “revata, idaṃ vāḷamigaṭṭhānaṃ, caṇḍānaṃ hatthiassādīnaṃ saddaṃ sutvā kiṃ karosī”ti? “Tesaṃ me, bhante, saddaṃ suṇato araññapīti nāma uppannā”ti. Satthā imasmiṃ ṭhāne revatattherassa pañcahi gāthāsatehi araññānisaṃsaṃ nāma kathetvā punadivase avidūraṭṭhāne piṇḍāya [M 2.0252] caritvā revatattheraṃ āmantetvā yehi bhikkhūhi therassa avaṇṇo kathito, tesaṃ kattarayaṭṭhiupāhanatelanāḷichattānaṃ pamussanabhāvamakāsi. Te attano parikkhāratthāya nivattā āgatamaggeneva gacchantāpi taṃ ṭhānaṃ sallakkhetuṃ na sakkonti. Paṭhamañhi te alaṅkatapaṭiyattena maggena gantvā, taṃdivasaṃ pana visamamaggena gacchantā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdantā jaṇṇukehi gacchanti. Te gumbe ca gacche ca kaṇḍake ca maddantā attanā vasitasabhāgaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ khadirakhāṇuke laggitaṃ attano chattaṃ sañjānanti, upāhanaṃ kattarayaṭṭhiṃ telanāḷiñca sañjānanti. Te tasmiṃ samaye “iddhimā ayaṃ [P 0.0527] bhikkhū”ti ñatvā attano parikkhāramādāya “dasabalassa paṭiyattasakkāro nāma evarūpo hotī”ti vadantā agamaṃsu.

Then the Teacher asked him: “Revata, this is a haunt of wild beasts. Hearing the sounds of fierce elephants, horses, and other animals, what do you do?” “When I hear their sounds, venerable sir, a delight in the forest arises in me,” he replied. On this occasion, the Teacher spoke to the Elder Revata on the benefits of the forest in five hundred verses. The next day, after going for alms in a nearby area, he addressed the Elder Revata and caused the monks who had spoken disparagingly of the elder to forget their staffs, sandals, oil flasks, and umbrellas. Though they returned to retrieve their requisites, walking back along the very path they had come, they could not recognize the place. For earlier they had traveled on a decorated and prepared path, but on that day they went by a rough path, squatting down here and there and proceeding on their knees. Crushing thickets, bushes, and thorns, they reached the area where they had stayed, and there they recognized their umbrellas stuck on acacia stakes, and their sandals, staffs, and oil flasks. At that moment, realizing, “This monk possesses psychic power,” they took their requisites and departed, saying, “So this is the kind of honor prepared for the Ten-Powered One!”

Purato āgate bhikkhū, visākhā upāsikā, attano gehe nisinnakāle pucchi – “manāpaṃ [V 2.0248] nu kho, bhante, revatassa vasanaṭṭhāna”nti? “Manāpaṃ, upāsike, nandavanacittalatāvanapaṭibhāgaṃ taṃ senāsana”nti. Atha tesaṃ pacchato āgate bhikkhū pucchi – “manāpaṃ, ayyā, revatassa vasanaṭṭhāna”nti? “Mā puccha, upāsike, kathetuṃ ayuttaṭṭhānaṃ, etaṃ ujjaṅgalasakkharapāsāṇavisamakhadiravanaṃ eva, tattha so bhikkhu vasatī”ti.

When the monks who had arrived ahead came, the female lay follower Visākhā, while seated in her house, asked them: “Venerable sirs, is the dwelling place of Revata agreeable?” “It is agreeable, lay follower, a counterpart to the Nandana and Cittalatā groves.” Then she asked the monks who arrived later: “Sirs, is the dwelling place of Revata agreeable?” “Do not ask, lay follower. It is a place unfit to describe—it is just a rough acacia forest with gravel, stones, and uneven ground. That is where that monk lives.”

Visākhā purimānaṃ pacchimānañca bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvā, “kesaṃ nu kho kathā saccā”ti pacchābhattaṃ gandhamālaṃ ādāya dasabalassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā satthāraṃ pucchi – “bhante, revatattherassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ekacce ayyā vaṇṇenti, ekacce nindanti, kimetaṃ, bhante”ti? “Visākhe, ramaṇiyaṃ vā hotu mā vā, yasmiṃ ṭhāne ariyānaṃ cittaṃ ramati, tadeva ṭhānaṃ ramaṇiyaṃ nāmā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Hearing the accounts of both the earlier and the later monks, Visākhā wondered, “Whose account is true?” After her meal, she took perfumes and garlands, went to attend upon the Ten-Powered One, paid homage, and sat to one side. She asked the Teacher: “Venerable sir, some venerables praise the Elder Revata’s dwelling place, while others disparage it. What is the meaning of this, venerable sir?” “Visākhā, whether it is delightful or not, whatever place the minds of the noble ones delight in, that place is itself delightful.” Then he spoke this verse:

“Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Yattha arahanto viharanti, taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyaka”nti. (dha. pa. 98; theragā. 991; saṃ. ni. 1.261);

“Whether in a village or in the forest, in a valley or on high ground, wherever the arahants dwell, that ground is a delightful place.”

Aparabhāge bhagavā ariyagaṇamajjhe nisinno theraṃ “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ lābhīnaṃ yadidaṃ, sīvalī”ti (a. ni. 1.198, 207) etadagge ṭhapesi.

On a later occasion, the Blessed One, seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones, placed the elder in the foremost position, saying: “Bhikkhus, foremost among my bhikkhu disciples who are recipients of requisites is Sīvalī.”

54. Athāyasmā sīvalitthero arahattaṃ patvā pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento [M 2.0253] padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Anuttānatthapadavaṇṇanameva karissāma.

54. Then the Venerable Sīvali, having attained arahantship and reached the foremost position, recollected his past kamma and, filled with gladness, he declared this apadāna of his past conduct, beginning with the words: “The Victor’s name was Padumuttara.” We shall provide a commentary only on the words with non-obvious meaning.

55. Sīlaṃ tassa asaṅkheyyanti tassa padumuttarassa bhagavato sīlaṃ asaṅkheyyaṃ.

55. His virtue is immeasurable: The virtue of that Blessed One, Padumuttara, is immeasurable.

“Nava koṭisahassāni, asītisatakoṭiyo;

Paññāsasatasahassāni, chattiṃsā ca punāpare.

“Nine thousand crores, eighty hundred crores, fifty hundred-thousands, and thirty-six more.”

“Ete saṃvaravinayā, sambuddhena pakāsitā;

Peyyālamukhena niddiṭṭhā, sikkhāvinayasaṃvare”ti. (visuddhi. 1.20; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.37) –

“These rules of restraint were proclaimed by the Self-Enlightened One; they are indicated by way of abbreviation in the training, discipline, and restraint.”

Evaṃ vuttasikkhāpadāni bhikkhūnaṃ sāvakapaññattivasena vuttāni. Bhagavato pana sīlaṃ asaṅkheyyameva [V 2.0249] saṃkhātuṃ gaṇetuṃ [P 0.0528] asakkuṇeyyanti attho. Samādhivajirūpamo yathā vajiraṃ indanīlamaṇiveḷuriyamaṇiphalikamasāragallādīni ratanāni vijjhati chiddāvachiddaṃ karoti, evameva padumuttarassa bhagavato lokuttaramaggasamādhi paṭipakkhapaccanīkadhamme vijjhati bhindati samucchindatīti attho. Asaṅkheyyaṃ ñāṇavaraṃ tassa buddhassa cattāri saccāni sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyadhamme saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhamme ca jānituṃ paṭivijjhituṃ samatthaṃ sayambhūñāṇasabbaññutaññāṇādiñāṇasamūhaṃ asaṅkheyyaṃ, atītānāgatapaccuppannādibhedena saṃkhāvirahitanti attho. Vimutti ca anopamāti saṃkilesehi vimuttattā sotāpattiphalādikā catasso vimuttiyo anupamā upamārahitā “imā viya bhūtā”ti upametuṃ na sakkāti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

The training rules thus stated were spoken as regulations for the disciples. The Blessed One’s virtue, however, is truly incalculable; the meaning is that it is impossible to count or reckon. His concentration is like a diamond: just as a diamond pierces and shatters gems such as sapphires, beryl, crystal, and cat’s-eye, riddling them with holes, so too the supramundane path concentration of the Blessed One Padumuttara pierces, breaks, and eradicates opposing and hostile states. His supreme knowledge is immeasurable: the meaning is that his collection of knowledges—the self-arisen knowledge, the knowledge of omniscience, and so on, which is capable of knowing and penetrating the Four Noble Truths, the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment, and conditioned and unconditioned phenomena—is incalculable, being without numerical distinction into past, future, and present. And his liberation is incomparable: the meaning is that because he is liberated from the defilements, the four kinds of liberation, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, are incomparable, without peer; it is not possible to make a comparison such as “they are like this.” The rest has a plain meaning.

Sīvalittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sīvali is complete.

4. Vaṅgīsattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vaṅgīsa

Catutthāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato vaṅgīsattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare mahābhogakule nibbatto vuddhippatto dhammaṃ sotuṃ [M 2.0254] gacchantehi nagaravāsīhi saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekabhikkhuṃ paṭibhānavantānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā satthu adhikārakammaṃ katvā – “ahampi anāgate paṭibhānavantānaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti patthanaṃ katvā satthārā byākato yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu ubhayasampattiyo anubhavitvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā mātu paribbājikābhāvena aparabhāge paribbājakoti pākaṭo vaṅgīsoti ca laddhanāmo tayo vede uggaṇhitvā tato ācariyaṃ ārādhetvā chavasīsajānanamantaṃ nāma sikkhitvā chavasīsaṃ nakhena ākoṭetvā – “ayaṃ satto asukayoniyaṃ nibbatto”ti jānāti.

The fourth apadāna, beginning, “The Victor named Padumuttara,” is the apadāna of the Elder Vaṅgīsa. He too had made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, and in existence after existence he accumulated wholesome deeds that served as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, he was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī into a family of great wealth. Having come of age, he went to the monastery with the city dwellers to listen to the Dhamma. While listening, he saw the Teacher place a certain bhikkhu in the foremost position among those with ready wit. Having performed a foundational service for the Teacher, he made an aspiration: “In the future, may I too be the foremost among those with ready wit!” Having received a prophecy from the Teacher, he performed wholesome deeds for the rest of his life and experienced the dual felicities of the human and deva worlds. At the arising of this Buddha, he was reborn into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī. Because his mother was a female wanderer, in the latter part of his life he became known as the wanderer Vaṅgīsa. Having mastered the three Vedas, he then satisfied his teacher and learned a mantra for knowing the skulls of the dead. By tapping a skull with his fingernail, he knows: “This being has been reborn in such-and-such a destiny.”

Brāhmaṇā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ jivikāya maggo”ti vaṅgīsaṃ gahetvā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo vicariṃsu. Vaṅgīso tivassamatthake matānampi sīsaṃ āharāpetvā nakhena ākoṭetvā – “ayaṃ satto asukayoniyaṃ nibbatto”ti vatvā mahājanassa kaṅkhācchedanatthaṃ te te jane āvāhetvā attano [V 2.0250] attano gatiṃ kathāpeti. Tena tasmiṃ mahājano [P 0.0529] abhippasīdati. So taṃ nissāya mahājanassa hatthato satampi sahassampi labhati. Brāhmaṇā vaṅgīsaṃ ādāya yathāruci vicariṃsu. Vaṅgīso satthu guṇe sutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitukāmo ahosi. Brāhmaṇā “samaṇo gotamo māyāya taṃ āvaṭṭessatī”ti paṭikkhipiṃsu.

The brahmins, thinking, “This is the path to our livelihood,” took Vaṅgīsa and wandered through villages, towns, and royal cities. Vaṅgīsa would have the skulls of even those who had been dead for three years brought to him, and tapping them with his fingernail, he would say: “This being has been reborn in such-and-such a destiny.” To cut off the doubt of the great crowd, he would invoke those very persons and have them declare their respective destinies. Because of this, the great crowd gained confidence in him. Relying on this, he received hundreds and thousands from the hands of the great crowd. The brahmins took Vaṅgīsa and wandered about as they pleased. Having heard of the Teacher’s virtues, Vaṅgīsa wished to approach the Teacher. But the brahmins prevented him, saying, “The ascetic Gotama will win you over with his magic.”

Vaṅgīso tesaṃ vacanaṃ anādiyitvā, satthu santikaṃ gantvā, paṭisanthāraṃ katvā, ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā taṃ pucchi – “vaṅgīsa, kiñci sippaṃ jānātī”ti? “Āma, bho gotama, chavasīsamantaṃ nāmekaṃ jānāmi, tena tivassamatthake matānampi sīsaṃ nakhena ākoṭetvā nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ jānāmī”ti. Atha satthā tassa ekaṃ niraye nibbattassa sīsaṃ, ekaṃ manussesu, ekaṃ devesu, ekaṃ parinibbutassa sīsaṃ āharāpetvā dassesi. So paṭhamasīsaṃ ākoṭetvā, “bho gotama, ayaṃ satto niraye nibbatto”ti āha. Sādhu vaṅgīsa, suṭṭhu tayā diṭṭhaṃ, “ayaṃ satto kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti pucchi. “Manussaloke”ti. “Ayaṃ kuhi”nti? “Devaloke”ti. Tiṇṇannampi nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Parinibbutassa pana sīsaṃ nakhena ākoṭento neva [M 2.0255] antaṃ na koṭiṃ passi. Atha naṃ satthā “na sakkosi, vaṅgīsā”ti pucchi. “Passatha, bho gotama, upaparikkhāmi tāvāti punappunaṃ parivattetvāpi bāhirakamantena khīṇāsavassa sīsaṃ jānituṃ na sakkoti. Athassa matthakato sedo mucci. So lajjitvā tuṇhī ahosi”. Atha naṃ satthā “kilamasi, vaṅgīsā”ti āha. “Āma, bho gotama, imassa nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ jānituṃ na sakkomi. Sace tumhe jānātha, kathethā”ti. “Vaṅgīsa, ahaṃ etampi jānāmi, ito uttaripi jānāmī”ti vatvā –

Disregarding their words, Vaṅgīsa went to the Teacher, exchanged friendly greetings, and sat down to one side. The Teacher asked him: “Vaṅgīsa, do you know any skill?” “Yes, Venerable Gotama, I know a mantra for knowing the skulls of the dead. With it, I can tap the skull of even one who has been dead for three years with my fingernail and know their place of rebirth.” Then the Teacher had the skull of one reborn in hell, one reborn among humans, one reborn among the devas, and one who had attained final Nibbāna brought and shown to him. Tapping the first skull, he said, “Venerable Gotama, this being was reborn in hell.” “Good, Vaṅgīsa, you have seen it well.” The Teacher then asked about the next, “Where was this being reborn?” “In the human world.” “And this one?” “In the deva world.” He stated the place of rebirth for all three. But when he tapped the skull of the one who had attained final Nibbāna, he could see neither beginning nor end. Then the Teacher asked him: “Are you unable, Vaṅgīsa?” “Behold, Venerable Gotama, I am still examining it.” But even after turning it over and over, he was unable to know the skull of one whose taints are destroyed by means of an external mantra. Then sweat broke out on his forehead. Ashamed, he became silent. The Teacher then said to him: “Are you weary, Vaṅgīsa?” “Yes, Venerable Gotama, I am unable to know this one’s place of rebirth. If you know, please tell me.” “Vaṅgīsa, I know this, and I know what is even beyond this,” he said:

“Cutiṃ yo vedi sattānaṃ, upapattiñca sabbaso;

Asattaṃ sugataṃ buddhaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

“One who knows in every way the passing away and rebirth of beings, unattached, a Well-Gone One, an Awakened One—that one I call a brahmin.”

“Yassa gatiṃ na jānanti, devā gandhabbamānusā;

Khīṇāsavaṃ arahantaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇa”nti. (dha. pa. 419-420; su. ni. 648-649) –

“One whose destination is unknown to devas, gandhabbas, and human beings, an Arahant with taints destroyed—that one I call a brahmin.” (Dhp 419–420; Snp 648–649)

Imā dve gāthāyo abhāsi. So tena hi, bho gotama, taṃ vijjaṃ me dethāti apacitiṃ dassetvā satthu santike nisīdi. Satthā “amhehi samānaliṅgassa demā”ti āha. Vaṅgīso “yaṃ kiñci katvā mayā imaṃ mantaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti brāhmaṇe upagantvā āha – “tumhe mayi [V 2.0251] pabbajante mā cintayittha, ahaṃ mantaṃ uggaṇhitvā sakalajambudīpe jeṭṭhako bhavissāmi, tumhākampi tena bhaddameva bhavissatī”ti [P 0.0530] so mantatthāya satthu santikaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Tadā ca thero nigrodhakappo bhagavato santike ṭhito hoti, taṃ bhagavā āṇāpesi – “nigrodhakappa, imaṃ pabbājehī”ti. Thero satthu āṇāya taṃ pabbājetvā “mantaparivāraṃ tāva uggaṇhāhī”ti dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ vipassanākammaṭṭhānañca ācikkhi. So dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ sajjhāyantova vipassanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Brāhmaṇā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “kiṃ, bho vaṅgīsa, samaṇassa gotamassa santike sippaṃ uggahita”nti pucchiṃsu. “Āma sikkhitaṃ”. “Tena hi ehi gamissāmā”ti. “Kiṃ sippasikkhanena, gacchatha tumhe na mayhaṃ tumhehi kattabbakicca”nti. Brāhmaṇā “tvampi dāni samaṇassa gotamassa vasaṃ āpanno, māyāya āvaṭṭito, kiṃ mayaṃ tava santike karissāmā”ti āgatamaggeneva pakkamiṃsu. Vaṅgīso vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ sacchākāsi.

He spoke these two verses. Then Vaṅgīsa, showing respect, said, “Well then, Venerable Gotama, give me that knowledge,” and he sat near the Teacher. The Teacher said: “We give it to one of similar appearance.” Thinking, “By whatever means, I must obtain this mantra,” Vaṅgīsa approached the brahmins and said: “Do not be concerned about my going forth. Once I have learned the mantra, I will become the foremost in all of Jambudīpa, and it will be for your good as well.” For the sake of the mantra, he approached the Teacher and asked for the going forth. At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was standing near the Blessed One. The Blessed One instructed him: “Nigrodhakappa, give this man the going forth.” In compliance with the Teacher’s command, the elder gave him the going forth and instructed him: “First, learn the mantra’s accessory practices,” and he explained the meditation subject on the thirty-two parts of the body and the meditation subject on insight. While reciting the meditation subject on the thirty-two parts of the body, he established the meditation subject of insight. The brahmins approached him and asked: “Well, Vaṅgīsa, have you learned a skill from the ascetic Gotama?” “Yes, I have learned it.” “Then come, let us go.” “What is the use of learning a skill? You go! I have no business with you.” The brahmins said: “Now you too have fallen under the sway of the ascetic Gotama, won over by his magic. What can we do in your presence?” And they departed by the way they had come. Vaṅgīsa developed insight and realized arahantship.

96. Evaṃ [M 2.0256] thero arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Anuttānatthameva vaṇṇayissāma.

96. Thus, having attained arahantship, the elder recollected his past kamma and, with joy arisen, he declared the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning: “The Victor named Padumuttara….” We shall explain only the meaning that is not obvious.

99. Pabhāhi anurañjantoti so padumuttaro bhagavā nīlapītādichabbaṇṇapabhāhi raṃsīhi anurañjanto jalanto sobhayamāno vijjotamānoti attho. Veneyyapadumāni soti padumuttarasūriyo attano vacanasaṅkhātena sūriyaraṃsiyā veneyyajanasaṅkhātapadumāni visesena bodhento pabodhento arahattamaggādhigamena phullitāni karotīti attho.

99. Pabhāhi anurañjanto (coloring with radiances): that Blessed One Padumuttara, dyeing them with the rays of the six colors—blue, yellow, and so on—blazing, adorning, and illuminating: this is the meaning. Veneyyapadumāni so (he, the lotuses to be trained): the sun Padumuttara, with the sun-rays that are his speech, especially awakens and fully awakens the lotuses that are the persons to be trained, causing them to blossom with the attainment of the path to arahantship: this is the meaning.

100. Vesārajjehi sampannoti –

100. Vesārajjehi sampanno (endowed with the grounds of self-confidence)—

“Antarāye ca niyyāne, buddhatte āsavakkhaye;

Etesu catuṭṭhānesu, buddho suṭṭhu visārado”ti. –

“Regarding obstructive qualities and the path of deliverance, regarding Buddhahood and the destruction of the taints; in these four grounds, the Buddha is perfectly self-confident.”

Evaṃ vuttacatuvesārajjañāṇehi sampanno samaṅgībhūto samannāgatoti attho.

Endowed with the four knowledges of self-confidence thus stated, furnished with them, possessed of them: this is the meaning.

105. Vāgīso vādisūdanoti vādīnaṃ paṇḍitajanānaṃ īso padhāno “vādīso”ti vattabbe da-kārassa ga-kāraṃ katvā evaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Sakatthaparatthavādaṃ sūdati paggharāpeti pākaṭaṃ karotīti vādisūdano.

105. Vāgīso vādisūdano: Vāgīsa means he is the lord (īso), the chief, of speakers (vādīnaṃ), that is, of wise people. It should be understood that this is said by changing the letter ‘d’ to ‘g’ when ‘vādīso’ should have been said. Vādisūdano: he makes flow (sūdati, paggharāpeti), makes manifest (pākaṭaṃ karoti), the teaching concerning one’s own welfare and the welfare of others; thus he is Vādisūdana.

110. Māramasanāti [V 2.0252] khandhamārādayo pañcamāre masati parāmasati viddhaṃsetīti māramasano. Diṭṭhisūdanāti vohāraparamatthasaṅkhātaṃ [P 0.0531] diṭṭhidassanaṃ sūdati paggharaṃ dīpetīti diṭṭhisūdano.

110. Māramasano: he touches (masati), crushes (parāmasati), and destroys (viddhaṃseti) the five Māras, beginning with the Māra of the aggregates; thus he is Māramasana. Diṭṭhisūdano: he illuminates (sūdati, dīpeti) the flowing forth (paggharaṃ) of the vision of views (diṭṭhidassanaṃ) designated as conventional and ultimate; thus he is Diṭṭhisūdana.

111. Vissāmabhūmi santānanti sakalasaṃsārasāgare santānaṃ kilamantānaṃ sotāpattimaggādiadhigamāpanena vissamabhūmi vissamaṭṭhānaṃ vūpasamanaṭṭhānanti attho.

111. Vissāmabhūmi santānaṃ (a land of rest for the continuity of beings): For the continuity of beings weary in the entire ocean of saṃsāra, he is a land of rest (vissāmabhūmi), a place of rest (vissamaṭṭhānaṃ), a place of appeasement (vūpasamanaṭṭhānaṃ), by leading them to attain the path of stream-entry and so on: this is the meaning.

132. Tatohaṃ vihatārambhoti tato paccekabuddhassa sarīradassanena ahaṃ vihatārambho vinaṭṭhasārambho, vinaṭṭhamāno nimmado hutvā pabbajjaṃ saṃ suṭṭhu yāciṃ saṃyāciṃ ārocesinti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

132. Tatohaṃ vihatārambho: ‘Then, on account of seeing the Paccekabuddha’s body, I was one whose effort was abandoned (vihatārambho), whose impetuosity was destroyed (vinaṭṭhasārambho), whose pride was destroyed, and having become free from conceit, I properly requested, earnestly beseeched, the going forth’: this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.

Vaṅgīsattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vaṅgīsa is complete.

5. Nandakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nandaka

Pañcamāpadāne [M 2.0257] padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato nandakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikārotiādi sabbaṃ pāṭhānusārena suviññeyyamevāti.

The fifth Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Venerable Nandaka, beginning with 'Padumuttaro nāma jino.' That he too had made his aspiration under former Buddhas, and so on—all this is to be easily understood in accordance with the text.

Nandakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nandaka is concluded.

6. Kāḷudāyittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kāḷudāyi

Chaṭṭhāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato kāḷudāyittherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto satthāraṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ kulappasādakānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapentaṃ disvā tajjaṃ abhinīhārakammaṃ katvā taṃ ṭhānantaraṃ patthesi. Satthāpi byākāsi. So yāvajīvaṃ kusalaṃ katvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto amhākaṃ bodhisattassa mātukucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase devalokato cavitvā kapilavatthusmiṃyeva amaccakule paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Bodhisattena saha ekadivaseyeva [V 2.0253] jāto, taṃdivasaṃyeva naṃ dukūlacumbaṭakena nipajjāpetvā bodhisattassa upaṭṭhānaṃ nayiṃsu. Bodhisattena hi saddhiṃ bodhirukkho, rāhulamātā, cattāro nidhī[P 0.0532], ārohaniyahatthī, kaṇḍako, channo, kāḷudāyīti ime satta ekadivase jātattā sahajātā nāma ahesuṃ. Athassa nāmaggahaṇadivase sakalanagarassa udaggacittadivase jātattā udāyītveva nāmaṃ kariṃsu. Thokaṃ kāḷadhātukattā pana kāḷudāyīti paññāyittha. So bodhisattena saddhiṃ kumārakīḷaṃ kīḷanto vuddhiṃ agamāsi.

The sixth Apadāna is the Apadāna of the Venerable Kāḷudāyi, beginning with 'Padumuttaro nāma jino.' This one too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara in the city of Haṃsavatī in a good family. Having reached maturity and listened to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher appointing a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who inspire faith in families. Having seen this, he made an aspiration for that very thing and longed for that same position. The Teacher too made a prediction for him. Having done good throughout his life and wandered among devas and humans, on the very day our Bodhisatta took conception, he passed away from the deva world and took rebirth in a minister’s family in Kapilavatthu itself. He was born on the very same day as the Bodhisatta. On that day, having laid him on a coil of fine cloth, they brought him to attend on the Bodhisatta. For along with the Bodhisatta, the Bodhi tree, Rāhula’s mother, the four great treasures, the state elephant, Kaṇṭhaka, Channa, and Kāḷudāyī—these seven were born on the same day and were thus called the 'co-natals.' Then, on his naming day, because he was born on a day of elation for the entire city, they gave him the name Udāyī. But because he was of a slightly dark complexion, he became known as Kāḷudāyī. He grew up playing childhood games with the Bodhisatta.

Aparabhāge lokanāthe mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitvā anukkamena sabbaññutaṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakke rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane viharante suddhodanamahārājā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā purisasahassaparivāraṃ ekaṃ amaccaṃ “puttaṃ me idhānehī”ti pesesi. So satthu dhammadesanāvelāyaṃ satthu santikaṃ gantvā parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ sutvā saparivāro [M 2.0258] arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Atha ne satthā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Sabbe taṃkhaṇaṃyeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā vassasaṭṭhikattherā viya ahesuṃ. Arahattappattato paṭṭhāya ariyā nāma majjhattāva honti, tasmā raññā pesitasāsanaṃ dasabalassa nārocesi. Rājā neva gato āgacchati, na sāsanaṃ suyyatīti aparampi amaccaṃ purisasahassaparivāraṃ pesesi. Tasmimpi tathā paṭipanne aparampīti etena nayena navapurisasahassaparivāre nava amacce pesesi. Sabbe gantvā arahattaṃ patvā tuṇhībhūtā ahesuṃ.

Later, when the Protector of the World had gone forth in the Great Renunciation, had gradually attained omniscience, had set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, and was dwelling near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the great king Suddhodana heard the news and sent a minister with a retinue of a thousand men, saying, 'Bring my son here.' That minister went to the Teacher during a Dhamma discourse, stood at the edge of the assembly, and after hearing the Dhamma, he and his retinue attained arahantship. Then the Teacher extended his hand, saying, 'Come, bhikkhus.' In that very moment, they all became like elders of sixty years’ standing, bearing bowls and robes created by psychic power. From the attainment of arahantship, noble ones are impartial; therefore, he did not deliver the king’s message to the One with Ten Powers. The king, thinking, 'The one who went does not return, nor is any message heard,' sent another minister with a retinue of a thousand men. When that one also acted in the same way, he sent another, and in this manner he sent nine ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand men. All of them went, attained arahantship, and remained silent.

Atha rājā cintesi – “ettakā janā mayi sinehābhāvena dasabalassa idhāgamanatthāya na kiñci kathayiṃsu, ayaṃ kho pana udāyī dasabalena samavayo sahapaṃsukīḷiko, mayi ca sinehavā, imaṃ pesessāmī”ti. Atha taṃ pakkosāpetvā, “tāta, tvaṃ purisasahassaparivāro gantvā dasabalaṃ idhānehī”ti vatvā pesesi. So pana gacchanto “sacāhaṃ, deva, pabbajituṃ labhissāmi, evāhaṃ bhagavantaṃ idhānessāmī”ti vatvā raññā “pabbajitopi mama puttaṃ dassehī”ti vutto rājagahaṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanāvelāya parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ sutvā saparivāro arahattaṃ patvā ehibhikkhubhāve patiṭṭhāsi. So arahattaṃ patvā – “na tāvāyaṃ dasabalassa kulanagaraṃ gantuṃ kālo, vassante pana upagate pabbatesu vanasaṇḍesu haritatiṇasañchannāya bhūmiyā gamanakālo bhavissatī”ti gamanakālaṃ āgamento vassante sampatte satthu kulanagaraṃ gantuṃ gamanavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇesi. Vuttañcetaṃ theragāthāya (theragā. 527-530) –

Then the king thought: 'All those people, because they lack affection for me, said nothing about bringing the One with Ten Powers here. But this Udāyī is of the same age as the One with Ten Powers, a childhood playmate, and he is affectionate toward me. I will send him.' Then, having summoned him, he said, 'My dear, go with a retinue of a thousand men and bring the One with Ten Powers here,' and he sent him. But as he was leaving, he said, 'Your Majesty, if I am able to go forth, then I will bring the Blessed One here.' When the king told him, 'Even if you have gone forth, you must show my son to me,' he went to Rājagaha. Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher's Dhamma discourse and hearing the Dhamma, he and his retinue attained arahantship and were established in the state of 'ehi-bhikkhu.' Having attained arahantship, he thought: 'This is not yet the time for the One with Ten Powers to go to his family’s city. But when the rainy season has arrived, when the ground in the mountains and forest groves is covered with green grass, that will be the time to go.' Awaiting the right time for the journey, when the rains arrived, he praised the beauty of the journey to the Teacher's family city. And this is stated in the Theragāthā (Thag 527–530):

“Aṅgārino [P 0.0533][V 2.0254] dāni dumā bhadante, phalesino chadanaṃ vippahāya;

Te accimantova pabhāsayanti, samayo mahāvīra bhāgī rasānaṃ.

“Now the trees are like glowing embers, venerable sir; seeking fruit, they have cast off their foliage. They shine as if aflame, great hero; it is the season for the partaking of saps.

“Dumāni phullāni manoramāni, samantato sabbadisā pavanti;

Pattaṃ pahāya phalamāsasānā, kālo ito pakkamanāya vīra.

“The trees are in bloom, delightful, their fragrance wafts in every direction. Having shed their leaves, hoping for fruit, it is time, O hero, to set out from here.

“Nevātisītaṃ [M 2.0259] na panātiuṇhaṃ, sukhā utu addhaniyā bhadante;

Passantu taṃ sākiyā koḷiyā ca, pacchāmukhaṃ rohiniyaṃ tarantaṃ.

“It is not too cold, nor yet too hot; the season is pleasant for travel, venerable sir. Let the Sākyans and the Koliyans see you crossing the Rohiṇī, facing west.

“Āsāya kasate khettaṃ, bījaṃ āsāya vappati;

Āsāya vāṇijā yanti, samuddaṃ dhanahārakā;

Yāya āsāya tiṭṭhāmi, sā me āsā samijjhatu.

“In hope the farmer ploughs his field, in hope the seed is sown; in hope the merchants, seeking wealth, travel to the sea. The hope on which I stand, may that hope of mine be fulfilled.

“Nātisītaṃ nātiuṇhaṃ, nātidubbhikkhachātakaṃ;

Saddalā haritā bhūmi, esa kālo mahāmuni. (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.225);

“Not too cold, not too hot, not a time of famine or hunger; the earth is green with fresh grass. This is the time, O great sage.

“Punappunañceva vapanti bījaṃ, punappunaṃ vassati devarājā;

Punappunaṃ khettaṃ kasanti kassakā, punappunaṃ dhaññamupeti raṭṭhaṃ.

“Again and again they sow the seed, again and again the king of devas sends rain; again and again the farmers plough the field, again and again grain comes to the country.

“Punappunaṃ yācanakā caranti, punappunaṃ dānapatī dadanti;

Punappunaṃ dānapatī daditvā, punappunaṃ saggamupenti ṭhānaṃ.

“Again and again do beggars roam, again and again do patrons give; having given again and again, again and again they go to a heavenly state.

“Vīro have sattayugaṃ puneti; Yasmiṃ kule jāyati bhūripañño;

Maññāmahaṃ sakkati devadevo, tayā hi jāto muni saccanāmo.

“A hero, it is said, purifies seven generations in the family in which one of vast wisdom is born. I believe, O Sakyan, O god among gods, that from you has been born the sage, true to his name.

“Suddhodano [P 0.0534] nāma pitā mahesino, buddhassa mātā pana māyanāmā;

Yā bodhisattaṃ parihariya kucchinā, kāyassa bhedā tidivamhi modati.

“The great seer’s father was named Suddhodana, and the Buddha’s mother was named Māyā. She who carried the Bodhisatta in her womb, at the breakup of the body, rejoices in heaven.

“Sā [V 2.0255] gotamī kālakatā ito cutā, dibbehi kāmehi samaṅgibhūtā;

Sā modati kāmaguṇehi pañcahi, parivāritā devagaṇehi tehi.

That Gotamī, having passed away, has fallen from here, endowed with divine sensual pleasures. Surrounded by those hosts of devas, she rejoices in the five strands of sensual pleasure.

“Buddhassa [M 2.0260] puttomhi asayhasāhino, aṅgīrasassappaṭimassa tādino;

Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsi sakka, dhammena me gotama ayyakosī”ti. (theragā. 531-536);

I am a son of the Buddha, the unassailable victor, of the incomparable Aṅgirasa, the Suchlike One. You, Sakka, are my father’s father; by Dhamma, O Gotama, you are my grandfather, Kosiya.”

“Ambā panasā kapiṭṭhā ca, pupphapallavalaṅkatā;

Dhuvapphalāni savanti, khuddāmadhukakūpamā;

Sevamāno ubho passe, gantukālo mahāyassa.

“Mango, jackfruit, and wood-apple trees, adorned with flowers and new leaves, drip with their constant fruits, like small honeycombs. Enjoying them on both sides of the path, it is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Jambū sumadhurā nīpā, madhugaṇḍidivapphalā;

Tā ubhosu pajjotanti, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Sweet rose-apples and nīpa trees, with fruits like heavenly lumps of honey; they illuminate both sides of the path. It is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Tiṇḍukāni piyālāni, soṇṇavaṇṇā manoramā;

Khuddakappaphalā niccaṃ, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Tinduka and piyāla trees, golden-hued and delightful, always have small, suitable fruits. It is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Kadalī pañcamocci ca, supakkaphalabhūsitā;

Ubhopassesu lambanti, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Banana and pañcamocī trees, adorned with well-ripened fruit, hang down on both sides of the path. It is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Madhupphaladharā niccaṃ, morarukkhā manoramā;

Khuddakappaphalā niccaṃ, gantukālo mahāyasa.

The delightful mora trees always bear honey-sweet fruit; they always have small, suitable fruits. It is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Hintālatālapantī ca, rajatakkhandhova jotare;

Supakkaphalasañchannā, khuddakappā madhussavā;

Phalāni tāni khādante, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Rows of hintāla and tāla palms shine like silver trunks; covered with well-ripened fruit, they are small, suitable, and drip with honey. While eating those fruits, it is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Udumbarāruṇāvaṇṇā[P 0.0535], sadāsumadhurapphalā;

Ubhopassesu lambanti, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Udumbara trees, the color of dawn, always bearing very sweet fruit, hang down on both sides of the path. It is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Itthambhūtā [V 2.0256] anekā te, nānāphaladharā dumā;

Ubhopassesu lambanti, gantukālo mahāyasa.

For you, there are many such trees bearing various fruits; they hang down on both sides of the path. It is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Campakā salaḷā nāgā, sugandhā māluteritā;

Supupphitaggā jotanti, sugandhenābhipūjayuṃ;

Sādarā vinatāneva, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Campaka, salaḷa, and nāga trees, fragrant, stirred by the wind; their well-blossomed tops are radiant, as if honoring you with their fragrance. As if bowing respectfully, it is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Punnāgā giripunnāgā, pupphitā dharaṇīruhā;

Supupphitaggā jotanti, sugandhenābhipūjayuṃ;

Sādarā vinatuggaggā, gantukālo mahāyasa.

Punnāga and mountain punnāga trees, flowering trees grown from the earth; their well-blossomed tops are radiant, as if honoring you with their fragrance. With their tips respectfully bent down, it is time to go, O one of great fame.

“Asokā [M 2.0261] koviḷārā ca, somanassakarā varā;

Sugandhā kaṇṇikā bandhā, rattavaṇṇehi bhūsitā;

Sādarā vinatuggaggā, samayo te mahāyasa.

Excellent asoka and koviḷāra trees, which bring delight; fragrant kaṇikāra trees in clusters, adorned with red hues. With their tips respectfully bent down, the time is yours, O one of great fame.

“Kaṇṇikārā phullitā niccaṃ, sovaṇṇaraṃsijotakā;

Dibbagandhā pavāyanti, disā sabbāni sobhayaṃ;

Sādarā vinatāneva, samayo te mahāyasa.

Kaṇikāra trees are always in bloom, shining with golden rays; divine fragrances waft, beautifying all directions. As if bowing respectfully, the time is yours, O one of great fame.

“Supattā gandhasampannā, ketakī dhanuketakī;

Sugandhā sampavāyanti, disā sabbābhigandhino;

Sādarā pūjayantāva, samayo te mahāyasa.

Ketakī and dhanuketakī trees, with beautiful leaves and rich in fragrance; their sweet scents waft forth, perfuming every direction. As if paying homage with respect, the time is yours, O one of great fame.

“Mallikā jātisumanā, sugandhā khuddamallikā;

Disā sabbā pavāyanti, ubho magge pasobhayaṃ;

Sādarā te palambanti, samayo te mahāyasa.

Mallikā, jasmine, and small fragrant jasmine; their scents waft in all directions, beautifying both sides of the path. They hang down respectfully for you; the time is yours, O one of great fame.”

“Sindhuvārā sītagandhā, sugandhā māluteritā;

Disā sabbābhipūjentā, ubho magge pasobhayaṃ;

Sādarā vinatuggaggā, samayo te mahāyasa.

“The sindhuvāra trees, cool-scented, fragrant, stirred by the wind, honoring all directions and beautifying both sides of the path, with their tops reverently bowed—it is your time, O one of great fame.”

“Sīhā [V 2.0257] kesarasīhā ca, catuppadanisevitā;

Acchambhītā surāpāne, migarājā patāpino.

“Lions and maned lions, attended by other quadrupeds, fearless of strong drink, majestic kings of beasts.”

“Sīhanādena pūjenti, sādarā te migābhibhū;

Maggamhi ubhato vūḷhā, samayo te mahāyasa.

“Those conquerors of beasts honor you reverently with a lion’s roar. Lined up on both sides of the path, they say: ‘It is your time, O one of great fame.’”

“Byagghā [P 0.0536] sindhavā nakulā, sādhurūpā bhayānakā;

Ākāse sampatantāva, nibbhītā yena kenaci;

Tehi te sādarā natā, samayo te mahāyasa.

“Tigers, lions, and mongooses, of fine form yet fearsome, moving as if flying through the sky, unafraid of anyone at all; by them you are reverently honored with a bow. It is your time, O one of great fame.”

“Tidhā pabhinnā chaddantā, surūpā sussarā subhā;

Sattappatiṭṭhitaṅgā te, ubho maggesu kūjino;

Sādarā hāsamānāva, samayo te mahāyasa.

“Six-tusked elephants in threefold rut, of beautiful form, sweet-voiced, and lovely, with their seven limbs firmly planted, trumpeting on both sides of the path; reverently, as if laughing, they say: ‘It is your time, O one of great fame.’”

“Migā varāhā pasadā, citrāsāvayavā subhā;

Ārohapariṇāhena, surūpā aṅgasaṃyutā;

Ubho magge gāyamānāva, samayo te mahāyasa.

“Deer, boars, and spotted antelopes, well-proportioned in height and girth, of fine form and endowed with graceful limbs; as if singing on both sides of the path, they say: ‘It is your time, O one of great fame.’”

“Gokaṇṇā [M 2.0262] sarabhā rurū, ārohapariṇāhino;

Surūpā aṅgasampannā, sevamānāva accharuṃ;

Sevamānā tehi tadā, samayo te mahāyasa.

“Gokaṇṇa, Sarabha, and Ruru deer, well-proportioned in height and girth, of beautiful form and endowed with perfect limbs, attending you as if they were celestial nymphs; thus attended by them then, it was your time, O one of great fame.”

“Dīpī acchā taracchā ca, tudarā varuṇā sadā;

Te dāni sikkhitā sabbe, mettāya tava tādino;

Te paccasevakā addhā, samayo te mahāyasa.

“Panthers, bears, and hyenas, always fierce and powerful; now they are all tamed by the loving-kindness of you, the Such-like One. They are indeed your attendants. It is your time, O one of great fame.”

“Sasā siṅgālā nakulā, kalandakāḷakā bahū;

Kasturā sūrā gandhā te, kevalā gāyamānāva.

“Hares, jackals, mongooses, and many black squirrels; musk deer, brave and fragrant, all as if singing.”

Samayo te mahāyasa;

“It is your time, O one of great fame.”

“Mayūrā [V 2.0258] nīlagīvā te, susikhā subhapakkhikā;

Supiñchā te sunādā ca, veḷuriyamaṇisannibhā;

Nādaṃ karontā pūjenti, kālo te pitudassane.

“They are peacocks with blue necks, with beautiful crests and lovely wings, with fine tails and sweet cries, resembling lapis lazuli gems. Crying out, they honor you, saying: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Suvaṇṇacitrahaṃsā ca, javahaṃsā vihācarā;

Te sabbe āsayā chuddhā, jinadassanabyāvaṭā;

Madhurassarena kūjanti, kālo te pitudassane.

“Golden-hued, variegated swans and swift swans that roam the sky—all of them are pure in heart, intent on seeing the Victor. They cry with a sweet voice: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Haṃsā koñcā sunadā te, cakkavākā nadīcarā;

Bakā balākā rucirā, jalakākā sarakukkuṭā;

Sādarābhinādino ete, kālo te pitudassane.

“Swans and sweet-sounding curlews, river-frequenting ruddy geese, beautiful cranes and egrets, cormorants and moorhens—these all cry out respectfully: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Citrā surūpā sussarā, sāḷikā suvataṇḍikā;

Rukkhaggā sampatantā te, ubho maggesu kūjino;

Tesu tesu nikūjanti, kālo te pitudassane.

“Variegated, beautiful, and sweet-voiced mynah birds and woodpeckers fly from treetop to treetop, chirping on both sides of the path. In all those places they warble: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Kokilā [P 0.0537] sakalā citrā, sadā mañjussarā varā;

Vimhāpitā te janataṃ, saddhimittādike surā;

Sarehi pūjayantāva, kālo te pitudassane.

“All the variegated cuckoos, ever sweet-voiced and excellent, astonishing the people, along with gods, friends, and others, as if honoring you with their songs, they cry: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Bhiṅkā kurarā sārā, pūritā kānane sadā;

Ninnādayantā pavanaṃ, aññamaññasamaṅgino;

Gāyamānā sareneva, kālo te pitudassane.

“Drongos, ospreys, and mynahs always fill the forest; making the woods resound, in harmony with one another, singing with their voices, they cry: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Tittirā [M 2.0263] susarā sārā, susarā vanakukkuṭā;

Mañjussarā rāmaṇeyyā, kālo te pitudassane.

“Sweet-voiced and lovely partridges, sweet-voiced jungle fowl, charming and delightful, all cry: ‘It is time for you to see your father.’”

“Setavālukasañchannā, supatitthā manoramā;

Madhurodakasampuṇṇā, sarā jotanti te sadā;

Tattha nhatvā pivitvā ca, samayo te ñātidassane.

“Lakes covered with white sand, with fine bathing spots, delightful, and filled with sweet water, always gleam for you. Having bathed and drunk there, it will be time for you to see your kinsmen.”

“Kumbhīrāmakarākiṇṇā[V 2.0259], valayā muñjarohitā;

Macchakacchapabyāviddhā, sarā sītodakā subhā;

“The cool and lovely lakes are crowded with crocodiles and makaras, encircled by muñja grass and red lotuses, and teeming with fish and turtles.”

Tattha nhatvā pivitvā ca, samayo te ñātidassane.

“Having bathed and drunk there, it will be time for you to see your kinsmen.”

“Nīluppalasamākiṇṇā, tathā rattuppalehi ca;

Kumuduppalasaṃkiṇṇā, sarā sobhantinekadhā;

Tattha sītalakā toyā, samayo te ñātidassane.

“Strewn with blue water lilies, and likewise with red ones, mingled with white lotuses, the lakes shine in many ways. There the waters are cool. It is time for you to see your kinsmen.”

“Puṇḍarīkehi sañchannā, padumehi samohatā;

Ubho maggesu sobhanti, pokkharañño tahiṃ tahiṃ;

Tatthodakāni nhāyanti, samayo te ñātidassane.

“Covered with white lotuses, overgrown with red lotuses, lotus ponds here and there beautify both sides of the path. There the waters are for bathing. It is time for you to see your kinsmen.”

“Setapulinasaṃkiṇṇā, supatitthā manoramā;

Sītodakamahoghehi, sampuṇṇā tā nadī subhā;

Ubho maggehi sandanti, samayo te ñātidassane.

“Strewn with white sandbanks, with fine fords, delightful, those beautiful rivers are full with great torrents of cool water. They flow on both sides of the path. It is time for you to see your kinsmen.”

“Maggassa ubhatopasse, gāmanigamasamākulā;

Saddhā pasannā janatā, ratanattayamāmakā;

Tesaṃ sampuṇṇasaṅkappo, samayo te ñātidassane.

“On both sides of the path are crowds of people from the villages and towns, faithful and confident, devoted to the Triple Gem. To fulfill their aspiration, it is time for you to see your kinsmen.”

“Tesu tesu padesesu, devā mānussakā ubho;

Gandhamālābhipūjenti, samayo te ñātidassane”ti.

“In those various regions, both gods and humans worship you with perfumes and garlands. It is time for you to see your kinsmen.”

Evaṃ [P 0.0538] thero saṭṭhimattāhi gāthāhi satthu gamanavaṇṇaṃ saṃvaṇṇesi. Atha kho bhagavā “kāḷudāyī mama gamanaṃ pattheti, pūressāmissa saṅkappa”nti tattha gamane bahūnaṃ visesādhigamaṃ disvā vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto rājagahato aturitacārikāvasena vuttappakāraphalāphale anubhavanto dvipadacatuppadādisamūhānaṃ sevanapūjāya pūjiyamāno vuttappakārasugandhapupphagandhehi gandhiyamāno gāmanigamavāsīnaṃ saṅgahaṃ kurumāno kapilavatthugāmimaggaṃ [M 2.0264] paṭipajji. Thero iddhiyā kapilavatthuṃ gantvā rañño purato ākāse ṭhito adiṭṭhapubbaṃ vesaṃ disvā, raññā – “kosi tva”nti [V 2.0260] pucchito “sace amaccaputtaṃ tayā bhagavato santike pesitaṃ na jānāsi, evaṃ jānāhī”ti vadanto –

Thus the elder praised the Teacher’s journey with about sixty verses. Then the Blessed One, thinking, “Kāḷudāyī desires that I make this journey; I will fulfill his aspiration,” and seeing that many would attain distinction during that journey, set out from Rājagaha. Surrounded by twenty thousand arahants, he proceeded by way of an unhurried tour, experiencing the fruits and results as described, being honored with the service and worship of hosts of bipeds and quadrupeds, perfumed by the fragrances of flowers as described, and bestowing his favor upon the inhabitants of the villages and towns, he took the road leading to Kapilavatthu. The elder, having gone to Kapilavatthu by psychic power, stood in the air before the king. Seeing his unprecedented appearance, the king asked, “Who are you?” The elder replied, “If you do not recognize the minister’s son whom you sent to the Blessed One, then know this,” and he said:

“Buddhassa puttomhi asayhasāhino, aṅgīrasassappaṭimassa tādino;

Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsi sakka, dhammena me gotama ayyakosī”ti. (theragā. 536) – gāthamāha;

He spoke this verse: ‘I am the son of the Buddha, the unendurable endurer, the Angirasa, the peerless Such-like One. You, O Sakyan, are the father of my Father; by the Dhamma, O Gotama, you are my grandfather.’”

Tattha buddhassa puttomhīti sabbaññubuddhassa ure vāyāmajanitāhi dhammadesanāhi jātatāya orasaputto amhi. Asayhasāhinoti abhisambodhito pubbe ṭhapetvā mahābodhisattaṃ aññehi sahituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā asayhassa sakalabodhisambhārassa, mahākaruṇākarassa ca sahanato tato parampi aññehi sahituṃ abhibhavituṃ asakkuṇeyyattā asayhānaṃ pañcannaṃ mārānaṃ sahanato abhibhavanato āsayānusayacaritādhimuttiādivibhāgāvabodhena yathārahaṃ veneyyānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi anusāsanīsaṅkhātassa aññehi asayhassa buddhakiccassa sahanato tattha vā sādhukārībhāvato asayhasāhino. Aṅgīrasassāti aṅgīkatasīlādisampattikassa. “Aṅgamaṅgehi niccharaṇakaobhāsassā”ti apare. Keci pana “aṅgīraso siddhatthoti imāni dve nāmāni pitarāyeva gahitānī”ti vadanti. Appaṭimassāti anupamassa iṭṭhādīsu tādilakhaṇasampattiyā tādino. Pitupitā mayhaṃ tuvaṃsīti ariyajātivasena mayhaṃ pitu sammāsambuddhassa lokavohāravasena tvaṃ pitā [P 0.0539] asi. Sakkāti vaṃsena rājānaṃ ālapati. Dhammenāti sabhāvena ariyajātilokiyajātīhi dvinnaṃ jātīnaṃ sabhāvasamodhānena. Gotamāti gottena rājānaṃ ālapati. Ayyakosīti pitāmaho ahosi. Ettha ca “buddhassa puttomhī”tiādiṃ vadanto thero aññaṃ byākāsi.

Herein, I am the son of the Buddha means: I am the legitimate son of the All-Knowing Buddha, born from the Dhamma teachings generated by the striving in his breast. Of the unendurable endurer: before his full enlightenment, he endured the entire store of requisites for enlightenment, which is unendurable for others apart from a great bodhisatta, and he endured great compassion; after his enlightenment, he endured and vanquished the five Māras, who are unendurable and cannot be vanquished by others; and he endured the Buddha’s duty of instructing trainees according to their dispositions, which is unendurable for others. Of the Angirasa: of one endowed with the attainment of virtue and so on, which he had taken upon himself. Others say it means ‘of one whose radiance issues from his every limb.’ Some, however, say: ‘Angirasa and Siddhattha—these two names were given by his father.’ Of the peerless: of the incomparable one. Such-like One: because he possesses the characteristic of steadfastness amidst desirable and undesirable things. You are the father of my Father: you are the father by worldly convention of my father, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is my father by way of noble birth. O Sakyan: he addresses the king by his lineage. By the Dhamma: by nature, that is, by the combination of the natures of the two births, the noble birth and the worldly birth. O Gotama: he addresses the king by his clan. You are my grandfather: you were my grandfather. Herein, by saying, ‘I am the son of the Buddha,’ etc., the elder was making a special declaration.

Evaṃ [M 2.0265] pana attānaṃ jānāpetvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhena raññā mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā attano paṭiyāditassa nānaggarasabhojanassa pattaṃ pūretvā patte dinne gamanākāraṃ dassesi. “Kasmā gantukāmattha, bhuñjathā”ti vutte, satthu santikaṃ gantvā bhuñjissāmīti. Kahaṃ pana satthāti? Vīsatisahassabhikkhuparivāro tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya maggaṃ paṭipannoti. Tumhe imaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjatha, aññaṃ bhagavato haratha. Yāva ca mama putto imaṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇāti, tāvassa itoyeva piṇḍapātaṃ harathāti. Thero bhattakiccaṃ katvā rañño ca parisāya ca dhammaṃ desetvā satthu āgamanato puretarameva rājanivesanaṃ ratanattayaguṇesu abhippasannaṃ karonto sabbesaṃ passantānaṃyeva satthu āharitabbabhattapuṇṇaṃ pattaṃ ākāse vissajjetvā sayampi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā [V 2.0261] piṇḍapātaṃ upanetvā satthu hatthe ṭhapesi. Satthāpi taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñji. Evaṃ saṭṭhiyojanaṃ maggaṃ divase divase yojanaṃ gacchantassa bhagavato rājagehato bhattaṃ āharitvā adāsi. Bhagavā kamena kapilavatthunagaraṃ patvā punadivase rājavīthiyaṃ piṇḍāya carati. Taṃ sutvā suddhodanamahārājā tattha gantvā, “mā evaṃ kattabbaṃ maññi, nayidaṃ rājavaṃsappaveṇī”ti. “Ayaṃ tumhākaṃ, mahārāja, vaṃso, īdiso amhākaṃ pana buddhavaṃso”ti vatvā –

Having thus made himself known, the king, joyful and delighted, had him seated on a magnificent couch, filled a bowl with various choice foods he had prepared, and gave him the bowl. When it was given, the elder showed his intention to leave. When asked, “Why do you wish to go? Eat here,” he replied, “I will eat after I have gone to the Teacher.” “But where is the Teacher?” “Surrounded by twenty thousand monks, he has set out on the road to see you.” “You eat this almsfood, and take another for the Blessed One. And until my son reaches this city, bring him almsfood from here.” The elder, having finished his meal, taught the Dhamma to the king and his retinue. Even before the Teacher’s arrival, he made the royal palace confidently devoted to the qualities of the Triple Gem. Then, in full view of everyone, he tossed the bowl full of food for the Teacher into the air, rose up into the sky himself, brought the almsfood, and placed it in the Teacher’s hands. The Teacher then partook of that almsfood. In this way, he brought food from the king’s house and gave it to the Blessed One each day as he traveled one yojana per day along the sixty-yojana path. The Blessed One in due course reached the city of Kapilavatthu. The next day, he was walking for alms along the royal street. Hearing this, King Suddhodana went there and said, “Sir, you should not do this. This is not the custom of the royal lineage.” The Buddha replied, “This, great king, is your lineage. But this is our lineage, the lineage of the Buddhas,” and he said:

“Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya, dhammaṃ sucaritaṃ care;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.

“One should arise and not be negligent; one should practice the Dhamma well. One who practices the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and in the next.”

“Dhammaṃ care sucaritaṃ, na naṃ duccaritaṃ care;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti. (dha. pa. 168-169) –

“One should practice the Dhamma well; one should not practice it badly. One who practices the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and in the next.”

Dhammaṃ desesi. Rājā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Tato rājā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā sakamandire bhojetvā sampavāretvā bhojanāvasāne dhammapālajātakaṃ (jā. 1.10.92 ādayo) sutvā sapariso anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahi. Aparabhāge setacchattassa heṭṭhā nipannova arahattaṃ patvā parinibbāyi.

He taught the Dhamma. The king was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then the king invited the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, fed them in his own palace, and served them to their satisfaction. At the conclusion of the meal, after listening to the Dhammapāla Jātaka (Jā 1.10.92ff.), he and his retinue were established in the fruit of non-returning. Later, while lying beneath a white parasol, he attained arahantship and attained final Nibbāna.

Tato bhagavā rāhulamātuyā bimbādeviyā pāsādaṃ gantvā tassā dhammaṃ [P 0.0540] desetvā sokaṃ vinodetvā candakinnarījātakadesanāya (jā. 1.14.18 ādayo) pasādaṃ janetvā nigrodhārāmaṃ agamāsi. Atha bimbādevī puttaṃ rāhulakumāraṃ āha – “gaccha, tava pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ yācāhī”ti. Kumāro “dāyajjaṃ[M 2.0266], me samaṇa, dehī”ti vatvā bhagavantaṃ anubandhitvā, “sukhā, te samaṇa, chāyā”ti vadanto gacchati. Taṃ bhagavā nigrodhārāmaṃ netvā “lokutaradāyajjaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vatvā pabbājesi. Atha bhagavā ariyagaṇamajjhe nisinno “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kulappasādakānaṃ yadidaṃ kāḷudāyī”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 225) theraṃ etadagge ṭhapesi.

Then the Blessed One went to the palace of Rāhula’s mother, Bimbādevī, taught her the Dhamma, dispelled her sorrow, and inspired confidence in her with a discourse on the Candakinnarī Jātaka (Jā 1.14.18ff.). He then returned to the Nigrodhārāma. Then Bimbādevī said to her son, Prince Rāhula: “Go, ask your father for your inheritance.” The prince followed the Blessed One, saying, “Give me my inheritance, ascetic,” and as he went, he said, “Pleasant is your shadow, ascetic.” The Blessed One led him to the Nigrodhārāma, said, “Take the supramundane inheritance,” and gave him the going forth. Then, seated amidst the assembly of noble ones, the Blessed One placed the elder in the foremost position, saying: “Bhikkhus, among my bhikkhu disciples who inspire confidence in families, the foremost is this one, that is, Kāḷudāyī” (AN 1.219, 225).

165. Thero pattaetadaggaṭṭhāno attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ [V 2.0262] pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādigāthāyo abhāsi. Tattha anuttānapadameva vaṇṇayissāma.

165. The elder, having attained this foremost position, recollected his past kamma and, filled with joy, proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct by reciting the verses beginning: “The Victor named Padumuttara….” Herein, we will comment only on the words that are not self-evident.

166. Guṇāguṇavidūti guṇañca aguṇañca guṇāguṇaṃ, vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ, kusalākusalaṃ vā taṃ jānātīti guṇāguṇavidū. Kataññūti aññehi kataguṇaṃ jānātīti kataññū, ekadivasampi bhattadānādinā katūpakārassa rajjampi dātuṃ samatthattā kataññū. Katavedīti kataṃ vindati anubhavati sampaṭicchatīti katavedī. Titthe yojeti pāṇineti sabbasatte nibbānapavesanupāye kusalapathe magge dhammadesanāya yojeti sampayojeti patiṭṭhāpetīti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva. Gamanavaṇṇanagāthānamattho theragāthāyaṃ vuttoyevāti.

166. Guṇāguṇavidū (Knower of virtue and fault): this means one who knows virtue and fault (guṇa and aguṇa), that is, praise and blame (vaṇṇa and avaṇṇa), or the skillful and unskillful. Kataññū (Grateful): this means one who knows the good done by others. He is called kataññū because he is capable of giving even his kingdom to one who has done him a favor, such as by offering food for a single day. Katavedī (Responsive to kindness): this means one who finds, experiences, or acknowledges what has been done for him. Titthe yojeti pāṇine (He establishes beings at the ford): this means he directs, connects, and establishes all beings in the path, the skillful path, the means for entering Nibbāna, by teaching the Dhamma. The rest has an obvious meaning. The meaning of the verses describing the journey has already been explained in the Theragāthā.

Kāḷudāyittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kāḷudāyī is concluded.

7. Abhayattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Abhaya

Sattamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato abhayattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimajinavaresu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vipaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle haṃsavatīnagare brāhmaṇakule nibbatto. So vuddhimanvāya vedaṅgapārago sakaparasamayakusalo ekadivasaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannamānaso bhagavantaṃ gāthāhi thomesi. So tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā puññāni katvā tato cuto devaloke nibbatto aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyevaṃ [M 2.0267] saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe bimbisārarañño putto hutvā nibbatti, abhayotvevassa nāmaṃ kariṃsu. So vayappatto nigaṇṭhehi saddhiṃ [P 0.0541] vissāsiko hutvā caranto ekadivasaṃ nigaṇṭhena nāṭaputtena satthu vādāropanatthāya pesito nipuṇapañhaṃ pucchitvā nipuṇabyākaraṇaṃ sutvā pasanno satthu santike pabbajitvā kammaṭṭhānānurūpaṃ ñāṇaṃ pesetvā nacirasseva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The seventh apadāna is that of the Venerable Elder Abhaya, beginning: “The Victor named Padumuttara….” He too, having made his aspiration under previous Supreme Jinas and in subsequent existences accumulated meritorious deeds that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family in the city of Haṃsavatī at the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. When he came of age, he mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and was skilled in his own and others’ philosophical systems. One day, after hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, with a confident mind he praised the Blessed One with verses. Having lived there for his full lifespan doing meritorious deeds, he passed away and was reborn in a deva world. Wandering thus through happy destinations, during the present Buddha-dispensation he was reborn in Rājagaha as a son of King Bimbisāra. They gave him the name Abhaya. When he came of age, he associated closely with the Nigaṇṭhas. One day, sent by Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta to challenge the Teacher to a debate, he asked a subtle question. Hearing the subtle explanation, he gained faith, went forth under the Teacher, and by directing his knowledge in accordance with his meditation subject, he soon attained arahantship.

195. So arahattaṃ patvā attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

195. Having attained arahantship, he recollected his past kamma and, filled with joy, proclaimed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with the words: “The Victor named Padumuttara….” All of this is easily understood.

Abhayattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Abhaya is concluded.

8. Lomasakaṅgiyattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Lomasakaṅgiya

Aṭṭhamāpadāne [V 2.0263] imamhi bhaddake kappetiādikaṃ āyasmato lomasakaṅgiyattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto kassapassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbatto saddho pasanno ahosi. Aparo candano nāma tassa sahāyo cāsi. Te dvepi satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā pasannamānasā pabbajitvā yāvajīvaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhitvā suparisuddhasīlā tato cutā devaloke nibbattitvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ dibbasukhaṃ anubhaviṃsu. Tesu ayaṃ imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sākiyakule nibbattitvā aparo candano devaputto hutvā tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti. Atha so sakyakulappasādakena kāḷudāyinā ārādhitena bhagavatā sakyarājūnaṃ mānamaddanāya kataṃ vessantaradhammadesanāyaṃ (jā. 2.22.1655 ādayo) pokkharavassaiddhipāṭihāriyaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pabbajitvā majjhimanikāye vuttaṃ bhaddekarattasuttantadesanaṃ sutvā araññavāsaṃ vasanto bhaddekarattasuttantadesanānusāsanaṃ (ma. ni. 3.286 ādayo) saritvā tadanusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasi karitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

The eighth apadāna is that of the Venerable Elder Lomasakaṅgiya, beginning: “In this fortunate eon….” He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and in subsequent existences accumulated meritorious deeds that serve as a basis for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family at the time of the Blessed One Kassapa; he was faithful and confident.
