Burning with what? Burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion; burning with birth, aging, and death, with sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs, I say. The ear is burning, sounds are burning… The nose is burning, odors are burning… The tongue is burning, tastes are burning… The body is burning, tangible objects are burning… The mind is burning, mental phenomena are burning, mind-consciousness is burning, mind-contact is burning, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is burning. Burning with what? Burning with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion; burning with birth, aging, and death, with sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs, and despairs, I say.”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati, yamidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Sotasmimpi nibbindati, saddesupi nibbindati…pe… ghānasmimpi nibbindati, gandhesupi nibbindati…pe… jivhāyapi nibbindati, rasesupi nibbindati…pe… kāyasmimpi nibbindati, phoṭṭhabbesupi nibbindati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati, dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati, manosamphassepi nibbindati, yamidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati[V 2.0281], virāgā vimuccati, vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti, ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti.

“Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, becomes disenchanted with forms, becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness, becomes disenchanted with eye-contact, and with whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. He becomes disenchanted with the ear, becomes disenchanted with sounds… he becomes disenchanted with the nose, becomes disenchanted with odors… he becomes disenchanted with the tongue, becomes disenchanted with tastes… he becomes disenchanted with the body, becomes disenchanted with tangible objects… he becomes disenchanted with the mind, becomes disenchanted with mental phenomena, becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness, becomes disenchanted with mind-contact, and with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. Becoming disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises in him: ‘It is liberated.’ He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”

Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ bhaññamāne tassa bhikkhusahassassa anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu.

And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of that thousand bhikkhus were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.

29. Evaṃ ādittapariyāyadesanaṃ sutvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ sampatto nadīkassapo thero somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ [M 2.0288] pakāsento padumuttarassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Tattha aggaphalanti uttamaphalaṃ, attanā ropitaambarukkhassa ādimhi gahitaphalaṃ vā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

29. Having heard this Discourse on Burning, the Elder Nadīkassapa attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Filled with joy, revealing the story of his own past deeds, he spoke the verses beginning: “The Blessed One Padumuttara….” Herein, ‘aggaphala’ means the supreme fruit, or the first fruit taken from the mango tree he himself had planted. The rest is easily understood.

Nadīkassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Nadīkassapa is complete.

3. Gayākassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gayākassapa

Tatiyāpadāne [P 0.0559] ajinacammavatthohantiādikaṃ āyasmato gayākassapattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ kusalaṃ upacinanto ito ekatiṃsakappe sikhissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbatto viññutaṃ patto nissaraṇajjhāsayatāya gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane assamaṃ māpetvā vanamūlaphalāhāro vasati. Tena ca samayena bhagavā eko adutiyo tassa assamasamīpenāgacchi, so bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito velaṃ olokento manoharāni kolaphalāni satthu upanesi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto nissaraṇajjhāsayatāya gharāvāsaṃ pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā dvīhi tāpasasatehi saddhiṃ gayāya viharati. Gayāya vasanato hissa kassapagottatāya ca gayākassapoti samaññā ahosi. So bhagavato saddhiṃ parisāya ehibhikkhūpasampadaṃ datvā nadīkassapassa vuttanayena ādittapariyāya desanāya ovadiyamāno arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

In the third Apadāna, that of the Venerable Gayākassapa begins: “Wearing a garment of antelope hide….” He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and having accumulated wholesome karma in various existences that served as a supporting condition for liberation, was reborn in a good family in this thirty-first aeon from today, during the time of the Blessed One Sikhī. Having come of age, with an inclination for renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic. He had a hermitage built in a forest region and dwelt there, living on roots and fruits of the forest. On one occasion, the Blessed One, alone and unaccompanied, came to the vicinity of his hermitage. Seeing the Blessed One, with a confident mind, he approached, paid homage, and stood to one side. Seeing it was the proper time, he offered delicious jujube fruits to the Teacher. Through that meritorious deed, he wandered through the round of rebirths among devas and humans. During the dispensation of the present Buddha, he was reborn in a brahmin family. Having come of age, with an inclination for renunciation, he abandoned the household life and went forth as an ascetic, dwelling at Gayā with two hundred ascetics. Because he dwelt at Gayā and was of the Kassapa clan, he received the name Gayākassapa. After the Blessed One gave him and his assembly the “Come, bhikkhu” ordination, he was instructed with the Discourse on Burning in the same way as Nadīkassapa, and was established in arahantship.

35. So arahattaṃ patvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento ajinacammavatthohantiādimāha[V 2.0282]. Tattha ajinacammavatthoti tāpasapabbajitattā ajinacammanivāsanapāvuraṇoti attho. Khāribhāradharoti tāpasakāle tāpasaparikkhāraparipuṇṇakājadharoti attho. Khārikatāpasaparikkhāre pūretvā. Kolaṃ ahāsi assamanti kolaphalaṃ assame pūretvā assame nisinnoti attho. Agopayinti [M 2.0289] pāṭhe kolaphalaṃ pariyesitvā assamaṃ gopesiṃ rakkhinti attho. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

35. Having attained arahantship and being filled with joy, he revealed the story of his past deeds by speaking the verses beginning: “Wearing a garment of antelope hide….” Herein, ‘wearing a garment of antelope hide’ means that because he had gone forth as an ascetic, he wore a lower garment and an upper robe of antelope hide. ‘Bearer of the carrying-pole’: during his time as an ascetic, he was a bearer of a carrying-pole full of the requisites of an ascetic. Having filled the ascetic’s carrying-basket with requisites. ‘I brought jujubes to the hermitage’ means having filled the hermitage with jujube fruits, I sat in the hermitage. In the reading ‘agopayiṃ’ (“I protected”), the meaning is: having searched for jujube fruits, I protected the hermitage, I guarded it. The meaning of the rest is all plain.

Gayākassapattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Gayākassapa is complete.

4. Kimilattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kimila

Catutthāpadāne nibbute kakusandhamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato kimilattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto kakusandhassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto parinibbute satthari [P 0.0560] tassa dhātuyo uddissa salalamālāhi maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā pūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena tāvatiṃsesu uppajjitvā aparāparaṃ devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kapilavatthunagare sakyarājakule nibbattitvā kimiloti tassa nāmaṃ akāsi. So vayappatto bhogasampattiyā pamatto viharati. Tassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ ñatvā saṃvegajananatthaṃ anupiyāyaṃ viharanto satthā paṭhamayobbane ṭhitaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ itthirūpaṃ abhinimminitvā purato dassetvā puna anukkamena yathā jarārogavipattīhi abhibhūtā dissati, tathā akāsi. Taṃ disvā kimilakumāro ativiya saṃvegajāto attano saṃvegaṃ pakāsento bhagavato pākaṭaṃ katvā laddhānusāsano arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

In the fourth Apadāna, the Apadāna of the Venerable Kimila begins with “When Kakusandha was extinguished....” This elder too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated merits in various existences that served as a basis for liberation. During the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha, he was born into a good family and attained understanding. After the Teacher had attained final Nibbāna, he had a pavilion built and decorated with salala garlands in honor of his relics, and he made offerings. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wandering repeatedly among devas and humans, in this Buddha-dispensation, he was born into the Sakyan royal family in the city of Kapilavatthu, and they gave him the name Kimila. Having reached adulthood, he lived heedlessly, indulging in his wealth. Knowing that his knowledge had matured, the Teacher, while dwelling at Anupiyā, created the form of a beautiful young woman in the prime of her youth and displayed it before him in order to inspire a sense of spiritual urgency. Then, gradually, he made her appear as if overcome by aging, sickness, and misfortune. Seeing this, Prince Kimila was greatly stirred. He expressed his spiritual urgency to the Blessed One, and having received instruction, he attained arahantship.

42. So arahattaṃ patvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute kakusandhamhītiādimāha. Brāhmaṇamhi vusīmatīti pañcahi vasitāhi vasippattamhi bhagavati. Brāhmaṇassa sabbaguṇagaṇehi maṇḍitattā abhivūḷhītattā brāhmaṇamhi kakusandhe bhagavati parinibbuteti attho. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ uttānamevāti.

42. Having attained arahantship and being filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his past deeds, beginning with: “When Kakusandha was extinguished….” Herein, “in the brahmin, the master” means in the Blessed One, who had attained mastery through the five masteries. Because he was adorned with all the collections of qualities of a brahmin and was exalted, “in the brahmin” refers to the Blessed One Kakusandha, who had attained final Nibbāna. The rest is all clear.

Kimilattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Kimila is complete.

5. Vajjiputtattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vajjiputta

Sahassaraṃsī [M 2.0290][V 2.0283] bhagavātiādikaṃ āyasmato vajjiputtattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayaṃ puññaṃ upacinanto ito catunavutikappe ekaṃ paccekabuddhaṃ bhikkhāya gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso kadaliphalāni adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde vesāliyaṃ licchavirājakumāro hutvā nibbatti, vajjirājaputtattā vajjiputtotvevassa samaññā. So daharo hutvā hatthisippādisikkhanakālepi hetusampannatāya nissaraṇajjhāsayova hutvā vicaranto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho satthu santike pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ katvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā aparabhāge aciraparinibbute satthari dhammaṃ saṅgāyituṃ saṅketaṃ katvā mahātheresu tattha tattha viharantesu ekadivasaṃ āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ sekhaṃyeva samānaṃ mahatiyā parisāya parivutaṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā tassa uparimaggādhigamāya ussāhaṃ janento –

The Apadāna of the Venerable Vajjiputta begins with “The Blessed One with a thousand rays….” He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas and accumulating merit in various existences as a foundation for liberation, ninety-four aeons ago saw a Paccekabuddha going for alms. With a confident mind, he gave him plantain fruits. By that meritorious deed, wandering among gods and humans, in this Buddha’s dispensation, he was reborn as a Licchavi prince in Vesāli. Being the son of a Vajji king, his designation was Vajjiputta. In his youth, even while learning elephant-craft and other skills, due to his natural capacity, he wandered with a mind inclined toward liberation. Hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, having gained faith, he went forth in the Teacher’s presence. Applying himself to insight meditation, he soon became one endowed with the six super-knowledges. Having attained the six super-knowledges, later, not long after the Teacher’s final Nibbāna, when the great elders had made an agreement to recite the Dhamma and were dwelling in various places, one day he saw the Venerable Ānanda—still a trainee—teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a great assembly. To inspire him to attain the higher path, he spoke this verse:

“Rukkhamūlagahanaṃ [P 0.0561] pasakkiya, nibbānaṃ hadayasmiṃ opiya;

Jhāya gotama mā ca pamādo, kiṃ te biḷibiḷikā karissatī”ti. (theragā. 119) – gāthaṃ abhāsi;

“Having resorted to a thicket at the foot of a tree, placing Nibbāna in your heart, meditate, O Gotama, and be not heedless! What will this chattering do for you?” (Theragāthā 119)

Tattha rukkhamūlagahananti rukkhamūlabhūtaṃ gahanaṃ, gahanañhi atthi, na rukkhamūlaṃ, rukkhamūlañca atthi, na gahanaṃ, tesu rukkhamūlaggahaṇena ṭhānassa chāyāya sampannatāya vātātapaparissayābhāvaṃ dīpeti, gahanaggahaṇena nivātabhāvena vātaparissayābhāvaṃ janasambādhābhāvañca dasseti, tadubhayena ca bhāvanāyogyataṃ. Pasakkiyāti upagantvā. Nibbānaṃ hadayasmiṃ opiyāti “evaṃ mayā paṭipajjitvā nibbānaṃ adhigantabba”nti nibbutiṃ hadaye ṭhapetvā citte katvā. Jhāyāti tilakkhaṇūpanijjhānena jhāya, vipassanābhāvanāsahitaṃ maggabhāvanaṃ bhāvehi. Gotamāti dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ gottenālapati. Mā ca pamādoti adhikusalesu dhammesu mā pamādaṃ āpajji. Idāni yādiso [M 2.0291] therassa pamādo, taṃ paṭikkhepavasena dassento “kiṃ te biḷibiḷikā karissatī”ti āha. Tattha biḷibiḷikāti biḷibiḷikiriyā, biḷibiḷitisaddapavatti yathā niratthakā, evaṃ biḷibiḷikāsadisā janapaññatti. Kiṃ te karissatīti kīdisaṃ atthaṃ tuyhaṃ sādhessati, tasmā janapaññattiṃ pahāya sadatthapasuto hohīti ovādaṃ adāsi.

Here, 'the thicket at the foot of a tree' means a thicket that is at the foot of a tree. For there are places that are thickets but not at the foot of a tree, and places that are at the foot of a tree but not thickets. By mentioning 'the foot of a tree,' it indicates the absence of the danger of wind and sun due to the place being endowed with shade. By mentioning 'thicket,' it shows the absence of the danger of wind due to being sheltered, and the absence of crowding by people. Both together signify its suitability for meditative cultivation. 'Having resorted to' means having approached. 'Having placed Nibbāna in the heart' means having established quiescence in the heart, having resolved in one's mind, 'By practicing thus, I shall attain Nibbāna.' 'Meditate' means to contemplate with the close scrutiny of the three characteristics; to cultivate the path-cultivation accompanied by the cultivation of insight. 'Gotama': he addresses the Treasurer of the Dhamma by his clan name. 'And be not heedless' means do not fall into heedlessness regarding the higher wholesome states. Now, to show the kind of heedlessness the elder had by way of refuting it, he said, 'What will this chattering do for you?' Here, 'chattering' (biḷibiḷikā) refers to the act of chattering; just as the utterance of the sound 'bili-bili' is meaningless, so too is popular talk, which is like chattering. 'What will it do for you?' means what kind of benefit will it accomplish for you? Therefore, he gave the advice: 'Abandoning popular talk, be intent on your own true welfare.'

Taṃ [V 2.0284] sutvā aññehi vuttena vissagandhavāyanavacanena saṃvegajāto bahudeva rattiṃ caṅkamena vītināmento vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā mañcake nisinnamattova “kiñci sayāmī”ti sīsaṃ bimbohanamasampattaṃ pādaṃ bhūmito uggataṃ sarīrassa ākāsagatakkhaṇeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Hearing that, stirred by the words spoken by another—words carrying the stench of the defilements—and filled with urgency, he spent much of the night in walking meditation. Having intensified his insight practice, he entered his dwelling. Just as he was about to lie down, thinking, 'I will rest a little,' with his head not yet having reached the pillow and his feet having lifted from the ground, in that very moment, he attained Arahantship.

49. Vajjiputtatthero aparabhāge somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sahassaraṃsī bhagavātiādimāha. Tattha sahassaraṃsīti ettha “anekasatasahassaraṃsī”ti vattabbe gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ “sahassaraṃsī”ti vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

49. Later, the Elder Vajjiputta, filled with joy, revealed the apadāna of his own past deeds, speaking, beginning with: 'The Blessed One, radiant with a thousand rays...' Here, it should be understood that 'radiant with a thousand rays' is said for the sake of metrical convenience, when 'radiant with countless hundreds of thousands of rays' should have been said. The rest is easily understood.

Vajjiputtattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Vajjiputta is finished.

6. Uttarattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uttara

Chaṭṭhāpadāne sumedho nāma sambuddhotiādikaṃ āyasmato uttarasāmaṇerassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro [P 0.0562] tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto sumedhassa bhagavato kāle vijjādharo hutvā ākāsena vicarati. Tena ca samayena satthā tasseva anuggaṇhanatthaṃ vanantare aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi chabbaṇṇabuddharaṃsiyo vissajjento. So antalikkhena gacchanto bhagavantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso ākāsato oruyha suvisuddhehi vipulehi kaṇikārapupphehi bhagavantaṃ pūjesi, pupphāni buddhānubhāvena satthu upari chattākārena aṭṭhaṃsu, so tena bhiyyosomattāya pasannacitto hutvā aparabhāge kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsesu nibbattitvā dibbasampattiṃ anubhavanto yāvatāyukaṃ tattha ṭhatvā tato cuto devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇamahāsālassa putto hutvā [M 2.0292] nibbatti, uttarotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇavijjāsu nipphattiṃ gantvā jātiyā rūpena vijjāya vayena sīlācārena ca lokassa sambhāvanīyo jāto.

In the sixth Apadāna is the apadāna of the Venerable novice Uttara, beginning with 'The Self-Enlightened One named Sumedha.' He too, having made his aspiration under former Buddhas and accumulating merits here and there as a supporting condition for liberation, became a knowledge-holder during the time of the Blessed One Sumedha and wandered through the sky. At that time, the Teacher, in order to favor him, sat down at the foot of a certain tree in a forest grove, emitting the six-hued Buddha-rays. As he was passing through the sky, he saw the Blessed One and, with a confident mind, descended from the sky and honored the Blessed One with very pure and abundant kaṇikāra flowers. By the Buddha's power, the flowers stood above the Teacher in the form of a canopy. Because of this, with his mind confident and with even greater gladness, he later passed away and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There he enjoyed divine fortune for his entire lifespan. Having passed away from there, he wandered among devas and humans. During the advent of this Buddha, he was reborn in Rājagaha as the son of a very wealthy brahmin, and his name was Uttara. Having reached maturity and attained proficiency in the brahminical sciences, he became esteemed by the world for his birth, beauty, knowledge, age, and virtuous conduct.

Tassa taṃ sampattiṃ disvā vassakāro magadhamahāmatto attano dhītaraṃ dātukāmo hutvā attano adhippāyaṃ pavedesi. So nissaraṇajjhāsayatāya taṃ paṭikkhipitvā kālena kālaṃ dhammasenāpatiṃ payirupāsanto tassa santike dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vattasampanno hutvā theraṃ upaṭṭhahati.

Seeing his good fortune, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, wished to give him his daughter in marriage and so made his intention known. But he, being inclined to renunciation, rejected the offer. From time to time, he attended upon the General of the Dhamma, and after hearing the Dhamma from him, he gained faith. He then went forth, became accomplished in the monastic duties, and attended upon the Elder.

Tena [V 2.0285] ca samayena therassa aññataro ābādho uppanno, tassa bhesajjatthāya uttaro sāmaṇero pātova pattacīvaramādāya vihārato nikkhanto antarāmagge taḷākassa samīpe pattaṃ ṭhapetvā udakasamīpaṃ gantvā mukhaṃ dhovati. Atha aññataro umaṅgacoro katakammo ārakkhapurisehi anubaddho aggamaggena nagarato nikkhamitvā palāyanto attanā gahitaṃ ratanabhaṇḍitaṃ sāmaṇerassa patte pakkhipitvā palāyi. Sāmaṇeropi pattasamīpaṃ upagato. Coraṃ anubandhantā rājapurisā sāmaṇerassa patte bhaṇḍikaṃ disvā “ayaṃ coro, iminā coriyaṃ kata”nti sāmaṇeraṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā vassakārassa brāhmaṇassa dassesuṃ. Vassakāro ca tadā rañño vinicchaye niyutto hutvā chejjabhejjaṃ anusāsati, so “pubbe mama vacanaṃ nādiyi, suddhapāsaṇḍiyesu pabbajī”ti (theragā. aṭṭha. 1.uttarattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) kammaṃ asodhetvā ghātukāmattāva jīvantameva taṃ sūle uttāsesi.

At that time, a certain affliction had arisen in the elder. To get medicine for him, the novice Uttara took his bowl and robe early in the morning and left the monastery. On the way, he placed his bowl near a pond and, going to the water's edge, washed his face. Just then, a housebreaker who had committed a theft was being pursued by guards. Fleeing from the city by the main road, he placed the bundle of jewels he had taken into the novice's bowl and ran away. The novice then approached his bowl. The king's men, who were chasing the thief, saw the bundle in the novice's bowl and thought, 'This is the thief! He committed the theft!' They bound the novice’s hands behind his back and brought him before Vassakāra the brahmin. At that time, Vassakāra had been appointed by the king to pass judgment and was prescribing punishments involving mutilation and execution. Thinking, 'Formerly, he did not accept my word but went forth among these worthless ascetics,' without investigating the case and out of a desire to kill him, he had him impaled alive on a stake.

Athassa bhagavā ñāṇaparipākaṃ oloketvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā vipphurantahatthanakhamaṇimayūkhasambhinnasitābhatāya paggharantajātihiṅgulakasuvaṇṇarasadhāraṃ viya jālāguṇṭhitamudutalunadīghaṅgulihatthaṃ uttarassa sīse ṭhapetvā “uttara, idaṃ te purimakammassa [P 0.0563] phalaṃ uppannaṃ, tattha tayā paccavekkhaṇabalena adhivāsanā kātabbā”ti vatvā ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desesi. Uttaro amatābhisekasadisena satthu hatthasamphassena sañjātappasādasomanassatāya uḷārapītipāmojjaṃ paṭilabhitvā yathāparicitaṃ vipassanāmaggaṃ samārūḷho ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā satthu ca desanāvilāsena tāvadeva maggapaṭipāṭiyā sabbe kilese khepetvā chaḷabhiñño [M 2.0293] ahosi. Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā sūlato uṭṭhahitvā parānuddayāya ākāse ṭhatvā pāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. Mahājano acchariyabbhutacittajāto ahosi. Tāvadevassa vaṇo saṃrūḷhi, so bhikkhūhi, “āvuso, tādisadukkhaṃ anubhavanto kathaṃ tvaṃ vipassanaṃ anuyuñjituṃ asakkhī”ti puṭṭho, “pageva me, āvuso, saṃsāre ādīnavo, saṅkhārānañca sabhāvo sudiṭṭho, evāhaṃ tādisaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavantopi asakkhiṃ vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā visesaṃ adhigantu”nti āha. “Pubbajātiyā daharakāle makkhikaṃ gahetvā nimbasūlakaṃ gahetvā sūlāropanakīḷaṃ paṭicca evaṃ anekajātisatesu sūlāropanadukkhamanubhavitvā imāya pariyosānajātiyā evarūpaṃ dukkhamanubhūta”nti āha.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving the maturity of his knowledge, went to that place. He placed on Uttara's head his soft, tender, long-fingered hand—veiled in a net of rays, shining with a white luster suffused with beams from his jeweled fingernails, like a flowing stream of molten gold and pure vermillion—and said: “Uttara, this is the fruit of your past kamma that has now arisen. You must endure it with the power of reflective patience.” Then he taught him the Dhamma appropriate to his disposition. Through the Teacher's touch, which was like an anointing with the deathless, confidence and gladness arose in Uttara, and he attained sublime rapture and joy. Having mounted the path of insight with which he was familiar, and because his knowledge had reached maturity, through the grace of the Teacher's teaching he immediately, by the sequence of the path, eradicated all defilements and became endowed with the six direct knowledges. Having attained the six direct knowledges, he rose from the stake and, standing in the air out of compassion for others, displayed a psychic feat. The great crowd was struck with amazement and wonder. Instantly, his wound healed. When the bhikkhus asked him, “Friend, how were you able to practice insight while enduring such suffering?” he replied, “Friends, the danger in saṃsāra has long been clear to me, and the nature of formations is well seen. Thus, even while enduring such pain, I was able to develop insight and attain a special distinction.” He further explained, “In a past life, when I was a boy, I caught a fly and, taking a neem thorn, played the game of impalement. Because of that, for many hundreds of births I endured the suffering of being impaled, and in this final life, I have experienced such suffering.”

55. Atha aparabhāge pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento sumedho nāma sambuddhotiādimāha. Tattha anuttānapadavaṇṇanameva karissāma.

55. Then, at a later time, recalling his past deeds and becoming joyful, he revealed the apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with the words: 'The Self-Enlightened One named Sumedha…' Therein, we shall provide a commentary only on the words whose meaning is not obvious.

57. Vijjādharo tadā āsinti bāhirakamantādivijjāsiddhiyā ākāsagāmisamattho hutvā caraṇavasena taṃ vijjaṃ rakkhitvā avināsetvā pariharaṇavasena vijjādharayoni āsiṃ ahosinti [V 2.0286] attho. Antalikkhacaro ahanti antaṃ pariyosānaṃ koṭiṃ likhate saṃkarissatīti antalikkhaṃ. Atha vā antaṃ pariyosānaṃ likhyate olokiyate etenāti antalikkhaṃ, tasmiṃ antalikkhe, ākāse caraṇasīlo ahanti attho. Tisūlaṃ sukataṃ gayhāti tikhiṇaṃ sūlaṃ, aggaṃ āvudhaṃ. Tisūlaṃ sundaraṃ kataṃ, koṭṭanaghaṃsanamaddanapaharaṇavasena suṭṭhu kataṃ sūlāvudhaṃ gayha gahetvā ambarato gacchāmīti attho. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattāva nayānuyogena suviññeyyamevāti.

57. 'At that time I was a knowledge-holder' (`vijjādharo tadā āsiṃ`): The meaning is this: having become capable of traveling through the sky by perfecting external knowledge such as spells, by means of practice I protected that knowledge, and by maintaining it without letting it perish, I was of the knowledge-holder class. 'I was a sky-farer' (`antalikkhacaro ahaṃ`): `Antalikkha` is so called because one marks (`likhate`) or gathers (`saṃkarissati`) the end (`antaṃ`), the limit, the edge. Or, it is `antalikkha` because the end or limit is marked or seen by means of it. The meaning is: 'In that `antalikkha`, the sky, I was one accustomed to travel.' 'Taking a well-made trident' (`tisūlaṃ sukataṃ gayha`): a sharp spear, a pointed weapon. 'A trident beautifully made' means a spear-weapon well-made for pounding, rubbing, crushing, and striking. The meaning is: 'Having taken this, I go through the sky.' All the rest is to be easily understood by applying the method in accordance with the principles stated previously.

Uttarattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Uttara is complete.

7. Aparauttarattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Apara-Uttara

Sattamāpadāne [M 2.0294] nibbute lokanāthamhītiādikaṃ āyasmato aparassa uttarattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu [P 0.0564] katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto ito catunnavutikappe siddhatthassa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā vayappatto viññutaṃ patvā sāsane laddhappasādo hutvā upāsakattaṃ nivedesi. So satthari parinibbute attano ñātake sannipātetvā bahupūjāsakkāraṃ saṃharitvā dhātupūjaṃ akāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sākete brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā uttaroti laddhanāmo vayappatto kenacideva karaṇīyena sāvatthiṃ gato kaṇḍambamūle kataṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ disvā pasīditvā puna kāḷakārāmasuttadesanāya abhivaḍḍhamānasaddho pabbajitvā satthārā saddhiṃ rājagahaṃ gantvā upasampadaṃ labhitvā tatheva caranto vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nacirasseva chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Chaḷabhiñño pana hutvā satthari sāvatthiyaṃ viharante buddhupaṭṭhānatthaṃ rājagahato sāvatthiṃ upagato bhikkhūhi – “kiṃ, āvuso, pabbajjākiccaṃ tayā matthakaṃ pāpita”nti puṭṭho aññaṃ byākāsi.

The seventh Apadāna, which begins, 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna...,' is the Apadāna of the venerable Elder Apara-Uttara. He too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulated in various existences merits that served as a basis for liberation. Ninety-four aeons ago, during the time of the Blessed One Siddhattha, he was born into a good family. Having reached maturity and gained understanding, he acquired faith in the Dispensation and declared himself a lay follower. After the Teacher’s Parinibbāna, he gathered his relatives, collected many offerings and honors, and performed a pūjā to the relics. By that meritorious deed, he wandered among devas and humans until, in this Buddha-era, he was reborn in a brahmin family in Sāketa and was named Uttara. When he came of age, he went to Sāvatthī on some business and, seeing the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, he was filled with confidence. Later, his faith having grown upon hearing the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, he went forth. Traveling with the Teacher to Rājagaha, he received the higher ordination. Practicing diligently, he developed insight and soon attained the six higher knowledges. Having attained the six higher knowledges, while the Teacher was dwelling at Sāvatthī, he went from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī to attend upon the Buddha. When the bhikkhus asked him, 'Friend, have you brought the goal of the homeless life to fulfillment?' he declared final knowledge.

93. Arahattaṃ pana patvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento nibbute lokanāthamhītiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānatthamevāti.

93. Having attained Arahantship and being filled with joy, he declared the apadāna of his past deeds, beginning with 'When the Lord of the World had attained Nibbāna....' All of this has a plain meaning because of the method explained above.

Aparauttarattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Apara-Uttara is complete.

8. Bhaddajittheraapadānavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhaddajit

Aṭṭhamāpadāne [V 2.0287] ogayhāhaṃ pokkharaṇintiādikaṃ āyasmato bhaddajittherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto brāhmaṇānaṃ vijjāsippesu pāraṃ gantvā kāme pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā araññāyatane assamaṃ [M 2.0295] kāretvā vasanto ekadivasaṃ satthāraṃ ākāsena gacchantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi. Satthā tassa ajjhāsayaṃ disvā ākāsato otari. Otiṇṇassa pana bhagavato madhuñca bhisamuḷālañca sappikhīrañca upanāmesi, tassa taṃ bhagavā anukammaṃ upādāya paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. So tena puññakammena tusitesu nibbatto tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto aparāparaṃ sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto vipassissa bhagavato kāle mahaddhano seṭṭhi hutvā aṭṭhasaṭṭhibhikkhusatasahassaṃ bhojetvā ticīvarena acchādesi.

In the Eighth Apadāna is the apadāna of the venerable Elder Bhaddajit, beginning with 'Having plunged into the lotus pond....' This elder too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas, accumulating in various existences merits that are a basis for liberation, was reborn in a brahmin family during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having attained understanding and mastered the brahminical sciences and arts, he renounced sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life. Dwelling in a hermitage in a forest abode, one day he saw the Teacher passing through the sky. With a serene mind, he raised his joined hands in reverence and stood there. The Teacher, perceiving his inclination, descended from the sky. When the Blessed One had alighted, he offered him honey, lotus-fibres and stalks, and ghee with milk. The Blessed One, out of compassion for him, accepted it, and after giving his blessing, he departed. By that meritorious deed, he was reborn in the Tusita realm, where he remained for his full lifespan. After passing away from there, he continued wandering only in happy destinations. During the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, he became a wealthy merchant. He fed sixty-eight hundred thousand bhikkhus and clothed them with the triple robe.

Evaṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ [P 0.0565] katvā devaloke nibbatti. Tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cavitvā manussalokesu uppanno buddhasuññe loke pañca paccekabuddhasatāni catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahitvā tato cuto rājakule nibbattitvā rajjaṃ anusāsanto attano puttaṃ paccekabodhiṃ adhigantvā ṭhitaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā tassa parinibbutassa dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ katvā pūjesi. Evaṃ tattha tattha tāni tāni puññāni katvā imasmiṃ buddhuppāde bhaddiyanagare asītikoṭivibhavassa bhaddiyaseṭṭhissa ekaputtako hutvā nibbatti, bhaddajītissa nāmaṃ ahosi. Tassa kira issariyabhogaparivārasampatti carimabhave bodhisattassa viya ahosi.

Having performed much merit, he was reborn in a deva world. Having lived there for his full lifespan, he passed away and was reborn in the human world at a time when the world was devoid of a Buddha. There, he attended upon five hundred Paccekabuddhas with the four requisites. After passing away from there, he was reborn in a royal family. While ruling the kingdom, he attended upon his son, who had realized the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. After his son’s Parinibbāna, he collected the relics, built a cetiya, and paid homage to it. Having thus performed various meritorious deeds in life after life, in this Buddha-era he was reborn in the city of Bhaddiya as the only son of the seṭṭhi Bhaddiya, who possessed a fortune of eighty crores. His name was Bhaddajit. It is said that his fortune, possessions, and retinue were like those of the Bodhisatta in his final existence.

Tadā satthā sāvatthiyaṃ vasitvā bhaddajikumāraṃ saṅgaṇhanatthāya mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ bhaddiyanagaraṃ gantvā jātiyāvane vasi tassa ñāṇaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno. Sopi uparipāsāde nisinno sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokento bhagavato santike dhammaṃ sotuṃ gacchantaṃ mahājanaṃ disvā, “katthāyaṃ mahājano gacchatī”ti pucchitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā sayampi mahatā parivārena satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanto sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍitova sabbakilese khepetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahatte pana tena adhigate satthā bhaddiyaseṭṭhiṃ āmantesi – “tava putto alaṅkatapaṭiyatto dhammaṃ suṇanto arahatte patiṭṭhāsi, tenassa idāneva pabbajituṃ yuttaṃ, no ce pabbajissati, parinibbāyissatī”ti. Seṭṭhi “na mayhaṃ puttassa daharasseva sato parinibbānena kiccaṃ [V 2.0288] atthi, pabbājetha na”nti āha. Taṃ satthā pabbājetvā upasampādetvā tattha sattāhaṃ vasitvā koṭigāmaṃ pāpuṇi, so ca gāmo gaṅgātīre ahosi[M 2.0296]. Koṭigāmavāsino ca buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ pavattesuṃ. Bhaddajitthero satthārā anumodanāya āraddhamattāya bahigāmaṃ gantvā “gaṅgātīre maggasamīpe satthu āgatakāle vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti kālaparicchedaṃ katvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā nisīdi. Mahātheresu āgacchantesupi avuṭṭhahitvā satthu āgatakāleyeva vuṭṭhāsi. Puthujjanā bhikkhū – “ayaṃ adhunā pabbajito, mahātheresu āgacchantesu mānathaddho hutvā na vuṭṭhāsī”ti ujjhāyiṃsu.

At that time, the Teacher, after dwelling at Sāvatthī, went to the city of Bhaddiya with a large community of bhikkhus in order to win over the youth Bhaddajit, and he stayed in the Jātiyā Grove, awaiting the maturing of his knowledge. Seated in the upper palace, Bhaddajit opened a lion-window and looked out. Seeing a great crowd going to hear the Dhamma from the Blessed One, he asked, 'Where is this great crowd going?' Upon hearing the reason, he too went to the Teacher with a large retinue. While listening to the Dhamma, though still adorned with all his ornaments, he eradicated all defilements and attained Arahantship. When he had attained Arahantship, the Teacher addressed the seṭṭhi Bhaddiya: 'Your son, while adorned and attired, listened to the Dhamma and has become established in Arahantship. It is fitting for him to go forth right now. If he does not go forth, he will attain Parinibbāna.' The seṭṭhi replied, 'My son has no need for Parinibbāna while still so young. Please give him the going-forth.' The Teacher gave him the going-forth and the higher ordination. After staying there for seven days, he reached Koṭigāma, a village on the banks of the Ganges. The villagers of Koṭigāma held a great almsgiving for the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. As soon as the Teacher began the blessing, the Elder Bhaddajit went outside the village. Thinking, 'I will rise when the Teacher arrives at the road near the bank of the Ganges,' he made a determination of time, sat down at the foot of a certain tree, and entered an attainment. Even when the great elders arrived, he did not rise; he rose only when the Teacher arrived. The worldling bhikkhus grumbled, 'This newly ordained one, stiff with conceit, did not rise when the great elders arrived.'

Koṭigāmavāsino satthu bhikkhusaṅghassa ca bahū nāvāsaṅghāṭe bandhiṃsu. Satthā “bhaddajissānubhāvaṃ pakāsemī”ti nāvāya ṭhatvā “kahaṃ bhaddajī”ti pucchi. Bhaddajitthero – “sohaṃ, bhante”ti satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā añjaliṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi. Satthā “ehi, bhaddaji, amhehi saddhiṃ ekanāvaṃ abhiruhā”ti. So uppatitvā satthu ṭhitanāvāyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Satthā gaṅgāya majjhe gatakāle, “bhaddaji, tayā mahāpanādakāle ajjhāvuṭṭharatanapāsādo [P 0.0566] kaha”nti āha. “Imasmiṃ ṭhāne nimuggo, bhante”ti. “Tena hi, bhaddaji, sabrahmacārīnaṃ kaṅkhaṃ chindā”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe thero satthāraṃ vanditvā iddhibalena gantvā pāsādathūpikaṃ pādaṅgulantarena sannirujjhitvā pañcavīsatiyojanaṃ pāsādaṃ gahetvā ākāse uppati, uppatanto ca paññāsayojanāni ukkhipi. Athassa purimabhave ñātakā pāsādagatena lobhena macchakacchapamaṇḍūkā hutvā nibbattā tasmiṃ pāsāde uṭṭhahante parivattitvā patiṃsu. Satthā te sampatante disvā “ñātakā te, bhaddaji, kilamantī”ti āha. Thero satthu vacanena pāsādaṃ vissajjesi. Pāsādo yathāṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhahi. Satthā pāraṅgato bhikkhūhi – “kadā, bhante, bhaddajittherena ayaṃ pāsādo ajjhāvuṭṭho”ti puṭṭho mahāpanādajātakaṃ (jā. 1.3.40 ādayo) kathetvā bahujanaṃ dhammāmataṃ pāyesi.

The residents of Koṭigāma fastened together many rafts of boats for the Teacher and the community of bhikkhus. The Teacher, thinking, 'I will reveal Bhaddajit’s spiritual power,' stood on a boat and asked, 'Where is Bhaddajit?' The Elder Bhaddajit replied, 'Here I am, venerable sir,' approached the Teacher, paid homage with joined palms, and stood there. The Teacher said, 'Come, Bhaddajit, board this one boat with us.' He leapt up and stood on the Teacher’s boat. When they reached the middle of the Ganges, the Teacher asked, 'Bhaddajit, where is the jeweled palace you inhabited during the time of Mahāpanāda?' 'It is sunk in this very spot, venerable sir,' he replied. 'Then, Bhaddajit, dispel the doubt of your companions in the holy life.' At that moment, the elder paid homage to the Teacher and, going by means of spiritual power, he seized the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, lifted the twenty-five-yojana-long palace, and rose into the sky. As he rose, he lifted it fifty yojanas high. Then his relatives from a past life—who, because of greed connected with that palace, had been reborn as fish, turtles, and frogs—tumbled out of the rising palace and fell. Seeing them falling, the Teacher said, 'Bhaddajit, your relatives are in distress.' At the Teacher’s word, the elder released the palace, and it settled back in its original place. After crossing to the far shore, the bhikkhus asked the Teacher, 'Venerable sir, when did the Elder Bhaddajit inhabit this palace?' The Teacher then narrated the Mahāpanāda Jātaka (Jā 1.3.40ff) and made the large crowd drink the deathless nectar of the Dhamma.

98. Thero pana arahattaṃ patto pubbasambhāraṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsetuṃ ogayhāhaṃ pokkharaṇintiādimāha. Tattha ogayhāhaṃ pokkharaṇinti puthunānāanekamahoghehi khaṇitattā “pokkharaṇī”ti laddhanāmaṃ jalāsayaṃ ogayha ogahetvā pavisitvā ajjhogāhetvā ghāsahetukhādanatthāya tattha pokkharaṇiyaṃ pavisitvā [M 2.0297] bhisaṃ padumapuṇḍarīkamūlaṃ uddharāmīti attho. Sesaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayattā uttānapadatthattā ca nayānusārena suviññeyyamevāti.

98. The elder, however, having attained Arahantship, recollected his accumulation of merit, and filled with joy, he began to proclaim the apadāna of his past deeds, saying, 'Having plunged into the lotus pond....' Therein, 'Having plunged into the lotus pond' means: having entered, plunged into, and submerged myself in the reservoir named 'Pokkharaṇī' because it was dug by the great and diverse efforts of many people; having entered that Pokkharaṇī for the sake of getting food to eat, 'I pull up lotus-stalks and the roots of red and white lotuses'—this is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand in accordance with the method, because the method has been stated above and the meaning of the words is plain.

Bhaddajittheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Bhaddajit is complete.

9. Sivakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sivaka

Navamāpadāne [V 2.0289] esanāya carantassātiādikaṃ āyasmato sivakattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto vipassissa bhagavato kāle kulagehe nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā pasannamānaso pattaṃ ādāya kummāsassa pūretvā adāsi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde rājagahe brāhmaṇakulagehe nibbattitvā sivakotissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So vayappatto vijjāsippesu nipphattiṃ gato nekkhammajjhāsayatāya kāme pahāya tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā vicaranto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto nacirasseva arahattaṃ [P 0.0567] pāpuṇi.

In the ninth Apadāna is the story of the Venerable Elder Sivaka, which begins: 'While wandering for alms…' This one too, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for turning away from the round of rebirth, was reborn in a good family in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached maturity, one day he saw the Blessed One wandering for alms-food. With a confident mind, he took his bowl, filled it with barley-meal, and gave it to him. By that meritorious deed, while transmigrating among devas and human beings, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn into a brahmin family in Rājagaha and was named Sivakoti. When he came of age, he attained proficiency in knowledge and crafts. Due to his inclination for renunciation, he abandoned sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life. While wandering, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and gained faith. He went forth and, while undertaking the practice of insight, before long he attained arahantship.

117. Arahattaṃ patvā somanassajāto attano pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento esanāya carantassātiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ suviññeyyamevāti.

117. Having attained arahantship, filled with joy, he disclosed the apadāna of his own former conduct, speaking the verses beginning: 'While wandering for alms…' All that is easily understood.

Sivakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Sivaka is complete.

10. Upavānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upavāna

Dasamāpadāne padumuttaro nāma jinotiādikaṃ āyasmato upavānattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayaṃ kira purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto kenaci kammacchiddena padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle dalliddakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto bhagavati parinibbute tassa dhātuṃ gahetvā manussadevanāgagaruḷayakkhakumbhaṇḍagandhabbehi sattaratanamaye sattayojanike thūpe kate [M 2.0298] tattha sudhotaṃ attano uttarāsaṅgaṃ veḷagge ābandhitvā dhajaṃ katvā pūjaṃ akāsi. Taṃ gahetvā abhisammatako nāma yakkhasenāpati devehi cetiyapūjārakkhaṇatthaṃ ṭhapito adissamānakāyo ākāse dhārento cetiyaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. Taṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya pasannamānaso ahosi. So tena puññakammena devamanussesu saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā upavānoti laddhanāmo vayappatto jetavanapaṭiggahaṇe buddhānubhāvaṃ disvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvā vipassanāya kammaṃ karonto chaḷabhiñño ahosi. Athāyasmā upavāno bhagavato upaṭṭhāko ahosi[V 2.0290]. Tena ca samayena bhagavato vātābādho uppajji. Therassa gihisahāyo devahito nāma brāhmaṇo sāvatthiyaṃ paṭivasati. So theraṃ catūhi paccayehi pavāresi. Athāyasmā upavāno nivāsetvā pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā tassa brāhmaṇassa nivesanaṃ upagañchi. Brāhmaṇo “kenaci maññe payojanena thero āgato bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “vadeyyātha, bhante, kenattho”ti āha. Thero tassa brāhmaṇassa payojanaṃ ācikkhanto –

In the tenth Apadāna is the story of the Venerable Elder Upavāna, which begins: 'The Victor named Padumuttara…' It is said that this one, having made his aspiration under previous Buddhas and accumulating in various existences merits that serve as a basis for turning away from the round of rebirth, due to some flaw in his kamma was reborn into a poor family in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached maturity, after the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, he took a relic. When a stūpa seven yojanas high and made of the seven kinds of gems was built by humans, devas, nāgas, garuḷas, yakkhas, kumbhaṇḍas, and gandhabbas, he tied his own well-washed upper robe to its pinnacle, making it a banner, and performed an act of worship. A yakkha general named Abhisammataka, appointed by the devas to guard the worship at the cetiya, took it and, becoming invisible, held it in the sky while circumambulating the cetiya three times. Seeing this, his mind became even more confident and joyful. Through that meritorious deed, while transmigrating among devas and human beings, during this Buddha-dispensation he was reborn into a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named Upavāna. When he came of age, he witnessed the Buddha’s spiritual power at the dedication of the Jeta’s Grove and gained faith. He went forth and, while undertaking the practice of insight, attained the six direct knowledges. Then the Venerable Upavāna became the Blessed One’s attendant. At that time, an ailment caused by wind arose in the Blessed One. The elder’s lay friend, a brahmin named Devahita, was living in Sāvatthī. He had invited the elder with an offer of the four requisites. Then the Venerable Upavāna, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, went to that brahmin’s residence. The brahmin, realizing, 'I suppose the elder has come for some purpose,' said: 'Speak, venerable sir, what is your need?' The elder, explaining his purpose to the brahmin, said:

“Arahaṃ sugato loke, vātehābādhiko muni;

Sace uṇhodakaṃ atthi, munino dehi brāhmaṇa.

“The Arahant, the Sugata in the world, the sage is afflicted by wind; if there is hot water, brahmin, give it to the sage.

“Pūjito pūjaneyyānaṃ, sakkareyyāna sakkato;

Apacitopaceyyānaṃ, tassa icchāmi hātave”ti. (theragā. 185-186) –

“Honored by the honorable, respected by the respectable, revered by the reverend—for him I wish to bring it.”

Gāthādvayaṃ abhāsi.

He spoke this pair of verses.

Tassattho – yo imasmiṃ loke pūjaneyyānaṃ pūjetabbehi sakkādīhi devehi mahābrahmādīhi ca brahmehi pūjito, sakkareyyānaṃ sakkātabbehi bimbisārakosalarājādīhi sakkato, apaceyyānaṃ apacāyitabbehi mahesīhi khīṇāsavehi apacito, kilesehi [P 0.0568] ārakattādinā arahaṃ, sobhanagamanādinā sugato sabbaññū muni mayhaṃ satthā devadevo sakkānaṃ atisakko brahmānaṃ atibrahmā, so dāni vātehi vātahetu vātakkhobhanimittaṃ ābādhiko jāto. Sace[M 2.0299], brāhmaṇa, uṇhodakaṃ atthi, tassa vātābādhavūpasamanatthaṃ taṃ hātave upanetuṃ icchāmīti.

Its meaning is as follows: He who in this world is honored by the honorable—by devas such as Sakka and by brahmās such as Mahābrahmā; who is respected by the respectable—by kings such as Bimbisāra and the king of Kosala; who is revered by the reverend—by great sages who are arahants; he is the Arahant because he is far from the defilements, the Sugata because of his sublime going, the Omniscient One, the Sage, my Teacher, the deva of devas, the Sakka beyond the Sakkas, the Brahmā beyond the Brahmās. He is now afflicted by an ailment due to the winds, with wind as its cause, with the disturbance of wind as its sign. If, brahmin, there is hot water, I wish to bring it, to offer it, for the purpose of pacifying his wind ailment.

Taṃ sutvā brāhmaṇo uṇhodakaṃ tadanurūpaṃ vātaharañca bhesajjaṃ bhagavato upanāmesi. Tena ca satthu rogo vūpasami. Tassa bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsi.

Hearing this, the brahmin brought the Blessed One hot water and a suitable medicine for dispelling the wind. And with that, the Teacher’s illness was pacified. The Blessed One gave a blessing in appreciation.

122. Athāyasmā upavāno aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttaro nāma jinotiādimāha. Tattha padumuttarotiādīni pubbe vuttatthāneva.

122. Then, at a later time, the Venerable Upavāna, recollecting his own past kamma, became filled with joy and disclosed the apadāna of his past conduct, speaking the verses beginning: 'The Victor named Padumuttara…' Therein, 'Padumuttara' and so on have the same meaning as stated before.

123. Mahājanā samāgammāti sakalajambudīpavāsino rāsibhūtāti attho. Citakaṃ katvāti yojanubbedhaṃ candanarāsicitakaṃ katvā bhagavato sarīraṃ tattha abhiropayiṃsūti sambandho.

123. ‘A great multitude having gathered’: the meaning is that the inhabitants of all Jambudīpa assembled in a crowd. ‘Having made a pyre’: the connection is that they made a pyre from a heap of sandalwood one yojana high and placed the Blessed One’s body upon it.

124. Sarīrakiccaṃ [V 2.0291] katvānāti ādahanāti agginā dahanakiccaṃ katvāti attho.

124. ‘Having performed the rites for the body’ means cremation; the meaning is, having performed the task of burning with fire.

127-28. Jaṅghā maṇimayā āsīti manussehi katathūpe jaṅghā pupphavāhatthaṃ caritaṭṭhānaṃ maṇimayā indanīlamaṇinā katāti attho. Mayampīti sabbe devā thūpaṃ karissāmāti attho.

‘The shanks were made of gems’: the meaning is that in the stūpa made by humans, the ‘shanks’ refers to the walkway for offering flowers, and ‘made of gems’ means made of sapphire. ‘We too’: the meaning is, ‘All we devas will also make a stūpa.’

129. Dhātu āveṇikā natthīti devamanussehi visuṃ visuṃ cetiyaṃ kātuṃ āveṇikā visuṃ dhātu natthi, taṃ dassento sarīraṃ ekapiṇḍitanti āha. Adhiṭṭhānabalena sakalasarīradhātu ekaghanasilāmayapaṭimā viya ekameva ahosīti attho. Imamhi buddhathūpamhīti sakalajambudīpavāsīhi katamhi imamhi suvaṇṇathūpamhi mayaṃ sabbe samāgantvā kañcukathūpaṃ karissāmāti attho.

129. ‘There are no separate relics’: this means there are no distinct relics for devas and humans to build separate cetiyas. To show this, he said: ‘The body was a single mass.’ The meaning is that by the power of his resolution, all the bodily relics became a single unit, like an image carved from a single solid block of stone. ‘In this Buddha-stūpa’: the meaning is, ‘Over this golden stūpa made by all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, we will all gather and build a casing-stūpa.’

133. Indanīlaṃ mahānīlanti indīvarapupphavaṇṇābhaṃ maṇi indanīlamaṇi. Tato adhikavaṇṇatā mahāmaṇi indanīlamaṇayo ca mahānīlamaṇayo ca jotirasamaṇijātiraṅgamaṇayo ca ekato sannipātetvā rāsī katvā suvaṇṇathūpe kañcukathūpaṃ katvā achādayunti sambandho.

133. ‘Sapphire, great blue gem’: a sapphire is a gem with the color and luster of a blue lotus flower. A great gem is one of superior color. The connection is that they gathered together sapphires, great blue gems, radiant gems, and gems of various colors, made a heap, and with it they made a casing-stūpa over the golden stūpa, thereby covering it.

144. Paccekaṃ [M 2.0300] buddhaseṭṭhassāti buddhuttamassa pati ekaṃ visuṃ uparichadanena thūpaṃ akaṃsūti attho.

144. ‘For the supreme Buddha individually’: the meaning is that for the supreme Buddha, each group made a separate stūpa as a covering over the existing one.

147. Kumbhaṇḍā guyhakā [P 0.0569] tathāti kumbhamattāni aṇḍāni yesaṃ devānaṃ te kumbhaṇḍā, paṭicchādetvā niguhitvā paṭicchādanato garuḷā guyhakā nāma jātā, te kumbhaṇḍā guyhakāpi thūpaṃ akaṃsūti attho.

147. ‘The Kumbhaṇḍas and Guyhakas likewise’: Kumbhaṇḍas are those devas whose testicles are the size of pots. Guyhakas are so called because they conceal and hide themselves from the Garuḷas. The meaning is that the Kumbhaṇḍas and Guyhakas also made a stūpa.

151. Atibhonti na tassābhāti tassa cetiyassa pabhaṃ candasūriyatārakānaṃ pabhā na atibhonti, na ajjhottharantīti attho.

151. ‘Its radiance they do not surpass’: the meaning is that the radiance of the moon, sun, and stars does not surpass, does not overwhelm, the light of that cetiya.

158. Ahampi kāraṃ kassāmīti tādino lokanāthassa thūpasmiṃ ahampi kāraṃ puññakiriyaṃ kusalakammaṃ dhajapaṭākapūjaṃ karissāmīti attho.

158. ‘I too will make an offering’: the meaning is, ‘At the stūpa of the Such-like One, the Protector of the World, I too will make an offering,’ which means, ‘I will perform a meritorious action, a wholesome deed, a worship with banners and flags.’

Upavānattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Upavāna is finished.

11. Raṭṭhapālattheraapadānavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Apadāna of Elder Raṭṭhapāla

Ekādasamāpadāne [V 2.0292] padumuttarassa bhagavatotiādikaṃ āyasmato raṭṭhapālattherassa apadānaṃ. Ayampi purimabuddhesu katādhikāro tattha tattha bhave vivaṭṭūpanissayāni puññāni upacinanto padumuttarassa bhagavato kāle tassa uppattito puretarameva haṃsavatīnagare gahapatimahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena gharāvāse patiṭṭhito ratanakoṭṭhāgārakammikena dassitaṃ aparimāṇaṃ kulavaṃsānugataṃ dhanaṃ disvā “imaṃ ettakaṃ dhanarāsiṃ mayhaṃ ayyakapayyakādayo attanā saddhiṃ gahetvā gantuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, mayā pana gahetvā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ mahādānaṃ deti. So abhiññālābhiṃ ekaṃ tāpasaṃ upaṭṭhahanto tena devalokādhipacce uyyojito yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā tato cuto devo hutvā nibbatti. So tattha devaloke devarajjaṃ karonto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā tato cuto manussaloke bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ samatthassa kulassa ekaputto hutvā nibbatti. Tena ca samayena padumuttaro nāma bhagavā loke uppajjitvā pavattitavaradhammacakko veneyyasattaṃ nibbānamahānagarasaṅkhātakhemantabhūmiṃ sampāpesi. Atha so kulaputto anukkamena viññutaṃ patto ekadivasaṃ upāsakehi [M 2.0301] saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gato satthāraṃ dhammaṃ desentaṃ disvā pasannacitto parisapariyante nisīdi.

In the eleventh Apadāna, the Apadāna of the Venerable Elder Raṭṭhapāla, beginning with 'of the Blessed One Padumuttara,' is stated. He too, having made his aspiration in the presence of previous Buddhas, accumulating merits in various existences that were a foundation for liberation, during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, even before his arising, was reborn in the city of Haṃsavatī in a wealthy householder's family. Having reached maturity, upon his father's passing, he became established in the household life. Seeing the immeasurable wealth inherited through his family lineage, shown by the treasurer of the jeweled treasury, he thought: "My ancestors and grandfathers could not take this much wealth with them; but it is proper for me to take it with me." Thus, he gave great gifts to the poor and needy. Attending upon an ascetic who had attained supernormal powers, he was urged by him to strive for sovereignty in the deva world. He performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, and after passing away from there, he was reborn as a deva. There, in the deva world, he reigned as a deva king for his entire lifespan. After passing away from there, he was reborn in the human world as the only son of a family capable of uniting a divided kingdom. At that time, the Blessed One named Padumuttara had arisen in the world, having set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, and led trainable beings to the secure land, which is the great city of Nibbāna. Then that young man, having gradually attained understanding, went one day with lay followers to the monastery. Seeing the Teacher expounding the Dhamma, his mind became joyful, and he sat down at the edge of the assembly.

Tena ca samayena satthā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ saddhāpabbajitānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi, taṃ disvā pasannamānaso tadatthāya cittaṃ ṭhapetvā satasahassabhikkhuparivārassa bhagavato mahatā sakkārena sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā paṇidhānaṃ akāsi. Satthā tassa anantarāyena [P 0.0570] ijjhanabhāvaṃ disvā “anāgate gotamassa nāma sammāsambuddhassa sāsane saddhāpabbajitānaṃ aggo bhavissatī”ti byākāsi. So satthāraṃ bhikkhusaṅghañca vanditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. So tattha yāvatāyukaṃ puññāni katvā tato cavitvā devamanussesu saṃsaranto ito dvānavutikappe phussassa bhagavato kāle satthu vemātikabhātikesu tīsu rājaputtesu satthāraṃ upaṭṭhahantesu tesaṃ puññakiriyāya sahāyakiccaṃ akāsi. Evaṃ tattha tattha bhave taṃ taṃ bahuṃ kusalaṃ upacinitvā sugatīsuyeva saṃsaranto imasmiṃ buddhuppāde kururaṭṭhe thullakoṭṭhikanigame raṭṭhapālaseṭṭhigehe nibbatti, tassa bhinnaṃ raṭṭhaṃ sandhāretuṃ samatthe kule nibbattattā raṭṭhapāloti vaṃsānugatameva nāmaṃ ahosi. So mahatā parivārena vaḍḍhanto anukkamena yobbanaṃ patto mātāpitūhi patirūpena dārena saṃyojetvā mahante ca yase patiṭṭhāpito dibbasampattisadisaṃ sampattiṃ paccanubhoti. Atha bhagavā kururaṭṭhe janapadacārikaṃ caranto thullakoṭṭhikaṃ anupāpuṇi. Taṃ sutvā raṭṭhapālo kulaputto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā satthu santike [V 2.0293] dhammaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho sattavāre bhattacchede katvā kicchena kasirena mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā satthu āṇattiyā aññatarassa therassa santike pabbajitvā yonisomanasikārena kammaṃ karonto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

At that time, the Teacher appointed a certain bhikkhu to the foremost position among those who had gone forth out of faith. Seeing this, with a pleased mind, he set his mind on that goal, and for seven days, with great honor, he offered a great almsgiving to the Blessed One, who was surrounded by a hundred thousand bhikkhus, and made an aspiration. The Teacher, seeing that his aspiration would succeed without obstacle, declared: "In the future, in the dispensation of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One named Gotama, he will be the foremost among those who have gone forth out of faith." He paid homage to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, rose from his seat, and departed. Having performed meritorious deeds there for as long as he lived, he passed away from there and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Ninety-two eons ago from now, during the time of the Blessed One Phussa, when the Teacher was being attended upon by three princes who were his step-brothers, he assisted them in their meritorious deeds. Thus, accumulating much wholesome kamma in various existences, he wandered only in happy destinations. In this Buddha's era, he was reborn in the household of the merchant Raṭṭhapāla in the town of Thullakoṭṭhika in the Kuru country. Because he was born into a family capable of uniting a divided kingdom, the name Raṭṭhapāla was his lineage name. Growing up with a large retinue, he gradually reached youth. His parents united him with a suitable wife and established him in great fame. He experienced prosperity comparable to divine happiness. Then the Blessed One, traveling on a tour through the Kuru country, arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. Hearing this, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the Teacher. Having heard the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, he acquired faith. Having refused food seven times, he persuaded his parents with difficulty and hardship to grant permission. He then approached the Teacher, requested ordination, and by the Teacher's command, he went forth in the presence of a certain elder. Applying himself with wise attention, he developed insight and attained arahantship.

179-180. Athāyasmā aparabhāge attano pubbakammaṃ saritvā somanassajāto pubbacaritāpadānaṃ pakāsento padumuttarassa bhagavatotiādimāha. Sunāgo so mayā dinnoti tadā mahādhanaseṭṭhi hutvā sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ dānamukhe vissajjanasamaye sattappatiṭṭho sundaro nāgo [M 2.0302] hatthirājā mayā dinno ahosi. Taṃ dassento īsādantotiādimāha. Īsādanto rathaīsappamāṇadanto, so mayā dinno hatthināgo. Urūḷhavāti rājāvahanayoggasamattho, rājāraho vā. Setacchattoti alaṅkāratthāya upaṭṭhahanasetacchattasahitoti attho. Pasobhitoti ārohapariṇāhavā rūpasobhāhi sampannoti attho. Sakappano sahatthipoti hatthialaṅkārasahito hatthigopakasahitoti attho. Itthambhūto hatthināgo padumuttarassa bhagavato mayā dinnoti attho.

179-180. Then, at a later time, the Venerable One, recollecting his past kamma, filled with joy, revealed the Apadāna of his former conduct, beginning with 'of the Blessed One Padumuttara,' and so forth. He said, 'A fine elephant was given by me.' At that time, having become a great wealthy merchant, at the time of relinquishing all his possessions by way of generosity, a beautiful elephant king, possessing the seven supports, was given by me. Illustrating that, he said, 'with tusks like chariot poles,' and so forth. Īsādanta means 'with tusks the size of a chariot pole.' That elephant was given by me. 'Urūḷhavā' means 'capable of being used for royal transport,' or 'worthy of a king.' 'Setacchatta' means 'accompanied by a white parasol held for the purpose of adornment.' 'Pasobhita' means 'endowed with an attractive appearance and well-proportioned form.' 'Sakappano sahatthipo' means 'with elephant trappings and elephant keepers.' The meaning is that such an elephant was given by me to the Blessed One Padumuttara.

181. Mayā bhattaṃ kāretvānāti mayā kārāpitavihāre vasantānaṃ koṭisaṅkhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ niccabhattaṃ paṭṭhapetvā mahesino niyyādesinti sambandho.

181. 'Having had food prepared by me' (Mayā bhattaṃ kāretvāna) – the connection is that, having established a perpetual meal for countless bhikkhus dwelling in the monasteries I had built, I dedicated it to the Great Seer.

183. Jalajuttamanāmakoti [P 0.0571] jalato jāto jalajo, kiṃ taṃ? Padumaṃ, padumena samānanāmattā uttamattā ca padumuttaro nāma bhagavāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

183. 'Jalajuttamanāmako' means 'born from water' (jalajo). What is that? A lotus (padumaṃ). The meaning is that the Blessed One is named Padumuttara because his name is associated with the lotus and because he is supreme. The rest is everywhere of obvious meaning.

Raṭṭhapālattheraapadānavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Apadāna of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla is concluded.

Chappaññāsamamahāvaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Fifty-sixth Great Chapter is concluded.

Iti visuddhajanavilāsiniyā apadāna-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus, in the Visuddhajanavilāsinī, the Apadāna Commentary.

Ettāvatā buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakattherāpadāna-aṭṭhakathā samattā.

Thus far, the Apadāna Commentary concerning Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Elder Disciples is concluded.

Nigamanakathā

The Conclusion

Sīhaḷadīpake [M 2.0303][V 2.0294] appicchatādiguṇavantānaṃ theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ ānandattherādīnaṃ sabbasattānaṃ taṇhāmānadiṭṭhādayo chedananiggahavivecanādyatthaṃ sattahi māsehi ativiya ārādhanena laddhakosallena bodhisambhāraṃ gavesantena satidhitigativīriyaparakkamantena mahāsamantaguṇasobhanena tipiṭakadharena paṇḍitena ābhataṃ imaṃ apadāna-aṭṭhakathaṃ sabbo sadevaloko jānātūti.

May the entire world with its devas know that this commentary on the Apadāna was composed in the island of Sīhaḷa by a learned Tipiṭaka-bearer—a lamp to the lineage of elders beginning with the venerable Ānanda, who are endowed with virtues such as fewness of wishes; one who is seeking the requisites for enlightenment, possessed of mindfulness, fortitude, progress, energy, and striving, and resplendent with the great all-round quality of virtue—who, for the purpose of cutting off, subduing, and discerning the craving, conceit, wrong views, and so on of all beings, attained skill through exceedingly great effort over seven months.

Anena lobhādimalā pajānaṃ, cakkhādirogā vividhā ca dukkhā;

Kalahādibhayā dukkhitā jātā, corādayonatthakarā ca loke.

Through this merit, may the defilements of beings, such as greed, and their various sufferings and diseases of the eye and so on, be destroyed. May those in the world afflicted by fear of quarrels and the like, and harm-doers such as thieves, cease to be.

Nassantu me pañca verā ca pāpā, nassantu gimhe yathā vuṭṭhivātā;

Aṭṭhaṅgikamaggavarena patvā, nibbānapuraṃ paṭipādayāmi.

May my five enmities and evils vanish; may they vanish like rain and wind in the hot season. Having reached the excellent Eightfold Path, I shall proceed to the city of Nibbāna.

Sabbadiṭṭhiñca maddanto, rāgadosādipāpake;

Saṃsāravaṭṭaṃ chinditvā, upemi saggamokkhake.

Crushing all wrong views and evils such as greed and hatred, having cut off the round of saṃsāra, I approach heaven and liberation.

Āṇākhettamhi [P 0.0572] sabbattha, avīcimhi bhavaggato;

Sabbe dhammānuyāyantu, tayo lokā utupi cāti.

Everywhere in the sphere of command, from Avīci up to the peak of existence, may all beings, the three worlds, and also the seasons, follow the Dhamma.

Apadāna-aṭṭhakathā samattā.

The Commentary on the Apadāna is completed.
